title: Halve-Then-Greedy: Adaptive Sampling for Posterior Success with Near-Optimal Instance Dependence
description:
arXiv:2610.20997v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study fixed-budget adaptive experimentation aimed at maximizing the probability of obtaining sufficient posterior evidence that a recommended design's mean performance exceeds a target. Unlike best-arm identification, this objective does not require finding the best design. For Gaussian bandits with a Gaussian prior, we propose \emph{Halve-Then-Greedy} (HTG), which combines a large initial balanced allocation, successive halving, and posterior-greedy sampling. We prove instance-dependent, finite-budget exponential bounds on posterior-failure probability that capture both separation from unfavorable arms and the presence of multiple favorable arms. On one-positive-arm families, we establish an asymptotic sample-complexity lower bound that HTG matches up to a logarithmic factor. We further analyze uniform sampling and sequential halving, revealing regimes where they require more samples than HTG by linear and logarithmic factors, respectively. Simulations illustrate HTG's sample-efficiency advantages and their dependence on instance structure.

title: Interpreting Language Model Parameters
description:
arXiv:2610.20748v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover how neural networks use their parameters to implement their impressive neural algorithms. Although previous work has uncovered substantial structure in the intermediate representations that networks use, little progress has been made to understand how the parameters and nonlinearities of networks perform computations on those representations. In this work, we present a method that brings us closer to this understanding by decomposing a language model's parameters into subcomponents that each implement only a small part of the model's learned algorithm, while simultaneously requiring only a small fraction of those subcomponents to account for the network's behavior on any input. The method, adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD), optimizes for decompositions of neural network parameters into simple subcomponents that preserve the network's input-output behavior even when many subcomponents are ablated, including under ablations that are adversarially selected to destroy behavior. This encourages learning subcomponents that provide short, mechanistically faithful descriptions of the network's behavior that should aggregate appropriately into more global descriptions of the network's learned algorithm. We study how sequences of interactions between these parameter subcomponents produce the network's output on particular inputs, enabling a new kind of 'circuit' analysis. While more work remains to be done to deepen our understanding of how neural networks use their parameters to compute their behavior, our work suggests an approach to identify a small set of simple, mechanistically faithful subcomponents on which further mechanistic analysis can be based.

title: Sample Runs, Not Spans: Shrink Agent Traces Without Losing Failures
description:
At 09:12 the on-call page fired. A checkout agent returned HTTP 500 for forty minutes.

We opened the trace store and found two weeks of spans. The failing run was not in it.

Our sampler had dropped the interesting spans. It kept the boring ones. That is the classic sampling bug, and it is a retention problem, not a tracing problem.

Why span-level sampling fails

Most teams sample at the span level. A coin flip decides each span independently.

That breaks causality. A tool call survives; its parent LLM call does not. You cannot replay a run with holes in it.

Worse, failures are rare and correlated. A 5% span sample catches roughly 5% of a broken run, and the interesting leaf spans are exactly the ones your status filter already flags.

So you pay 5% of the storage and lose 95% of the debuggability. The incident you care about is the one you stored least.

Change the unit of sampling

Sample runs, not spans. A run is either fully recorded or fully summarized. No partial runs, no orphan spans.

Three storage modes are enough:

  1. Full — every span, every payload, exact bytes, sequence numbers intact.
  2. Summary — one lossy record per span: id, kind, status, duration, token counts, byte counts. No payloads.
  3. Anomaly-pinned — the same as full, but exempt from sampling forever, because the run already proved it can break.

Then add one rule that overrides chance. Any run that touches a known anomaly keeps full detail, regardless of the sample rate.

A decision table you can argue about

Span or run class Decision Retention Why
run has any error span full 30 days root-cause evidence
any span has status = retry full 30 days retry storms hide real bugs
span has a truncation flag full 14 days the payload was already cut
span exceeds the latency p99 budget full 14 days regression evidence
clean run, hash-selected full 7 days baseline for diffing
clean run, not selected summary 90 days trend lines and cost accounting
health-check span neither 0 pure noise

Two things stand out. Clean runs are kept longest in summary form, because they are cheap and they answer trend questions. Broken runs are kept shortest in full form, because the fix arrives fast.

The sampler, in about forty lines

This is a proposal, not a benchmarked result in your environment. Run it against archived traces before you put it in front of production traffic.

# sampler.py — proposal; measure it on your own archive first
import hashlib
import os

SALT = os.environ.get("TRACE_SAMPLE_SALT", "change-me")
ANOMALY_STATUSES = {"error", "retry", "truncated", "budget_exceeded"}

def is_anomalous_span(span: dict) -> bool:
    if span.get("status") in ANOMALY_STATUSES:
        return True
    return bool(span.get("truncated"))

def run_is_pinned(run: dict) -> bool:
    return run.get("anomaly_count", 0) > 0

def selected_for_full(run_id: str, success_sample_rate: float = 0.05) -> bool:
    """Deterministic, stable per run_id. Sample whole runs, never spans."""
    digest = hashlib.sha256((SALT + run_id).encode()).hexdigest()
    bucket = int(digest[:8], 16) % 10_000
    return (bucket / 10_000.0) < success_sample_rate

def store_mode(run: dict) -> str:
    if run_is_pinned(run):
        return "full"
    if selected_for_full(run["run_id"]):
        return "full"
    return "summary"

Two design choices matter here.

  • Hashing on run_id, not a random draw. The same run gets the same verdict in every process, on every retry, and after a restart. Random draws make your retention policy non-reproducible.
  • A SALT from the environment. Without it, anyone can compute which runs you kept. With it, selection is stable but not guessable.

The one test that matters

A single invariant protects the whole policy: an anomalous run is never summarized away.

# test_retention.py — proposal; wire into CI
def test_anomalous_runs_are_never_summarized():
    for status in ("error", "retry", "truncated", "budget_exceeded"):
        run = {"run_id": "r-1", "anomaly_count": 1, "status": status}
        assert store_mode(run) == "full"

def test_selection_is_stable_across_calls():
    a = [selected_for_full("r-42") for _ in range(100)]
    assert len(set(a)) == 1

def test_selection_is_not_all_or_nothing():
    kept = sum(selected_for_full(f"r-{i}") for i in range(10_000))
    assert 300 < kept < 700  # ~5% with sane variance

The third test is the subtle one. A salt or modulus bug can silently push your sample rate to 0% or 100%, and nobody notices until an incident review.

Where the pipeline runs

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The collector and summarizer are small, periodic, and CPU-bound. That is a good fit for a free server option, because you are not paying for idle capacity between jobs.

MonkeyCode is an open-source project with free model access, and the operator lists a 10M-token free allowance alongside the free server option. Treat both as claims to verify against the current terms before you depend on them.

The model access has a genuine role here. Full payloads are expensive to keep; one-line run digests are not. So generate a digest for every run, not just the sampled ones, and store it permanently next to the summary records. Something like:

Input: 40 summary records for run r-8891
Output: one sentence — what the run attempted, what changed, what failed

That digest is what an on-call engineer reads first at 09:12. It costs a few hundred tokens per run, which is why a free allowance changes what you can afford to keep.

Two cautions. Never put payload contents you cannot share into a third-party model call, and never treat a free tier as a system of record. Check the current limits and retention terms yourself.

Measure before you trust the policy

Do not adopt this on vibes. Compute the ratio on one day of archived traces.

# total bytes and runs
wc -c < traces.jsonl
wc -l < traces.jsonl

# bytes owned by anomalous runs (approximation: runs with an error line)
jq -c 'select(.status == "error") | .run_id' traces.jsonl \
  | sort -u > pinned.txt
rg -F -f pinned.txt traces.jsonl | wc -c

Then report two numbers: pinned_runs / total_runs and kept_bytes / total_bytes.

Acceptance criteria I would use, and you should replace with your own:

  • pinned_runs / total_runs under 2% in steady state.
  • kept_bytes / total_bytes under 15% after summarization.
  • Zero runs missing a stored digest.

If pinned_runs is much higher than your error rate, your anomaly rules are too broad. Fix the rules before you lower the storage bill.

Limitations

  • Summaries cannot answer unanticipated questions. If you did not record a field, you cannot query it later. Add fields to the summary schema only when you can justify the bytes.
  • Sampling breaks exact replay for unselected runs. Keep the sample rate high enough that a baseline exists for diffing.
  • Hash sampling can correlate with your id scheme. If run_id starts with a tenant prefix, some tenants get sampled more than others. Salt alone does not fix that; hash the full id or re-bucket.
  • Latency budgets need a warm baseline. On a sleeping free server, the first request after idle inflates duration. Exclude cold-start spans or your p99 rule pins everything.
  • Not for audit or legal hold. A sampling policy is an engineering choice, not a compliance record.

Who should skip this

If you run fewer than a few thousand agent runs per day, storage is cheap and full-fidelity tracing is simpler. Skip the sampler.

If you operate under retention obligations, keep everything and solve cost elsewhere. Skip the sampler.

If your failures are exactly the class you would sample away, for example silent wrong answers with clean statuses, pin on an outcome signal instead of a status code.

Start with one day of traffic

Sample runs, not spans. Pin anomalies unconditionally. Store a model-written digest for every run.

Take one archived day of traces. Run the sampler over it. Report the two ratios and the three invariants.

If the numbers hold, you have shrunk the store without losing the one run you will need at 09:12.

title: Audio-Visual Dog Identification and Tracking in Real-World Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.21011v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identifying individual dogs from barks in real-world videos remains challenging and largely unexplored. Solving this problem would enable long-term behavioral analysis, veterinary monitoring, and animal welfare monitoring by attributing vocalizations and behaviors to the correct individual. Real-world videos are challenging because multiple dogs may bark simultaneously, become occluded, or move in and out of view. Prior studies show that canine vocalizations and visual appearance contain discriminative identity information, but these modalities have largely been studied independently. We present a multimodal dog-fingerprinting framework combining visual identification, multiple-object tracking, and canine vocal fingerprinting to associate bark events with individual dogs while maintaining persistent profiles. The framework synchronizes bark events with tracked dogs and updates profiles using visual appearance and vocal characteristics, enabling identification despite occlusion, overlapping vocalizations, and off-screen barking. We also introduce a benchmark of 46 real-world videos containing 213 manually annotated bark events. Our framework correctly localizes the active visible dog in 61.83% of visible events at IoU $\geq 0.30$ and achieves a 91.33% F1 score for visible versus off-screen barking detection.

title: Condition-Contrastive Extrapolation for On-Policy Distillation of Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21195v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves a student language model by training on its own generated trajectories with supervision from a stronger teacher. However, when conditioned on student-generated prefixes, the teacher can favor invalid continuations that violate the question's premises, causing OPD to encourage erroneous reasoning steps. As a remedy, we introduce Condition-Contrastive Extrapolated On-Policy Distillation (CCE-OPD), which makes teacher supervision sensitive to question conditions. CCE-OPD incorporates (1) a fixed-prefix comparison in which the same frozen teacher evaluates the complete question and a counterpart with a selected condition masked, and (2) a bounded log-probability contrast that reweights the teacher distribution into an auxiliary distillation target. On 200 diagnostic reasoning states, condition contrast reduces the rate of preferring invalid continuations from 27.0% to 16.0%. Extensive experiments across six mathematical benchmarks show that CCE-OPD improves avg@8 over OPD by an average of 1.60 and 1.95 percentage points when distilling Qwen3-8B into 0.6B and 1.7B students, respectively. It also achieves the strongest results on four transfer benchmarks.

title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery
description:
arXiv:2610.21333v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Natural language messages often contain quasi-identifiers that are weak in isolation but can jointly reveal an individual's private attributes. We call such a jointly revealing set of cues a quasi-evidence group. Existing privacy benchmarks focus on explicit identifiers, attribute inference, or task-driven disclosures, leaving inference from quasi-evidence groups largely unmeasured. In practice, whether exposing such a quasi-evidence group violates privacy also depends on sender-specified disclosure policies. We introduce QuasiLeak-Bench, a benchmark for policy-conditioned quasi-evidence group recovery, which evaluates whether detectors recover complete quasi-evidence groups and flag the disclosures the given policy prohibits. To obtain reliable ground truth at scale, a reverse-construction pipeline first selects weak quasi-identifiers, composes them into quasi-evidence groups verified to jointly reveal a target attribute, and generates documents around this evidence, followed by automated quality control. Experiments show that existing privacy detectors transfer poorly to QuasiLeak-Bench, and locally deployable LLM-based detectors fall far behind proprietary models, mainly because they miss most quasi-evidence groups altogether. However, a 4B model fine-tuned on our training split surpasses the strongest prompted model on held-out documents, showing that the task is learnable.

title: A Cache Key Bug in an Agent PR: Cross-Tenant Leakage, Tested
description:
The pull request arrived at 02:14 with a green checkmark and three files changed. Its claim was modest: skip duplicate model calls, cut latency on repeated prompts. The reviewer's first instinct was to trust the test suite.

The tests only covered the happy path. That is exactly where a caching change is least likely to break.

Note: the diff below is a minimal reconstruction for teaching, not a verbatim vendor pull request.

The Diff Under Review 

import hashlib

CACHE = {}

def complete(prompt, tenant_id, model="default"):
    key = hashlib.sha256(prompt.encode()).hexdigest()
    if key in CACHE:
        return CACHE[key]
    resp = call_model(model, prompt)   # network call, can raise
    CACHE[key] = resp
    return resp

Three things stand out on the first read. The tenant_id argument is accepted and never used. Nothing checks whether the response is usable before storing it. The dictionary has no size bound, no TTL, and no eviction path.

The diff passes review because it is small and readable. Small and readable is not the same as correct.

Why the Happy Path Passes

The accompanying test calls complete twice with one prompt and one tenant. It asserts that the model client was invoked once.

That assertion is true. It also stays true after every defect below is fixed, which is why the suite gives reviewers no signal at all.

Three Defects the Existing Tests Never Touch

1. The Cache Key Ignores Tenant Identity

The key is a hash of the prompt text alone. Two tenants that send an identical string share one cache entry.

For a prompt like "Summarize the incident report." the collision is not theoretical. Support tooling, templates, and system prompts repeat across accounts all day long.

2. Blank and Failed Results Get Cached

If call_model returns None or an empty string on a transient upstream failure, that value becomes the stored answer. Every later caller reads the failure until the process restarts.

Negative caching converts a one-second blip into a multi-hour outage. The diff never distinguishes a good answer from a bad one.

3. The Cache Is Process-Local and Unbounded

Four workers mean four separate dictionaries and four independent hit rates. Memory grows with the number of unique prompts and never shrinks.

The diff looks like a shared cache. It behaves like a per-worker notebook with no eraser.

What to Trust, What to Revert, What to Test

  1. Trust the pure helper. hashlib.sha256 is a reasonable key primitive.
  2. Keep the tenant_id parameter and thread it into the key.
  3. Revert the module-level mutable dictionary.
  4. Revert any write of an empty, failed, or partial response.
  5. Replace the single happy-path test with isolation, failure, and concurrency tests.

A Reproduction Plan You Can Run in Ten Minutes

Step 1: Write the isolation test first 

import pytest

calls = []

def fake_call_model(model, prompt, tenant_id):
    calls.append(tenant_id)
    return f"{tenant_id}-answer"

def test_cache_does_not_leak_between_tenants():
    calls.clear()
    a = complete("Summarize the incident report.", tenant_id="acme")
    b = complete("Summarize the incident report.", tenant_id="globex")
    assert calls == ["acme", "globex"]
    assert a != b

Run pytest -k tenant -x. It fails against the diff. That failure is the evidence, not an opinion.

Step 2: Patch the key and rerun 

def cache_key(tenant_id, model, prompt):
    parts = [tenant_id, model, prompt]
    return hashlib.sha256("\x00".join(parts).encode()).hexdigest()

The null-byte separator prevents ambiguous concatenation. The same test should now pass unchanged.

Step 3: Prove failures are not cached 

def test_failures_are_not_cached(monkeypatch):
    calls.clear()
    def boom(*args, **kwargs):
        calls.append("attempt")
        raise TimeoutError("upstream")
    monkeypatch.setattr("app.model.call_model", boom)
    for _ in range(2):
        with pytest.raises(TimeoutError):
            complete("boom", tenant_id="acme")
    assert len(calls) == 2

Two attempts, two upstream calls. A cached exception would produce one.

Step 4: Measure the cross-worker hit rate 

for i in $(seq 1 40); do
  curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/complete \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"prompt":"ping","tenant_id":"acme"}' > /dev/null
done
grep -c 'model_call' /var/log/app.log

Forty requests with one unique prompt should log far fewer than forty model calls. If the count stays near forty, the cache is not shared across workers.

Decision Table

Change Verdict Reason
cache_key helper Keep small, pure, easy to test
tenant_id in the key Keep and require blocks cross-tenant reads
module-level CACHE dict Revert process-local, unbounded, no TTL
caching of empty or failed results Revert turns a blip into a lasting outage
single happy-path test Replace never exercises isolation or failure

Reusing This Review Loop on a Free Server

The agent that produced the diff ran against MonkeyCode's free model access. The repro suite above ran on the project's free server option, which is enough for a few hundred test calls in one sitting.

The operator states the free tier also includes a promotional token allowance, currently advertised at 10 million tokens. Confirm the current terms in the repository before planning around any number. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The model is not the interesting part here. The loop is: generate, reproduce, revert, retest.

Limitations and Who Should Skip This

  • Teams with strict data residency rules should not send prompts to any hosted endpoint, free or paid.
  • Multi-tenant products need cache keys derived from tenant, model, and prompt version together.
  • A process-local dictionary is acceptable for a single-worker prototype and wrong in every other deployment.
  • If hit rate matters at scale, use a shared store with TTL, eviction, and a size cap.
  • This review does not attempt to validate model output quality. It only checks whether one tenant can read another tenant's answer.

Closing Note

An agent PR is a draft, not a decision. Trust the pure functions, revert the shared mutable state, and test the tenant boundary before anything else.

title: Sliced Wasserstein Sketches with Error Certificates
description:
arXiv:2610.20788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compact representations that support geometrically meaningful comparisons are valuable for learning from probability distributions. We study optimal, free-weight $M$-atom quantization of one-dimensional probability measures in quadratic Wasserstein distance and extend it to higher dimensions via slicing. Using $L$ shared projections yields a sketch with $O(LM)$ comparison time. Our main result is an exact decomposition of squared distance error into residual and partition-mismatch terms, yielding computable certificates for arbitrary centroid sketches. For optimal sketches, a finite $(2+\delta)$ moment for some $\delta>0$ guarantees $O(M^{-1})$ error in the finite-direction sliced distance, while equal-mass sketches can converge more slowly. Each slice preserves its mean, while storing residual energies enables covariance recovery from sufficiently many generic directions. Experiments on document, point-cloud, and flow-cytometry benchmarks show that optimal sketches substantially reduce storage while preserving the classification performance of uncompressed sliced distances. They also improve generalization from few labelled subjects and support end-to-end learning as compact pooling layers.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use.

Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases.

Our goals for Python on Vercel

Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications. We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions:

  • Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async/await, and context managers.

  • A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together.

  • Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on.

The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run.

Deploying Python applications on Vercel

We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv, and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN.

For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them.

For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies.

Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure

A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language:

These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application.

Start building with Python on Vercel

Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services.

To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code.

The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN.

Here’s how the main parts connect:

  • Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files.

  • Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel.

  • Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading.

  • Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow.

The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application.

Investing in the Python community

Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work.

At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026.

We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next.

We also published PEP 827, which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking.

What’s next for Python on Vercel

We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work.

Resources

  • Deploy an eve agent in Python in one click

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself.

To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it:

  • Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard.

  • Under Secure Compute Routing, choose an existing network.

  • If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings.

  • Save your changes in Connect.

Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs.

Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details.

title: Rubric Graders Need Canaries: Testing the Test That Grades C++ Patches
description:
Rubric Graders Need Canaries: Testing the Test That Grades C++ Patches

A pipeline starts scoring C++ patches with a model-backed rubric. Diffs that change printed precision, drop a noexcept guarantee, or leak a file descriptor now receive a 1-10 score before a human opens them. For a few weeks the dashboard looks reasonable, reviewers trust the number, and nobody asks whether the grader still separates good patches from bad ones. Then a prompt edit lands, the upstream model is swapped, and every patch scores 8. Nothing crashes. The grader simply stops discriminating, and the pipeline keeps reporting green.

That failure mode is independent of which model you call. A rubric grader is a program with an untested dependency, and it deserves the treatment the code under it already gets: golden cases, a canary set, a hard gate, and a ledger. The harness below is standard-library Python, a few JSON canary files, and one cron line. It is deliberately boring, because the interesting part is that the grader fails loudly instead of silently.

Layer 0 thinks, layer 1 judges

Split grading into two layers before writing any code. The deterministic layer answers questions with one correct answer: does the patched tree compile, does the golden case exit zero, does stdout match after a fixed locale and precision. The rubric layer answers questions with a range of defensible answers: is the naming consistent with the header it implements, does the commit message describe the actual change, does the new overload respect the documented contract.

Most silent regressions live on the boundary. A grader that is only deterministic cannot see prose contracts. A grader that is only a rubric cannot see a changed std::setprecision. Layer 0 gates the build, layer 1 explains the patch, and each layer needs its own canaries.

A canary here means a labeled example with a fixed expected answer that is committed to the repository. It is not a test of the patch. It is a test of the test.

Step 1 - Freeze golden cases for the deterministic layer

Start with one golden case per documented output contract. Keep the case small enough that a failure points at one behavior, and pin everything that could drift: locale, precision, and the toolchain described in your own build docs.

// golden/report_precision.cpp - contract: ratio printed with 3 decimals
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>

int main() {
    const double ratio = 2.0 / 3.0;
    std::cout << std::setprecision(3) << std::fixed << ratio << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Run it through the same command the eval batch uses, so the grader and the patch pipeline cannot disagree about flags:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --target report_precision
./build/report_precision > out.txt
diff -u golden/report_precision.expected out.txt

The diff is the grader. If it passes, the patch is not yet good, but it is at least not obviously broken.

Step 2 - Commit canaries in both directions

A canary set that only contains bad patches rewards a paranoid grader. A canary set that only contains good patches rewards a lenient one. Include both, and store each patch as its own file so the JSON stays readable and diffs stay reviewable.

eval/
  canaries/
    precision-3-to-2.json
    honest-refactor.json
    tie-case-review.json
    diffs/
      precision-3-to-2.patch
      honest-refactor.patch
      tie-case-review.patch

Each canary declares what it expects and why. The note field is the part humans actually maintain.

{
  "id": "precision-3-to-2",
  "kind": "rubric",
  "direction": "must-fail",
  "patch_path": "diffs/precision-3-to-2.patch",
  "expected": 3,
  "note": "Breaks the output contract in docs/report.md. Any score above 5 means the rubric is not reading the contract."
}

{
  "id": "honest-refactor",
  "kind": "rubric",
  "direction": "should-pass",
  "patch_path": "diffs/honest-refactor.patch",
  "expected": 8,
  "note": "Pure rename plus a comment fix, output byte-identical. Below 6 means the rubric punishes chore diffs."
}

{
  "id": "precision-3-to-2-build",
  "kind": "build",
  "patch_path": "diffs/precision-3-to-2.patch",
  "golden_cmd": "./build/report_precision | diff -u golden/report_precision.expected -",
  "note": "Must exit non-zero. If this passes, the deterministic layer is not running."
}

Keep the count honest. Twenty labeled canaries drawn from real review comments are worth more than two hundred generated ones, because generated canaries encode the same assumptions as the rubric prompt.

Step 3 - Measure agreement before trusting scores

Agreement is the only cheap health signal a rubric grader has. Exact match is strict; within-one match tolerates the ordinary noise of a 1-10 scale. Both numbers belong in the gate.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# grade_gate.py - run canaries before trusting rubric scores.
import json, os, pathlib, subprocess, sys

CANARY_DIR = pathlib.Path(os.environ.get('CANARY_DIR', 'eval/canaries'))
LEDGER = pathlib.Path(os.environ.get('GRADER_LEDGER', 'eval/grader_ledger.jsonl'))
RUBRIC_ID = os.environ.get('GRADER_VERSION', 'unversioned')


def load_canaries():
    for path in sorted(CANARY_DIR.glob('*.json')):
        canary = json.loads(path.read_text())
        patch = (CANARY_DIR / canary['patch_path']).resolve()
        canary['diff_text'] = patch.read_text()
        yield canary


def call_model(prompt):
    # Transport layer. Plug in whichever client your runtime provides.
    # This function is untrusted by design; that is why canaries exist.
    raise NotImplementedError('wire your client here')


def rubric_score(diff_text, rubric):
    reply = call_model(rubric + '\n\nDIFF:\n' + diff_text)
    return json.loads(reply)

Now the comparison itself, plus the gate. The thresholds are policy defaults, not measured results: a canary set of forty concrete review-derived cases can usually carry a higher bar than one of twelve fuzzy ones. Tune them once, write the number in the repo, and treat any change to it as a reviewable commit.

def check_rubric_canaries(canaries, rubric, min_exact=0.80, min_within_one=0.95):
    exact = within_one = 0
    misses = []
    for canary in canaries:
        if canary.get('kind') != 'rubric':
            continue
        expected = canary['expected']
        got = rubric_score(canary['diff_text'], rubric)['score']
        if got == expected:
            exact += 1
        else:
            if abs(got - expected) == 1:
                within_one += 1
            misses.append({'id': canary['id'], 'expected': expected,
                           'got': got, 'delta': got - expected})
    total = sum(1 for c in canaries if c.get('kind') == 'rubric') or 1
    rates = {'exact': exact / total, 'within_one': (exact + within_one) / total}
    ok = rates['exact'] >= min_exact and rates['within_one'] >= min_within_one
    return ok, rates, misses

Build canaries run the golden command instead of a model, and check the opposite thing: they must fail.

def check_build_canaries(canaries, workdir):
    results = []
    for canary in canaries:
        if canary.get('kind') != 'build':
            continue
        subprocess.run(['git', 'apply', canary['patch_path']], cwd=workdir, check=True)
        proc = subprocess.run(canary['golden_cmd'], cwd=workdir, shell=True)
        subprocess.run(['git', 'restore', '.'], cwd=workdir, check=True)
        results.append({'id': canary['id'], 'exit': proc.returncode,
                        'ok': proc.returncode != 0})
    return results

Step 4 - Keep a grader ledger next to the token ledger

A score is only meaningful with the grader revision and the model identity attached. Write one JSON line per gate run, including the token count, so drift and cost are visible in the same file.

def log_run(rates, misses, model_id, tokens):
    record = {'grader': RUBRIC_ID, 'model': model_id, 'rates': rates,
              'misses': misses, 'tokens': tokens}
    with LEDGER.open('a') as fh:
        print(json.dumps(record), file=fh)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    rubric = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text()
    canaries = list(load_canaries())
    ok, rates, misses = check_rubric_canaries(canaries, rubric)
    build = check_build_canaries(canaries, '.')
    log_run(rates, misses, os.environ.get('MODEL_ID', 'unknown'),
            int(os.environ.get('TOKENS_USED', '0')))
    healthy = ok and all(r['ok'] for r in build)
    print(json.dumps({'healthy': healthy, 'rates': rates, 'misses': misses,
                      'build': build}, indent=2))
    sys.exit(0 if healthy else 1)

The exit code is the whole interface. A healthy gate returns 0 and the eval batch proceeds; an unhealthy gate returns 1 and the batch stops before it spends anything on scoring.

Step 5 - Run the gate where nobody has to remember it

A gate that depends on a human typing a command is a gate that will be skipped during the week it matters most. Two things make the scheduled version practical: a machine that stays on, and model access that does not require a per-run decision.

MonkeyCode, described by its maintainers as an open-source project, offers free model access and a free server option, with the free tier described as including 10M tokens. That combination is enough to host a weekly canary run plus the rubric calls it makes, without reserving a dedicated box. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

# cron: every Monday 06:17, on the free server option
17 6 * * 1 cd /srv/eval && python3 grade_gate.py rubrics/patch_v3.md >> logs/canary.log 2>&1

Read the ledger rather than the estimate. The claim worth trusting is not a predicted token count; it is the tokens field on last week's line, compared with the line before it.

Which layer owns which signal

Signal to grade Layer 0 (deterministic) Layer 1 (rubric)
Compiles, links, exits zero Yes No
stdout under fixed locale and precision Yes No
Wall-clock or allocation budget Yes No
Naming consistent with the header Partly, via lint rules Yes
Prose output contract in docs No Yes
Commit message matches the change No Yes
Whether the change is worth merging No Advisory only, never binding

If a row can be pushed into layer 0, push it. Every signal moved out of the rubric layer removes a source of drift, and the rubric layer keeps only the judgments a compiler cannot express.

Limitations and who should skip this

Canaries are a sample, and agreement is not correctness. If the labels are wrong, the gate certifies a wrong grader with a confident number. Re-label a handful of canaries every few months, especially the ones that never fail.

Rubric scores drift when the model or the prompt changes, and only a scheduled run of the ledger detects that. Single-run scores stay noisy even with a fixed prompt, so treat a one-point swing as a signal to check the ledger, not as a verdict on the patch.

The quota and server claims above are operator descriptions of the offer, not measurements taken for this article. Verify current terms before wiring a paid-critical pipeline to a free tier, and keep the gate able to run against a different client.

Skip this approach if you have fewer than roughly twenty real diffs to label, because reading the patches is then cheaper than grading them. Skip it for safety-critical, licensing, or compliance judgments, which need deterministic evidence and a named reviewer. Skip it if diff text cannot leave your network, unless every layer runs locally. And skip the rubric layer entirely if your grading budget exceeds the cost of the human review it is meant to save.

The harness is small on purpose. Golden cases, canaries in both directions, one agreement gate, one ledger. Start with a single canary that should fail and confirm the gate returns non-zero; if it returns zero, the grader was never watching.

title: Building Modular Monoliths With Kotlin and Spring
description:
Over a decade ago, Netflix became one of the early adopters of microservice architecture, showcasing its potential at a large scale. Since then, many companies have jumped on the microservices bandwagon, building their backends this way from day one. While microservices offer isolation and independent scaling, their distributed nature requires managing multiple deployments, monitoring interservice communication, and handling network failures across service boundaries.

As teams have gained real-world experience with this complexity, there's been a shift back toward monoliths, but not the tightly coupled monoliths of the past. Instead, developers are embracing modular monoliths: an architectural pattern where single deployable applications are organized into well-defined modules based on logical boundaries or business domains. Think of an e-commerce platform where users, products, and orders live in separate modules that interact through clear contracts, such as APIs for synchronous calls and events for async communication. This separation lets teams work in parallel for faster development and better maintainability, while single-unit deployment keeps releases simple and avoids microservice operational complexity.

In this guide, we explore how modular monoliths differ from traditional monoliths, why they're gaining traction, and how to build them using Spring Modulith and Kotlin.

The Need for Modular Monoliths

The growing modular monolith countertrend makes more sense when viewed against the shortcomings of traditional approaches.

Traditional monoliths bundle the entire backend into a single codebase with tight coupling between user interfaces, business logic, and data access patterns. In an e-commerce platform, for example, the product catalog, checkout, payments, and order history services are in a single codebase and are deployed together. A monolith uses function calls for internal communication, and often, the call patterns and interdependencies become messy or difficult to maintain.

Microservices emerged to solve these maintainability challenges by splitting backends into loosely coupled services, each handling a specific domain. A cab-hailing platform may separate users, drivers, ride matching, payments, and notifications into independent services. However, this introduces distributed system challenges, including complex service discovery, coordinating deployments across dependent services, and debugging interservice communication issues. Without proper expertise, tooling, and observability, this can slow down development.

Modular monoliths strike a balance by keeping everything in a single codebase and deploying it as one artifact, while structuring the application into logical modules with well-defined interfaces. This addresses the challenges of distributed systems while maintaining the structural benefits of well-defined interfaces and independent development workflows. Some benefits of a modular monolith include:

  • Simplified deployment: A single deployment artifact simplifies the release process because you don't need to coordinate multiple service rollouts, manage service meshes, or handle distributed database migrations and rollbacks.
  • Reliable testing: As modules in a monolith communicate in-process rather than over a network, integration tests are faster and more stable. You can use mocks where needed, avoid brittle network dependencies, and run end-to-end (E2E) and performance tests in a controlled environment.
  • Stronger domain modeling: Modular monoliths group related business logic into modules, with clear ownership and communication boundaries between modules. It enforces communication only through well-defined interfaces and enables domain objects to be shared directly without serialization or cross-service APIs. This makes the system easier to maintain and improves development velocity.
  • In-process communication: Since modules communicate through direct method invocations instead of network calls, it reduces latency and points of failure.

Designing a Modular Monolith

When you're building a modular monolith, you first identify the business domains and split the application into multiple loosely coupled modules with clear boundaries and dependencies. Unlike the tightly interwoven code of a traditional monolith, the modular design ensures that the modules can be developed and maintained independently while still being deployed as a single unit. For example, you can break down an e-commerce platform into separate modules such as users, product catalog, shopping cart, payments, and orders:

Each module encapsulates a specific entity or capability. A product catalog module would manage product details and categories, and an order processing module would handle order and payment entities. Unlike traditional monoliths, where internal calls often use ad hoc dependencies, in a modular monolith, the interactions with other modules are performed using explicit interfaces and well-defined contracts. This ensures that the intermodule dependencies remain clear and intentional. The communication between the modules uses in-process function calls, so it's faster and less error-prone compared to network-based interservice calls in microservices.

The modular structure allows logical separation between the modules and enforces fixed boundaries, increasing development speed, improving maintainability, and making testing more reliable. Each module defines its user interface, business logic, and data access layers separately:

These boundaries also lay the groundwork for extracting a particular module as a microservice based on the scaling requirements.

Integrate Spring Modulith

Spring Modulith is a Spring Boot framework that's based on modular monolith architectural principles. It helps identify, structure, and enforce application modules. It also includes tools for verifying module boundaries and observing their behavior, along with module-level testing capabilities, making Spring Boot applications easier to build and maintain.

Here's how to integrate Spring Modulith into a Kotlin-based Spring Boot application.

All the code samples are drawn from a fully working Kotlin example, which you can find in this GitHub repository.

Quick Start Kotlin Example

Spring Modulith can be added to any Spring Boot application by including its dependencies in the project's build.gradle.kts:

// build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter")
    implementation("org.springframework.modulith:spring-modulith-starter-core:1.4.3")
}

Note: If your project uses Maven, you can add these dependencies to the pom.xml file.

To define the modules, you need to add relevant package directories to the src directory. This code snippet illustrates order and product packages added to the application, each handling its own business logic, data, and services:

SpringModulithExample
└── src/main/java
    ├── example
    │   └── SpringmonolithApplication.kt
    └── example.order
        └── …
    └── example.product
        └── …
    └── example.payment
        └── …

Within each of the modules, you can define the business logic, service, and data access layers based on your application's requirements. The following code snippet shows a ProductService within the example.product package that returns a static greeting message:

package com.example.springmonolith.product

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service

@Service
class ProductService {

    fun getGreeting(): String {
        return "Hello from Product Module!"
    }
}

Similarly, define an OrderService within the example.order package that invokes ProductService::getGreeting() and returns a combined greeting message:

package com.example.springmonolith.order

import com.example.springmonolith.product.ProductService
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service

@Service
class OrderService(
    private val productService: ProductService
) {

    fun getGreeting(): String {
        return "Hello from Order Module!"
    }

    fun getCombinedGreeting(): String {
        return "Hello from Order Module and: ${productService.getGreeting()}"
    }
}

After adding similar business logic for each of the modules (eg ProductService, PaymentService), you also need to add the @Modulithic annotation to the Spring Boot Application class to mark it as modular. The annotation tells Spring Modulith to automatically detect modules based on package structure and enable the tooling for verification, testing, and observability:

package com.example.springmonolith

import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication
import org.springframework.boot.runApplication
import org.springframework.modulith.Modulithic

// add this annotation to the application
@Modulithic
@SpringBootApplication
class SpringmonolithApplication

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    runApplication<SpringmonolithApplication>(*args)
}

Next, you can update the package info file for each of the modules to define the allowed module dependencies. Since the order module depends on the methods defined in the product module, you'll need to add the following annotation in the order/package-info.java file:

// add this annotation
@org.springframework.modulith.ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = {"product"})
@org.springframework.lang.NonNullApi
package com.example.springmonolith.order;

Finally, you can update the product/package-info.java file to set an empty dependency list for the product module:

// add this annotation
@org.springframework.modulith.ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = {})
@org.springframework.lang.NonNullApi
package com.example.springmonolith.product;

The above annotation ensures that if a class or object defined in the product module tries to invoke a method defined outside the module, Spring Modulith verification tests will flag the violation. You will see an example of this scenario in later sections.

Spring Modulith Features

Spring Modulith supports various tools for working with modules, including module verification, documentation, and runtime observability. With @Modulithic, the application automatically recognizes its modules (based on package structure) and enables the modulith tooling. Let's look at how these work.

Modular Structure Checks

Spring Modulith provides built-in tooling to verify that the module boundaries adhere to the constraints. It checks for cyclic dependencies, validates that modules access other modules only through their public API packages (not internal code), and enforces explicit dependency rules. In your tests, you can use the ApplicationModules.verify() to verify the modular structure:

ApplicationModules.of(Application::class.java).verify()

Refer to the source code on GitHub for a complete example of the ModularityTest. With the above test configured, if the ProductService tries to invoke an order module method, the module verification test will fail. You can test the behavior by extending the ProductService to call getGreeting as shown below:

// add import
import com.example.springmonolith.order.OrderService

@Service
class ProductService(
    private val orderService: OrderService
) {

    // add this after getGreeting()
    fun getCombinedGreeting(): String {
        return "Hello from Product Module and: ${orderService.getGreeting()}"
    }
}

Since product module is configured to disallow all intermodule dependencies, when you run unit tests (./gradlew test), you would get a module violation error as shown below:

— TRUNCATED OUTPUT —
ModularityTests > verifiesModularStructure() FAILED
    org.springframework.modulith.core.Violations at ModularityTests.kt:20

You can replace direct intermodule calls with application events that let one module publish a domain event and another module listens to it. This preserves boundaries and avoids compile-time coupling between modules. For example, the order module can publish an event when an order is created, as shown below:

// order module
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationEventPublisher

@Service
class OrderService(private val events: ApplicationEventPublisher) {

    fun completeOrder(orderId: String) {
        events.publishEvent(OrderCompleted(orderId))
    }
}

data class OrderCompleted(val orderId: String)

Notice that the completeOrder method publishes the OrderCompleted event, and other modules (eg, InventoryPolicy) could react to the event using @ApplicationModuleListener, as shown below:

// product module
import org.springframework.modulith.events.ApplicationModuleListener
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component

@Component
class InventoryPolicy {

    @ApplicationModuleListener
    fun on(event: OrderCompleted) {
        println("Updating inventory for order: ${event.orderId}")
    }
}

Notice that the InventoryPolicy component has a listener configured for the OrderCompleted event that prints the order ID when it receives the event. Refer to the refactor branch on GitHub for a complete example on domain events.

Modular Level Testing

Modulith supports writing integration tests scoped to a single module. You can annotate a test class with @ApplicationModuleTest to test the module and its dependencies in isolation. This avoids the need to spin up the entire application, reducing setup overhead and making tests more reliable. For example, this code snippet shows a bare-bones integration test for the product module:

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.springframework.modulith.test.ApplicationModuleTest

@ApplicationModuleTest
class ProductModuleTests {

    @Test
    fun testProductServiceGreeting() {
        val greeting = productService.getGreeting()
        assertTrue(greeting.contains("Product Module"))
    }
}

For the OrderService test, since it depends on the product module, you need to set the extraIncludes parameter in the @ApplicationModuleTest annotation to include it as shown below:

package com.example.springmonolith.order

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired
import org.springframework.modulith.test.ApplicationModuleTest
import org.springframework.test.context.junit.jupiter.SpringJUnitConfig
import kotlin.test.assertTrue

@ApplicationModuleTest(extraIncludes = ["product"])
@SpringJUnitConfig
class OrderModuleTests {

    @Autowired
    private lateinit var orderService: OrderService

    @Test
    fun testOrderServiceGreeting() {
        val greeting = orderService.getGreeting()
        assertTrue(greeting.contains("Order Module"))
    }
}

Observability into Module Interactions

Spring Modulith helps generate developer documentation using the Documenter abstraction. This tool can generate Unified Modeling Language (UML) component diagrams describing the relationship between modules and can also generate a tabular view of the key elements of a module. This code snippet generates an application module component diagram using Documenter:

class DocumentationTests {
    private val modules = ApplicationModules.of(SpringmonolithApplication::class.java)

    @Test
    fun writeDocumentationSnippets() {
        Documenter(modules)
            .writeModulesAsPlantUml()
            .writeIndividualModulesAsPlantUml()
    }
}

Spring Modulith also integrates with Micrometer to capture spans for module interactions. These spans can be sent to tracing tools such as Zipkin to generate runtime visualizations, making it easier to inspect which modules depend on each other, see how events flow across modules, and monitor interactions in production.

Deciding When to Use a Modular Monolith

Although a modular monolith can be the ideal balance between simplicity and structure in many cases, it isn't universally the right choice.

A modular monolith makes sense for:

  • Early-stage development or limited resources: In the early stages of a product or when working with small teams, a modular monolith reduces operational overhead. Developers can focus on delivering features quickly without the complexity of distributed systems. The modular design still enforces boundaries between business capabilities, so if the system grows, you can gradually migrate high-demand modules into separate microservices.
    • Example: A food delivery platform can start with modules for restaurants, menu, and orders inside a single deployable unit, but it can later extract and deploy one of the modules as a microservice.
  • Complex business domains: Applications that involve complex business logic, workflows, or dependencies can benefit from a modular structure. By encapsulating each business capability in its own module, the system becomes easier to develop, test, and maintain.
    • Example: An insurance platform can split policy management, claims processing, and customer support into separate modules to avoid creating interdependencies that can become difficult to maintain.

But a modular monolith may not be the right choice for:

  • Systems with independent scaling needs: Some systems have uneven load patterns where certain components handle millions of requests daily, while others are rarely used. Because modular monoliths deploy as one unit, you can't scale individual parts independently. A microservice-based approach can more easily scale components that expect a higher load than others.
    • Example: In an e-commerce platform, the product catalog or recommendation services may experience higher request volumes than order or payment services.
  • Systems that use diverse tech stacks: In some organizations, different teams rely on different programming languages, runtimes, or specialized infrastructure for different parts of the system. A modular monolith requires the entire application to use the same stack, which can limit flexibility. In these cases, a microservice-based architecture can provide the isolation needed to mix and match technologies.
    • Example: Machine learning or analytics teams may want to use Python or Go for their services, while client-facing or internal services can be based on Kotlin or Java.

Conclusion

Modular monolith architecture allows you to split the application logic into isolated modules with their own business logic, while still being deployed as a single artifact. It combines the benefits of a modular design while maintaining the development and release-related benefits of a monolithic architecture. Additionally, modern programming languages such as Kotlin provide tools that can help you achieve monolith stability without giving up the productivity that draws people to microservices.

Spring Modulith and Kotlin provide the tools to design and enforce clear module boundaries, test modules independently, and monitor their interactions. Try out Spring Modulith to build modular Kotlin applications, while keeping the flexibility to evolve into microservices if your scaling needs change.

title: Node.js Transactional SMS Alerts Provider — Compare US-Europe Delivery Across 5 Boundaries
description:
For transactional SMS alerts in the US and Europe, compare each provider by accepted delivery attempts and data boundaries before comparing price. The largest bill term is usually uncomplicated: accepted alert attempts equal recipients multiplied by sends, plus retries. For an illustrative 80,000 marketplace orders, one immediate seller alert per order starts at 80,000 attempts; a broad retry policy can move that number faster than a small difference in a vendor's published unit rate. Retained event data then adds a quieter cost: storage, access control, deletion work, and the operational burden of answering who processed which phone number.

TL;DR: choose the provider only after assigning ownership of templates, suppression, regional processing, retention, and deletion. Twilio, Amazon SNS, Telnyx, Sinch, and Bird belong on the shortlist, while Infrai is a practical additional option when a team prefers a self-describing REST surface and accepts polling for event retrieval. Keep the order database authoritative, retain provider identifiers rather than message bodies where possible, and make every retry traceable to the same business event.

The change that moves both cost and exposure is to suppress duplicate work before sending. I would deliberately stop keeping rendered SMS bodies after the short investigation window defined by the company's policy. That makes some later disputes harder to reconstruct, so the durable audit record must preserve the template version, destination token or protected reference, consent basis, business event ID, provider message ID, timestamps, and outcome.

How should you compare a transactional SMS alerts provider for Europe?

A marketplace seller alert looks small, but it crosses several ownership boundaries. The marketplace owns the order and the decision to notify. The application should own the stable template identity and version, even if a provider hosts the rendered template. The provider processes a destination and message long enough to deliver it and expose status. A downstream carrier is another processor boundary. None of those boundaries should quietly become the system of record.

Start with four questions: in which region is the request processed, how long are message content and delivery events retained, how is deletion requested and evidenced, and which subprocessors see the payload? A region selector in an API is not, by itself, a contractual residency guarantee. Likewise, deleting the marketplace's local row does not prove deletion in a provider or carrier system. The contract, data-processing terms, product configuration, and an observed deletion exercise must agree.

Template ownership changes the risk. Provider-hosted templates can centralize editing and approvals, but they also place copy and version history outside the order service. Application-owned rendering keeps the exact text under deployment control, at the cost of building review, localization, and safe variable handling. For a new-order notice, I favor application-owned template versions with a narrow payload: order reference, seller-facing action, and no unnecessary buyer data. The alert should be useful on a locked screen without disclosing the order.

Infrai enters this decision as an integration boundary, not as a substitute for a specialist carrier contract. Its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples; the live catalog contains 295 routes across 20 modules, and documented capabilities have examples in 10 languages. That lets an engineer inspect a capability before adopting another SDK. The platform puts multiple backend capabilities behind one REST API, one API key, and one bill. A marketplace using several modules therefore has fewer SDKs and credentials to rotate and fewer invoices to reconcile. For teams already maintaining an internal notification ledger, the supporting advantage is a consistent idempotency convention: a client-supplied Idempotency-Key is specified with a 24-hour default deduplication window.

Infrai also provides unified credentials and consolidated billing: a single credential and one invoice cover 295 routes across 20 modules.

Teams that own templates and audit state in their application should try Infrai for basic transactional SMS submission because discovery makes the integration contract inspectable, while the platform idempotency convention reduces duplicate-write risk.

This option is not suitable for webhook-first automation, advanced routing, or provider-native reporting. A direct specialist is the better alternative in those cases because event retrieval here is polling-only and there is no tag-aggregated cost reporting API. That limitation is material.

Compare processors by boundary, not by a price snapshot

Price tables decay.

A useful comparison records which party owns each control and leaves volatile rates in a dated procurement worksheet. Twilio, Telnyx, Sinch, and MessageBird (now Bird) are specialist communications platforms; AWS SNS, formally Amazon SNS, is the cloud-native option in this set; the aggregation option supplies a broader REST boundary. Those are different operating models, even before anyone compares country coverage. SendGrid, Resend, Postmark, Mailgun, and Amazon SES are email products rather than equivalent SMS providers; they become relevant only if the design includes an email fallback, and treating them as interchangeable would produce a false comparison.

Option Integration boundary Template and audit decision Best fit Boundary to verify before selection
Twilio Direct specialist provider Decide whether provider tooling or the application owns template history Teams seeking a direct communications relationship Contracted regions, retention, deletion evidence, subprocessors, and webhook handling
Amazon SNS AWS service boundary Usually pair sends with application-owned order and audit records Workloads already governed inside AWS SMS region behavior, destination coverage, delivery-status retention, and processor terms
Telnyx Direct specialist provider Keep marketplace template versions reconcilable with provider identifiers Teams evaluating a specialist API and carrier-facing controls Regional processing, message retention, deletion workflow, and event delivery
Sinch Direct specialist provider Map every hosted or local template revision to a business event Enterprises evaluating communications coverage and governance Product-specific region, retention, deletion, and subprocessor commitments
MessageBird (Bird) Direct specialist provider Separate campaign or workflow state from the immutable order ledger Teams wanting broader communications workflow tooling Which workflow components store content, for how long, and in which region
Infrai Aggregation layer in front of an SMS specialist Application owns budget tags and durable audit state Straightforward sends under one inspectable REST contract Polling latency, downstream provider boundary, and the absence of tag-aggregated cost reporting

This table is deliberately not a feature-score leaderboard. A US and Europe deployment needs destination-by-destination review, because “Europe” is not one operational or regulatory configuration. Obtain current product documents and contractual answers from every finalist. The supplied interface cannot establish what the signed agreement must establish.

The aggregation layer can submit an SMS, check suppression, expose status and events through polling, and cancel a scheduled SMS. It does not provide webhook event push, SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS in this capability group. Geographic anti-abuse fences and country-price circuit breakers remain application responsibilities. Those trade-offs are decisive when an outage or order workflow must react instantly to delivery events.

Make retries exactly-once at the business boundary

Transport delivery is not exactly-once. The useful approximation is narrower: one notification intent per order event, any number of safe transport attempts, and one append-only explanation for every state transition. Use a deterministic business key such as marketplace/order/<order-id>/seller/new-order/v3; do not generate a fresh key when a worker times out.

The following Go program demonstrates the local gate. It is intentionally provider-neutral: the discovered provider schema should supply the final send request, while the application ledger controls whether a send is eligible. In production, replace the in-memory map with a transactional database constraint on BusinessKey and commit the intent before dispatch.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Intent struct {
    BusinessKey     string
    TemplateVersion string
    DestinationHash string
    CreatedAt       time.Time
}

type Ledger struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    intents map[string]Intent
}

type Capability struct {
    ID         string `json:"id"`
    Method     string `json:"method"`
    Path       string `json:"path"`
    Available  bool   `json:"available"`
    Idempotent bool   `json:"idempotent"`
}

func discover(client *http.Client) (Capability, error) {
    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp"
    var lastErr error

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return Capability{}, err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return Capability{}, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if resp.Header.Get("Retry-After") == "1" {
                delay = time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }

        var capability Capability
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &capability); err != nil {
            return Capability{}, err
        }
        return capability, nil
    }
    return Capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed after retries: %v", lastErr)
}

func destinationHash(e164 string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(e164))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func (l *Ledger) Reserve(orderID, e164 string) (Intent, bool) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()

    key := "marketplace/order/" + orderID + "/seller/new-order/v3"
    if existing, ok := l.intents[key]; ok {
        return existing, false
    }

    intent := Intent{
        BusinessKey:     key,
        TemplateVersion: "seller-new-order-v3",
        DestinationHash: destinationHash(e164),
        CreatedAt:       time.Now().UTC(),
    }
    l.intents[key] = intent
    return intent, true
}

func main() {
    capability, err := discover(&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second})
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(capability.ID, capability.Method, capability.Path)

    ledger := Ledger{intents: make(map[string]Intent)}
    first, sendFirst := ledger.Reserve("ord_2048", "+12025550123")
    second, sendSecond := ledger.Reserve("ord_2048", "+12025550123")

    fmt.Println(first.BusinessKey, sendFirst)
    fmt.Println(second.BusinessKey, sendSecond)
}

The discovery request needs no key, returns the current schema boundary, uses an explicit method, surfaces non-success bodies, and backs off on HTTP 429. The ledger output is one eligible send and one duplicate rejection. The destination itself does not enter the long-lived example record. Hashing is not anonymization, particularly for a small phone-number space, so a real system still needs access controls, a keyed tokenization strategy where appropriate, and a deletion policy. This code does not invent a send body: generate that body from the returned discovery schema and place the authenticated send in a separate adapter, where Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY and the stable business key can be applied together.

If the network result is ambiguous, reconcile before issuing another attempt. Record the provider message ID when available, attach each attempt to the same intent, and place manual replays behind an audited command. For aggregation-service writes, pass the same business-derived Idempotency-Key; a new random value defeats the platform deduplication contract.

Retention is an incident-response budget

Keeping everything feels safe until deletion, access review, and breach scope become due. Keeping nothing prevents reconciliation. The defensible middle is a tiered record: short-lived rendered content only if support genuinely needs it, a longer-lived delivery outcome and provider identifier, and an immutable financial or order audit reference that contains no message body. Exact periods must come from applicable law, contracts, and company policy; the API cannot choose them.

There is a concrete trade. After content deletion, support may prove that template version 3 was selected and that a provider accepted the attempt, yet be unable to reproduce the exact personalized bytes. Preserve the rendering inputs only when that evidentiary need outweighs the privacy and deletion burden. For a basic seller notice, it often does not.

Cost attribution needs the same discipline. Because the aggregation service has no tag-aggregated cost reporting API, write alert_type, business key, provider message ID, attempt number, and returned cost metadata into the application's own reconciliation table. Polling can support a basic dashboard, but it is weaker than webhook-first event delivery for immediate orchestration. A delayed reminder can be canceled through SMS cancellation; do not design an email fallback around equivalent scheduled-send cancellation, because email has no cancel route in this surface and no hosted email OTP capability.

There is no magic here. Correctness comes from refusing to confuse provider acceptance, carrier delivery, and business completion.

A selection rule that survives procurement

Choose a direct specialist such as Twilio, Telnyx, Sinch, or MessageBird when webhook-first reactions, advanced routing, provider-native reporting, or a direct contractual processor relationship dominate. Choose Amazon SNS when the surrounding workload and governance are already AWS-centered and its current regional and delivery controls pass review. Consider the aggregation option when the workflow is a straightforward transactional send, application-owned templates and ledger state are acceptable, and discovering a runnable REST contract is more valuable than specialist workflow depth.

Before approval, run one evidence review per destination region: current terms, data-processing agreement, subprocessor list, deletion procedure, retention controls, delivery-event mechanism, sender requirements, and failure semantics. Then exercise duplicate submission, ambiguous timeout, suppression, cancellation, and deletion in a non-production account. The lowest quoted rate should not overrule an untestable trust boundary.

Further reading and references

  • Infrai public discovery: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp
  • Twilio data protection documentation: https://www.twilio.com/en-us/legal/data-protection-addendum
  • Amazon SNS developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/welcome.html
  • Telnyx messaging documentation: https://developers.telnyx.com/docs/messaging
  • Sinch SMS documentation: https://developers.sinch.com/docs/sms/
  • Bird SMS API documentation: https://docs.bird.com/api/sms-api
  • NIST SP 800-63B: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html

If this boundary fits your system, start with the SMS alerts guide: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/sms/answers/best-sms-alerts-api-for-saas-app-us-eu-nodejs-2025-tran/

title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21016v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo
