title: ZoomCap: Evidence-Routed Visual Zooming for Recoverable Visual Information Transfer
description:
arXiv:2610.21320v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detailed captions transfer visual information into vision-language model supervision, but quality is easily conflated with length: long single-pass outputs still miss small objects, text, and spatial relations or promote uncertain observations into confident claims. We formulate fine-grained captioning as recoverable visual information transfer, in which a teacher acquires missing evidence under a finite observation budget and converts it into reusable supervision. ZoomCap uses a draft caption to route conditional knowledge retrieval, OCR-sensitive reading, coverage-gap recovery, and adaptive visual zooming, allocating deeper crops only to the most complex eligible region, deriving spatial relations from grounded geometry, and fusing non-duplicate evidence. We also introduce FactCycle, which scores caption-derived atomic claims on two blind anchors--source image (truthfulness) and reconstruction (realizability)--separating fabrication from generator loss claim by claim; human and multi-judge comparisons complement this fact-level view. Against Qwen3.5-397B-A17B captions, ZoomCap achieves an 81.9% human tie-adjusted preference score with a teacher over 10x smaller, and FactCycle counts 52.4 transferred claims per image vs. 31.5 for ScaleCap. The evidence also transfers: in continual pre-training, ZoomCap-450K improves the 11-benchmark average by 1.31-2.38 points over the strongest competing corpus and Ling-Tiny-VL-v3 gains 1.4 points on a production document/OCR monitor suite (1.5 on perception) at 60B tokens; in medical pre-training, 2.64M ZoomCap-captioned images improve five VQA benchmarks by 3.04 points (vs. 1.76 for same-image Gemini-3.1-Pro captions).

title: Realtime Host Handoff Recovery: WebRTC Failure Handling for Consultation Rooms
description:
Use a realtime API surface that matches host handoff, then make recovery explicit in the video consultation room. The deciding constraint is trust: a replacement host must receive a narrowly scoped token, while the browser must be able to prove which room state it has actually observed.

Short answer: keep authentication, subscription state, and business events as separate state machines, and reconcile them with stable identifiers after every reconnect.

The experiment: a host handoff is a state transition

Imagine a clinician's browser loses its uplink during a consultation. A second clinician takes over. The simple implementation treats “connected” as proof that the handoff worked. That is the trap. A WebRTC peer connection can be alive while the application subscription is stale, and a valid token can outlive the business event that revoked the first host.

I model the room with three clocks: token expiry, realtime subscription, and the clinical business event. They can disagree. The handoff command carries a server-created room identifier and a monotonically increasing event identifier. The new host asks for current presence, compares that identifier, and only then enables controls. It feels slower than optimistic UI for one frame. It is much easier to audit.

The useful measurement is not a glossy latency number. Measure how often a reconnect converges to one host, how many duplicate events are discarded, and how often an unauthorized client is denied. Your mileage may vary with mobile radio conditions; I’m not sure a lab Wi-Fi test tells you much here.

How should realtime failure handling protect host handoff and token scope?

Start with an explicit state table. “Expired” is not the same thing as “disconnected,” and neither means the consultation ended.

State Client action Server decision
Token expired Stop publishing; request a fresh scoped token Re-check role and room version
Subscription dropped Reconnect with backoff, then fetch presence Replay or return the current stable identifier
Duplicate event Compare event identifier and ignore an old one Keep delivery at-least-once safe
Partial handoff Show read-only controls until reconciliation Reject writes from the old host

This separation also makes authorization tests concrete. Try an expired token, a token for another room, and a valid token with an old role. Then add 400 ms latency and duplicate delivery. A green path is not evidence that the workflow is safe.

A small Node.js reconciliation loop

The presence read is deliberately boring. It is a recovery checkpoint, not a second source of business truth. The route below is the documented presence lookup; the room and event identifiers returned by your application service remain the authoritative records.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required (use the service's v1 base URL)");

async function readPresence(channel: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/realtime/presence/get/${encodeURIComponent(channel)}`,
      {
        method: "GET",
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
      },
    );

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`presence lookup failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("presence lookup rate-limited after retries");
}

The plain REST shape is useful when the room service is already in Node.js but the mobile client is not: there is no SDK version to coordinate, and any HTTP-capable worker can perform the same checkpoint. Infrai's other practical advantage here is a single key and billing surface for adjacent backend capabilities, while this article's decision still rests on scope and recovery semantics. Keep the key on your server; never forward it to a browser.

Keep it server-side.

Where the common room providers fit

There is no universal winner. The right choice depends on how much of the room lifecycle you want to operate and how much control your authorization model needs.

Option Strength for a consultation room Trade-off to validate
Pusher Familiar pub/sub primitives for broadcasting a handoff event You still own media, token scope, and recovery ordering
Ably Managed realtime delivery with presence concepts Validate retention and replay behavior against your audit requirements
PubNub Broad realtime messaging and presence tooling Provider-specific event semantics can increase migration work later
Plain WebRTC plus your service Maximum control over token scope and business events You operate signaling, reconnect behavior, and observability
Infrai realtime surface One HTTP interface can fit a server-side presence checkpoint without installing an SDK It is not a complete media room by itself; pair it with a WebRTC room layer

The catch is important: a REST presence checkpoint does not replace media negotiation, TURN capacity, or clinical audit storage. Choose a managed room provider when your team cannot operate those pieces. Stick with plain WebRTC when protocol control is the product. Choose the Infrai surface when a small, language-neutral backend checkpoint is the missing piece, not because a single API magically removes the rest of the system.

Run the same scenario against every candidate: clinician A publishes, the network drops, clinician B receives a scoped token, and the old browser retries an event. Assert that the old write is rejected, the duplicate is harmless, and a reconnect converges on one stable room and event identifier. Record authentication failures separately from subscription failures and business-event failures; combining them produces an attractive dashboard that cannot explain a patient-facing incident.

I would ship only after those assertions pass under realistic latency and authorization permutations. The implementation is small. The state contract is the real feature.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://docs.livekit.io/
  • https://www.twilio.com/docs/video
  • https://docs.daily.co/

title: Beyond Retrieval Failure: Understanding Why LLMs Miss Evidence in Multi-Hop RAG
description:
arXiv:2610.21184v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires an agent to retrieve evidence for a sequence of dependent sub-questions. When a wrong answer lacks a required passage, the passage may be inaccessible to the retriever, or the agent may have failed to issue a query that would retrieve it. Standard retrieval evaluations conflate these two causes. We study how much apparent retrieval failure is instead caused by search drift: the search no longer tracks an unanswered sub-question. Holding the retriever, corpus, and generation model fixed, we introduce ExecutionRAG, a training-free requirement register that records open sub-questions and their supporting evidence. The register changes search guidance but not evidence access, so each gold passage it recovers certifies that the passage was reachable by the original retriever. On 1,000 MuSiQue questions, the number of wrong answers with unretrieved required evidence falls from 382 to 234 with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and from 383 to 274 with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. These counts correspond to 69% to 44% and 66% to 48% of each system's wrong answers, respectively. Crucially, evidence recovery does not produce a proportional reduction in total error: premature resolutions and abstentions increase as missing-evidence failures decrease. The central finding is therefore a shift in the remaining bottleneck, from guiding search toward required evidence to verifying that the retrieved evidence is sufficient.

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: Same Context, Different Agents: A Behavioral Study of Semantic Layers, Orchestration and Compaction in Data Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.20959v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Answering questions over heterogeneous data means combining evidence from files, databases, documents and the web. Data agents automate this, but their success depends on context. Three context-engineering techniques (CETs) help by shaping it: semantic layers describe the data, orchestration splits work among agents, and compaction condenses interaction history. Existing studies validate each CET alone, leaving open how agent behavior shapes its effect. We present a comprehensive analysis of the three CETs, alone and combined, with seven large language models (LLMs) on 1,514 long-horizon tasks from five benchmarks, covering behavior, accuracy and cost. We find that data agents without CETs form three behavior groups: investigators, premature answerers that answer without inspecting data, and early stoppers that give up. Each CET delivers its known benefit, from more investigation to smaller prompts, but only the behavior group it matches turns that benefit into accuracy, such as premature answerers under orchestration. For investigators, the same CETs can hurt: the semantic layer stops them from looking, orchestration makes them overconfident, costing 5 percentage points, and compaction makes them repeat steps. Combining CETs yields smaller gains and losses than their sum. We derive guidance for choosing CETs by agent behavior, task demands and accuracy-cost trade-offs.

title: AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.20675v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions on agent components such as tools, skills, and memory under matched conditions. We study three open-source models and three open-source harnesses on five answer-based benchmarks, with two models also tested on two interactive benchmarks. We find that harnesses do not consistently improve the accuracy of reasoning: gains on questions unsolved by the model alone can be outweighed by losses on questions it answers correctly without tools. This inconsistency extends to component interventions: neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably improves accuracy. Behavior and output-token use must be assessed with correctness: low token entropy can accompany wrong answers, and less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer when accuracy falls. AlphaDiana links answer correctness and execution status to traces and resource records for comparing agents and diagnosing failures under shared task and resource policies.

title: Rubric Judgments Lack Uncertainty: Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.21214v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess large language model (LLM) outputs by decomposing quality into multiple criteria and assigning each a binary judgment from an LLM verifier. However, judgment certainty varies substantially across criteria. Existing methods uniformly aggregate these judgments into a final score, implicitly treating every criterion as equally certain and overlooking this heterogeneity. As a result, uncertain judgments remain incorporated into reward estimation without distinction, potentially yielding misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning (RL). To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW), a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level judgment uncertainty via conformal calibration. Specifically, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal $p$-values with provable coverage guarantees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment.

title: Twitter Added id_str in 2010 Because JavaScript Can't Hold a Java long
description:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On October 18, 2010, Twitter told every developer on its API that tweet IDs were about to change shape. A new generator called Snowflake would produce 64-bit IDs, and TechCrunch's write-up of the notice put the date plainly: "on November 26, these IDs will go longer than 53 bits." The fix Twitter shipped was blunt. Starting October 22, every ID in a JSON response would come back twice, once as a number and once as a string. In the words of developer advocate Matt Harris, quoted in the same article: "To allow javascript and JSON parsers to read the IDs we need to include a string version of any ID."

That string field is id_str, and it is still in the API. The current X developer docs tell v1.1 clients to "always use id_str", and v2 skipped the number entirely: IDs come back as strings by default.

Sixteen years later, the same bug still ships. A Spring Boot or Ktor service returns a Long ID, a TypeScript client calls JSON.parse, and the last few digits change. No exception. No warning in the console. The client then sends the wrong ID back to the server, and you get a 404 on a record that exists, or a hit on a different record whose ID happens to be the rounded value.

Why Twitter needed 64 bits in the first place

Snowflake was built for Twitter's move from MySQL to Cassandra. The original README is direct about the motive: "there is no sequential id generation facility in Cassandra, nor should there be." The requirements were uncoordinated generation across machines, rough time ordering, and IDs that stay under 64 bits.

The layout it settled on:

  • 41 bits of millisecond timestamp against a custom epoch ("gives us 69 years")
  • 10 bits of machine ID, for up to 1024 machines
  • 12 bits of sequence number, rolling over every 4096 IDs per machine

That is 63 bits of payload, which fits a signed 64-bit integer: a Java long, a Kotlin Long, a Scala Long. The Java Language Specification gives long the range -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807. Every JVM backend can hold a Snowflake ID without thinking about it. The trouble starts when the ID leaves the JVM.


A JVM long has 64 bits to spend. A JavaScript number has 53 for the integer part.

53 bits of mantissa versus 64 bits of long

A JavaScript number is an IEEE 754 double. MDN's page on Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER spells out the consequence: a double "only has 52 bits to represent the mantissa," plus one implicit leading bit, so it can only safely represent integers between -(2^53 - 1) and 2^53 - 1. That ceiling is 9007199254740991.

Past it, a double still exists for every power of two, but not for every integer. Just above 2^53 the gap between neighbouring doubles is 2. Just above 2^60 it is 2^(60-52), which is 256. Modern Snowflake IDs live up there, so a parsed ID snaps to the nearest representable double, and two real IDs generated a moment apart can land on the same one.

You can see it in four lines:

const body = '{"id": 9007199254740993}';
const order = JSON.parse(body) as { id: number };

console.log(order.id);                       // 9007199254740992
console.log(Number.isSafeInteger(order.id)); // false

MDN shows the same collapse from the arithmetic side: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 evaluates to true. The X docs use 10765432100123456789, which is past even a Java long's ceiling, and show it printing back as 10765432100123458000.

None of this breaks the JSON spec. RFC 8259, section 6 "allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted," and names only the integers in [-(2^53)+1, (2^53)-1] as the range where implementations "will agree exactly on their numeric values." Jackson writing 9007199254740993 is valid JSON. JSON.parse rounding it is also valid. The contract between them is the bug.

TypeScript does not help here. JSON.parse returns any, your as { id: number } is a promise you made to the compiler, and the value already satisfies number. The type system checks the shape, and the shape is fine.

Why BigInt doesn't fix JSON.parse

The natural reaction from a JVM developer is: JavaScript has arbitrary-precision integers now, so parse into BigInt. Two things get in the way.

First, JSON.parse never produces a BigInt. Numbers become doubles during parsing, before your code sees anything. The MDN JSON.parse page is explicit that the reviver "is run after the value is parsed," so numbers "will have already been converted to JavaScript numbers, and may lose precision in the process." Writing BigInt(value) inside a classic two-argument reviver gives you an exact BigInt of the wrong number.

Second, the trip back is closed by default. Per MDN's BigInt page, calling JSON.stringify() on any value containing a BigInt throws a TypeError unless you supply a toJSON or a replacer.

So BigInt is a fine type to hold an ID once you have the exact digits. It cannot recover digits the parser already threw away. The digits have to survive the parse, which means either they arrive as a string, or the parser hands you the source text.


Above 2^53, distinct IDs can parse to the same JavaScript number.

Fix it on the JVM side: make the ID a string in the contract

The fix Twitter chose, and the one Discord documents for its own Snowflake IDs ("they are always returned as strings in the HTTP API"), is to put the ID on the wire as a JSON string. Keep Long in the database and in your domain model. Change only the serialized form.

With Jackson, a per-field annotation does it:

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonFormat;

public record OrderDto(
    @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING)
    long id,
    long totalCents
) {}

In Jackson 2, the number serializers return ToStringSerializer.instance when the shape is STRING, so id goes out as "9007199254740993" with the quotes. The annotation lives in jackson-annotations, which the Spring team notes kept its package unchanged when Spring Boot 4 moved to Jackson 3 under tools.jackson, so the same line works across that upgrade.

If every Long in your API is an identifier, you can register the serializer by type instead. On Spring Boot 3 with Jackson 2:

@Bean
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer longsAsStrings() {
    return b -> b
        .serializerByType(Long.class, ToStringSerializer.instance)
        .serializerByType(Long.TYPE, ToStringSerializer.instance);
}

Be careful with that one. It also quotes counts, cents and timestamps that never needed it. Jackson's blunter switch, JsonWriteFeature.WRITE_NUMBERS_AS_STRINGS (off by default), "forces all regular number values to be written as JSON Strings," doubles included. Per field is usually the honest scope.

On Ktor with kotlinx.serialization, the library ships a serializer for exactly this case. The LongAsStringSerializer docs describe it as "intended to be used for interoperability with external clients (mainly JavaScript ones)":

import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable
import kotlinx.serialization.builtins.LongAsStringSerializer

@Serializable
data class OrderDto(
    @Serializable(with = LongAsStringSerializer::class)
    val id: Long,
    val totalCents: Long,
)

Then write it down. If you publish an OpenAPI spec, the ID is type: string, not type: integer, format: int64, so generated TypeScript clients get string too.

Fix it in the TypeScript client

On the client, type the ID as what it is on the wire: a string. A branded type keeps it from mixing with other strings:

type OrderId = string & { readonly __brand: "OrderId" };

interface Order {
  id: OrderId;
  totalCents: number;
}

You compare it, put it in URLs and send it back. You almost never do arithmetic on an ID, so a string loses nothing. If you need ordering or math, convert with BigInt(order.id) at that moment, from exact digits.

Sometimes you don't own the server and it still sends bare numbers. For that case, TC39 added source text access to JSON.parse; the proposal is at stage 4. For primitive values, the reviver gets a third context argument whose source property is "the original JSON string representing this value" (MDN). MDN's compatibility data lists it in Chrome 114, Firefox 135, Safari 18.4, Node.js 21, Deno 1.33 and Bun 1.1.43.

type Ctx = { source?: string };

function idsAsStrings(key: string, value: unknown, ctx?: Ctx) {
  if (key !== "id" || typeof value !== "number") return value;
  if (ctx?.source === undefined) {
    throw new Error("JSON.parse source access not supported");
  }
  return ctx.source; // the exact digits, before rounding
}

const order = JSON.parse(text, idsAsStrings) as Order;

The reviver throws when the runtime doesn't pass context, because falling back to String(value) would hand you the rounded digits as a string, which is the original bug wearing a disguise. And you need the raw text to call it: Response.json() takes no reviver, so read the body with await res.text() and parse it yourself.

The same proposal added JSON.rawJSON for the outbound direction. A replacer like typeof v === "bigint" ? JSON.rawJSON(v.toString()) : v lets JSON.stringify emit a BigInt as a bare JSON number without precision loss, when a server insists on numeric IDs in request bodies.

If you own the server, the one-line @JsonFormat change is the whole fix, and it costs less to ship before your ID generator crosses 2^53 than after the first 404 on a record that exists.

If this was useful

This bug lives exactly on the seam between the JVM and TypeScript: a Long that is perfectly safe on one side and quietly lossy on the other. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript is the book I wrote for that seam, mapping what you already know from Java and Kotlin (variance, null safety, sealed hierarchies, coroutines) onto how TypeScript does the same jobs.

It's part of The TypeScript Library, five books with a clear path through them. Books 1 and 2 are the core path. If you come from the JVM, book 3 stands in for book 1. If you ship TypeScript at work, book 5 is the production layer:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

title: FocusOPD: Structure-Guided On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21250v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation enables rectified-flow models with diffusion-transformer architectures to combine task-specific capabilities within a single student. However, matching model outputs does not guarantee that their internal representations are aligned, and it remains unclear where and when additional feature supervision is most useful. We analyze the teacher-student feature mismatch across Transformer blocks and denoising timesteps, and find that the mismatch is concentrated in deeper Transformer blocks during early denoising and persists after OPD distillation, indicating ineffective distillation. Motivated by this observation, we introduce FocusOPD, which augments the base OPD objective with token-wise directional feature alignment restricted to deep layers and early denoising steps. Across two rectified-flow backbones and multiple OPD objectives, FocusOPD improves capability transfer in compositional generation, text rendering, and preference-based evaluation. On the primary benchmark, it improves over DiffusionOPD from 0.953 to 0.967 on GenEval, from 23.797 to 23.944 on PickScore, and from 6.052 to 6.199 on LAION-Aesthetic. Ablations show that selective deep and early supervision is more effective and efficient than alignment over the full network and trajectory.

title: The AI Automation Billing Trap Nobody Explains (Zapier vs Make vs n8n)
description:
If you are building AI workflows for your business or clients, you are probably choosing between the big three: Zapier, Make, and n8n.
Most people just look at the starting price tier (like "$20/month"), enter their credit card details, and hit subscribe.
That is a massive mistake. Here is why.
The real trap isn't the monthly base fee; it's how these platforms count your usage when AI gets involved. A single AI loop that processes incoming leads, filters them, runs a prompt, and updates a database can cost you $30 on one platform and explode to $400+ on another within a single week.
Here is the quick breakdown of how they quietly drain your budget:
• Zapier (The Task Trap): Zapier charges per completed "Task". It sounds fair, but if your workflow uses filters, paths, or webhooks, those tasks vanish instantly. It has the best UI and integrations, but scaling high-volume AI loops here will break the bank.
• Make (The Operation Explosion): Make charges per "Operation". Every single bubble or module that touches data counts as an execution. If an AI module processes 10 items in a bundle, that counts as 10 separate operations. It is much cheaper than Zapier for bulk data, but a poorly optimized workflow can eat through your monthly limit in 48 hours.
• n8n (The Fair Competitor): n8n is built heavily for advanced workflows and developers. Their cloud version is priced fairly, but their real superpower is the Open-Source Community Edition. If you know how to self-host it on a basic $5 VPS or your own machine, your execution costs drop to literally zero.

We got tired of the marketing hype and affiliate sales pitches. So, we opened the pricing pages, read all the small print, and calculated the exact multi-tier billing math by hand.

title: IneqAgent: Agentic Inequality Proving in Lean with Symbolic Computation
description:
arXiv:2610.20681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Formal inequality proving requires mathematical reasoning and exact computation, often connected through intermediate lemmas and goal reformulations. We introduce IneqAgent, an agentic framework combining LLM reasoning with symbolic computation for inequality proving in Lean4. Lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and symbolic backend selection. Complementary sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends produce exact certificates for local Lean proof generation. The agent integrates these proofs with LLM-generated steps and uses Lean feedback to construct complete proofs checked against the original theorem statements. On four benchmarks, IneqAgent with DeepSeek-V4-Flash solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%), achieving the highest overall success rate among the evaluated methods. Across four backbones, it achieves higher success rates at low LLM inference cost thresholds than Direct Agent using the same backbone, with lower mean inference costs over each method's successful runs. We also obtain Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture in dimensions four and five, and certify the Holens--Djokovic $(4,4)$ inequality, implying Merris's conjecture in dimension four.

title: Replicable Dueling Bandits
description:
arXiv:2610.20908v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dueling bandits choose each comparison based on earlier noisy outcomes, so two runs on the same preferences can compare different pairs. We study replicable dueling bandits, where two executions with shared internal randomness and independent comparison outcomes must select the same ordered pair in every round with probability at least $1-\rho$. Building on Beat-the-Mean, whose scores change as arms are eliminated and need not rank the best arm highest, we design the first such algorithms with sublinear regret. Under relaxed stochastic transitivity with parameter $\gamma\ge 1$ and the stochastic triangle inequality, we design an algorithm that achieves expected regret $\widetilde{O}(\gamma^8 K^4 H_{\mathrm{p}}/\rho^2)$, where $H_{\mathrm{p}}=\sum_{i=2}^{K}(P_{1i}-1/2)^{-1}$. Under strong stochastic transitivity, we design an algorithm based on simultaneous elimination that improves the dependence on $K$ and achieves $\widetilde{O}(K^2 H_{\mathrm{p}}/\rho^2)$ regret. For linear dueling bandits, we design an algorithm that achieves regret $\widetilde{O}(d^3\sqrt{T}/(c_\mu\rho))$. Experiments on synthetic and language-model preferences show replicability, with sublinear regret.

title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight
description:
arXiv:2610.21018v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.

title: An AI Agent Is Running a Real Microbusiness Solo. Here's the Function Split Worth Studying.
description:
In mid-October, Alex Finn posted that his Grok Bot — the same class of consumer agent most people use to draft emails — had built a use-case website on its own, decided to monetize it with sponsors, kept shipping updates without being asked, and closed its first sponsor. Finn's remaining job: running the social media accounts. Everything else ran agent-side.

Label this honestly: it's one source, from the person with every incentive to promote it, and the revenue is real-but-small — first sponsor money, not a payroll. Treat it as anecdote, not proof.

But it's the first plausible report of a consumer agent operating a real (if tiny) business end-to-end, and it makes a question concrete that most owners only ask abstractly: if you had an agent like that, which functions of your business could it actually own?

Most coverage of "AI runs a business" runs it through hype or threat. Both skip the exercise an owner can do in twenty minutes. That exercise — function allocation — is the part worth stealing.

Task Delegation Is Not Function Ownership

There's an important distinction hiding here, because "delegate to AI" already has a playbook — the junior agent drafts, a human reviews every output before it ships. That's task delegation. It's the right pattern for most work, and it's not what happened in this case.

Function ownership is different: the agent runs the entire loop, the output goes to real people without a human looking at it first, and the human only audits results — weekly, not per-output.

  • A task delegate drafts your follow-up emails. You read each one and send.
  • A function owner maintains your website, publishes updates, answers the inbound, invoices the customer. You review traffic and revenue on Friday.

The test is brutal and simple: does the work leave the building without a human in the loop? If yes, the agent owns the function. If a human signs off on each output, you've delegated a task — which is fine, and much safer, but it's a different bet.

The Agent-First Seats

Look at what held up as agent-owned in the reported case, and why each survived:

  • The website. Built and maintained by the agent. Bad output is immediately visible to anyone who visits.
  • Continuous updates. The agent shipped improvements unprompted. A dud update shows up in the numbers within days.
  • Inbound negotiation. The agent handled sponsor inquiries through to a closed deal — inside authority limits someone set up front.
  • The records. Tracking what shipped, what earned, what's owed. Bookkeeping-ish work with a paper trail.

There's a shared property: the feedback loop is external and fast. A weak update surfaces as traffic loss in days. A misjudged reply bounces back as an email. The work self-corrects before small errors compound into big ones. Fast, visible, cheap-to-fix feedback is what makes a function ownable.

The Human-Kept Seats

Notice where the human stayed in the same case: the public-facing voice. Social media ran through Finn — because the brand's face is an asset that an agent can degrade faster than any dashboard can measure.

For your business, the human-kept seats are the ones that fail that external-fast-feedback test:

  • Your name in public. Reputation damage is slow to surface and expensive to repair — the opposite of a fast feedback loop.
  • Key client relationships. An agent can draft; the relationship compounds because a specific human answers.
  • Judgment calls with compounding downside. Pricing strategy, hiring, which market to enter. Wrong answers take months to show up, and by then the cost is sunk.
  • Anything where being wrong is invisible until it's expensive. If you can't check the output cheaply on a weekly cadence, you can't own-by-audit.

Calibrate the Expectation Before You Run It

The payday in this case is a first sponsor on a niche website — dollars, not millions. If the pattern works at all, it frees the owner's time and adds small revenue streams, not a payroll.

The reason to pay attention isn't the money. It's that the boundary of "ownable" just moved — the same way website builders moved it and Zapier moved it. Each shift lets a smaller business cover one more seat without a hire. The allocation exercise is how you catch that shift early instead of paying for software and people who duplicate it.

Run the Allocation Exercise on Your Business Tonight

This takes twenty minutes and one page:

  1. List your functions. Marketing, sales, fulfillment, support, records, admin. Six rows.
  2. Apply the ownership test to each row. Three questions: Can output leave without human review? Is the feedback loop fast and external? Is being wrong cheap and visible?
  3. Score it. Three yeses → pilot it as function ownership. Two → task delegation (drafts plus review). One or zero → human seat, and stop feeling guilty about it.
  4. Start with exactly one function. Give the agent the seat, set its authority limits in writing, and audit weekly — results only, not outputs. If the audit passes four weeks in a row, hand it the next function.

The mistake to avoid is confusing the two modes. An agent that drafts well isn't ready to own the function; an agent that owns the inbox shouldn't also get the brand. Most failed AI rollouts in small businesses happen when a task delegate gets promoted to function owner without the feedback loop to support it.

Want the full framework? The AI Agent Owner's Playbook covers function allocation, authority limits, and the weekly audit format in one walkthrough — $49 CAD, instant download.

title: DST-Net: Decomposed Spatio-Temporal Network for Time Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.21123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Series decomposition has emerged as a widely acknowledged paradigm in deep time series forecasting models. However, existing approaches predominantly employ a homogeneous modeling strategy for all subsequences, thereby overlooking the distinct inductive biases inherent in different components. We identify that the trend component exhibits dominant spatial coupling across channels but carries significant temporal redundancy, whereas the seasonal component is characterized by local temporal evolution but remains susceptible to attention distraction. To address this, we propose a novel disentangled architecture that tailors specific modeling strategies to align with the intrinsic properties of each component. For the trend branch, we design a Latent Graph Block, employing latent graph modeling to capture global topological dependencies and system-wide co-movements. Conversely, for the seasonal branch, we introduce a Gaussian Multi-scale Attention mechanism to mitigate attention distraction. By injecting learnable Gaussian priors, we impose structural constraints that compel the model to focus on multi-granular local contexts, effectively filtering out global noise and accurately capturing local evolutionary phases. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

title: Recursive Reward Improvement via Adversarial Meta-Prompt Evolution
description:
arXiv:2610.21040v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) has gained wide attention for its ability to work with limited data. In a proposer-solver loop, a proposer model writes training tasks and a solver model learns to solve them through reinforcement learning. Such loops have succeeded in mathematics and coding, where every answer can be checked automatically. Open-ended expert tasks, like clinical report generations, have no answer key, which makes simple question-answer generation not viable. Here the proposer must also write a rubric that lists the content an answer should include and the errors it should avoid. However, the unique challenge behind model-written rubric is the comprehensiveness of it. For naively generated rubric, solvers tend to exploit it, naming the expected topics without the substance behind them, which corrupts the learning process. To solve this problem, we introduce RRI, Recursive Reward Improvement, which uses a reward hacking adversary to supervise the reward. Before the solver trains on a generated task, an adversary writes an answer that games its rubric while being as useless as possible, the same model writes an honest answer without seeing the rubric, and up to two repair steps revise the rubric to make the honest answer win. The exploits found also rewrite how future tasks and rubrics are generated. On HealthBench Professional, RRI improves the adjusted score over the Generation Only self-improvement baseline by 10.9 points at 9B and 12.4 at 27B, and by 10.3 points without any external model. In particular, the gains are largest on difficult and writing tasks. We show that the 27B model trained on the HealthBench Professional description improves by 6.6 points on PRBench Hard and 8.0 on ProfBench without seeing a task from either. We further analyze the exploitable points of model-generated question-rubric pairs to facilitate future research on open-ended self-play.

title: How to build an AI chat UI with shadcn/ui and the Vercel AI SDK that survives real users
description:
The demo takes an afternoon. useChat from the AI SDK, a list of messages, a textarea, and tokens stream onto the screen. Everyone on the team is impressed.

Then a real person uses it. They hit Enter while composing Japanese and send half a word. They stop a reply and the UI shows nothing. A tool call wants approval mid-stream and there is no UI for that. They scroll up to re-read something and the view yanks them back to the bottom with every token.

I have built this screen more times than I would like, most recently as the blocks behind HextaUI. This is the checklist of what a chat UI has to handle before it is done, with the shadcn/ui and AI SDK specifics for each.

Start from message parts, not strings

The AI SDK's useChat returns messages made of parts: text, reasoning, tool calls with their state, sources, files. Render the parts, not a concatenated string. Every feature below depends on it.

import { isToolUIPart } from "ai"

{message.parts.map((part, i) => {
  if (isToolUIPart(part)) return <ToolCall key={i} part={part} />
  switch (part.type) {
    case "text":
      return <Markdown key={i} text={part.text} />
    case "reasoning":
      return <Thinking key={i} text={part.text} />
    case "source-url":
      return <Source key={i} url={part.url} />
    default:
      return null
  }
})}

Tool parts are typed tool-<name>, so isToolUIPart is the reliable check.

Keep your blocks free of the SDK import. Take parts as props. Then the same components work with a LangGraph backend or your own server once you map its output to the same shape.

The composer

The textarea is where most of the bugs live.

Enter sends, Shift+Enter breaks a line. Everyone does this. Almost nobody handles composition. When someone types Japanese, Chinese or Korean, the IME is open and Enter confirms the candidate, not the message. Check event.nativeEvent.isComposing and bail:

function onKeyDown(event: React.KeyboardEvent<HTMLTextAreaElement>) {
  if (event.key !== "Enter" || event.shiftKey) return
  if (event.nativeEvent.isComposing) return
  event.preventDefault()
  submit()
}

Grow with the text, within limits. One line to start, up to about eight rows, then scroll. Animate the height change, and never through React state on every keystroke. Measure scrollHeight in a layout effect and set the height on the DOM node. Any setState in a native input listener will eventually drop or delay keys under load.

Drafts survive a reload. Save the draft to localStorage keyed by chat id, debounced. People lose long prompts to accidental refreshes and never forgive you.

Queue messages typed during a reply. If the model is still writing and the user sends another message, either disable sending or queue it and send when the stream ends. Silently dropping it is the worst option and it is the default.

Attachments show progress and retry. Uploads fail. Show the failure on the attachment card with a retry, not as a toast that disappears.

Streaming that reads well

Models emit tokens in bursts. If you render exactly what arrives, text stutters: nothing, then twelve words, then nothing. Smooth it. Reveal characters at a steady pace that speeds up when the buffer grows, so you never fall far behind the stream but never stutter either.

Markdown during streaming has its own trap: half-typed syntax. The model has written **bold and not yet closed it, so your renderer shows literal asterisks for a frame, then bold text. Hold back incomplete inline syntax until it closes, or until the stream ends.

Code blocks need the same care. Highlight incrementally and never re-highlight the whole block on every token.

Stop, retry, edit and versions

Stop should leave the partial reply on screen, with a visible "Stopped" marker so the user knows it is incomplete. Do not delete it.

Retry on a failed reply is a button on the message, not a hidden gesture. Connect it to regenerate().

Edit an earlier message creates a branch. Both the old and new reply exist. Show a small 1 / 2 switcher on the message so the user can flip between versions. This is where a lot of homegrown chat UIs give up, and it is the feature people miss most from ChatGPT and Claude.

Failed replies get a reason and a retry. "Something went wrong" with no action is a dead end.

Scrolling

Follow new tokens when the user is at the bottom. The moment they scroll up, stop following, and show a "jump to latest" button with a count of what they missed. When they jump, follow again.

Loading older history at the top must not move the view. Measure the scroll height before and after you prepend, and adjust scrollTop by the difference in the same frame.

If the user sends a message, scroll so their message pins to the top of the viewport and the reply streams below it. That is how the two big chat apps behave now and users expect it.

Tool calls and approvals

The AI SDK gives each tool part a state: input-streaming, input-available, output-available, output-error, and with human-in-the-loop, approval-requested, approval-responded and output-denied. Every state needs a look.

Reads and searches can fold into a one-line summary. Edits, commands and errors should stay expanded. Approvals block the stream and need a clear Allow and Deny, plus a way to say "do this instead" that sends text back to the model as the denial reason.

Show the result when it is useful. A file edit opens into a diff. A command opens into a terminal with the output. A search opens into results. A tool call that only says "Done" teaches users to ignore tool calls.

Thinking and sources

Reasoning parts should be collapsible and collapsed by default once the answer starts. While the model is still thinking, a live label that follows each step ("Searching docs", "Reading three files") is far more reassuring than a spinner.

Citations belong next to the claims they support, inline, not in a list at the bottom nobody reads.

Accessibility you cannot skip

  • New messages announce through a role="log" region, so screen reader users hear replies.
  • The stop button is reachable by keyboard and has a label.
  • Streaming text should not fire a hundred live-region announcements. Announce when the message completes, or at sentence boundaries.
  • Every icon-only button has aria-label.

Putting it together

If you want the pieces, shadcn/ui shipped AI Elements in October 2026: 21 patterns you copy into your project and compose yourself, including Chat, Prompt Input, Reasoning and Tool. Vercel's earlier AI Elements library is being deprecated at the end of November 2026 in favor of them.

If you want the screens already assembled with the states above worked out, that is what the HextaUI blocks are: a Chat Thread with stop, retry and versions, Tool Calls with every AI SDK state and approvals, Streaming and Markdown that never show half-typed syntax, and a Prompt Input that handles CJK input, uploads, queues and drafts. Prompt Input is free. The rest is a one-time purchase. All of it reads AI SDK message parts and none of it imports the SDK, so it works with any backend you can map.

You can try the whole thing assembled as a chat app at hextaui.com/blocks/hexta-ai before installing anything.

FAQ

Do I need the Vercel AI SDK to use these patterns? No. The message-parts shape is the useful part. Any backend works once you map its output to parts.

How do I handle Enter with an IME? Check event.nativeEvent.isComposing in your keydown handler and return early.

Should streaming text update a live region on every token? No. Announce at completion or at sentence boundaries, or screen readers become unusable.

What happens to a stopped reply? Keep the partial text and mark it as stopped. Never delete what the user has already read.

title: AI acceptable use policy for employees: what works
description:
Somewhere in your organisation this morning, someone pasted a client contract, a candidate CV or an unreleased financial projection into a personal ChatGPT account. This is not a hypothetical risk to manage next quarter: 66% of office professionals admit using AI tools at work even when they believed their employer did not permit it. The reflex response, a blanket ban, does not work. It simply pushes confidential data onto personal smartphones and unmonitored home networks. This article sets out the working alternative for a 20 to 200 person firm: a two-page AI acceptable use policy you can write this week, a sanctioned tool under company accounts, and a private gateway for the work that must stay inside your perimeter. With the numbers.

An effective AI acceptable use policy for employees sets clear data classification boundaries, specifies sanctioned corporate tools, and establishes a no-blame incident reporting path. Rather than attempting an outright ban, a workable policy gives staff approved, low-friction alternatives so confidential company and client data never enters public AI models. For a 20 to 200 person organisation, this means combining a two-page policy document with company-managed accounts and a self-hosted private gateway for sensitive workloads.

The urgency is driven by frontline behaviour. A PagerDuty survey published in June 2026 found that two-thirds (66%) of office professionals have used AI tools at work despite believing it was not permitted under company policy (PagerDuty). The same survey found 88% have shared work-related information with public AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini: 43% shared emails, 40% meeting notes, 34% customer data, and 31% financial information or confidential company documents.

If your instinct as a leader is to issue a strict ban or block AI domains at the perimeter firewall, the evidence suggests that the ban has already failed. Worse, it actively increases your exposure. When staff need to summarise twenty pages of meeting notes before a 2:00 PM executive call, they do not abandon the technology; they open ChatGPT on a personal smartphone, tether to a 5G hotspot, or forward the document to a personal webmail address.

Here is what actually works, what it costs, and how a 20 to 200 person organisation can put a working system in place within 30 days.

Why do employees ignore AI bans and leak company data?

The PagerDuty Shadow AI Survey was conducted by Wakefield Research among 1,250 office professionals in non-IT roles at organisations with annual revenue of USD 500 million or more, across the United States, United Kingdom, Australia and Japan (PagerDuty). While your organisation in the UAE or GCC is likely smaller, there is no evidence that staff behaviour differs when deadlines loom. The direction of travel is unambiguous.

Two operational figures matter most to technical and business leadership:

First, the volume of confidential material entering public models is accelerating rapidly. Figures compiled by Unio Digital from vendor security research put the share of corporate data entering AI tools that is sensitive at 34.8%, up from 10.7% two years earlier (Cyberhaven, 2025). The same review highlights that 77% of employees paste data directly into generative AI prompts, and 82% of those pastes originate from personal accounts rather than corporate workspaces (LayerX, 2025).

Second, the financial and operational cost when that exposure triggers a security incident is severe. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach 2026, as compiled in the Unio Digital review, found that security incidents involving shadow AI had more than doubled to 43% of organisations, averaging USD 5.39 million per incident (Unio Digital).

The lesson for a mid-market firm is not that you will necessarily face a USD 5.39 million breach bill; those samples skew towards multinational enterprises. The immediate takeaway is that shadow AI use is near-universal, it directly involves your most sensitive commercial material, and it is happening right now through unmanaged personal channels that your IT and security teams cannot audit.

Why do blanket AI bans fail in practice?

Blocking external AI domains at your office firewall feels decisive during an executive committee meeting. In practice, it creates a dangerous illusion of security.

Start with how your team actually works. Because 82% of corporate data pastes into generative AI tools originate from personal accounts (Unio Digital), the corporate network perimeter is largely irrelevant. Consumer ChatGPT accounts retain chat history by default and use prompt inputs to train and refine foundation models unless an individual user navigates deep into settings to opt out. A consumer account is not covered by your master service agreements, your non-disclosure agreements, or enterprise data protection commitments.

Furthermore, consumer account credentials represent an active secondary risk. Over 225,000 OpenAI credentials captured by infostealer malware were listed for sale on dark web illicit marketplaces in 2024 (Unio Digital). When an employee uses their personal account on an unmanaged personal device, any paste containing client confidential data sits inside an account that may already be compromised by infostealer malware. A firewall ban does not remove the data from these insecure environments. It simply removes your security team from the conversation, pushing usage to mobile browsers and home Wi-Fi networks where data loss prevention (DLP), conditional access, and audit logging cannot reach.

Bans also inflict direct damage on talent retention. In the PagerDuty study, 77% of office professionals stated that their employer's AI restrictions limit their professional growth, while 75% said they would be likely to look for a new role that offered better AI skills development (PagerDuty). Forcing high-performing analysts, software engineers, and project managers to work with one hand tied behind their backs creates resentment.

The practical alternative is not unconstrained permission. It is a three-part operating model: a concise, practical acceptable use policy, an approved commercial tool provisioned under company accounts, and a self-hosted private gateway for the sensitive workloads that cannot leave your perimeter.

How to write an AI acceptable use policy for employees

An AI acceptable use policy for employees should never be a 40-page legal dissertation. Lengthy governance manuals are rarely read, harder to remember, and virtually impossible for frontline managers to enforce. A policy that works must fit on two pages, present a clear mental model, establish a sanctioned path that is more convenient than personal workarounds, and provide a clear procedure for when someone makes a mistake.

The policy should centre on a strict three-tier classification model that tells staff exactly where different types of data may go:

  • Red (Restricted): Client personal data, Emirates ID numbers, bank details, unreleased financial projections, payroll files, intellectual property, and anything covered by an NDA. This tier must never be submitted to a hosted multitenant AI tool. It is routed exclusively to your internal private gateway.
  • Amber (Internal): Internal strategy memos, project roadmaps, non-sensitive source code, and business context that contains no personal identifiers or confidential financial metrics. Hosted commercial tools under corporate accounts are permitted only after redaction.
  • Green (Public): Public marketing collateral, standard boilerplate text, generic coding syntax queries, synthetic test data, and general brainstorming. Any sanctioned corporate tool is approved.

Below is a functional policy template. Customise the bracketed operational fields, keep the length under two pages, and issue it immediately:

ACME AI Acceptable Use Policy (v1.0, dated DD Month YYYY)

1. Purpose. This policy defines how we use artificial intelligence tools
   at work. Its goal is to enable productive, safe AI adoption, not to
   prohibit it.

2. Sanctioned tools. Staff may use AI exclusively via corporate accounts:
   - ChatGPT Business (under the ACME corporate workspace)
   - Microsoft Copilot Chat (authenticated with your corporate Entra ID account)
   - The ACME Internal AI Gateway at https://ai.internal for Red and Amber data
   Using personal accounts, consumer logins, or unapproved third-party AI
   extensions for company work is strictly prohibited.

3. Data classification rules. Before submitting information, classify it:
   RED: Client PII, national identity numbers, financial records, HR files,
   unreleased company metrics, NDA-governed material. Gateway only.
   AMBER: Internal memos, architectures, source code. Sanctioned hosted
   tools permitted ONLY after redacting identifiers.
   GREEN: Public content, generic drafting, open syntax questions.
   Sanctioned tools permitted freely.

4. Redaction protocol. When preparing Amber content for hosted tools:
   replace client and employee names with placeholders such as [Client A];
   strip account numbers, phone numbers, and addresses; retain only the
   abstract structure required to complete the task.

5. Human accountability. You remain personally responsible for deliverables.
   Verify all facts, calculations, statutory citations, and code outputs
   before sharing with clients or deploying to production.

6. Transparency. Inform clients or counterparties when AI has generated a
   substantial part of a deliverable whenever contracts or regulations require it.

7. No-blame incident reporting. If you inadvertently paste Red data into an
   unapproved or hosted tool, notify [Head of IT] within 24 hours. Prompt
   reporting carries no disciplinary sanction. Concealing a known data leak
   is a disciplinary offence.

8. Governance. This policy is reviewed quarterly by [Head of IT].

Two operational principles ensure this policy succeeds:

First, your sanctioned path must deliver superior performance: low-latency models, generous usage caps, and zero friction. If the internal gateway is slow or difficult to access, staff will revert to consumer accounts.

Second, enforce network boundaries pragmatically. Block consumer AI login pages on managed laptops via your secure web gateway or endpoint management profile. Configure endpoint DLP rules to detect patterns like UAE Emirates ID numbers (784-XXXX-XXXXXXX-X) and international bank account numbers (IBANs) in browser clipboard events. You cannot control personal mobile devices directly, but you can remove friction from the corporate path and maintain an auditable record of compliance.

Which AI tools should your company policy sanction?

The fastest risk-reduction step an organisation can take is migrating employees from unmanaged personal accounts to a corporate workspace. The contractual and technical differences between consumer and enterprise tiers are fundamental.

OpenAI does not use data submitted to ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, or the OpenAI API to train its models by default (OpenAI enterprise privacy). Workspace administrators retain administrative oversight, user provisioning, and retention controls, with deleted conversations purged from OpenAI operational systems within 30 days. ChatGPT Business is priced at USD 25 per seat per month on monthly billing, or USD 20 per seat per month on annual billing, with an upgraded Premium seat at USD 125 monthly or USD 100 annually, specifically accommodating organisations sized from 2 to 200 seats (OpenAI Business pricing).

For organisations running on Microsoft 365, Microsoft Copilot Chat accessed via an Entra ID corporate account provides commercial data protection at no additional cost (Microsoft Learn). Prompts and responses do not cross the Microsoft 365 tenant boundary, are not inspected by humans, are not used to train foundation models, and inherit corporate audit logging and eDiscovery retention policies.

When developing custom internal tooling using the OpenAI API, inputs have not been used for model training by default since 1 March 2023 (OpenAI platform data controls). API operational logs are retained for abuse monitoring for up to 30 days, and organisations handling highly regulated workloads can apply for zero data retention (ZDR).

Route Direct cost Used for model training Governance and controls
Personal accounts (status quo) USD 0 direct Yes, by default unless opted out Zero administrative visibility; personal email logins
ChatGPT Business USD 25/seat monthly; USD 20/seat annual No, by default Central admin console, SSO, seat lifecycle, 30-day purge
Microsoft Copilot Chat (work account) Included with Entra ID corporate plans No, protected M365 tenant boundary, corporate audit logs, eDiscovery
OpenAI API (custom applications) Usage-based token pricing No, default policy since March 2023 30-day abuse monitoring logs; zero retention on approval
Private self-hosted gateway GPU compute leasing Never, runs isolated weights Complete data residency, raw prompt audit logs, local weights

A critical constraint for GCC organisations to evaluate: major providers such as OpenAI do not offer an in-country UAE data processing boundary for these software-as-a-service plans. For standard drafting and day-to-day administrative tasks, this trade-off is often acceptable when paired with strict Amber redaction rules. However, for sensitive client files, national identity data, and regulated records, cross-border data transfer without explicit legal grounds introduces significant compliance exposure.

When is a private AI gateway worth paying for?

Consider a typical GCC operational structure: an 80-person professional services consultancy in Dubai operating on Microsoft 365. The organisation comprises advisory, marketing, and client delivery teams. Approximately 25 staff members routinely handle Red or Amber material: financial models, audit schedules, M&A due diligence files, and human resources records. The remaining 55 staff members conduct general analysis, drafting, and research.

A private gateway consists of dedicated GPU hardware running open-weight inference models behind a unified reverse proxy. The proxy handles user authentication, per-department token allowances, and immutable local logging. Your staff interact with standard web interfaces or internal scripts, but the inference processes execute on private hardware hosted within a local data centre. Prompts and responses remain strictly within your controlled perimeter.

We deploy and manage these environments for clients within our AI infrastructure service, placing FastLLM Proxy in front of model instances. FastLLM Proxy acts as an OpenAI-compatible gateway that centralises request routing, enforces department quotas, and manages access controls across private GPU instances and external hosted endpoints.

Three triggers indicate that your organisation requires a private gateway:

  1. Data residency mandates: Client agreements, public sector contracts, or regional data protection statutes requiring that personal and financial information never leave the UAE.
  2. High volume of confidential data: When sensitive workflows are executed daily, human redaction discipline inevitably slips under pressure. Technical segregation prevents leaks by design.
  3. Regulatory auditability: Regulated entities in financial services, legal, and healthcare sectors must produce verifiable audit trails detailing who issued each prompt, what model generated the response, and where the compute was located.

To evaluate the operational expenditure, consider indicative pricing from GPU providers. Using Hyperstack published rates as an industry benchmark:

  • NVIDIA L40 (48 GB VRAM): USD 1.00 per hour on demand, translating to approximately USD 730 per month running 24/7 (roughly AED 2,700). An L40 runs OpenAI's open-weight gpt-oss-20b model (requiring approximately 16 GB VRAM) or high-performance 32B parameter models in 4-bit quantisation with ample headroom.
  • NVIDIA H100 (80 GB VRAM): USD 2.50 per hour on demand, amounting to roughly USD 1,825 per month (approximately AED 6,700), or from USD 1.75 per hour on reserved terms (roughly USD 1,280 per month). OpenAI's deployment guidelines show that gpt-oss-120b requires approximately 60 GB of VRAM, running on a single H100 instance (OpenAI cookbook).

The production inference layer is powered by vLLM, an open-source, Apache 2.0 licensed serving engine featuring continuous batching, PagedAttention memory management, and an OpenAI-compatible API structure supporting hundreds of model architectures.

The service commands for standard open-weight architectures illustrate the operational simplicity:

# Launch gpt-oss-120b on a single 80 GB GPU instance (requires ~60 GB VRAM)
vllm serve openai/gpt-oss-120b --max-model-len 32768

# Launch gpt-oss-20b on an L40 instance (requires ~16 GB VRAM)
vllm serve openai/gpt-oss-20b --max-model-len 32768

Internal developers and chat user interfaces connect to the gateway by modifying the base URL in the standard OpenAI client:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

For a total monthly budget between USD 1,830 and USD 2,925, the firm eliminates shadow AI, provides high-speed tooling for general staff, and guarantees that sensitive client data never leaves an audited, local GPU instance. Compared against the IBM benchmark cost of USD 5.39 million per shadow AI incident (Unio Digital), the business case is clear.

How do you roll out an AI policy in 30 days?

Deploying this framework across a mid-sized organisation requires an orderly progression over four weeks:

Week 1: Policy sign-off and baseline tooling

Finalise your organisation's two-page acceptable use policy using the template provided. Secure executive sign-off from legal, operations, and IT leadership. Procure an initial pool of five to ten ChatGPT Business seats or confirm Microsoft Copilot commercial protections in your Entra ID tenant. Implement standard web filtering rules blocking consumer generative AI sign-up pages on managed endpoints, and configure endpoint DLP to alert when UAE Emirates ID numbers or IBAN strings appear in web paste events.

Week 2: Private gateway staging and integration

Spin up your dedicated GPU instance. Deploy vLLM with your chosen open-weight model weights and configure the reverse proxy layer. Configure departmental API keys with strict monthly token quotas, log retention policies, and rate limits. Onboard the 25 staff members handling sensitive workflows to test latency, prompt responsiveness, and usability.

Week 3: Departmental practical training

Policy adoption fails when training is limited to mass email announcements. Conduct one-hour interactive sessions with each department. Review real-world emails and documents from their daily workflow, demonstrating how to categorise items into Red, Amber, and Green. Teach practical redaction techniques, verify that users can access their sanctioned accounts, and reiterate the non-punitive incident reporting policy.

Week 4: Production cutover and exception management

Decommission ad-hoc developer access and unapproved API trial accounts. Move the remaining corporate staff onto their sanctioned commercial accounts. Publish the official directory of approved AI tools on the intranet alongside the two-page policy, and schedule the first quarterly governance review. The audit logs generated by your gateway and administrative consoles now form your operational compliance baseline.

UAE AI compliance: what does the PDPL require by 2027?

For organisations operating in the United Arab Emirates, establishing AI governance is no longer just a cybersecurity best practice; it is an immediate statutory requirement.

Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data (PDPL) requires full compliance by 1 January 2027 (WCR Legal). The UAE PDPL is a consent-first framework. Unlike the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the UAE federal statute does not recognise "legitimate interests" as a lawful basis for processing personal information.

Relying on informal assumptions while employees feed client or employee data into public machine learning systems exposes the organisation directly to statutory sanctions. Administrative fines under the PDPL reach up to AED 5 million (approximately USD 1.36 million) for severe violations, and regulatory compliance guidance explicitly instructs organisations processing UAE personal data at scale to maintain documented AI usage policies covering approved tools and permitted use cases (WCR Legal).

In financial free zones, strict supervision is already in effect:

  • DIFC: DIFC Data Protection Regulation 10 has been active since January 2026, establishing mandatory requirements for AI impact assessments, transparency disclosures, and rigorous record-keeping for high-risk data processing, backed by statutory fines between USD 25,000 and USD 50,000 per violation (WCR Legal).
  • ADGM: The Data Protection Regulations 2021 (DPR 2021) closely mirror international standards, requiring strict technical safeguards, documented transfer mechanisms, and verifiable audit trails for automated processing.

A practical corporate posture recognises that the two-page acceptable use policy, commercial workspaces, and a private inference gateway are not separate initiatives. Together, they constitute the exact compliance package an auditor or regulatory authority will examine: a defined policy, sanctioned tooling, boundary protections against unauthorised processing, and verifiable logs demonstrating where data was processed.

What should your organisation do next?

Take these operational steps immediately:

  1. This week: Adapt the acceptable use template to your organisation's reporting lines and get it approved. Enable commercial data protection in your Microsoft 365 environment or purchase a starter tier of ChatGPT Business seats. Review your standard client engagement contracts to identify existing data processing restrictions.
  2. This month: Evaluate your sensitive data exposure.
