title: Dusting the Phantom: Gaussian Allocation for Fading Dynamic Content
description:
arXiv:2610.21302v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dynamic Gaussian representations have made high-quality, real-time volumetric video increasingly practical, yet challenging motion can still break their reconstruction: small fast-moving objects may disappear, and fine textures in highly dynamic regions are often lost. In particular, simply training longer or using more Gaussians may still fail to recover small, fast-moving objects. We argue that the key bottleneck is not representational capacity itself, but where and when Gaussian primitives are allocated. Existing allocation strategies rely on current Gaussian locations and often overlook the spatiotemporal destinations of relocated Gaussians. To address these limitations, we introduce two complementary strategies. First, Seed Injection identifies under-reconstructed dynamic regions using temporal appearance changes and reconstruction errors, and initializes new Gaussians at geometrically plausible 3D locations through multi-view observations, independent of existing Gaussian locations. Second, Temporal Biased Relocation uses time-resolved optimization signals to guide the spatiotemporal placement of relocated Gaussians. Both strategies maintain a fixed Gaussian budget without modifying the underlying representation. Experiments across multiple dynamic-scene datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction quality, particularly in highly dynamic regions, recovering small, rapidly moving objects and fine-grained appearance details.

title: Sign Betting for Misspecified Regression: Variance Adaptivity and Optimal Approximation
description:
arXiv:2610.20903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study bounded regression under model misspecification, evaluating a function $f$ by its $L_1(P_X)$ distance to the conditional mean $\eta(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$, rather than the standard $L_2(P_X)$. This $L_1$ metric is natural for downstream decision problems such as bandits and reinforcement learning. We analyze the min--max estimator of Baraud & Maillard (2025), which we call \emph{sign-betting regression}. Our main results show that sign-betting regression achieves high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequalities under misspecification. Under realizability, our bound adapts to the average conditional variance and recovers the variance-adaptive rate of Li et al. (2026). We further characterize the optimal universal approximation factor for proper learning by showing that sign betting achieves factor 3, while no proper learner can satisfy a distribution-free, high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequality with a universal approximation factor strictly below 3. We extend the upper-bound analysis beyond finite classes and complement the theory with experiments in synthetic and real-world model-selection tasks.

title: I Built G-Buudddyy : Bringing AI-Powered Experiences Beyond the Screen
description:
AI Garden Buddy

Less scrolling. More growing.

AI Garden Buddy is a local-first gardening assistant that uses AI to help people start gardening. It recommends suitable plants, generates a personalized seven-day gardening plan, and suggests one small outdoor task to complete each day.

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass.

Live Demo

Live Application: https://hacktoberfest-tawny.vercel.app/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/yogesh968/hacktoberfest

Note: AI plan generation requires the FastAPI backend and Ollama. The deployed frontend needs a reachable backend to generate plans for online users.

Features

  • Personalized Plant Recommendations: Suggests plants based on city, garden type, sunlight, and gardening experience.
  • Seven-Day Gardening Plan: Generates a practical daily schedule based on available time.
  • Daily Outdoor Tasks: Provides actionable gardening activities with instructions and estimated completion times.
  • Progress Tracking: Allows users to mark tasks as complete and record reflections in their browser.
  • Safety Notes: Highlights considerations such as plant toxicity, heat exposure, heavy pots, and tools.
  • Uncertainty Notes: Explains limitations, including the lack of live weather and frost-date information.
  • Local AI Inference: Runs a Gemma model locally through Ollama.
  • Structured Output Validation: Uses JSON Schema and Pydantic to validate AI-generated plans.
  • Reliable Error Handling: Reports model failures instead of presenting fabricated AI-generated plans.

Tech Stack

Frontend

  • React 18
  • Vite 6
  • Tailwind CSS v4
  • lucide-react
  • Fontsource

Backend

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Pydantic v2
  • Uvicorn
  • httpx
  • pydantic-settings

AI and Testing

  • Google Gemma
  • Ollama
  • JSON Schema
  • pytest
  • ESLint

How It Works

  1. The user enters their city, garden type, sunlight conditions, experience level, and available daily time.
  2. The React frontend sends the information to the FastAPI backend.
  3. The backend sends a prompt and JSON Schema to a Gemma model through Ollama.
  4. Pydantic validates the generated response.
  5. The frontend displays the gardening plan, plant recommendations, safety notes, and daily task.
  6. The user completes the outdoor task, marks it as done, and records a reflection.

Architecture 

React + Vite Frontend
        |
        v
FastAPI Backend
        |
        v
Ollama Inference Runtime
        |
        v
Gemma AI Model
        |
        v
Validated Gardening Plan
        |
        v
Outdoor Task and Progress Tracking

Getting Started

Prerequisites

  • Python 3.10 or later
  • Node.js and npm
  • Ollama
  • Sufficient memory and disk space for your selected AI model

1. Clone the Repository 

git clone https://github.com/yogesh968/hacktoberfest.git
cd hacktoberfest

2. Download the AI Model

Install Ollama and run:

ollama pull gemma3:4b

Alternatively, use the smaller model:

ollama pull gemma3:1b

3. Set Up the Backend 

cd backend
python -m venv .venv

Activate the environment.

Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

macOS/Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Copy the example environment file:

# Windows
copy .env.example .env

# macOS/Linux
cp .env.example .env

4. Set Up the Frontend

Open another terminal from the repository root:

cd frontend
npm install

Copy the frontend environment file:

# Windows
copy .env.example .env

# macOS/Linux
cp .env.example .env

For local development, configure the backend URL:

VITE_API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000

5. Run the Application

Start Ollama if it is not already running:

ollama serve

Start the backend from the backend directory:

uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000

Start the frontend from the frontend directory:

npm run dev

Open the application:

  • Frontend: http://localhost:5173
  • Backend API Documentation: http://localhost:8000/docs

Make sure the model configured in the backend has been downloaded.

API Overview

GET /api/health

Checks backend health and model connectivity.

POST /api/garden-plan

Generates a personalized gardening plan.

Example request:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/garden-plan \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"city":"Pune","garden_type":"balcony","sunlight":"partial_sun","experience":"beginner","minutes_per_day":15}'

Use the exact request fields and accepted values defined by the backend's Pydantic model.

Reliability and Error Handling

The backend uses multiple validation layers to improve reliability:

  • Ollama structured outputs constrain the response using JSON Schema.
  • Pydantic validates the generated response.
  • Additional checks enforce application-specific requirements, including seven days and between two and six plant recommendations.
  • Invalid output triggers one retry.
  • If validation still fails, the backend returns a clear error.

When AI generation is unavailable, the application can display general gardening advice labelled "Not AI-generated" instead of pretending it came from the model.

Testing

The backend includes 13 automated API tests using pytest.

The tests use a fake HTTP transport instead of Ollama, allowing API behavior and failure scenarios to be tested without running an actual model.

Coverage includes:

  • Valid plans
  • Malformed model output and retry behavior
  • Ollama being unavailable
  • Missing models
  • Request timeouts
  • Invalid form input

Run the backend tests:

python -m pytest -q

Run frontend checks from the frontend directory:

npm run lint
npm run build

Privacy

With the default local configuration:

  • User inputs are sent to the local FastAPI backend and Ollama service.
  • The backend does not log the city or other form inputs.
  • Task completion and reflections are stored in the browser.
  • Local AI inference does not require a hosted AI API key.

These privacy statements apply to the local configuration. A remote backend or cloud model may process data outside the user's computer.

Limitations

  • The application does not automatically retrieve live weather or frost-date information.
  • Plant recommendations may not account for every local growing condition.
  • Smaller AI models may occasionally generate invalid or imperfect responses.
  • Generation speed depends on the user's hardware.
  • Users should verify plant toxicity and local growing advice, especially around children and pets.

Model Licensing

Gemma models have their own licensing terms. Gemma 3 is distributed under Google's Gemma Terms of Use, which differ from an OSI-approved open-source license.

Check the applicable terms for the specific model version you use. The application's code license and the AI model's license are separate.

Contributing

Contributions and suggestions are welcome.

  1. Fork the repository.
  2. Create a branch for your changes.
  3. Implement your changes and add tests where appropriate.
  4. Run the relevant tests and code-quality checks.
  5. Submit a pull request describing your changes.

Please do not commit secrets, environment files, or other sensitive information.

Future Improvements

  • Integration with verified weather and climate information
  • Multilingual gardening assistance
  • Plant images with appropriate attribution
  • Saved gardening plans and streaks
  • Improved regional plant recommendations
  • Simplified local setup using Docker Compose

Acknowledgements

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass.

AI Garden Buddy explores how locally run AI can help people move from browsing and learning to taking meaningful action in the real world.

Less scrolling. More growing.

title: Understanding Parameters and EventCallbacks in Blazor
description:
Understanding Parameters and EventCallbacks in Blazor

In Blazor, a component can receive information from its parent through parameters. Parameters are declared with the [Parameter] attribute, allowing a parent component to provide values such as text, numbers, dates, or Boolean values.

Blazor also supports EventCallback, which lets a child component notify its parent when a user performs an action. For example, a child can raise a callback after a button is clicked, while the parent decides what should happen next. This keeps reusable components focused on displaying information and reporting user actions.

The following two Razor components are provided separately. The code blocks are kept together without explanatory text between them.

@page "/parameters-demo"

<h3>Parent Component</h3>

<p>Message received: @receivedMessage</p>

<ChildComponent Name="Ayush"
                OnMessageSent="HandleMessage" />

@code {
    private string receivedMessage = "No message received yet.";

    private void HandleMessage(string message)
    {
        receivedMessage = message;
    }
}

// GymCard.razor    
<div class="card gym-card h-100 shadow-sm">
    <div class="card-body d-flex flex-column">
        <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-start gap-2 mb-3">
            <h5 class="fw-bold mb-0">@GymName</h5>
            <span class="badge @(Status == "Active" ? "bg-success" : "bg-secondary")">
                @Status
            </span>
        </div>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-geo-alt me-2"></i>@Address, @CityName
        </p>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-telephone me-2"></i>@Phone
        </p>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-envelope me-2"></i>@Email
        </p>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-clock me-2"></i>
            @OpeningTime.ToString(@"hh\:mm") - @ClosingTime.ToString(@"hh\:mm")
        </p>

        <p class="gym-detail">
            <i class="bi bi-people me-2"></i>
            Class capacity: @TotalClassCapacity
        </p>

        <div class="d-flex flex-wrap gap-2 mb-3">
            <span class="facility-badge">
                Locker: @(LockerFacility ? "Yes" : "No")
            </span>
            <span class="facility-badge">
                Parking: @(ParkingAvailable ? "Yes" : "No")
            </span>
        </div>

        <div class="d-flex gap-2 mt-auto">
            <button type="button"
                    class="btn btn-outline-primary btn-sm flex-fill"
                    @onclick="EditGym">
                <i class="bi bi-pencil me-1"></i>Edit
            </button>

            <button type="button"
                    class="btn btn-outline-danger btn-sm flex-fill"
                    @onclick="DeleteGym">
                <i class="bi bi-trash me-1"></i>Delete
            </button>
        </div>
    </div>
</div>

@code {
    [Parameter] public Guid Id { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public string GymName { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    [Parameter] public string Address { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    [Parameter] public string CityName { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    [Parameter] public string Phone { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    [Parameter] public string Email { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    [Parameter] public TimeSpan OpeningTime { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public TimeSpan ClosingTime { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public int TotalClassCapacity { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public bool LockerFacility { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public bool ParkingAvailable { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public string Status { get; set; } = "Active";

    [Parameter] public EventCallback<Guid> OnEdit { get; set; }
    [Parameter] public EventCallback<Guid> OnDelete { get; set; }

    private Task EditGym() => OnEdit.InvokeAsync(Id);
    private Task DeleteGym() => OnDelete.InvokeAsync(Id);
}


=========================================================================================

@page "/admin/gyms"
@attribute [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]

@using System.Net.Http.Json
@using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations
@using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms
@using GymManagement.Client.Components.Admin

@inject HttpClient Http
@inject IJSRuntime JS

<PageTitle>Manage Gyms</PageTitle>

<div class="container-fluid py-4">
    <div class="d-flex flex-wrap justify-content-between align-items-center gap-3 mb-4">
        <div>
            <h2 class="fw-bold mb-1">Manage Gyms</h2>
            <p class="text-secondary mb-0">Add, update, search, and manage gyms.</p>
        </div>

        <button class="btn btn-primary" @onclick="OpenAddForm">
            <i class="bi bi-plus-circle me-1"></i>Add Gym
        </button>
    </div>

    <div class="card shadow-sm border-0 mb-4">
        <div class="card-body">
            <div class="row g-3">
                <div class="col-12 col-md-8">
                    <label class="form-label">Search gyms</label>
                    <input class="form-control"
                           @bind="searchText"
                           @bind:event="oninput"
                           placeholder="Search name, city, phone, or email..." />
                </div>

                <div class="col-12 col-md-4">
                    <label class="form-label">Sort by</label>
                    <select class="form-select" @bind="sortBy">
                        <option value="name">Gym name</option>
                        <option value="city">City</option>
                        <option value="status">Status</option>
                    </select>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>
    </div>

    @if (isLoading)
    {
        <div class="text-center py-5">
            <div class="spinner-border text-primary"></div>
            <p class="text-secondary mt-2">Loading gyms...</p>
        </div>
    }
    else if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(errorMessage))
    {
        <div class="alert alert-danger">
            @errorMessage
            <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger ms-2"
                    @onclick="LoadGymsAsync">Retry</button>
        </div>
    }
    else if (FilteredGyms.Count == 0)
    {
        <div class="alert alert-info">No matching gyms found.</div>
    }
    else
    {
        <div class="row g-4">
            @foreach (var gym in FilteredGyms)
            {
                <div class="col-12 col-md-6 col-xl-4" @key="gym.Id">
                    <GymCard Id="@gym.Id"
                             GymName="@gym.GymName"
                             Address="@gym.Address"
                             CityName="@gym.CityName"
                             Phone="@gym.Phone"
                             Email="@gym.Email"
                             OpeningTime="@gym.OpeningTime"
                             ClosingTime="@gym.ClosingTime"
                             TotalClassCapacity="@gym.TotalClassCapacity"
                             LockerFacility="@gym.LockerFacility"
                             ParkingAvailable="@gym.ParkingAvailable"
                             Status="@gym.Status"
                             OnEdit="OpenEditForm"
                             OnDelete="DeleteGymAsync" />
                </div>
            }
        </div>
    }
</div>

@if (showForm)
{
    <div class="modal-backdrop-custom">
        <div class="card modal-card shadow-lg">
            <div class="card-header bg-white d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center">
                <h5 class="mb-0">@(isEditMode ? "Edit Gym" : "Add Gym")</h5>
                <button class="btn-close" @onclick="CloseForm"></button>
            </div>

            <div class="card-body">
                <EditForm Model="@formModel" OnValidSubmit="SaveGymAsync">
                    <DataAnnotationsValidator />
                    <ValidationSummary />

                    <div class="row g-3">
                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Gym name</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.GymName" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.GymName)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">City</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.CityName" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.CityName)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-12">
                            <label class="form-label">Address</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.Address" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.Address)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Phone</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.Phone" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.Phone)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Email</label>
                            <InputText class="form-control" @bind-Value="formModel.Email" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.Email)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Opening time</label>
                            <InputText type="time" class="form-control"
                                       @bind-Value="formModel.OpeningTime" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Closing time</label>
                            <InputText type="time" class="form-control"
                                       @bind-Value="formModel.ClosingTime" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Total class capacity</label>
                            <InputNumber class="form-control"
                                         @bind-Value="formModel.TotalClassCapacity" />
                            <ValidationMessage For="@(() => formModel.TotalClassCapacity)" />
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6">
                            <label class="form-label">Status</label>
                            <InputSelect class="form-select" @bind-Value="formModel.Status">
                                <option value="Active">Active</option>
                                <option value="Inactive">Inactive</option>
                            </InputSelect>
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6 form-check ms-2">
                            <InputCheckbox class="form-check-input"
                                           @bind-Value="formModel.LockerFacility" />
                            <label class="form-check-label">Locker facility</label>
                        </div>

                        <div class="col-md-6 form-check ms-2">
                            <InputCheckbox class="form-check-input"
                                           @bind-Value="formModel.ParkingAvailable" />
                            <label class="form-check-label">Parking available</label>
                        </div>
                    </div>

                    <div class="d-flex justify-content-end gap-2 mt-4">
                        <button type="button" class="btn btn-outline-secondary"
                                @onclick="CloseForm" disabled="@isSaving">
                            Cancel
                        </button>
                        <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary" disabled="@isSaving">
                            @(isSaving ? "Saving..." : isEditMode ? "Update Gym" : "Save Gym")
                        </button>
                    </div>
                </EditForm>
            </div>
        </div>
    </div>
}

@code {

    }

    private List<GymCardModel> gyms = new();
    private GymFormModel formModel = new();
    private bool isLoading;
    private bool isSaving;
    private bool showForm;
    private bool isEditMode;
    private string searchText = "";
    private string sortBy = "name";
    private string errorMessage = "";

    private List<GymCardModel> FilteredGyms =>
        gyms.Where(g =>
                string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(searchText) ||
                g.GymName.Contains(searchText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                g.CityName.Contains(searchText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                g.Phone.Contains(searchText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                g.Email.Contains(searchText, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            .OrderBy(g => sortBy switch
            {
                "city" => g.CityName,
                "status" => g.Status,
                _ => g.GymName
            })
            .ToList();

    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync() => await LoadGymsAsync();

    private async Task LoadGymsAsync()
    {
        isLoading = true;
        errorMessage = "";

        try
        {
            var result = await Http.GetFromJsonAsync<List<GymCardModel>>("api/GymCenter");
            gyms = result ?? new();
        }
        catch
        {
            errorMessage = "Unable to load gyms. Check the API URL and connection.";
        }
        finally
        {
            isLoading = false;
        }
    }

    private void OpenAddForm()
    {
        formModel = new GymFormModel();
        isEditMode = false;
        showForm = true;
    }

    private void OpenEditForm(Guid id)
    {
        var gym = gyms.FirstOrDefault(g => g.Id == id);
        if (gym is null) return;

        formModel = new GymFormModel
        {
            Id = gym.Id,
            GymName = gym.GymName,
            Address = gym.Address,
            CityName = gym.CityName,
            Phone = gym.Phone,
            Email = gym.Email,
            OpeningTime = gym.OpeningTime.ToString(@"hh\:mm"),
            ClosingTime = gym.ClosingTime.ToString(@"hh\:mm"),
            TotalClassCapacity = gym.TotalClassCapacity,
            LockerFacility = gym.LockerFacility,
            ParkingAvailable = gym.ParkingAvailable,
            Status = gym.Status
        };

        isEditMode = true;
        showForm = true;
    }

    private async Task SaveGymAsync()
    {
        if (!TimeSpan.TryParse(formModel.OpeningTime, out var opening) ||
            !TimeSpan.TryParse(formModel.ClosingTime, out var closing) ||
            closing <= opening)
        {
            await ShowMessageAsync("Invalid hours",
                "Closing time must be later than opening time.", false);
            return;
        }

        isSaving = true;

        try
        {
            var payload = new
            {
                formModel.Id,
                formModel.GymName,
                formModel.Address,
                formModel.CityName,
                formModel.Phone,
                formModel.Email,
                OpeningTime = opening,
                ClosingTime = closing,
                formModel.TotalClassCapacity,
                formModel.LockerFacility,
                formModel.ParkingAvailable,
                formModel.Status
            };

            HttpResponseMessage response = isEditMode
                ? await Http.PutAsJsonAsync($"api/GymCenter/{formModel.Id}", payload)
                : await Http.PostAsJsonAsync("api/GymCenter", payload);

            var result = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<OperationResponse>();

            if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode || result?.Success != true)
            {
                await ShowMessageAsync("Unable to save gym",
                    result?.Message ?? "The API could not save the gym.", false);
                return;
            }

            showForm = false;
            await LoadGymsAsync();
            await ShowMessageAsync("Success", result.Message, true);
        }
        catch
        {
            await ShowMessageAsync("Error", "An error occurred while saving the gym.", false);
        }
        finally
        {
            isSaving = false;
        }
    }

    private async Task DeleteGymAsync(Guid id)
    {
        var confirmed = await JS.InvokeAsync<bool>(
            "gymUi.confirmDelete", "Delete gym?", "The gym will be soft-deleted if allowed.");

        if (!confirmed) return;

        try
        {
            var response = await Http.DeleteAsync($"api/GymCenter/{id}");
            var result = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<OperationResponse>();

            if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode || result?.Success != true)
            {
                await ShowMessageAsync("Unable to delete",
                    result?.Message ?? "The gym could not be deleted.", false);
                return;
            }

            await LoadGymsAsync();
            await ShowMessageAsync("Success", result.Message, true);
        }
        catch
        {
            await ShowMessageAsync("Error", "An error occurred while deleting the gym.", false);
        }
    }

    private void CloseForm()
    {
        if (!isSaving) showForm = false;
    }

    private Task ShowMessageAsync(string title, string message, bool success) =>
        JS.InvokeVoidAsync("gymUi.showMessage", title, message, success).AsTask();
}

        if (response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
        {

            var token = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<TokenResponse>();

title: ToolBottleneckBench: Measuring Tool-Agent Performance under Controlled Pressures and Fixed Harness Budgets
description:
arXiv:2610.21098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The success score of a tool agent reflects both its model and the budgets of the harness that runs it. We present ToolBottleneckBench, a benchmark that measures tool-agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets. Synthetic enterprise tasks stay fixed while one pressure varies: the registered tool catalog, the visible tool menu, the certified workflow, or the encoding of returned records. An exact grader records the first unmet obligation of each failed episode and the harness limit, if any, that ended it. Across 21 model and harness configurations, the visible menu is the only one of the three pressures that act on the model with a large penalty, and this penalty tracks truncation at the completion cap. Raising the cap sixteenfold removes most of the penalty in the truncation-heavy configurations. Most failures end at a harness limit, and the failure record identifies the assigned pressure no more reliably than a count of tool calls. The repairs that help change which tools reach the model or who issues the calls, and only two repairs, neither improving model behavior, beat every configuration switch. We recommend reporting pressure effects with the harness budgets under which they were measured. We release the benchmark at https://github.com/zichuanxu/tool-bottleneck-bench.

title: Jev-as-a-Judge for RAG Claim Verification: Confidence-Gated Cascading Between a Non-Generative Verifier and a Frontier LLM
description:
arXiv:2610.20634v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation asks one question at volume: does this evidence support this claim? The answer is one bit, yet most pipelines obtain it from a text generator and pay generation prices for the prose wrapped around it. We compare a non-generative decision model, which returns a typed value from a declared enumeration together with a native probability and no text, against a frontier LLM configured as an engineer would deploy it for binary classification. Both answer the same 495 human-labelled claims from LLM-AggreFact, so every comparison is within-item. We report three things. First, the two systems are statistically indistinguishable on the metric this task is conventionally scored by, a paired difference of -0.56 points, Jev minus Astra, at a 187-fold cost difference. Second, that tie carries almost no information about deployment: the systems disagree on 15.2% of claims, and the cheaper one admits 23.2% of the claims annotators marked unsupported against the frontier model's 14.1%. A component whose job is to catch unsupported claims should be judged on that rate, and the conventional headline hides it. Third, because the errors differ they compose: routing the claims the cheap model is confident about and escalating the rest reaches 74.10 at USD 2.92 per thousand claims against 73.83 at USD 8.93, with the threshold chosen out of fold. But a matched random-escalation control at in-sample thresholds, spending the same budget by coin flip, does as well, so what buys the saving is the escalation share and not the probability that picks what to escalate. Measured against the cheap model it is built from, the cascade costs 61-fold more for 0.83 points, 95% CI [-3.36, 4.86], and it is the more permissive guard of the two. Equal accuracy conceals unequal errors. All predictions, prompts, pricing and code are released.

title: AI Governance That Does Not Slow You Down: The Minimum Operating Model for UAE Enterprises
description:
Most UAE organisations run AI in production without a named owner, a clear intake route, or proof of why models access sensitive data. A 40-page policy will not fix this. Four small, load-bearing artefacts will, giving technical leaders provable governance that aligns directly with ISO/IEC 42001 and the UAE AI Charter.

Most UAE organisations now run artificial intelligence in production in some form: a customer service assistant on the web portal, a document summarisation pipeline in legal, or a coding assistant deployed across engineering teams. Yet when asked three basic questions that a board, an enterprise client or an auditor will pose, most technology leaders cannot answer with verifiable proof. Who is the named individual accountable for this system? Why is this specific model permitted to process this specific dataset? Where is the immutable audit log confirming that policy was enforced?

The typical response to this uncertainty is to commission a 40-page AI governance policy, assemble a committee, and consider appointing a Chief AI Officer. For most enterprises in the UAE and wider GCC, both instincts are counterproductive. A dense policy document that developers and product owners do not read does not mitigate operational risk. When a failure occurs, an ignored policy serves only as documented negligence.

What engineering leaders and risk officers actually need is a lightweight, enforceable operating model. You can establish provable AI governance in about six weeks using four load-bearing artefacts: a one-page use-case intake form with an objective risk scoring table, a named accountable owner per system paired with a 45-minute monthly review, an architectural enforcement layer that intercepts model traffic, and a live model and agent register.

This operating model satisfies the governance expectations of regional regulators and international counterparties. By designing these four artefacts intentionally, the exact same document set maps directly to clauses 4 through 10 of ISO/IEC 42001 and the core principles of the UAE AI Charter.

The gap is operating roles, not appetite

The narrative that regional organisations are hesitant to adopt AI is contradicted by industry data. A global study by the Dubai Future Foundation and IBM found that roughly 20% of UAE organisations have AI governance platforms in place, compared with 12% globally, alongside strong regional leadership across core AI adoption metrics. Executive research cited by CDO Magazine indicates that 100% of GCC chief executive officers are either investing in AI today or plan to invest within twelve months.

The regional market does not suffer from a lack of tooling or ambition. The breakdown occurs in operational execution: enterprise platforms are acquired, but everyday accountability remains unassigned. Teams deploy workloads using shared API credentials, use cases bypass formal intake, and nobody can produce a definitive list of models operating across internal environments.

This gap becomes urgent when external scrutiny arrives. Enterprise clients in banking, government and healthcare are embedding detailed AI assurance questionnaires into procurement tenders, demanding proof of human oversight and data residency before signing contracts.

Simultaneously, the regulatory posture across the Gulf is maturing. The UAE Charter for the Development and Use of AI establishes 12 core principles, prioritising human oversight, accountability, data privacy and transparency. Regulatory analysis by Latham & Watkins highlights that UAE authorities are systematically moving from voluntary, principles-based frameworks toward binding expectations in critical sectors, with public services and regulated industries leading the transition.

Voluntary guidelines do not withstand commercial procurement or compliance audits. Building an agile operating model now prevents governance from becoming an expensive, disruptive crisis later.

The four artefacts at a glance

Enterprise governance must not become an administrative bottleneck. The framework below replaces slow committee approvals and unverified rules with four concrete artefacts:

Artefact Structural format Creation effort Operational replacement
1. Intake form and tier table One-page document: scope, data classification, autonomy level, blast radius, risk tier Half a day to draft Ad-hoc approvals in messaging channels that cannot be audited
2. Named owner and monthly review Single accountable person per system, 45-minute monthly cadence with fixed agenda 1 hour per month Multi-departmental committees that meet twice yearly
3. Enforcement layer Model gateway with team-scoped access tokens, token quotas, and structured logging 2 to 4 days of infrastructure setup Unenforced acceptable use policies buried in employee handbooks
4. Model and agent register Tabular register: unique ID, owner, data categories, assigned tier, next review date 1 day to populate Tribal knowledge that disappears when a lead developer resigns

These four artefacts require approximately one working week of collective effort to establish. If an external consultancy proposes a six-month governance design phase before implementing basic intake and technical controls, they are delivering administrative overhead rather than operational resilience.

Artefact 1: the one-page intake form with a stop/go tier table

Every AI deployment, including shadow tools already running in engineering or marketing teams, must pass through an intake form. This document must remain strictly one page, take under ten minutes to complete, and capture six mandatory fields:

  1. System function: a concise summary of what the system does, written in plain business English.
  2. Data categories touched: explicit classification of input data (for example: public information, internal operations, personally identifiable data, electronic medical records, or payment card details).
  3. Decision autonomy: the precise level of human intervention required before an output triggers an action.
  4. Blast radius: the tangible downside if the system produces hallucinations, biased output, or erroneous decisions.
  5. System owner: the named individual accountable for ongoing operation and maintenance.
  6. Calculated risk tier: derived deterministically from the scoring rubric below.

To prevent subjective disputes over whether a use case is dangerous, use an objective scoring formula. Evaluate three dimensions on a 1 to 3 scale: Data Sensitivity, System Autonomy, and Blast Radius.

Assigned points Data sensitivity System autonomy Blast radius
1 point Public data or synthetic datasets Advisory output only: a human reviews and manually acts on every output Internal operational impact: errors are immediately reversible with zero external visibility
2 points Internal confidential data: non-personal commercial documentation Supervised execution: the system drafts an action that executes upon one-click human approval Customer-facing impact: errors reach clients or partners but remain technically recoverable
3 points Personal data, sensitive health records, or regulated financial data Autonomous execution: the system takes direct action via APIs without prior human sign-off Irreversible harm: direct financial loss, regulatory breach, or severe safety impact

Sum the scores across all three dimensions to assign the operational tier:

Total score Classification Authorisation route Operational turnaround
3 to 4 points Tier 1: Green Named system owner approves; entry is recorded in the register Within 48 hours
5 to 7 points Tier 2: Amber Evaluation at the next monthly review; operational conditions assigned Up to 30 days
8 to 9 points Tier 3: Red Deployment prohibited until technical controls are verified and executive sponsor signs off Strict freeze until controls exist

Worked deployment scenarios

Consider a private healthcare operator in Dubai seeking to deploy an LLM assistant to draft responses to incoming patient inquiries in its contact centre.

  • Data Sensitivity: 3 points (touches patient inquiries containing identifiable medical symptoms).
  • System Autonomy: 1 point (the system generates a draft response inside the CRM; human staff read, edit, and send the message).
  • Blast Radius: 2 points (an erroneous message sent to a patient could cause confusion, though clinical staff can issue immediate corrections).

Total score: 6 points (Tier 2, Amber).

At the monthly review, the project is approved subject to three mandatory conditions: model traffic must route exclusively through an internal gateway with zero data retention by external API vendors, prompts must pass through an automated de-identification filter before leaving the local boundary, and 5% of all agent-approved messages must undergo weekly quality sampling. Intake to conditional clearance takes 18 days. A year earlier, this exact project would have languished in legal limbo for months because there was no transparent mechanism to evaluate its risk.

Now consider the same healthcare provider evaluating an AI agent that automatically adjusts patient appointments directly inside the electronic health record system without human mediation.

  • Data Sensitivity: 3 points (direct access to patient scheduling records).
  • System Autonomy: 3 points (writes directly to production databases via automated functions).
  • Blast Radius: 2 points (a scheduling error displaces real clinical visits, impacting patient care).

Total score: 8 points (Tier 3, Red).

The table halts unmediated production deployment immediately. The engineering team is directed to re-architect the service into a Tier 2 workflow: the model may propose schedule optimisations to a human coordinator, but direct database writes are locked until automated rollbacks and audit safeguards are proven.

This intake rubric aligns conceptually with the govern, map, measure, and manage core functions outlined in the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Because enterprise buyers widely recognise this taxonomy, internal tier assignments translate cleanly when international clients conduct vendor risk assessments.

Artefact 2: a named owner per system and a 45-minute monthly review

Quarterly steering committees do not govern software effectively. By the time a quarterly agenda is finalised, engineering teams have already shipped code or abandoned the project. Real governance requires a short, monthly operating cadence.

The operating model requires exactly two roles, adapting guidance on agile AI oversight structures from Trustible:

  1. The Executive Sponsor: a single executive (such as the CTO, CIO, or Chief Risk Officer) who maintains institutional authority over the tier table and serves as the final escalation authority for Tier 3 projects. The sponsor attends only the opening ten minutes of the review.
  2. The System Owner: a designated individual (not a team alias or department) assigned to every AI asset. The system owner is personally accountable for completing the intake form, verifying operational constraints, monitoring accuracy, and reporting incidents. If an AI workload lacks an accountable human owner, it is decommissioned.

The monthly review is scheduled for 45 minutes on a fixed recurring date, chaired by an operational lead:

  • Minutes 0 to 10: Triage new intakes. Review all Tier 1 and Tier 2 submissions logged over the preceding month. Confirm or adjust assigned tiers (the Executive Sponsor participates in this segment).
  • Minutes 10 to 20: Scheduled Tier 2 reviews. Examine running systems approaching their mandatory six-month reassessment. Review changes in underlying foundation models, prompt changes, or shift in data inputs.
  • Minutes 20 to 35: Incident evaluation and audit logs. Review reported anomalies, prompt injection attempts, output degradation, or gateway policy violations. Determine required mitigations.
  • Minutes 35 to 45: Register hygiene. Flag systems with expired review dates, identify unmaintained prototypes, and issue termination notices for orphaned systems.

Meeting minutes are recorded directly into the model register. This practice prevents governance drift, ensuring that risk registers and operational realities remain identical.

Artefact 3: an enforcement layer, not a written rule

The failure of traditional IT governance lies in treating policies as compliance reading material rather than technical guardrails. If a company policy states that external models must not process proprietary customer data, but engineers hold raw API keys in local development environments, that policy provides zero operational security.

Technical rules must be enforced at the network and runtime layers. The core architectural component is a unified model gateway: an OpenAI-compatible proxy situated between internal software applications and all downstream model providers (whether hosted externally or deployed in private data centres).

This architecture is precisely what FastLLM Proxy implements: routing, tenant token budgets, model allowlists, and end-to-end request logging consolidated into a single control plane. Engineering teams configure their SDKs to point to the internal gateway URL, keeping credentials entirely out of application source code.

# Production gateway policy configuration
team_identifier: contact-centre-ops
api_key_ref: env:CONTACT_CENTRE_GATEWAY_TOKEN
routing:
  default_provider: self-hosted-gpu
  allowed_models:
    - internal/llama-3.1-70b-instruct  # On-premise infrastructure; data remains in-country
    - cloud/gpt-4o-mini                 # Permitted strictly for de-identified general drafting
quotas:
  monthly_spend_limit_usd: 3000
  rate_limit_requests_per_minute: 120
  alert_threshold_percentage: 80
security_enforcement:
  pii_scrubbing_mode: redact_before_egress
  log_prompt_payloads: false          # Prevents recording sensitive health or personal data
  log_structured_metadata: true        # Records timestamp, user context, token counts, latency

With an enforcement proxy operational, compliance rules become automated routing logic:

  • The rule stating sensitive records must remain within national borders is enforced by restricting the team API key to self-hosted models running on domestic infrastructure.
  • The rule capping experimental AI spend is enforced via automated token quotas that throttle traffic when budgets are exhausted.
  • The requirement to provide auditable evidence to regulators is satisfied by structured metadata logs that record every invocation without persisting sensitive payload text.

The second half of technical enforcement involves standardising prompt configuration. If system instructions reside inside arbitrary application scripts, prompt updates cannot be peer-reviewed. Deploying a version-controlled repository such as PromptForge ensures prompt engineering changes are tracked through pull requests, tested against benchmarks, and deployed consistently.

Storing approved architecture patterns, tier criteria and registry data in an accessible system like Kryton lets human engineers and automated tools reference identical operating parameters. Governance artefacts that are isolated from developer workflows will be bypassed.

Artefact 4: the model and agent register

The model and agent register serves as the central inventory of all artificial intelligence assets across the enterprise. It provides immediate answers during board reviews, customer security audits, and regulatory inquiries.

Rather than maintaining static spreadsheets that quickly become obsolete, define the register in structured text formats that can integrate with continuous integration checks:

# Enterprise Model and Agent Register Entry
- system_id: sys-2025-cc-drafter
  system_name: Contact Centre Patient Message Assistant
  system_owner: a.almansoori@enterprise.ae
  operational_tier: Tier 2 (Amber)
  approval_date: 2025-05-10
  mandatory_review_date: 2025-11-10
  data_classification:
    - patient_medical_inquiries
    - synthetic_reference_templates
  allowed_endpoints:
    - internal/llama-3.1-70b-instruct
  gateway_team_scope: contact-centre-ops
  enforced_controls:
    - automated_pii_redaction
    - outbound_gateway_only
    - weekly_human_audit_sample_pct: 5
  incident_history:
    - date: 2025-07-22
      summary: Hallucinated clinic opening hours
      resolution: System prompt updated in PromptForge with canonical schedule reference

This register provides continuous visibility. If a model identifier surfaces in gateway logs that does not exist in the register, an unapproved system has been detected automatically.

In enterprise deployments across the UAE, runtime isolation tools such as Kuvryn AI simplify this tracking. By hosting autonomous agents and internal model servers within segregated workspaces on sovereign GPU clusters, infrastructure metrics automatically mirror the system register, eliminating manual reconciliation.

One document set, two assurance frameworks

Establishing governance around these four artefacts provides immediate regulatory alignment. The structure satisfies the dual requirements of international certification under ISO/IEC 42001 and local compliance with the UAE AI Charter without requiring duplicative documentation.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 represents the international management system standard for artificial intelligence, establishing auditable requirements across clauses 4 through 10. Industry timelines published by accredited certifiers like Konfirmity show that achieving ISO 42001 certification typically spans 4 to 9 months, with significantly compressed timelines for enterprises that already maintain an active ISO 27001 Information Security Management System.

The table below demonstrates how the four small artefacts satisfy mandatory ISO clauses while fulfilling the operational principles established by the UAE government:

Operational artefact ISO/IEC 42001 clause mapping UAE AI Charter principles fulfilled
1. One-page intake form and tier table Clause 4 (Context of the organisation)
Clause 6.1 (Actions to address AI risks)

When a commercial partner or statutory auditor requests evidence of your AI governance framework, you do not need to hand over an abstract policy manual. You provide the intake criteria, the system register showing clear human ownership, the gateway configurations enforcing security boundaries, and the minutes of recurring monthly reviews.

If your enterprise requires an initial baseline assessment to map these controls across legacy workloads, Azrty's AI strategy & readiness consulting provides an accelerated diagnostic. We evaluate how your organisation operates across systems, workflows and data pipelines, identifying precisely where artificial intelligence yields measurable commercial returns, what infrastructure changes are required, and what controls must be established first. Azrty is a UAE company based in Dubai. Our own team in the UAE does the consulting, the deployment and the support for our clients.

The six-week implementation roadmap

To establish this operating model without stalling delivery, execute the deployment as an agile, six-week sequential project:

Week 1: Foundations & Sponsor Alignment
  └── Finalise intake form & 3×3 risk scoring table
  └── Secure Executive Sponsor sign-off (CTO / Head of Risk)

Weeks 2–3: Enterprise Discovery & Registration
  └── Scan gateway/network logs for existing AI traffic
  └── Survey development leads to compile undocumented workloads
  └── Populate baseline Model & Agent Register

Week 3: Ownership Assignment
  └── Assign named individual owner to every active system
  └── Flag orphan workloads for immediate deprecation

Weeks 3–4: Gateway Infrastructure Deployment
  └── Stand up unified proxy (FastLLM Proxy)
  └── Migrate client API credentials to team-scoped gateway tokens
  └── Configure token limits, logging policies, and PII filters

Week 4: The Inaugural Monthly Review
  └── Convene 45-minute review session
  └── Classify legacy systems into Tier 1, 2, or 3
  └── Define binding remediation milestones for Tier 2 systems

Weeks 5–6: Operational Hardening
  └── Ingest production prompts into versioned library (PromptForge)
  └── Publish registry and documentation into Kryton knowledge base
  └── Lock production CI/CD pipelines to enforce gateway routing

Immediate priorities

  1. Week 1: Define the intake document and risk scoring table. Drafting requires approximately two hours; securing formal approval from the Executive Sponsor requires a single one-hour briefing.
  2. Weeks 2 to 3: Inventory current operational systems. Review existing firewall and API logs to identify external model providers currently receiving queries. Distribute a single-question inquiry to software and business team leads to capture unlisted workloads. Construct the initial draft of the register.
  3. Week 3: Enforce operational accountability. Assign a specific, named human owner to every active deployment. If a workload has no identifiable owner willing to assume accountability for its behaviour, schedule it for retirement.
  4. Weeks 3 to 4: Deploy the gateway layer. Implement the proxy endpoint, update application configuration files to route through the gateway, invalidate direct provider API keys, and implement baseline logging and budget caps.
  5. Week 4: Conduct the inaugural monthly review. Dedicate 45 minutes to tiering the existing inventory. Establish remediation requirements for any workloads processing customer or sensitive data.
  6. Weeks 5 to 6: Consolidate operational workflows. Move production prompts into a versioned library, publish the completed register to your internal engineering knowledge base, and formalise upcoming review dates.

Once these six weeks are complete, resist the urge to draft additional theoretical documentation. Allow the operating model to run for three consecutive review cycles. The empirical data recorded in your gateway logs and system register will reveal precisely which operational risks require further refinement. Practical governance is built through operational visibility, unambiguous personal accountability, and deterministic technical enforcement.

  • Regulatory Overview: Latham & Watkins on UAE AI Regulation and Authority Oversight

title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21165v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.

title: Value-Informed Schedule Trimming for Accelerated Sequential Monte Carlo Guidance in Discrete Diffusion
description:
arXiv:2610.20669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive. Active guidance steps require additional reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but commonly used schedules are fixed heuristics whose effectiveness can vary substantially across tasks. We propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects guided timesteps under a fixed budget. VISTA formulates sparse guidance as approximation of the ideal full-guidance probability path and derives an estimable upper bound on \(\ell_1\) path deviation. Using value statistics collected from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA optimizes the resulting empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming. The warmup generations can be retained as model outputs, and after schedule selection VISTA has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation tasks, VISTA discovers task-dependent schedules and outperforms hand-designed sparse schedules in most tested settings, while approaching or exceeding full-guidance performance on several task metrics. In toxic-text generation, for example, VISTA attains a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio compared with 1.00 for full guidance while reducing post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35$\times$ speedup.

title: Temporal Specification Guidance for Text-to-Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.20822v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.
