title: A large-scale climate-aware satellite image dataset for domain adaptive land-cover semantic segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.21238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A few well-annotated datasets for land-cover semantic segmentation have recently been introduced to advance the field of earth observation technologies. However, these datasets overlook the significant diversity among geographic areas with different climates, which can greatly impact and diversify land cover. Consequently, this leads to a domain gap in remote sensing images and severe performance degradation of the segmentation models. To enhance land-cover semantic segmentation with improved generalization ability, we conducted the first investigation into the impact of climate on this task. In this paper, we present a unique large-scale Climate-Aware Satellite Images Dataset (CASID) specifically designed for domain adaptive land-cover semantic segmentation. It consists of 980 satellite images with a size of 5000 x 5000 pixels, collected from 30 different regions around Asia, covering over 24,500 square kilometers. These images are gathered from four distinct climate zones, namely temperate monsoon, subtropical monsoon, tropical monsoon, and tropical rainforest. It includes four sub-datasets/domains, each representing one of the aforementioned climate zones. This characteristic makes CASID the first climate-aware land-cover semantic segmentation dataset with multiple domains. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the samples from the four climate zones, emphasizing differences in global image features, image texture, category distribution, spectral value, and object shape. These analyses offer valuable insights for subsequent research in this field. Moreover, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the latest semantic segmentation and unsupervised domain adaptation methods on the CASID dataset. These results serve as a robust baseline for future research endeavors. Our dataset will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Linwei-Chen/CASID.

title: RoboCloth: A Large-Scale Real Cloth Material Dataset for Neural Reflectance Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.21090v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present RoboCloth, a dataset of 500 real cloth materials captured under flexible, calibrated camera and lighting configurations, where both are robotically controlled during acquisition. Each material is imaged in approximately 580 high-dynamic range frames spanning a wide view-light hemisphere; camera poses are refined via structure-from-motion and aligned to the robot frame, yielding per-material sparse surface geometry and structured per-point reflectance observations ready for neural material training. We demonstrate the value of this data through a two-stage neural reconstruction pipeline: Stage 1 trains a shared MLP decoder on our corpus to learn cloth material priors; Stage 2 then freezes the decoder and fits a dense 2048x2048 latent texture to each target material. Evaluating on held-out materials from our own dataset and on the independent UBO2014 benchmark, we show that a decoder trained on our captures outperforms decoders trained on existing measured reflectance datasets and analytic PBR fitting, transferring to unseen acquisition systems without modification. The dataset, calibration files, observation tensors, and train/test splits are released under CC BY 4.0 on the Hugging Face Hub.

title: The SEO Score Trap: How to Prove Search Visibility in the Age of AI Answers
description:
An evidence-first field manual for technical SEO, GEO, AEO, and the difficult work of measuring whether an optimization actually mattered.

For: technical SEOs, developers, founders, content strategists, and teams responsible for organic discovery

A website can score 98/100 in an audit and still send search engines toward the wrong URL. It can pass every automated check and publish nothing worth citing. It can appear in an AI answer and receive no useful visit. It can even gain citations while losing conversions.

These are not paradoxes. They are different outcomes, measured at different points in a system that the SEO industry often compresses into a single number.

The number is attractive because it looks decisive. A red warning gives a team something to fix. A green score gives a founder something to show. A dashboard makes progress visible. But arithmetic does not make the underlying measurement complete. If a tool cannot tell you what it observed, what it inferred, what remains unknown, and how to verify the proposed fix, its precision is mostly cosmetic.

The real job is not to make a website's score rise. It is to understand how a page moves from a URL that exists to information that can be retrieved, trusted for a particular purpose, cited accurately, and eventually used by a person.

That is the thread connecting traditional SEO, answer engine optimization (AEO), and generative engine optimization (GEO). The labels are different; the need for evidence is not.

This guide turns that principle into a working method. It covers technical discovery, canonicalization, rendering, structured data, content quality, AI crawler controls, emerging AI visibility reports, and a repeatable way to test changes without mistaking correlation for causation. It distinguishes documented platform behavior from hypotheses that still need testing. It does not promise rankings, traffic, or citations that no practitioner can guarantee.

In this guide

  1. The score is a map, not the territory
  2. Treat visibility as a chain, not a metric
  3. Start with what the server actually returns
  4. An audit finding must survive scrutiny
  5. What makes a page worth retrieving and citing
  6. SEO, AEO and GEO: what the evidence says in 2026
  7. Crawlers, permissions and the false promise of one AI switch
  8. How to measure AI visibility without fooling yourself
  9. Prioritize causes, then test interventions
  10. A live editorial audit and a technical example
  11. A practical toolset and primary sources

1. The score is a map, not the territory

An SEO score is the output of a particular model. It depends on which URLs a tool visited, which checks it runs, the conditions under which it ran them, the evidence it could retrieve, and the weights it assigns to its findings. Two products can examine the same website and produce different scores without either calculation being arithmetically wrong. They may be measuring different things.

Scoring is not inherently bad. A consistent score can help someone orient themselves, compare the same template over time, or decide which category needs inspection first. It becomes dangerous when a summary is mistaken for a diagnosis, a Google metric, a forecast, or evidence that a site is ready for AI search.

Imagine two audit reports.

The first page receives 94/100. Its title is present, images have dimensions, lab performance looks acceptable, and almost every on-page test passes. Yet the product URL declares the homepage as its canonical, appears in the XML sitemap, and receives internal links alongside several parameterized versions. The number looks healthy; the URL signals disagree. The work is not to recover six points. It is to determine which URL the site intends search engines to understand as the representative page and to align the evidence with that decision.

The second page receives 63/100 because an automated report flags missing alt text on decorative SVGs, several headings, and a long script. Adding keyword-heavy alt text to decorative graphics may make the accessible experience worse. The large script may be essential to the page. The audit has identified things to inspect; it has not proved three defects.

A universal 0–100 SEO score is not published by Google. Google documents technical eligibility, search policies, and best practices; it does not certify third-party audit grades as a proxy for ranking. Meeting technical requirements does not guarantee indexing or serving. Google's starting point is its Search technical requirements and helpful-content guidance, not a vendor's color scale.

The useful question is not “How do I get from 82 to 95?” It is “Which important condition is wrong, how do we know, and what would prove the repair worked?”

Before treating a score as a decision, establish five things:

  • Scope. Was the tool testing one URL, a representative template, a sampled crawl, or the whole site? A homepage scan cannot describe a catalogue of 80,000 products.
  • Evidence source. Did a claim come from raw HTML, a browser-rendered DOM, a lab performance trace, field data, server logs, a third-party API, or a heuristic?
  • Applicability. Does the rule make sense for this page? A non-product article should not fail a product-price test.
  • Inference. Which part is observed, and which part is an explanation proposed by the tool?
  • Reproducibility. Can another person run the same test against the same URL and understand why the result was produced?

If those questions are unanswered, the score may still be useful for navigation. It is not enough to justify a costly change.

2. Treat visibility as a chain, not a metric

“Visibility” covers several different events. A page can succeed at one and fail at the next. The model below is diagnostic, not a claim that every platform follows one identical pipeline.

Access: can the system fetch the resource through its redirects, robots rules, authentication, CDN, and firewall? A successful request proves only that one request worked under one set of conditions.

Interpretation: can the system obtain the facts that matter? Main content may be missing from the initial response, injected through JavaScript, hidden in an image, or inconsistent with structured data. A page may load successfully and still leave product identity, authorship, price, or compatibility ambiguous.

Indexing and representation: has a search system retained or selected this URL as a representative page? Discovery, crawling, indexing, canonicalization, and serving are not synonyms. A fetched URL may not be indexed; an indexed page may not be selected for a query.

Retrieval and selection: does the page help answer this particular question? A general explainer may be irrelevant to a request for current pricing, regional rules, compatibility, or a measured benchmark. Generative systems can combine different sources and return different citations for similar prompts. Their full selection processes are not all public.

Citation and outcome: is the source actually cited, does it support the nearby claim, and does that exposure help a person? A citation can be correct but commercially irrelevant. A brand can be mentioned without a clickable source. Neither an impression nor a citation is automatically a conversion.

These distinctions are practical, not semantic:

Observed problem Investigate first What it does not prove
Crawler receives an error Response, redirects, CDN/WAF rules, access That every crawler receives the same response
Page is not indexed URL diagnostics, directives, canonicals, internal discovery, content That one missing tag caused the exclusion
Indexed page rarely appears Query fit, demand, competing pages, usefulness, architecture That the audit score is too low
Page is absent from a prompt sample Query selection, access, page value, variability, competitor coverage That it is invisible to every AI system
Citations rise but qualified visits do not Query relevance, referral behavior, page proposition, measurement That the work succeeded or failed commercially

Do not use evidence from one stage as proof of success at another. A crawl pass is not an indexing report. Indexing is not ranking. Ranking is not citation. A citation is not a conversion.

3. Start with what the server actually returns

A strong investigation starts with a specific URL and a reproducible request—not a hundred generic recommendations.

Get the response, headers, and body separately

For a public page, a first-pass fetch can be recorded with:

curl -sS -L --max-redirs 10 \
  -D response-headers.txt \
  -o response-body.html \
  -w 'final_url=%{url_effective}\nstatus=%{http_code}\nredirects=%{num_redirects}\ntime_total=%{time_total}s\n' \
  --max-time 30 \
  'https://www.example.com/products/widget'

This saves redirect and final-response headers separately from the body. It does not run JavaScript, emulate Googlebot, prove which canonical Google selected, or show how every AI system sees the page. It is a narrow observation. A 200 OK can still return the wrong page; a soft 404 can also return 200; a redirect can end at an irrelevant URL; and a CDN or firewall can treat automated clients differently.

Inspect status, redirects, canonical, robots directives, title, primary content, internal links, and structured data. Compare the initial response with a browser-rendered DOM when JavaScript matters. Do not treat a generic curl request as equivalent to a verified search crawler; use provider diagnostics and logs when crawler-specific behavior is material.

Do not confuse crawl control with indexing control

robots.txt expresses crawl preferences to compliant crawlers. It does not reliably guarantee that a URL never appears in search: a blocked URL can sometimes be discovered through links without its content being fetched. A noindex directive is intended to prevent indexing by systems that support it, but the crawler generally must fetch the resource to read the directive. Blocking a page while expecting Google to see its noindex tag can therefore defeat the intended outcome. Google's indexing-control guidance explains the distinction.

The X-Robots-Tag header can carry indexing directives for HTML and non-HTML resources. Authentication, application permissions, CDN rules, and WAF challenges are different again: they can prevent the request from reaching the content. Record which control was observed and which system it is intended to affect.

Canonicalization is a set of signals

Suppose a page exists at https://example.com/product/widget, a www variant, and a tracking-parameter variant. Redirects, rel="canonical", sitemap entries, and internal links should support the site's intended URL policy. Google describes redirects and canonical annotations as strong signals and sitemap inclusion as a weaker one. They are signals, not commands that override all other evidence. See Google's canonicalization documentation.

“Canonical present” is not the same as “canonical correct.” Check whether the target is intended, returns a valid response, is indexable, and is supported by internal links and sitemap entries. A self-referencing canonical is common and often sensible, but is not an unconditional law for every URL.

Compare rendered content and field performance

JavaScript is not inherently an SEO defect. Google can process JavaScript, but rendering adds another stage where content and signals can fail or differ. Compare the initial response with the rendered DOM for primary copy, title, canonical, robots directives, links, and product facts. Google's JavaScript SEO guide documents the relevant constraints. The question is not “Does this site use React?” but “Can the systems that matter obtain the needed content reliably?”

A sitemap helps search engines discover URLs; it does not command indexing. Important indexable pages should also be discoverable through meaningful internal links. On large sites, sample deliberately: core templates, revenue-critical pages, recently deployed templates, regional variants, filtered categories, and unusual code paths.

Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Google's “good” thresholds at the 75th percentile are LCP at or below 2.5 seconds, INP at or below 200 milliseconds, and CLS at or below 0.1. See Google's Core Web Vitals guidance. A Lighthouse run is a lab test; CrUX and other field datasets represent real-user experience over a reporting window. They answer different questions. No URL-level field data is not the same as a failing field metric.

Finally, resource size does not prove the cause of poor performance. Identify the resource type, initiator, timing, and role before proposing a fix. The aim is a better user experience, not a cleaner-looking waterfall chart.

4. An audit finding must survive scrutiny

An audit result is only useful when another person can understand what was observed, why it matters, and how to verify the proposed intervention without guessing what the tool intended.

Compare these statements:

“Page speed is poor. High impact. Fix JavaScript.”

And:

“In the 16 October desktop lab run, the LCP element was the hero image. The image request began after a client-side component executed. This test did not establish the URL's field LCP. Inspect whether the image can be discovered earlier in the initial document, make one change, and repeat the same lab configuration before evaluating field data when enough becomes available.”

The second finding is not merely more cautious. It is more actionable. It separates observation from interpretation, identifies a limitation, and proposes a test that could falsify the diagnosis. It does not pretend to know the exact effect on rankings.

A robust finding record should contain:

Field What to preserve
Target URL, resource, template, or site area
Observation Exact value or output seen, not just a label
Method Request type, tool, test conditions, and evidence source
Time Timestamp and relevant environment, including locale or device where material
Expected state The condition the page is intended to meet, with the reason why
Interpretation The probable implication, clearly distinguished from the observation
Next action A change or further test that could address the cause
Verification The evidence required after deployment to call the change successful
Unknowns What this test cannot establish, such as current index state or ranking cause

Use an Evidence-to-Outcome loop: observe, prove, intervene, verify, measure. Keep each step separate. A tool can record an observation automatically, but it must not convert a guess about cause into a fact merely by placing it in a red card. The loop closes only when the production change is verified at the correct layer and the intended outcome is measured with a suitable source.

The following example is illustrative; the values are not a live-site measurement:

{
  "findingId": "CANONICAL_TARGET_MISMATCH",
  "targetUrl": "https://example.com/products/widget",
  "observedAt": "2026-10-16T12:00:00Z",
  "evidenceSource": "rendered_html",
  "observed": {
    "httpStatus": 200,
    "canonicalUrl": "https://example.com/"
  },
  "expected": {
    "canonicalUrl": "https://example.com/products/widget"
  },
  "assessment": "confirmed_mismatch",
  "notEstablished": [
    "Google-selected canonical",
    "Current indexed representation",
    "Ranking impact"
  ]
}

The final three lines matter as much as the finding itself. They stop an auditor from confusing the page's current HTML with what Google has selected or from claiming a ranking impact that the evidence did not measure.

Distinguish “fail” from “unknown”

A report should represent at least six meaningful states: confirmed failure, warning, pass, unknown, not applicable, and not run. They are not cosmetic variations.

“Unknown” means the evidence was insufficient. “Not run” means no test was executed. “Not applicable” means the rule does not fit the resource. None of those means “fail.” A page without a product offer should not be penalized for lacking product-price markup. A crawler that could not reach a page should not confidently report that the page lacks a canonical; it did not inspect the canonical at all.

Severity and confidence should also be separate. A potentially severe issue backed by weak evidence deserves quick verification. A low-severity issue observed with certainty may be safe to defer. One red badge cannot communicate both facts.

A report becomes trustworthy when it is willing to say “we do not know yet.” That is not a failure of automation. It is the boundary between evidence and fiction.

5. What makes a page worth retrieving and citing

Technical access explains whether a system can reach a page. It does not explain why the page should be selected for a particular question. That depends on relevance, usefulness, the evidence on the page, competing sources, and platform-specific behavior.

The weakest approach to GEO is to optimize for an imagined machine evaluator: repeat question phrases, add arbitrary FAQ blocks, generate near-duplicate pages, sprinkle statistics without context, or publish llms.txt as if it were a ranking switch. Such tactics can create the appearance of work without helping a reader make a decision.

The stronger approach is to make the page resolve a real information need better than the available alternatives.

Make the page's purpose and evidence clear

A product page should make identity, price, availability, compatibility, limitations, and next steps clear where those facts matter. A technical guide should state the recommended action and the conditions under which it applies. An original research page should disclose its sample, method, dates, exclusions, and limits. Readers should not have to reverse-engineer the purpose of a page before deciding whether to trust it.

For consequential claims, give the reader a trail: what exactly is being claimed, who is responsible for it, what source supports it, when and where it applies, and what could make it incomplete or false. “This feature improves performance by 40%” is meaningless without a definition of performance, baseline, sample, method, and conditions. A research paper citation does not justify generalizing from a benchmark to every commercial AI system.

The standard is not “every sentence needs a citation.” It is “the claim driving the recommendation can be checked.”

Keep every representation of a fact consistent

A company can have several versions of one fact: the visitor-facing page, initial HTML and rendered DOM, structured data or product feed, and statements elsewhere on the web. Search systems and AI products may encounter different subsets of these representations. When they disagree, adding schema does not repair the underlying information problem.

Imagine a product shown as $79 on its page, $69 in JSON-LD, $79 in a feed, and $99 in an old comparison article. Every URL may load correctly. Every piece of markup may validate. The public record is still inconsistent. Establish the authoritative fact, correct the representations under the site's control, update or retire stale pages, and check what the relevant services actually show.

The same issue appears when a SaaS landing page promises an integration that its documentation says is unavailable, when a company uses three names for one product, or when a PDF preserves a claim that the HTML page has corrected. Sometimes the right unit to audit is the fact and its lineage, not just the URL.

Schema describes the page; it does not certify it

Structured data gives supported search systems explicit clues about page meaning and can enable eligible rich results. Valid markup does not guarantee that a result feature will appear, and markup cannot make inaccurate visible content trustworthy. Google's structured data introduction and policy documentation explain the intended role.

Treat schema as a structured representation of real page content, not an alternate reality in which a publisher can declare better facts than a visitor sees. When a price, review score, date, author, or availability is wrong, fix the underlying source of truth as well as the markup.

Original information is the defensible advantage

The strongest differentiator is something a competitor cannot reproduce merely by rewriting the same five sources: a measured test, a useful dataset, an informed teardown, a decision framework, a first-hand account, or a transparent record of a failure and its fix. Not every page needs a lab experiment. A maintained reference table, a useful calculator, trustworthy compatibility information, or a clear answer to a specialized question can add real value. The requirement is additional value, not theatrical novelty.

Google's guide to generative AI features emphasizes valuable, non-commodity content and unique points of view. Its people-first guidance asks whether content adds original information or analysis rather than merely rewriting what is already available. That is sound editorial practice whether or not an AI system ever cites the page.

Freshness is factual, not typographical. Changing a date does not make a claim current. A meaningful update corrects an error, changes an important fact, adds a better test, replaces an obsolete instruction, or explains what has changed. Record the version or date of behavior described in fast-moving fields, and distinguish durable principles from product details likely to change.

6. SEO, AEO and GEO: what the evidence says in 2026

SEO is the established discipline of helping people and search systems discover, understand, and select useful pages. AEO, or answer engine optimization, is an industry term for making information useful in answer-oriented systems. GEO, or generative engine optimization, usually refers to work intended to improve a source's chance of being retrieved, mentioned, or cited in generated responses. Neither AEO nor GEO has a single universally accepted technical specification or scoring standard.

These labels can describe different measurement goals. They do not justify inventing separate rules for every AI product.

What Google has documented

Google's official guide, last updated on 10 July 2026, says that existing SEO best practices remain relevant to AI Overviews and AI Mode. A page must meet Search technical requirements and be eligible to appear with a snippet; crawling, indexing, and serving are not guaranteed even when requirements and best practices are met.

The guide directly addresses several popular GEO claims. Google Search does not require llms.txt or other special machine-readable files, does not require content to be broken into tiny chunks, does not require a special writing style just for AI, and does not require a special Schema.org type for AI Overviews or AI Mode. Google says it ignores llms.txt for Search visibility. Another service may choose to use such a file, but that is a different claim from improving Google Search visibility. Read Google's guide to generative AI features.

The same guide warns against inauthentic mentions and large volumes of pages created mainly to manipulate rankings or AI responses. A service built around boilerplate pages, artificial mentions, or a mysterious “AI score” with no transparent method deserves scrutiny.

What GEO research establishes

Aggarwal and colleagues' GEO: Generative Engine Optimization was published at ACM SIGKDD 2024. It introduced a framework and benchmark for studying how content changes affect visibility in generative responses. The authors reported gains of up to 40% for certain methods in their tested settings, with effects varying across domains. Read the paper.

Its important contribution is methodological: define prompts and conditions, measure visibility in the tested system, and compare interventions. The headline number is not an expected lift for a random website. It does not prove that adding statistics or quotations will improve any particular site by 40%, and it does not disclose the full retrieval algorithms of today's Google, Bing, ChatGPT, Claude, or other products.

What changed in measurement in 2026

Google announced dedicated Search Generative AI performance reports in Search Console on 3 June 2026 and said the rollout reached websites worldwide by 31 August. The reports show impressions in generative AI features in Search—including AI Overviews and AI Mode—and related AI features in Discover. The documented dimensions include pages, countries, devices for Search, and dates. See Google's announcement and Search Console help page.

This is more useful than inferring visibility from a handful of manually entered questions, but it is not a transcript of every prompt or every internal retrieval decision. Use the report for the evidence it exposes, not for claims it cannot support.

Microsoft introduced AI Performance reporting in Bing Webmaster Tools in February 2026 to expose citations across supported Copilot, Bing, and partner experiences. In June it announced preview capabilities for intent and topic groupings, citation share, and comparisons over time. Citation Share is an observational measure of a site's portion of citations for a grounding query—not a ranking score, traffic share, or content-quality grade. On 13 October, Microsoft announced a beta Topics Portfolio grouping grounding queries into broader themes. The company warns that topic classifications and some aggregate volumes are approximate and should be treated as directional signals. See the February announcement, June update, and October announcement.

The reports are not interchangeable. Different systems define and expose citation activity differently, so a manual ChatGPT prompt test cannot automatically be compared with a provider's official citation-share metric.

For every GEO claim, ask which platform it concerns, what was measured, which queries were included, over what dates, and which outcome changed. Without those boundaries, a recommendation is a hypothesis—not an established best practice.

7. Crawlers, permissions and the false promise of one AI switch

A common mistake is to treat all AI-related crawlers as one thing. Providers use separate user agents for different jobs, and the distinction matters to publishers making access decisions.

OpenAI documents three relevant mechanisms:

User agent Documented role Practical implication
OAI-SearchBot Search discovery for ChatGPT search features Blocking it can prevent a site from appearing in ChatGPT search answers, according to OpenAI's documentation.
GPTBot Crawling content that may be used to improve foundation models The training-related control is separate from the search control.
ChatGPT-User Access associated with certain user-initiated actions It is not the automatic search crawler and should not be treated as the same control.

These roles and controls are described in OpenAI's crawler documentation. OpenAI states that OAI-SearchBot and GPTBot settings are independent; a site owner can permit the search crawler while disallowing the training crawler. The documentation also explains that user-initiated access works differently from automatic crawling.

Anthropic similarly documents separate crawlers: ClaudeBot for potential model-training data collection, Claude-SearchBot for search, and Claude-User for user-directed retrieval. Blocking one does not express the same preference as blocking all of them. See Anthropic's site-owner documentation.

Google's Googlebot and Google-Extended also serve different purposes. Site owners should read the provider's current explanation before editing robots.txt; the directive that governs ordinary Search crawling is not a universal switch for every Google AI use.

The operational lesson is not “allow every bot.” It is to make an explicit content-access decision based on the use case, then verify the actual user-agent rules and any CDN or firewall behavior. Keep in mind that robots.txt communicates instructions to compliant crawlers; it is not authentication and is not a substitute for protecting private data.

Do not silently block a search crawler and later interpret absent citations as evidence that the content is low quality. Conversely, allowing a crawler only makes access possible; it does not guarantee selection, citation, or traffic.

8. How to measure AI visibility without fooling yourself

A screenshot of one answer is useful for debugging and poor as a measurement program. Generated answers can vary with wording, locale, timing, model version, available sources, and product behavior. One successful citation proves that citation can happen, not that visibility is stable.

Define a small experiment before inspecting the answers. Start with customer questions and important tasks, not prompts selected because they flatter the site. A B2B software company might test product comparisons, compatibility, implementation, pricing, limitations, and alternatives. A publisher might test explanations, current facts, and research questions. A local business needs queries tied to service and location.

A practical exploratory pilot might use 30 fixed prompts across informational, comparison, and commercial intent, then run each prompt three times on each of three explicitly named surfaces: 270 observations before reviewing citation quality. That is a manageable pilot, not a universal sample-size standard or proof of statistical significance. A formal study should be designed around the variability and decision it needs to support.

Preserve the exact prompt, platform, product surface or model version when exposed, timestamp, language, region, account state where relevant, answer, cited URLs, and page versions under test. Do not rewrite a prompt after an unfavorable response and merge the new result into the original series. Version the query set when it changes.

Measure different outcomes separately

Citation coverage is the proportion of eligible prompt-runs in which the target domain receives at least one relevant citation. Define “eligible” before testing and keep the denominator stable.

Citation coverage = (eligible runs with a relevant target-domain citation / all eligible runs) × 100%

Citation accuracy is the proportion of reviewed target-domain citations that genuinely support the nearby claim. A URL listed at the end of an answer but unrelated to the claim is not a successful supporting citation.

Citation prominence records where the source appears under a consistent, documented rubric—for example, directly beside the supported claim or only in a general list. This is a study-specific annotation, not a universal platform metric.

Factual fidelity checks whether the answer represents the source accurately: price, date, capability, limitation, or quantity. Share of citations in the test set compares the target with a fixed competitor set for the same prompt-runs. Its denominator must remain stable, and it should not be compared directly with a provider's official metric unless the definitions and coverage are genuinely equivalent.

Business outcome means relevant referral sessions, qualified leads, sign-ups, purchases, or another explicit goal. It requires analytics or other first-party evidence. A report about AI impressions must not be relabeled as conversions.

These measures can move in different directions. Coverage might rise while citation accuracy stays flat. Citations can fall after a platform update even though the site did not change. A small number of highly relevant citations may be commercially valuable while the aggregate count remains low.

Use first-party reports before manual prompting

For Google AI features, inspect the Generative AI performance report in Search Console alongside broader Search performance. Use the dimensions the report actually exposes—such as pages, countries, devices, and dates—and compare equivalent periods. Record substantial site changes during the same window; a before-and-after chart does not establish causality when other changes occurred.

For supported experiences covered by Microsoft, use the Bing Webmaster Tools AI Performance report. Examine cited pages and grounding queries, and use intent, topic, and comparison views where available. Remember that Topics Portfolio was announced as a beta with approximate aggregate values and AI-generated topic classifications.

Manual tests complement those provider reports when you need to inspect individual citations or cover questions not exposed by first-party reporting. They should not replace provider data with a much smaller sample that looks more decisive than it is.

Audit the support, not just the citation

Does the cited page actually state the claim? Is it current? Does it refer to the right product, market, and date range? Is the page accessible without an interaction the retrieval system may not perform? Has the answer omitted a limitation that changes the meaning?

If an answer cites a site but misrepresents it, log that as a fidelity failure. A brand mention without a clickable source may matter in another way, but record it as a mention rather than a citation. For a commercial audit, the real question is not only “How often were we cited?” It is “For which valuable questions are we accurately represented, which facts are getting lost, and does that exposure reach our intended audience?”

Finally, treat an increase after a rewrite as an association until the evidence supports a stronger claim. Retrieval may have changed because of the content, competitors, product updates, demand, or the platform itself. Record the timeline and plausible confounders. Where the decision warrants it, compare updated pages with suitable unchanged pages, while acknowledging the limitations of non-randomized SEO comparisons.

9. Prioritize causes, then test interventions

Once issues are credible, teams still need to decide what to do first. The answer should not come from the brightest color in the dashboard.

Evaluate a finding on four dimensions:

  • Impact: if the diagnosis is correct, how important is the affected page or user journey?
  • Confidence: how strong is the evidence that the problem exists and that the proposed intervention addresses it?
  • Scope: how many important URLs or templates could be affected, and are there dependencies that might make a global fix risky?
  • Cost and reversibility: how difficult is the change to implement and validate, and how easy is it to roll back if the assumption fails?

This is a decision aid, not a mathematical formula that produces an objectively correct priority. A high-impact, low-confidence diagnosis often calls for a fast verification step before a broad implementation. A confirmed template defect affecting thousands of revenue-critical pages may justify early action even if its precise ranking effect cannot be forecast.

Do not add imagined gains together

Audit reports sometimes forecast that one fix may recover 10%, another 15%, and a third 20%, then present the sum as an expected traffic gain. Unless those estimates are independently measured and the effects are known to be additive, the total is fiction. The interventions may overlap, share the same affected URLs, or depend on one another.

Use a baseline, a specific change, an agreed success measure, and a verification window. Do not claim the score increase itself is the business result. Record both intended and unintended consequences: an implementation can make one metric better while accidentally removing useful content, changing a canonical, or slowing another template.

For performance, compare comparable lab runs and field data when available. For indexing, re-check the response and use the provider's URL diagnostics. For AI citations, repeat the query set and track platform reports. For revenue, inspect relevant analytics. No single measurement covers all four.

The work is finished only when the production change has been verified at the correct layer. A source file change is not a deployed change. A deployed canonical is not proof that Google has selected it. A content update is not proof that an AI product has retrieved it. A citation is not proof of commercial impact.

10. A live editorial audit and a technical example

The strongest way to demonstrate an evidence-first standard is to apply it to the auditor. A review of the publicly visible copy of AuditMe's own SEO Score Checker and Website SEO Checker, conducted on 16 October 2026, found several claims worth examining. This is a review of the claims on those pages—not a full technical crawl, a test of the audit engine's output, or a study of ranking outcomes. That boundary matters.

The copy contained several assertions that need narrower wording or evidence before a skeptical reader can verify them.

Claim pattern on the public pages Evidence problem A more defensible treatment
The score's component factors are weighted by their known influence on rankings, and improving the score directly improves ranking chances. A proprietary score is a model created by the tool. Its weights are not Google's weights, and a higher composite score does not prove a ranking effect. Explain that the score summarizes the checks the product measures. Describe what each check observed and verify any claimed downstream impact separately.
Every page should have exactly one H1, alt text should be added to every image, and fixed title or content lengths indicate quality. These are too broad to be universal pass/fail rules. Decorative images often need empty alt text; an arbitrary word-count threshold is not evidence of usefulness. Label thresholds as heuristics, explain the case they help detect, and distinguish accessibility conventions from search requirements. Assess content by purpose and usefulness, not word count alone.
Structured data can increase click-through rate by a fixed 20–30%. A single percentage without a clearly applicable study, sample, and measurement context implies a general effect that cannot be assumed for every site or result feature. Say that valid structured data can make a page eligible for supported rich results. Measure CTR for the specific implementation and query set instead of promising a standard uplift. Google's structured data guidance does not guarantee an appearance or a particular CTR gain.
The “AI readiness” layer includes llms.txt, crawler access, schema coverage, and date freshness as signals that decide whether engines can cite a page. Access, retrieval, selection, and citation are separate events. Google specifically says llms.txt is not needed for its Search AI features; requirements differ across providers. A changed date is not proof of a meaningful update. Report provider-specific crawler access separately from measured citations. Treat files as useful only where a named system documents that it consumes them, and update a page date only when the content materially changes. See Google's current guide.
A “State of SEO” statistic says 68% of analyzed sites lost organic traffic because of overlooked issues. The visible page copy does not give the reader a linked methodology that establishes the sample, time period, definition of traffic loss, exclusions, and basis for attributing the cause. Link the report and methodology, including the sampling frame and limitations, or remove/qualify the statistic until those details are available.

This review does not establish that AuditMe's scoring engine is inaccurate, nor does it compare the product with competitors. It shows something more limited—and still valuable: even a tool built to evaluate other websites must hold its own claims to the same evidence standard. Strong marketing makes a promise. Strong technical publishing also shows the reader the basis, scope, and limits of that promise.

That is an editorial audit, not a ranking experiment. To see how the same discipline applies to technical findings, consider a separate fictional ecommerce example. The details below are illustrative; they are not a report or measured result from a live website.

Canonical mismatch

The product page returns 200 OK, but its rendered HTML declares the homepage as canonical. The product URL appears in the sitemap and receives internal links from category pages. The homepage is not a duplicate of the product page.

The engineer first confirms the intended URL policy. If the product is meant to be its own representative URL, the template is corrected and the production response re-tested. Sitemap and internal links are checked for consistency. That verifies the implementation-level fix; it does not prove Google has selected the intended canonical. URL Inspection and post-recrawl monitoring are separate steps.

Performance warning

A comparable lab trace identifies the hero image as the LCP element and shows its request starting after a client-side component executes. Field data is insufficient for this exact URL, so the team does not label real-user LCP as failing.

The engineer makes one targeted change to expose the important image earlier and reserve its dimensions, then repeats the same lab conditions. The result records whether the request starts sooner and the trace improves. Field data is reviewed when sufficient representative user data exists. This is a test of delivery, not a forecast of ranking gains.

“Low AI readiness”

The team replaces the label with a testable question: does the product page appear as a useful source for a fixed set of comparison and specification questions that prospective customers actually ask?

It verifies that the page is public, important facts are available in crawlable content, the visible price agrees with structured data, and specifications are not trapped in an image or interaction. It records a baseline using a versioned prompt set and available provider reports. If the page is rarely cited, the team compares the cited alternatives and looks for a substantive gap—missing compatibility details, an unclear limitation, no documented test, or stale availability.

A meaningful improvement might be a verified compatibility table or a transparent comparison based on published specifications, provided it genuinely helps customers. llms.txt, arbitrary FAQ blocks, and dozens of near-duplicate pages are not default solutions.

The same queries are tested after publication and each citation is inspected for accuracy. The result may be positive, neutral, or inconclusive; all three are legitimate. The final record contains a verified technical correction, a controlled performance test, and an AI visibility measurement. They remain separate because each answers a different question.

11. A practical toolset and primary sources

Different tools answer different questions. Use the source closest to the event being investigated, then add context from other systems where necessary.

Question Useful starting point What it is good for
What did the server return? curl, browser DevTools, server and CDN logs Status, redirects, headers, body, and request-specific behavior
What does Google report for this URL? Search Console URL Inspection Google's indexed and tested URL information within the tool's stated limits
How is the site performing in Google Search and AI features? Google Search Console First-party Search data and the generative AI performance reporting that is available for the property
What is the user's real performance experience? PageSpeed Insights, CrUX, and first-party real-user monitoring Field experience and lab diagnostics, kept separate
Is the page eligible for a supported rich result? Rich Results Test and structured data policies Markup validation and supported-feature eligibility, not a guarantee the feature will appear
Is the site being cited in covered AI search experiences? Bing Webmaster Tools, Google's AI report, and versioned manual tests Provider-specific visibility evidence, interpreted using each system's metric definitions
How are AI crawlers controlled? Current official crawler documentation, robots.txt, CDN/WAF rules, and logs Distinguishes search, training, and user-initiated retrieval controls

A useful SEO score checker can point to areas worth inspecting. A broader website audit can help organize findings. The right tool should make its evidence available and make uncertainty visible rather than asking the user to trust a grade.

For an initial technical overview, use the AuditMe SEO Score Checker. For a broader scan of a website's SEO issues, use the AuditMe Website SEO Checker. Treat their outputs as the start of the investigation: verify consequential findings against the actual page, the relevant first-party data, and the behavior of the system you are trying to understand.

Primary sources and further reading

  • Google Search Central, Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search, updated 10 July 2026.
  • Google Search Central, Search technical requirements.
  • Google Search Central, Block Search indexing with noindex.
  • Google Search Central, Consolidate duplicate URLs and specify a canonical.
  • Google Search Central, JavaScript SEO basics.
  • Google Search Central, Core Web Vitals and Google Search.
  • Google Search Central, Structured data introduction and structured data policies.
  • Google Search Central, Search Generative AI performance reports in Search Console, 3 June 2026; rollout completed worldwide by 31 August 2026.
  • Microsoft Bing Webmaster Blog, AI Performance in Bing Webmaster Tools, 10 February 2026.
  • Microsoft Bing Search Blog, Intents, Topics, Citation Share and Compare, 16 June 2026.
  • Microsoft Bing Webmaster Blog, Topics Portfolio beta in AI Performance, 13 October 2026.
  • OpenAI, Overview of OpenAI Crawlers.
  • Anthropic, Website crawlers and site-owner controls, 7 April 2026.
  • Aggarwal et al., “GEO: Generative Engine Optimization”, ACM SIGKDD 2024.

The standard worth keeping

Stop asking whether a website is “AI-ready” as if readiness were a permanent property that a tool can certify. Ask a more precise set of questions: Can the relevant system retrieve the page? Does the page expose the facts needed for this task? Is it selected for a defined query? Is it cited accurately? Does that exposure help the intended audience?

Those questions do not fit neatly into one score. They do lead to better engineering, better content, and more defensible decisions.

An audit should not promise certainty where the system is opaque. It should reduce uncertainty one verifiable finding at a time.

Disclosure: AuditMe publishes the tools linked in this article. This guide is educational and is not an independent comparative benchmark of SEO products. The worked investigation is illustrative, not a claim of measured results from a live website. No score, markup change, crawler rule, or GEO/AEO technique guarantees rankings, traffic, or AI citations.

title: The N+1 Query Problem — "It works locally, but is extremely slow in production"
description:
The scenario: Your API loads 100 users and their orders. It works locally — but becomes extremely slow in production. What could be causing it?

One of the most common (and sneaky) causes: the N+1 Query Problem. 🐢

What Is It?

Suppose the application needs to display 100 users along with their orders. You'd expect the database to fetch everything together in one efficient round-trip. But here's what often actually happens:

1️⃣ The application sends one query to fetch all 100 users.
2️⃣ It then sends one additional query per user to fetch that user's orders.

Result:

  • ✅ 1 query to fetch the users
  • ❌ 100 additional queries — one per user — to fetch their orders

That's 101 database queries for a single API request.

This is the textbook N+1 Query Problem:

1 query fetches the parent records, then N additional queries fetch the related records
individually — one per parent row.

With 100 users, this might go unnoticed in a local test with a fast local DB and no network latency. With 10,000 users, the same code path triggers 10,001 queries — and it becomes catastrophic in production, especially over a real network to a real database.

Why It Hurts

Every additional query introduces:

  • Network round-trip time (multiplied by N)
  • Database connection pool usage (queries competing for limited connections)
  • Query-processing/parsing overhead per call
  • More load on the database server
  • Significantly higher API response time — often the actual root cause of "works locally, slow in prod," since local dev DBs have near-zero latency per query while production round-trips add up fast.

Why Does It Happen?

Most commonly with an ORM using lazy loading. The application loads the users first (one query). Later, when code accesses user.getOrders() inside a loop, the ORM silently and transparently issues another database query per user at that exact point — invisible in the code (it just looks like a normal getter call), which is exactly why it's easy to miss in code review and easy to reproduce only under realistic data volumes.

How to Fix It

🔗 1. Fetch related data together (join fetch)

Use a join or fetch strategy that retrieves the parent (users) and the related child data (orders) together, in a single query, instead of triggering a separate query per parent row.

📦 2. Use batch fetching

Instead of loading orders one user at a time, retrieve the orders for multiple users in one batch query (e.g., WHERE user_id IN (1, 2, 3, ..., 100)). This can turn 100 queries into a small handful — often reducing hundreds of queries down to just a couple.

🎯 3. Fetch only the required fields (projections)

If the API only needs a user's name, order number, and status, don't load the complete User,Order, and every related entity graph. Project only the fields actually needed for the response — less data over the wire, less mapping overhead, and often avoids triggering lazy-loaded associations entirely. — less data over the wire, less mapping overhead, and often avoids triggering lazy-loaded associations entirely.

📄 4. Add pagination

Never load thousands of users (and their orders) in a single request. Retrieve a bounded page and only the data needed for that page — this caps the worst-case query count and payload size regardless of how large the underlying table grows.

How Do You Detect the N+1 Problem?

  • Enable database query logging (e.g., Hibernate's show-sql / format_sql, or the database's own slow-query log) and actually read what gets generated for a given endpoint.
  • Monitor the number of queries per API request — a sudden spike proportional to the result set size (e.g., queries scale linearly with the number of users returned) is the classic signature.
  • Use an APM tool (e.g., New Relic, Datadog, Elastic APM) — most surface a per-request query count and flag "N+1 detected" patterns automatically.
  • Look for repeated queries with different IDs in the log — the same SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? template repeated 100 times with different parameter values is the smoking gun.
  • Test using realistic data volumes — this bug is invisible with 3 test users locally and becomes an incident with 10,000 users in production; load/integration tests need production-like data sizes to catch it before release.

Spring Boot / JPA: Which Fix Should You Prefer?

A common follow-up question: "Which approach do you prefer in Spring Boot — fetch joins, entity graphs, batch fetching, or DTO projections?"

There isn't a single universally-correct answer — it depends on the access pattern — but here's how to reason about the trade-offs:

Approach How it works Best when Watch out for
Fetch Join (JOIN FETCH in JPQL) Single SQL query joins parent + child in one round-trip You always need the child collection alongside the parent for this query Fetching multiple collections with JOIN FETCH in one query causes a Cartesian product explosion (rows multiply); JPA restricts fetching more than one List-type collection this way
Entity Graph (@EntityGraph) Declaratively specifies which associations to eagerly fetch, per query/method, without changing the entity's default fetch type globally You want eager fetching for specific use cases but keep lazy loading as the sane default elsewhere Still one query per graph, but multiple collections in the same graph can hit the same Cartesian-product issue as fetch joins
Batch Fetching (@BatchSize, or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size) Lazy loading still triggers on access, but Hibernate batches the next N pending lazy loads into one IN (...) query instead of one-by-one You have unavoidable lazy access patterns (e.g., generic repository code used in many contexts) and want a broad, low-effort mitigation Doesn't eliminate extra queries entirely, just batches them — still more than a single join, though far better than true N+1
DTO Projections (JPQL constructor expressions, Spring Data interface projections, or a mapper) Query selects only the exact fields needed directly into a DTO — no entity graph traversal at all Read-only / API-response use cases where you don't need full entity objects or their lazy associations Loses JPA entity features (dirty checking, lazy nav) — but for a read API, you don't want those anyway

Default preference: start with DTO projections for read-heavy API endpoints — they sidestep the N+1 problem entirely because there's no entity graph to lazily traverse in the first place, and they also naturally satisfy "fetch only the required fields" (fix #3) at the same time. Reserve fetch joins / entity graphs for cases where you genuinely need full entity objects (e.g., you're about to modify and save them), and use batch fetching as a safety net for lazy-loaded associations you can't easily eliminate across a large, shared codebase.

🔗 Related

  • Designing APIs for Massive Datasets — takes pagination (fix #4) and field projection (fix #3) further for very large datasets: cursor-based pagination, sparse fields, DB-level filtering, caching, and compression.
  • Caching Strategies — caching read-heavy query results to avoid re-paying the query cost at all.

title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
description:
arXiv:2610.20665v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

title: A Self-Improving Agent that Grows its Own DSL: Oracle-Free Operator Induction for Exact Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.20809v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A self-improving agent has to decide which new skills to keep, and in practice it keeps whatever earns a high reward, convinces a judge model, or compresses its library, even when the skill is wrong. That is fine until the answers have to be exactly right: over a table of transactions, a total is either right or wrong. We ask a harder question: can an agent grow what it can compute with no reward, no judge, and no answer key, and still be exactly right? A single frozen model runs two nested loops over a small, exact domain-specific language (DSL). The inner loop answers new questions only when two independently written expressions agree on every record. The outer loop discovers its own missing capability and authors an operator for it, admitted only when an independent second implementation agrees and the result obeys a conservation law, all without ground truth. The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set, and the outer loop self-extends on disjoint starting sets, inventing operators outside the starting closure; a no-induction control answers none of the new questions. The admission rule is empirically sound: it rejects 138 of 138 buggy operator variants under an independent reference, even one written by a different model family, where the admit-if-it-runs, self-consistency, and compression signals the field relies on admit most of them. Unmodified, the same mechanism self-extends on two further domains with unrelated schemas, business-ledger and clinical-encounter question answering, growing their answerable sets more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold. The loop transfers across model families too: run with further proposers, the gate stays sound and independent families self-extend comparably, with only the induction yield tracking each proposer's DSL fluency.
