title: Quantile-Guided Diffusion for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.20739v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantile forecasts summarize uncertainty at each future time step, while diffusion forecasters represent it through sampled future trajectories. We study how predicted quantiles can serve as distributional controls for diffusion forecasting. Specifically, we investigate how the mechanism of quantile integration affects its effectiveness in guiding a pretrained diffusion forecaster. We find that residual control throughout the denoising network yields the most consistent improvements. We instantiate this approach as Control-TS, which learns a quantile-control pathway while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. Across eight benchmarks, Control-TS consistently improves the backbone's CRPS, achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art forecasting models, and retains its gains in capacity-matched comparisons. Further analyses examine how these gains depend on quantile granularity, predictor choice, and forecast quality. Finally, we introduce the Conditional Linear Predictive Score (CLPS), which complements distributional metrics by evaluating the downstream forecasting utility of generated futures. Together, these findings support predicted quantiles as an effective interface between explicit uncertainty estimates and diffusion-based trajectory generation.

title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
description:
arXiv:2610.20778v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.

title: How to trace and evaluate an AI agent in Microsoft Foundry, from the first trace to production monitoring
description:
Microsoft Foundry splits agent observability into three capabilities, and each one answers a different question. Tracing shows what the agent did during a run, evaluation scores how good its answers were against criteria you choose, and monitoring keeps asking both questions once the agent is in front of users. This post goes through them in the order you'll usually need them, using the official Python samples, and it says which parts Microsoft labels as generally available and which as preview, because that label decides how much weight each piece can carry.

What's generally available and what isn't

Tracing is generally available for prompt agents and hosted agents, while workflow agents and external agents are still in preview. Microsoft's Build announcement from June 3, 2026 says tracing and evaluations reached general availability in the spring, but the reference pages still attach preview labels to individual pieces. On the agent evaluators page, Task Adherence, Task Completion, Intent Resolution, Customer Satisfaction, Output Quality and Tool Use Quality are labeled preview, while the tool evaluators such as Tool Call Accuracy don't carry any label at all. On the monitoring page, agent metrics, recurring evaluations, red team scans and alerts are labeled preview, and the page says Microsoft doesn't recommend its preview items for production workloads. The GitHub Action for evaluations is in preview too. I checked these labels on October 14, 2026, and since they change quickly, it's worth reopening the linked pages before you build on any of them.

Step 1, connect Application Insights and read your first trace

Tracing for prompt agents and hosted agents works on the server side, so you don't need to change anything in your code. With the New Foundry toggle turned on, open your project, go to Agents, select Traces and choose Connect, then attach an existing Application Insights resource or create a new one. From that point the runs of an agent hosted in Foundry are recorded through OpenTelemetry, including the model calls, the tool invocations, the decisions the agent took and its dependencies on other services, as described in the observability overview.

To read the traces you'll need the Log Analytics Reader role on the connected Application Insights resource, plus Privileged Monitoring Data Reader when the underlying Log Analytics tables are protected. After you run the agent once, the Traces tab lets you search, filter and sort the traces from the last 90 days, open one to step through its spans, or search by Response ID or Trace ID and open a Conversation ID to see the history, token counts, run steps, tool calls, inputs and outputs. If nothing shows up, the setup page recommends waiting a few minutes and refreshing before you head to its troubleshooting section. That page also covers client side tracing with azure-core-tracing-opentelemetry, which is optional and meant for the code of your own application.

Step 2, evaluate the agent with a small dataset

A trace tells you what happened but not whether the answer was good, and that's the job of evaluation. The sample below follows the official page on evaluating your AI agents, with the rubric generation step removed so it only uses evaluators that ship with Foundry. You'll need the Foundry User role on the project, which Microsoft renamed from Azure AI User without changing the role IDs, and a chat completion model deployment that acts as the judge for the evaluators that use a model.

That page asks for azure-ai-projects 2.4.0 or later, while other pages in the same documentation list lower minimums, so it's safer to install the latest release.

pip install "azure-ai-projects>=2.4.0" azure-identity

Set the environment variables AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT and AZURE_AI_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME, then create a JSONL file called test-queries.jsonl where each line holds a query field. These three lines are only example questions, so swap them for the questions your agent gets.

{"query": "What is the difference between an Azure region and an availability zone?"}
{"query": "When should I use Azure Functions instead of a virtual machine?"}
{"query": "How do I stop a storage account from being publicly accessible?"}

The first part of the script creates the clients and uploads the dataset to your project.

import os
import time

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient

endpoint = os.environ["AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"]
model_deployment = os.environ["AZURE_AI_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME"]
AGENT_NAME = "my-agent"  # replace with the name of your agent

project_client = AIProjectClient(endpoint=endpoint, credential=DefaultAzureCredential())
client = project_client.get_openai_client()

dataset = project_client.datasets.upload_file(
    name="agent-test-queries",
    version="1",
    file_path="./test-queries.jsonl",
)

The second part defines what to measure and creates the evaluation. Coherence is scored by the judge deployment, while Violence comes from the risk and safety group, which the official sample runs without a judge deployment.

from azure.ai.projects.models import TestingCriterionAzureAIEvaluator
from openai.types.eval_create_params import DataSourceConfigCustom

testing_criteria = [
    TestingCriterionAzureAIEvaluator(
        type="azure_ai_evaluator",
        name="Coherence",
        evaluator_name="builtin.coherence",
        initialization_parameters={"deployment_name": model_deployment},
        data_mapping={
            "query": "{{item.query}}",
            "response": "{{sample.output_text}}",
        },
    ),
    TestingCriterionAzureAIEvaluator(
        type="azure_ai_evaluator",
        name="Violence",
        evaluator_name="builtin.violence",
        data_mapping={
            "query": "{{item.query}}",
            "response": "{{sample.output_text}}",
        },
    ),
]

data_source_config = DataSourceConfigCustom(
    type="custom",
    item_schema={
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["query"],
    },
    include_sample_schema=True,
)

evaluation = client.evals.create(
    name="Agent Quality Evaluation",
    data_source_config=data_source_config,
    testing_criteria=testing_criteria,
)

The third part starts the run. With the azure_ai_target_completions source, Foundry sends every query to the agent named in the target and evaluates the answers it gets back, which is why the mappings above read from sample.output_text.

eval_run = client.evals.runs.create(
    eval_id=evaluation.id,
    name="Agent Evaluation Run",
    data_source={
        "type": "azure_ai_target_completions",
        "source": {"type": "file_id", "id": dataset.id},
        "input_messages": {
            "type": "template",
            "template": [
                {
                    "type": "message",
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": {"type": "input_text", "text": "{{item.query}}"},
                }
            ],
        },
        "target": {"type": "azure_ai_agent", "name": AGENT_NAME},
    },
)

while True:
    run = client.evals.runs.retrieve(run_id=eval_run.id, eval_id=evaluation.id)
    if run.status in ["completed", "failed"]:
        break
    time.sleep(5)

print(f"Status: {run.status}")
print(f"Report URL: {run.report_url}")

In the response, result_counts gives the total, passed, failed and errored rows, per_testing_criteria_results breaks the same numbers down by evaluator, and each row carries a score, a label, a reason, a threshold and a passed flag for every evaluator. The report_url opens the same results in the Foundry portal, where they also show up under the Evaluations tab, and the reason field is where I'd start reading when a row fails.

If your agent calls tools, the tool use evaluators are the ones worth adding next. Tool Call Accuracy checks that the agent made the right calls with correct parameters and without redundancy, Tool Selection checks that it chose the tools it needed and no extra ones, Tool Input Accuracy checks the parameters, Tool Output Utilization checks whether the agent used the results correctly, and Tool Call Success checks that the calls ended without technical errors. Four of them take tool_definitions as an input, and Tool Call Accuracy scores on a scale of one to five before a threshold turns that score into a pass or a fail.

What it costs and where it's restricted

Risk and safety evaluations, which include the Violence evaluator used above, and agents playground evaluations are billed on consumption, and playground evaluations are enabled by default for every Foundry project. To turn them off, clear all the evaluators in the playground's metrics selector. Some features also have regional restrictions, namely rubric generation, synthetic and trace based dataset creation, and the risk and safety evaluators, so check the supported regions before you run the sample in a project you already have. The monitoring data itself lives in the connected Application Insights resource, so its retention and billing follow however you've configured that resource.

Step 3, keep evaluating after release

The monitoring page describes continuous evaluation, which runs an evaluation on sampled traffic while the agent serves users. The code below creates an evaluation with an azure_ai_source and attaches a rule that runs it whenever a response from the named agent completes. The project managed identity needs the Foundry User role for continuous evaluation rules to run, and the rule is capped by max_hourly_runs, which the sample sets to 100 and which Microsoft documents as the default limit per hour. Once the cap is reached, further runs are skipped until the next hour or until you raise the value.

import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient
from azure.ai.projects.models import (
    EvaluationRule,
    ContinuousEvaluationRuleAction,
    EvaluationRuleFilter,
    EvaluationRuleEventType,
)

endpoint = os.environ["AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"]
agent_name = os.environ["AZURE_AI_AGENT_NAME"]

with (
    DefaultAzureCredential() as credential,
    AIProjectClient(endpoint=endpoint, credential=credential) as project_client,
    project_client.get_openai_client() as openai_client,
):
    eval_object = openai_client.evals.create(
        name="Continuous Evaluation",
        data_source_config={"type": "azure_ai_source", "scenario": "responses"},
        testing_criteria=[
            {
                "type": "azure_ai_evaluator",
                "name": "violence_detection",
                "evaluator_name": "builtin.violence",
            }
        ],
    )

    rule = project_client.evaluation_rules.create_or_update(
        id="my-continuous-eval-rule",
        evaluation_rule=EvaluationRule(
            display_name="My Continuous Eval Rule",
            description="Runs on agent response completions",
            action=ContinuousEvaluationRuleAction(
                eval_id=eval_object.id, max_hourly_runs=100
            ),
            event_type=EvaluationRuleEventType.RESPONSE_COMPLETED,
            filter=EvaluationRuleFilter(agent_name=agent_name),
            enabled=True,
        ),
    )
    print(f"Rule created (id: {rule.id})")

To read the results, open the agent in the Foundry portal and select Monitor. The dashboard shows token usage, latency, run success rate, evaluation metrics and red teaming results for the time range you pick, and the documentation gives two starting points for interpreting it. Latency above ten seconds may point to model throttling, complex tool calls or network issues, and a run success rate below 95 percent warrants an investigation of the failed runs.

Running the same evaluation on every commit

You can also run the evaluation from Step 2 in a pipeline through the microsoft/ai-agent-evals@v3-beta GitHub Action, which the documentation labels as preview. The step below goes after the checkout and an Azure login step that uses OpenID Connect, so the workflow also needs the id-token: write permission and the client, tenant and subscription IDs stored as GitHub Actions variables.

      - name: Run Evaluation
        uses: microsoft/ai-agent-evals@v3-beta
        with:
          azure-ai-project-endpoint: "<your-ai-project-endpoint>"
          deployment-name: "<your-deployment-name>"
          agent-ids: "<your-ai-agent-ids>"
          data-path: ${{ github.workspace }}/path/to/your/data-file

The agent-ids input takes values such as my-agent:1,my-agent:2, an optional baseline-agent-id sets the version used as the comparison, and the results show up in the workflow run summary with the score of each metric, confidence intervals and, when you compare several agents, a pairwise statistical comparison that tells you whether a difference is meaningful or just random variation. That makes it a reasonable quality gate for changes to an agent's instructions or model, since the same dataset runs against both versions.

If you'd rather see the three pieces working together before you try them, the Azure Friday episode Observe and evaluate agents for quality and safety in Microsoft Foundry walks through evaluation, tracing and monitoring with a live demo in the Foundry portal and in Visual Studio Code.

Which of those three questions is the hardest to answer about your agents today, what they did, how good their answers were, or whether they stay that good after release?

title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.20731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.

title: GBase Database Server Sizing: How to Choose the Right Hardware Tier
description:
Choosing hardware for GBase Database (GBase 8s) isn't about buying the most expensive server. It's about matching resources to your workload.

A practical starting point is to evaluate three deployment tiers: development, small-to-medium workloads, and large-scale enterprise systems.

1. Three GBase Database Hardware Tiers

The following specifications are illustrative planning references. Verify them against the official hardware requirements for your GBase 8s version and target platform before deployment.

Tier Typical workload CPU Memory Storage
Minimum Development and debugging 2 × 2-core CPUs, 2.0 GHz 4 GB 100 GB+
Mid-range Fewer than 100 concurrent users; TPS below 50; data under 100 GB 4 × 4-core CPUs, 3.0 GHz 16–64 GB ECC 1 TB+ enterprise SSD
High-end More than 1,000 concurrent users; TPS above 500; data at least 1 TB 64+ cores 128 GB ECC 2 TB+ SSD; dedicated storage as needed

Important: These tiers are starting points, not universal sizing guarantees. Actual performance depends on transaction complexity, workload mix, indexing, availability requirements, and storage architecture.

2. Three Principles for Database Capacity Planning

First, estimate concurrency and transaction throughput.

Concurrent sessions and transactions per second (TPS) help determine CPU capacity and memory requirements. Benchmark representative workloads rather than relying on user counts alone.

Second, size storage for both capacity and performance.

Data volume determines baseline storage needs, but transaction workloads also depend on IOPS, latency, log-write performance, and growth forecasts. Storage requirements should reflect measured workload characteristics.

Third, leave room for peak demand and growth.

Plan for peak concurrency, data expansion, maintenance operations, and recovery requirements. Sizing a server at its minimum capacity can leave little room for unexpected workload spikes.

3. Why Memory Matters for GBase Database

For an OLTP database such as GBase Database, memory configuration affects caching, concurrency, and overall workload performance.

Insufficient shared memory can prevent instance initialization or constrain workload capacity. However, simply adding RAM doesn't guarantee better performance: shared-memory parameters must also be configured appropriately for the operating system and GBase 8s instance.

Final Takeaway

Effective GBase Database server sizing starts with workload metrics, not hardware price tags.

Estimate concurrency, TPS, data volume, I/O requirements, and future growth. Then validate your proposed configuration through workload testing before production deployment.

How does your team size database servers: workload benchmarks, vendor recommendations, or previous project experience?

title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.20686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.

title: How to Add, Read, Edit, and Delete Excel Comments in Java
description:
When working with Excel spreadsheets, you may need to add information that doesn't belong directly in a cell, such as the reason for a price change, an explanation of an unusual value, or a reminder to verify certain data.

Excel comments let you attach these notes to individual cells without changing their values. You can also use Java to add, read, update, or remove them programmatically.

This article covers these four operations with complete Java examples.

1. Add the Maven Dependency

To get started, add an Excel processing library to your Java project. If you're using Maven, include the following repository and dependency in your pom.xml file:

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <name>e-iceblue</name>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.xls.free</artifactId>
        <version>16.3.1</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

2. Add Comments to Excel Cells in Java

To add a comment to an Excel cell, use the CellRange.addComment() method. It returns an ExcelComment object, which you can use to set the comment text and adjust its appearance.

For the examples below, we'll use a workbook named sales.xlsx, with the following data on its first worksheet:

Product Quantity Unit Price Amount
Product A 20 49 980
Product B 15 60 900

The table occupies cells A1:D3. We'll add a note explaining the price in C2 and another reminding us to verify the amount in D3:

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class AddExcelComments {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            // Load the Excel file
            workbook.loadFromFile("sales.xlsx");

            // Get the first worksheet
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            // Add a comment to cell C2
            ExcelComment comment1 =
                    sheet.getCellRange("C2").addComment();

            comment1.setText(
                    "The unit price was updated this month.");

            // Set the comment box size
            comment1.setWidth(220);
            comment1.setHeight(60);

            // Keep the comment box hidden by default
            comment1.setVisible(false);

            // Add a comment to cell D3
            ExcelComment comment2 =
                    sheet.getCellRange("D3").addComment();

            comment2.setText(
                    "Please verify this amount.");
            comment2.setAutoSize(true);

            // Save the modified workbook
            workbook.saveToFile(
                    "sales-with-comments.xlsx",
                    ExcelVersion.Version2016);

        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The program creates sales-with-comments.xlsx, with a comment attached to each of the two cells.

Besides setting the text, you can control how a comment appears:

  • setWidth() and setHeight() specify the comment box dimensions.

  • setAutoSize(true) adjusts the box size to fit its text.

  • setVisible(false) keeps the comment box from being displayed continuously.

Setting a comment's visibility to false doesn't remove it. The comment remains attached to the cell and can still be viewed in Excel.

3. Read Comments from an Excel Worksheet

You may also need to inspect comments already stored in a workbook, such as when checking notes left during a review.

The Worksheet.getComments() method provides access to the comments collection for a worksheet. You can iterate through it and retrieve each comment's text and location.

The following example reads all comments from the workbook created in the previous section:

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class ReadExcelComments {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            // Load the Excel file
            workbook.loadFromFile(
                    "sales-with-comments.xlsx");

            // Get the first worksheet
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            // Get the number of comments
            int count = sheet.getComments().getCount();

            System.out.println("Total comments: " + count);

            // Read each comment
            for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {

                ExcelComment comment =
                        sheet.getComments().get(i);

                System.out.println("Comment " + (i + 1));
                System.out.println("Row: " + comment.getRow());
                System.out.println("Column: " + comment.getColumn());
                System.out.println("Text: " + comment.getText());
                System.out.println("----------------");
            }

        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The program prints the number of comments and the row, column, and text of each one.

If you already know which cell contains the comment, there's no need to loop through the entire collection. You can retrieve it directly using getComment():

ExcelComment comment =
        sheet.getCellRange("C2").getComment();

if (comment != null) {
    System.out.println(comment.getText());
}

The null check matters because not every cell has a comment. It prevents a NullPointerException when the requested cell has none.

4. Edit an Existing Excel Comment

Comments sometimes need to be updated as the information in a spreadsheet changes.

For example, suppose the unit price in C2 has now been verified. We can replace the original comment with "The current unit price has been verified."

There's no need to remove the existing comment and create a new one. Simply retrieve it with getComment() and update its text using setText().

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class EditExcelComment {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            // Load the workbook containing comments
            workbook.loadFromFile(
                    "sales-with-comments.xlsx");

            // Get the first worksheet
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            // Get the existing comment in C2
            ExcelComment comment =
                    sheet.getCellRange("C2").getComment();

            // Update the comment
            if (comment != null) {

                comment.setText(
                        "The current unit price has been verified.");

                // Resize the comment box to fit the text
                comment.setAutoSize(true);
            }

            // Save the updated workbook
            workbook.saveToFile(
                    "sales-edited-comments.xlsx",
                    ExcelVersion.Version2016);

        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

After running the code, open sales-edited-comments.xlsx to see the updated comment in C2.

Only the comment text and its box sizing are changed. The cell's value remains the same.

You can also modify other comment properties, such as its dimensions, visibility, and text formatting, without recreating the comment.

5. Delete Comments from Excel Cells

Once a note is no longer needed, you can remove it from the worksheet.

Suppose the amount in D3 has been checked, and the reminder to verify it is no longer relevant.

Use getComment() to retrieve the comment, then call remove() to delete it.

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class DeleteExcelComment {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            // Load the workbook containing comments
            workbook.loadFromFile(
                    "sales-with-comments.xlsx");

            // Get the first worksheet
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            // Get the comment in cell D3
            ExcelComment comment =
                    sheet.getCellRange("D3").getComment();

            // Remove the comment if it exists
            if (comment != null) {
                comment.remove();
            }

            // Save the modified workbook
            workbook.saveToFile(
                    "sales-removed-comment.xlsx",
                    ExcelVersion.Version2016);

        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The resulting file, sales-removed-comment.xlsx, no longer contains the comment in D3. The value stored in that cell is preserved, as are the comments in other cells.

If you need to remove comments from several known cells, you can repeat the same operation for each one.

6. A Few Things to Keep in Mind

Traditional Comments vs. Threaded Comments

The examples in this article work with traditional Excel cell comments, which are called Notes in newer versions of Microsoft Excel.

These are different from modern threaded comments, which support replies and @mentions. The APIs shown here should not be assumed to work with threaded comments.

Check Whether a Comment Already Exists

Before adding a comment to a cell, consider whether it already has one.

If your goal is to update an existing note, use getComment() followed by setText() rather than creating another comment.

Save Changes to the Workbook

Adding, editing, or deleting a comment changes the workbook in memory. To write those changes to an Excel file, you must call workbook.saveToFile().

The examples save their results to new files so that the original workbook remains unchanged. If you need to overwrite an existing file, it's worth keeping a backup.

title: Amazon DynamoDB Streams now supports timestamp-based stream processing
description:
Amazon DynamoDB Streams now supports timestamp-based stream processing, enabling you to begin reading stream records from a specific point in time. Previously, you could only start from the oldest retained record (up to 24 hours old) or from new records written after you start consuming the stream. Now, you can supply a timestamp and begin processing at the first record written at or after that time using the AT_TIMESTAMP shard iterator type.

Timestamp-based stream processing can be used with the Amazon Kinesis Client Library (KCL) through the DynamoDB Streams Kinesis adapter. It helps you avoid reprocessing entire retained streams or missing records when resuming stream consumption, supporting common use cases such as recovery after an interruption, data replay for debugging and auditing by reading from a specific point in the past, skipping a backlog by resuming from a recent timestamp near the latest records, and synchronizing after a restore by beginning at the export timestamp following a point-in-time recovery (PITR) export.

Timestamp-based stream processing is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. There is no additional charge for this feature beyond standard GetRecords API request charges. To get started, see Amazon DynamoDB Streams timestamp documentation in the DynamoDB developer guide.

title: Object Storage Backups: Private Access, Retention, and S3-Compatible Delivery
description:
When a game backend writes a nightly database dump, the important constraint is not finding a public URL. It is keeping the bytes private while making a restore download boring and dependable. Short answer: choose private object storage with signed links when day-level retention is enough; choose a dedicated backup system when you need immutable versioned copies.

That decision also determines whether the application has to proxy a 4 GB export. A worker can upload directly to an object store, record the object key in the ledger, and hand an operator a time-limited download link later. The app moves metadata, not the file.

A restore is the first acceptance test

For app data backups, “cheapest” is a three-part number: stored bytes, bytes downloaded during a restore, and request volume. A storage service that looks inexpensive per gigabyte can still be a poor fit if restore traffic is unpredictable or if its tooling forces a custom client. S3-compatible commands and libraries keep a scheduled dump script small, which is useful when the script must be audited six months after it was written.

The backup object should be private by default. Name it with fields you can filter by prefix, such as prod/us-east/db/2026-08-19T02-00Z.sql.gz; server-side metadata search is limited, so the object key becomes part of the index. Keep a database row with the exact key, checksum, creation time, and retention deadline. That row is your audit trail when someone asks which dump was restored, and it gives a reconciliation job enough data to distinguish a missing object from a stale manifest, a distinction that matters when an operator is deciding whether to retry a restore or page the backup owner.

A signed download is an authorization decision, not a new copy. The API creates a URL that expires; the restore service streams from storage to the operator or restore job. There is no permanent public-read ACL in this model, so it is unsuitable for a game launcher that needs an eternal asset URL, a static site, or an image host.

Keep it private.

Short-lived links are easier to reason about. I use a 15-minute window for an interactive restore and log the request ID beside the restore ticket. Your mileage may vary: an overnight transfer over a constrained link may justify a longer window, but that is a policy choice that belongs in configuration, not in a hard-coded URL.

What should private S3-compatible storage provide for app data backups?

The minimum useful contract is deliberately plain:

  1. A private bucket and an object write operation.
  2. A signed read operation for an operator or restore worker.
  3. Lifecycle expiration with a day-level boundary.
  4. Predictable listing by key prefix.
  5. A client-side checksum and an idempotent write record.

The day-level boundary matters. Lifecycle can expire old backups, but it cannot express “delete this at 02:15,” and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule. Set the retention deadline in your own job, then let lifecycle provide a second, coarse safety net.

There is a harder boundary: no object versioning and no object lock (WORM) means an overwrite is not recoverable from the bucket. A ransomware-style credential leak can replace yesterday’s dump with a valid-looking object. For financial or regulatory records that must not change, use a backup platform or an external immutable repository; object storage alone is the wrong control.

Strict compare-and-swap writes are another gap. Without an If-Match condition, two workers can race to the same key. Generate unique keys, serialize promotion in a database or queue, and treat the object checksum as evidence. Exactly-once is a mindset here: retries must be harmless even when the network response is lost.

The upload path should be small and repeatable

The following sketch keeps the application out of the byte path. It uses the documented storage routes for writing an object and creating a signed URL, reads the key from the environment, and makes retries explicit. The request body in a real backup worker would be the dump stream; this small example uses a byte slice so the control flow is visible.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, path string, body []byte, idem string) ([]byte, error) {
    base := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if base == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    url := base + path
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("storage request failed (%s): %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 60 * time.Second}
    bucket := "backup-prod"
    key := "prod/us-east/db/2026-08-19T02-00Z.sql.gz"
    putPath := strings.NewReplacer("{bucket}", bucket, "{key}", key).Replace("/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}")
    if _, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPut, putPath, []byte("backup bytes"), "backup-2026-08-19T02-00Z"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    presignPath := strings.NewReplacer("{bucket}", bucket, "{key}", key).Replace("/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}")
    link, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, presignPath, nil, "sign-2026-08-19T02-00Z")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(link))
}

The idempotency key is stable for the logical backup, not for each network attempt. In production I would also persist the checksum before publishing the database row, then verify the downloaded bytes during a restore. That ordering gives reconciliation something concrete to compare.

Where each storage option fits

The alternatives are not interchangeable once retention and access policy enter the design. AWS S3 is the reference point for S3 tooling and is the natural choice when your organization already depends on its broader backup controls. Cloudflare R2 and Backblaze B2 are credible candidates to price and test for the same private-object workflow. A unified API such as Infrai is useful when the application already has several backend dependencies and one key and one bill reduce credential and invoice reconciliation; its discovery surface and consistent HTTP conventions also keep a small Go worker portable.

Option Private signed downloads Retention and recovery question Good fit
AWS S3 Yes, through the established S3 ecosystem Validate versioning and object-lock policy for your account Teams needing the broadest surrounding AWS controls
Cloudflare R2 Evaluate with the same private-bucket and signed-link test Confirm lifecycle and restore behavior for your regions Workloads already close to Cloudflare delivery
Backblaze B2 Evaluate S3-compatible tooling and private access Confirm retention, replication, and restore operations Teams optimizing a simple backup store
Unified REST storage API Private bucket plus signed access, with one key and bill across backend services Day-level lifecycle; no object versioning or WORM in this model App teams that value one control plane and can add immutable storage separately

Do not turn that table into a benchmark it cannot be. Run a representative dump, a restore, and a failed retry in the regions you actually serve. Record storage, egress, request counts, latency, and the operator steps required to prove which object was restored.

The catch is compliance. If an auditor requires an unalterable seven-year record, the unified object store is not suitable by itself; stick with a dedicated backup platform or add an immutable external target. It is also a poor fit for browser-direct uploads that require self-service CORS configuration, because that workflow needs a separately managed CORS policy. For permanent public links, choose a public asset service instead.

A rollout that preserves the audit trail

Start with one non-production game shard. Create a private bucket, write keys with an environment and timestamp prefix, and set a one-day-or-longer lifecycle rule that matches the retention policy. Keep the manifest in your database, including checksum and restore owner. Then execute three tests: a normal scheduled dump, a duplicate retry with the same idempotency key, and a restore through an expired signed link followed by a newly issued link.

Promote only after the reconciliation report is boring. If the report cannot explain a missing object, pause and fix the manifest or the retention rule before adding more shards. That discipline is more valuable than shaving a fraction from a storage quote.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html

title: Connect devices, sensors and custom hardware to business workflows
description:
Connected hardware is most valuable when it supports a clear operational response. A sensor reading, button press or machine state becomes useful when the platform knows which asset it belongs to, whether the information is current and who should act when something needs attention.

The project should therefore begin with the workflow, not a catalogue of devices.

Define the event and response

Write down what needs to be observed or controlled. Examples include temperature leaving an agreed range, a tank reaching a threshold, an asset arriving at a site or a manual inspection being confirmed.

Then define the response. Who receives the information? Is acknowledgement required? What evidence closes the event? What happens outside business hours? This turns a reading into an operational requirement.

Reuse existing equipment where practical

An older asset may already expose a relay, serial port or industrial protocol. An off-the-shelf product may provide an API or export. Assess the supported interface, documentation, ownership and maintenance implications before adding new hardware.

Where no suitable interface exists, an external sensor or custom gateway may bridge the gap without replacing the asset. The design should respect warranties, electrical isolation, environmental conditions and safe installation.

Treat connectivity as variable

Sites may have weak mobile coverage, restricted networks or periods without power. Decide what the device should do while offline, how much information it stores and how duplicate events are prevented after reconnection.

Show the last contact time in the platform. A missing reading should not be displayed as a normal value. For important processes, create a separate alert for loss of communication and retain a manual check.

Identify every device and asset

Use stable identifiers for the physical unit, installed asset and site. Record commissioning, firmware, calibration and maintenance information where relevant. If hardware is moved or replaced, preserve the history without assigning new readings to the wrong asset.

Avoid using a network address or user-entered label as the only identity. Both can change.

Secure the full path

Limit each device to the services and actions it needs. Protect credentials, rotate them where supported and plan how a lost or retired device is disabled. Validate incoming data and record the source and receipt time.

Remote control requires additional safeguards. Separate monitoring from control, confirm the current state and require appropriate approval for consequential commands.

Connect readings to work

A graph can help with investigation, but daily users often need an exception queue, assigned task and response history. Link the device event to the asset, site and responsible team. Suppress repeated notifications for the same unresolved condition while preserving the underlying readings.

Managers can then review recurring issues and response performance. Leadership can see trends across an asset portfolio without losing the source evidence.

Pilot in the real environment

Test power loss, connectivity loss, invalid readings and physical conditions. Confirm installation and replacement procedures. Establish a baseline and run the connected workflow alongside the current check until the team trusts it.

SuperJupiter designs connected-device platforms and custom integrations as part of a complete operational view. Tell us what asset, signal and response you need to connect.

title: SkillNEO: Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization of Agent Skills
description:
arXiv:2610.20926v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent skills turn procedural knowledge into reusable artifacts, allowing LLM agents to accumulate and refine expertise through experience. Building on this, skill evolution iteratively improves skills using execution feedback. However, improvement may require several interdependent edits, so low-reward versions can still be worth developing. Requiring immediate reward gains can discard useful partial repairs before their benefits emerge. Non-elitist evolution allows new versions to receive further edits despite scoring below earlier ones. For agent skills, this calls for evidence of what to preserve and repair next. We introduce SkillNEO (Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization for Agent Skills), which separately selects a version to use and versions to keep improving. Comparing how related versions perform the same task reveals working steps to preserve and remaining failures to fix. It can also revisit and revise earlier versions using later evidence. Across 86 SkillsBench tasks in eight domains, including software engineering and office work, SkillNEO raises GPT-5.4 Mini's average reward from 49.1% to 66.4%, within GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna's original-skill range. Mini executes tasks, proposes revisions, and edits skills; final evaluation uses the same task instances. Gains span all eight domains. The same skills improve stronger models without further editing. On the 41 tasks with modified skills, reuse improves Luna by 10.5 percentage points and places GPT-5.5 10.6 points above its published original-skill reference. Execution records show these skills can benefit stronger models even when Mini still fails some task requirements. Search histories also show lower-scoring versions leading to skills ultimately selected for use. Together, these findings show that skill evolution can turn a weaker model's partial progress into reusable procedural knowledge for improving more capable agents.

title: Can World and Action Modeling Benefit Each Other under Unified Causal Training?
description:
arXiv:2610.21095v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.

title: FlowBudget: Training-Free Sampling-Budget Estimation for Flow Matching Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler--Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget

title: The Spike Dies When Two Runs Disagree
description:
The Spike Dies When Two Runs Disagree

Consider a worker that retries a failed job three times, and occasionally performs the same side effect twice. Nobody in the incident thread disagrees about the symptom, but everyone disagrees about the cause, and the argument has already outlasted the fix it is about. Someone proposes asking an AI coding assistant to patch it, and the thread splits a second time: half the team wants the diff now, the other half refuses to trust a patch nobody can reproduce.

That split is not a debate about model quality, and no amount of opinion will settle it. What settles it is evidence narrow enough to be produced inside one meeting block: two attempts, one hypothesis, and a kill rule written down before either attempt starts. A spike is not a smaller project; it is a bet with a deadline, and a bet that cannot lose is not a bet.

Write the hypothesis before the clock starts

The spike begins with a single sentence that predicts a specific, falsifiable outcome. Vague goals such as "evaluate the assistant on our codebase" produce hours of pleasant activity and no verdict, because nothing in them can be contradicted. The card below is the correct size for the exercise, and it is short enough to be read aloud before anyone types a prompt.

Hypothesis: the failing test retries_spec::replays_side_effect_once fails because
            the retry wrapper re-enqueues before the first attempt is acknowledged.
Prediction: a patch that acknowledges before re-enqueue makes the test pass twice
            on HEAD <sha>, touching the retry wrapper and nothing else.
Kill criteria: baseline test already green, two runs disagree on outcome, the two
            diffs share no file, or 90 minutes elapse.
Out of scope: production config, performance, security review.

Three properties make this useful. The base revision is pinned, so a moving branch cannot contaminate the comparison. The prediction names an observable result instead of an intention, so "it feels better" is never an outcome. And the kill criteria are checkable by a script, which matters because the person running the spike is the person most motivated to keep it alive.

One passing run is mostly a coincidence

A single attempt that turns a red test green tells you that something worked once. It does not tell you whether the assistant found the cause or merely found a way past the assertion, and those two futures look identical in a terminal. Cheap sampling makes both futures visible: run the same unmodified prompt twice, on the same revision, in two disposable worktrees, then compare outcomes and diffs side by side.

Two runs do not prove correctness, and the protocol never claims they do. They bound how much confidence a 90-minute budget can honestly buy, and they convert a matter of taste into a pair of files on disk. When two runs disagree, the disagreement itself is the finding: the prompt, the test, or the model is unstable, and none of those three should be shipped over.

The discipline that makes this work is refusing to coach the second run. If the first attempt fails and the operator rewrites the prompt, pastes the stack trace, or points at the guilty file, the two runs are no longer samples of the same process. The second run then demonstrates the operator's understanding, which was never the open question.

A harness that shares one ninety-minute clock

The script below creates the worktrees, records the base revision, checks that the target test actually fails before the assistant touches anything, and saves each attempt's patch, diff stat, and test result. One deadline is computed at the start and shared by both runs, so no run receives a private 90 minutes.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# spike.sh - two-run, time-boxed spike harness. Illustrative: adapt the paths and commands.
set -euo pipefail

TEST_CMD=${TEST_CMD:-"npm test -- --runInBand"}
ASSISTANT_CMD=${ASSISTANT_CMD:-"./scripts/ask-assistant.sh"}  # your client, your model
PROMPT=${PROMPT:-"spike/hypothesis.md"}
BUDGET=${BUDGET:-5400}              # 90 minutes of wall clock for the whole spike
RUNS=${RUNS:-2}

OUT="spike/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
mkdir -p "$OUT"
deadline=$(( $(date +%s) + BUDGET ))
left() { echo $(( deadline - $(date +%s) )); }

for n in $(seq 1 "$RUNS"); do
  wt="$OUT/wt$n"
  git worktree add --detach "$wt" HEAD >/dev/null 2>&1      # docs: git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree
  git -C "$wt" rev-parse HEAD > "$OUT/run$n.base"

  # 1. Baseline must fail, or the hypothesis is rejected before any model call.
  if timeout "$(left)"s bash -c "cd '$wt' && $TEST_CMD" > "$OUT/run$n.before" 2>&1; then
    echo "run$n: baseline already green - hypothesis rejected" > "$OUT/verdict.txt"
    exit 2
  fi

  # 2. Exactly one attempt per run, with the prompt piped in unchanged.
  timeout "$(left)"s bash -c "cd '$wt' && $ASSISTANT_CMD < '$PROMPT'" > "$OUT/run$n.answer" 2>&1 || true

  # 3. Evidence: what changed, and whether the test passes now.
  git -C "$wt" diff      > "$OUT/run$n.patch"
  git -C "$wt" diff --stat > "$OUT/run$n.stat"
  if timeout "$(left)"s bash -c "cd '$wt' && $TEST_CMD" > "$OUT/run$n.after" 2>&1; then
    echo pass > "$OUT/run$n.result"
  else
    echo fail > "$OUT/run$n.result"
  fi
done

python3 spike/verdict.py "$OUT"

Two details are easy to get wrong. timeout measures wall clock, so a run that hangs on a prompt cannot borrow time from the next one; the semantics are documented in the coreutils manual. And the worktrees are detached at HEAD, which means the spike never touches the branch a human is working on, while git worktree remove --force and git worktree prune clean up afterwards.

Two transcripts, four possible verdicts

The reduction step is deliberately blunt. It reads the two result files, the two base revisions, and the file lists from the diff stats, then emits exactly one verdict without weighting anything and without asking for a summary.

# spike/verdict.py - reduce two spike runs to one verdict.
import json, pathlib, sys

out = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
runs = {}
for result_file in sorted(out.glob("run[0-9]*.result")):
    name = result_file.name.split(".")[0]
    runs[name] = {
        "result": result_file.read_text().strip(),
        "base": (out / f"{name}.base").read_text().strip()[:12],
        "touched": sorted((out / f"{name}.stat").read_text().splitlines()),
    }

outcomes = [run["result"] for run in runs.values()]
bases = {run["base"] for run in runs.values()}
overlap = set.intersection(*(set(run["touched"]) for run in runs.values())) if runs else set()

if len(runs) < 2:
    verdict, why = "kill", "the spike did not finish both runs inside the budget"
elif len(bases) > 1:
    verdict, why = "kill", "runs started from different revisions"
elif outcomes == ["pass", "pass"] and overlap:
    verdict, why = "ship-to-review", "both runs passed and touched at least one identical file"
elif outcomes == ["pass", "pass"]:
    verdict, why = "kill", "two passes with disjoint diffs; the cause was not identified"
else:
    verdict, why = "kill", "runs disagree on outcome"

(out / "verdict.json").write_text(json.dumps({"verdict": verdict, "why": why, "runs": runs}, indent=2))
print(verdict, "-", why)
Run 1 Run 2 Diffs share a file Verdict
pass pass yes ship to review
pass pass no kill
pass fail either kill
fail fail either kill, and rewrite the hypothesis
any unfinished - kill, with no partial credit

The harshness is the point. A spike that ends with a patch, two transcripts, and a written reason for killing it has produced real value, because the next person will not spend another afternoon on the same argument. "Ship to review" is not "ship": the patch still goes through normal review, and the reviewer still asks the questions a two-run protocol cannot answer.

Where free model access changes the arithmetic

The protocol above doubles the number of attempts and test executions, which is exactly the kind of cost that pushes teams toward sampling once and calling it evidence. MonkeyCode, the open-source project behind this outreach, currently offers free model access and a free server option, which removes the per-attempt price argument from the decision and lets the second run happen as a matter of routine rather than as a favor.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Two honest qualifications belong here. The free tier, including any token allowance, is defined by the project and changes over time, so read the current terms on the project page instead of planning around a number quoted in a blog post. And the assistant invocation in the harness is a placeholder on purpose: the interface for talking to a hosted model is a project detail, so check the repository for its current client shape rather than assuming a command-line tool that may not exist.

Where the free server option genuinely participates is the clock. If the harness runs on a machine that is not the developer's laptop, a slow test suite no longer competes with an editor, and the 90 minutes are spent where the work actually happens. A long run can be detached and its log followed, but the deadline must stay attached to the process.

# Illustrative: detach the spike so the 90-minute clock outlives the terminal session.
cd ~/repo && PROMPT=spike/hypothesis.md nohup ./spike.sh > spike.log 2>&1 &
tail -f spike.log

Limits, and who should skip this entirely

The protocol measures agreement between two samples, and nothing else. It cannot separate a flaky test from a flaky model, so a suite that already fails intermittently will generate kills for the wrong reason; stabilize the flake first or the spike is just noise. It says nothing about performance, security, or behavior under production load, and it never justifies skipping review.

Some teams should not use it at all. Anyone who needs the fix today should fix it today, because a spike is the wrong instrument for an outage. Teams in regulated environments that require auditable tooling and data handling agreements should confirm those constraints before sending code to any hosted assistant. And anyone evaluating a model rather than a bug should choose a different design, because two runs on one test is far too small a sample for that question.

The useful version of this workflow ends with a small directory of evidence: two patches, two base revisions, two test logs, and one verdict with a reason attached. If a spike that costs nothing to repeat is the interesting part, the free model access and free server option are the cheapest way to find out whether your hypothesis survives its first honest disagreement.

title: Compute that takes any shape
description:
Workloads differ in how long they run, how much memory they take, and how much of the environment they control. That previously meant a different compute primitive for each job, so product iterations required provisioning infrastructure, not just working on a feature.

We built Vercel so that none of this has to be your problem. The compute layer is a single system with a simple job. Take any workload, assemble the machine it needs, swap configuration on the fly, and absorb burst capacity in real time.

We call this Fluid.

Builds ran on it first, then sandboxes, and now functions. If you've shipped on Vercel, you've been on Fluid without knowing it.

Fluid compute now runs over 15 million builds a day, 25 million sandboxes a week, and a trillion requests a month.

A history of compute

Changing a machine used to mean changing it by hand. You went down to the computer store, bought a hard drive or a stick of RAM, and swapped it in yourself.

Then you could rent bare metal when you needed it, and use it to serve a website, host a database, or send email.

Then the cloud let you request a machine in any configuration you wanted, choose its operating system, use it, and throw it away when you were done.

For agents, even the cloud is too slow. A standard VM can't provision fast enough to keep up with how they work, but this is where Fluid excels.

How a workload runs on Fluid

When a workload comes in, Fluid assembles a machine to fit its shape. If an agent needs to run code, Hive provides an isolated VM, usually one already warm, so it's ready instantly. Your own image boots on top as the environment. A Drive connects, and your files are right where you left them, because storage was never tied to the machine.

Each workload needs something different. A build is compute-bound, so it wants a beefy machine, heavy on CPU and memory. A function is IO-bound, loading specific code to run the instant a request lands, usually on a small VM. A sandbox is flexibility-bound, taking whatever configuration the work calls for with a Drive attached for user data.

Fluid compute is the execution model that all of this leans on. Many requests run on one instance, instead of each spinning up its own. Work starts immediately, and with Active CPU pricing, you pay for CPU only while your code is working, not while it waits on a database or a model.

Hive

Hive is the "hardware." We built it to control our own compute. It provisions the isolated machines every workload runs on. It picks the right machine for the job, keeps each one isolated in our multitenant environment, and does it at global scale. Hive gives every product one control-plane API, so our teams build on the same foundation instead of each maintaining their own.

Fluid images

Fluid images is the environment. Until now the OS was fixed. You ran the one the cloud gave you, not the one you chose. Now you push your own image to Vercel Container Registry, and run it across sandboxes and functions. In the background, Vercel converts images into a Fluid image in a format we call VHS (Vercel Hive Snapshot), the optimized boot format behind Dockerfile deploys and sandbox custom images, so it can resume rather than boot and a custom machine is ready in milliseconds. It uses the same technology behind Sandbox Snapshots, so optimizations in one product carry to the rest. v0 already uses it to build and run its own development environments.

Vercel Drives

Vercel Drives is the storage. Your files live in portable, durable storage that travels with the workload instead of being stranded on one machine's disk. Storage that outlives the compute attached to it is what makes the rest of the system work. Drives aren't bound to a single machine, you can swap the compute underneath it and pick up exactly where you left off in the next session. Drives attach to sandboxes today, in private beta, and extend to the rest of Fluid from there.

One system underneath

These are different shapes of the same system, not separate platforms. Because it's one compute layer underneath every product, a gain in boot time, isolation, scheduling, or caching lands across functions, sandboxes, and builds at once, instead of being rebuilt three times. New shapes of compute can be added without rebuilding the foundation. You don't end up with separate primitives that drift apart.

And it's real, not a diagram: Hive provisions a full VM in milliseconds and brings your filesystem state along with it, so you get isolation stronger than an isolate or a container, without paying for it in startup time.

The agent workload

For an agent to move fast, it needs the right machine, and it needs it immediately. The faster the machine assembles, the faster the agent works.

An agent runs untrusted code, so the machine needs a secure boundary. It brings its own tools, so the machine needs its own environment. And because an agent spins up and tears down constantly, its state has to outlive the compute. Fluid assembles that machine immediately, and then a fresh one for the next task.

For years, the machine was a fixed thing, and you fit your work to it.

In Fluid you describe the work, and the machine forms around it.

Read more

title: Open-world AI: a Tale of Three Requirements
description:
arXiv:2610.20782v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The closed world asks AI for specialized competence and lets it manufacture the iid data its theory assumes: a fixed criterion licenses collecting examples until the task is covered. The open world asks for versatility --- taking up tasks a machine was not built for, from few examples and with little prior from a human designer --- and offers data that is grouped, not shuffled. Its tasks are not known in advance, so a machine must do inference-time learning (1st requirement). Modeling tasks as sharing latent factors and decomposing the training objective, we derive two more: a *rich representation*, retaining more than iid generalization requires, and a predictive disentanglement that aligns inputs and outputs into matched low-dimensional groups. The analysis further predicts the need for a consistent inner learner, and the benefit of long contexts spanning related tasks. We test these claims on language models up to 8B, asking whether a model has a property (qualitative) rather than how much it wins (quantitative). Models that meet the requirements improve as data from related tasks accumulates; the rest degrade, and neither scale nor layer-type interleaving repairs this.

title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.20795v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.

title: KBS: A Korean Benchmark Suite for Foundation Model Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.21227v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a Korean Benchmark Suite (KBS) comprising Ko-ARC, Ko-GSM8K, Ko-EQ-Bench, Ko-WinoGrande, Ko-LAMBADA, and Ko-IFEval, covering six capabilities across 9,396 items. The suite combines review, localization, direct Korean construction, and redesign for Korean, avoiding a translation-only approach to benchmark adaptation. We evaluate Korean-developed models, multilingual open models, and closed API models under protocols that account for model access, prompt format, and scoring differences. Results show that Korean benchmark scores depend on task construction, scoring rules, prompting, and model post-training. These findings suggest that Korean evaluation should report both final scores and the settings used to obtain them.

title: A Large-Scale Dataset for Multi-Class Financial News Classification in Brazilian Portuguese
description:
arXiv:2610.20630v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The development of Financial Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems for Brazilian Portuguese is hindered by the scarcity of domain-specific datasets. To address this, we present a large-scale corpus of approximately 160,000 Brazilian Portuguese financial news articles collected from web sources. To establish initial benchmarks for a weakly supervised multi-class classification approach based on semantic similarity, we annotated subsets of this corpus both manually and using a Large Language Model (LLM). We evaluated three similarity-based methods -- cosine similarity, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and FAISS-based nearest-neighbor search -- using multilingual semantic embeddings. Our experiments reveal that the task is highly sensitive to label quality and class distribution. On the manually labeled subset, KNN achieved the best performance (47.3% accuracy, 31.9% F1-score), closely followed by FAISS. Conversely, on the LLM-annotated subset, while accuracy reached approximately 50%, F1-scores dropped to near 20%, highlighting the negative impact of label imbalance and noisy weak annotations. These findings establish foundational baselines for a challenging task, underscoring the critical need for high-quality manual annotations. Ultimately, this dataset and our preliminary results provide a reference point for future research in Brazilian Portuguese Financial NLP.
