title: Weekend Build Log: A Notes Index That Ships Without an API Key
description:
Your notes folder is a landfill. The fix you wrote three weeks ago is inside it somewhere.

You open far too many files and find nothing. So Saturday gets one query: type a word, get the right section.

This is that build log. Three commands, one SQLite file, one optional model call.

The scope cut

Weekend projects die from ambition, not from bugs. Pick one input, one query, one output.

My fence for Saturday:

  1. Input: a folder of Markdown files.
  2. Output: the top ten matching sections in a terminal.
  3. Budget: four hours, then stop.

Everything else goes into SKIPPED.md. You will read that file on Sunday and feel fine.

Step 1: Prove the index works with no API key

Start with SQLite FTS5. It ships inside Python, and it needs no network at all.

Check it exists before writing more code:

python -c "import sqlite3; sqlite3.connect(':memory:').execute('CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE t USING fts5(x)'); print('fts5 ok')"

If that fails, your Python links an old SQLite. Stop and fix the environment first.

Now the indexer. It splits each file on headings, so a hit points at a section, not a whole file.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""index_notes.py - index a Markdown folder, then search it. Stdlib only."""
import hashlib
import json
import pathlib
import re
import sqlite3
import sys

DB = pathlib.Path("notes.db")
STORE = pathlib.Path("summaries.json")
HEADING = re.compile(r"^#{1,6}\s+(.*)$", re.M)


def connect():
    con = sqlite3.connect(DB)
    con.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
    return con


def chunks(text):
    parts = HEADING.split(text)
    if len(parts) == 1:
        return [("", text)]
    return [(parts[i].strip(), parts[i + 1].strip()) for i in range(1, len(parts), 2)]


def index(con, root):
    summaries = json.loads(STORE.read_text()) if STORE.exists() else {}
    con.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS notes")
    con.execute(
        "CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE notes USING fts5("
        "path UNINDEXED, title, body, summary, tokenize='porter')"
    )
    root = pathlib.Path(root)
    n = 0
    for md in sorted(root.rglob("*.md")):
        rel = str(md.relative_to(root))
        text = md.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
        for title, body in chunks(text):
            h = hashlib.sha1((title + "\n" + body).encode()).hexdigest()
            con.execute(
                "INSERT INTO notes (path, title, body, summary) VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
                (rel, title, body, summaries.get(h)),
            )
            n += 1
    con.commit()
    print(f"indexed {n} chunks from {root}")


def search(con, query, limit=10):
    sql = (
        "SELECT path, title, summary, "
        "snippet(notes, 2, '[', ']', ' ... ', 12) "
        "FROM notes WHERE notes MATCH ? ORDER BY rank LIMIT ?"
    )
    for path, title, summary, snip in con.execute(sql, (query, limit)):
        print(f"\n{path} :: {title or '(intro)'}")
        if summary:
            print(f"  summary: {summary}")
        print(f"  {snip}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cmd = sys.argv[1]
    con = connect()
    if cmd == "index":
        index(con, sys.argv[2])
    elif cmd == "search":
        search(con, " ".join(sys.argv[2:]))
    else:
        sys.exit("usage: index_notes.py index <folder> | search <query>")

Two decisions matter. The table is rebuilt on every run. Summaries live in a JSON file, not in the database.

Both are wrong at a scale you do not have yet. Both save you an hour on Saturday.

Run it, and run this smoke test before you trust it:

mkdir -p /tmp/notes
printf '# Alpha\nsqlite fts5 is fine\n' > /tmp/notes/alpha.md
python index_notes.py index /tmp/notes
python index_notes.py search fts5

You should see alpha.md and the sentence around the match. If not, fix that before adding anything.

Step 2: Search before you generate

Search first, model second. If keyword search already finds your section, you just saved a batch and a bill.

FTS5 ranking is boring, and boring is a feature on a Saturday.

The honest weakness is synonyms. You type "auth", the note says "login". Keyword search misses it.

Step 3: Add a model only to the part that needs it

Enrichment is the only step here that needs a model, and it is also the step you can skip.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

MonkeyCode is the tool I reached for on this step, because its free model access makes a batch job cheap to try. The script below assumes an OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions route. If your dashboard shows a different path, change one line. It reads the base URL, key, and model id from the environment, so nothing here hardcodes a model name.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""enrich.py - optional. One model call per chunk. Resumable via summaries.json."""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import pathlib
import sys
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

from index_notes import STORE, chunks

BASE = os.environ.get("MONKEYCODE_BASE_URL", "").rstrip("/")
KEY = os.environ.get("MONKEYCODE_API_KEY", "")
MODEL = os.environ.get("MONKEYCODE_MODEL", "")


def pending(store, root, limit):
    todo = []
    for md in sorted(pathlib.Path(root).rglob("*.md")):
        text = md.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
        for title, body in chunks(text):
            h = hashlib.sha1((title + "\n" + body).encode()).hexdigest()
            if h not in store:
                todo.append((h, title, body))
            if len(todo) >= limit:
                return todo
    return todo


def summarize(title, body):
    payload = {
        "model": MODEL,
        "temperature": 0,
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": "Summarize for keyword search. Max 20 words. Plain text only."},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"{title}\n\n{body[:2000]}"},
        ],
    }
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{BASE}/chat/completions",
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as r:
        return json.loads(r.read())["choices"][0]["message"]["content"].strip()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if not (BASE and KEY and MODEL):
        sys.exit("set MONKEYCODE_BASE_URL, MONKEYCODE_API_KEY, MONKEYCODE_MODEL")
    root = sys.argv[1]
    batch = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 50
    store = json.loads(STORE.read_text()) if STORE.exists() else {}
    todo = pending(store, root, batch)
    print(f"{len(todo)} chunks need a summary")
    for h, title, body in todo:
        try:
            store[h] = summarize(title, body)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            print("stopping on HTTP", e.code, e.read()[:200])
            break
        except Exception as e:
            print("stopping on", type(e).__name__, e)
            break
        STORE.write_text(json.dumps(store, indent=0))
        time.sleep(0.2)
    print(f"{len(store)} summaries on disk")

Run it in small batches, then re-index:

export MONKEYCODE_BASE_URL="..."   # copy from your dashboard
export MONKEYCODE_API_KEY="..."
export MONKEYCODE_MODEL="..."
python enrich.py ~/notes 50
python index_notes.py index ~/notes

The script writes after every success, so a crash costs one call. A 429 stops the batch instead of hammering the endpoint.

Step 4: Move the slow part off your laptop

The batch touches every changed note. That is a night job, not a foreground one.

MonkeyCode advertises a free server option alongside its free model access. Treat every availability claim in this article as operator-stated and short-lived: quotas, model ids, and limits change, so read the pricing page on the day you build.

A nightly line is enough:

0 3 * * * cd ~/notes-index && python enrich.py ~/notes 200 >> enrich.log 2>&1 && python index_notes.py index ~/notes >> enrich.log 2>&1

Cap the work per night. A fixed batch size is a budget you can predict.

Decision table

Your situation Add the model? Why
Under ~200 notes, you search by word No FTS5 rank is already enough
You forget your own vocabulary Yes, summaries only Synonyms get a place to live
You want "meaning" search Neither You need embeddings and a vector store
Air-gapped or offline machine No Enrichment needs the network
You will not watch a bill Start free, set a batch cap Free tiers end, jobs keep running

What I skipped

  1. No UI. The terminal is the interface.
  2. No incremental indexing. A full rebuild is fine at this size.
  3. No watcher process. Cron is enough.
  4. No PDF or Office parsing. Markdown only.
  5. No embeddings. That is a different weekend.

The SKIPPED.md list is the point. Write it before you start, not after you quit.

Limits and who should not use this

Summaries drift. Re-run enrichment when notes change, or your index describes an older version of you.

Full rebuilds get slow past a few tens of thousands of chunks. Measure your own folder; do not take my word for it.

Skip this approach if you need semantic search, multi-user access, or live sync. Skip it if you cannot keep an API key out of a public repo.

Start with the offline index. It ships whether or not the model answers, and that is the only promise a weekend needs.

If you do want to try the paid-parts-for-free route, point MONKEYCODE_BASE_URL at your own key and run one fifty-chunk batch first.

title: Free AWS practice exams: how to actually use them well
description:
Most of us have wasted at least one practice exam. You sit down, blast through 65 questions, glance at the score, feel either great or terrible, and then move on. Maybe you retake it a day later, accidentally memorize a few answers, and convince yourself you're ready.

That's not preparation. That's pattern matching.

I've been through the AWS certification cycle a few times now (SAA, DVA, and recently SAP), and I've learned that how you use practice exams matters way more than how many you take. Here's the approach that actually works.

What a practice exam is actually for

A good practice exam isn't a study tool. It's a diagnostic tool. Think of it like a test suite for your knowledge. You're not running it to make the tests pass. You're running it to find out what's broken.

A well-designed mock mirrors the real certification exam blueprint: same domain weighting, same question format, same time pressure. The goal is to surface your weak domains before you pay $300 for the real thing and find out the hard way.

There are a bunch of free options out there. I've been using mockapi.vip lately for AWS, Azure, and CompTIA practice questions. Every answer comes with an explanation, which turns out to be the most important feature. I'll get into why below.

Your first attempt should be a clean run

Here's the first principle: your first attempt at a full-length mock should simulate real exam conditions.

That means:

  • Set a timer (65 questions in 130 minutes for most AWS exams)
  • No second monitor with docs open
  • No "let me just check this one thing"
  • No phone

I know it's tempting to look things up as you go. Don't. The entire point is to get an honest baseline. If you cheat your practice exam, you're only cheating your own feedback loop.

My personal exam-day simulation checklist

  • [ ] Close all browser tabs except the exam
  • [ ] Phone in another room
  • [ ] Timer set (visible but not distracting)
  • [ ] Water bottle ready
  • [ ] No music, no podcasts
  • [ ] Flag uncertain questions, but don't dwell

After you finish, write down your score and note which questions you flagged as uncertain, even if you got them right. A lucky guess isn't knowledge.

The review phase is where the real learning happens

This is where most people cut corners, and it's where the bulk of the value lives.

Go through every single wrong answer. Not just the ones you got wrong, but also the ones you flagged. For each one:

  1. Read the explanation carefully
  2. Identify which domain or topic it falls under
  3. Ask yourself: did I not know this, or did I misread the question?

Here's a simple tracking format I use:

Missed questions log, AWS SAA mock #1

# Domain Topic Root cause Action
12 Networking VPC peering vs Transit GW Didn't know Study VPC architectures
27 Security KMS key policies Misread question Re-read; tricky "LEAST privilege" q
34 Storage S3 lifecycle transitions Confused Glacier tiers Review storage class comparison
41 Compute ECS vs EKS use cases Guessed correctly Still need to study

The "Root cause" column is everything. There's a huge difference between "I didn't know this existed" and "I knew the concept but got tripped up by the wording." They require completely different fixes.

Map your weak domains

After your review, you should have a clear picture of which exam domains need work. AWS exams publish their domain breakdown. For example, the Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03) looks roughly like:

Domain 1: Secure Architectures         30%
Domain 2: Resilient Architectures       26%
Domain 3: High-Performing Architectures 24%
Domain 4: Cost-Optimized Architectures  20%

If you're missing 60% of your security questions but acing cost optimization, you don't need to re-study everything. You need to spend a week deep-diving into IAM policies, KMS, Security Groups vs NACLs, and encryption patterns.

The retake strategy

Here's where the method comes together. After spending focused time on your weak domains:

Wait at least a week, then take another mock. If your platform supports filtering by domain, target just the weak areas. On mockapi.vip, the explanations map to exam domains, which makes it straightforward to focus your retake on what actually needs work.

If domain filtering isn't available, take another full-length mock but pay special attention to your previously weak areas. Your score trajectory across attempts should look something like this:

Mock 1 (baseline):     62%  -> Identified weak: Security, Networking
Mock 2 (after study):  74%  -> Improved Security, still weak Networking
Mock 3 (after study):  82%  -> Passing range, schedule the real exam

The threshold I use: if you're consistently scoring 80%+ on practice mocks, you're probably ready. Most AWS exams have a passing score around 720/1000 (roughly 72%), so 80% gives you a comfortable buffer for exam-day nerves.

Mistakes that will cost you

Don't memorize answers. If you take the same exact mock three times, you will start recognizing questions by their first few words. That's useless. Use different question sets or wait long enough between retakes that the specifics fade.

Don't skip the explanations for correct answers. Sometimes you picked the right answer for the wrong reason. The explanation might reveal a concept you didn't fully understand.

Don't take a mock the night before your real exam. If you score poorly, you'll psych yourself out. If you score well, you'll get overconfident. The night before is for rest.

Don't use practice exams as your only study method. Mocks are diagnostic. Pair them with documentation, hands-on labs, or video courses. The ideal loop looks like this:

Study -> Mock -> Review -> Targeted study -> Mock -> Review -> Schedule exam

On free vs. paid exams

You don't necessarily need to spend money on practice exams. There are legitimate free options with quality explanations. I mentioned mockapi.vip earlier, and it's been solid for my recent prep. Good coverage across the AWS exam domains, clear explanations for each answer. The important thing is that whatever you use has up-to-date questions aligned to the current exam version and detailed explanations, not just "A is correct."

Paid options sometimes offer more questions or advanced analytics, but for most people, a free set used properly beats a paid set used carelessly.

Putting it all together

Here's the full method, condensed:

  1. Take one full mock under real exam conditions
  2. Score it honestly, and flag uncertain correct answers too
  3. Review every wrong and flagged answer, log root causes
  4. Identify your weakest domains
  5. Study those domains specifically for a week
  6. Retake and measure improvement
  7. Repeat until you're consistently hitting 80%+
  8. Schedule the real exam

Practice exams are the highest-signal feedback loop you have in cert prep. Use them deliberately, and you'll walk into the testing center knowing exactly where you stand.

Good luck out there.

title: Building and Deploying an Interactive Sales Dashboard with Streamlit, GitHub Actions and Streamlit Community Cloud
description:
¿Por qué Streamlit?

Hay muchas herramientas para construir dashboards en Python y R. Un resumen rápido:

Herramienta Lenguaje Ideal para Curva de aprendizaje
Streamlit Python Apps de datos rápidas, prototipos y demos Muy baja
Dash (Plotly) Python Dashboards empresariales con callbacks finos Media
Bokeh Python Gráficos interactivos y streaming de datos Media
Seaborn Python Gráficos estadísticos estáticos (reportes) Baja
Shiny R / Python Apps reactivas, muy usado en estadística Media

Elegí Streamlit porque un script de Python normal se convierte en una app web, sin HTML, CSS ni JavaScript. Cada vez que el usuario mueve un filtro, Streamlit vuelve a ejecutar el script de arriba hacia abajo. Ese modelo mental es muy simple.

Arquitectura del proyecto 

.
├── app.py                     # Interfaz de Streamlit + gráficos
├── src/data.py                # Lógica de datos (sin Streamlit → testeable)
├── data/sales.csv             # Dataset sintético (6 000 pedidos 2024-2025)
├── scripts/generate_data.py   # Generador reproducible del dataset
├── tests/                     # Tests unitarios + smoke test de la app
├── .streamlit/config.toml     # Tema visual
├── .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
├── requirements.txt
└── requirements-dev.txt

La decisión de diseño más importante es separar la lógica (src/data.py) de la interfaz (app.py). Así puedo probar los cálculos con pytest sin levantar un navegador.

Paso 1: Los datos

Para no depender de datos privados, generé un dataset sintético pero realista con numpy y una semilla fija (seed=42), así siempre sale igual. Incluye:

  • 5 regiones del Perú (Lima, Arequipa, Trujillo, Cusco, Piura)
  • 5 categorías (Electronics, Home, Sports, Clothing, Beauty)
  • 2 canales (Online y Store)
  • Estacionalidad: picos en julio (Fiestas Patrias) y en noviembre-diciembre
  • Crecimiento de ~20 % en 2025 respecto a 2024 
# scripts/generate_data.py (fragmento)
dates = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2025-12-31", freq="D")
weights = np.ones(len(dates))
weights[dates.month.isin([7])] *= 1.4        # Fiestas Patrias
weights[dates.month.isin([11, 12])] *= 1.8   # Campaña navideña
weights[dates.year == 2025] *= 1.2           # Crecimiento anual
weights /= weights.sum()

order_dates = rng.choice(dates, size=N_ORDERS, p=weights)

Paso 2: La lógica de negocio (testeable)

En src/data.py están las funciones puras que usa el dashboard:

def filter_sales(df, start, end, regions=None, categories=None, channels=None):
    mask = (df["order_date"].dt.date >= start) & (df["order_date"].dt.date <= end)
    if regions:
        mask &= df["region"].isin(regions)
    if categories:
        mask &= df["category"].isin(categories)
    if channels:
        mask &= df["channel"].isin(channels)
    return df.loc[mask]


def compute_kpis(df):
    revenue = float(df["revenue"].sum())
    profit = float(df["profit"].sum())
    orders = int(df["order_id"].nunique())
    return {
        "revenue": revenue,
        "profit": profit,
        "orders": orders,
        "avg_ticket": revenue / orders if orders else 0.0,
        "margin": profit / revenue if revenue else 0.0,
    }

Si un filtro está vacío, se toma como "todos". Además, compute_kpis no divide entre cero cuando no hay datos. Ambos casos tienen su test.

Paso 3: El dashboard con Streamlit + Plotly

Carga con caché y filtros en la barra lateral 

import plotly.express as px
import streamlit as st
from src.data import breakdown, compute_kpis, filter_sales, load_sales, monthly_revenue

st.set_page_config(page_title="Sales Dashboard", page_icon="📊", layout="wide")

@st.cache_data
def get_data():
    return load_sales()

df = get_data()

st.sidebar.header("Filters")
min_d, max_d = df["order_date"].min().date(), df["order_date"].max().date()
date_range = st.sidebar.date_input("Date range", (min_d, max_d), min_value=min_d, max_value=max_d)
start, end = date_range if len(date_range) == 2 else (min_d, max_d)

regions = st.sidebar.multiselect("Region", sorted(df["region"].unique()))
categories = st.sidebar.multiselect("Category", sorted(df["category"].unique()))
channels = st.sidebar.multiselect("Channel", sorted(df["channel"].unique()))

data = filter_sales(df, start, end, regions, categories, channels)

@st.cache_data hace que el CSV se lea una sola vez, aunque el script se vuelva a ejecutar con cada clic.

Tarjetas de KPIs 

k = compute_kpis(data)
c1, c2, c3, c4, c5 = st.columns(5)
c1.metric("Revenue", f"S/ {k['revenue']:,.0f}")
c2.metric("Profit", f"S/ {k['profit']:,.0f}")
c3.metric("Orders", f"{k['orders']:,}")
c4.metric("Avg. ticket", f"S/ {k['avg_ticket']:,.2f}")
c5.metric("Margin", f"{k['margin']:.1%}")

Gráficos

Usé Plotly Express porque sus gráficos ya son interactivos (zoom, hover, ocultar series):

monthly = monthly_revenue(data)
fig_trend = px.line(monthly, x="month", y=["revenue", "profit"], markers=True)
fig_trend.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
st.plotly_chart(fig_trend, width="stretch")

El dashboard final tiene:

  1. Tendencia mensual de ingresos y utilidad
  2. Ingresos por categoría (barras horizontales)
  3. Ingresos por región (barras)
  4. Online vs. tienda (dona)
  5. Mapa de calor categoría × región
  6. Tabla de pedidos filtrados con botón para descargar CSV Para probarlo en local: 
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
streamlit run app.py

Paso 4: Tests automáticos

Hay dos tipos de pruebas:

Unitarias, para la lógica de datos:

def test_monthly_revenue_totals_match(df):
    m = monthly_revenue(df)
    assert m["revenue"].sum() == pytest.approx(df["revenue"].sum())
    assert len(m) == 24  # ene-2024 .. dic-2025

Smoke test de la app completa, con AppTest. Streamlit ejecuta la app sin navegador y podemos interactuar con los widgets:

from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest

def test_region_filter_updates_kpis():
    at = AppTest.from_file(APP, default_timeout=60).run()
    total_orders = at.metric[2].value
    at.sidebar.multiselect[0].select("Cusco").run()
    assert not at.exception
    assert at.metric[2].value != total_orders

Así compruebo que la app no lanza excepciones y que los filtros cambian los KPIs.

Paso 5: Despliegue automatizado con GitHub Actions

Esta es la parte clave. Streamlit Community Cloud redespliega la app cada vez que cambia la rama a la que está conectada. Si la conecto a main, cualquier error llegaría directo a producción.

La solución: conectar Streamlit Cloud a una rama production que solo GitHub Actions actualiza, y solo si los tests pasan.

push a main ──► GitHub Actions: ruff + pytest
                     │ (solo si todo pasa ✅)
                     ▼
         promueve el commit a la rama `production`
                     │
                     ▼
  Streamlit Community Cloud detecta el cambio ──► redeploy
                     │
                     ▼
     Actions verifica que la URL pública responda HTTP 200

# .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  test:
    name: Lint & test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: requirements-dev.txt
      - run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - run: ruff check .
      - run: pytest -v

  deploy:
    name: Deploy to Streamlit Community Cloud
    needs: test
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    environment:
      name: production
      url: ${{ vars.APP_URL }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Promote tested commit to the production branch
        run: git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/production --force
      - name: Wait for Streamlit Cloud and check the public URL
        if: vars.APP_URL != ''
        run: |
          sleep 60
          for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
            code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -L "${{ vars.APP_URL }}")
            echo "Attempt $i -> HTTP $code"
            [ "$code" = "200" ] && exit 0
            sleep 30
          done
          exit 1

Puntos importantes:

  • needs: test → el job de deploy espera a que pasen los tests.
  • if: ... refs/heads/main → los pull requests se prueban, pero no se despliegan.
  • permissions: contents: write → permite que el workflow haga push a la rama production.

- environment: production → GitHub muestra el historial de despliegues y el link de la app en la página del repo.

Paso 6: Publicar en Streamlit Community Cloud

  1. Entra a share.streamlit.io e inicia sesión con GitHub.
  2. Haz clic en Create app → Deploy a public app from GitHub.
  3. Configura:
    • Repository: IkerASierraR/streamlit-sales-dashboard
    • Branch: production
    • Main file path: app.py
    • App URL: iker-sales-dashboard
  4. Haz clic en Deploy. Streamlit instala requirements.txt y en uno o dos minutos la app está en línea.
  5. En GitHub, ve a Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables y crea APP_URL con la URL pública. Así se activa la verificación automática. Desde ese momento, el flujo de trabajo es: 
git add .
git commit -m "feat: add new chart"
git push

…y en unos minutos el cambio está publicado. Sin tocar ningún servidor. 🚀

Resultado

✅ Dashboard interactivo con 5 KPIs, 5 gráficos, filtros y descarga de CSV
✅ Repositorio público con código, tests y documentación
✅ Pipeline de CI/CD: lint → tests → deploy → verificación
✅ App pública y gratuita en Streamlit Community Cloud

🔗 Pruébalo aquí: https://iker-sales-dashboard.streamlit.app

IkerASierraR / streamlit-sales-dashboard

Conclusiones

  • Streamlit permite pasar de un análisis en pandas a una app web en muy pocas líneas.
  • Separar la lógica de la interfaz hace que el dashboard sea fácil de probar.
  • Una rama production controlada por CI es una forma simple y gratuita de tener despliegue continuo seguro en Streamlit Community Cloud.
  • La misma idea sirve para otras herramientas: Dash o Shiny en Render, Hugging Face Spaces, Railway, etc. Si te sirvió, deja un ❤️ o un comentario. ¡Gracias por leer!

title: SHIP: Structured and Hierarchical Insight with Privacy
description:
arXiv:2610.21048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Extracting insights from textual data while protecting user privacy is increasingly important. Existing methods produce private insights in diverse forms for different analytical purposes, making their utility difficult to assess and compare. In this work, we formulate differentially private (DP) insights as reusable representations for answering analytical queries, providing a common basis for utility assessment. Answering these queries, however, requires fine-grained details and cross-attribute statistics that existing representations may omit. To capture this information, we introduce Structured and Hierarchical Insight with Privacy (SHIP), which automatically maps queries to attributes, builds a hierarchical hybrid taxonomy, and releases a DP synthetic table for further analysis. We also develop an evaluation protocol based primarily on QA performance and structured fidelity. Our experiments demonstrate SHIP's strong performance on both measures relative to existing private insight baselines, while identifying queries that remain challenging for structured representations.

title: Pre-Installation Dependency Check Script for GBase Database (GBase 8s)
description:
Missing system dependencies are a common source of Linux installation problems. When installing GBase Database (GBase 8s), discovering a missing library halfway through deployment can mean unnecessary troubleshooting and delays.

A better approach is to check the environment before running the installer.

1. Run a Dependency Pre-Check

On RPM-based Linux systems, the following Bash script checks whether a list of specified packages is installed:

#!/bin/bash

PKGS="libaio libgcc libstdc++ ncurses pam unzip libtinfo tar"

missing=0

for pkg in $PKGS; do
    if rpm -q "$pkg" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        echo "OK      $pkg"
    else
        echo "MISSING $pkg"
        missing=1
    fi
done

if [ "$missing" -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "All packages in the check list are installed."
else
    echo "Some packages are missing. Review them before installation."
    exit 1
fi

Save the script as check_deps.sh, then run:

chmod +x check_deps.sh
./check_deps.sh

2. Understand the Results

  • OK: The specified RPM package is installed.
  • MISSING: The package name was not found in the RPM database. Verify the correct package name for your operating system.

Package names and dependencies vary across Linux distributions and versions. For example, libstdc++ is a common RPM package name, while compat-libstdc may refer to a legacy package available only on certain platforms.

Java packages and compatibility libraries should only be added to the checklist when required by your specific GBase Database installation package and deployment documentation.

3. Resolve Missing Dependencies

Before installing missing packages, confirm that they are required for your target GBase 8s version and supported operating system.

On systems using YUM, you can install a verified package with:

sudo yum install <package-name>

For newer systems, the package manager may be DNF instead.

Important: This script checks package installation status; it does not verify library compatibility, CPU architecture, configuration, or whether the database can initialize successfully.

Final Takeaway

A GBase Database pre-installation dependency check helps identify potential issues before deployment begins. Combine it with checks for disk space, shared memory, environment variables, and platform compatibility to build a more reliable installation workflow.

For multi-node deployments, standardizing these checks can reduce repeated troubleshooting and improve consistency.

title: SATOR: Backpropagation-Free 3D Test-Time Adaptation via Sample-Adaptive Token Routing
description:
arXiv:2610.21367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.

title: MeddeX: A Retrieval-Augmented LLaMA-3 System with Gemini Vision for Evidence-Backed Medical Report Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.20632v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern healthcare generates increasingly complex medical reports that challenge clinical professionals in terms of time and interpretive burden. Manual review processes are slow, error-prone, and difficult to scale. This paper presents MeddeX, a Medical Report Analyzer that combines a QLoRA fine-tuned LLaMA-3 (8B) model with Retrieval-Augmented Gen eration (RAG) and a multimodal Gemini Vision layer to deliver accurate, concise, and evidence-backed summaries of medical documents. The system handles text-native PDFs, scanned image based PDFs, and direct radiological images through an intelligent hybrid extraction pipeline that includes a novel garbage-text detection mechanism for corrupted and UTF-16-encoded doc uments. Beyond single-report Q&A, MeddeX introduces report scoped retrieval for precise contextual grounding, an automated longitudinal report comparison engine, and a self-healing backfill pipeline that lazily processes legacy documents on demand. A FastAPI backend, Supabase vector store, and Next.js fron tend complete the end-to-end architecture. Evaluation against the base LLaMA3-Med42-8B model demonstrates consistent improvements across ROUGE-1 (+9.2%), ROUGE-2 (+10.0%), ROUGE-L (+11.8%), BLEU (+71.4%), and BERTScore (+0.8%), validating the benefit of domain-specific fine-tuning. MeddeX represents a practical and robust step toward AI-assisted clinical decision support.

title: CoSTA: Compressed Speech Token Adaptation for Efficient Spoken Dialogue Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21143v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.

title: Learning When to Withdraw: Curriculum Coverage and Rule-Specific Failures in Fine-Tuned Language Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using language agents must revise prepared actions when evidence changes or authority is revoked. Selective withdrawal means suspending affected actions, preserving supported work, and resuming only after sufficient repair. We study supervised fine-tuning in NAQD-Env, a synthetic environment with explicit dependencies and a deterministic reference policy. Four LoRA checkpoints of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct compare an original curriculum with an enriched one, the latter under three system-prompt framings with identical views and targets. Three instruction-tuned baselines and all four checkpoints are evaluated under three inference prompts on fresh validation cases, held-out dependency families, and held-out structural combinations. Under the naqd prompt, SFT checkpoints reach decision agreement of 0.77-0.92 and withdrawal recall of 0.46-0.86, versus 0.45-0.63 and at most 0.06 for the baselines. Rule-level diagnostics qualify these gains. The original-curriculum checkpoint wrongly withdraws 26 of 34 actions with surviving alternative support; enriched checkpoints withdraw 0-1. Conversely, all SFT checkpoints narrow prohibited combinations less often than the 7B and 8B baselines, a case absent from both curricula. Delegation results show more withdrawal but poorer preservation of independently authorized actions, and all four checkpoints omit valid event reports. Framing contrasts vary across metrics and splits and do not establish a reproducible advantage or equivalence. One training run per arm, jointly changed curriculum properties, prior evaluation exposure, and baseline-SFT quantization differences limit causal attribution. The contribution is a method for detecting rule-specific regressions that aggregate accuracy can conceal, not evidence that fine-tuning alone ensures agent safety.

title: Bellman-Consistent Trajectory RL for LLM Arithmetic Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.21060v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To address sparse terminal rewards in LLM arithmetic reasoning, we propose a Bellman-consistent trajectory RL method. Our framework introduces Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (TBRM) to transform sparse rewards into dense token-level signals. We integrate a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) group strategy to reduce gradient variance of Bellman residuals and use hindsight goal relabeling to accelerate intermediate learning. Evaluated on the Countdown task, our method alleviates optimization bottlenecks and stabilizes gradient variance significantly better than GRPO. The TBRM-RLOO framework boosts Pass@1 to 0.55--0.64 and achieves a state-of-the-art Pass@16 accuracy of 76.0--84.0\%, outperforming the SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines. Our approach demonstrates exceptional single-sample efficiency and successfully circumvents standard performance plateaus via test-time scaling.

title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
description:
arXiv:2610.21046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.

title: Persistent memory for eve agents

eve agents can now retain context across sessions and use it in future conversations.

Persistent memory is organized into slots. You can define named slots in files under agent/memory/. Each slot specifies a provider, which stores and retrieves the memory, and a scope, which determines who or what shares it. For example, you can keep separate memory for each authenticated user.

Before each turn, eve retrieves relevant memory and adds it to the model's context. Depending on the provider, memory can be updated automatically after a turn, through tools the agent uses, or through both methods.

To add eve's built-in file memory provider, run:

The command creates a file memory slot scoped to each authenticated caller:

For agents deployed on Vercel, file memory uses a private Vercel Blob store so saved memories persist across restarts and deployments.

title: L2G-SR: Learning to Guide LLM-based Symbolic Regression
description:
arXiv:2610.20685v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Symbolic regression searches for an equation that explains observed data. Numerical error is commonly used to guide the search, but it alone can favor an accurate surrogate over a candidate with the right structure. We propose L2G-SR, a framework for LLM-based symbolic regression that guides search with a learned structural verifier. We construct structural supervision signal using tree edit distance (TED), accounting for commutative operators and alternative expression forms. A verifier first aligns numerical observations with the formulas, then learns to score a candidate's structural similarity to the target formula. At search time, the target formula is hidden and the verifier complements numerical error in parent selection. An analyst then uses verifier feedback and diagnostic tools to propose revisions, which a generator converts into refined expressions. On LLM-SRBench, L2G-SR achieves state-of-the-art numerical fit, equation level accuracy and TED across the evaluated LLM backbones and domains. L2G-SR demonstrates the value of learned structural guidance for LLM-based symbolic regression.

title: LEV: Thinking Fast and Deep with Looped Decision Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20951v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models answer typed questions about an input with one probability per option, computed in a single forward pass without generating text. Like the fast System 1 of dual-process theory, they answer at once, but their depth is fixed at training time, so they spend the same computation on easy and hard questions. Models that reason in generated text can think longer, but they pay for every extra step in decoded tokens. We present LEV, a decision model that thinks deeper by rerunning its layers in a loop instead of generating tokens. LEV builds on a language model pretrained as a loop, reads the options after every loop step and trains all steps jointly, so one checkpoint can answer at any depth. On three looped backbones, accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions, and a 2.6B LEV goes from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench. On-demand depth, set per question by a small stopper with a threshold fitted on unlabelled requests, saves 15% to 24% of the computation at a cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above a fixed mix of depths. On a locked test set, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non-looped) models and cascades of the same latency below 50 ms.

title: Prune the Summary, Not the History: Source-Judged Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.20927v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents rely on context compaction: when the interaction history outgrows the context window, a compressor replaces it with a natural-language summary. We show that these summaries contain more than a record of what happened. Compaction prompts ask for decisions and next steps, so each summary mixes facts established by the environment with reasoning written by the compressor, and the agent cannot tell the two apart afterwards. In an analysis of a widely used structured compressor, 83% of failed runs trace back to an action that carries out a specific summary entry, most of which no environment output supports. We propose Source-Judged Compaction (SJC), a training-free post-processing step that scores each summary entry for whether it has a source in the environment outputs or the previous summary, and removes the entries that do not. It changes neither the agent nor the compressor and adds one inexpensive judge request per compaction. The judge is Jev, a non-generative decision model that answers the source question with a calibrated probability instead of text. On AppWorld and OfficeBench with two agent models, SJC improves cross-run reliability over the underlying compressor by 2.1%-8.9% without increasing the agent's token usage.

title: Stop Guessing. Let the Algorithm Find the Sweet Spot.
description:
Simulated annealing gives a search permission to get worse before it gets better. The useful part is learning when that permission pays off.

There is a familiar ritual in software engineering: increase the thread count, change the batch size, run the benchmark, and squint at the result. Then change another number.

Eventually, something looks better, and we call it optimized.

But better than the previous attempt is a low bar. How much of the search space did we explore? What did each experiment cost? Does the improvement survive a different workload?

Those questions are the difference between tuning by habit and running an optimization experiment.

Simulated annealing is one way to run that experiment. Its most interesting feature is also its least intuitive: sometimes it accepts a worse candidate on purpose.

Let's examine why, implement the rule in Rust, and compare it with greedy search, random search, and a grid. Every method gets the same evaluation budget. The experiment is small enough to run locally and check exhaustively.

Why the first valley can trap you

Imagine walking through a mountain range at night, trying to find its lowest point. You can see nearby terrain, so you keep taking downhill steps.

Eventually, every nearby step leads uphill. You have found a local minimum. Another valley might be deeper, but your rule prevents you from crossing the ridge.

That is the problem with accepting only immediate improvements. Whether a solution is a local minimum also depends on the moves your search permits. A larger jump might cross a barrier that a small step cannot.

Simulated annealing sometimes accepts uphill moves. It borrows its name from the connection between cooling physical materials and searching for low-energy configurations, developed in Kirkpatrick, Gelatt, and Vecchi's 1983 paper.

In the algorithm, energy becomes an objective score. Temperature becomes a parameter controlling the willingness to accept regressions. Cooling gradually reduces that willingness.

This creates a route out of some local minima. A finite run can still miss the best solution.

The acceptance rule

Suppose lower scores are better. Calculate the change from the current candidate:

delta = score(candidate) - score(current)

Accept improvements and ties. For a worse candidate, draw a uniform random number between zero inclusive and one exclusive, then accept when it is smaller than:

p = exp(-delta / temperature)

This is the usual Metropolis acceptance rule for symmetric proposals, used in the original simulated annealing paper. Symmetric means the chance of proposing a move equals the chance of proposing its reverse.

For a regression of two score units, the probability is about 82% at temperature 10, 14% at temperature 1, and effectively zero at temperature 0.1.

Temperature has the same units as the score. Multiply every score by 1,000 and keep the old temperature, and you have changed the search's behavior. A cooling schedule is a design choice, not a magic constant.

Also keep two records: where the search is now and the best candidate it has ever found. Exploring a worse configuration should not erase a better answer.

Define what good means before searching

Consider these hypothetical service settings:

Setting Allowed values Count
Worker threads Every integer from 1 to 64 64
Batch size Every integer from 32 to 4,096 4,065
Timeout 50 to 2,000 milliseconds, stepping by 10 196

That is 50,991,360 configurations. At one evaluation per second, sequential exhaustive search would take about 590 days, before repeats or setup costs.

The hard part starts before choosing a search algorithm. What makes a configuration good?

One possible objective is:

score = 0.5 * (p99_latency / reference_latency)
      + 0.3 * (memory / reference_memory)
      - 0.2 * (throughput / reference_throughput)

Fix those positive reference values before the experiment. The ratios are dimensionless; the weights express your priorities. Changing the scales during the search would make scores from different iterations incomparable.

Hard requirements need separate treatment. If a configuration violates a memory cap, correctness invariant, or latency limit, reject it as infeasible. A throughput gain should not quietly compensate for breaking a requirement.

Even among feasible candidates, there may be several reasonable trade-offs. A candidate lies on the Pareto frontier if no feasible alternative improves an objective without worsening another. A weighted score expresses a preference among trade-offs; it does not discover your priorities for you.

The most important function is the one that decides what good looks like.

Give the algorithm something we can verify

For an executable demonstration, use a smaller problem where we can check the answer exhaustively.

The companion Rust project searches a 64 by 64 grid of abstract parameter indices. Each index maps onto a coordinate between -5.12 and 5.12. Its objective is the two-dimensional Rastrigin function:

E(x, y) = x*x + y*y + 20
        - 10*cos(2*pi*x) - 10*cos(2*pi*y)

The quadratic terms pull the search toward the center. The cosine terms add many local valleys. These scores have no latency, throughput, or dollar units. This is a deterministic mathematical experiment.

The continuous function reaches zero at the origin. Our even-sized grid does not contain the origin, so we enumerate all 4,096 grid points to find the discrete optimum. That enumeration is a separate reference calculation, unavailable to the search algorithms.

The comparison fixes these choices before running:

  • 256 objective evaluations per run, including the initial candidate and repeated proposals.
  • The same initial point, index (63, 63), for each method.
  • 30 seeds, numbered 1 through 30, for the stochastic methods.
  • Annealing and greedy search share a neighborhood: move one index by a signed step of 1 through 8. An out-of-range proposal stays in place and still costs an evaluation.
  • Annealing cools geometrically from 20 to 0.1 over its 255 proposals. Greedy search accepts only improvements or ties.
  • Random search samples the whole grid with replacement. Grid search uses a fixed 16 by 16 subset, rounding evenly spaced coordinates to integer indices.

Equal evaluation counts make one cost comparable. They do not give all methods identical information or movement rules. The starting point, neighborhood, grid spacing, and cooling schedule remain consequential choices.

The Rust loop

The project has no external Rust dependencies. Its seeded generator makes the search repeatable on the tested toolchain. This is the loop from the implementation; validation, random generation, and candidate construction live in the companion source.

/// Minimize an objective while retaining the best state ever visited.
pub fn anneal<S: Clone>(
    initial: S,
    mut score: impl FnMut(&S) -> f64,
    mut neighbor: impl FnMut(&S, &mut Rng) -> S,
    seed: u64,
    schedule: Schedule,
) -> Result<Outcome<S>, String> {
    schedule.validate()?;
    let mut rng = Rng::new(seed)?;
    let mut current = initial;
    let mut current_score = finite(score(&current))?;
    let mut result = Outcome {
        best: current.clone(),
        best_score: current_score,
        evaluations: 1,
        accepted_uphill: 0,
    };

    for proposal in 0..schedule.evaluations - 1 {
        let candidate = neighbor(&current, &mut rng);
        let candidate_score = finite(score(&candidate))?;
        result.evaluations += 1;
        let delta = finite(candidate_score - current_score)?;
        let temperature = schedule.temperature(proposal);
        if delta <= 0.0 || rng.unit() < (-delta / temperature).exp() {
            result.accepted_uphill += usize::from(delta > 0.0);
            current = candidate;
            current_score = candidate_score;
            if current_score < result.best_score {
                result.best = current.clone();
                result.best_score = current_score;
            }
        }
    }
    Ok(result)
}

The boundary handling matters. We choose signed moves with equal probability and leave invalid moves at the current point. Simply clamping an arbitrary move to the nearest boundary would accumulate probability there and lose the symmetry assumed by this acceptance rule.

The implementation also rejects invalid settings and nonfinite objective values, counts evaluations explicitly, and tests that a temporarily worse current state cannot overwrite the best result.

A separate unit test makes the barrier explicit: three adjacent states have costs 1, 2, 0. Starting at the first state, greedy search cannot cross the middle state. With the test's fixed seed and temperature, annealing accepts the uphill move and then reaches zero. That tiny fixture verifies the mechanism; it is not evidence that annealing usually wins.

Run it and compare the evidence

The companion project includes the Rust source, raw results, an independent results checker, and a plotting script. Clone it and run:

git clone https://github.com/copyleftdev/simulated-annealing-article.git
cd simulated-annealing-article
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target
cargo test --locked
cargo run --release --locked -- results/raw.csv
python3 scripts/verify.py --reproduce
python3 scripts/analyze.py

Python analysis uses the standard library. Add Matplotlib to regenerate the figures with python3 scripts/analyze.py --plots.

Method Median best score Best to worst score Exact grid optimum hits
Annealing 2.565 2.565 to 2.565 30/30
Greedy 2.565 2.565 to 2.565 30/30
Random 4.220 2.565 to 8.425 5/30
Coarse grid 3.480 3.480 to 3.480 No (deterministic)

Lower is better. The exhaustive grid optimum is 2.564508, and both annealing and greedy search reached it in all 30 runs. Annealing accepted between 14 and 33 uphill moves per run, but those moves did not improve its final score over greedy search here.

That result is a useful correction to the valley metaphor. Our neighborhood allows jumps of up to eight index positions. The cosine ripples repeat roughly every six positions, so greedy search can jump across hills without accepting a worse landing point. This experiment gives us no reason to prefer annealing over this greedy baseline on final score.

Random search reached the optimum in five runs. The coarse grid returned the same result every time; repeating it creates no new statistical evidence. Its chosen spacing misses the central indices 31 and 32, so its result is sensitive to grid alignment. These are observed score ranges, not confidence intervals or a universal ranking.

The raw CSV also records search duration. With such a cheap objective, optimizer overhead and machine conditions can substantially affect timing. An evaluation count is not a measurement of infrastructure savings.

There is a second check: after each run selects its best candidate, the harness shifts each coordinate by either -0.1 or +0.1, evaluates all four combinations, and records their mean score. These four evaluations are outside the 256-call search budget and its timer, and the search never sees their scores. This tests sensitivity to a small, specified change in the formula. It does not simulate production traffic or establish robustness to measurement noise.

That distinction matters. Thirty seeds describe variation in search outcomes on one fixed problem. They are not thirty independent workloads.

Try breaking the optimizer

A passing test suite deserves a challenge too. We used cargo-mutants to alter the library and rerun its tests. The original eight Rust tests missed 53 of 181 generated mutations, including deleting the minus sign in the acceptance formula.

After adding acceptance and contract tests, 153 mutations triggered test failures. Two survived: they permute symmetric terms in the shifted-score average, preserving its mathematical value. Another 25 did not compile, and one caused a nonterminating loop detected by a timeout. We report those categories separately in the mutation review.

The statistical check drives the real kernel through one million uphill proposals across five predeclared temperatures. At a score difference of 2 and temperature 2, expected acceptance is about 36.79%; observed acceptance was 36.988%. Every case fell within the predeclared tolerance of about 0.635 percentage points.

That tolerance uses a Hoeffding bound under ideal independent random draws. Our fixed pseudorandom streams make this a reproducible regression check, not a certification of randomness. The statistical review records all cases and assumptions. The expanded suite has 23 tests; production optimizer code and benchmark results are unchanged.

The optimizer proposes. The testing harness disposes.

A real service adds a complication: measurements fluctuate.

A noisy score can make a regression look like an improvement. Searching thousands of configurations also creates thousands of opportunities to get lucky. The most impressive single measurement may be the least trustworthy result.

For service tuning, make the evaluator earn its authority:

  1. Fix the workload, objective, constraints, and search budget before comparing methods.
  2. Repeat measurements, control warmup and machine conditions, and interleave candidates when drift could bias the comparison. Charge those repetitions to the evaluation budget.
  3. Evaluate finalists on reserved workloads, including skewed inputs, contention, and failure cases. Report variability alongside the central estimate.
  4. Check correctness and operational limits before promoting a candidate. Keep a rollback path and monitor the deployed result.

Once reserved workloads influence another round of tuning, they become development data. A fresh evaluation set is needed for a fresh generalization claim.

Accepting a worse candidate is a search decision inside an evaluation environment. It does not require deploying that candidate to customers.

Where this becomes an engineering habit

The same framing gives several everyday tuning problems a concrete shape:

Problem Candidate decisions Objective and constraints
Service performance Workers, batching, queue depth Minimize cost per completed request while meeting latency and correctness limits
AI agent orchestration Model routing, retry budget, verification threshold Minimize cost on a fixed task set while meeting quality and latency requirements
Test scheduling Test order and assignment to workers Minimize completion time while preserving the required suite and dependencies
Infrastructure sizing Instance mix, capacity, scaling thresholds Minimize cost under representative demand while meeting capacity and recovery requirements

Applying search to these problems requires a candidate representation, legal moves, and a trustworthy evaluator. In an agent system, for example, a cheap answer is useful only if the quality check deserves trust. Evaluators can be fooled or overfit too.

The separation is useful: a search proposes configurations, an evaluator measures outcomes, and a deployment process decides what can ship.

You do not need to adopt annealing to adopt that architecture.

Make annealing earn its place

Start with a baseline you can understand. If the space is small, enumerate it. If a coarse grid or random search gives good results within the budget, that is valuable evidence.

Annealing becomes interesting when useful local moves exist but a search that accepts only improvements gets trapped. Its neighborhood and temperature schedule still need attention. If objective evaluations are expensive, compare methods designed to spend fewer evaluations. If useful gradients exist, consider methods that exploit them.

The cost of tuning the optimizer also belongs in the accounting. Trying twenty cooling schedules and reporting only the best is another search, with another budget.

The engineering habit is simple: define success, constrain the experiment, compare alternatives, and keep the evidence. Repeat when the environment changes.

Sometimes a better answer is on the other side of a hill. Sometimes a simpler search already finds it. Measure which situation you are in.

What configuration have you spent hours tuning manually, and what would a trustworthy objective function for it look like?

Disclosure: AI agents drafted and revised this article, implemented the experiment, and performed technical review. The numerical results come from executing the accompanying code.

title: L2GSSL: Label-Efficient Local-to-Global Self-Supervised Learning for Volumetric Healthcare Data
description:
arXiv:2610.21356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Healthcare institutions routinely accumulate high-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes, but only a fraction can be annotated by experts. We present L2GSSL, a local-to-global self-supervised learning framework that leverages unlabeled volumes by decomposing pretraining into intra-slice and inter-slice representation spaces. A slice encoder learns view-invariant local features, and a global encoder aggregates the resulting tokens to model volumetric context. The stop-gradient isolates the local space from the global objective, while slice-wise execution and a three-phase schedule support training under constrained GPU memory. On LIDC-IDRI lung nodule malignancy classification, L2GSSL reaches $0.9229$ AUROC with only $10\%$ of the labels and $0.9377$ with $25\%$, exceeding the volume-level VICReg by $0.0229$ and $0.0294$, respectively. With all labels, the strongest supervised baseline exceeds L2GSSL by only $0.0044$ AUROC, consistent with self-supervised pretraining providing its greatest value when annotations are limited. Without adaptation to the external LNDb cohort, a model fine-tuned on $25\%$ of LIDC-IDRI obtains $0.8138$ AUROC and $0.7589$ AUPRC, improving over the strongest evaluated self-supervised baseline by $0.1130$ and $0.0954$. Experiments across data sources, thoracic and abdominal anatomy, downstream tasks, and two backbones examine healthcare-data variety, while lesion-slice masking shows that the predictions depend on lesion-bearing content.

title: TIL: GBase Database Installation Can Fail When `/tmp` Runs Out of Space
description:
One easily overlooked cause of GBase Database (GBase 8s) installation failures is insufficient temporary disk space.

During installation, the installer may need to extract files and create temporary data. If /tmp is on a small dedicated partition, it can run out of space before the installation completes.

A useful rule of thumb is to check whether /tmp has enough free space for the installer and its temporary files. The required capacity depends on the package and installation method, so don't assume that one fixed ratio works for every GBase Database installation.

1. Check /tmp Before Installation

Run:

df -h /tmp
df -i /tmp

The first command checks available disk space; the second checks available inodes. Either resource can become a bottleneck.

2. Use a Larger Temporary Directory

If /tmp doesn't have enough space, you may be able to use a directory on a larger filesystem:

mkdir -p /opt/tmp
chmod 700 /opt/tmp
export TMPDIR=/opt/tmp

Important: Run the installer using the appropriate account and verify that the installer honors TMPDIR. Some installation tools use their own temporary paths, so setting this variable alone may not resolve every issue.

3. Why This Matters for GBase Database Deployment

Insufficient temporary space can interrupt GBase Database installation, complicate silent deployments, and cause failures across batch installation workflows.

Before deploying GBase Database (GBase 8s), make temporary storage checks part of your standard Linux pre-installation checklist.

A few seconds spent checking disk space can save hours of troubleshooting.

title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
description:
arXiv:2610.21055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.20818v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.
