title: Find Inactive Users in Jira and Confluence
description:
Atlassian bills every user who has access to an app, whether they log in or not. Their words: users "are automatically counted towards billing even if they don't accept your invite or log in." You can find the inactive ones for free with Atlassian's own export. On 15 October we released Cost Slasher, a beta app that adds per-app inactivity policies and time away on top. It doesn't remove anyone for inactivity until you've verified it on your own site.

Prices went up this week. Since 13 October, Jira Standard's first 100 users cost $9.70 a month each, up from $9.05. So around renewal most Jira admins end up asking the same question. Who here hasn't opened Jira in two months, and why am I paying for them?

Below: the free way to find them, what Cost Slasher does today and what stays switched off, the arithmetic on what an idle seat costs against what the app costs, how to install it, and what I got wrong. The screenshots come from the production install on our demo site, taken the evening it went public.

If I were the admin deciding, I'd want to know this first:

  1. Automatic release ships switched off, and until it's on the app doesn't read your users' last-active dates.
  2. The warning period can't go below 24 hours.
  3. Unknown activity means the seat stays.
  4. A seat counts as reclaimed only when the access is verified gone.
  5. Time away releases your licence for the absence and keeps your place in the seat pool.
  6. JSM agents get a policy but no automatic release.
  7. It isn't cheap at 100 users.

How to find inactive users in Jira without an app, and what the export misses

You don't need any app to find inactive users in Jira Cloud. Atlassian already has the data.

  1. Go to admin.atlassian.com, open your organization, then Directory and Users.
  2. Export the users of the site. The CSV has a Last seen in column per app, which Atlassian defines as "the date the user last viewed the app's workspace for a minimum of 2 seconds." (Export users from a site)
  3. Sort by that column and pick a cut-off (60 or 90 days, your call). Take out admins and service accounts, then anyone you know is on leave.
  4. Remove app access or deactivate them, by hand or in bulk (Atlassian's bulk steps).

You can get the same dates from the Organizations REST API as last-active dates, with one line of fine print: "The data for the last activity may be delayed by up to 24 hours." Atlassian's pricing FAQ gives the same advice I'm giving: "Deactivate inactive users that aren't using your cloud product(s) so they no longer count towards your monthly bill."

That's fine once a year. The second time hurts. Nobody warned the people you removed, so the first you hear of it is "I can't open Jira" from someone back from paternity leave. The spreadsheet doesn't know who is on leave, and unless you keep notes there's no record of who removed whom, or why. Atlassian has no built-in inactivity deactivation that I could find: AX-1169, "Deactivate inactive user based on activity", has sat at Under Consideration since May 2019 and has 781 votes.

In my earlier post on Atlassian license management I had a CogniRunner AI agent do this job from a paragraph of instructions, and I said there that if license management is the only job, a deterministic tool is the simpler path. Cost Slasher is ours.

How Cost Slasher's inactivity policy works: allowance, warning period, restore protection, exclusions

Each app gets its own policy, because someone who reads Confluence daily and opens Jira twice a quarter shouldn't be warned off Confluence. Jira and Confluence seats each get one, and so do JSM agent seats (agent seats only, never customer portal access).

The inactivity allowance is how long someone can go without opening the app before a warning is due (30 days by default). The warning period is how long after the warning reaches them before the seat can go. It defaults to 48 hours and can't be set below 24.

Restore protection keeps a seat safe for a while after someone's access comes back (48 hours by default), so a person who just returned isn't warned again on day one. Exclusions are accounts left out of automatic release for that app, say a finance lead who opens Jira twice a year.

When release is on, activity comes from Atlassian's Organizations API, the same last-active dates as the export, read with your organization's Admin API key. That key can do far more than read dates. It lives in Forge secret storage, scoped to the installation. Cost Slasher doesn't create or rotate it, and our AWS side never receives it. Remove API key in the app takes it out of Cost Slasher and blocks new changes, but it doesn't revoke the key in Atlassian Administration. Do that there.

I put the 24-hour floor in the code as a constant, with the comment "Last-active reporting can lag by one day; every policy must allow that lag." If the data can be a day late, a 12-hour warning could run out and release the seat of someone who used Jira this morning, before Atlassian's data shows the visit.

Why the beta does not remove inactive users from Jira automatically yet

The listing's release notes say: "Automatic release stays off until recovery, warnings, activity and capacity are verified." Off is the default for every new policy. Saving a policy with release switched on is refused until activity, recovery and capacity are verified (plus agent activity, for JSM). Even then, no seat goes until a warning has been confirmed delivered and the full warning period has run.

Here's what each check means on your site. Recovery: you've put Cost Slasher's recovery link into Atlassian's native access-denied message and tested it with a real account that lost its paid seat. Warnings: a warning counts from confirmed delivery, not from the moment it was handed to the mail service. Warnings go out as email through Amazon SES in our AWS Ireland region. Activity: a test account opens the app inside a window of at most 72 hours, and the app must then find that exact visit in Atlassian's activity data for that app. Capacity: the app has finished reading who already holds each managed seat, so it knows the real count before it changes anything.

Until then, the app doesn't read your users' activity for that app. My access shows Activity unavailable, nobody gets an inactivity warning, and if you want a seat back you release it yourself. One kind of release does run on its own, switch or no switch: if a managed account is suspended, leaves the organization or drops out of the eligibility group, the app releases that seat. You do that in People: pick the app, select the accounts, add a reason, preview exactly which accounts change, then apply. The listing summary calls this "Beta; access changes require verified setup."

With release on, unknown activity still stops it. The guide is blunt: "Unknown or unparseable activity is not a never-used account and is not a release candidate." A never-used account is different: if Atlassian's answer is complete and has no date for that app, the allowance counts from the day Cost Slasher granted the seat or, for a seat that was already there when you installed it, from the day the app took it over.

Why so careful? A seat you paid for one month too long is cheap. Removing the release manager's Jira access on release morning isn't. Most of the licence apps I looked at advertise the automatic part first ("Auto-Schedule deactivation/suspension of inactive users", "Deactivate and offboard by inactivity threshold (3 days to 6 months)"). I shipped the off switch first, and you turn it on per app once the checks pass on your site.

Confluence inactive users and JSM agents: one policy per product

Cost Slasher installs on Jira and opens in Confluence on the same site. Confluence is the common case for a separate policy: plenty of people live in Confluence and rarely open Jira, and one site-wide rule would warn the wrong people.

JSM agents are different. You can set an agent policy and limit agent seats. Automatic agent release stays disabled, though. Atlassian's last-active data records a page view of two seconds or more, which can't tell an agent who works tickets from one who glanced at the queue. Agent seats also cost more (Service Collection, the plan JSM is now sold as, is $26.90 per agent a month at Standard for the first 15 agents), so a wrong release costs more too.

What ships today: My access, time away, a seat cap, reports and audit

My access is the page members see first: their access per app, the inactivity allowance, the last observed activity, and a button to check or restore. Checking grants nothing. Restoring is a separate click. It's also how people ask for a seat in the first place.

People who already lost their seat can't open the app, so recovery starts outside it. You paste a generated message into Atlassian's access-denied settings, and it links to a recovery page on cost-slasher.leanzero.net. Signing in there only asks Atlassian who you are, and signing in alone grants nothing. (Other apps offer self-service restore too. miniOrange and OSCi advertise it, for example.)

Time away is the feature I haven't seen on the other licence apps' listings (we read ten). A member enters when they leave and when they're back, previews it, then confirms. The licence is released for the absence, and the return seat stays reserved in the pool, so nobody else takes it. Restore is scheduled to start 30 minutes before the recorded return, and there's an "I'm back early" button. It only works if they're still eligible when they come back.

A seat limit with a queue. Each app's managed group has a seat limit. When it's full, a request waits with an expiry (24 hours by default) and the app picks waiting requests up in order as seats free. The limit covers access granted through Cost Slasher's group. Access granted through other groups isn't counted against it.

Management reports download as PDF, CSV or JSON. They hold aggregates only, with no individual names. Type in a monthly seat price and you get an estimate, which the app labels "a planning estimate" that "does not prove invoice savings".

The audit log records who acted, on which account, through which entry point, and the outcome of each stage. You can filter by period, category, outcome, app, actor or account, and the download holds all matching events, across pages.

There are five roles (Member, Operator, Routing manager, Auditor, Administrator), each scoped to sites and apps, and a REST API with scoped tokens that expire.

If your groups come from SCIM, this part matters. Cost Slasher reads a SCIM-managed group only as an eligibility source and never writes to it. Seats are granted through a separate destination group that the app has verified it can write to, and routing rules (add, mirror or move) show a preview first.

What the Atlassian cloud price increase 2026 does to an idle seat

No customer has run Cost Slasher yet, so this is Atlassian's price list and a calculator, done with their tables on 15 October 2026.

Take a 250-user Jira Standard site on monthly billing, and say 25 people (10%) haven't opened Jira in 90 days. Atlassian prices monthly seats in bands, so the last 150 users pay the 101-250 rate.

Before 13 Oct From 13 Oct
Jira Standard, users 1-100 $9.05 $9.70
Jira Standard, users 101-250 $7.65 $8.20
250 users, monthly bill $2,052.50 $2,200.00
25 idle seats, per month $191.25 $205.00
25 idle seats, per year $2,295 $2,460

If the same 25 people also hold Confluence Standard ($5.45 per user per month in the 101-250 band), that's another $136.25 a month, or $1,635 a year.

Cost Slasher is priced on the Jira user count, $1.32 a month for each of the first 100 users and $0.40 for each user after that up to 5,000. Once those 25 are gone the site has 225 users, which comes to $182 a month, $2,184 a year. That's about the cost of 22 idle Jira seats at $98.40 a year each, or 13 people who hold both Jira and Confluence. Up to 10 users it's free, permanently.

So on Jira alone at 10% idle it's close to break-even, and in this beta the seats are released by you, not by the app. What you'd be paying for is the policy and audit trail around each change, plus time away and the seat queue. Automatic release comes once you've verified it. Atlassian's usage billing from 3 December 2026 also pools allowances such as Rovo credits per paid user, so a removed seat shrinks that pool a little (I measured what 25 Rovo credits per user actually buys).

Annual plans are different. You pay for a tier. You only save when you drop to a lower one at renewal. Jira Standard's 300-user tier is $25,500 a year and the 200-user tier is $18,000, so getting a 280-person site under 200 is worth $7,500 a year. Cost Slasher's annual price at 300 users is $2,120.

And the competition, from each app's live pricing on the same day:

App Vendor Annual, 100 users Annual, 500 users
Manage Users for Jira Cloud Bloompeak $200 $600
License Cost Optimizer for Jira Atlassway $790 $2,700
User Management for Jira & Auto-deactivation miniOrange $850 $2,100
Kantega User Management & License Optimizer Kantega SSO $850 $2,100
User Management for Jira TechTime $1,000 $2,375
Flexible User License OSCi $1,000 $2,375
User Management and License Optimizer resolution $1,000 $3,450
Cost Slasher LeanZero $1,320 $2,920

At 100 users we're the most expensive. At 500 only resolution costs more. Kantega's listing says it is fully hosted on Atlassian's infrastructure, and resolution's says Cloud Fortified. Ours is neither yet. For Jira alone at 100 users I probably wouldn't pay $1,320 for it. If your people also hold Confluence or JSM agent seats, or you lose a day every time someone comes back from leave to a missing licence, I think the sum changes. And if all you want is a sorted list of last-active dates, the export from the first section is free.

Install it and the first ten minutes

First, where your data goes, because a security reviewer will ask before step 4. The app calls api.atlassian.com and cost-slasher.leanzero.net. Recovery sign-in, the controller registry (which tracks each installation's controller), shared organization budgeting and email notifications run in AWS Ireland, behind CloudFront. The Admin API key stays in Forge. Our privacy declaration states that the app doesn't support data residency, so if your organization requires Runs on Atlassian, this isn't the app for you today.

  1. Install Cost Slasher from the Marketplace listing on your Jira Cloud site. The listing has a Try it free button, and sites with up to 10 Jira users pay nothing.
  2. Open Apps → Cost Slasher. Members see My access first. The first site admin to open it gets a setup guide that shows one next step at a time. Opening setup doesn't call Atlassian's organization API or change any licence.
  3. Run Storage safety. It tests the app's own Forge SQL storage on your site with throwaway records and checks they get cleaned up. It touches nothing in Jira. Our demo install passed all 88 units.
  4. Enter your Organization ID, Directory ID and an organization Admin API key.
  5. Request pairing from LeanZero. Recovery runs through our service, so this step needs us. Ask through the support portal.
  6. Map each app: an eligibility group, a destination group that grants the paid app, and a seat limit. Applying a mapping creates a policy with automatic release off and starts a read-only count of who already holds each seat. It doesn't grant anyone a seat.
  7. Look at Policies, Operations and People.

The last setup section, Controller shutdown, is the brake. It freezes new work at the revision you reviewed and cancels only operations proven never to have started. Existing paid access is kept. This short film walks through it on the production app:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cklgkAo2b24

We published four more the same evening, on privacy and release notes, roles and scope, the REST API's scoped tokens and usage coverage.

Where I was wrong while building it

This post. The first draft said Cost Slasher finds your inactive users. Then our red-team pass read the code. With release off, the app doesn't read your users' activity, and off is how the beta ships. The title had to change. So did the excerpt, the hero image and five sentences. A launch post that oversold its own beta was the one thing I'd told myself not to write.

A 204 isn't a freed seat. Removing someone from a group returns 204, but they may still get the same app from another group. In my CogniRunner drill the removal returned 204 and the count did drop, but the agent had no way to read the person's groups back. Cost Slasher counts a seat as reclaimed only after it reads back that effective access is gone, and the 4 October commit that fences inactivity releases added 73 test cases.

Two UX defects only showed up when we recorded the demo films. The empty-list message appeared on the last page of 12 lists and the exclusion picker, as if those lists were empty. And the setup page contradicted itself about recovery pairing when pairing was healthy. Both were fixed on 4 October. I should have clicked through those pages myself.

The demo site's first signed request failed with a 503. This was on 15 October, release day. The new production secrets sat in a different AWS namespace from the one our gateway role could read. A narrow permission grant fixed it. The enrollment tool now refuses a mismatched namespace before it writes anything.

The Marketplace shows version 3.2.0. Inside the app the footer says "App release 0.4.4", which is the same build under our own numbering.

Who should install it now

Ten users or fewer? Install it. It costs nothing.

If you're bigger and want inactive users removed on a schedule tonight, this beta isn't it yet, and I'd rather lose that sale than remove the wrong person. If you want a written inactivity policy per app and time away that keeps someone's place, install it and tell us through the support portal what breaks. The Cost Slasher product page has the full manual.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

title: TRACER: A Multimodal Harness for Patient Care in Hospitals
description:
arXiv:2610.21266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.

title: Pinterest Scraper in Go: Board RSS, Pin Pages, and a Saves Tracker in SQLite (2026)
description:
Pinterest is quietly one of the best datasets for anyone working in e-commerce, home decor, food, or fashion. Saves are a pretty honest signal of what people actually want to buy or make, and they show up weeks before a trend hits other platforms.

Getting that data out is a different story. In this post I'll build a small Go tool that:

  1. Reads the latest pins from any public board or profile
  2. Opens each pin and pulls out title, outbound link, domain, creation date, repins, and saves
  3. Stores a snapshot on every run in SQLite, so you can see which pins are picking up saves

Everything here was tested against live Pinterest pages in October 2026. I'll also point out the parts that are flaky, because a few of them surprised me.

Before you start: stick to public data, keep request rates low, and read Pinterest's Terms of Service. If you only need data for accounts you own or manage, the official API v5 is the cleaner route (more on that below).

Your options, briefly

  • Official API v5. Needs a registered app, OAuth, and approval; new apps start on limited trial access. It's built around accounts that authorize your app, so it isn't a way to read arbitrary public boards.
  • Internal /resource/... endpoints. The web app's own JSON calls. They work until they don't: parameters change without notice and they're much more likely to get you rate limited.
  • RSS + pin pages (this post). Every public profile and board still has an RSS feed, and every pin page ships its data as embedded JSON. No login, no headless browser.

Step 1: The RSS feed gives you pin URLs

This part is pleasantly boring. Two URL patterns:

https://www.pinterest.com/<username>/feed.rss         # a profile's latest pins
https://www.pinterest.com/<username>/<board-slug>.rss  # one board

Each feed returns the 25 most recent pins with a title, link, thumbnail, and pubDate. That limit matters, and I'll come back to it. Parsing it in Go needs nothing beyond the standard library:

type rssFeed struct {
    Channel struct {
        Title string    `xml:"title"`
        Items []rssItem `xml:"item"`
    } `xml:"channel"`
}

type rssItem struct {
    Title   string `xml:"title"`
    Link    string `xml:"link"`
    PubDate string `xml:"pubDate"`
}

Step 2: A polite fetch helper

Pin pages are big (more than 1 MB of HTML each), and Pinterest does return 429 if you hammer it. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter keep things civil:

// fetch does a polite GET with retries and exponential backoff.
func fetch(url string) ([]byte, error) {
    var lastErr error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        if attempt > 0 {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            time.Sleep(wait + time.Duration(rand.Intn(1000))*time.Millisecond)
        }
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", url, nil)
        req.Header.Set("User-Agent", userAgent)
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", "en-US,en;q=0.9")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            continue
        }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            continue
        }
        switch {
        case resp.StatusCode == 200:
            return body, nil
        case resp.StatusCode == 429 || resp.StatusCode >= 500:
            lastErr = fmt.Errorf("%s: HTTP %d", url, resp.StatusCode)
            continue
        default:
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: HTTP %d", url, resp.StatusCode)
        }
    }
    return nil, lastErr
}

Setting Accept-Language matters more than you'd think. Pinterest localizes heavily, and without it you may get titles and SEO descriptions in whatever language it guesses from your IP.

func boardFeed(user, board string) ([]rssItem, error) {
    url := fmt.Sprintf("https://www.pinterest.com/%s/%s.rss", user, board)
    if board == "" {
        url = fmt.Sprintf("https://www.pinterest.com/%s/feed.rss", user)
    }
    body, err := fetch(url)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    var feed rssFeed
    if err := xml.Unmarshal(body, &feed); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("parse rss: %w", err)
    }
    return feed.Channel.Items, nil
}

Step 3: Where the pin data actually lives

My first attempt parsed the application/ld+json block on the pin page. It has a nice SocialMediaPosting object with a "Saves" counter. It worked on the first pin I tried, and then failed on 25 out of 25 pins in my first real run.

Fetching the same pin six times in a row explained it: the JSON-LD block was there once. Pinterest streams the page, and which blocks make it into the HTML varies from request to request.

What is consistently there is one or more <script data-relay-completed-request="true"> tags. Each one calls window.__PWS_RELAY_REGISTER_COMPLETED_REQUEST__(key, json), and the JSON contains a v3GetPinQueryv2.data object with the pin. A single pin is often split across several of these blocks, and some fields (especially aggregatedPinData.aggregatedStats.saves) only appear in one of them. So the trick is to parse all of them and merge:

type Pin struct {
    ID        string
    URL       string
    Title     string
    Link      string // outbound destination, if any
    Domain    string
    Image     string
    Author    string
    Board     string
    Published string
    Repins    int
    Saves     *int // nil when Pinterest didn't include it in this response
}

var relayRe = regexp.MustCompile(`(?s)<script data-relay-completed-request="true"[^>]*>window\.__PWS_RELAY_REGISTER_COMPLETED_REQUEST__\("[^"]*",(.*?)\);?</script>`)

type pinData struct {
    EntityID   string `json:"entityId"`
    Title      string `json:"title"`
    SeoTitle   string `json:"seoTitle"`
    Link       string `json:"link"`
    Domain     string `json:"domain"`
    CreatedAt  string `json:"createdAt"`
    RepinCount int    `json:"repinCount"`
    ImageLarge string `json:"imageLargeUrl"`
    Pinner     *struct {
        Username string `json:"username"`
    } `json:"pinner"`
    Board *struct {
        URL string `json:"url"`
    } `json:"board"`
    AggregatedPinData *struct {
        AggregatedStats struct {
            Saves *int `json:"saves"`
        } `json:"aggregatedStats"`
    } `json:"aggregatedPinData"`
}

type relayPayload struct {
    Data struct {
        Pin *struct {
            Data *pinData `json:"data"`
        } `json:"v3GetPinQueryv2"`
    } `json:"data"`
}

var errNoPinData = errors.New("no pin data in page")

func first(vals ...string) string {
    for _, v := range vals {
        if v != "" {
            return v
        }
    }
    return ""
}

// scrapePin merges every relay block on the page: Pinterest splits one pin
// across several blocks, and some fields (like saves) only show up in one.
func scrapePin(url string) (*Pin, error) {
    body, err := fetch(url)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    p := &Pin{URL: url}
    found := false
    for _, m := range relayRe.FindAllSubmatch(body, -1) {
        var r relayPayload
        if json.Unmarshal(m[1], &r) != nil || r.Data.Pin == nil || r.Data.Pin.Data == nil {
            continue
        }
        d := r.Data.Pin.Data
        found = true
        p.ID = first(p.ID, d.EntityID)
        p.Title = first(p.Title, d.Title, d.SeoTitle)
        p.Link = first(p.Link, d.Link)
        p.Domain = first(p.Domain, d.Domain)
        p.Published = first(p.Published, d.CreatedAt)
        p.Image = first(p.Image, d.ImageLarge)
        if d.RepinCount > p.Repins {
            p.Repins = d.RepinCount
        }
        if d.Pinner != nil {
            p.Author = first(p.Author, d.Pinner.Username)
        }
        if d.Board != nil {
            p.Board = first(p.Board, d.Board.URL)
        }
        if d.AggregatedPinData != nil && d.AggregatedPinData.AggregatedStats.Saves != nil {
            p.Saves = d.AggregatedPinData.AggregatedStats.Saves
        }
    }
    if !found {
        return nil, errNoPinData
    }
    return p, nil
}

Two field notes:

  • repinCount is not the save count. On one pin I saw repinCount: 9 next to saves: 417. The aggregated saves number is the one that matches what users see.
  • Saves are often missing. In a 25-pin run, saves came back on only about a third of the pins. That's why Saves is a pointer: I'd rather store NULL than a fake zero that wrecks your growth charts.

Step 4: Store snapshots, not rows

The value is in the change over time, so pins go in once and every run appends a snapshot:

const schema = `
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pins (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, url TEXT, title TEXT, link TEXT, domain TEXT,
  image TEXT, author TEXT, board TEXT, published TEXT, first_seen TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS snapshots (
  pin_id TEXT, taken_at TEXT, repins INTEGER, saves INTEGER,
  PRIMARY KEY (pin_id, taken_at)
);`

func save(db *sql.DB, p *Pin) error {
    now := time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)
    _, err := db.Exec(`INSERT INTO pins (id,url,title,link,domain,image,author,board,published,first_seen)
        VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?) ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING`,
        p.ID, p.URL, p.Title, p.Link, p.Domain, p.Image, p.Author, p.Board, p.Published, now)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = db.Exec(`INSERT INTO snapshots (pin_id,taken_at,repins,saves) VALUES (?,?,?,?)`,
        p.ID, now, p.Repins, p.Saves) // a nil *int is stored as NULL
    return err
}

And the main loop, with a random 2 to 4 second pause between pins:

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 2 {
        log.Fatal("usage: pinscrape <user> [board-slug]")
    }
    user, board := os.Args[1], ""
    if len(os.Args) > 2 {
        board = os.Args[2]
    }

    db, err := sql.Open("sqlite", "pins.db")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()
    if _, err := db.Exec(schema); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    items, err := boardFeed(user, board)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    log.Printf("feed returned %d pins", len(items))

    for _, it := range items {
        p, err := scrapePin(it.Link)
        if err != nil {
            log.Printf("skip %s: %v", it.Link, err)
            continue
        }
        if err := save(db, p); err != nil {
            log.Printf("db: %v", err)
        }
        saves := "?"
        if p.Saves != nil {
            saves = fmt.Sprint(*p.Saves)
        }
        fmt.Printf("%-20s saves=%-6s repins=%-4d %s\n", p.ID, saves, p.Repins, p.Title)
        time.Sleep(time.Duration(2000+rand.Intn(2000)) * time.Millisecond)
    }
}

Install the SQLite driver (pure Go, no cgo) and run it against a board:

go mod init pinscrape
go get modernc.org/sqlite
go build -o pinscrape .
./pinscrape pinterest                 # profile feed
./pinscrape <username> <board-slug>   # a single board

Real output from Pinterest's own profile feed (trimmed):

feed returned 25 pins
424605071146015538   saves=418    repins=2    Burgundy food table
424605071146015535   saves=?      repins=9    The Christmas Centerpiece That Makes a Table Feel Instantly Magical
skip https://www.pinterest.com/pin/424605071146015533/: no pin data in page
424605071146015511   saves=6462   repins=5    Aesthetic gift wrapping idea
424605071146015505   saves=3063   repins=6    Christmas champagne

Run it from cron once a day, then ask SQLite which pins are gaining traction:

SELECT p.title,
       MIN(s.saves) AS first_saves,
       MAX(s.saves) AS latest_saves,
       MAX(s.saves) - MIN(s.saves) AS gained
FROM snapshots s
JOIN pins p ON p.id = s.pin_id
WHERE s.saves IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY p.id
ORDER BY gained DESC
LIMIT 20;

MIN and MAX skip NULLs, which is exactly what you want when saves only show up on some runs.

Where this approach hits a wall

  1. 25 pins per feed, no pagination. RSS only shows the newest 25. To build history for a big board you have to start tracking early and keep running; you can't backfill old pins this way.
  2. No keyword search. RSS covers profiles and boards. Searching Pinterest for "christmas tablescape" means the search page, which renders client-side and leans on the internal endpoints.
  3. Flaky fields. Around 1 in 8 pin pages in my test had no pin data at all, and saves were missing more often than not. Retry missing pins on the next run instead of hammering them immediately.
  4. Bandwidth. 25 pins is roughly 30 MB of HTML. Fine for a few boards, painful for thousands.
  5. Markup drift. v3GetPinQueryv2 is an internal query name. When it changes, your scraper returns zero pins. Alert on that instead of silently storing nothing.

When you'd rather not maintain it

If you need keyword search, deeper pagination, or more volume than a cron job can handle politely, a scraping API takes over the fetching. I use ScrapeAtlas* for this. Its /v1/pinterest/search endpoint takes a query and an optional cursor, and /v1/pinterest/board takes a board url. Both return a pins array plus a cursor for the next page:

type apiResp struct {
    Status string  `json:"status"` // success, partial, failed, challenged
    Cursor *string `json:"cursor"`
    Pins   []struct {
        ID        string `json:"id"`
        Title     string `json:"title"`
        URL       string `json:"url"`
        CreatedAt string `json:"created_at"`
    } `json:"pins"`
}

func searchPins(query, cursor string) (*apiResp, error) {
    q := url.Values{"query": {query}}
    if cursor != "" {
        q.Set("cursor", cursor)
    }
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/pinterest/search?"+q.Encode(), nil)
    req.Header.Set("x-api-key", os.Getenv("SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY"))
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    var r apiResp
    return &r, json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&r)
}

Check status either way: partial means you got usable pins but some fields were missing (the response's coverage.warnings tells you which, for example missing_pin_counts). The same pins and snapshots tables work for both sources.

Wrapping up

  • A handful of boards, tracked daily: RSS plus pin pages, as above, works well and costs nothing.
  • Make missing data explicit: store NULL for saves you didn't get and merge every relay block on the page.
  • Search or scale: that's where the DIY version stops being fun, and an API or a lot of proxy work comes in.

If your run starts returning "no pin data" on every pin, Pinterest has probably renamed the query. Leave a comment and I'll update the parser.

*I build it.

title: Vercel for Enterprise
description:
AI adoption in the enterprise is growing rapidly, and expanding beyond engineering users.

In the last three months, token usage by enterprise companies on AI Gateway has quadrupled, and OpenAI recently reported that from August 2025 to June 2026, non-developer Codex users grew 189x.

Our customers call these builders citizen developers. They know their part of the business better than anyone else, and with AI they can create the software they need to ship work faster and deliver better customer experiences.

Building has never been easier, but that also means that control and governance have never been harder. Employees are using AI tools whether they are approved or not, and if a citizen developer vibe codes a login page incorrectly, private data can reach the public internet.

Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control.

Enterprise Apps and Agents

We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar.

Today, we are expanding the platform:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) on AWS is generally available, giving you the full Vercel developer experience, while keeping compute and data inside your AWS boundary.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization through Vercel Connect is launching in public beta, giving agents the ability to access connected services on behalf of employees through your IdP.

title: How AI Coding Tools Leak Your API Keys, And What I Built to Stop It
description:
Last week I watched Claude Code read my .env file, extract my OpenAI API key, and paste it into a curl command in a shell script it was writing for me. The key worked. The script worked. And my sk-proj- key was now sitting in a file on disk, in Claude's session history, and in Anthropic's API logs.

I didn't ask Claude to use the key. It just... did what a helpful agent does. It saw the environment, understood the task, and wired things up. That's the whole point of AI coding tools. It's also the problem.

The threat is not hypothetical

GitGuardian's State of Secrets Sprawl 2026
reports 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025, a
34% year-over-year increase. AI-service secrets separately increased 81% year
over year; that category-specific figure does not apply to all secrets.

Here is one common high-risk pattern when an AI coding tool has dotenv access:

  1. You have a .env file with OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-abc123...
  2. The AI agent reads that file to understand your project
  3. Your real API key is now inside the LLM's context window

Once a secret enters the context window, several downstream systems can become exposure paths:

  • Session logs. Most AI tools persist conversation history. Your key is sitting in a JSON file in ~/.claude/ or ~/.cursor/, probably unencrypted.
  • Prompt injection. A malicious README, dependency, or code comment can instruct the LLM to exfiltrate environment variables. This isn't theoretical — Check Point Research demonstrated it with CVEs against both Cursor and Claude Code: crafted prompts that trick the agent into sending secrets to attacker-controlled servers.
  • Malicious MCP servers. The Model Context Protocol lets AI tools call external services. A compromised MCP server can request environment context and receive your real keys.
  • Accidental commits. The AI writes code that hardcodes a key, or generates a test fixture with real credentials. You review it quickly, approve, and push.

The standard advice — "just don't put secrets in .env" — ignores reality. Developers need secrets in their environment to build software. The question isn't whether AI will read your .env. It's what it finds when it does.

Phantom tokens: keep real credentials out of the AI boundary

I built Phantom to reduce that exposure at the architecture
level. The core idea: replace heuristically detected, Phantom-managed dotenv
secrets with phantom tokens — cryptographically random placeholders that
are not accepted as credentials by the upstream provider.

Here's what your .env looks like before and after running phantom init:

# Before
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-abc123def456ghi789...
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_51HG7a9s8d7f6g5h4j3k2l1...
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-example...
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=3000

# After
OPENAI_API_KEY=phm_a7f3b9e2d1c4f8a6b3e7d2c5f9a1b4e8...
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=phm_c3d7f2a9e1b5d8c4a7f3b6e2d9c1a5f8...
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=phm_e8b2d5a9c3f7e1b4d8a2c6f3e7b1d5a9...
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=3000

Those phm_ tokens use 256 bits of CSPRNG output. They are not provider
credentials and cannot be redeemed directly against OpenAI, Anthropic, or
Stripe. They are still mappings worth protecting. Client headers and bodies
never resolve them, but a stolen live proxy bearer can authorize exact routes
that inject their own credentials. Rotate an exposed project token. Non-secret config values such as NODE_ENV and PORT
are normally left untouched by the detection heuristics.

Your real secrets are stored through the platform credential backend (macOS
Keychain, the Linux kernel keyring, or Windows Credential Manager), with an
encrypted-file fallback when its passphrase can be persisted and verified.
Linux kernel-keyring entries do not survive a reboot.

The reverse proxy: route-owned authentication

When you run phantom exec -- claude, Phantom starts a local HTTP reverse proxy on 127.0.0.1 and rewrites the base URLs in your environment:

OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/openai
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/anthropic
STRIPE_API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/stripe

Here's the full request lifecycle:

Your code / AI agent
     |
     |  POST http://127.0.0.1:PORT/openai/v1/chat/completions
     |  Client request (no credential substitution)
     v
Phantom Proxy (localhost)
     |
     |  1. Authenticate session and match exact route
     |  2. Inject route-owned key into fixed auth header
     |  3. Forward client headers/body without token resolution
     |  4. Forward over TLS to api.openai.com
     |  5. Drop request buffers; the session lookup copy remains until proxy exit
     v
OpenAI API (real endpoint, HTTPS)
     |
     |  Response returns through content-aware scrubbing
     v
Your code / AI agent

This is not a MITM proxy. It does not inject CA certificates or break TLS. Your code sends plaintext HTTP to localhost; the proxy initiates a fresh TLS connection to the upstream API. This is a standard reverse proxy pattern — the same architecture as nginx sitting in front of an application server.

Key design decisions:

  • Reviewed routes. Agentic proxy sessions accept Phantom's exact built-in service definitions and reject repository-authored proxy destinations. This constrains injection, but endpoint integrity, DNS/TLS, the local account, and the configured provider remain in the threat model.
  • Localhost only. The proxy binds to 127.0.0.1, never 0.0.0.0. It is not reachable from the network.
  • Ephemeral ports. Each session gets a random high port, reducing the window for local process abuse.
  • Session-scoped proxy authentication. phantom exec gives the child process fresh phm_ placeholders and a fresh proxy bearer. Client placeholders never resolve; the bearer becomes invalid when that proxy exits. Project tokens stored in dotenv are different values and persist until phantom rotate.

Supported SDKs that honor Phantom's implemented base-URL overrides can work
without source changes. This is not a claim for every HTTP client or protocol.
Protected database connection strings currently make phantom exec fail
closed; Phantom does not inject them into the child environment.

Real usage: three commands 

# 1. After installing the reviewed v0.7.9 GitHub release, initialize the project
$ phantom init
-> Found .env with 5 entries
-> Detected 3 secret(s): OPENAI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
-> Skipped 2 non-secret(s): NODE_ENV, PORT
-> Stored real values in OS keychain
-> Rewrote .env with phantom tokens
ok Project initialized. Run `phantom exec -- <cmd>` to start coding.

# 2. Work with AI — supported SDK routes use the proxy
$ phantom exec -- claude
-> Proxy listening on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port
-> Proxying: OPENAI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
-> Starting: claude

# The app loads phm_ tokens; Claude uses value-blind MCP metadata.
# The SDK hits localhost; the matched route injects its fixed auth header and forwards to the real API.
# Supported SDK calls use the reviewed local proxy route; MCP stays value-blind.

# 3. Deploy — push real secrets to your platform
$ phantom sync --platform vercel
-> Synced 3 secrets to Vercel (real values, not phantom tokens)

MCP server for AI-native secret management

Phantom also ships an MCP server so Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and Codex can manage secrets natively — listing, adding, rotating — without ever seeing a real value:

$ phantom setup --client claude

The release-schema-verified catalog currently contains 54 unique tools covering
vault status, init, safe interactive secret entry, checks, diagnostics, cloud
sync, audit, validation, rotation, expiry, compliance, and team vaults. The
deprecated plaintext add tool refuses secret values through MCP, so real
credentials stay out of the agent context. Runtime tools/list is canonical.

Architecture: modular Rust workspace 

phantom-core     Config, .env parsing, token generation (256-bit CSPRNG, phm_ prefix)
phantom-vault    VaultBackend trait: OS keychain + encrypted file fallback
phantom-proxy    HTTP reverse proxy (hyper), token replacement, TLS forwarding (reqwest)
phantom-cli      clap-based CLI with agent readiness, proxy, sync, audit, teams
phantom-mcp      MCP server (rmcp SDK), stdio transport, schema-verified catalog
workspace/kernel Value-blind setup plus fail-closed governed-execution foundations

The vault uses ChaCha20-Poly1305 for encryption with Argon2id key derivation
(for the encrypted file fallback). Major vault retrieval, serialization, and
decrypted-file buffers use targeted zeroization, while some proxy lookup copies
remain ordinary strings. Zeroization is defense in depth, not a complete
memory-erasure guarantee. CI runs the Rust test suite and clippy before release.

The cloud client can encrypt a vault payload before upload so the vault API
stores ciphertext rather than decrypted secret values. That property does not
remove the client, account, endpoint, or deployed-service trust boundaries.

Why not existing tools?

I looked at the landscape before building this.

1Password / HashiCorp Vault — Enterprise secret-management systems with
different runtime models. Environment-injection workflows such as op run can
still expose a value to an agent that can inspect that process environment;
their current product capabilities should be evaluated independently.

Doppler / Infisical — Centralized secret-management systems that can inject
real values at runtime. If an agent can inspect the target environment, that
specific integration pattern may cross the agent context boundary.

dotenvx — Encrypts .env files at rest, which is useful. But at runtime, secrets are decrypted into real environment variables. The AI sees them.

The design gap Phantom targets is narrower: agent workflows where readable
dotenv values or real process-environment credentials can enter model context,
transcripts, generated files, or tool calls.

Get started 

phantom init

Install the checksum-verified v0.7.9 GitHub release binaries using the
current platform instructions before running
this command. Three commands establish the local boundary for supported API routes. Keep
dotenv reads denied, review the generated config, and use the documented
recovery and CI controls for the rest of the system.

Phantom's local CLI and proxy are MIT-licensed Rust software and do not require
the hosted service for local protection. Hosted packaging and future pricing
are separate from the open-source license.

  • Website: phm.dev
  • GitHub: github.com/ashlrai/phantom-secrets
  • Docs: phm.dev/docs/getting-started

If you've ever pasted an API key into an AI coding tool and felt a twinge of guilt — you were right to. But you don't have to stop using AI to fix it.

title: Build a Resume-Safe Batch Summarizer: A Case Study on a Free Server
description:
It is 1 a.m., the fan is loud, and the lid is closed. Somewhere in that folder of lecture notes, a job is either still moving or already dead, and you have no way to tell which until morning.

That gap is the whole reason this article exists. I wanted one small project — summarize every file in a folder — and I wanted a crash to cost me exactly one file. Not the whole night, not the whole budget. So the learning question here is narrow: when a batch job dies in the middle, what is the smallest piece of state that lets you restart without paying twice? If you can answer that in your head before reading on, you already own this idea.

The project, end to end

I called it nightshift. One folder of note files goes in, one append-only ledger.jsonl comes out, and every line in that ledger is a claim about a single file: "I was processed, here is the result, here is the model and prompt version that produced it." That's it. No database, no queue service, no framework.

The reason I reached for MonkeyCode here is boring and practical: the free model access gives me an endpoint I don't have to pay for to run a batch of a few hundred small calls, and the free server option means the job can keep running after my laptop sleeps. Both are availability claims from the operator rather than things I've audited myself. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The allowance I was told to expect is on the order of ten million free tokens, and there is a free server option alongside it. Treat those numbers as a starting point to confirm on the project page before you plan a semester around them — I have not measured the quota, and you shouldn't assume it is permanent either.

Prerequisites, exactly

Python 3.11 or newer (I ran this on 3.11.9), standard library only, and a folder of text files. That's the whole list. I deliberately keep the fixture .txt files so nothing in this article depends on network access — if you have PDFs, extract them to text first with pdftotext and let the runner stay ignorant of file formats.

Here is the naive version I started from, and I want you to see it fail before I fix it:

for p in Path("corpus").rglob("*.txt"):
    summary = call_model(p.read_text())
    open("out.jsonl", "a").write(json.dumps({"file": str(p), "summary": summary}) + "\n")

Three things go wrong. Kill it at file 211 and the next run re-sends files 1 through 210 — you paid twice for the same text. Key your output on the path and a renamed copy becomes a brand new call. And a plain write without a flush can leave a half-written line that poisons every later read. None of these are exotic; they are just invisible until the second run.

The artifact

Save this as nightshift.py. It is the entire runner.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""nightshift.py - resumable batch summarizer. Python 3.11+, stdlib only."""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

PROMPT_VERSION = "sum-v1"
LEDGER = Path("ledger.jsonl")
SUFFIXES = {".txt", ".pdf"}


def fingerprint(path: Path, model: str) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    h.update(path.read_bytes())
    h.update(model.encode("utf-8"))
    h.update(PROMPT_VERSION.encode("utf-8"))
    return h.hexdigest()[:16]


def load_done(ledger: Path) -> dict:
    done = {}
    if not ledger.exists():
        return done
    for lineno, line in enumerate(ledger.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(), 1):
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        try:
            rec = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            print(f"warning: torn line {lineno} ignored", file=sys.stderr)
            continue
        done[rec["key"]] = rec
    return done


def append(ledger: Path, rec: dict) -> None:
    with ledger.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        fh.write(json.dumps(rec, sort_keys=True) + "\n")
        fh.flush()
        os.fsync(fh.fileno())


def stub_model(text: str, model: str) -> str:
    if not text.strip():
        raise ValueError("empty input: no text to summarize")
    words = text.split()
    return f"[{model}] {len(words)} words; first: {' '.join(words[:3])}"


def summarize(path: Path, model: str) -> str:
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
    if os.environ.get("NIGHTSHIFT_STUB") == "1":
        return stub_model(text, model)
    raise SystemExit("no client wired; see the endpoint section")


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    root = Path(argv[1] if len(argv) > 1 else "corpus")
    model = os.environ.get("NIGHTSHIFT_MODEL", "stub-model")
    files = sorted(p for p in root.rglob("*") if p.is_file() and p.suffix in SUFFIXES)
    done = load_done(LEDGER)

    todo, seen, skipped = [], set(), 0
    for p in files:
        key = fingerprint(p, model)
        if key in done or key in seen:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        seen.add(key)
        todo.append((key, p))

    print(f"corpus={len(files)} todo={len(todo)} skipped={skipped}")
    for key, p in todo:
        try:
            summary = summarize(p, model)
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"FAIL {p.name} {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
            append(LEDGER, {"key": key, "file": p.name, "status": "error",
                            "error": type(exc).__name__})
            continue
        append(LEDGER, {"key": key, "file": p.name, "status": "ok",
                        "model": model, "prompt": PROMPT_VERSION,
                        "summary": summary})
        print(f"OK   {p.name}")

    poison = sum(1 for r in load_done(LEDGER).values() if r["status"] == "error")
    print(f"poison={poison}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv))

The fingerprint function is the load-bearing part. It hashes the file bytes, the model name, and the prompt version together, so the same text under a different model is a different job — which is what you want when you swap endpoints, and mildly annoying the first time it silently re-runs everything. That annoyance is the point. A cache that ignores the model is a cache that lies.

The failing input, and the run you can reproduce

Build a fixture with one deliberately broken file. The empty one is my poison file.

mkdir -p corpus
printf 'attention is a lookup table\n' > corpus/a.txt
printf 'a softmax turns scores into weights\n' > corpus/b.txt
: > corpus/c.txt
cp corpus/a.txt corpus/dup_of_a.txt

Now run it offline. The stub keeps the whole exercise network-free.

NIGHTSHIFT_STUB=1 NIGHTSHIFT_MODEL=stub-model python3 nightshift.py corpus

Expected output on the first run:

corpus=4 todo=3 skipped=1
OK   a.txt
OK   b.txt
FAIL c.txt ValueError: empty input: no text to summarize
poison=1

Read the counters slowly, because each one is a decision. skipped=1 is dup_of_a.txt: identical bytes plus identical model plus identical prompt version produced a key already seen in this pass, so it never left the machine. That deduplication is free, and I did not write a single line of code for it. FAIL c.txt is the empty file — most model endpoints reject a blank prompt, so I raise the same way the stub does, and the failure path deliberately writes an error record instead of a summary.

And poison=1 is the trap I want you to notice. The error record uses the same key, so load_done counts it as handled and the next run will not retry it. That is the right default for a batch you are paying for — one broken file shouldn't burn retries forever — but it means a poisoned key sits there quietly until you delete its line by hand. Delete the line, and only that file re-runs.

Run it a second time:

corpus=4 todo=0 skipped=4
poison=1

Zero todo. Nothing resent, nothing re-billed, and the crash boundary is now the only file that was in flight when the process died. That is the property I wanted at 1 a.m.

The ledger itself is the last thing worth inspecting:

{"file": "a.txt", "key": "…", "model": "stub-model", "prompt": "sum-v1", "status": "ok", "summary": "[stub-model] 5 words; first: attention is a"}

The key is a 16-hex-character digest in the real file; I elided it because yours will differ from mine and the counts will not.

Moving it to the free server

Here is where the free server option actually earns its place. My laptop sleeps, and a sleeping laptop is a job that stops without telling you. A box that stays awake turns a 40-minute batch into something you check over breakfast.

Two commands do the trip. Ship the corpus and the script, then start the run detached so an SSH hiccup doesn't kill it:

rsync -av corpus/ box:~/nightshift/corpus/
rsync -av nightshift.py box:~/nightshift/
ssh box 'cd ~/nightshift && NIGHTSHIFT_MODEL=<model-id> nohup python3 nightshift.py corpus > run.log 2>&1 &'
ssh box 'tail -f ~/nightshift/run.log'
rsync -av box:~/nightshift/ledger.jsonl ./ledger.jsonl

Notice what I did not do: I did not try to make the remote box reliable. I made it disposable. The ledger is the only state that matters, it is append-only, and it travels back over rsync in a second. If the free server is reclaimed tomorrow, I lose the run in progress and nothing else — which is exactly the trade I want from something I am not paying for.

When should you run where? I use three rules:

Situation Run it on Why
Under ~50 files, one-off Your laptop Setup cost outweighs the benefit
Long batch, sleeps overnight Free server Keeps running when your lid closes
Deadline or SLA attached Paid endpoint Free tiers carry no promises
Anything confidential Neither You cannot send the text to a third party at all

That last row is not rhetorical. Lecture notes you wrote are fine. A friend's medical records, an employer's internal docs, or someone else's copyrighted book are not — no free tier makes that decision for you.

Common mistakes I hit while writing this

Using the file path as the key instead of the content hash. It works perfectly until you reorganize your folders, and then every file is new.

Forgetting to version the prompt. Change one word in your instruction, rerun, and now your ledger holds two incompatible generations of summaries with no way to tell them apart. PROMPT_VERSION costs you one line.

Retrying on a timer instead of on a key. Time-based retry logic guesses. A ledger does not guess; it knows whether the key is present.

And the one I still catch myself doing: writing to the ledger before the call succeeds. Order matters here. Call, then append, never the reverse.

What I actually learned

A batch job is not a loop. It is a loop plus a durable claim about what already happened, and the claim is worth more than the loop. Once the key exists, retries, model swaps, machine swaps, and crashes all collapse into the same boring question: is this key in the set?

I also stopped treating the free server as an environment and started treating it as a spot to stand. Something you can lose without losing work is a much better fit for a free tier than hoping it behaves like a paid one.

How to swap in a real endpoint: replace the body of summarize with an HTTP call, set NIGHTSHIFT_STUB to nothing, and keep the guard that raises when neither is configured. The exact request shape belongs to whichever endpoint you were given, and I have not run this particular client, so treat it as a sketch rather than tested code:

# SKETCH - unexecuted. Adapt the payload and the response path to your endpoint.
import urllib.request

def call_endpoint(text: str, model: str) -> str:
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        os.environ["NIGHTSHIFT_URL"],
        data=json.dumps({"model": model, "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize in one sentence:\n{text}"}]}).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json",
                 "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['NIGHTSHIFT_KEY']}"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as resp:
        return json.load(resp)["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

Who should not use this approach? Anyone whose batch has a deadline attached, anyone processing text they are not allowed to send off-device, and anyone who needs to cite an exact model version months later in published work. A free tier plus a hand-rolled ledger is a good fit for a student's overnight notes job, and a poor fit for a pipeline with a contract behind it.

Your turn, and I am more interested in the diagnosis than the applause. Suppose c.txt is the second file in a 400-file run and the process dies at file 300. On restart, which counters change, and which file never gets a second chance no matter how many times you rerun? If you can predict that from the code above, you have the pattern — and a good extension exercise is splitting skipped into two counters, one for keys already in the ledger and one for duplicates caught inside the current pass, so the log stops conflating them.

title: Causal Syntax Circuits in CodeLMs: Budget and Probe Decide What Looks Localised
description:
arXiv:2610.20683v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Code models write Python when the prompt does not say which language to use. We ask a mechanistic question about that habit: is it produced by a small, findable group of components inside the model? We run one pipeline---mean ablation, activation patching, greedy circuit extraction, a random-control significance test, and activation steering---over 55 model-language settings spanning ten open code models (five base and five instruction-tuned), three target languages (Rust, C#, PHP), two prompt suites, and two component budgets. We report five findings. First, the preference is large, grows with model size, and survives instruction tuning: it is larger on every instruction-tuned checkpoint than on its base version, by 12% on average. Second, its measured size is mostly a property of the probe; replacing our aligned prompts with XLCoST parallel functions takes the same measurement on the same models from about 1.6 to about 0.01. Third, whether the preference looks localised depends on how many components the search may keep: with a budget of 12, 1 of 15 settings yields a circuit that beats size-matched random controls after multiple-comparison correction, and with a budget of 40, 6 of 15 do. Fourth, interventions that a smaller-budget study reports as uniformly failing do sometimes succeed: patching makes a Python prompt prefer target syntax in 2 of 45 settings, and steering changes the most likely next token in 9 of 45. Fifth, every circuit whose effect is significant but points away from the target language comes from a setting where circuit extraction failed, which makes such results a diagnostic rather than a phenomenon. The practical lesson is that a claim about whether a behaviour is localised can turn on analysis choices that papers rarely report. We release the full grid so those choices can be varied.

title: VLA-$\Delta$: Learning Physical State Transition for Vision-Language-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21306v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$\Delta$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$\Delta$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta

title: OmicsBench: a long-horizon multi-turn benchmark of AI agents on research-study-scale bioinformatics
description:
arXiv:2610.21074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational biologists increasingly delegate substantial analyses to AI agents in long-horizon, multi-turn sessions, yet most benchmarks of agents' bioinformatics capabilities pose a single short task with a single-shot prompt. We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents. Each of its 97 tasks links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph, for 662 underlying subtasks in all. Each subtask is posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on incorrect answers. Across 12 models on three harnesses, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and no combination comes near saturating the benchmark, with mean scores of 0.43 to 0.57 out of a possible 1 without in-context feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it. Multi-turn evaluation also uncovers behavior that single-shot prompts cannot, as agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier subtasks, and in-context feedback helps agents recover some of that loss. Because deterministic scoring gives no qualitative account of how an agent failed, we also introduce an unsupervised failure mode discovery pipeline that describes, embeds, and clusters agents' failed attempts to surface emergent failure modes. Applied to OmicsBench, this pipeline exposes qualitative shortcomings in how agents carry out bioinformatics analyses, ranging from agents applying their own statistical filters in place of the specified ones to agents writing whole answers from memory.

title: Java Operators in GenAI
description:
Introduction

Java operators help developers perform calculations, comparisons, and logical operations.

They are useful when building AI-powered applications.

In GenAI, operators can validate user inputs and evaluate AI response scores.

They also help control application logic and decision-making.

What Are Java Operators?

Java operators are symbols used to perform operations on variables and values, such as addition, comparison, and logical evaluation.

Syntax / Example 

int tokenCount = 150;
int maxTokens = 200;
double confidenceScore = 0.92;

System.out.println(tokenCount < maxTokens);
System.out.println(confidenceScore >= 0.90);
System.out.println(tokenCount + 50);

Practical Example

In a Java-based AI application, comparison operators can check whether a response meets a confidence-score threshold, while arithmetic operators can calculate token usage.

Key Takeaways

  • Arithmetic operators perform calculations.
  • Comparison operators compare values.
  • Logical operators combine conditions.
  • Operators help implement AI application rules.
  • They support validation and decision-making.

Conclusion

Java operators are useful for controlling logic in GenAI applications. They help developers compare values, perform calculations, and evaluate conditions. Understanding operators makes it easier to build reliable Java-based AI systems.

Which Java operator would you use to validate an AI response score?

title: Go 1.27 Has Generic Methods. They Can't Satisfy an Interface, and That's the Point
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

func GetAs[V any](c *Cache, key string) (V, bool) belongs on the cache. Until this year it had to live at package scope, because Go would not let a method declare its own type parameters.

Go 1.27, released in August 2026, changes that. The release notes call it "widely anticipated", and the standard library ships the first example: math/rand/v2 now has a method (*Rand) N[Int intType](Int) Int, next to the generic function N it already had. Calling it looks like any generic function call, with the type argument inferred from the argument:

r := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2))
backoff := r.N(500 * time.Millisecond) // Int = time.Duration

The same paragraph of the release notes ends with the catch: "methods of interfaces may not declare type parameters nor can interface methods be implemented by generic methods."

That sentence will trip up anyone who reaches for an interface the moment they see a useful method.

A cache with a generic Get

Start with a module whose go.mod says go 1.27. The go directive sets the language version, and the compiler rejects features newer than it, so an older directive turns the method below into an error.

The cache stores values of any type. Before 1.27, typed retrieval needed a package-level helper. Now it is a method:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

type User struct {
    ID   int
    Plan string
}

// Cache stores values of any type under string keys.
type Cache struct {
    mu   sync.RWMutex
    data map[string]any
}

func NewCache() *Cache {
    return &Cache{data: make(map[string]any)}
}

func (c *Cache) Set(key string, v any) {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()
    c.data[key] = v
}

// Get returns the value under key as a V. ok is false
// when the key is missing or holds a different type.
func (c *Cache) Get[V any](key string) (V, bool) {
    c.mu.RLock()
    defer c.mu.RUnlock()
    v, ok := c.data[key].(V)
    return v, ok
}

func main() {
    c := NewCache()
    c.Set("user:42", User{ID: 42, Plan: "pro"})
    c.Set("hits", 17)

    u, ok := c.Get[User]("user:42")
    fmt.Println(u.Plan, ok) // u.Plan is "pro", ok is true

    _, ok = c.Get[string]("hits")
    fmt.Println(ok) // false: "hits" holds an int
}

Cache itself is not generic: the spec allows a method to declare type parameters "possibly in addition to type parameters declared by the receiver specification", so a plain struct qualifies. And the call site must spell out [User], because V appears only in the results and there is nothing to infer it from. From the spec: "Like a generic function, a generic method must be instantiated before it can be called or used as a value."

The lock is a sync.RWMutex so concurrent readers don't block each other. The type assertion c.data[key].(V) handles both failure cases at once: a missing key yields a nil any, and the assertion on nil fails the same way a wrong type does.

Try to put Get in an interface

Now the reflex: you want to mock this cache in tests, so you write an interface for it.

// Attempt 1: rejected by the parser.
type TypedStore interface {
    Get[V any](key string) (V, bool)
    Set(key string, v any)
}

This never reaches type checking. The compiler's parser has a dedicated message for it, "interface method must have no type parameters", and the spec states the rule directly: "Interface methods cannot declare type parameters, but they may use type parameters from the interface declaration."

Fine, you think: drop the type parameter and ask for the any version. c.Get[any] has exactly that signature.

// Attempt 2: the interface compiles, the assertion doesn't.
type Getter interface {
    Get(key string) (any, bool)
}

var _ Getter = (*Cache)(nil) // compile error

The build fails because *Cache does not implement Getter. The Go blog post on generic methods uses this exact situation, where T.M[int] has the same signature as I.M, and explains why it still doesn't count: "interface implementation is a property of a (possibly instantiated) type, not of any particular method." The accepted proposal by Robert Griesemer puts it more bluntly: "a generic concrete method does not match against an interface method with the same name and signature."

So a generic method is invisible to interface satisfaction, in both directions. Interfaces can't ask for one, and a type can't use one to answer an interface.

Why the compiler says no

An interface value is two words: a pointer to a table and a pointer to the data. Russ Cox's write-up of Go's interface layout describes that table as metadata followed by "a list of function pointers", and a method call through the interface jumps through one of those pointers. One method, one slot, one compiled function.

A generic method compiles to a family of instantiations, and the compiler only generates the ones some call site asks for. When you call c.Get[User] on a concrete *Cache, the compiler sees User and builds that version.


One slot per interface method, but a generic method has no single body to put in it.

Through an interface, that knowledge is gone. The code that calls s.Get[V] might live in a package compiled long after the one that defines *Cache, asking for a V nobody has seen. The blog post spells out the two ways out, and why Go took neither. Generating T.M "with every possible type argument" is "impractical". Passing the type argument at run time as a boxed value would let one compiled body serve every instantiation, "at the cost of indirect call overhead", and that cost would land on direct calls too.

The result is no hidden runtime cost on direct calls and no unbounded code generation. Generic methods are for organizing code on concrete types, and interfaces work exactly as before.

The refactor: keep the interface non-generic

The fix is to split the cache into two layers. The interface carries the non-generic primitive. The type-safe convenience sits on top of it, written once. Replace the Get from the first listing with the version below.

// Store is the contract. No type parameters anywhere.
type Store interface {
    Load(key string) (any, bool)
    Set(key string, v any)
}

func (c *Cache) Load(key string) (any, bool) {
    c.mu.RLock()
    defer c.mu.RUnlock()
    v, ok := c.data[key]
    return v, ok
}

// Lookup works on any Store, not only *Cache.
func Lookup[V any](s Store, key string) (V, bool) {
    v, _ := s.Load(key)
    t, ok := v.(V)
    return t, ok
}

// Get replaces the earlier version: sugar over Lookup.
func (c *Cache) Get[V any](key string) (V, bool) {
    return Lookup[V](c, key)
}

var _ Store = (*Cache)(nil) // compiles

*Cache satisfies Store because Load and Set are ordinary methods. The generic Get is still there, and it doesn't interfere, because it sits outside what interfaces can see. Your test fake implements two plain methods, and Lookup works against it unchanged.


The interface holds the plain primitive. The generic layer sits above it.

If every value in a given cache has the same type, the other refactor is to move the type parameter from the method to the type. A type parameter on the type is different from one on the method. Generic interfaces like the one below have been legal since Go 1.18:

type Typed[V any] interface {
    Get(key string) (V, bool)
}

type TypedCache[V any] struct {
    mu   sync.RWMutex
    data map[string]V
}

func (c *TypedCache[V]) Get(key string) (V, bool) {
    c.mu.RLock()
    defer c.mu.RUnlock()
    v, ok := c.data[key]
    return v, ok
}

var _ Typed[User] = (*TypedCache[User])(nil)

Here Get is not a generic method. V is fixed the moment you write TypedCache[User], so the method has one concrete signature and fits one interface slot. You pay with one cache per value type.

When a generic function is still the better choice

Generic methods fix the package-scope problem from the opening. The blog post's example is a Map method on a list, where chained calls read left to right instead of inside out. Generic methods still don't replace generic functions, and three cases favor the function.

The code holds an interface. A generic method lives on one concrete type. Lookup above works on every Store, including fakes and wrappers you haven't written yet. A method can't do that. The same goes for test doubles: in Go the usual seam for one is an interface, and an interface can only hold non-generic methods. Keep the generic part thin and put the behavior behind the plain method, as Load does above.

You need a tighter constraint than the type declares. The spec says receiver type parameter constraints "are implied by the receiver base type definition", so a method can't narrow them. A Sum over a List[E any] has to be a function:

type List[E any] []E

// A method can't add a numeric constraint to E.
func Sum[E int | int64 | float64](l List[E]) E {
    var s E
    for _, x := range l {
        s += x
    }
    return s
}

Something discovers methods through reflection. The proposal says generic methods "won't be accessible via reflection (by name or index) for the same reason that uninstantiated generic functions are not accessible." Code that looks methods up dynamically through reflect will not find them.

Use the generic method when the operation belongs to one concrete type and every caller already has that type in hand. Use the function when the operation belongs to a contract.

If this was useful

Rules like this one feel arbitrary until you know the language underneath them. If the "why" section was the part you enjoyed, The Complete Guide to Go Programming goes deep on the language, the runtime, the standard library and concurrency.

title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
description:
arXiv:2610.20865v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. The standard response is to build a long-context drafter, by training or fine-tuning one, or by using a multi-token-prediction head shipped inside the target checkpoint. We argue this is unnecessary, because the drafters in use are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the entire prefix, so distant context already reaches them without their own attention, and verification corrects what they miss. We therefore freeze released short-context drafters and run them far past their training length under two inference-time mechanisms, one bounding the attention cache they see, which fixes their cost, and one re-basing their rotary position indices into the trained range. No weight is touched and the only tunable saturates early, so one vLLM-side configuration spans 4k to two million tokens, costing at most 0.16x of speedup at short length. We prove when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged, and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens, across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora. The claim concerns the flatness rather than the multiple, and removing either mechanism eliminates it. The gain is conditional on the speculative cost per emitted token staying below the matched target-only cost.
