title: BD-HazardVLM: Probing Vision-Language Models for Latent Defensive-Driving Hazards in Bangladesh Road Scenes
description:
arXiv:2610.20627v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used for driving-scene understanding, yet their defensive reasoning under weakly structured Global South traffic remains unclear. We introduce BD-HazardVLM, a diagnostic benchmark of 500 Bangladesh road-scene images, comprising 375 from RSUD20K and 125 from TFP-BD, annotated for hazard presence, primary hazard category, risk timing, severity, defensive actions, visible evidence, and hallucination- and Western-road-bias traps. We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and MiniCPM-V-4.6 using a shared zero-shot task definition and structured output schema. Binary hazard-presence accuracy ranges from 88.0 percent to 89.2 percent, essentially matching the 89.0 percent majority-class baseline. Fine-grained reasoning is substantially weaker: category accuracy remains below 40 percent, risk-timing accuracy ranges from 1.6 percent to 12.4 percent, and exact defensive-action matching remains below 2 percent. Although InternVL3-8B achieves the highest severity accuracy at 61.2 percent, it has zero recall on the 58 high-severity cases. Qwen exhibits severe category mode collapse, while all models show weak latent-hazard anticipation and near-zero self-reported trap recognition. For the evaluated models, these findings show that coarse hazard recognition does not imply reliable fine-grained defensive-driving reasoning and motivate geographically diverse safety evaluation.

title: CoTranslator: Reverse to Forward Chain-of-Thought Translator for Reasoning Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.20828v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning distillation requires chain-of-thought (CoT) data with correct answers, but obtaining such data efficiently remains challenging. Forward CoT generation (FCG) followed by rejection sampling (RS) produces verified, question-only responses, yet may require many teacher calls for difficult problems. Reverse CoT generation (RCG) is cheaper because it conditions on the known answer, but access to this answer can lead to post-hoc rationalization and a mismatch with the student's answer-free inference setting. We propose CoTranslator, which learns to translate reverse CoT responses toward the distribution of verified forward responses. Trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses, it supports large-scale generation and verification of student training data. Across six student models evaluated on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improves average accuracy over semantic suppression by up to $5.82$ percentage points. For two 4B students, it retains $95.0\%$ of rejection sampling's average accuracy while using $35.9\%$ of its estimated compute. Without retraining, the same translator transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher, and STEM problems, improving average STEM accuracy by $4.88$ and $4.31$ percentage points for 4B and 8B students, respectively. These results show that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable approach to reasoning distillation.

title: Cloud Testing vs On-Premise Testing: Choosing the Right Testing Environment
description:
Testing infrastructure can be managed internally or accessed through a cloud-based testing platform. The right approach depends on an organization's testing requirements, infrastructure, and security constraints.

Modern applications need to be tested across a growing mix of devices, operating systems, networks, browsers, and geographic locations. For mobile applications in particular, access to physical devices and different network conditions can affect test coverage and performance visibility.

This guide compares cloud and on-premise testing across scalability, security, device coverage, and performance to help you choose the right approach.

What Is Cloud Testing?

Cloud testing uses remotely hosted infrastructure to test applications without requiring teams to build and maintain the entire testing environment themselves. Teams can access browsers, operating systems, and real devices through the cloud and run tests remotely.

This allows teams to scale test execution, expand device and browser coverage, run tests in parallel, and test applications across different networks and geographic locations. For mobile applications, cloud testing can also provide access to real devices without requiring teams to maintain their own physical device lab.

What Is On-Premise Testing?

On-premise testing uses infrastructure that is hosted and managed within an organization's own environment. This can include test servers, physical devices, internal networks, and other resources required to run and manage tests.

It gives teams greater control over infrastructure, data, security, and test environments. This makes on-premise testing useful for organizations with strict security or compliance requirements, restricted applications, or environments that cannot be accessed through external infrastructure.
However, teams are also responsible for provisioning, maintaining, scaling, and upgrading the infrastructure, which can increase operational overhead as testing requirements grow.

Cloud Testing vs. On-Premise Testing: Key Differences

Cloud Testing vs. On-Premise Testing: Pros and Cons

The trade-offs become clearer when you look at how each approach affects infrastructure, testing coverage, and day-to-day operations.

Cloud Testing
Cloud testing reduces the need to build and maintain testing infrastructure internally. Teams can access testing environments remotely and scale them based on demand.

Key advantages

  • Faster scalability: Add devices and testing capacity without purchasing new hardware.
  • Broader test coverage: Access more devices, operating systems, browsers, and environments.
  • Lower maintenance: The provider manages much of the underlying infrastructure.
  • Remote access: Distributed teams can access the same testing environments from anywhere.

Key limitations

  • Less infrastructure control: Teams have limited control over the underlying hardware and environment.
  • Provider dependency: Availability, device selection, and supported capabilities depend on the provider.
  • Security considerations: Sensitive applications may require private, dedicated, or controlled deployments.
  • Usage-based costs: Costs can increase as testing volume and infrastructure usage grow.

On-Premise Testing
On-premise testing gives organizations direct ownership of their testing infrastructure. This provides greater control but also makes the organization responsible for managing it.

Key advantages
Greater control: Teams control the hardware, software, networks, and test environments.
Security and isolation: Suitable for sensitive applications and restricted environments.
Customization: Infrastructure can be configured around specific testing requirements.
Air-gapped testing: Works well for environments that cannot connect to external infrastructure.

Key limitations

  • Higher infrastructure overhead: Teams must purchase, configure, and maintain the required hardware.
  • Limited scalability: Expanding capacity requires additional infrastructure.
  • Device management: Organizations must procure, maintain, replace, and update physical devices.
  • Geographic limitations: Testing across locations, carriers, or network conditions may require additional infrastructure.

When Should You Choose Cloud Testing?

Cloud testing is a strong fit when your testing strategy requires broad coverage, rapid scaling, or access to infrastructure that would be difficult to build internally.
1. You need broad device coverage
Access a wider range of devices, operating systems, and browsers without purchasing and maintaining them internally.
2. You need to scale testing quickly
Add testing capacity as test volume grows without investing in additional physical infrastructure.
3. You run tests in parallel
Run tests across multiple devices and environments simultaneously to reduce execution time.
4. You test across locations and networks
Test applications across different geographic locations, network conditions, and, where supported, carrier environments.
5. You have distributed testing teams
Give QA and engineering teams remote access to the same testing infrastructure without requiring access to a physical lab.
6. You want to reduce infrastructure overhead
Let the cloud provider handle much of the infrastructure provisioning, maintenance, and upgrades.

When Should You Choose On-Premise Testing?

On-premise testing is a better fit when infrastructure control, isolation, or specific security requirements are more important than rapid scalability.
1. You need direct infrastructure control
Manage the hardware, software, networks, and test environments according to your organization's requirements.
2. You handle sensitive applications or data
Keep testing infrastructure and data within your organization's controlled environment.
3. You require air-gapped testing
Run tests in environments that must remain isolated from external networks and infrastructure.
4. You need highly customized environments
Configure testing infrastructure around specific application, network, or hardware requirements.
5. You need access to restricted internal systems
Test applications and services that cannot be exposed to external testing infrastructure.
6. You already have suitable infrastructure
Continue using existing hardware and test environments when they provide the device coverage and capacity your teams need.

Can You Combine Cloud and On-Premise Testing?

Yes. A hybrid testing setup allows teams to use both cloud and on-premise infrastructure based on the requirements of each workload.
1. Keep sensitive testing on-premise
Use internal infrastructure for applications, data, or systems that require strict security, isolation, or compliance controls.
2. Use the cloud for scale and coverage
Use cloud infrastructure when you need broader device coverage, parallel execution, geographic access, or additional testing capacity.
3. Extend existing infrastructure
A hybrid model can complement an existing on-premise lab rather than requiring teams to replace it entirely.
4. Choose the environment per workload
Not every test needs the same infrastructure. Teams can run restricted tests on-premise while using cloud infrastructure for mobile, browser, regression, or large-scale device testing.

The next section should naturally move from the decision framework into HeadSpin's role, without turning into an abrupt product pitch.

How HeadSpin Supports Cloud and On-Premise Testing

HeadSpin gives teams access to real devices, networks, and testing infrastructure across multiple deployment options. This allows organizations to choose the level of control and coverage they need without limiting testing to a single infrastructure model.
1. Test on real devices
Access physical Android and iOS devices, tablets, Smart TVs, and other connected devices without maintaining the entire device inventory internally.
2. Test across real networks
Test applications under different network conditions and access SIM-enabled devices across locations to evaluate how network changes affect application performance.
3. Scale testing across locations
Scale Testing helps to access devices across 50+ global locations to expand geographic coverage and test applications closer to the conditions users experience in different markets.
4. Choose the right deployment model
HeadSpin supports shared cloud, dedicated cloud, on-premise, and air-gapped deployments, allowing organizations to balance scalability, security, and infrastructure control.
5. Capture performance beyond test results
HeadSpin captures 130+ performance KPIs across the application, device, and network layers, helping teams understand not just whether a test passed, but how the application performed during testing.

Cloud Testing vs. On-Premise Testing: Which Is Better?

There is no single answer for every organization. Cloud testing is generally better suited to teams that need scalability, broad device coverage, geographic access, and lower infrastructure overhead. On-premise testing is a better fit when infrastructure control, isolation, or highly customized environments are priorities.

For many enterprises, the practical choice is not one or the other. A combination of cloud and on-premise testing can provide the scalability and coverage of the cloud while keeping sensitive or restricted workloads under internal control.

title: CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF
description:
arXiv:2610.21138v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feedback noise is pervasive in preference data, arising from subjective human judgments, annotation mistakes, and imperfect LLM judges. Standard reward modeling trained on such feedback yields a biased estimate of the clean risk. Although classical denoising methods are directly applicable to noisy feedback learning, they generally assume a uniform noise ratio across samples. However, this assumption fails for feedback data, where noise is intrinsically sample-wise. To address this challenge, we propose CleanRM, which uses a few clean feedback to calibrate sample-wise noise ratios via optimal transport. Specifically, CleanRM aligns the joint distribution of preferences reverted from noisy feedback with that of clean feedback and then trains the reward model using a noise-corrected surrogate loss. Theoretically, we prove that the resulting objective is unbiased with respect to the clean risk. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CleanRM outperforms state-of-the-art denoising baselines and yields more effective downstream RLHF alignment.

title: Defining and Generating Compositional Structure
description:
arXiv:2610.20922v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compositional structure is pervasive in nature and across scales: atoms combine into molecules, molecules into cells, and cells into organisms, while further compositional hierarchies appear within each level. More broadly, compositionality, the reuse and recombination of parts into novel structures, is a fundamental source of interesting complexity in both natural and artificial systems. Yet despite its importance, and despite our apparent ease in recognizing it, mathematical accounts capturing what we intuitively mean by compositional structure remain limited. Here, we fill this gap by formalizing a simple idea: compositional structure emerges when parts, considered together, reveal shared structure that is not captured when those parts are modeled separately. We express this idea using algorithmic information theory, the mathematics of information and compression, which provides a natural way to identify structure in arbitrary data without specifying in advance what that structure must look like. Applied across scales, our definition informs where and how compositional structure emerges within an object. Using tractable approximations, we then invert the framework to generate compositional objects: we specify the desired form of their compositional structure without prescribing their particular content, and optimize directly over strings and images. The resulting objects exhibit readily recognizable hierarchical reuse and part-whole organization, suggesting that the definition captures compositional structure rather than merely complexity, regularity, or shared information. Finally, we discuss implications for machine learning, including a new perspective on depth in neural architectures and principles for constructing compositional data curricula capable of supporting open-ended learning.

title: Context Injection and Long-Horizon Reliability: Separating Duplicate Recognition, Local Processing, and Counter Tracking
description:
arXiv:2610.20633v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon failures of language models are usually measured as end-task success or as a horizon length. We instead score, step by step, three components of a 400-step ledger task in which every step is easy in isolation and the model's own answers are re-injected into its context: recognising a record already seen 5 to 300 steps earlier, processing the current record locally, and writing a counter incremented at every step. On Qwen3-8B (non-thinking, 20 seeds, replicated on a second machine and backend), with every step scored component by component, two results hold. First, duplicate-recognition errors rise late in the episode -- from 0.0019 to 0.011 per step at risk across step 200 -- while the counter makes no error in 8,000 steps and local processing is descriptively stable; the rise combines long-distance recall errors and rising false alarms. Second, a block of irrelevant content inserted before each step makes the counter fail in 20 of 20 seeds on each machine, against none without it, while its effect on local processing is much smaller and not distinguishable from none. Three pre-registered follow-ups probe the counter. Its value depends on the value present in the response history: a corrupted value persists without correction in every seed, and an exact external reminder, repeated before each message, re-aligns it within one to two steps. Under the irrelevant block, no counter error was observed when an exact compact reminder of the state, supplied externally by an oracle, preceded each message (0 of 20 seeds with an error, against 15 without it), and this reminder outperformed a length-matched neutral text; whether a single reminder suffices was not conclusive, and the absence of damage to the other components was not established. An aggregate or exclusive error classification can hide the difference we report.

title: Mutable retry state inside authenticated encrypted DTN mailboxes
description:
Mutable retry state inside authenticated encrypted DTN mailboxes

Most mesh people talk about routing first. I spend more time worrying about what happens when a message never gets delivered at all.

GhostWire is a Rust mesh-protocol experiment: libp2p, XChaCha20-Poly1305, Kademlia-backed offline mailboxes, and DTN store-carry-forward routing. The mailbox layer has one awkward requirement:

  • sender seals a message for the recipient’s public key
  • recipient is offline
  • one or more peers stores the sealed envelope
  • retries happen without re-sealing the payload

That seemingly small requirement forces a design decision that I became uncomfortable with and want to put in front of people who understand AEAD better than I do.

The envelope 

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct MailboxEnvelope {
    pub recipient_id: String,
    pub ephemeral_pub: String,
    pub ciphertext: Vec<u8>,
    pub nonce: String,
    pub created_at: u64,
    pub message_id: String,
    pub attempts: u32, // deliberately excluded from AAD
}

impl Drop for MailboxEnvelope {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.ciphertext.zeroize();
    }
}

The encrypted mailbox AAD is bound to immutable metadata:

  • recipient identity
  • ephemeral key
  • nonce
  • message ID
  • creation timestamp

attempts is intentionally not in the AAD.

Tradeoff A: include retry state in AAD

This is the clean cryptographic posture. The authenticator describes everything about the record, including mutable control state.

The practical problem: if retry state changes, the previous authenticator is invalidated. That means either:

  1. re-seal every time under the same recipient key, destroying a useful property
  2. predefine every possible retry counter, which is absurd
  3. let recipients reject or duplicate records every time a signer’s local counter changes

A strict AEAD model collides with retry policy changes.

Tradeoff B: exclude mutable retry state from AAD

The record authorizes what matters:

  • who gets it
  • who sealed it
  • when it was created
  • which message identifier it carries

Retries are a local delivery/cost concern layered above the sealed payload. AAT in this case is concerned with authenticity of intent, not anti-replay accounting for every delivery attempt.

I chose B because the alternative re-creates a seal for every attempt.

What I do not like: a future reader could miss that state at a glance. I need better documentation and possibly a separate signed receipt so retry behavior is non-cryptographically attested.

Retry state should become a proven promise

Instead of dropping attempts into AAD, the more honest pattern seems to be:

  • keep ciphertext immutable and bound to the original AD
  • keep retry-state metadata outside it
  • expose an API boundary that returns a signed envelope descriptor only when attempts are changed
  • audit every state mutation separately from payload readability

This treats the cryptographic envelope as an evidence object and the delivery system as a policy object. That is better than pretending one signature can mean both things.

The more serious concern: accidental ciphertext copies

MailboxEnvelope derives Clone, and this type can travel through serde serializations.

Drop zeroization only affects the dropped allocation. If:

  • a cloned mailbox copy is held elsewhere
  • a temporary serialization buffer is allocated
  • transport middleware buffers bytes

then “the original object was zeroed” is not the same as “all copies disappeared.” Production Rust code has libraries specifically for this: secrecy, zeroize-on-drop patterns, and more explicit small-source handling.

I am not yet sure this level of copy-safety is necessary for ciphertext that is, by design, something one recipient is supposed to decrypt. It may still matter against heap snapshots, debug traces, or process forensics, but the right point is an operational requirement, not an automatic obvious gate.

If you work in Rust cryptography, I want one concrete answer

When ciphertext is being handled by protocols at multiple layers, what is the least effortful and still correct handling model?

  1. Manual Drop plus short-lived scope?
  2. secrecy::Expose and CryptographicBuffer wrapper everywhere?
  3. Accept temporary copies but only allow canonical object copies to remain live for bounded durations?

I am especially interested in patterns that are realistic at 100+ messages/second, not “never instantiate temporary slices.”

What stayed out of this post

GhostWire’s roadmap includes post-quantum key exchange, mix routing, and AI-assisted pathing, but none of that improves the trust model if mailbox confidentiality is sloppy. The mailbox layer is intentionally primitive because it is where subtle assumptions become failures.

If you have experience implementing this kind of encrypted storage in the Rust ecosystem, the comments here are the part I want most.

title: UltraDiff: Transferring High-Fidelity Priors to Compressed Latent Spaces for High-Resolution Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.21202v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-resolution synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) faces a fundamental trade-off between computational cost and generative fidelity. This trade off is largely governed by the latent compression factor f (e.g. f8 denotes f=8 and f32 f=32). While aggressive compression (f32) significantly improves efficiency, it suffers from severe information loss and ambiguity compared to standard f8 models. We propose UltraDiff, a framework that reformulates this challenge as joint latent diffusion learning followed by marginal score distillation. We introduce MixTeacher, a dual branch DiT that models the joint f8-f32 distribution, utilizing shared attention to resolve the ambiguity of the compressed space with high fidelity f8 priors. Crucially, we propose vector field distillation in the native f32 space. Theoretically, this compels the student to learn the conditional expectation of the teacher trajectory, effectively filtering out compression artifacts. Across the evaluated 1K to 4K settings, UltraDiff approaches f8 level quality while preserving f32 efficiency. With 20 sampling steps on a single A100 GPU, it generates a 2K image in 6.2 seconds over 40 times faster than our f8 baseline.

title: When Reasoning Traces Conflict with Evidence: How Answer Configuration Shapes Evidence Following
description:
arXiv:2610.20805v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A reasoning trace retained at answer time plays two roles: it can raise accuracy, and it can compete with the current evidence when the two disagree. We disentangle these roles by crossing verified evidence versions with the traces generated from each and answering from the same traces and evidence under two configurations: continuation of the model's own thinking and a separate answer call. Across three model families (gpt-oss, Gemma4, Qwen3) on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, the separate call raises evidence-following over continuation by 29.9 to 60.6 points. On the same pairs, removing the trace lowers accuracy by similar amounts under both configurations. Yet continuation repeats the stale conclusion in most conflicts, and the separate call follows the current evidence far more often. Benefiting from a trace and deferring to it are therefore distinct properties. Further analyses show that the final line of a trace carries most of its value, gold evidence helps most before the trace is written, distractors weaken correction under a separate call, and renewed reasoning, unlike a verification instruction, follows the current evidence in most conflicts. Because trace deletion alone cannot reveal which source an answer follows, evaluations should report both properties together with the answer configuration.

title: Malformed Metrics Query JSON: Implementing Defensive Alert Worker Boundaries
description:
TL;DR: Treat a malformed metrics-query response as an explicit unknown result, never as zero failures. For a marketplace's nightly data pipeline, attach tenant, pipeline stage, and run identifiers before logs enter shared storage; measure stored bytes by those dimensions; retain compact audit records for every query; and alert separately when the monitoring response cannot be proved valid. The least complex implementation is a strict Go decoder at the worker boundary plus a small, bounded quarantine record containing a digest and a truncated payload.

This ordering matters because the monitoring bill is usually discussed after the parser breaks, although the bill determines what evidence will still exist when it does. The useful quantity is not an advertised unit price. It is attributable stored volume:

daily bytes = sum(encoded event bytes × copies × retention path)

Measure that term first. A worker that silently converts a bad response into an empty result can suppress the failure alert and also assign the query's retrieval cost to an unclassified bucket. That is a correctness defect with an accounting symptom.

What is the bill actually made of?

For this workload, separate ingestion, retained storage, query scanning, and duplicated copies. CloudWatch's public pricing page, for example, describes log ingestion in per-GB terms; the durable lesson is that bytes crossing the ingestion boundary are a cost driver, while the exact commercial rate is deliberately outside this design. Compression, indexing, regional replication, and query execution may add different meters in a particular system, so exporting one total invoice number into a dashboard does not create cost attribution.

Start with an inventory measured from the encoded records, not from an estimate of source rows. The following program accepts an illustrative nightly volume, average encoded size, copy count, and retention days. The sample inputs are an arithmetic demonstration, not a benchmark: 8,000,000 records, 420 bytes each, two retained copies, and 14 days.

package main

import "fmt"

func gib(bytes uint64) float64 {
    return float64(bytes) / (1024 * 1024 * 1024)
}

func main() {
    const records uint64 = 8_000_000
    const encodedBytes uint64 = 420
    const retainedCopies uint64 = 2
    const retentionDays uint64 = 14

    daily := records * encodedBytes * retainedCopies
    retained := daily * retentionDays
    fmt.Printf("daily_ingested_gib=%.2f retained_gib_days=%.2f\n", gib(daily), gib(retained))
}

The multiplication exposes the dominant term without pretending every backend bills identically. Run it again with measurements from each pipeline stage. If catalog_export emits ten times the bytes of settlement_reconcile, optimize the former first even when the latter has the more alarming event count.

Cost attribution must be present at emission time. A useful minimum is marketplace_account, pipeline_stage, run_id, event_class, and outcome. Keep bounded values; a raw error message or order identifier used as a label can create an uncontrolled number of index terms. The high-cardinality detail belongs in the log body, while the stable dimensions belong in the fields used for allocation and filtering.

Do not infer ownership later from free-form text. It fails audit review because the mapping can change after the charge was incurred.

How should an alert worker defensively parse a malformed metrics query JSON response?

The response boundary needs three distinct checks: syntactic JSON validity, the expected envelope shape, and semantic validity of the values used by the alert. HTTP success alone proves none of them. A body containing valid JSON such as {"status":"ok"} is still unusable if the worker's contract requires a numeric failure count and a query identifier.

Model the outcome as valid, invalid, or transport_error. Two states are insufficient. In particular, do not use a zero value as the fallback for a missing number: zero means the pipeline was observed and no failures matched, whereas invalid means the observation could not be completed.

This complete program uses only the Go standard library. UseNumber delays numeric conversion, DisallowUnknownFields detects contract drift rather than ignoring it, the second decode rejects trailing JSON values, and validation refuses blank identifiers, negative counts, or a run mismatch.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
)

type QueryResult struct {
    QueryID     string      `json:"query_id"`
    RunID       string      `json:"run_id"`
    FailureCount json.Number `json:"failure_count"`
}

func parseResult(body []byte, expectedRun string) (QueryResult, error) {
    var result QueryResult
    decoder := json.NewDecoder(bytes.NewReader(body))
    decoder.UseNumber()
    decoder.DisallowUnknownFields()

    if err := decoder.Decode(&result); err != nil {
        return result, fmt.Errorf("decode response: %w", err)
    }
    if err := decoder.Decode(&struct{}{}); !errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
        if err == nil {
            return result, errors.New("response contains a trailing JSON value")
        }
        return result, fmt.Errorf("inspect response suffix: %w", err)
    }
    if result.QueryID == "" || result.RunID == "" || result.FailureCount == "" {
        return result, errors.New("response omits a required field")
    }
    if result.RunID != expectedRun {
        return result, errors.New("response run_id does not match the requested run")
    }
    count, err := result.FailureCount.Int64()
    if err != nil || count < 0 {
        return result, errors.New("failure_count must be a non-negative integer")
    }
    return result, nil
}

func main() {
    tests := [][]byte{
        []byte(`{"query_id":"q-41","run_id":"run-2026-10-08","failure_count":3}`),
        []byte(`{"query_id":"q-42","run_id":"run-2026-10-08","failure_count":`),
        []byte(`{"query_id":"q-43","run_id":"run-2026-10-08"}`),
        []byte(`{"query_id":"q-44","run_id":"wrong-run","failure_count":0}`),
    }
    for _, body := range tests {
        result, err := parseResult(body, "run-2026-10-08")
        fmt.Printf("query=%q count=%q valid=%t error=%v\n",
            result.QueryID, result.FailureCount, err == nil, err)
    }
}

Strict unknown-field rejection is a conscious trade-off. It turns an additive upstream field into a visible compatibility event, which is appropriate when this narrow envelope is an internal contract and deployment is coordinated. For a public or independently evolving API, decode a versioned envelope and tolerate documented additive fields instead. The invariant is narrower: the worker must prove the fields that drive the alert, bind them to the requested run, and reject ambiguous values.

Preserve evidence without retaining every successful payload

Parsing is only half the incident record. For every attempt, write an immutable audit event with the request ID, run ID, pipeline stage, account allocation key, response class, byte length, content digest, parser version, and final decision. Store the raw body only in a bounded quarantine path when the class is invalid; cap its length before persistence and apply access controls appropriate to the data it may contain.

The digest answers a narrow but important question: did two workers receive the same bytes? It does not establish what the remote system intended to send, and it must not be used as a substitute for the response body during diagnosis. Likewise, retries must reuse an idempotency key derived from the logical query and pipeline run, while each attempt receives its own attempt number. The logical decision record is written once; attempt records remain append-only.

That is the exactly-once mindset in practical form. Network delivery is allowed to repeat. The alert decision is not.

A parser failure should open a monitoring-integrity alert whose fingerprint is based on stable dimensions such as operation, schema version, and parser error class, rather than the raw body or request ID. Sentry documents how event grouping and custom fingerprints influence which events become one issue; the general lesson applies without requiring a particular incident tool. Stable grouping prevents every nightly run from becoming a separate incident while retaining run IDs in the event details for reconstruction.

Make the alert state machine explicit

After parsing, the decision table is small enough to review with both operations and finance:

Observation Pipeline alert Integrity alert Cost allocation
Valid count is zero Closed Closed Requested account and stage
Valid count is positive Open Closed Requested account and stage
JSON or schema is invalid Unknown, never closed Open Requested account and stage plus invalid_response
Transport fails after retry budget Unknown, never closed Open Requested account and stage plus transport_error

The distinction between open and unknown is operationally useful. Reusing the pipeline-failure alert for parser defects obscures whether the marketplace job failed or its observer failed. Closing an existing failure alert on unknown evidence is worse: it converts loss of visibility into apparent recovery.

Deploy the contract parser behind recorded fixtures for truncated input, HTML accidentally returned as a body, valid JSON with missing fields, decimal counts, negative counts, duplicate logical responses, and a mismatched run ID. The HTML fixture should fail at decoding; no special content sniffing is required for correctness. Also test the retry boundary with a fake transport so that two deliveries produce two attempt records but one logical decision.

These tests serve auditability as much as reliability. A reviewer can trace the decision from requested run, through exact response classification, to the alert transition and its allocation key.

Retention is a decision about future evidence

The change that moves the dominant storage term is usually selective retention, not parser micro-optimization. Keep compact audit events for all queries, full invalid responses for a short and explicitly governed quarantine period, and aggregated counts for trend analysis. Stop keeping full successful query payloads once the audit event and verified aggregate have been committed.

This deliberately removes the ability to replay an old successful response byte for byte after its retention window. If a later parser defect is discovered, the team can reconstruct which parser version made the decision and compare the stored count and digest, but it cannot reinterpret a body that no longer exists. That loss should be accepted in a retention review, with compliance and incident-reconstruction requirements setting the window; it should not emerge accidentally from a storage cleanup.

The final control is reconciliation. Compare the count of scheduled pipeline runs with valid decisions, invalid decisions, and exhausted transports for the same allocation period. Those categories must account for every run exactly once. Any remainder is a missing observation, and any excess is a duplicate logical decision, even if every individual worker log line looks healthy.

title: PEDBench: Can Speech Models Detect Phonetic Errors?
description:
arXiv:2610.20830v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Phonetic error detection (PED) aims to identify phoneme-level substitutions, deletions, and insertions and is essential for educational and clinical speech assessment and intervention. Despite recent advances in speech models for phoneme recognition, their ability to reliably detect fine-grained phonetic errors remains unclear because of a lack of high-quality evaluation data. To address this gap, we introduce PEDBench, the first PED benchmark spanning a continuum from natural to controlled speech. It comprises real-world recordings of spoken errors made by children (N=334), scripted error productions by human actors (N=1,188), and synthetic error productions generated using phone-conditioned text-to-speech (N=1,083). All phonetic annotations were transcribed and verified by two phonetically trained annotators. Our evaluation of 13 state-of-the-art speech models shows that they fail to reliably detect phonetic errors, even under controlled conditions with acted and synthetic speech, where acoustic variability is reduced. The models also exhibit low precision, frequently misclassifying correctly pronounced phonemes as errors. Our speech-language models, fine-tuned on synthetic data, outperform commercial and open-source baselines on word-level PED, although a sim-to-real domain gap remains. We plan to publicly release our code and recipes, along with our acted and synthetic datasets, to support the development of more accurate PED systems.

title: Multimodal AI Detection for Math-Heavy Scientific Text
description:
arXiv:2610.21062v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models become increasingly capable of generating, and assisting with, scientific writing, there is a need for greater transparency and disclosure around the use of AI in research. Consequently, a veritable subfield of research and a number of commercial services aim to flag AI-generated content automatically. However, existing detectors which rely only on text extracted from PDFs fail to benefit from the rich visual information contained in the formatting of math-heavy scientific content. To study this, we select human-written proof and prose passages from pre-2022 arXiv LaTeX sources and re-generate them using 15 modern LLMs within the context of the same paper. This leaves us with coupled human and AI outputs in three different representations: the LaTeX source, a rendered image of the PDF, and the text extracted from the PDF. We find that the accuracy of the state-of-the-art Pangram 4 drops significantly as the mathematical content in a passage increases, especially when evaluated on text as opposed to LaTeX. However, this is not an inherent limitation of detecting AI-generated math: finetuning Qwen-3.5-27B based detectors on this domain recovers the gap, with LaTeX inputs performing significantly better than text since they preserve more formatting information. Since LaTeX sources are rarely available in practice, we also train SnapJudge: an image-based detector operating on screenshots of both prose and proofs from papers. At 0.1% false positive rate, SnapJudge achieves a detection rate of 92% on proofs and 93% on prose generated by frontier models, substantially outperforming both Pangram 4 and our text-based detector. We release our data, models and code at https://nlplab.cs.duke.edu/snapjudge.

title: Giving an Open-Weight Language Model the Vote in Among Us Meetings
description:
Meetings are the part of Among Us that a language model looks made for. The crew is trying to find the few hidden impostors among them. When a body is found, everyone talks, states where they were, accuses someone and votes, and whoever gets the most votes is thrown off the ship. My simulator's bots normally vote with small recurrent networks trained on thousands of meetings, which read who saw whom and who accused whom and output a suspicion score for each player. I expected that handing the meeting to a real language model, one that could argue, ask questions and catch lies, would make the crew better at finding impostors. Across six setups it never did.

The setup

The model is gpt-oss:20b, an open-weight model from OpenAI, running locally through Ollama. In a meeting every surviving player, crewmate or impostor, is a separate prompt to the same model, and its reply is that player's speech and vote. A crewmate's prompt contains only what that player could know: where it walked, who it saw and when, any kill or vent it witnessed, and the table of where everyone claims to have been. An impostor's prompt also contains its real movements, marked secret, and permission to lie. Movement, tasks and kills between meetings stay with the trained bots; only the meetings change.

There were three meeting formats. In the first, players speak in rounds and may ask each other structured questions ("where were you 20 seconds ago?"). In the second, each crewmate's prompt also includes the voting network's guesses as an "instinct" (described below). In the third, players hold a free conversation in turns, again with the instinct.

The comparison is the same bots in the same lobby with the trained networks doing all the voting, crew and impostors alike, over 300 games. So the language model replaces both sides' votes at once, and a worse result for the crew could come from worse crew votes or from better impostor talk; the runs below cannot tell those apart. I measured the baselines after the language-model runs, on the current version of the simulator. Five of the six language-model runs used an earlier version, which I mark. The bots come from different leagues (training runs), and each league trained its own voting network.

Eight players, two impostors

These used the bots from my second league. The network baseline did not record wrongly ejected crewmates.

who votes games crew wins impostors ejected per game crewmates ejected per game
the trained networks (current version) 300 52.0% 0.99 not recorded
gpt-oss, rounds and questions (earlier version) 16 2 (12.5%) 0.06 0.94
gpt-oss, rounds and questions plus the instinct (earlier version) 16 8 (50%) 1.00 0.63
gpt-oss, conversation plus the instinct (earlier version) 16 6 (37.5%) 0.81 0.69

On its own the language model did much worse than the networks. The crew ejected an impostor once in sixteen games and an innocent crewmate almost every game, and won 2 games of 16 where the networks' crew wins about half. That gap is well beyond chance (one-sided Fisher exact test, p = 0.0017), with the caveat that the simulator version differed.

The "instinct" put the voting network's numbers into each crewmate's prompt as a line of text. It opens "Your instinct (a trained model reading everything YOU saw, plus the accusations so far; it picks the right impostor about 70% of the time, so weigh it with the facts):" and then gives each other player's percentage chance of being an impostor. The 70% in that line was my rough estimate when I wrote the prompt, not a measurement. With the instinct and the rounds format, the crew won 8 of 16, indistinguishable from the networks (p = 0.54). If the model mostly voted the way the instinct line pointed, that is the result you would expect; I did not measure how often it did.

Fifteen players, three impostors

In these lobbies the crew wins more often under both kinds of voting, and the ordering held. All three runs use the conversation format with the instinct.

bots networks voting (300 games, current version) gpt-oss, conversation plus the instinct
league 2 89.7% 10 of 12 (83%), earlier version
league 4 84.7% 11 of 20 (55%), earlier version
league 6 93.3% 16 of 20 (80%), current version

The league 6 row is the only like-for-like comparison: same bots, same simulator version, same settings, run on the same day. Sixteen of 20 against 280 of 300 is a one-sided Fisher exact p of 0.052, and the 95% interval on 16 of 20 is 58% to 92%. On its own, that row is suggestive rather than settled. The league 4 gap is far larger (p = 0.0025), but between that run and its baseline I changed how meetings treat a running sabotage and what impostors know when they shut doors, so I would not lean on it.

Counting across all six setups: in one the language model was clearly worse than the networks (eight players, no instinct). In the five with the instinct it matched the networks once and fell short four times, by margins that are individually too small or too confounded to be conclusive. I have no setup in which it did better.

What it costs

A 15-player game with gpt-oss meetings took 524 seconds of wall-clock time on average in the league 6 run. Nearly all of that was about 4 meetings' worth of turns, at one model call per player per turn. The networks' votes need no model calls at all. That would be a fair price for better votes, and the votes were not better.

Why I think it happens

This part is my reading rather than a measurement. The networks have an unfair advantage that is also the point: they were trained on the outcomes of thousands of meetings in this simulator, so their suspicion scores are calibrated against who actually turned out to be an impostor here. The language model brings general knowledge of how deception sounds. An impostor here does not sound like anything; it names a room, and the only way to catch the lie is to check that claim against who could have seen that room. The prompts contain what each player saw. Nothing in the results suggests the model made that check reliably, and with the network's numbers in the prompt it did no better than the network.

An earlier benchmark of mine, which ranked language models on spotting liars in Mafia, found first-day accusations at chance. There, on the first day, nothing about the liars is knowable yet. Here the evidence is in each crewmate's prompt, which makes falling short of a small network harder to excuse.

The simulator, the meeting prompts and the measurement scripts were written by Claude Code at my direction. The code is not public. Every figure above comes from the result files the runs wrote, and the significance tests are recomputed from those counts.

title: Route an Incoming OSS Patch by Blast Radius Before a Model Drafts the Review
description:
Route an Incoming OSS Patch by Blast Radius Before a Model Drafts the Review

A review queue that looks calm and is not

On a Monday morning, the maintainer of a small Python library opens the pull request list and finds eleven items waiting. Four are dependency bumps, three fix docstring typos, two add small features, one only rewrites tests, and one rewrites the argument parser from scratch. The natural instinct is to open the parser rewrite first, because it is the largest and most intimidating diff in the queue.

That instinct is expensive and frequently wrong. A three-line change to a lockfile can break every downstream install, while a two-hundred-line refactor inside a well-covered module may be exactly what the existing tests already describe. Review attention is finite, and it should follow risk rather than diff size.

The workflow below is a composite illustration rather than a report from one named repository. It defines a small routing procedure that assigns each incoming patch a tier, then decides which tiers may receive model-drafted review notes and which must not. Every command in it is ordinary git, so it runs against any clone without extra services.

Three signals that predict review cost

Diffs carry a few cheap, language-agnostic signals that correlate with how much human attention a patch will consume. None of them is a correctness signal, and none of them replaces reading the code.

Signal Why it raises review cost Cheap check
Build or dependency files Changes install resolution, CI images, and lockfile integrity for everyone Basename match against a known build-file set
Public surface paths Alters behaviour callers depend on, including undocumented callers Path prefix match (src/, lib/, pkg/)
No test delta Removes the fastest way to falsify the claimed behaviour Marker match (tests/, spec/, test_)
Wide file spread Suggests a cross-cutting change with more integration edges Count of files in --numstat
Large net change Longer to read, more places for a silent regression to hide Sum of added and removed lines

The first three signals are properties of what the patch touches, and the last two are properties of how much it touches. Combining them produces a coarse but useful ordering, and the ordering is what the routing script encodes.

A routing script for a fresh clone

The script below reads a diff between a base ref and a head ref, scores it, and prints a tier. It has no dependencies outside the standard library, and it is written as a starting point rather than a finished product, so pinning your own path globs and build-file set is expected.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Route an incoming OSS pull request by blast radius.

Usage:
    python review_route.py --base origin/main --head pr-4821
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import subprocess

PUBLIC_PREFIXES = ("src/", "lib/", "pkg/", "internal/api/")
BUILD_FILES = {
    "pyproject.toml", "setup.py", "setup.cfg", "requirements.txt",
    "package.json", "package-lock.json", "Cargo.toml", "Cargo.lock",
    "go.mod", "go.sum", "Makefile", "Dockerfile",
}
TEST_MARKERS = ("/tests/", "/test/", "spec/", "test_", "_test.")


def git(*args: str) -> str:
    proc = subprocess.run(["git", *args], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return proc.stdout


def numstat(base: str, head: str) -> list[tuple[int, int, str]]:
    rows = []
    for line in git("diff", "--numstat", f"{base}...{head}").splitlines():
        added, removed, path = line.split("\t", 2)
        rows.append((int(added) if added.isdigit() else 0,
                     int(removed) if removed.isdigit() else 0,
                     path))
    return rows


def classify(rows):
    added = sum(r[0] for r in rows)
    removed = sum(r[1] for r in rows)
    paths = [r[2] for r in rows]
    public = any(p.startswith(PUBLIC_PREFIXES) for p in paths)
    build = any(p.split("/")[-1] in BUILD_FILES for p in paths)
    tests = any(any(m in p for m in TEST_MARKERS) for p in paths)
    return added, removed, public, build, tests, len(paths)


def tier_for(files, added, removed, public, build, tests) -> tuple[int, str]:
    score = 0
    score += 3 if build else 0
    score += 2 if public else 0
    score -= 2 if tests else 0
    score += 1 if files > 5 else 0
    score += 1 if (added + removed) > 200 else 0
    if score >= 4:
        return score, "T0 human-only review"
    if score >= 2:
        return score, "T1 human review; model may draft notes"
    return score, "T2 model draft first; human sign-off"


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--base", default="origin/main")
    ap.add_argument("--head", default="HEAD")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    rows = numstat(args.base, args.head)
    added, removed, public, build, tests, files = classify(rows)
    score, tier = tier_for(files, added, removed, public, build, tests)
    print(f"base={args.base} head={args.head}")
    print(f"files={files} +{added} -{removed}")
    print(f"public_surface={public} build_files={build} tests_touched={tests}")
    print(f"score={score} tier={tier}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Sample output 

$ python review_route.py --base origin/main --head pr-4821
base=origin/main head=pr-4821
files=7 +412 -96
public_surface=True build_files=False tests_touched=True
score=2 tier=T1 human review; model may draft notes

A one-line lockfile bump from the same queue scores differently, because build=True adds three points and tests=False adds two more. That inversion is the point of the exercise: the smallest diff in the queue is not the cheapest one to review.

How to read the tiers in practice

  • T0 — human-only review. Dependency and lockfile edits, authentication or authorization paths, CI workflow files, and any patch that deletes or weakens tests. No model-drafted note should precede a human read here.
  • T1 — human review, model notes allowed. Public surface changes that ship with tests. A model may summarize the diff or list untested branches, but the review comment itself is written by a person.
  • T2 — model draft first. Test-only changes, internal helpers, docstring fixes, and small additions behind private names. A draft is useful here because the acceptance criteria are usually mechanical.

Two rules keep the tier list honest. First, a maintainer's knowledge of their own codebase always overrides the score, because the score has never read the code. Second, the tier decides who drafts the first comment, never whether the patch gets merged.

Where free model access fits in the queue

Drafting review notes for a T2 patch is a low-stakes use of a hosted model, since the reviewer still reads the diff before responding. MonkeyCode is an open-source project whose operator states it offers free model access and a free server option, which matters mainly for contributors who do not want a paid API key attached to routine review work.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Two boundaries are worth stating plainly. Model access is used only for T1 and T2 drafting, and T0 patches are read by a human before anything else happens. Availability, model selection, and any usage limits are operator-stated and change over time, so confirm the current terms on the project page rather than trusting a figure quoted in an older post.

Two runs, then mechanical verification

The weakest part of model-drafted review notes is that they cite symbols and files that may not exist. A cheap protocol removes most of that noise, and it has three steps.

  1. Run the drafting prompt twice with different phrasing or sampling settings, and collect both answer sets as JSONL.
  2. Keep only claims that appear in both runs with the same file and the same symbol, which discards most one-off hallucinations.
  3. Verify every surviving claim mechanically against the patch before it reaches the contributor.

The drafting prompt should require one JSON object per line, with a file, a symbol, and a short note, and it should forbid claims that cannot name a symbol. Claims without a symbol are opinions, and opinions belong in the human review, not in an automated pass.

The verification script

The script below keeps only claims that survive two mechanical checks: the file appears in the patch, and the symbol resolves at the head revision. It is deliberately narrow, and it proves existence rather than correctness.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Keep only model review claims that resolve mechanically against the patch.

Input JSONL, one claim per line:
    {"file": "src/parser.py", "symbol": "parse_args", "note": "..."}
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import subprocess
import sys


def git(*args: str):
    proc = subprocess.run(["git", *args], capture_output=True, text=True)
    return proc.returncode, proc.stdout


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("claims")
    ap.add_argument("--base", default="origin/main")
    ap.add_argument("--head", default="HEAD")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    _, changed_raw = git("diff", "--name-only", f"{args.base}...{args.head}")
    changed = set(changed_raw.split())

    kept, dropped = [], []
    with open(args.claims, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line in handle:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            claim = json.loads(line)
            path, symbol = claim["file"], claim["symbol"]
            reasons = []
            if path not in changed:
                reasons.append("file not in patch")
            rc, hits = git("grep", "-n", "-F", symbol, args.head, "--", path)
            if rc != 0 or not hits.strip():
                reasons.append("symbol not found at head")
            record = {**claim, "rejected_because": reasons}
            (dropped if reasons else kept).append(record)

    print(json.dumps({"kept": kept, "dropped": dropped}, indent=2))
    print(f"kept={len(kept)} dropped={len(dropped)}", file=sys.stderr)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

What the filter does not catch

A symbol that exists can still be described incorrectly, and the filter says nothing about whether a suggested change is right. Claims that survive both checks are candidates for human reading, not conclusions, and the rejection list is often the more informative output because it shows which class of claims the model tends to fabricate.

Limitations and who should not adopt this

  • Very small repositories. The script overhead exceeds the review time saved, and a maintainer who already knows every file gains nothing from a tier column.
  • Repositories without tests. The tests=False penalty has no meaning when no test suite exists, so the score degenerates into a diff-size rank.
  • Monorepos with sparse paths. Public prefix matching needs per-package configuration, and a single global glob set will misclassify most of the tree.
  • Security-sensitive patches. A tier score is the wrong instrument for vulnerability fixes, and those should bypass the routing pipeline entirely.
  • Projects that forbid hosted tooling. If repository policy excludes third-party model services, run the routing script alone and stop before the drafting step.

The scripts above are a starting point rather than a benchmarked tool, and they have not been validated across every language layout. Treat the build-file set and prefix list as configuration to maintain, not as constants.

A twenty-minute checklist

  1. Add review_route.py to a scripts directory and adjust PUBLIC_PREFIXES and BUILD_FILES for your language.
  2. Run it against the three oldest open pull requests and compare the tiers with your own intuition.
  3. Fix the scoring only where your intuition is consistently right and the script is consistently wrong.
  4. Draft notes for one T2 patch twice, and diff the two answer sets before verifying anything.
  5. Run verify_claims.py and read the rejected list first, because it reveals the failure mode fastest.
  6. Record which tiers produced useful notes, and drop model drafting from any tier that did not earn its place.

The procedure is deliberately unglamorous, and its value comes from being repeatable on a Monday morning when eleven patches are waiting. If you want to try the drafting step without wiring up local inference, the free model access and free server option described by MonkeyCode are a reasonable place to start, beginning with the T2 queue and a small rejected-claims list.

title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation
description:
arXiv:2610.20667v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

title: Does Latent Chain-of-Thought Actually Reason? A Single, Unifying Taxonomy for Latent Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.21182v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent chain-of-thought replaces written reasoning steps with continuous hidden states, giving models additional steps to compute before answering. It remains unclear what computation these steps actually perform. High task accuracy and decodable intermediate answers do not establish that a model uses its latent chain to reach an answer. We study this question across twenty-one model-task configurations covering three training recipes, three reasoning tasks, and two backbones. We combine chain deletion and content replacement with probes and trajectory analysis to test whether the chain affects the answer, what it encodes, and how its states change. On logical tasks, COCONUT often carries an answer that is already readable before the chain begins. Its states settle early, and deleting the chain leaves predictions almost unchanged. Per-step supervision produces an ordered layout of reasoning steps and can make the model depend on the chain. Yet even an ordered chain can act as a placeholder, with deletion hurting performance while content replacement leaves answers unchanged. On arithmetic tasks, all tested recipes show dependence on chain content. These results show why readable latent states alone are insufficient evidence of reasoning. We introduce a taxonomy that separates what a chain represents from how the model uses it. Seen this way, earlier reports no longer compete: placeholder tokens, collapsed superposition and step-dependent causal roles are each consistent with a different kind of chain, each obtained on a different task, training recipe or measurement. Once a study says which property it tested, whether the model uses the chain, what the chain holds, or how its state moves, claims about latent reasoning can be compared.

title: My demo runs with no backend: a mock axios client that mirrors the real API
description:
The hardest part of shipping a product demo isn't the demo itself. It's that the demo needs a backend, and backends need servers, and servers need babysitting. I wanted a demo page anyone could click through — login, dashboard, user management — with zero infrastructure behind it.

So I built a fake API that mirrors the real one. One seam, and the entire frontend switches over without knowing.

In client.js, the axios client is created behind a single branch:

const client = isDemoMode() ? createDemoClient() : axios.create({
  baseURL: `${import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL || 'http://localhost:8000'}/api`,
  headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
});

isDemoMode() just reads VITE_DEMO_MODE=true from the build. The public preview build sets it; the shipped product doesn't. Everything else in the app — AuthContext, the pages, the components — imports the same client and calls the same endpoints: POST /auth/login, GET /auth/me, GET /dashboard/stats, apiResource users.

The mock, demoMock.js, implements those endpoints against in-memory arrays. The critical discipline: it returns the exact response shapes the real API returns. POST /auth/login returns { token, user }. The user object carries id, name, email, role, created_at — same fields as the Laravel UserResource. Validation failures come back as 422-shaped errors with an errors object.

Why this matters more than it sounds: if the mock drifted from the real API — say it returned username where Laravel returns name — the demo would silently test a frontend that doesn't match the product. Mirroring the response shapes means the demo is also a regression test for my frontend's assumptions. When I change the real API, the demo breaks visibly, and I fix the mock in the same commit.

I seed it with an admin (admin@demo.io) plus eight sample users, and mutations go to the in-memory array — you can create and delete users in the demo and it all "works", resetting on reload. Honest limits: the demo banner says data is simulated. No fake permanence.

The pattern generalises beyond demos. Anytime your frontend depends on an API you don't want to run — a third-party sandbox, a service under development, a test environment — write the mock to the response-shape contract, not to vibes. Your future self, debugging why the mock behaves differently, will thank you.

This exact setup ships in my Laravel + React SaaS starter kit, so a buyer can try every flow in the live preview and then run the same code against the real Laravel API: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig ($19, one-time).

title: The Screenshot Was Ready. The Status Bar Wasn’t.
description:
A practical Android screenshot workflow for controlling battery, carrier, signal and status-bar details before export.

The app screen looked right. The message was clear. The layout was ready to share.

Then the status bar ruined the consistency.

One screenshot showed 18% battery. Another showed 77%. A third had a different network state, carrier label, Wi-Fi indicator, or notification icon.

For a tutorial, product presentation, portfolio, store asset, or social post, those small differences can make a polished sequence look accidental.

A small strip can change the whole screenshot

The Android status bar takes up very little space, but visually it matters.

When screenshots are captured at different times, the top bar may change automatically:

  • battery percentage
  • charging state
  • carrier
  • signal
  • Wi-Fi
  • LTE / 5G
  • notification indicators
  • app name or other presentation details

Retaking every screenshot is slow.

Cropping the top can remove useful context.

Leaving everything untouched can make a set of screenshots inconsistent.

The practical need is not to change the real state of the phone. It is to control the visual presentation of the screenshot.

A controlled screenshot workflow

That is the problem Nullun is designed around.

The workflow is simple:

  1. Import the screenshot.
  2. Configure the battery and supported status-bar elements.
  3. Preview the final presentation inside the app.
  4. Keep the visual language consistent across multiple screenshots.
  5. Export or share the finished result when Lifetime access is enabled.

The editor can be useful when a screenshot sequence needs a repeatable visual state instead of whatever happened to be visible on the phone at capture time.

Precise battery values for repeatable scenarios

Some screenshots need a specific battery level.

A battery-saving tutorial may need 10%.

A product presentation may look cleaner with 75% across every screen.

A low-power example may need a warning state.

The goal is consistency in the visual, not changing the phone's real battery.

Status-bar consistency for multi-screen work

For developers and creators, a screenshot is often part of a larger set:

  • documentation
  • app tutorials
  • feature walkthroughs
  • marketing images
  • portfolios
  • UI demonstrations
  • social content

If each screenshot uses a different carrier, signal state, battery percentage or Wi-Fi state, the sequence can look fragmented.

A controlled status bar helps the screenshots behave like one visual system.

Free editing, Lifetime output

Nullun's current model separates creation from external output.

Free users can:

  • import
  • edit
  • configure
  • preview the result inside the app
  • view History internally

Lifetime unlocks external output such as:

  • Share
  • Save
  • Export
  • History Share
  • History Export

This keeps the app usable before purchase while reserving the final portable result for Lifetime.

The status bar should support the message

The status bar should not become the subject of the screenshot.

It should quietly support the content below it.

That is the idea behind Nullun: make the top layer deliberate, repeatable and visually consistent before the image leaves the app.

title: Reference-Guided Turn-Taking Style Transfer for Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20763v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models decide at every frame whether to take the floor, defining a conversational personality -- yet each set of weights encodes exactly one, which human speakers bracket rather than share. Existing controls mostly act from outside; none identifies the quantity that sets how much the model speaks. We identify it: a single late-layer residual-stream direction, the initiative vector, extracted from the model's own conversations without training or annotation. The same direction reads the decision, anticipating onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it: scaled during generation, it moves speech ratio from 6-12% to 42-61% (no steering: 21-30%), consistently across conversations, weights, and corpora. A short reference recording suffices to transfer a speaker's turn-taking style to the model, and the transfer is reference-specific: swapping in another speaker's reference worsens the match in 93-98% of cases, whereas the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering. Turn-taking style is not frozen into the weights but a direction that can be read, shifted, and calibrated per person. Audio examples are available at https://elpsykongloo.github.io/initiative-vector/.

title: Semantic Latent Alignment for Flow Matching with Invertible Bi-Lipschitz Adapters
description:
arXiv:2610.21332v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained latent spaces trade compression, reconstruction, and the learnability of the coordinates a downstream generator has to work in, which complicates adapting these spaces to different domains or tasks: continued training is expensive, and without a new alignment objective it often fails to improve downstream generation. We instead leave the encoder and decoder fixed and change only the coordinates between them, using an invertible bi-Lipschitz adapter aligned offline to a semantic teacher and frozen during class-conditional flow matching. Invertibility preserves compatibility with the pretrained autoencoder, while the bi-Lipschitz constraint limits how far alignment can distort its latent geometry. This provides a simple way to improve semantic organization while retaining the compression and reconstruction properties of the original latent space. On two medical imaging datasets, constrained latent adaptation improves feature metrics, seed stability and counterfactual edit strength, while remaining competitive on downstream classification. In contrast, unconstrained adaptation can become highly anisotropic and sensitive despite remaining invertible, highlighting the importance of controlling geometric distortion. Our results suggest that carefully constrained post-hoc adaptation offers a parameter-efficient and tuning-free alternative to jointly modifying the representation during generative training.

title: StepSafe: Learning Timely Intervention with Context-Aware Safety Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.20960v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety in agentic systems is inherently sequential: whether an action is safe depends on prior actions, tool outputs, information disclosures, and interactions among agents. Recent work has shifted agent safety guardrails from post-hoc trajectory-level assessment toward step-level action diagnosis and proactive risk prediction, yet existing training objectives provide limited supervision for how step evidence accumulates over time and when it becomes sufficient to justify intervention. We propose \methodlong~(ASPO): a training framework for step-level timely intervention. Pre-fix level stage alignment allows crediting each decision at its own step: it compares each response with the other responses sampled at the same prefix and rewards the action that fits the stage, continuing before the risk is visible, asking while clarification can still avert harm, and stopping before harm is irreversible. Adaptive feedback self-distillation further credits the reasoning behind each decision, with the model itself as a teacher that sees the step annotations on intervention steps and rules mined from its own false alarms on safe steps. Its training data carry a violation taxonomy and an intervention window at every step and are extended through self-evolving multi-agent red-teaming. Finally we present \textsc{StepSafe}, a step-level reasoning guardrail with timely intervention, that achieves the state-of-the-art peformance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks on safety-utility pareto curve with Youden's $J$ of 53.0 (4B) against 46.2.

title: SIEVE: Overcoming Topological Obstruction in Equivariant Self-Supervised Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.21087v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We identify a theoretical incompatibility between 3D point cloud masked autoencoding and SE(3)-equivariant networks. We prove that standard masking triggers a topological collapse, effectively forcing the model to hallucinate orientation without a reference frame. To resolve this, we introduce SIEVE (Scalar Invariant Extraction Via Equivariance), an SE(3)-equivariant self-supervised framework that compresses point cloud geometry into invariant scalar embeddings. At its core is the spherical projection mask, which preserves global pose while obfuscating local semantics, sidestepping the obstruction by construction. Experiments confirm that SIEVE circumvents the predicted collapse where constant and noise masks fail. On downstream point cloud tasks, the resulting embeddings improve over coordinate-based baselines and hand-crafted geometric descriptors, with the largest gains on generalization to unseen shape categories.

title: Hybrid Generative-Tagging Decoding for Efficient Product Attribute-Value Extraction
description:
arXiv:2610.21329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribute-value extraction is important for building high-quality product catalogs in e-commerce. Existing systems either rely on generative or tagging strategies for extracting the attribute names and their corresponding values. Tagging models directly label spans in the source, making them fast and grounded, but they cannot produce values that require reformatting or generate rare attribute names outside their label space. Generative models avoid these drawbacks by generating both attribute names and values token by token, but this auto-regressive nature makes them slow and limits attribute coverage. We introduce hybrid generative-tagging decoding, a novel model architecture that combines tagging source spans and open-ended generation. For frequent attributes whose values are copyable, a tagging head extracts values directly from the source. This lets the generative head focus on the remainder - rare attributes outside the tagger's label space and non-copyable values, including implicit or normalized values. Integrated into vLLM inference, the hybrid decoder raises attribute coverage by 10% and extracts 63% more correct attribute-value pairs at no precision cost, while reducing latency by 44%.
