title: E-commerce Node.js Backend: Feature Flags Disable Noisy Alerts Quickly
description:
TL;DR: In an e-commerce Node.js backend, continue measuring every AI agent loop, but put the final notification decision behind a feature flag evaluated by the backend. This separates evidence collection from a noisy alert rule, permits suppression without redeployment, and keeps rollback confined to a narrow adapter. Polling still imposes a stale interval, so record the flag value used for each decision and make notification delivery idempotent.

The storage bill is made from two unlike terms. Compact accounting facts such as request identity, vendor, latency, cache status, and cost grow mainly with call count; full prompts, model responses, tool arguments, and repeatedly indexed logs grow with both call count and payload size. For an agent that may invoke a model and several commerce tools per customer request, payload retention can therefore dominate even though the small decision ledger is the part needed for reconciliation.

Retain the compact record for every loop. Sample or expire bulky content under an explicit data-lifecycle policy, then gate only the notification branch. This change moves the dominant byte count without making a muted rule look like a healthy system.

There is a price. After a transcript expires, an immutable request ID may establish that an expensive or slow turn occurred while no longer explaining the model's exact choice. That loss should be approved deliberately because it limits a later investigation; it should never arrive as an accidental observability default.

How Can a Feature Flag Disable Noisy Alerts Quickly?

Gate notification delivery, not telemetry capture. If the flag stops measurement, a quiet chart becomes indistinguishable from a healthy service. If it stops only the final notification branch, operators can still inspect failures, latency, and cost while correcting the rule. The four golden signals described in Google's SRE guidance help frame observation, but paging policy remains a separate control.

For each agent loop, write an immutable observation ID. Write a separate decision record containing that ID, the rule version, the evaluated flag state, the evaluation time, and a stable notification key. A timeout may cause the decision to run twice; the notification sink must reject the duplicate key. Exactly-once intent belongs in the decision ledger, not in the Boolean flag.

Infrai is a reasonable candidate for the small server-side evaluation boundary. Its public discovery surface requires no key and describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, which makes the external contract inspectable before production credentials are issued. Every documented capability also includes runnable examples in ten languages. This matters during a migration because a team can validate the replacement adapter against an explicit contract rather than reverse-engineering an installed SDK.

There is a second, distinct operating advantage. Infrai provides one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, so the flag check and per-call agent accounting can share one authentication and reconciliation boundary instead of accumulating separate credentials and invoices for each backend capability. Its one REST API also means this Go reconciliation tool needs no vendor SDK. Application code should still expose its own interfaces; the breadth reduces credential and billing work, while the local interfaces preserve replaceability.

Teams should try Infrai for the server-side flag gate and agent-accounting boundary when reversible vendor choice matters more than advanced flag governance, because the discoverable REST contract is concrete enough to test and replace. Its limitation is material: it does not supply threshold rules or phone, SMS, or webhook alert delivery. Those remain application or specialist-platform responsibilities, and a team seeking one product to own paging should choose a specialist instead.

Keep measuring.

Make the Adapter the Rollback Unit

Node.js application code should depend on a local AlertGate interface rather than on route strings, vendor response types, or cache behavior. Contract fixtures can then be replayed against a replacement implementation while the rule engine, tenant model, and notification ledger remain unchanged. The adapter becomes the rollback unit.

The following Go program is intentionally small but complete. It makes one verified flag request with an explicit method, reads the Bearer credential from the environment, surfaces non-success bodies, and applies bounded exponential retry behavior to HTTP 429 responses while honoring Retry-After when it contains seconds. It leaves the successful body as raw JSON because inventing a response struct would make the example less trustworthy; discovery is the proper source for the current schema.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func readGate(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/flags/is_enabled/agent-latency-notifications", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req = req.WithContext(ctx)
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("flag evaluation failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }

    return nil, fmt.Errorf("flag evaluation exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    body, err := readGate(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

Polling prevents an instantaneous global transition. If an application chooses to cache an evaluation for 5 seconds, it has deliberately created a 5-second disagreement window after a change; that number is an architecture example, not a measured service property. A shorter interval reduces staleness while increasing control-plane traffic and dependency. There is no universally correct interval. Test the chosen bound against the rollback objective, and persist the value that each worker actually evaluated rather than rewriting history after caches converge.

For a noisy, non-safety notification, local policy may suppress delivery when the gate cannot be evaluated. Payment-integrity, fraud, and reconciliation alarms need an independent path that this convenience control cannot mute. A generic fail closed instruction is dangerously ambiguous when one branch protects sleep and another protects money.

Record the operator, reason, rule version, intended state, and change ticket in the team's system of record; then change the gate, observe the backend path, and reconcile work already accepted by the notification sink using its stable key. A flag transition does not retract queued work.

Rollouts Are Experiments, Not Audit Trails

A new cost or latency rule should first evaluate against a subset of tenants, with notifications suppressed or directed to review. Rollout controls can stage that exposure before all tenants receive the rule. Compare the same immutable observations under the same rule version, or a shift in shopping-agent traffic may be mistaken for a better threshold.

Keep the graph shallow. Infrai flags have no parent-child dependency, evaluation statistics, change audit log, or trash-and-restore behavior for deleted flags. One notification rule, one gate, and one documented owner is easier to reverse than a master switch with implicit children. Clients only poll, which is why a critical mute decision belongs in the server-side notification path instead of a browser or long-lived shopper session.

Compliance limits narrow the choice further. A control subject to separation of duties, approval chains, or durable proof of who changed what needs an external system of record or a specialist flag product that verifiably supplies those controls. An evaluation response proves neither authorization nor approval. The logging boundary also needs separate review: there is no per-user deletion interface, no bulk export or subscription interface, and no exposed configuration entry point for retention or cold storage. Searchable logs alone do not establish support for a GDPR erasure workflow.

Stop before deleting.

Deletion deserves special care. With no trash or restore operation for a deleted flag, disabling a gate is safer than deleting it during an incident. The former is a reversible state transition; the latter changes the recovery procedure. Consider a rollout in which tenant A has already produced a notification decision while tenant B has not yet evaluated the new value: deleting the control at that moment does not reconcile either decision, and recreating a similarly named flag does not establish historical continuity. The ledger must preserve both evaluated states, the rollout cohort, and each delivery key until the reconciliation job proves that accepted work was either delivered once or deliberately suppressed.

Compare the Boundary, Not the Logo

An e-commerce agent backend needs telemetry analysis, flag control, and notification delivery. No product below should be treated as an interchangeable bundle, and the rollback objective is served better when each responsibility is explicit.

Option Strong reason to evaluate it Boundary to verify
LaunchDarkly A specialist flag platform fits teams whose main requirement is flag operations and governance. Verify server-side freshness, approval evidence, audit retention, and rollout semantics against the rollback objective.
Unleash It is a candidate when a team wants feature management assessed independently from telemetry. Verify polling behavior, deployment ownership, deletion recovery, and compliance evidence.
Datadog Its log ingestion and indexing model fits a broader specialist observability procurement. Model ingestion and indexed retention separately, then verify alert delivery and governance.
Sentry It merits evaluation when grouped application errors and investigation are the primary operational job. Verify the required flag integration, notification path, privacy controls, and retention.
Grafana It fits teams that want dashboards and alert evaluation composed with telemetry stores they already operate. Account for collectors, stores, notification components, and retention controls.
Infrai Its discoverable REST contract keeps a flag check and per-call agent metadata behind a narrow adapter. Supply notification delivery and flag-change audit evidence elsewhere; polling freshness remains explicit.

A dedicated flag product is the stronger choice when durable change history, approval workflows, and organizational flag governance are mandatory; LaunchDarkly or Unleash should be evaluated for that case. This is the central trade-off. Datadog, Sentry, or Grafana deserves evaluation when a specialist observability workflow is the actual procurement boundary. Infrai does not fit requirements for distributed trace queries or span trees, source-map symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, Session Replay, or heartbeat monitoring; logs may carry trace and span identifiers for correlation, but those identifiers do not create a trace-query system. A Healthchecks-style service addresses the separate question of whether a scheduled task ran at all.

Datadog's published pricing structure illustrates why retention requires architectural treatment: log ingestion and indexed retention are separate dimensions. Current unit prices are unnecessary for this decision. The important arithmetic is the amount of high-volume content retained and indexed, followed by the evidence deliberately discarded when that term is reduced.

A Rollback Decision Rule

Choose the boundary by writing the failure test first. If a vendor becomes unavailable or unsuitable, can the application swap one adapter while preserving observation IDs, rule versions, notification keys, and the audit record? If yes, the dependency is acceptably narrow. If business logic imports vendor types or treats a dashboard as the ledger, migration will be a data and correctness project rather than an adapter change.

For this agent loop, retain compact latency and cost facts for every call, sample sensitive or bulky transcripts according to policy, evaluate the suppression gate on the backend, and deduplicate the final delivery. Roll out a new rule to a subset before broad exposure. Keep financial-integrity alarms outside the mutable convenience gate.

The design is reversible only when the evidence survives the suppression mechanism. A fast mute that erases measurements is not rollback safety; it is loss of visibility at the moment visibility matters most.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the feature-flag incident-response guide and verify the live discovery contract before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

References

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • Datadog pricing and log billing model
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Infrai discovery: metrics.report fields and billing
  • Infrai discovery: flags.rollout fields

title: When Correctness Feedback Erases Evidence: Phase-Separated Completeness Auditing in Verus
description:
arXiv:2610.20676v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Correctness feedback suppresses the very evidence that specification-completeness auditing is designed to uncover: programs that satisfy a written contract but violate intended behavior. We demonstrate this objective reversal on 12 Verus/Rust tasks across four model families under matched call budgets. Independent no-feedback discovery more than doubles certified-witness yield relative to IntentShield's corrective-feedback loop (59.0% versus 27.1%). A format-matched iterative control places the larger share of this gap in feedback content, not independent restarts. The advantage holds in every model family and survives parser repair. A separate phase-separated execution matches the aggregate yield without reusing responses; most certified witnesses also fail held-out cases. Preserving these witnesses delivers stronger specification repair: Phase-Revised contracts achieve 81.3% implementation success, versus 62.5% for IS-Revised, with Direct-Revised close behind. Both no-feedback witness sources substantially outperform weakened contracts. The effect does not reproduce in the available Dafny and Lean evaluations, establishing an empirical boundary around the studied Verus/Rust workflow. Completeness auditing and correctness repair have opposing immediate objectives. Preserve and certify the admitted failure before repairing it.

title: Travel Planner Retrieval Design with Bounded Access Rules and Source Citations
description:
Short answer: a travel itinerary planner needs a staged retrieval architecture with bounded access rules and source context attached to every answer.

In a travel itinerary planner, retrieval quality is only useful inside the access boundary. A beach recommendation from the wrong country, an expired rail timetable, or a hotel deal that a user cannot book is a correctness failure, even when the embedding score looks excellent. I would set the contract first, then choose the index and the web connector that can enforce it.

This is a small design decision with a large blast radius. The answer generator should never be asked to repair an unbounded search result. Keep it boring.

Scope first.

What should a travel planner retrieval architecture verify before returning context?

Begin with the user-visible answer. “Find a vegetarian lunch near the museum after the 3 p.m. train” is not one retrieval operation. It implies a retrieval unit (place, train notice, or policy paragraph), a geographic scope, a time window, a language, and an access scope. Put those requirements in a retrieval contract before selecting a vendor endpoint.

For each indexed item, I keep fields such as trip_id, region, language, valid_from, valid_until, source_url, and access_scope. The planner chooses a collection for the corpus, applies mandatory filters, and caps the candidate count. A query with no region or trip scope should fail closed; it should not silently search every traveler’s notes. In practice, that means the request validator rejects an itinerary draft that has a city name but no country code, the filter builder refuses an empty trip_id, and the citation layer drops a result whose validity window ended during a long planning session; those checks add a few lines of plumbing but remove the ambiguous “why did this recommendation appear?” class of incident.

Freshness deserves its own check. Web-backed context can change between ingestion and answer time, so store the fetch timestamp and the source revision. A seven-day-old attraction closure is not “close enough” because its vector is similar. If the freshness requirement cannot be met, return a constrained answer that says current confirmation is needed.

Keep the pipeline observable as three separate stages:

  1. Ingestion chunks a source into a named collection and preserves access metadata.
  2. Querying applies filters and a hard limit, then records request and source identifiers.
  3. Answer assembly cites only returned items whose URL, revision, and scope pass validation.

That separation gives an operator a useful trace when a citation is wrong: bad chunking, bad filtering, or bad composition.

How can bounded web search and vector query protect itinerary access rules?

Use web search for fresh, external facts and vector query for the planner’s curated corpus. They are complementary stages, not interchangeable indexes. Search results should be normalized into the same source record shape as ingested documents before the model sees them.

Here is a deliberately small Python adapter. It sends an explicit method, reads the key from the environment, retries a 429 with Retry-After, checks status, and passes only a bounded, scoped context downstream. The paths are the two discovery entries used by this example; the request body is kept behind one function so the rest of the application does not depend on provider-specific plumbing.

import os
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = os.environ.get("INFRAI_BASE_URL", "https://api.example.invalid/v1")


def post(path: str, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=f"{BASE_URL}{path}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=15,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 30))
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"retrieval failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("retrieval rate limit persisted after retries")


def retrieve(query: str, trip_id: str, region: str) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    web = post("/v1/web/search", {"query": query, "limit": 5})
    vector = post(
        "/v1/vector/query",
        {
            "collection": "itinerary-public",
            "query": query,
            "top_k": 5,
            "filter": {"trip_id": trip_id, "region": region, "access_scope": "traveler"},
        },
    )
    candidates = (web.get("results") or []) + (vector.get("matches") or [])
    return [item for item in candidates if item.get("source_url") and item.get("region") == region][:8]

The exact field schema still belongs in the discovery contract and your tests; the important invariant is that a returned item carries scope and source context. I would also log the normalized source ID, not the full traveler query, when privacy requirements make raw query logging inappropriate. Don't log what you don't need.

Infrai fits this adapter when a team wants one REST surface and one key and bill across retrieval and other backend capabilities. That reduces credential and invoice sprawl, while plain HTTP keeps the integration language-neutral. It does not decide your chunk size, freshness SLA, or authorization policy for you.

Which retrieval options fit a quality-versus-latency budget?

A fair comparison starts with the operational shape of the corpus, not a feature checklist. Pinecone is a managed vector service with a focused indexing workflow. Weaviate offers an open-source core and a managed option, useful when self-hosting or schema control matters. Elasticsearch combines lexical, filtering, and vector search in one search stack, which can be valuable for exact station names and fuzzy descriptions. An HTTP aggregation layer can simplify access to several backend capabilities, but it adds another contract to monitor.

Option Useful fit Trade-off to test
Pinecone Teams prioritizing managed vector operations Extra service boundary for web freshness and policy data
Weaviate Teams wanting schema-rich search with self-hosting choice More operational decisions around modules and deployment
Elasticsearch Hybrid lexical, metadata, and vector queries Tuning and operating a broader search platform
Infrai Teams preferring one REST API and one credential across backend services Validate retrieval semantics and regional access filters against your contract

The benchmark should use a labeled set of real itinerary questions. Record recall of the required source, citation validity, and p95 retrieval latency at the same time. A tiny set of 50–100 questions with labels for region, date, and access scope catches more policy mistakes than a large set of unlabeled queries. I am not sure your mileage will match a vendor demo; traffic shape, language mix, and freshness windows dominate the result.

The catch is that a single global collection may be unsuitable when tenants require hard isolation or when retention rules differ. Use separate collections, or stick with a search system that can prove document-level filtering, when an accidental cross-trip result would be a compliance event. For exact timetable identifiers, keep a lexical path available even if vector recall wins on paraphrased place descriptions.

A rollout rule for citations, monitoring, and change control

Ship ingestion and querying behind separate feature flags. First replay the labeled evaluation set and inspect failures by stage. Then shadow live queries, comparing candidate scope and freshness without changing user-visible answers. Only after citation validity is stable should the generator consume the new context.

Every answer should retain a compact trace: collection, filter values, source IDs, source URLs, revision or fetch time, and the retrieval limit. Alert on missing source fields, out-of-window documents, and a sudden drop in labeled recall. Do not use a fluent answer as the health check.

When the corpus changes, rerun the same labels. If latency rises, reduce candidate limits or split collections before weakening access filters. Retrieval quality and latency are negotiable; authorization is not.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html

title: All-in-One Memory: Process-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Memory Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21147v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. However, existing memory methods often optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, without a shared reward space for evaluating search, writing, and stopping decisions. To address this, we propose All-in-One Memory (AiO-Mem), which organizes these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state and directly evaluates the semantic quality of each action in a unified reward space. AiO-Mem compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, providing a shared substrate for retrieval and memory writing. A unified memory policy actor then rolls out complete interaction trajectories over this shared evidence state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model is trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level DPO to assign process scores to the collected trajectories. These scores are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by Process-Aligned DAPO (PA-DAPO) to optimize the memory policy. Across long-context memory benchmarks, AiO-Mem consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.

title: Confidence-Calibrated Inference Expansion for Evaluator-Guided Test-Time Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.20836v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluator-guided reasoning presents a local control problem at every step: trust the current answer, return a fallback, or spend more inference. We formulate this choice as a compute-aware three-action controller, scoring terminal actions by predicted answer success and expansion by a rollout-based continuation-success surrogate, with compute cost priced explicitly. A local action-gap analysis characterizes when score errors can change a decision, while an expected regret bound accounts for errors along the realized expansion path. Guided by this analysis, we learn and calibrate action-specific confidence estimates, with local uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. On held-out width expansion and revision tasks, the controller improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively. Across four Qwen3-8B seeds, compute is lower than fitted Q in both settings, while utility differences are small and mixed. The results frame evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty, rather than a uniformly stronger reasoner.

title: Rubric First, Box Second: A Bootcamp Lab Where the Setup Is the Deliverable
description:
The short version: in a bootcamp lab, the environment is part of the answer. If a classmate can't rebuild your box from your repo and get the same bytes back, then your clever prompt never mattered. So this lab grades setup, checkpoints, and a rubric — before it grades the agent at all.

Why flip the order?

Most AI labs hand students a working sandbox and a problem. The sandbox is invisible, so the lesson students actually absorb is "the sandbox was just there." That's a bad lesson to carry into a job.

Free tiers make it worse. A free model sitting behind a shared queue is not guaranteed to be the same model tomorrow. A free server is not the same machine next week. Neither of those is a defect — it is the honest shape of free infrastructure. But it means the reproducible part of your work has to be the contract: what you pinned, what you recorded, and what you can rebuild from scratch.

Hence the flip. Deliverable one is a shell script. Deliverable four is a rubric. The agent run sits in the middle, where it belongs.

The lab contract

Four artifacts, one repo:

  1. bootstrap.sh — rebuilds the box from nothing.
  2. manifest.json — pins inputs, model identity, and budget.
  3. checkpoints/ — three named checks a stranger can run.
  4. rubric.json — the scoring rules, written by the student.

Nothing here is exotic. That's the point. If it feels boring, you're doing it right.

Artifact 1: a bootstrap that assumes amnesia 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# lab/bootstrap.sh — rebuild from an empty box. Bash 5+, Debian-ish target.
LAB_ROOT="${LAB_ROOT:-$HOME/lab}"
python3 -m venv "$LAB_ROOT/.venv"
"$LAB_ROOT/.venv/bin/pip" install --quiet -r "$LAB_ROOT/requirements.txt"
mkdir -p "$LAB_ROOT/runs"
git -C "$LAB_ROOT" rev-parse --short HEAD > "$LAB_ROOT/runs/git-sha.txt"
date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ        > "$LAB_ROOT/runs/built-at.txt"
echo "built $(cat "$LAB_ROOT/runs/git-sha.txt") at $(cat "$LAB_ROOT/runs/built-at.txt")"

Two rules for students:

  • It must run on a box where $LAB_ROOT does not exist yet.
  • It must print a build stamp. No stamp, no credit.

Why so strict? Because "it works on my machine" is a sentence, not evidence.

Artifact 2: pin the model, don't assume it

This is where free access actually changes the design. The project this lab is built around — the open-source coding agent from MonkeyCode — is described by its operator as offering free model access and a free server option.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I am deliberately not quoting a token quota or a machine spec here. Those numbers move, and a bootcamp that hard-codes them teaches students to trust a stale README. Check the project's own page the morning you run the lab, and write down what you found. That check is itself worth a point.

What you do pin is which model actually answered:

{
  "schema": 1,
  "runtime": "python3.11",
  "model": { "alias": "student-default", "recorded_id": "fill-me-in", "fallback": "fill-me-in" },
  "inputs": { "fixture": "fixtures/issue-0007.md", "sha256": "fill-me-in" },
  "budget": { "max_calls": 40, "max_wall_clock_s": 900 },
  "rebuild": { "script": "bootstrap.sh", "verified_at": null }
}

rebuild.verified_at stays null until the student has run bootstrap.sh twice, on two fresh boxes. That one field kills more hand-waving than any rubric line I've ever written.

Artifact 3: three checkpoints

Not one checkpoint. Three, and each must be cheap enough to run on a whim.

  1. Cold — bootstrap.sh on an empty box, then print the build stamp.
  2. Frozen — re-run the agent with the fixture hash unchanged; assert the output hash equals run one's output hash.
  3. Fenced — assert the diff touches only paths listed in allowed_paths.

A checkpoint is a command, not a paragraph:

$ ./checkpoints/frozen.sh
frozen: output hash 3f9c...  == run-001   OK

If a checkpoint needs three sentences of explanation to run, it isn't a checkpoint. It's a wish.

Artifact 4: stretch goals

Stretch goals are where the lab stops being a tutorial and starts being work:

  • Swap the model alias and keep the same score.
  • Cut wall clock by a third without losing a single checkpoint.
  • Add one rubric criterion that would catch a specific cheat, then explain who it punishes unfairly by accident.

That third one is the best hour of the week. Students grumble, then quietly rewrite the criterion twice.

The fair rubric

A rubric is only fair if two people applying it in the same room land on the same number. Otherwise you're not grading work, you're grading mood.

{
  "criteria": [
    {"id": "R1", "name": "rebuild", "weight": 3, "pass": "bootstrap.sh runs on an empty box and prints a build stamp"},
    {"id": "R2", "name": "repro",   "weight": 3, "pass": "two runs from the same manifest produce identical output bytes"},
    {"id": "R3", "name": "log",     "weight": 2, "pass": "runs/latest.json names model id, fixture hash, and call count"},
    {"id": "R4", "name": "scope",   "weight": 2, "pass": "no edits outside allowed_paths"}
  ],
  "disagreement_rule": "if two graders differ on any criterion, neither score counts until both re-read the manifest"
}

And a twenty-line grader, so the rubric is executable instead of decorative:

import json, sys

def grade(rubric_path, run_path):
    rubric = json.load(open(rubric_path))
    run    = json.load(open(run_path))
    earned = 0
    for c in rubric["criteria"]:
        ok = bool(run.get("checks", {}).get(c["id"]))
        print(f"{c['id']:>3}  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {c['name']}")
        earned += c["weight"] if ok else 0
    total = sum(c["weight"] for c in rubric["criteria"])
    return earned, total

if __name__ == "__main__":
    earned, total = grade(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])
    print(f"score {earned}/{total}")
    sys.exit(0 if earned == total else 1)

Then the drill that makes it real: two students grade the same run file, separately, no talking. Different score? The rubric is broken, not the run. Fix the wording of the criterion and try again. That loop — not the agent output — is the skill being taught.

Limitations, honestly

  • Free infrastructure recycles. A box can vanish between checkpoint two and three. That is the lesson, but it also eats lab time.
  • Shared queues make wall clock noisy. So don't grade speed. Grade recorded call counts.
  • The grader reads logs, not code. Pair it with a human read, or students optimize for the log format.
  • bootstrap.sh assumes network access and a Debian-ish base. Porting it elsewhere is part of the assignment, not a footnote.
  • These scripts are a skeleton. I haven't validated them across a distro matrix — adapt, then stamp your own manifest.

Who should not use this

  • Teams that need one fixed production model with compliance paperwork. Pin something stable instead.
  • Courses where the environment isn't the lesson. A pure algorithms unit gets overhead and nothing back.
  • Anyone who can't tolerate a free tier that changes shape mid-semester. Grade the contract, or pay for predictable hardware.

Try it, then break it

Run the lab once with a classmate grading you blind. Then ask the only question that survives contact with a deadline: could a stranger rebuild this from your repo on a Tuesday you didn't plan for?

If you'd rather not provision anything yourself just to find out, the free server option and the free model access are the cheapest way to start — check the project page for what's actually available today.

title: DLOSAC: Joint Spatial-Geometric Image Estimation via Delaunay-Guided Local Optimization RANSAC
description:
arXiv:2610.21215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable image geometric estimation from noisy matching points is typically addressed using RANSAC, often combined with local optimization to refine inliers and model parameters. However, existing paradigms are predominantly residual-centric; even heuristic attempts to enforce spatial uniformity suffer from a sequential, two-stage nature that inherently decouples distribution optimization from geometric refinement, preventing an effective trade-off. In this paper, we propose DLOSAC, a local optimization framework that jointly incorporates both geometric consistency and spatial distribution information. We begin by constructing a Delaunay triangulation over candidate inliers to explicitly encode neighborhood topology. The geometric module introduces an edge-based consistency metric to evaluate geometric errors, while the spatial module derives distribution descriptors from triangle areas and edge attributes to quantify the clustering of inliers. Finally, we combine edge-based geometric constraints, spatial distribution regularization, and traditional point-level geometric constraints to improve the quality of geometric parameters. Extensive experiments on six publicly available real-world datasets, covering three types of geometric estimation tasks, achieve state-of-the-art performance.

title: FGSS-BO: Feedback-Guided Hypothesis Management for LLM-Based Bayesian Optimization
description:
arXiv:2610.21246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-guided Bayesian optimization (BO) uses past observations to guide search, but proposed directions and their revision can remain implicit. We propose Feedback-Guided Search State (FGSS), a structured hypothesis-management interface connecting language-based guidance to observed evidence, executable parameter interventions, and comparative support updates. An LLM reflector proposes and revises hypotheses; a deterministic curator validates them and maintains identities and test records. The evolving state guides candidate construction and priorities. Instantiated on LLAMBO, FGSS-BO retains its surrogate and default expected improvement selection, with a bounded testing policy. On two retrospective protocol/media tasks with nearest-neighbor response oracles, it attains higher sample mean final best and search AUC than the matched LLAMBO baseline and evaluated non-LLM baselines. Prose-reflection and EI-only controls show mixed component effects. Six direct-training hyperparameter-optimization tasks show task-dependent transfer, strongest on diabetes SVM; exact-grid and reaction controls examine other settings. FGSS exposes hypotheses, their execution, and cross-round revisions for inspection while supporting search gains in selected settings.

title: When Reality Outpaces Cognition: A New Scaling Principle for Reliable Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2610.20764v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper challenges the understanding capabilities of existing AI paradigms and emerging world models by asking a fundamental question: How quickly can reality change before an intelligent system can no longer reliably perceive, reason, and act? We formulate this as a theory- and model-agnostic challenge in which systems must infer reliable actions for increasingly distant future states across a growing observation--reality gap. We operationalize this challenge through the effective Speed of Coherent Cognition (\(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\)), defined as the highest tested Speed of Reality (\(S_R\)) through which a system continuously satisfies a predefined behavioural reliability criterion from baseline. As a proof of concept, reinforcement-learning agents are trained at the baseline \(S_R\) and evaluated, without retraining, as \(S_R\) is increased by up to \(50\times\) while computational resources remain fixed. We compare Transformer and gated-MLP baselines with \(Co^4\), an architecture inspired by cellular mechanisms implicated in conscious processing and awake thought. Across the tested scenarios, \(Co^4\) achieves substantially higher \(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\) than the baselines, motivating \(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\) as a new benchmark and the scaling of coherent cognition as a principle for reliable AI.

title: OLED Monitors and Dark Mode: Why CSS Inversion Often Beats Your OS Settings
description:
OLED Monitors and Dark Mode: Why CSS Inversion Often Beats Your OS Settings

If you have an OLED monitor or OLED laptop screen, you've probably noticed that "true black" matters. OLED pixels that display pure black are literally off — no backlight, zero power, perfect contrast. This is why dark mode on OLED feels so different from LCD.

But there's a problem: OS-level dark mode doesn't actually control websites.

The Gap Between OS Dark Mode and Web Dark Mode

When you enable dark mode on macOS or Windows, you're changing the OS theme. Apps that respect your preference (VS Code, Slack, etc.) switch to dark. Your browser's chrome (the toolbar, tabs, sidebar) also goes dark.

But websites? They're in charge of their own styling. A site only goes dark if:

  1. The site explicitly supports prefers-color-scheme: dark in its CSS, OR
  2. Something forces it to

Most sites don't support it well. Some support it partially. Some ignore it completely.

How Browser-Level Dark Mode Forcing Works

A Firefox extension like NightOwl uses CSS inversion to force dark mode on any page regardless of whether the site implemented it:

html {
  filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg);
}

img, video, canvas, svg {
  filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg);
}

The invert(1) flips all colors. The hue-rotate(180deg) corrects the hue shift so that reds stay red and blues stay blue — just inverted in brightness. The second rule re-inverts images and videos so they still look correct.

This is crude but effective. Every white background becomes dark gray/black. Every dark text becomes light.

Why This Matters Specifically for OLED

On an LCD screen, the difference between "very dark gray" and "pure black" is cosmetic. The backlight is always on.

On OLED, pure black (#000000 or close) turns pixels off entirely. This means:

  • No light bleed from the display
  • Noticeably better battery life on laptops (less power to unlit pixels)
  • Dramatically better perceived contrast ratios (infinite contrast)

OS dark mode on Chrome/Firefox gives you dark browser chrome but still renders white pages. Every tab you open with a white background is blasting your OLED pixels at full brightness. CSS inversion flips that so most of the page is dark.

The Trade-offs

Pros of CSS inversion:

  • Works on any site, immediately, without site support
  • Per-domain toggle (you can leave specific sites as-is)
  • No account or cloud sync needed

Cons:

  • Colors can look slightly "off" on sites with unusual color schemes
  • Some gradients or design-heavy sites look weird
  • Not as polished as a site's native dark mode when the site actually implements it well

When to use native dark mode instead:

  • Sites like GitHub, Figma, Notion that have excellent native dark themes — let those sites control their own theming
  • Sites where color accuracy matters (photo editors, design tools)

When CSS inversion wins:

  • Documentation sites, news sites, forums, wikis — anything that's mostly text on white
  • Sites that partially support dark mode but miss elements (navigation stays white, etc.)
  • Any stubborn site that ignores prefers-color-scheme

A Practical Workflow

On NightOwl: enable dark mode globally, then whitelist the 3-5 sites where you want native theming (GitHub, your design tools, whatever). This gives you forced dark on 95% of sites while preserving intentional designs where they matter.

For OLED users specifically: the battery life improvement from not blasting full white on dozens of tabs is real. It's not dramatic per tab, but over a full day of browsing it adds up.

The underlying point: OS dark mode and browser dark mode solve different problems. OS dark mode controls native app theming. Browser-level CSS inversion forces dark on the web. If you care about OLED efficiency or just want consistent dark across all sites, you need both.

title: Vercel Daemons is now in public beta

Vercel Daemons is now in public beta, allowing you to run long-running processes that pull and execute work from Vercel Queues, databases, or third-party systems without requiring an HTTP server:

Daemons run containers on Fluid compute and deploy alongside your app in the same project. Vercel builds your image and maintains the instance count you configure in each region, restarting instances that exit or crash.

title: Node.js Scheduled Data Cleanup: BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or Hosted Queue for Small SaaS
description:
Short answer: for a small edtech SaaS sending scheduled shipment updates, start with a hosted queue plus cron, and choose BullMQ or RabbitMQ only when you are ready to own their delivery machinery.

Keep it boring.

Measure twice.

A shipment update is a deceptively small feature. A teacher changes a delivery window, and thousands of learners may need the same notice. The real decision is delivery guarantee: can a message be delivered at least once, can a duplicate be harmless, and can an operator see a stuck job before support does?

The field guide: pick a queue by the failure you can operate

Option Pick this when Delivery shape Operational catch
BullMQ with Redis Your team already runs Redis and wants a Node.js-native job API At-least-once workers with retries You own Redis persistence, upgrades, and worker supervision
RabbitMQ You need broker-level routing and have messaging operations experience Explicit acknowledgements and redelivery Topology, monitoring, and capacity become part of the product
Hosted queue You want cron-triggered dispatch with minimal platform work At-least-once delivery; make consumers idempotent You accept one provider's limits and outage surface
Inngest You want managed event steps and retries Provider-managed workflow delivery Its workflow model can exceed a single queue need

For a small SaaS, the hosted row is usually the least expensive in human time and the easiest to explain during an incident. That is a judgment about operations, not a promise about a vendor invoice.

How should a small SaaS choose BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or a hosted queue for scheduled cleanup and fan-out?

Start with the work unit. A cron trigger should enqueue a compact record range or cursor, then a worker loads the rows and sends updates. Do not put a deletion manifest or a full subscriber list into one message: the queue message limit is 256KB. A cursor such as {\"shipmentId\":\"shp_4821\",\"page\":7} is easier to retry and audit.

Delivery is at-least-once. I once treated a retry as a rare edge case and let the handler append a notification row before checking its idempotency key; a timeout after the insert produced duplicate mail on the next attempt. The fix was boring and effective: derive a stable job key from shipment ID plus page, then make the database write conditional. Five minutes later, the retry was harmless.

Here is the small handoff I use for a Node.js worker. It publishes a batch and reports a failed item through the same base URL and key. The response body is retained as evidence for the run; a real service would also persist the request ID beside its job key. Infrai offers one key, one bill, and one plain REST API for both dispatch and captured errors keeps the contract stable when the backend provider changes. No SDK install is required.

const baseUrl = "https://api.example.invalid/v1";
const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const headers = {
  Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
};

async function publishShipmentPage(shipmentId: string, page: number) {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/queue/publish_batch`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers,
    body: JSON.stringify({
      messages: [{
        idempotency_key: `shipment:${shipmentId}:page:${page}`,
        payload: { shipmentId, page },
      }],
    }),
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`queue publish failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  const result = await response.json();
  if (result.failed?.length) {
    await fetch(`${baseUrl}/errors/capture`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers,
      body: JSON.stringify({
        message: "shipment fan-out publish reported a failed item",
        context: { shipmentId, page, result },
      }),
    });
  }

  return result;
}

publishShipmentPage("shp_4821", 7).catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

The important detail is the handoff: queue output and captured errors are visible under one key, so a dead-letter spike can be investigated beside application errors. Infrai's differentiator here is the contract: swapping the backend behind a capability does not force a code rewrite, and the same plain REST surface covers dispatch and observability. An SQS plus Sentry setup can do the same job, but it means two sign-ups, two credential sets, and glue code to correlate message IDs with error events.

Retries need backoff, and a standard queue has no Kafka-style replay or multi-consumer-group history. Keep the queue for work dispatch, not as your audit log. If a cleanup job runs longer than 900 seconds, let cron enqueue it and have a worker consume pages; do not make cron host the long task.

What each serious option looks like in production

BullMQ is a sensible pick when Redis is already a staffed dependency and every service is TypeScript. Its familiar worker model makes local development pleasant. The catch is that Redis operations are now coupled to shipment reliability; persistence settings and failover are your responsibility.

RabbitMQ fits teams that need routing keys, exchanges, or established AMQP tooling. It is a strong broker, but it asks for more topology and monitoring discipline than a single cleanup pipeline usually justifies. Stick with it when those routing semantics are a requirement, not because the name sounds more durable.

A hosted queue fits the small-SaaS boundary when one queue, a cron trigger, and idempotent workers cover the workflow. Amazon SQS is the obvious comparison for teams already deep in AWS. The trade is concentration: one provider, one bill, and one outage surface. That is acceptable only if your runbook includes provider status checks, bounded retries, and a way to pause fan-out.

Limits that should change your design

The queue does not provide DAG orchestration, a join primitive, native debounce, or throttle. Delayed messages top out at seven days, retention at 30 days, and FIFO deduplication at five minutes. Cron does not replay triggers missed while paused, and its run output keeps only the first 4KB. Push targets must be publicly reachable HTTPS endpoints.

Those boundaries are design inputs. In a busy enrollment week, a page can fan out to 10,000 subscribers while the cleanup cursor remains a few dozen bytes; that asymmetry is why I separate scheduling, dispatch, and durable audit state instead of forcing one tool to do all three. Store the durable audit record in Postgres, claim pages with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and enqueue IDs or cursors. If your requirement is a replayable event stream or a multi-stage workflow, choose a system built for that job instead.

References

  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html

title: This Week in Open Source for October 15, 2026
description:
by Daryl Ducharme, Open Source Programs Office

This Week in Open Source for October 15, 2026

A look around the world of open source

After speaking about the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol and Model Context Protocol (MCP) in Toronto last week (which I recapped in Tag-Team Transmission), open agent boundaries were clearly still on my mind while collecting this week's reads. As AI agents, terminal tools, and embedded micro-apps move deeper into everyday software workflows, a central tension keeps surfacing across the open source community: where do human judgment, interface trust, and maintainer sustainability fit in? Whether teams are wiring up open protocols in the Unix shell, running multimodal retrieval locally on a laptop, or stewarding decades-old kernel infrastructure, the healthiest open source architectures don't replace human agency—they give workers clearer boundaries, inspectable tools, and a genuine seat at the controls.

Upcoming Events

🗓️ October 2026

  • All Things Open 2026 (October 19–20, 2026) — Raleigh, North Carolina, USA. One of the largest community-focused open source conferences on the U.S. East Coast exploring open source software, AI engineering, and maintainer sustainability—featuring Googlers Andrew Brogdon, Mark Techson, and Marc Dougherty speaking on "Where Is My Futuristic App? Generative UI and the Open Future" and Abdel Sghiouar on "Taming Agentic AI: How to Run Agents-Generated Code Safely on Kubernetes", alongside the Google Community Lounge with the Flutter team.
  • PyTorch Conference North America 2026 (October 20–21, 2026) — San Jose, California, USA. Two days of open source machine learning innovation across the PyTorch ecosystem—featuring a keynote by Google's Bill Jia ("Workload Fungibility in the Age of Agents") and technical sessions from Googlers Chris Jones, Sandeep Pokkunuri, Rob Mulla, Ankita Luthra, Trinadh Kotturu, Claudio Basile, Qi Zhou, Jago Macleod, and Aleksey Vlasenko on TorchTPU, vLLM, SGLang, Ray, and Kubernetes.
  • AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026 (October 22–23, 2026) — San Jose, California, USA. Linux Foundation and Agentic AI Foundation conference focused on building and scaling production agentic systems with open standards—featuring keynotes by Google's Sarah Drasner and Chi Wang, plus sessions from Googlers Alan Blount (on A2UI), Junjie Bu (on interoperable agent discovery), Amit Handa (on agentic commerce), Dominic Farolino (on MCP Apps + WebMCP), and Prerna Kakkar & Kurtis Van Gent (on EvalBench).
  • GitHub Universe 2026 (October 28–29, 2026) — San Francisco, California, USA & Virtual. Annual global developer gathering highlighting open source workflows, collaborative security, and multi-model AI-assisted software engineering.

🗓️ November 2026

  • Open Source in Finance Forum (OSFF) New York (November 4–5, 2026) — New York, New York, USA. Dedicated industry conference examining open source compliance, supply-chain security, and collaborative innovation across regulated financial institutions.
  • SeaGL (Seattle GNU/Linux Conference) 2026 (November 6–7, 2026) — Seattle, Washington, USA & Virtual. Free, grassroots technical summit dedicated to spreading awareness and knowledge of free and open source software, hardware, and culture.
  • KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 (November 9–12, 2026) — Salt Lake City, Utah, USA. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation's flagship conference uniting adopters and maintainers around Kubernetes and cloud-native infrastructure—featuring over 35 sessions and keynotes from Googlers including Abdel Sghiouar, Jago Macleod, Tim Hockin, Kaslin Fields, John Belamaric, Dawn Chen, Janet Kuo, Benjamin Elder, Antonio Ojea, Lior Lieberman, Michelle Au, and Braydon Kains across Kubernetes SIGs, etcd, containerd, Gateway API, CEL admission policies, and agent sandboxes.
  • SFSCON (South Tyrol Free Software Conference) 2026 (November 13–14, 2026) — Bolzano, Italy. One of Europe's longest-running Free Software conferences bringing together public-sector decision-makers and developers to advance digital sovereignty and open infrastructure.

🗓️ December 2026

  • Yocto Project Virtual Summit 2026.12 (December 1–3, 2026) — Virtual. Community summit for embedded Linux engineers and maintainers building custom, reproducible Linux distributions across edge and IoT hardware.
  • Open Source Summit Japan 2026 (December 7–9, 2026) — Tokyo, Japan. The Linux Foundation's premier Asia-Pacific conference connecting open source developers, kernel maintainers, and enterprise leaders across cloud, embedded Linux, and open AI, including sessions from Google engineers such as Anurag Sinha.
  • OpenCompliance Summit 2026 (December 10–11, 2026) — Tokyo, Japan. Specialized gathering uniting legal, security, and OSPO practitioners around OpenChain, SPDX, software bills of materials (SBOMs), and global open source supply-chain compliance.

Open Source Reads and Links

  • [Blog] Meet the A2A CLI: discover, message, and manage agents from your terminal — In Developer Relations, few things beat showing a protocol live in a terminal during a conference talk without a complex web stack in the way. The new Apache 2.0 A2A CLI lets you discover, message, and wrap any stdin/stdout script into a streaming Agent2Agent server with --exec—raising an interesting question: does meeting developers in the Unix shell matter more for open protocol adoption than heavy SDKs?
  • [Blog] Talking to Agents with a2a (as a human!) — Right after the MCP Dev Summit in Toronto, Marc Dougherty shared a post that uncovered even more about the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol by flipping the lens from autonomous systems to human-to-agent interfaces with A2UI. Building a2term so agents render interactive terminal confirmation forms before acting raises a compelling question: could open agent protocols also save humans from enterprise UI bloat?
  • [Article] Dreamforce 2026 — When major enterprise platforms start telling customers they may never need to log into a web UI again because every workflow is now an API, MCP tool, or CLI command, where does the user interface go? RedMonk's Rachel Stephens examines this shift toward headless software and asks a question every open source protocol builder should ponder: when third-party agents mediate our data and workflows, how well does trust actually travel?
  • [Blog] EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model — Moving RAG setups fully on-device opens up real-world possibilities—from kiosks in low-connectivity areas and offline backup systems to hardware that ships with all of its own help and support docs onboard. With Google DeepMind's Apache 2.0 release of EmbeddingGemma 2 fitting multimodal search into 567MB of RAM, what new resilient tools become possible when devices don't need an internet connection to know how they work?
  • [Blog] Atproto Web Tile Embeds — Seeing AT Protocol Web Tiles in the wild sparks curiosity about what new publishing patterns become possible when open protocols move beyond text and static images. Nathan Cassell walks through embedding a live, sandboxed 3D Web Tile straight from a personal data server into a blog post—making us wonder what developers might build when interactive micro-apps can travel anywhere without phoning home.
  • [Report] Navigating Open Source Governance in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: The 2026 State of OSPOs and Open Source Management — Working in an OSPO myself, seeing how other teams operate is essential for improving how we serve as liaisons between our organizations and the broader open source ecosystem. With the Linux Foundation and TODO Group's 2026 survey finding 79% of AI-involved OSPOs shaping model policy and 69% piloting agentic workflows, how can we ensure enterprise AI governance also supports upstream maintainers?
  • [Report] Celebrating 35 Years of Linux: The Open Source Engine Powering Three Decades of Global Innovation and Infrastructure — It is incredible to see the success of the Linux kernel and distributions across enterprise software development—and to ponder how a project from the early 1990s has kept up with so many technological shifts. As Linux Foundation Research celebrates 35 years of Linux across billions of devices and every top-500 supercomputer, how can the community's model of continuous adaptation guide the next generation of maintainers?

Which of these stories will you be chatting about at your next meetup or conference? Let us know! Share with us on our @GoogleOSS X account or our @opensource.google Bluesky account.

title: What Should We Remove? Evaluating the Reliability and Costs of RLVR Data Decontamination
description:
arXiv:2610.21229v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) math corpora are routinely screened for benchmark overlap, but the reliability and data-loss costs of cleaning policies remain underexamined. We audit sixteen open RLVR math corpora comprising 1,673,514 corpus-specific training items against six benchmarks containing 1,949 questions. We evaluate eight policies based on exact, lexical, and semantic matching using 594 independently and blindly dual-reviewed training-benchmark pairs. Calibration and held-out sets have disjoint benchmark questions and training-example families. A separate review of all 83 candidate matches for 80 sampled training items measures item-level false removal. At cosine threshold 0.80, 52 of 59 sampled removals (88%) were confirmed false removals; this is not a demonstrated population rate. No semantic threshold in our preregistered grid (0.80-0.98) meets the 90% conservative-precision target on calibration. The existing judge-adjudicated policy achieves 98.1% resolved precision and 98.2% candidate-frame recall on held-out corpora. It has zero confirmed false removals among six sampled removals, with one unresolved case; this does not establish zero risk. Within the evaluated candidate frame, this policy offers a more favorable precision-recall balance than the semantic-threshold alternatives tested. Recall does not measure contamination outside the candidate frame. We release reviewed labels, per-policy decisions, and coverage accounting to support evaluation of cleaning reliability and cost rather than overlap counts alone.

title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards
description:
arXiv:2610.20814v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.

title: ControlFlow3D: Distilling Multi-View Knowledge into Latent Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
description:
arXiv:2610.21190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Point cloud upsampling is essential for 3D applications but remains challenging due to sparse, under-constrained observations. Multi-view images can resolve geometric ambiguity, but existing multi-modal methods do not fully exploit visual cues. We propose ControlFlow3D, a framework that distills knowledge from pretrained foundation models into a lightweight generation network during training, enabling strong performance without multi-view images available at test time. Specifically, our method performs conditional flow matching in a structured latent space defined by a frozen 3D encoder. Multi-view image tokens and 3D latent tokens are jointly clustered into shared prototypes via unsupervised soft KMeans; the resulting prototypes guide the flow trajectory through velocity control and are aligned by a consistency loss that progressively transfers image knowledge into the base network. A Mamba-based geometry decoder then maps latent features to dense coordinates with linear complexity. We also construct ShapeNetPU, a 35K-object multi-modal benchmark that is 31 times larger than prior datasets. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its strong generalization capability.

title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: Lessons from GitLab's PostgreSQL Architecture
description:
Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: Lessons from GitLab's PostgreSQL Architecture

Running a standard schema migration on a small staging database is trivial: you run ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN bio text; and it finishes in 10 milliseconds.

However, when your PostgreSQL database holds billions of rows, multi-terabyte tables, and thousands of concurrent transactions per second (as GitLab.com does), a naive migration can trigger table-wide ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks. In seconds, transaction queues back up, connection pools exhaust, and your application goes down.

GitLab has pioneered some of the most rigorous, battle-tested patterns for zero-downtime database migrations in the open-source world.

In this guide, we will unpack GitLab’s database architecture rules and show you how to apply these enterprise patterns to your own production systems.

1. The PostgreSQL Locking Hierarchy: Understanding the Danger

Every schema alteration in PostgreSQL requests a lock. Understanding which locks conflict with standard reads (SELECT) and writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) is essential:

Operation Lock Mode Acquired Blocks Concurrent Reads? Blocks Concurrent Writes?
SELECT AccessShareLock No No
UPDATE / DELETE RowExclusiveLock No No
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ShareUpdateExclusiveLock No No
ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN AccessExclusiveLock Yes Yes
CREATE INDEX (Standard) ShareLock No Yes

The Trap: Lock Queues

Even if an ALTER TABLE statement only takes 2 milliseconds to run, if it is forced to wait behind an active, long-running SELECT query, it waits in the lock queue.

While it waits, every single subsequent query behind it is blocked. Within 30 seconds, your entire application server runs out of database connections.

2. Rule 1: Always Use Low Lock Timeouts

In GitLab Core, migrations never wait indefinitely for locks. They configure strict lock timeouts and retry loops:

class AddStatusToDeployments < Gitlab::Database::Migration[2.2]
  # Limit waiting for the lock to 500ms
  SET_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 500

  def change
    # Set statement and lock timeouts for this transaction
    execute("SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '500ms';")
    execute("SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5s';")

    add_column :deployments, :status, :smallint, default: 0, null: false
  end
end

If the migration cannot acquire the required lock within 500ms, it aborts cleanly, releasing the queue, and can be retried safely without taking down web traffic.

3. Rule 2: Never Create Indexes Synchronously

A standard CREATE INDEX locks the target table against writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) for the entire duration of the index build. On a 100-million-row table, this can lock your database for 30 minutes!

The GitLab Pattern: add_concurrent_index

GitLab provides helper methods that disable DDL transactions and invoke PostgreSQL’s CONCURRENTLY engine:

class AddIndexToIssuesTitle < Gitlab::Database::Migration[2.2]
  disable_ddl_transaction! # Required for concurrent indexing

  def up
    add_concurrent_index :issues, :title, name: 'index_issues_on_title'
  end

  def down
    remove_concurrent_index_by_name :issues, 'index_issues_on_title'
  end
end

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds the index in the background using two table scans, allowing concurrent reads and writes to proceed uninhibited.

4. Rule 3: Safe Column Deletions (The 3-Phase Strategy)

Dropping a column directly from a live table (ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone;) instantly breaks existing application workers that are caching table columns in memory.

GitLab enforces a strict 3-phase deployment cycle across separate releases:

Release N (Phase 1):
  Ignore column phone in application models (ActiveRecord / ORM).
  New code no longer reads or writes the column.

Release N+1 (Phase 2):
  Mark column phone as ignored in DB schema.
  Remove column references from all background jobs.

Release N+2 (Phase 3):
  Safely execute: ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone;
  Zero application crashes.

In code, this is handled via ignore_column:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  # Inform the ORM to stop including this column in queries
  self.ignored_columns += %i[deprecated_token]
end

5. Rule 4: Batched Background Migrations (BBM)

What happens when you need to update 50,000,000 rows (e.g., populating a new UUID column)?

Running UPDATE users SET uuid = gen_random_uuid(); in a single transaction will blow up WAL logs, exhaust memory, and lock rows for hours.

GitLab solves this using Batched Background Migrations (BBM):

  1. Break the table down into discrete chunks (e.g., batches of 5,000 IDs).
  2. Execute the batch update asynchronously inside background worker jobs (Sidekiq).
  3. Throttle execution based on database replication lag: if replicas fall behind by more than 8 seconds, the background migration pauses automatically! 
class BackfillProjectTokens < Gitlab::Database::Migration[2.2]
  restrict_gitlab_migration gitlab_schema: :gitlab_main

  def up
    queue_batched_background_migration(
      job_class_name: 'BackfillProjectTokens',
      table_name: :projects,
      column_name: :id,
      job_arguments: [],
      batch_size: 5_000,
      sub_batch_size: 250,
      interval: 2.minutes
    )
  end
end

The migration runs smoothly over the course of several hours in the background while users experience 0.00ms of downtime or query slowdown.

6. Key Takeaways for High-Scale Applications

  1. Guard with Lock Timeouts: Never allow a migration to queue indefinitely; fail fast if locks conflict.
  2. Build Indexes Concurrently: Never run CREATE INDEX synchronously on live tables.
  3. Phase Destructive Operations: Delete columns and rename tables across at least two consecutive deployment cycles.
  4. Batch Data Updates: Throttle heavy data transformations against database replication lag.

Resources & Links

  • GitLab Database Documentation: docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/database/
  • GitLab Profile: gitlab.com/hrlpavan
  • GitLab Contributor Profile: contributors.gitlab.com/users/hrlpavan
  • GitHub: @hrlpavan

How does your team handle high-concurrency database migrations? Let’s talk database internals in the comments below!
