title: CoTS: Competitive Token Selection for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20642v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent latent reasoning methods move beyond discrete Chain-of-Thought (CoT) by replacing sampled tokens with continuous soft embeddings or hidden states, enabling richer intermediate representations and preserving alternative reasoning paths. However, the need for latent reasoning varies across decoding steps: confident predictions favor discrete commitment, whereas ambiguous steps benefit from preserving multiple plausible alternatives. Existing approaches typically handle this variation through either global soft activation or hard switching based on uncertainty thresholds, treating latent intervention as an all-or-nothing decision rather than continuously adapting its strength. To address this limitation, we propose Competitive Token Selection (CoTS), a training-free framework that reframes latent intervention from binary mode selection into continuous allocation at the token level. CoTS uses the probability competition between the two most likely candidates to dynamically balance discrete commitment and soft exploration at each reasoning step. The second candidate represents the strongest alternative to the model's preferred continuation, so the separation between the two directly reflects the stability of the current discrete choice. When one candidate clearly dominates, CoTS keeps the representation close to the sampled discrete token to preserve a stable reasoning trajectory; as the competition strengthens, it increases the contribution of the soft representation to retain plausible alternatives. This competition-based allocation requires neither manually tuned switching thresholds nor mixing coefficients, and introduces no additional forward passes. Experiments across six reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that CoTS consistently outperforms standard CoT and state-of-the-art training-free latent reasoning methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/OkinoYu/CoTSReasoning.

title: Perception or Reasoning? Diagnosing and Tackling Reinforcement Learning Bottlenecks in VLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.21380v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning has brought strong gains to language model reasoning, but its improvements on visual tasks remain less consistent. One difficulty is that visual task failures can arise from different sources: the same benchmark may be limited by perception for one model and by reasoning for another. We introduce Perception and Reasoning Attribution (PARA), which measures the remaining perceptual and reasoning headroom of each model--benchmark pair by comparing how many current errors are recovered with more accurate visual information versus a stronger reasoner. Across 4 vision-language models and 17 multimodal benchmarks, PARA broadly agrees with the expected characteristics of existing benchmarks while revealing substantial model-specific variation. More importantly, it shows that RL gains become smaller as perceptual headroom increases, but larger when reasoning explains more of the recoverable errors, suggesting that current RL exploits reasoning headroom more effectively than perceptual headroom. Motivated by this gap, we analyze how existing RL objectives affect visual perception and find that reward- and token-level signals influence visual attention only indirectly. We therefore propose GRAD, a group-relative attention distillation objective that uses the best rollout in each group to directly guide the visual attention of weaker rollouts. GRAD consistently improves performance across two model scales and seven benchmarks, and further complements existing RL methods.

title: The AI experience doesn’t care about your org chart
description:
AI is bringing content design, enterprise content strategy, knowledge management, and model behavior into the same user experience. Our ways of working haven’t caught up.

Imagine a finance manager trying to understand why a supplier hasn’t been paid.

The enterprise application shows that the invoice has been approved. The manager asks the AI assistant when the supplier can expect payment, and the assistant explains that the invoice has completed the approval process and is ready for payment.

Except it isn’t.

The invoice is blocked because of a discrepancy between the invoiced amount and the purchase order. Approval and payment eligibility are different things, governed by different parts of the business process.

The assistant hasn’t necessarily misunderstood the approval status. But it has failed to understand what that status means in relation to everything else.

Maybe it retrieved documentation about invoice approvals without the information about payment blocks. Maybe the underlying business concepts aren’t represented consistently across systems. Maybe it didn’t have access to the current payment status. Or maybe it had the right information and still failed to interpret it correctly.

Those are different problems, often owned by different teams.

But from the user’s perspective, it’s one experience — and it’s broken.

This is one of the most consequential challenges emerging as AI becomes part of enterprise software. We’re bringing together content and knowledge ecosystems that we’ve historically managed separately, and we haven’t yet developed the ways of working to manage their interdependence.

We’re going to need more than better AI models, better content systems, or better design guidelines. We’re going to need to rethink how these things work together.

We’re talking about more than one AI transformation

One thing that makes this moment difficult to navigate is that we tend to talk about AI and content as though we’re discussing a single change.

We’re not.

In a 2026 article for Nielsen Norman Group, Sarah Gibbons articulated four different meanings of “AI design”: designing with AI, designing AI products, designing for AI agents, and designing the AI itself.

That distinction is useful because the implications for content work are dramatically different depending on which kind of AI design we’re talking about.

Consider two scenarios.

In the first, a product team uses AI to accelerate its existing design process. It has a content design system with established terminology, voice and tone guidelines, and interaction patterns. Designers use AI to generate candidate UI copy, and content designers review and refine it before shipping.

AI has changed how efficiently the team produces content, but the fundamental model is familiar. People design and approve a defined set of content before it ships, and the product displays that content according to established rules and conditions.

In the second scenario, the product generates content dynamically for each user, drawing on information about their task, their context, the state of the system, and relevant enterprise knowledge.

The content designer can’t anticipate or approve every possible sentence. Instead, they help design the system that determines what the experience should communicate, under what conditions, with which constraints, and how to evaluate whether it’s working.

That’s a fundamentally different design challenge.

And then there’s another dimension: an AI agent that needs to understand the same product well enough to take action on behalf of a user. The information and structures that make sense to humans may not be sufficient for an agent. The system needs reliable representations of concepts, relationships, actions, constraints, and permissions.

Those three situations map to the first three of Gibbons’s categories. The fourth, designing the AI itself, is what is being called things like model design, model behavior, context architecutre, or content engineering — and it shapes all of the others.

These scenarios don’t replace one another. They increasingly coexist, sometimes within the same product.

We’re only beginning to understand what that means for content work.

Specialization is increasing. So is interdependence.

There’s been considerable discussion about whether content design is splitting into different specializations.

One direction moves deeper into content systems: structured content, reusable patterns, guidelines, standards, and the infrastructure that allows content design decisions to scale.

Another moves toward model behavior design: shaping how AI systems communicate, interpret intent, manage ambiguity, explain their decisions, and respond in different situations.

I see value in recognizing these areas of expertise. They involve different technical knowledge, methods, and deliverables.

But there’s another area where content designers need to develop greater expertise: the semantic and context architecture that allows systems to work with meaning.

Taxonomies, ontologies, and knowledge graphs are becoming increasingly relevant to the experiences we’re designing.

These aren’t interchangeable technologies. Taxonomies help organize and classify concepts. Ontologies define concepts and relationships within a domain. Knowledge graphs can represent interconnected information in ways that systems can query and use.

Together, these kinds of structures can help establish shared meaning across systems.

A broader context architecture also needs to account for information about the user’s task, the current state of the product, relevant business rules, permissions, and other conditions that determine what information is appropriate at a particular moment.

For content designers, learning these concepts well enough to communicate with technical teams is a start.

But content designers should also learn to actively help shape the semantic architecture of the experiences they design.

Information architects, knowledge engineers, data specialists, and enterprise architects bring essential expertise to that work. Content designers add what has always been central to our discipline: terminology, conceptual models, information organization, user mental models, and the relationship between language and understanding.

The decisions encoded in a semantic model can have direct consequences for how a user experiences a product.

If a system represents two business concepts as equivalent when users understand them as distinct, that mismatch may surface in navigation, generated explanations, recommendations, or agent behavior.

That’s a UX problem, even if its source is several layers removed from the interface.

This is also why I’m cautious about drawing hard boundaries between emerging content specializations.

We need people who go deep into content systems, model behavior, and semantic architecture. But their work needs to share patterns, concepts, and principles if the experience is going to feel coherent.

An enterprise user might move between a traditional interface, dynamically generated explanations, an AI conversation, and an agent performing a task.

Those interactions won’t use identical language or behave in identical ways, nor should they. But they need to share an understanding of how the product works.

Specialization makes sense. Separation is where I get concerned.

AI is bringing separate content ecosystems into the same experience

The challenge becomes even larger when we look beyond UX content design.

Enterprises have long divided responsibility for content and knowledge across different domains.

UX content design teams work on product experiences, language, interaction patterns, and design systems. Technical communication teams create and maintain product documentation, help content, and educational materials. Marketing, support, and other functions manage their own content ecosystems.

Content strategy and content ops establish content models, workflows, governance, lifecycle processes, and systems for managing content at scale, but usually within individual domains rather than across them.

Information architecture shapes how information is organized, labeled, and connected within each of these domains. Knowledge management varies even more: in some organizations it means maintaining documentation and knowledge bases, and in others it means capturing, sharing, and applying organizational expertise.

Now AI engineering teams are building systems that retrieve knowledge, assemble context, generate responses, and enable agents to act, often drawing on content and information governed by all these different functions.

These connections aren’t entirely new. Documentation has always needed to reflect how products actually work. Terminology in an interface should be consistent with the language in support content. But teams could often manage these dependencies through periodic reviews, handoffs, and separate publication processes.

AI is changing the nature of that dependency.

An AI assistant might draw on technical documentation to answer a question within a product. The semantic architecture can influence what information it retrieves and how it interprets that information. Content design patterns can shape how the assistant communicates its response. And business rules and permissions can determine what actions an agent can take on the user’s behalf.

The experience is increasingly assembled from information and design decisions managed by different teams, sometimes in real time.

That creates new operational challenges. When something goes wrong, no single team may have the visibility or authority to diagnose and fix the problem. And a change made in one system can have consequences for experiences that another team owns.

This is why content ops and design ops need to work much more closely together. But the coordination can’t stop there. It also needs to involve the people responsible for enterprise knowledge, semantic architecture, AI engineering, and evaluation.

We need to scale coordinated decisions

Large enterprises have always struggled to scale content design.

One response has been to invest in reusable patterns, standards, guidelines, design systems, and operational processes that allow teams to create more consistent experiences without requiring a content designer to personally review every decision.

But another response, less often acknowledged, has been to accept uneven quality. When headcount shrinks or demand exceeds capacity, some experiences simply receive less attention. That compromise was never ideal, but organizations could often contain its consequences within particular products or channels.

AI makes that compromise harder to sustain. Inconsistencies in terminology, guidance, or source content can now influence generated responses and actions across many interactions.

Investments in reusable systems are becoming even more essential. AI can also make them more powerful by bringing guidance directly into the tools and workflows where experiences are designed and built.

But scaling content production isn’t the same as scaling content design.

AI can help us generate more content, more quickly. That doesn’t guarantee the content is appropriate, coherent, accurate, or useful.

Scaling content design means making good design decisions repeatable across an organization.

And increasingly, those decisions don’t live in one team’s tools or processes.

Consider what happens when an enterprise changes the terminology for an important business concept.

Traditionally, a content design team might update the design system and work with product teams to change UI strings. A documentation team might update help content and published materials according to its own release process.

Now we may also need to consider whether the change affects a taxonomy or ontology, what an AI assistant retrieves, which terms it uses in generated explanations, how an agent interprets a request, and what our evaluation tests consider a correct response.

Who identifies all those dependencies? Who decides which changes are significant? How do the changes move through the different systems? How do we know when they’re complete?

These are operational questions.

Combining all these functions into one organization could create as many problems as it solves.

What we need is a more integrated operating model: shared standards where they matter, clear ownership, connected workflows, and governance that accounts for how decisions propagate across systems.

In practice, that means:

  • Shared governance of enterprise terminology and semantic standards, so a change to an important business concept is made deliberately and carried everywhere it matters.
  • Content design patterns that inform both traditional interfaces and AI behavior, so the product communicates as one product.
  • Workflows that identify which experiences need review when enterprise knowledge changes, so teams find the dependencies before users do.
  • Feedback loops that run in the other direction, so what we learn about AI behavior and user understanding reaches the teams who can fix the source.

That last one deserves more attention than it usually gets.

If testing reveals that an AI assistant consistently misunderstands a business concept, how does that information reach the teams responsible for the underlying knowledge, semantic structure, or content model?

If a documentation team discovers that users misunderstand a particular process, how does that insight influence the design of the product and its AI interactions?

We’ve spent years developing ways to scale the work within content functions. Now we need to get better at scaling the work across them.

Evaluation is becoming part of content and experience operations

Evaluation is another area where this interdependence becomes clear.

With traditional UI content, we can review a relatively stable set of artifacts before they ship. We can assess the language, test it with users, and make revisions.

When an AI system generates responses dynamically, we can’t review every possible output in advance.

Instead, we need to evaluate the system’s behavior across different situations and continue evaluating it as the system, its knowledge, and its users’ needs change.

We’re still at a very early stage of learning how to do this well.

Much of the initial work must be exploratory. People examine outputs, identify patterns, form hypotheses about why something went wrong, and determine what needs to change.

As with the invoice, the cause can sit in several places. Sometimes the issue is with the model’s behavior. Sometimes the system retrieved the wrong information. Sometimes the underlying content was incomplete, outdated, or contradictory. Sometimes the system lacked the context necessary to interpret the request correctly.

And sometimes the response is factually accurate but still represents a poor experience.

It might misunderstand the user’s intent, communicate uncertainty inappropriately, fail to explain an important limitation, or suggest an action without adequately establishing what the user wants.

These are different kinds of problems, and they require different kinds of expertise.

I expect we’ll get much better at translating what we learn into evals: repeatable tests that assess how AI systems perform against defined expectations. These can help us identify recurring failures, assess the impact of changes, and improve the system over time.

But first, we need to understand what we’re evaluating.

It’s not enough to ask whether a response is accurate. We also need to ask whether it was appropriate in context, supported the user’s goals, and made sense as part of the overall experience. And when the system recommends or takes action, we need to evaluate whether users understand what’s happening and retain appropriate control.

Go back to the finance manager. An evaluation that only checked whether the assistant described the approval status accurately would have passed that response. The manager still wouldn’t know when the supplier would be paid.

One tempting response to poor AI outputs is to give the system more context. But more isn’t necessarily better. Irrelevant, outdated, or conflicting information can actually make responses less reliable. The challenge is determining which knowledge, rules, and details about the user’s task are needed in a particular situation, and using evaluation to understand whether we’re providing the right context.

This is another place where content designers and strategists, design researchers, AI engineers, and the people responsible for enterprise knowledge and semantic architecture need to work closely together.

As these practices mature, we’ll be able to automate more of our evaluations. But human judgment will remain essential, not only for assessing outputs, but for identifying new failure patterns and refining our understanding of what good AI behavior looks like.

This is particularly important for experience quality, where success depends on context, user expectations, and judgments that aren’t always easily reduced to pass-or-fail criteria. Automated evals and human evaluation will need to work together, each informing and improving the other.

The operational challenge will be to turn what we learn through evaluation into improvements across the systems involved.

An evaluation finding shouldn’t stop at identifying a bad response. It should help us diagnose what needs to change, whether that’s the model’s instructions, the knowledge it retrieves, the semantic architecture, the interaction patterns, or even the underlying business process. And that diagnosis needs to reach the people who can address it.

Those changes then need to be governed, tested, and maintained.

Evaluation used to be a checkpoint at the end of the design process. It’s becoming one of the ways we maintain the experience itself.

Enterprise knowledge is becoming part of experience architecture

There’s a larger shift underneath all of this.

We’ve often treated content as something we produce, manage, and deliver through products and systems.

But AI is making content and knowledge increasingly important to what those products and systems can understand, communicate, and do.

Enterprise knowledge is becoming part of experience architecture.

That doesn’t mean every document becomes a product component, or that every content specialist needs to become an AI engineer.

It means decisions about how information is structured, represented, governed, and made available can directly shape the behavior and quality of an experience.

And it means the distinction between designing an experience and designing the knowledge that supports it is becoming harder to maintain.

I’m not suggesting that anyone has figured out the right organizational structures or operating models for this work. I certainly haven’t. We’re just beginning to understand the scope of the transformation, and the practices we need will develop through experimentation, collaboration, and learning from real systems.

But I’m increasingly convinced that improving each discipline independently won’t be enough.

We’ll need deeper expertise in content systems, model behavior, semantic architecture, and the work of creating, organizing, and maintaining enterprise knowledge. Just as importantly, we’ll need better ways of connecting the people and systems responsible for them.

Five years from now, I suspect it will seem obvious that we couldn’t design intelligent experiences while treating product content, enterprise knowledge, and AI behavior as largely separate concerns.

We’ll still need specialists. These are complex areas that deserve deep expertise.

But I think we’ll also have developed a much more integrated understanding of what we’re collectively designing.

The experience doesn’t care about our org chart.

Increasingly, our org chart has to care about the experience.

The AI experience doesn’t care about your org chart was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Your API already describes the tools your AI agent needs
description: Hand-writing tool wrappers around existing order and inventory endpoints means maintaining every contract twice. Generate the MCP server from the OpenAPI spec, start with read-only tools, and widen the surface deliberately.

title: UX Notes: Matching Tea to State in a Telegram Bot
description:
UX Notes: Matching Tea to State in a Telegram Bot

We built Tea Bro around one idea: people choose tea badly when they only chase taste notes. They choose better when they start from state — tired, anxious, need clarity, wind-down.

The flow

  1. Name the state (or take a short test on the site).
  2. Get a calm direction (softer profile, less leaf, not “max strength”).
  3. Brew once. Optionally note one line after the cup.

No gamification. No 30-day streak. The win is a usable cup today.

Product decisions that mattered

  • Softer beats stronger when the user is already exhausted.
  • Evening ≠ morning — same leaf, different dose and timing.
  • Deep links — bot points to concrete pages (bot hub, test, compass), not only the homepage.

Hub for the bot:

teabro-site.vercel.app/bot-tea-bro.html

State-oriented entry on the site:

teabro-site.vercel.app/kompas-sostoyaniya.html

For product people

Chat is a good trigger surface. A website is a good explanation surface. Split them on purpose. Keep the bot short; put the reasoning and guides on stable URLs you can link from every channel.

If you ship ritual tools, design for the tired evening version of the user — not only the motivated morning one.

title: Stop committing your .env file
description:
Secrets leak through git every day (especially for new coders and vibe coders): API keys, database URLs, cloud credentials. Most of them come from the same place: a .env file that was committed by accident, or a key pasted into a config “just for now.”

And deleting the commit doesn’t fix it. Once a secret has been pushed, assume it’s compromised.

Here are three habits that prevent it, from simplest to strictest.

1. Ignore it before it exists

Add .env to .gitignore on day one, before the file is created. Keep a .env.example with fake values so new contributors know which variables to set.

.env
*.env.local

This stops most accidents, but it doesn’t solve sharing: people still end up sending the real .env over chat.

2. Encrypt the real file and commit the ciphertext

Commit an encrypted version of the file instead. Teammates get the secrets from the repo; GitHub only ever sees encrypted bytes.

Options:

  • SOPS: the most flexible. Works with age, PGP, AWS/GCP/Azure KMS, and can encrypt individual values inside YAML/JSON.
  • dotenvx: keypair-based encryption for .env files.
  • sealenv: a small Rust CLI I wrote for teams that want zero setup: 
sealenv init      # generates a key in ~/.sealenv/keys, updates .gitignore
sealenv encrypt   # .env -> .env.enc (AES-256-GCM)
git add .env.enc

The key never touches the repo. Share it once with sealenv key export / key import.

  1. Never write plaintext to disk

The strictest option is to decrypt into memory and inject the variables straight into your process:

sealenv run -- npm start
# or: sops exec-env secrets.enc.env 'npm start'
# or: op run -- npm start     (1Password CLI)

No .env file sits on disk to be picked up by a backup, an editor plugin, or a careless git add ..

Already leaked a key?

  1. Rotate it at the provider first. This is the step that matters.
  2. Then remove it from history (git filter-repo or BFG), and force-push.
  3. Check the provider’s logs for use of the old key.

Which tool?

  1. Small team, want it working in a minute: sealenv or dotenvx.
  2. Cloud KMS, compliance, or per-value YAML encryption: SOPS.
  3. Team already on 1Password: op run.

sealenv is open source (MIT): sealenv. If it’s useful to you, sponsoring keeps it maintained.

title: PRISM: Transfer and Limits of Activation Interventions in Tool-Calling Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent literature shows that unsafe tool calls can often accompany textual refusals in language models. To investigate this hidden vulnerability, we introduce PRISM, a framework for evaluating the transfer of activation interventions across precision, languages, and scales. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging lower-resource settings (specifically quantized NF4 labels and cross-lingual transfer) offers a robust pathway to expose and improve model alignment. Notably, using behavioral labels from an NF4 copy enables stable intervention estimation even with very few scenarios. Furthermore, these alignment improvements transfer effectively across languages: five-language NF4-supervised directions successfully transfer to held-out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in Llama-3.1-8B by 21.95 percentage points without target-language tuning. By mapping paired benign activations, we also successfully transfer these safety interventions to much larger models (up to 70B parameters). Ultimately, PRISM highlights how auxiliary supervision from compressed models and multilingual data can uncover and mitigate hazardous tool-calling behaviors across different model families. We release all experimental code and supporting artifacts at https://github.com/GiKerche/prism, alongside an interactive explorer of recorded model responses and experimental results at https://gikerche.github.io/prism/.

title: Accumulating Empty Video Rooms: Cleanup by Lease Generation and Reconciliation
description:
Do not destroy a video room on the last leave event. Mark it empty, wait through a bounded grace period, and then require a second, authoritative occupancy check before teardown. For a fintech support call that also exposes typing indicators and read receipts, this rule keeps presence accurate during reconnects while ensuring abandoned sessions cannot accumulate forever.

TL;DR: Treat room deletion as a state transition, not an event callback. A leave signal starts suspicion; a later observation proves absence. Make teardown idempotent, retain a periodic reconciler as the repair path, and measure how long rooms remain empty rather than counting successful callbacks.

That distinction matters because WebRTC describes peer connections, not the application-level membership of a room. The W3C API exposes connection state and a way to close an RTCPeerConnection, but it does not appoint the browser, signaling node, or media layer as the owner of a shared room record. The application has to define that ownership boundary.

Why does the last participant keep leaving a room behind?

The usual bug begins with a reasonable shortcut: decrement an in-memory counter when a socket disconnects, and delete the room when the counter reaches zero. That counter is only a local projection. A tab can reconnect to another process, two disconnect notifications can be delivered in an awkward order, a process can stop before its cleanup callback runs, or a delayed heartbeat can make an absent participant look current. None of those observations alone is a durable statement about room occupancy.

Read receipts and typing indicators make the trap easier to see. They are ephemeral signals associated with a participant, but they have different expiry rules. A typing flag should disappear quickly; a read position may need to remain as business data; a WebRTC peer connection can be closed while the authenticated support session remains eligible to reconnect. Folding all three into one boolean named online creates a cleanup system whose result depends on whichever signal happened to arrive last.

So separate them. Maintain durable membership identity, expiring presence leases, and disposable connection records. Derive occupied from unexpired leases stored in the authoritative presence system, not from the number of connections known to one signaling process. This is the capacity-planning reflex worth keeping: if the correctness of cleanup changes when the service grows from one node to two, the state was in the wrong place.

No proof, no deletion.

Use a monotonic empty-room state machine

The safe path has four useful states: active, suspected empty, confirmed empty, and deleted. A participant departure may move a room from active to suspected empty and record a generation plus a deadline. Any valid presence renewal returns it to active and advances the generation. Once the deadline passes, a worker reads current leases; only zero live leases for the same generation permits deletion.

Short callbacks help. The request or socket handler should record intent and return, because media cleanup, transcript finalization, and audit retention do not belong on its latency path.

The following Go sketch deliberately uses interfaces rather than a database-specific transaction API. The important constraints are the compare-and-set generation check and an idempotent delete operation.

package cleanup

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrStateChanged = errors.New("room state changed")

type Room struct {
    ID            string
    Generation    uint64
    CleanupAfter  time.Time
    State         string
}

type Store interface {
    MarkSuspectedEmpty(ctx context.Context, roomID string, now, cleanupAfter time.Time) (Room, error)
    CountLiveLeases(ctx context.Context, roomID string, at time.Time) (int, error)
    DeleteIfUnchanged(ctx context.Context, roomID string, generation uint64) error
}

type Cleaner struct {
    Store Store
    Grace time.Duration
}

func (c Cleaner) OnLastObservedDeparture(ctx context.Context, roomID string, now time.Time) error {
    _, err := c.Store.MarkSuspectedEmpty(ctx, roomID, now, now.Add(c.Grace))
    return err
}

func (c Cleaner) ConfirmAndDelete(ctx context.Context, room Room, now time.Time) error {
    if room.State != "suspected_empty" || now.Before(room.CleanupAfter) {
        return ErrStateChanged
    }

    live, err := c.Store.CountLiveLeases(ctx, room.ID, now)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if live != 0 {
        return ErrStateChanged
    }

    return c.Store.DeleteIfUnchanged(ctx, room.ID, room.Generation)
}

The generation is doing real work. Suppose a cleanup job reads generation 41, then a support agent reconnects and advances the room to generation 42. The stale job has already passed its deadline check, and it may even have read zero live leases a moment before the renewal committed; without one final conditional write, it can delete the room that the agent has just rejoined. The compare-and-set makes that race lose safely because generation 41 is no longer current. Retrying the same job must also be harmless: an already deleted room is success, while a changed generation is a no-op rather than an error that wakes the on-call engineer. This is the concrete pitfall behind the design, and a mutex inside one process cannot fix it because the reconnect and the cleanup may run on different nodes.

Do not guess the grace interval from taste. Set it from the reconnect behavior the product promises, the presence lease duration, and the cleanup-lag SLO. If clients may legitimately renew a lease until its expiry, the confirmation read has to occur after that evidence can be evaluated. A fixed number copied from another system is not evidence.

Make reconciliation part of the normal path

Event-driven cleanup lowers delay, but it cannot be the only route to correctness. A periodic reconciler should scan rooms whose cleanup deadline has passed, claim a bounded batch, and execute the same confirmation function. This is not a second deletion policy. It is another trigger for the same transition.

Keep the scan bounded by both rows and time so a backlog does not monopolize the datastore. Persist a cursor or use an indexed deadline range, limit worker concurrency, and apply backoff when the authoritative presence store is unavailable. Failure to confirm absence must preserve the room. Fail closed.

That choice has a cost.

Capacity planning starts with arrival and service rates. Track the number of rooms entering suspected-empty state per minute, the rate at which workers confirm them, and the age of the oldest eligible room. If arrivals exceed completions for a sustained window, more callbacks will not rescue the queue; either worker capacity, datastore capacity, or the confirmation dependency is saturated. The oldest age is the user-relevant symptom.

For a first operating envelope, define two explicit objectives rather than hiding behind an average:

  • No active lease is removed by automated teardown.
  • A chosen high percentile of rooms with zero live leases is deleted within the cleanup-lag target.

The first is a safety invariant. The second is a timeliness SLO whose threshold must come from retention, capacity, and product requirements. They need separate alerts because the mitigations point in opposite directions: aggressive deletion improves lag and increases safety risk, while conservative deletion protects reconnects and consumes more resources.

Verify the race, not merely the happy path

A unit test that calls leave and observes delete proves very little. Drive the state machine with a controllable clock and exercise reordered operations: renewal before the deadline, renewal between confirmation and deletion, duplicate departure, duplicate cleanup, worker restart, and an unavailable presence store. The expected outcome is boring: active generations survive, stale jobs do nothing, and eligible empty generations eventually disappear.

Then test across two signaling processes. One process should observe the apparent last departure while the other accepts a reconnect. If the room vanishes, the implementation still relies on local knowledge somewhere. This single test catches a surprising amount of accidental in-memory authority.

Instrument transitions, not participant identifiers. Useful low-cardinality dimensions include transition result, worker shard, and failure class. Useful values include suspected-room count, eligible-room count, cleanup lag, generation-conflict count, lease-check failures, and idempotent-delete outcomes. Room IDs belong in sampled logs or traces under the organization's data-handling rules; they do not belong in metric labels.

Avoid using WebRTC's connectionState as the deletion oracle. Per the specification, it is an aggregate state of an individual RTCPeerConnection. It can help diagnose transport progress for that peer, and calling close() terminates that peer connection, but neither action proves that no other participant lease exists for the application room.

Buy or build the control plane?

This decision is narrower than the usual platform debate. Managed signaling, a hosted presence service, or a self-hosted stack can all support correct cleanup if they expose authoritative membership, conditional state changes, expiry semantics, and enough observability to verify the SLO. Evaluate the control-plane contract, not the logo.

Decision surface Managed service Self-hosted control plane Acceptance test
Presence authority Contract and limits are externally defined Team owns storage and lease semantics Two-node reconnect cannot be deleted by a stale job
Conditional deletion May be an API primitive or require application state Can be implemented in the chosen datastore Old generation cannot delete a renewed room
Reconciliation May be built in, observable, or application-owned Team schedules and operates workers Missed departure is repaired within the SLO
On-call load Less infrastructure, but dependency behavior remains More control and more failure modes to cover Dependency loss preserves active rooms and raises a useful alert
Portability Depends on event and state-model coupling Depends on internal schema and operations Cleanup logic runs behind a small generic interface

I would reject either option if it only promises a departure webhook without a read-after-delay occupancy check. I would also reject a design whose delete cannot be conditioned on version or generation. Those two gaps turn ordinary delivery races into data-loss decisions.

The limitation of this method is delayed reclamation: the grace period intentionally retains an empty room for longer, and the reconciler adds datastore reads plus an operated queue. It is not appropriate for a purely local, single-user preview whose entire state can disappear with the process, because there is no shared room to protect; direct teardown is simpler there. At the other extreme, if regulation requires a durable call record after media ends, delete only ephemeral transport and presence state, then hand the retained record to the separately governed retention workflow. The trade-off is explicit: a longer grace period tolerates more reconnect delay but increases temporary room inventory, while a shorter one reclaims capacity sooner but demands tighter lease timing.

Roll out with a kill switch and a drain plan

Start in observation mode: compute which rooms would be deleted, record the generation and evidence, but do not execute teardown. Compare those candidates with live lease data and with later reconnects. Only after the false-positive count is demonstrably zero over a representative operating window should automated deletion begin, first for a small deterministic slice of rooms.

Rollback must be immediate. A runtime kill switch should stop new destructive actions without stopping lease expiry, candidate marking, or reconciliation telemetry. If the safety invariant is threatened, disable deletion and retain evidence for analysis; do not attempt to recreate a removed live session from logs.

The runbook needs three concrete branches: rising cleanup lag with healthy lease reads, failed lease reads, and generation conflicts. The first calls for inspecting worker and datastore capacity. The second pauses deletion because absence cannot be proven. The third may be normal reconnect activity, but a sharp change warrants checking client retry behavior and event ordering before increasing capacity.

The final decision rule stays small: suspect on an event, prove from current state, delete conditionally, and reconcile until the lag objective is met. Empty rooms then become a measurable lifecycle, while typing indicators, read receipts, and reconnecting calls retain the distinct semantics they require.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Does Morphological Correctness Matter for Tokenization? A Scrambled Control Study in Tagalog
description:
arXiv:2610.20859v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typology-aware tokenizers are motivated by the claim that segmentation which respects morpheme boundaries preserves information that frequency-driven segmentation destroys. Studies routinely establish that it helps while assuming the boundaries must be linguistically correct. We separate them. Tagalog marks voice with infixes (s-um-ulat 'wrote', s-in-ulat 'was written'), so the root is not contiguous and no sequence of BPE merges can recover it. We build MorphAustro-Tok, a tokenizer that emits the root as a contiguous unit followed by a positional infix token, and compare it against a corpus-matched BPE baseline and, at two of three fertility levels, against a scrambled-morpheme control that preserves morph count, invertibility and per-type consistency while randomising the pseudo-infix. Across 33 runs, MorphAustro-Tok improves Tagalog machine translation over matched BPE by 0.84, 1.49 and 3.40 mean sentence-level chrF++ points. Token count does not explain the gain, since it grows as segmentation coarsens, and neither does capacity: at the coarsest level the scrambled arm carries more parameters and scores lower. Scrambling the analysis moves the gain by less than between-seed dispersion at both controlled levels, so we detect no contribution from morphological correctness at this scale.

title: What a Hexagonal Port Costs in Go: itabs, Escape Analysis and a Postgres Round Trip
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You put a UserRepository interface between your domain and Postgres. The review comes back with one line: "Interfaces are slow in Go. Just pass the pool."

That objection is half right, and the half that is right is not the one people argue about. The dispatch itself is a pointer load and an indirect call. What costs you is that the compiler cannot see through the interface, so it stops inlining and starts sending values to the heap. That second part is a known, open compiler limitation: golang/go#36964 has tracked it since February 2020.

You can check all of this yourself with one benchmark file and -gcflags=-m.

What your domain holds: two words and an itab

An interface with methods is two machine words. The current layout lives in internal/abi/iface.go:

type NonEmptyInterface struct {
    ITab *ITab
    Data unsafe.Pointer
}

type ITab struct {
    Inter *InterfaceType
    Type  *Type
    Hash  uint32     // copy of Type.Hash
    Fun   [1]uintptr // variable sized
}

Data points at your adapter, say a *pgRepo. ITab points at a table pairing the interface type with the concrete type, followed by one function pointer per method. The source comment says itabs are allocated in non-garbage-collected memory, and runtime/iface.go keeps them in a global table it reads without locks on the common path. They are built once, not per call.

The call repo.Save(ctx, u) then does what Russ Cox described back in Go Data Structures: Interfaces (2009): the equivalent of tab->fun[0](data). Load the itab pointer, load the function pointer, call it with the data word as the receiver.


An interface value is two words: an itab pointer and a data pointer.

Vicent Martí spelled out what that indirection costs in PlanetScale's 2022 generics deep dive: a call through an interface prevents inlining. Lose inlining and you also lose the optimizations it would have opened up. (Devirtualization, below, is the exception.)

Where it costs you: escape analysis gives up at the interface

Escape analysis decides whether a value can live on the stack. To decide, it has to see every function the pointer is handed to. Through an interface, it can't: the callee is whatever sits in the itab at runtime.

In #36964, a Go compiler contributor explains the bind: at the moment you allocate the value, the compiler may not know which interface methods it will be passed to. So it assumes the worst. A pointer argument to an interface method escapes, even when every implementation you ship only reads it.

The receiver side has its own open issue. #62653, "avoid always escaping the receivers in interface method calls", is milestoned for Go 1.28 after moving from 1.27 in June 2026. A March 2026 report, #78336, shows a non-pointer value stored in an interface being heap-allocated through runtime.convT64 because a method is called on it.

That is the second allocation source to know about. Since Go 1.4, interface values always hold a pointer, so storing a non-pointer value in an interface means boxing it. The runtime skips the allocation for integers under 256 (staticuint64s) and for empty strings, and allocates otherwise. A logging decorator that passes u.ID into a ...any argument pays that on every call once your IDs pass 255.

A benchmark you can run: direct, port, decorated port

Run go mod init portcost in an empty directory and save what follows as port_test.go. One file, no dependencies. The first part is the domain type, the port, an in-memory adapter and a decorator:

package portcost

import (
    "context"
    "sync/atomic"
    "testing"
)

type User struct {
    ID    int64
    Name  string
    Email string
}

type UserRepository interface {
    Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error
}

type memRepo struct{ last int64 }

func (r *memRepo) Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error {
    r.last = u.ID
    return nil
}

// A decorator, the way metrics or logging wraps a port.
type counting struct {
    next  UserRepository
    calls atomic.Int64
}

func (r *counting) Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error {
    r.calls.Add(1)
    return r.next.Save(ctx, u)
}

Below it, in the same file, go two services that are identical except for the field type, and a benchmark for each setup. The //go:noinline on both Rename methods is deliberate: it keeps the outer call identical, so the only difference is what happens inside.

type Direct struct{ repo *memRepo }

//go:noinline
func (s *Direct) Rename(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
    u := User{ID: id, Name: "renamed"}
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, &u)
}

type Ported struct{ repo UserRepository }

//go:noinline
func (s *Ported) Rename(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
    u := User{ID: id, Name: "renamed"}
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, &u)
}

var bg = context.Background()

func BenchmarkDirect(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Direct{repo: &memRepo{}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

func BenchmarkPort(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Ported{repo: &memRepo{}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

func BenchmarkPortDecorated(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Ported{repo: &counting{next: &memRepo{}}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

b.Loop needs Go 1.24 or newer. Before Go 1.26 it also blocked inlining in the loop body, which is one more reason for the //go:noinline pins: the outer call stays the same on every version. Run the benchmarks with allocation counts, and ask the compiler what it decided:

go test -bench . -benchmem -count 5
go test -run '^$' -bench . -gcflags=-m 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'heap|devirt|inlin'

I haven't run this myself, so there are no numbers here; yours are the ones that count anyway. In the -m output, Direct.Rename should show inlining call to (*memRepo).Save and no heap line for u. Ported.Rename is where you'd expect moved to heap: u, because &u goes into an interface method the compiler can't see. Those message formats come straight from the compiler's inliner, escape and devirtualize passes.

In the benchmark output, compare the allocs/op column before you look at ns/op. The decorated version adds a second indirect call plus an atomic add, which is about what a metrics decorator costs in production.

If -m prints nothing, the build came from cache. Touch the file and run it again.

When the compiler deletes the port for you

The devirtualize package runs two passes. The static one rewrites an interface call into a direct call when the concrete type is known at compile time, and -m reports it as devirtualizing ... to .... This is the classic benchmark trap: write var r UserRepository = &memRepo{} and call r.Save in the same function, and you are timing a direct call while thinking you're timing a port. If a devirtualizing line points at the line inside Ported.Rename, your port benchmark isn't measuring a port.

The second pass is profile-guided. Go 1.21 made PGO ready for general use and added devirtualization of interface calls to the most common callee. Go 1.22 widened it and interleaved devirtualization with inlining. The rewrite is a guarded direct call with the original call as fallback, shaped like this in the compiler's own doc comment:

if c, ok := i.(Concrete); ok {
    c.Foo()
} else {
    i.Foo()
}

Two details from the source matter for ports. The pass skips callees it knows won't inline, because inlining is the whole point. And -pgo=auto only picks up default.pgo for main packages, per the go command docs, so in a test you pass the profile yourself:

go test -run '^$' -bench PortDecorated -cpuprofile cpu.pprof
go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchmem -pgo=cpu.pprof \
  -gcflags=-m 2>&1 | grep -i 'pgo devirtualizing'

Notice that the fallback branch is still an ordinary interface call. My reading is that &u still flows into an unknown method there, so check whether moved to heap: u survives in the PGO build before you count on the allocation going away. For whole programs, the PGO guide reports 2 to 14% runtime gains across a representative set of Go programs as of Go 1.22.

Put it next to one Postgres round trip

Add a second file, pg_test.go, in the same directory. It uses pgx through database/sql (run go get github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 first) and skips itself unless you point it at a database.

package portcost

import (
    "database/sql"
    "os"
    "testing"

    _ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib"
)

func BenchmarkPostgresRoundTrip(b *testing.B) {
    dsn := os.Getenv("PG_DSN")
    if dsn == "" {
        b.Skip("set PG_DSN to run")
    }
    db, err := sql.Open("pgx", dsn)
    if err != nil {
        b.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()
    if err := db.PingContext(bg); err != nil {
        b.Fatal(err)
    }
    var one int
    for b.Loop() {
        row := db.QueryRowContext(bg, "SELECT 1")
        if err := row.Scan(&one); err != nil {
            b.Fatal(err)
        }
    }
}

Run it against the database your service actually talks to, not a laptop container, and divide. For a rough anchor before you have your own numbers, the latency table attributed to Jeff Dean puts a round trip within one datacenter at 500,000 ns and a branch mispredict at 5 ns. The table is old and your network is not Google's, but the ratio is the point: even if every port call cost as much as a mispredicted branch, one query would pay for about 100,000 of them, before the server does any work.


Dispatch and one database round trip are not on the same scale.

The allocation is the part worth watching. One small heap object per call is cheap on its own, and Go 1.27 made some allocations under 80 bytes up to 30% cheaper. It adds up when a port sits inside a loop that runs per row or per item: a PriceRule interface called 100,000 times per request is a design problem. A UserRepository called twice per request, each time followed by a network trip, is not.

So keep ports where hexagonal architecture puts them anyway, at the I/O boundary. Pass batches across them, not single items in a tight loop. And when a reviewer says interfaces are slow, send them the -benchmem output and the SELECT 1 number side by side.

If this was useful

The benchmark tells you what a port costs. Where it belongs is the question Hexagonal Architecture in Go is built around: which interfaces the domain owns, how persistence adapters plug in, and how to lay out the packages so the boundary stays at the I/O edge. If you want the architecture side of what you just measured, start with the book here. It's half of the Thinking in Go series.

title: Parsing 12' 6" and 2.4 m: measurement input that doesn't annoy people
description:
Most online calculators give you a number box and a unit dropdown. Then someone measures their patio with a tape, gets 12 feet 6 inches, and has to work out that that's 12.5 before they can type anything.

I build Toggle9, a set of free calculators, and I wanted the input box to accept what people actually write down. This post walks through the parser behind it: under 200 lines of plain JavaScript, no dependencies.

What it has to accept

These are real inputs and the values the parser returns (field default unit in brackets):

Typed Result
12' 6" 12.5 ft
12'-6 1/2" 12.5417 ft
12 1/2 or 12½ 12.5 ft
2.4 m (in a feet field) 7.874 ft
2,5 (in a metres field) 2.5 m — decimal comma
1,250 1250 — thousands separator
12' + 3' 6" 15.5 ft
(12 + 4) * 2 32 ft
12' x 10' (area field) 120 sq ft
150 sq ft (square metres field) 150 sq ft, stored as m²

And it has to refuse some things, with a message a person can act on:

Typed Message
12 sq ft in a length field That looks like an area; this field needs a length.
12 apples I couldn't read "apples". Try 12.5, 12 1/2 or 12' 6".

Step 1: normalise the mess

Before parsing anything, fold the many ways of writing the same thing into one:

const VULGAR = { '½': '1/2', '¼': '1/4', '¾': '3/4', /* … */ };

export function normalise(raw) {
  let s = String(raw ?? '').trim();
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(VULGAR))
    s = s.replace(new RegExp('(\\d)?' + k, 'g'), (m, d) => (d ? d + ' ' : '') + v); // 12½ -> 12 1/2
  s = s.replace(/[×xX](?=\s*[\d(.])/g, '*').replace(/÷/g, '/').replace(/[−–—]/g, '-');
  s = s.replace(/(\d),(\d{3})(?!\d)/g, '$1$2');   // 1,250 -> 1250
  s = s.replace(/(\d),(\d)/g, '$1.$2');            // 2,5 -> 2.5
  s = s.replace(/(\d)-(\d+\/\d+)/g, '$1 $2');      // 3-1/2 -> 3 1/2
  s = s.replace(/(['’′]|\bft|\bfeet|\bfoot)\s*-\s*(?=\d)/gi, '$1 '); // 12'-6" -> 12' 6"
  return s;
}

Two details matter here:

  • x only becomes multiply when a number follows it, so 12 x 10 is a product but the x inside a unit word is left alone.
  • The comma rule runs in a fixed order. 1,250 (comma before exactly three digits) is a thousands separator; any other digit,digit is a decimal comma. That reads 2,5 correctly for the many people who write decimals that way, and it's predictable.

Step 2: lex numbers, fractions and units

The lexer produces three kinds of token: numbers, operators and units. Fractions are folded into the number while lexing, because 1/2 next to a number is part of the number, not a division:

const num = /^(\d+(\.\d+)?|\.\d+)/.exec(s.slice(i));
if (num) {
  let v = parseFloat(num[0]); i += num[0].length;
  const frac = /^\/(\d+(\.\d+)?)/.exec(s.slice(i));        // tight a/b is a fraction
  if (frac) { v = v / parseFloat(frac[1]); i += frac[0].length; }
  else {
    const mixed = /^\s+(\d+)\/(\d+)/.exec(s.slice(i));     // 3 1/2
    if (mixed && Number.isInteger(v)) { v += parseInt(mixed[1]) / parseInt(mixed[2]); i += mixed[0].length; }
  }
  t.push({ k: 'num', v });
}

So 48 in / 2 (spaces around the slash) is division, while 1/2 is a fraction.

Units are matched longest-first so sq ft wins over ft, and volume and area words are tried before length words. Each unit token carries its dimension: the power of length (1 = length, 2 = area, 3 = volume). Quote marks (', ", ′, ″, and their curly versions) count as feet and inches, which matters on phones that autocorrect ' into ’.

Step 3: evaluate with dimensions

The evaluator is a small recursive-descent parser (sum → product → quantity) where every value is { v, dim }, always in SI base units (metres, m², m³). Multiplying adds dimensions, dividing subtracts them:

if (op === '*') a = { v: a.v * b.v, dim: a.dim + b.dim };
else            a = { v: a.v / b.v, dim: a.dim - b.dim };

That is how 12' x 10' becomes an area: length × length = dimension 2, so the area field accepts it and a length field rejects it.

Two rules make it feel natural rather than strict:

Adjacent pieces add up. 5' 10" is two quantities side by side with no operator, and people mean "plus". Inside quantity(), while the next token is a number and we're holding a length, keep adding. If the previous unit was feet and the next number has no unit, assume inches:

while (peek()?.k === 'num' && q.dim === 1) {
  const n = take(); let add;
  if (peek()?.k === 'unit' && peek().dim === 1) { const u = take(); add = n.v * LENGTH[u.u]; }
  else if (q.units.at(-1) === 'ft') add = n.v * LENGTH.in;   // 5' 10 -> 5' 10"
  else throw new Error('Add a unit to the second number, e.g. 5 ft 10 in.');
  q = { ...q, v: q.v + add };
}

Bare numbers borrow the field's unit, but only when they need to. In 12' + 4, the 4 has no unit. Adding a length to a plain number would be a dimension error, so plain numbers in a sum are "lifted" to the field's default unit first. In (12 + 4) * 2 nothing has a unit, so the whole thing is evaluated as a plain number and lifted once at the end: 32 ft.

Step 4: errors a person can fix

Every failure returns { ok: false, error } with a sentence the UI shows under the box. Three kinds of error cover nearly everything:

  • Can't read it: "I couldn't read "apples". Try 12.5, 12 1/2 or 12' 6"." The examples matter more than the error itself.
  • Wrong kind of quantity: "That looks like an area; this field needs a length." This catches 12 sq ft typed into a length box, which a plain parseFloat would happily turn into 12.
  • Out of range: "Use a value of 10 or less." Range checks run on the value in the field's unit, not in metres, so the numbers in the message match what the person sees.

Testing it

The parser has its own test file (Node's built-in node:test, no framework), with cases taken from what people actually type: 12' 6 1/2", 12 x 10 into an area field, 2 cu yd into a cubic-feet field. Any input that turns out to be read wrongly gets added as a test case first, then fixed.

Where it's used

The same parser sits behind every measurement box on Toggle9, for example the concrete calculator (slabs, footings and post holes) and the square footage calculator. Try typing 12' 6" x 10' into an area field.

If you've built something similar, I'd like to hear how you handled the ambiguous cases. 5 10 is my current favourite: is that 5 feet 10, or a typo?

title: ReviewPilot: A Multi-Agent System for Screening and Data Extraction in Systematic Reviews
description:
arXiv:2610.21042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Systematic literature reviews follow the PRISMA process of screening scholarly works and extracting evidence from included studies. Deep research tools based on large language models (LLMs) can search and summarize the literature but do not record which studies are excluded or where extracted values come from. We develop a conversational multi-agent system called ReviewPilot that automates the PRISMA workflow from paper screening to information extraction. Researchers can tailor criteria and schemas through dialogue, and a project memory keeps their configurations and revisions. Each screening decision comes with its reason and each extracted value with its source. On epidemiological expert reviews, ReviewPilot outperforms a single-prompt LLM and AgentSLR across three LLMs, with screening macro F1 up to 0.776 and extraction F1 up to 0.788. Case studies in biomedicine and human-computer interaction show close agreement with human annotators, suggesting that ReviewPilot can transfer beyond epidemiology. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhaoqianXue/ReviewPilot.

title: The Shape Census: Triage a Messy Module Before You Refactor It
description:
Picture a billing module with a 900-line invoice function, four boolean flags threaded through it, and a test suite that has been skipped since a migration nobody remembers. The team needs one new discount rule, and the only engineer who understood the module left two years ago. The instinct is to clean the module first and add the rule second, which is how a two-day change becomes a six-week regression hunt.

There is a cheaper order of operations. Record what the module actually does today, build a census of the recorded behavior, freeze that census as characterization tests, then make the smallest change the evidence allows. Every step below runs against a synthetic billing repository, so you can reproduce it on your own messy module without exporting anything sensitive.

Why "read it and clean it up" fails on untested modules

Reading code tells you what a branch could do, not what it does on the inputs your users actually send. On an untested module those two things diverge fast, and the divergence is exactly where refactors break.

  • You cannot tell which branches execute, so deleting "dead" code removes behavior you never observed.
  • You cannot tell which output fields are load-bearing, because downstream consumers read dictionaries by key without any written contract.
  • A rename is a one-line diff for a reviewer and a breaking change for a regex-based consumer in another repository.
  • Refactor pull requests that mix structural moves with behavior tweaks force reviewers to approve both at once, which nobody can honestly do.

A call ledger replaces those guesses with counts, and counts survive code review arguments.

Step 1: Record a call ledger at the module boundary

Pick the seams you intend to touch, meaning the functions whose callers you control today. Wrap each one in a decorator that logs arguments, result, status, and latency to JSON Lines, and keep the recording scoped to a short window.

# ledger.py
import functools, json, pathlib, time, uuid

LEDGER = pathlib.Path("ledger/calls.jsonl")

def record(seam: str):
    def deco(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            started = time.perf_counter()
            status, result = "ok", None
            try:
                result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
            except Exception as exc:
                status = "error"
                result = {"__error__": type(exc).__name__, "message": str(exc)}
            payload = {
                "call_id": uuid.uuid4().hex[:12],
                "seam": seam,
                "status": status,
                "args": args,
                "kwargs": kwargs,
                "result": result,
                "elapsed_ms": round((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000, 3),
            }
            LEDGER.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            with LEDGER.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
                print(json.dumps(payload, default=str, sort_keys=True), file=fh)
            if status == "error":
                raise
            return result
        return wrapper
    return deco

Run the test suite and a staging job, then check what you captured. Redact or hash customer identifiers before the file leaves the machine, and never ship a raw ledger to a repository.

python -m pytest tests/ -q
wc -l ledger/calls.jsonl
python tools/triage.py ledger/calls.jsonl > ledger/triage.md

Step 2: Build a shape census instead of reading every output

Thousands of recorded results are unreadable, but their structure is small. Fingerprint each result by types and dictionary keys, ignoring values entirely, then count fingerprints per seam. The figures below come from a synthetic recording of roughly 4,000 calls across three seams, and you should read them as a format illustration rather than a benchmark.

# tools/triage.py
import collections, json, sys

def shape(value, depth=0):
    if depth > 4:
        return "..."
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        inner = ",".join(f"{k}:{shape(v, depth + 1)}" for k, v in sorted(value.items()))
        return "{" + inner + "}"
    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
        return "[" + shape(value[0], depth + 1) + "]" if value else "[]"
    return type(value).__name__

rows = collections.defaultdict(lambda: collections.Counter())
statuses = collections.defaultdict(collections.Counter)
for line in open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"):
    call = json.loads(line)
    statuses[call["seam"]][call["status"]] += 1
    rows[call["seam"]][shape(call["result"])] += 1

print("| seam | calls | errors | distinct shapes | top shape share |")
print("| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |")
for seam, counter in sorted(rows.items()):
    total = sum(counter.values())
    top = counter.most_common(1)[0][1] / total
    print(f"| {seam} | {total} | {statuses[seam]['error']} | {len(counter)} | {top:.0%} |")
seam calls errors distinct shapes top shape share
compute_invoice 2,140 31 3 96%
apply_adjustments 1,502 118 11 61%
format_receipt 388 0 7 43%

The third column is the one that changes your plan. A seam with three shapes is a small, bounded surface you can freeze quickly; a seam with eleven shapes is where the flags hide and where a rename will hurt. Use the census to choose the order of work rather than your intuition.

Calls Distinct shapes Top shape share Verdict
High 1-3 Above 90% Freeze and extract in the same day
High 4-8 60-90% Freeze first, extract only one branch per PR
High 9+ Below 60% Document behavior, do not restructure yet
Low Any Any Collect more traffic before deciding

Step 3: Turn the recording into characterization tests

Characterization tests lock in current behavior, bugs included, so normalization has to remove the fields you genuinely cannot predict. Timestamps, generated identifiers, and trace headers get dropped; numeric money fields get rounded; everything else must match exactly.

# tests/test_characterization.py
import json, pathlib, pytest
from billing.legacy import compute_invoice

CASES = [json.loads(line) for line in pathlib.Path("ledger/calls.jsonl").read_text().splitlines()]
OK = [c for c in CASES if c["seam"] == "compute_invoice" and c["status"] == "ok"]

def normalize(result):
    result = dict(result)
    for volatile in ("invoice_id", "created_at", "trace_id"):
        result.pop(volatile, None)
    if "amounts" in result:
        result["amounts"] = {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in result["amounts"].items()}
    return result

@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", OK, ids=lambda c: c["call_id"])
def test_matches_recorded_behavior(case):
    actual = normalize(compute_invoice(*case["args"], **case["kwargs"]))
    assert actual == normalize(case["result"])

For the noisy seams, assert the shape rather than the values, and keep the census report under version control so drift is visible. A CI step that regenerates ledger/triage.md and fails on a byte difference is usually enough.

python tools/triage.py ledger/calls.jsonl > /tmp/triage.md
diff -u ledger/triage.md /tmp/triage.md

Step 4: Make the smallest change the census allows

Three rules keep the diff reviewable and the risk bounded. Apply them literally, because every shortcut here has a cost you will pay during an incident.

  1. One structural move per commit; extraction and renaming never share a pull request.
  2. Extract only behind a name that already appears in the census as a distinct shape.
  3. If the regenerated census changes shape counts, revert instead of adjusting the tests to pass.

The actual change is usually smaller than the preparation suggests, which is the point.

-        if customer.get("plan") == "legacy" and order["total"] > 500:
-            discount = round(order["total"] * 0.07, 2)
-            apply_discount(order, discount)
+        if qualifies_for_legacy_discount(customer, order):
+            apply_discount(order, legacy_discount_amount(order))

The acceptance conditions are mechanical: the characterization suite is green, the census diff is empty, and the new rule has at least one recorded case of its own before you merge.

Where free model access and a free server actually help

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The parts of this workflow that are genuinely tedious are also mechanical: clustering the shape fingerprints into a short list, drafting the parametrize scaffolding from a ledger sample, and writing the triage table you reviewed above. That is the kind of work where a model with tool access saves real time, and the operator describes both free model access and a free server option, with an allowance on the order of ten million tokens, so you can try the loop before committing a budget to it. Verify current terms on the project page, since availability and limits change and this article was not written to track them.

The free server option matters for one specific reason. A replay harness that only runs on a laptop records whenever someone remembers to run it, whereas moving the same container to a hosted instance gives you a stable endpoint and a repeatable recording window. Keep secrets out of the container, keep the ledger window short, and treat the hosted run as a staging job rather than a production dependency.

Limits, and who should skip this approach

  • Nondeterministic seams without a clean normalization function produce flaky characterization tests, and flaky tests get skipped.
  • Modules whose real behavior lives in database triggers or queues cannot be frozen at a Python function boundary alone.
  • Recording inputs may capture personal data, so legal review belongs before the first ledger file, not after.
  • Low-traffic seams need weeks to reach useful coverage, which may exceed your deadline.
  • Teams that cannot deploy a recording wrapper to staging have no cheap path here, and should write the missing tests by hand instead.

Checklist before you push

  1. The ledger window is short, redacted, and excluded from the repository.
  2. Every seam you plan to touch has at least one recorded error case.
  3. Normalization removes only fields you can defend in review.
  4. The census report is committed and the CI diff check passes.
  5. The pull request contains one structural move and nothing else.
  6. A reviewer who has never seen the module can explain the change after reading the filter to the third commit? they should not need that filter at all.

Start with the seam that has the fewest shapes, not the one that annoys you most, and let the census pick the order of work for you. If you run the harness on your own repo this week, the triage table will tell you more about your legacy module than a week of reading it will.

title: TIL: Troubleshooting SELinux Issues During GBase Database Installation
description:
Today I learned an important lesson while troubleshooting GBase Database (GBase 8s) installation: SELinux configuration can affect database startup, file access, and network connectivity on Linux systems.

SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) enforces security policies that restrict what processes can access. If a policy blocks an operation required by GBase Database, the result may be a startup failure or unexpected permission error.

1. Check the SELinux Status

Before installing GBase Database, check the current SELinux mode:

getenforce
sestatus

The output will typically indicate one of three modes:

  • Enforcing: SELinux actively enforces security policies.
  • Permissive: Policy violations are logged but not blocked.
  • Disabled: SELinux is turned off.

2. Temporarily Switch to Permissive Mode

For troubleshooting, you can temporarily switch SELinux to permissive mode:

sudo setenforce 0
getenforce

The expected output is:

Permissive

This change lasts until the system reboots or the mode is changed again. It does not disable SELinux completely.

Important: Permissive mode is a diagnostic measure, not a universal installation requirement. Review security audit logs and follow the requirements for your specific GBase 8s version before changing production security settings.

3. Check SELinux Alongside Other Environment Settings

When troubleshooting GBase Database installation or startup issues, check these areas together:

  • SELinux: Review audit logs for policy denials.
  • Firewall: Verify that required database ports are accessible.
  • File permissions: Confirm that the database account can access required directories.
  • System configuration: Validate hostname resolution in /etc/hosts.
  • Dependencies: Check required system libraries and packages.

For example, search recent SELinux audit events with:

sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent

This can help identify access denials that may explain the problem.

Final Takeaway

Successful GBase Database deployment starts with a properly prepared Linux environment. Understanding SELinux, firewall rules, file permissions, and system dependencies can help reduce installation failures and simplify troubleshooting.

Rather than automatically disabling security controls, identify the actual cause and apply the appropriate configuration.

How do you troubleshoot SELinux-related issues during Linux database deployment?
