title: Probe-and-Resume: When and How to Evaluate Agent Execution
description:
arXiv:2610.21088v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time search can improve agent performance by exploring alternative actions and using a critic to select promising branches. We study this approach in terminal-based computer-use environments, which expose only a partial view of a large underlying state, and find that the Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) configuration we evaluate does not significantly improve task success. We identify two sources of poor critic performance: the agent's observations omit environment state needed for evaluation, and intermediate states offer limited evidence of whether a trajectory will succeed. At intermediate states, critics rank continuations only modestly better than chance, and environment access improves this little. We study when to invoke a critic and what access to give it to evaluate a node. Our findings motivate a policy that invokes the critic only at nodes the agent believes are final, rather than during partial progress. Further, the policy gives the critic read, write, and execute access to a fork of the computer's current and initial state, allowing it to probe and perform potentially destructive actions to surface any hidden state the trajectory omits. We call the resulting design Probe-and-Resume: when the agent claims to be done, the critic probes a fork of its state, and a rejected agent resumes where it stopped. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, this raises success by 8.4 percentage points over MCTS with conventional critics, and approaches the success rate of the Codex CLI agent with the same underlying model at less than half its cost.

title: O-RAN-Native Jamming Detection Under Network Heterogeneity
description:
arXiv:2610.20816v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Radio-frequency jamming threatens cellular network operations in contested environments. The Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture exposes per-User Equipment (UE) telemetry through the E2 interface, enabling Key Performance Indicator (KPI)-based jamming detection without proprietary hardware. However, operational deployment demands detection methods that generalize across heterogeneous networks. We propose a Statistical Ensemble Method (SEM) combining adaptive Median Absolute Deviation (MAD)-based baseline detection, count-based anomaly detection, and abrupt change detection through a weighted voting system. SEM operates in two modes: a cold-start mode requiring no labeled data for immediate deployment, and a supervised mode where parameters are refined offline via grid search as labeled data accumulates. We evaluate SEM against five machine learning (ML) classifiers and five deep learning (DL) sequence models using approximately 25 hours of testbed data comprising logs from eight heterogeneous 5G environments, employing both single-environment and multi-environment leave-one-out (LOO) validation. Our analysis indicates that under conditions not encountered during training (distribution shift), learning-based models tend to lose recall and miss jamming events, whereas SEM, even in cold-start mode, maintains detection capabilities at the cost of false alarms. Furthermore, SEM's parameter optimization can be mapped to O-RAN's Non-RT RIC as an rApp for continuous refinement, allowing operators to transition to learning-based alternatives once corpus coverage is sufficient.

title: Wrong Votes, Right Gradients: Why Majority-Vote Rewards Track Verifiable RL
description:
arXiv:2610.20898v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with self-generated labels, such as majority vote over a model's own samples, often recovers most of the gain of training with verifiable rewards. This is puzzling from the usual prompt-level view, in which majority vote only returns a model's modal answer and cannot add information about correctness. We argue that the relevant unit is the batch-level update. Because parameters are shared, a prompt's own gradient accounts for less than 1\% of the change in that prompt's output at practical batch sizes, so a wrong label matters only to the extent that label errors share a direction across prompts. We decompose the majority-vote update into shrinkage and misdirection relative to the gold update, and show that misdirection vanishes with batch size whenever errors are incoherent across prompts, however often the labels are wrong. Measuring per-response gradients on five models, we find that majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, that the majority-vote update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other, and that its noise-corrected cosine with the gold update is 1 within error. Randomly flipping up to 30\% of gold labels leaves the update direction intact, while the same fraction flipped by a shared rule destroys it, and rewards that favor a kind of response on every prompt, such as a learned reward model, fall measurably short. The equivalence holds at every checkpoint we examine but is local: gold-reward training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy. Error coherence, not error rate, determines when self-generated labels can stand in for verification.

title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation
description:
arXiv:2610.21304v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.

title: Managing the Relationship with Service Providers: How Easy Is It?
description:
Managing the Relationship with Service Providers: How Easy Is It?

Most engineering organizations depend on service providers more than they admit. Cloud platforms, payment processors, SaaS tools, managed support teams, outsourced development partners, and staffing firms now sit inside the critical path of many products. When those relationships work, nobody notices them. When they fail, the failure shows up as an outage, a missed audit, a surprise invoice, or a team that cannot ship.

The uncomfortable question is simple: how easy is it to manage these relationships well? For most teams the honest answer is "not very easy". Contracts are signed by procurement, technical contacts change, service levels are written but never measured, and the provider's account manager becomes the only person who knows what was promised. This article looks at why provider management is hard, what makes it easier, and how engineering leaders can build a practical system around it. Java examples are included where automation makes the process more reliable.

Why provider relationships are harder than they look

Service providers differ from internal teams in three important ways. First, their incentives are partly outside your control. A provider wants renewals, expansion, and a healthy margin. Your interests are uptime, predictable cost, and the ability to leave if needed. Those goals overlap, but they are not identical.

Second, information is asymmetric. The provider knows its architecture, its staffing, its roadmap, and its internal incidents. You usually see only what it chooses to show you, through status pages, quarterly reviews, and the reports you remember to request.

Third, the relationship is spread across people. Procurement negotiated the contract. Finance pays the invoices. Engineering consumes the service. Security reviews the data processing terms. Nobody owns the whole picture, so problems fall into gaps between these groups.

These three factors explain why provider management often feels reactive. A dispute surfaces, someone searches for the contract, and the team discovers that the notice period for cancellation was missed last quarter.

Step 1: Know what you actually depend on

You cannot manage what you have not listed. Start with an inventory of every external service your systems or teams rely on. For each entry, record:

  • Service and purpose: what it does for you and which products depend on it.
  • Criticality: what happens if it is unavailable for one hour, one day, or one week.
  • Data involved: whether personal, financial, or confidential data flows through it.
  • Owner: an internal person accountable for the relationship, not just the contract.
  • Contract terms that matter: renewal date, notice period, price escalation, service levels, and exit obligations.

The inventory should live somewhere searchable and kept current, not in a spreadsheet that one person updates once a year. A simple structure in code can make it queryable and testable. The sketch below models a provider record and flags relationships that are overdue for review or approaching a notice deadline:

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.List;

public enum Criticality { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL }

public record ServiceProvider(
        String name,
        String purpose,
        Criticality criticality,
        boolean handlesPersonalData,
        String internalOwner,
        LocalDate contractRenewal,
        int noticeDays,
        LocalDate lastReview) {

    public LocalDate noticeDeadline() {
        return contractRenewal.minusDays(noticeDays);
    }
}

public final class ProviderReviewPolicy {

    private static final int MAX_DAYS_BETWEEN_REVIEWS = 90;

    public List<String> findAttentionItems(List<ServiceProvider> providers, LocalDate today) {
        return providers.stream()
                .filter(p -> p.criticality() == Criticality.HIGH || p.criticality() == Criticality.CRITICAL)
                .flatMap(p -> {
                    java.util.List<String> items = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
                    if (p.lastReview() == null
                            || p.lastReview().plusDays(MAX_DAYS_BETWEEN_REVIEWS).isBefore(today)) {
                        items.add(p.name() + ": business review overdue");
                    }
                    if (!today.isBefore(p.noticeDeadline()) && today.isBefore(p.contractRenewal())) {
                        items.add(p.name() + ": notice period is running, decide renew or exit");
                    }
                    return items.stream();
                })
                .toList();
    }
}

The value here is not the code itself. It is the habit of asking the same questions for every provider and getting a list of items that need attention before the deadline arrives.

Step 2: Make service levels measurable

Many provider contracts contain service level agreements that look reassuring on paper. An uptime target of 99.9 percent sounds strong until you calculate that it allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime per month. Before signing or renewing, translate every commitment into a number you can observe, and decide how you will observe it.

Three questions help. What exactly is measured, and by whom? How is downtime defined, and does a degraded but working service count? What credit or remedy applies, and is it meaningful compared to the cost of the outage?

Measurement should not depend only on the provider's own reports. Where possible, monitor the service from your side: synthetic checks, error rates on your integration points, latency from your regions, and the number of support tickets your team opens. When the provider's report and your measurements disagree, you have a concrete basis for a conversation.

Some teams wrap provider calls in a small client that records latency and failures, so the data exists even when nobody asks for it. A minimal example with a timeout and a circuit breaker shows the idea:

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public final class ProviderClient {

    private final String providerName;
    private final MetricsRecorder metrics;
    private int consecutiveFailures = 0;
    private long openUntilMillis = 0;

    private static final int FAILURE_THRESHOLD = 5;
    private static final Duration OPEN_DURATION = Duration.ofSeconds(30);

    public ProviderClient(String providerName, MetricsRecorder metrics) {
        this.providerName = providerName;
        this.metrics = metrics;
    }

    public synchronized <T> T call(Supplier<T> request, T fallback) {
        if (System.currentTimeMillis() < openUntilMillis) {
            metrics.record(providerName, "short_circuited");
            return fallback;
        }
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            T result = request.get();
            consecutiveFailures = 0;
            metrics.record(providerName, "success", System.nanoTime() - start);
            return result;
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            consecutiveFailures++;
            metrics.record(providerName, "failure", System.nanoTime() - start);
            if (consecutiveFailures >= FAILURE_THRESHOLD) {
                openUntilMillis = System.currentTimeMillis() + OPEN_DURATION.toMillis();
                consecutiveFailures = 0;
            }
            return fallback;
        }
    }

    public interface MetricsRecorder {
        void record(String provider, String outcome);
        void record(String provider, String outcome, long durationNanos);
    }
}

This pattern does two things. It protects your system when the provider degrades, and it produces evidence. A quarterly report built from these metrics is far more persuasive than a memory of "it felt slow last month".

Step 3: Assign one accountable owner per relationship

Every provider needs an internal owner who is accountable for the relationship as a whole. That person does not have to do all the work, but they should know the contract's key dates, the current service performance, the open issues, and the escalation path.

The owner's job includes a short recurring review. For critical providers, a monthly operational check covers incidents, support responsiveness, and upcoming changes. A quarterly business review covers cost, roadmap alignment, and whether the relationship still fits your needs. Annual reviews cover the market: is there a better option, and what would switching cost?

A common failure is treating the provider's account manager as the owner. That person works for the provider. Their job is to renew the contract, and they are good at it. Your owner's job is to protect your interests, which sometimes means pushing back on them.

Step 4: Plan for exit before you need it

Ease of managing a provider depends heavily on how easy it would be to leave. Teams often discover too late that their data cannot be exported in a usable format, that a proprietary API has no equivalent elsewhere, or that the contract requires a twelve-month notice for termination.

Exit planning does not require building an identical replacement for every service. It requires knowing the answers to a few questions: Can we export our data, in what format, and how long would it take? Which parts of our code depend on provider-specific features, and how isolated are they? Is there a realistic alternative, and what would migration cost in time and money?

Architectural isolation helps here. Wrapping a provider behind an internal interface, as in the client above, confines vendor-specific details to one place. The interface does not need to be perfectly portable. It only needs to make the cost of change visible and bounded.

Step 5: Govern changes and risk together

Providers change things constantly: pricing, terms, subprocessors, data locations, supported versions, and features. Each change can affect your risk profile, and many arrive as an email nobody reads. A lightweight intake process helps. Route provider notices to a shared channel that the owner monitors. For each notice, decide whether it requires action, an update to the inventory, or a review with security or legal.

Security and compliance deserve their own checkpoints. Before onboarding a provider that handles personal or financial data, confirm the data processing terms, the certifications the provider holds, where data is stored, and how access is revoked when your contract ends. Revisit these at each renewal, because the provider's answers can change without much notice.

Step 6: Measure the relationship, not just the invoices

A useful scorecard for each critical provider includes a small number of measures reviewed consistently:

  • Availability and incident count measured from your side, with the provider's reported figures alongside.
  • Response and resolution time for the support requests you open, compared to the contract.
  • Total cost of ownership, including the internal time spent managing the provider, not only the invoice.
  • Change frequency and surprise rate, meaning how often the provider changes something that affects you without enough notice.
  • Owner's confidence rating, a simple score from one to five, updated monthly. A declining score often predicts problems before the metrics show them.

The point is to see trends. A provider that is slightly slower each quarter is a different conversation from one that had a single bad week.

Common mistakes

  • Signing without reading the exit terms. Notice periods and data return clauses matter more than the discount.
  • Letting the provider define success. Their dashboard shows what they choose to measure.
  • Spreading ownership across departments. When everyone is responsible, nobody is.
  • Ignoring the cost of management. A cheap provider that consumes a senior engineer's time every week is not cheap.
  • Waiting for a crisis to start the review. The best time to discuss service levels is before the outage.

A practical ninety-day plan

Days 1 to 30: Build the inventory of external services, with owners and contract dates. Identify the five providers whose failure would hurt most, and mark their notice deadlines in the team calendar.

Days 31 to 60: For those critical providers, translate service levels into measurable targets, add monitoring from your side, and schedule the first monthly operational review. Document the exit path for the most critical one.

Days 61 to 90: Introduce the scorecard, start the quarterly business review, and set up a shared intake for provider notices. Review the inventory with procurement, finance, and security so the owners know who to call for what.

Key takeaways

  • Provider relationships are hard to manage because incentives, information, and responsibility are spread across the organization.
  • Start with an inventory that records criticality, data, owners, and contract deadlines.
  • Turn service level promises into numbers you can observe yourself, and keep evidence.
  • Give every critical relationship one accountable internal owner who is not the provider's account manager.
  • Plan your exit before you need it, and isolate provider-specific code behind your own interfaces.
  • Track a scorecard over time, because trends reveal problems that single incidents hide.

So, how easy is it to manage service providers? It can be easy enough, once the relationship is visible, measured, and owned. The effort is modest compared to the cost of discovering a missed notice deadline or an unmeasured outage in the middle of a critical launch.

title: SSR vs. CSR vs. SSG: How Netflix Cut Time-to-Interactive by 50% by Shipping Less JavaScript
description:
SSR vs. CSR vs. SSG: How Netflix Cut Time-to-Interactive by 50% by Shipping Less JavaScript

In 2017, Netflix's logged-out homepage was carrying about 300 kB of JavaScript. Some of it was React, some was utility libraries like Lodash, and some was the data needed to hydrate React's state. React itself was only around 45 kB of that. But when the team removed client-side React, several libraries, and the code that depended on them, the total dropped by more than 200 kB, and the page's time-to-interactive improved by over 50%. React didn't disappear: Netflix kept using it on the server to produce the initial HTML, and it prefetched React in the background so the rest of the sign-up flow, a single-page app, still loaded fast. That prefetching cut time-to-interactive by 30% on later navigations.

The lesson isn't "React is slow." It's that how a page gets built, and how much JavaScript has to run before it works, can matter more than which framework you picked. That decision is the heart of rendering strategy: do you build the HTML in the browser (client-side rendering, CSR), on the server for each request (server-side rendering, SSR), or ahead of time at build (static site generation, SSG)?

The stakes are measurable. Google's Core Web Vitals want a Largest Contentful Paint of 2.5 seconds or less, an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, and a Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less, judged at the 75th percentile of real visits. And Google's own documentation notes that the default strategy for single-page apps today is client-side rendering, while encouraging server-side rendering or pre-rendering if you're free to choose. This guide breaks down what each approach does, where the real numbers come from, and how to decide, page by page.

If you're newer to frontend work, our React & Frontend roadmap covers the fundamentals this comparison builds on.

This post originally appeared on the Ciphemic Academia blog.

The Short Version

  • Client-side rendering (CSR): the server sends a nearly empty HTML page and a JavaScript bundle. The browser runs the JavaScript, fetches data, and builds the page.
  • Server-side rendering (SSR): the server builds the full HTML for each request and sends it. The browser shows it right away, then JavaScript "hydrates" the page to make it interactive.
  • Static site generation (SSG): the HTML is built once, at build time, and served as plain files from a CDN. Every visitor gets the same pre-built page.

If you want one default: decide per page, not per site. Use SSG for content that rarely changes, like blog posts, docs, and marketing and course pages. Use SSR for public pages that are personalized or change on every request. Use CSR for app-like screens behind a login, where search engines never look.

What All Three Are Actually Trying to Solve

Before the differences, the shared goals:

  • Showing real content quickly, which Google measures as Largest Contentful Paint
  • Responding fast when users interact, measured as Interaction to Next Paint
  • Keeping the layout stable so content doesn't jump around, measured as Cumulative Layout Shift
  • Being understood by crawlers and link previews, so search engines and social sites can read your content
  • Keeping infrastructure and developer effort reasonable, since every rendering choice has a cost somewhere

The strategies differ in where and when the HTML gets built, and each answer shifts the costs to a different place.

Client-Side Rendering (CSR)

What it actually is: the browser does the rendering. The server returns a minimal HTML shell and a JavaScript bundle. The browser downloads, parses, and runs the bundle, which fetches data from an API and builds the page. A default Vite or Create React App project works this way.

A small example (what the server sends for a client-rendered app):

<body>
  <div id="root"></div>
  <script type="module" src="/assets/index.js"></script>
</body>

The visible content only exists after the script runs and builds it inside #root.

Where it shines:

  • Rich interactivity: once loaded, navigation between screens is instant because only data moves, not whole pages
  • Simple hosting: static files plus an API, with no render server to run
  • Clean separation: the front end and back end can be built and deployed independently
  • A natural fit behind a login: dashboards and admin tools don't need to rank in search

Where it struggles:

  • A blank screen until JavaScript arrives: the user sees little until the bundle downloads, parses, and executes, which hurts Largest Contentful Paint
  • JavaScript cost on slower devices: a heavy bundle can make interactions sluggish on mid-range phones, which hurts Interaction to Next Paint
  • SEO risk: Googlebot can render JavaScript, but pages go through a crawl queue and then a render queue, so there's a delay, and Google notes that other search engines may ignore JavaScript entirely
  • Weak link previews: social platforms often read the initial HTML for titles and images, which a bare shell doesn't contain

Who this suits: logged-in application interiors, internal tools, and anything where search visibility doesn't matter.

Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

What it actually is: the server runs your components for each request, fetches the data, and sends complete HTML. The browser can display that immediately. Then the JavaScript bundle loads and hydrates the page, attaching event handlers so it becomes interactive.

A small example (Next.js, Pages Router; other frameworks have equivalents):

// pages/courses/[slug].jsx
export async function getServerSideProps({ params }) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/courses/${params.slug}`);
  const course = await res.json();
  return { props: { course } };   // runs on the server for every request
}

export default function CoursePage({ course }) {
  return <h1>{course.title}</h1>;
}

Where it shines:

  • Real content in the first response: users and crawlers get meaningful HTML immediately, which helps both Largest Contentful Paint and indexing
  • Fresh and personalized data: every request can reflect the current database state or the current user
  • Good link previews: titles and images are in the HTML
  • Secrets stay on the server: API keys and database access never reach the browser

Where it struggles:

  • Server cost per request: you pay compute for every page view, and a slow database makes every page slow
  • Time to first byte depends on your backend, since the server has to finish rendering before it can send anything
  • Hydration cost: the page can look ready before it responds to clicks, and shipping a large bundle for hydration is exactly the overhead Netflix removed from its landing page
  • More infrastructure: you need a server or edge runtime, plus a caching strategy so you don't render the same page repeatedly (a cache like the ones in our Redis vs. Memcached guide often helps)

Who this suits: public pages that must be indexed and also change per request or per user, such as product pages, search results, and personalized landing pages.

Static Site Generation (SSG)

What it actually is: pages are rendered once during the build and saved as HTML files. A CDN serves those files directly, so there's no server work per visit. Many frameworks add incremental regeneration, where a page is rebuilt in the background after a set time or on demand, so static pages can stay reasonably fresh.

A small example (Next.js, Pages Router, with regeneration):

// pages/blog/[slug].jsx
export async function getStaticPaths() {
  const slugs = await getAllPostSlugs();
  return { paths: slugs.map((slug) => ({ params: { slug } })), fallback: 'blocking' };
}

export async function getStaticProps({ params }) {
  const post = await getPost(params.slug);
  return { props: { post }, revalidate: 3600 };   // rebuild at most once an hour
}

export default function BlogPost({ post }) {
  return <article><h1>{post.title}</h1></article>;
}

Where it shines:

  • Speed: pre-built files from a CDN are typically the fastest way to deliver a page, which supports strong Core Web Vitals
  • Low cost and high resilience: no per-request compute, and static hosting keeps working under traffic spikes
  • Strong SEO: complete HTML is there from the first byte
  • Smaller attack surface: there's no server running your rendering code for every request

Where it struggles:

  • Content freezes until the next build or revalidation: that's fine for a blog post and wrong for live inventory
  • Build time grows with page count: thousands of pages can mean slow builds unless you regenerate incrementally
  • Per-user content needs another route: anything personalized has to be fetched client-side or handled by a different strategy
  • Rebuilds need automation: content changes should trigger builds, which is where a CI/CD pipeline, like those in our GitHub Actions vs. Jenkins vs. CircleCI comparison, comes in

Who this suits: blogs, documentation, marketing sites, and course or catalog pages whose content changes occasionally, not on every request.

Side-by-Side Comparison

CSR SSR SSG
Where HTML is built In the browser On the server, per request At build time
First content on screen After JavaScript runs In the first response In the first response, from a CDN
Interactivity After the bundle loads After hydration After hydration (if any JavaScript ships)
SEO and link previews Weakest, depends on JS rendering Strong Strong
Data freshness As fresh as the API Fresh on every request As of the last build or revalidation
Server cost Low (static files plus API) Highest (compute per request) Lowest
Hosting Any static host Needs a server or edge runtime Any static host or CDN
Main risk Slow first paint, empty shell for crawlers Server load, hydration overhead Stale content, long builds
Typical use Logged-in apps, dashboards Personalized or fast-changing public pages Blogs, docs, marketing, catalogs

How This Fits a Career Path

  • Frontend and full-stack engineers: choosing a rendering strategy per route is part of building any serious site, and it shows up in code reviews and architecture discussions
  • Performance-focused roles: you'll own Core Web Vitals, which means understanding how rendering, bundle size, and caching combine; our logs vs. metrics vs. traces post covers the measurement side
  • SEO-aware developers: knowing what a crawler sees in the initial HTML is a practical skill that separates strong frontend engineers from average ones
  • Interviews: "SSR, CSR, or SSG for this page, and why?" is a common frontend and system design question, and the best answers decide per page with reasons

How to Choose Without Overthinking It

  1. Ask who needs to find the page. If search engines or link previews matter, don't rely on a bare client-rendered shell. Choose SSG or SSR.
  2. Ask how often the content changes. Rarely, as with blog posts and docs: SSG, with regeneration if you need occasional updates. On every request or per user: SSR.
  3. Use CSR where search doesn't matter. Logged-in dashboards and tools are a good fit.
  4. Do the view-source test. Open View Page Source on a page you care about. If the article text isn't in that HTML, a crawler's first look sees an empty shell.
  5. Send less JavaScript regardless of strategy. Netflix's win came mainly from running less code in the browser, not from switching strategy.
  6. Measure real users, not your laptop. Core Web Vitals are judged at the 75th percentile across mobile and desktop, so check field data in Search Console or PageSpeed Insights.
  7. Don't build new sites around dynamic rendering. Google describes serving crawlers a different version than users as a workaround, not a long-term solution.

A note on honesty: the Netflix numbers describe one page, the logged-out homepage, in 2017, and engineers have pointed out that the story is as much about running less JavaScript as about any one framework. Netflix still used React on the server and for the rest of its sign-up flow. Core Web Vitals are one signal among many, and the relevance of your content matters more than shaving a few milliseconds. Thresholds can change, so check Google's current documentation. Modern frameworks also let you mix strategies within one app, so the clean categories here blur in practice.

Common Mistakes When Choosing a Rendering Strategy

  • Using one strategy for the whole site. Marketing pages, logged-in screens, and personalized pages have different needs.
  • Building public content pages as pure client-side apps. Blogs and course pages that need to rank shouldn't depend on a render queue.
  • Assuming SSR automatically means fast. A slow backend or a huge hydration bundle can erase the benefit.
  • Shipping a huge JavaScript bundle under any strategy. Bundle size drives interactivity problems everywhere.
  • Forgetting Open Graph and meta tags in the HTML. Link previews read the initial response, not the post-JavaScript page.
  • Lazy-loading the main above-the-fold image. That's usually your Largest Contentful Paint element, so it should load as early as possible.
  • Letting content load in late and shift the layout. Reserve space for images and embeds to protect your Cumulative Layout Shift score.
  • Using SSG without a refresh plan. Stale pages quietly erode trust, so decide how and when content gets rebuilt.
  • Not caching SSR responses. Re-rendering identical pages on every request wastes compute.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is client-side rendering bad for SEO?

It isn't banned, since Googlebot renders JavaScript, but pages are queued for rendering, which adds delay and risk, and other search engines may not run JavaScript at all. For public content that needs to rank, server-side or static rendering is the safer choice.

What is hydration?

After the server sends HTML, the browser downloads the JavaScript and attaches event handlers and state to that existing markup, which is what makes the page interactive. Until hydration finishes, the page may look ready but not respond.

SSR or SSG for a blog?

SSG for most blogs. The content changes rarely, static files are fast and cheap, and you can trigger a rebuild when you publish. Add incremental regeneration if you need updates without a full rebuild.

Can I mix these in one app?

Yes, and most real apps do. Modern frameworks let you choose per route, so a marketing page can be static while a dashboard is client-rendered and a search page is server-rendered.

Do I need Next.js to use SSR or SSG?

No. Frameworks like Astro, Remix, Nuxt, and SvelteKit offer similar capabilities, and you can build static or server-rendered pages without a framework. Next.js is just a popular example.

How do interviewers evaluate this topic?

Usually by giving you a page and asking how you'd render it. A strong answer decides per page, names the trade-offs in speed, freshness, SEO, and cost, and mentions measuring Core Web Vitals instead of guessing.

Decide Per Page, Then Measure

The Netflix story and Google's guidance point to the same habit: choose how each page gets built based on who needs it and how fresh it must be, send as little JavaScript as you can, and check real-user numbers instead of trusting a rule of thumb. Explore the React & Frontend roadmap to practice building the same page three ways and see the trade-offs for yourself.

title: SMS Alert API Alternatives Explained (Europe GDPR and US Startup Support)
description:
Choose an SMS alert API by the evidence it lets your system retain, not by the apparent simplicity of its send call. For US and EU loan-application updates, my recommendation is to put consent, destination policy, sender eligibility, idempotency, and an append-only audit record in your own critical path; then select a provider whose operating model fits the response-time and channel breadth you actually need. Infrai is workable for plain alerts when polling is acceptable and your application owns the compliance logic. Twilio, Vonage, and Sinch deserve equal consideration when a broader communications suite or provider-specific workflow is the stronger requirement.

Short answer: no provider turns a phone number and a message into a compliance decision. The durable architecture makes that decision before transmission and records enough evidence to explain it afterward.

Which SMS alert API alternatives support US and Europe compliance?

This architecture decision record starts with four invariants. First, a loan update cannot be sent unless the application has a current consent record for the destination and purpose. Second, the country inferred by the application must be allowed by an explicit policy; absence from the policy means deny. Third, one business event produces at most one accepted send operation, even if a worker crashes after the provider accepts it. Fourth, every decision leaves an audit record containing the business event ID, policy version, consent reference, message classification, chosen sender, provider request reference, and final disposition.

The last two invariants are related but not interchangeable. An idempotency key prevents duplicate effects within a defined deduplication window; an audit trail explains what the system believed before, during, and after that window. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window, so I would still make the loan event ID unique in the application database rather than treating provider retention as permanent exactly-once delivery.

Exactly once is an aspiration. The enforceable design is an atomic local transition, an idempotent remote request, and reconciliation.

No evidence, no send.

Failure boundaries matter here. A malformed phone number fails before policy evaluation. Missing consent fails closed. An unknown country never falls through to a default sender. A timeout after submission is ambiguous and must be retried with the same key, while HTTP 429 requires bounded exponential backoff that honors Retry-After. Delivery status is later evidence, not permission retroactively granted.

Sender registration and sender-listing capabilities support production setup where local sender rules apply, but the application still has to choose an eligible sender. Inbound messages are retrieved by polling, which can cover simple STOP and HELP processing but is a poor match for conversational, low-latency support. There is no built-in geographic fence or by-country spend circuit breaker, so both belong before the send operation. I chose an application-owned deny-by-default map because a provider-side sender list answers a different question: what can be used, rather than what this lender has authorized for this event.

The decision is about evidence, latency, and scope

The following comparison is deliberately qualitative. Published prices and country rules move; neither should be frozen into an architecture record without a dated procurement review.

Option Best fit for this decision Boundary to test before adoption
Twilio Teams that want a mature, provider-specific messaging workflow and detailed guidance on SMS segmentation Verify current sender registration, inbound handling, and country obligations for every launch market
Vonage Messages API Teams evaluating SMS alongside a broader messaging API Confirm the exact inbound and status event model, regional processing terms, and sender support for the intended countries
Sinch SMS Teams that want an established SMS platform and are prepared to integrate its callbacks and compliance processes Confirm sender availability, opt-out handling, data location, and evidence retention contractually
AWS SNS Systems already organized around AWS identities, logs, and operational controls Validate origination identities, two-way requirements, country coverage, and the evidence exported to the lender's audit store
Infrai Plain alerting where one REST contract and one key across many backend capabilities reduce integration and reconciliation work Inbound events are pull-based; geo-fencing and country spend controls remain application responsibilities
Amazon SES An email fallback for teams already using AWS; it is not an SMS replacement Keep email consent, domain authentication, suppression, and channel-specific evidence separate from the SMS decision

This is not a feature-count contest. Twilio documents how GSM-7 and UCS-2 affect segmentation, a detail that can alter both delivery behavior and cost when loan status text contains non-GSM characters. The same message-body test belongs in any provider evaluation, including Vonage, Sinch, AWS SNS, and the final option in the table. Separately, GDPR requires a lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimization, and demonstrable compliance; selecting an EU-capable vendor does not transfer those controller obligations out of the application.

Amazon SES belongs in the table only as an adjacent channel decision. A lender may use email when its product policy permits that fallback, but substituting email does not make an SMS alert requirement disappear, and the email side has its own evidence: authenticated sending domains, suppression state, consent purpose, and delivery events. Keeping that distinction visible prevents a broad “communications” procurement exercise from pretending that all channels have interchangeable sender rules or opt-out semantics.

Infrai's differentiator is breadth behind a consistent REST API: its self-describing discovery catalog reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules under one key, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. Public request and response schemas reduce the friction of reviewing a payload contract before it reaches a regulated workflow; the shared idempotency convention reduces a different kind of friction during retry design. Neither point compensates for polling latency, missing geo controls, or the absence of voice, WhatsApp, RCS, and SMTP relay.

Put policy before the network

The critical path below is a runnable Go client for the one verified send operation, POST /v1/sms/send. It reads the exact JSON payload from SMS_PAYLOAD_JSON because no request fields should be guessed, reads credentials and the deployment base URL from the environment, checks every response, surfaces error bodies, reuses the business event ID as the idempotency key, and applies bounded 429 retry behavior. The compliance gate must run before this client is called.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func send(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, baseURL, key, eventID string, payload []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            baseURL+"/v1/sms/send", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", eventID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 { return body, nil }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("sms send returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    baseURL, key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    eventID, payload := os.Getenv("LOAN_EVENT_ID"), []byte(os.Getenv("SMS_PAYLOAD_JSON"))
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || eventID == "" || len(payload) == 0 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, LOAN_EVENT_ID, and SMS_PAYLOAD_JSON")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := send(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, baseURL, key, eventID, payload)
    if err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The network client is only half of the guarantee. A real service needs a database uniqueness constraint on the event ID and an outbox or equivalent transaction boundary; otherwise two processes can both submit before either stores its receipt. Store message classification and a content hash when retaining the full body would violate minimization policy; retain the body only when the compliance and support case justifies it. This is the trade-off I would document: more local state and reconciliation work in exchange for evidence that remains coherent through a timeout, a worker restart, or a provider migration.

I initially considered treating an HTTP success as the final ledger event, then rejected that model because its failure story is incomplete. Consider the awkward sequence: the provider accepts loan-1042-approved-v1, the connection drops before the response reaches the worker, and the worker restarts. The local row still says “pending,” yet the external effect may already exist. On restart, the worker reads the same outbox row and resubmits with the same idempotency key; it does not mint a new key for attempt two. If the response is accepted, the worker stores the provider request reference and advances the row. If ambiguity remains, reconciliation polls status rather than guessing. The audit stream records each attempt and its outcome, while the business-event uniqueness constraint ensures that another process cannot create a second logical send. That is why I chose a little more state. A dashboard screenshot cannot reconstruct this sequence, and an application log that expires after a week cannot carry a lender's long-term evidence policy.

Retries preserve identity.

Reconciliation then compares accepted submissions with polled status and inbound records. Because the email and SMS namespaces do not emit webhook events, the polling worker needs a persisted cursor, overlap between windows, deduplication by provider record ID, and an alert for stale progress. A three-minute poll may be perfectly adequate for STOP processing in a low-volume alert service, but that number is an internal service-level choice, not a platform guarantee.

Why reject a provider-owned compliance boundary?

The rejected design sends first and relies on provider dashboards, sender registration, or suppression behavior as the system of record. It is attractive because the initial integration is smaller. It also separates the loan decision from its evidence: the provider can show that a message was submitted, yet the lender may still be unable to show which consent and country policy authorized that submission.

There is a valid use case for the rejected option. A prototype using synthetic recipients, no regulated customer data, and no production traffic can use a provider console to test copy and segmentation before the audit subsystem exists. The boundary must be explicit, short-lived, and incapable of reaching real borrowers.

For production, record consent withdrawal locally before the next send can be admitted. Polling for inbound STOP and HELP messages should feed the same suppression decision, with repeated records handled idempotently. If the product requirement changes from alerts to real-time two-way support, polling becomes the architectural reason to reconsider the provider rather than something to disguise with a tighter loop.

Decision

For a startup delivering loan-application alerts in the US and EU, I would adopt the provider-neutral policy and audit layer first, then choose among Twilio, Vonage, Sinch, AWS SNS, and Infrai after a country-by-country sender and data-processing review. The last option fits when plain SMS alerts, pull-based event handling, and a broad single-contract backend surface are acceptable. It does not fit a design that requires real-time inbound webhooks, managed geographic enforcement, or voice and rich-messaging channels.

The acceptance test is concrete: replay one business event twice and observe one provider submission; deny an unlisted country before any network call; trace an accepted alert back to consent and policy versions; process the same inbound opt-out twice without changing the outcome; and reconcile every ambiguous timeout. Pass those tests before debating unit price.

Policy wins.

References

  • EUR-Lex: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 5
  • Twilio: SMS character limits and message segmentation
  • Twilio: Messaging compliance
  • Vonage: Messages API documentation
  • Sinch: SMS API documentation
  • AWS: SMS messaging with Amazon SNS
  • AWS: Amazon SES documentation
  • FCC: Robotexts and unwanted texts

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

  • Automatic framework support: FastAPI, Flask, and Django applications are automatically recognized and configured, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the Vercel CDN.

  • Native Python runtime and tooling: Vercel runs CPython on Linux and supports uv and pyproject.toml for dependency management.

  • Compute for APIs and workers: Scale request-driven applications with Fluid compute and run long-running pull-based workloads with Vercel Daemons.

Native Python SDKs

Within your application, Python SDKs let you build agents, run untrusted code, and orchestrate durable workflows.

  • Sandbox: Give your application or agent an isolated Linux VM on demand.

  • AI SDK for Python (Beta): Generate or stream model responses and call tools. Get started with uv add ai.

  • Workflow SDK for Python (Beta): Persist execution state and retry failed workflow steps.

  • Queues (Beta): Send and receive messages for background work.

  • Connect: Obtain credentials for calling external APIs.

  • Blob: Upload and retrieve files in object storage.

Use the SDKs individually or combine them in the same Python application.

Your frontend and backend, together

For full-stack applications, Vercel Services allows you to deploy your frontend and backends together in one project, with shared previews and atomic deployments and rollbacks. Within that project, you can view logs by service and connect backends privately through service bindings.

For a frontend in frontend/ and a FastAPI app defined in backend/main.py, add this vercel.toml at the repository root.

Requests under /api/ reach matching FastAPI routes with the path unchanged, while other requests reach the frontend. Run both services locally with vercel dev, then deploy them together from the same repository.

Read the Python documentation to get started.

title: A Jury, Not an Electorate: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Ensembles of Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21085v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An ensemble of language models is a jury, not an electorate. The answers are testimony from witnesses of unknown reliability, and the question is not what the majority said but who is credible. Most ensemble methods assign each expert a fixed reputation, often learned from labels. We ask whether it can instead be inferred from the pattern of agreement and disagreement among the experts. We model the experts as a jury: each question has a latent true answer, each expert reports it with unknown reliability, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (EM) from unlabelled answer configurations alone. We show that its decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts' answer distributions. What changes is not how the jury votes, but how it learns whom to trust. On a 1560-question benchmark, the jury, with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision. Instead, it outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark.

title: AdaLoop: Thinking with the Vision Encoder
description:
arXiv:2610.21323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) treat the vision encoder as a static feature extractor: it encodes an image once, independently of the question, and leaves subsequent reasoning to the language model. Yet different questions may require different visual operations and processing depths. We present AdaLoop, a framework for question-conditioned visual recurrence in VLMs. AdaLoop adapts visual computation to the question and reuses the encoder's transformations across multiple iterations, with the pretrained vision weights frozen. We also introduce VisRO, a procedural dataset and generation pipeline for training and evaluating vision-centric reasoning. On six VisRO tasks, AdaLoop outperforms standard fine-tuning and question-conditioned single-pass baselines with matched training data and optimizer updates. These gains hold across three VLM families on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples. Our findings suggest that pretrained vision encoders can contribute to reasoning through task-directed, iterative visual computation.

title: Learning Topology-Aware Representations for Mechanics-Relevant TPMS Metamaterials
description:
arXiv:2610.20684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning informative representations of mechanical Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) metamaterials is important for mechanics analysis and structural design, yet existing methods have rarely explicitly supervised learned representations with information about global structural connectivity that is relevant to mechanical response. We propose a topology-aware representation learning framework that integrates persistent homology into a DMAE backbone to explicitly encode global structural connectivity. A persistence-guided masking strategy prioritizes patches associated with persistent topological features, while an auxiliary persistent-homology decoder encourages the latent representation to retain information about topological feature counts across connected components, tunnels, and voids. We evaluate the learned representations on two complementary TPMS datasets using family classification, mechanical-property classification, unsupervised clustering, and regression. Across the two datasets, our method demonstrates strong performance in both structural family and mechanical-property classification, improving family classification by up to 3.9% while achieving the best linear-probe performance. More notably, unsupervised property-clustering performance improves by up to 26.7% and 51.5% across the two datasets, while strong regression performance is retained with $R^2=0.993$. These results establish persistent topology as an effective inductive bias for representation learning of complex three-dimensional mechanical metamaterials.

title: Rate Limiting Like Gandalf: Building a Distributed Cache with Redis
description:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")

Ever had your API melt down because a sudden traffic spike hammered every endpoint at once? I remember a late‑night deploy where our “simple” in‑process counter crashed under a flash sale, and the pager started singing like a busted karaoke machine. We needed a way to throttle requests without turning every service into a bottleneck or rewriting the whole stack.

The problem boiled down to: how do we share a counter across many instances, keep it fast, and survive node failures?

A naïve approach—each service keeps its own local counter—fails the moment you scale beyond one node. A centralized DB works but adds latency that kills throughput. Enter Redis: an in‑memory key‑value store that can be replicated, clustered, and accessed with sub‑millisecond latency. It felt like discovering a hidden armory in a dungeon—suddenly we had the right tool for the job.

The Revelation (The Insight)

The magic insight is decoupling the rate‑limit decision from the storage mechanism by using a token bucket algorithm implemented with a single Redis key per client (or IP, or API key).

Here’s why this beats the usual alternatives:

Approach Pros Cons
Local in‑memory counter Zero network latency No shared state → limits are per‑instance, easy to bypass
Central SQL/NoSQL DB Strong consistency Higher latency, more operational overhead
Redis + Lua script Atomic increment & expiry, O(1) time, built‑in TTL for auto‑cleanup Requires Redis cluster, but that’s a solved problem for most teams

The critical insight is that we can let Redis do the heavy lifting atomically with a Lua script, so we never read‑modify‑write in two steps (which would invite race conditions). The script returns the current token count and, if allowed, decrements it—all in one round trip.

ASCII diagram of the flow 

+----------------+      Lua Script (EVAL)      +----------------+
|  Service A     |  --------------------->    |   Redis Cluster  |
|  (or B, C…)   |  <--------------------     |   (key: bucket) |
+----------------+      (INCR + EXPIRE)       +----------------+
        |                                               |
        |  Decision: allow/deny based on tokens       |
        v                                               v
+----------------+                               +----------------+
|  HTTP Response |                               |  TTL refresh   |
+----------------+                               +----------------+

The bucket key holds two fields: tokens (remaining permits) and timestamp (last refill). On each request we:

  1. Refill tokens based on elapsed time (now - last_refill).
  2. Cap at the max bucket size.
  3. If tokens >= 1, consume one and reply 200.
  4. Else reply 429 Too Many Requests.

All of this happens inside Redis, guaranteeing that two concurrent requests can’t both see the same token count and both slip through.

Wielding the Power (Code & Examples)

The Struggle (Before) 

# Bad: naive per‑process counter (race condition city)
import time
from flask import Flask, request, abort

app = Flask(__name__)
counter = 0          # ← only one process sees this
LIMIT = 100          # requests per minute
WINDOW = 60          # seconds

@app.before_request
def limit():
    global counter
    now = time.time()
    if not hasattr(limit, "reset"):
        limit.reset = now
        counter = 0
    if now - limit.reset > WINDOW:
        limit.reset = now
        counter = 0
    if counter >= LIMIT:
        abort(429)
    counter += 1

What’s wrong? If you run three Gunicorn workers, each gets its own counter. Three workers × 100 = 300 effective limit—your rate limit is basically useless. Plus, the global variable isn’t safe across threads or processes.

The Victory (After)

We’ll use the redis-py client and a Lua script that does the token‑bucket math atomically.

import time
import redis
from flask import Flask, request, abort

app = Flask(__name__)
r = redis.Redis(host='redis-cluster', port=6379, decode_responses=True)

# Lua script stored as a string; we'll load it once at startup
LUASCRIPT = """
local key = KEYS[1]
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])   -- max tokens
local refill_rate = tonumber(ARGV[2])  -- tokens per second
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local bucket = rcall('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'timestamp')
local tokens = tonumber(bucket[1]) or limit
local last = tonumber(bucket[2]) or now

-- refill
local delta = math.max(0, now - last)
tokens = math.min(limit, tokens + delta * refill_rate)

local allowed = 0
if tokens >= 1 then
    tokens = tokens - 1
    allowed = 1
end

rcall('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'timestamp', now)
rcall('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(limit / refill_rate) + 5)  -- auto‑clean
return allowed
"""

# Register the script (returns a SHA we can call with EVALSHA)
SCRIPT_SHA = r.script_load(LUASCRIPT)

def allow_request(client_id: str, limit: int = 100, per_seconds: int = 60) -> bool:
    """Return True if request is allowed, False otherwise."""
    key = f"rate_limit:{client_id}"
    now = time.time()
    refill_rate = limit / per_seconds  # tokens per second
    # EVALSHA returns 1 (allowed) or 0 (denied)
    result = r.evalsha(SCRIPT_SHA, 1, key, limit, refill_rate, now)
    return bool(result)

@app.before_request
def enforce_limit():
    # Use IP or API key as the client identifier
    client_id = request.remote_addr  # or request.headers.get('X-API-Key')
    if not allow_request(client_id, limit=100, per_seconds=60):
        abort(429)

@app.route('/api/hello')
def hello():
    return {"msg": "Hello, traveler!"}

What changed?

  • We moved state to Redis, so every service instance sees the same bucket.
  • The Lua script guarantees the read‑modify‑write cycle is atomic—no race conditions even under thousands of concurrent requests.
  • Keys auto‑expire (EXPIRE) after a bit of idle time, keeping memory usage bounded.

Common Traps to Avoid

  1. Using GET/SET separately – If you fetch the token count, then decrement it in a second command, two threads can interleave and both think they have a token. Always wrap the logic in a Lua script (or use Redis’ INCRBY with a custom TTL trick, but Lua is clearer).
  2. Forgetting to set an expiration – Without EXPIRE, idle clients will linger forever, wasting memory. A short TTL (a few multiples of the refill interval) lets Redis reclaim keys automatically.

Why This New Power Matters

Now you can drop this snippet into any service—Flask, FastAPI, Node.js, Go—and instantly get a globally consistent rate limiter that scales horizontally with your Redis cluster. No more per‑instance guesswork, no more surprise 429s during a flash sale, and no extra latency that makes users feel like they’re stuck in a loading screen.

You’ve turned a flimsy, local counter into a resilient, shared guardrail—think of it as giving your API a magical shield that only lets through the worthy adventurers.

Your Turn

Grab a Redis instance (even a free tier on Redis Cloud works), copy the Lua script above, and try limiting a public endpoint with a different algorithm—maybe a fixed‑window counter or a sliding‑window log. Compare latency, memory usage, and ease of tuning. Share your findings in the comments; I’d love to hear what quest you embark on next!

Happy coding, and may your rate limits always be just right. 🚀

title: A Quarantine Ledger for Agent Patches
description:
A CI suite runs 300 tests. Two of them fail on almost every diff. The failures land in files nobody touched.

Reviewers learn to scroll past red. An agent opens forty diffs a week. Each one looks green except the usual two. The suite stops being a gate and becomes wallpaper.

This post describes a workflow for that situation. It has three parts: a quarantine ledger with expiry dates, a property harness for agent patches, and a fixture budget that makes silent fixture edits visible. Every snippet below is runnable pytest against a small synthetic importer. The counts are illustrative, not measured.

The ledger

A ledger is one JSON file in the repo. Each entry names a test, an owner, a reason, and an expiry date.

{
  "tests": [
    {
      "id": "tests/test_billing.py::test_retry_after_webhook",
      "owner": "payments",
      "reason": "clock-dependent, fails ~3 of 20 runs on clean main",
      "opened_at": "2026-10-16",
      "expires_at": "2026-11-13"
    }
  ]
}

A conftest hook reads the ledger at collection time. Unexpired entries get skipped. Expired entries run again, which is the enforcement you want. The skip markers themselves are plain pytest, documented at https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/skipping.html.

# conftest.py
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path
import pytest

LEDGER = Path("quarantine.json")
RUN_LOG = Path("artifacts/quarantine-run.json")


def pytest_collection_modifyitems(config, items):
    entries = json.loads(LEDGER.read_text())["tests"] if LEDGER.exists() else []
    today = time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    by_id = {e["id"]: e for e in entries}
    report = {"date": today, "skipped": [], "expired": [], "runnable": 0}

    for item in items:
        entry = by_id.get(item.nodeid)
        if entry and entry["expires_at"] > today:
            item.add_marker(pytest.mark.skip(reason=f"quarantined: {entry['reason']}"))
            report["skipped"].append(item.nodeid)
        else:
            if entry:
                report["expired"].append(item.nodeid)
            report["runnable"] += 1

    RUN_LOG.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    RUN_LOG.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2))

Expiry is the whole point. A skip without a date is a deletion in disguise. The run log also gives you one number to watch. The skipped count should fall over a quarter. If it rises, the suite is decaying faster than you repair it.

Properties instead of examples

Agent patches tend to preserve shapes and break rules. An example test asserts that row 42 credits ten dollars. A property test asserts that accepted plus rejected equals input, for any input.

Here is the code under test, small enough to reason about.

# app/importer.py
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class ImportResult:
    accepted: int
    rejected: int
    credited_sum: int
    checksum: int


class Importer:
    def __init__(self, conn):
        self.conn = conn

    def run(self, rows):
        accepted = rejected = credited = 0
        for row in rows:
            if row["amount"] == 0:
                rejected += 1
                continue
            cur = self.conn.execute(
                "insert or ignore into ledger_row (id, amount, currency) values (?, ?, ?)",
                (row["id"], row["amount"], row["currency"]),
            )
            if cur.rowcount == 1:
                accepted += 1
                credited += row["amount"]
        self.conn.commit()
        checksum = self.conn.execute(
            "select coalesce(sum(id), 0) from ledger_row"
        ).fetchone()[0]
        return ImportResult(accepted, rejected, credited, checksum)

And the fixtures, with an in-memory database and a seeded generator.

# tests/conftest.py
import random
import sqlite3
import pytest
from app.importer import Importer


class Snapshot:
    def __init__(self, conn):
        self.conn = conn

    def count(self, table):
        return self.conn.execute(f"select count(*) from {table}").fetchone()[0]

    def sum(self, table, column):
        return self.conn.execute(
            f"select coalesce(sum({column}), 0) from {table}"
        ).fetchone()[0]


@pytest.fixture
def snapshot():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    conn.execute(
        "create table ledger_row (id integer primary key, amount integer, currency text)"
    )
    yield Snapshot(conn)
    conn.close()


@pytest.fixture
def importer(snapshot):
    return Importer(snapshot.conn)


@pytest.fixture
def rows():
    def build(seed, n=40):
        rng = random.Random(seed)
        return [
            {
                "id": rng.randrange(10_000),
                "amount": rng.randrange(-500, 500),
                "currency": rng.choice(["USD", "EUR"]),
            }
            for _ in range(n)
        ]

    return build

Two properties carry most of the weight here: idempotency and conservation.

# tests/properties/test_import_properties.py
import pytest

pytestmark = pytest.mark.property

SEEDS = range(1, 26)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_import_is_idempotent(seed, importer, snapshot, rows):
    batch = rows(seed)
    first = importer.run(batch)
    assert snapshot.count("ledger_row") == first.accepted

    second = importer.run(batch)
    assert second.accepted == 0
    assert snapshot.count("ledger_row") == first.accepted


@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
def test_rejection_never_breaks_totals(seed, importer, snapshot, rows):
    batch = rows(seed)
    result = importer.run(batch)
    assert result.accepted + result.rejected == len(batch)
    assert snapshot.sum("ledger_row", "amount") == result.credited_sum

Twenty-five seeds across two properties is fifty cheap runs. That is a friendlier signal than one hand-written example. It also survives refactors better, because the invariant does not move when the row format does. When a property fails on seed 17, you keep seed 17 forever as a regression.

A fixture budget

Fixtures are shared state that agents can quietly rewrite. Pin a fingerprint and fail the build when the fixture set drifts.

# tests/test_fixture_budget.py
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

PINNED = "9f2c41ab77de0013"  # update only in the same diff as a ledger entry


def fixture_fingerprint(root="tests/fixtures"):
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    for path in sorted(Path(root).rglob("*")):
        if path.is_file():
            digest.update(path.name.encode())
            digest.update(path.read_bytes())
    return digest.hexdigest()[:16]


def test_fixtures_did_not_drift():
    assert fixture_fingerprint() == PINNED, "fixture set changed; justify it in the diff"

This test is intentionally annoying. It forces the patch author to state why the fixture moved. Most agent diffs leave fixtures alone, so the cost is near zero. The benefit arrives the day a diff rewrites a fixture to match a bug.

Re-entry

Quarantine ends with evidence, not optimism. Run the test against clean main, twenty times, before you delete the entry.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/reentry.sh <nodeid>
set -euo pipefail
TEST_ID="$1"
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  pytest "$TEST_ID" -q || { echo "flake on run $i"; exit 1; }
done
python - "$TEST_ID" <<'PY'
import json, pathlib, sys
path = pathlib.Path("quarantine.json")
data = json.loads(path.read_text())
data["tests"] = [t for t in data["tests"] if t["id"] != sys.argv[1]]
path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2))
print("removed", sys.argv[1])
PY

Twenty passing runs on clean main is a weak guarantee, and you should say so out loud. It still beats deleting a skip because the log annoyed someone.

Deciding what to do

What you observe Ledger action Effect on the merge gate
Fails 2 of 10 runs on clean main Open entry with a 30-day expiry Excluded from the verdict, still recorded
Fails only on the agent diff No entry Merge blocked, treat as a real regression
Passes locally, fails in CI Freeze clock, timezone, locale New entry for the environment diff
Diff edits fixtures Fingerprint test fails Author must justify the change
Property fails on one seed Keep that seed as a regression Merge blocked until fixed

The rule behind the table is simple. Unknown failures lose their vote. Known failures keep it.

Where MonkeyCode fits

MonkeyCode is the operator's open-source project, and the fit here is narrow. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The operator states that free model access and a free server option are available, with a free allowance of 10 million tokens.

I have not verified quotas, hardware, or how long the offer lasts. Treat every limit as changeable and check the current terms before designing a nightly job around it. If the numbers hold for you, the free model access is where patch generation happens, and the free server option is where the repeated sweeps run. Fifty property runs per diff adds up quickly, and that repeated compute is exactly what a metered runner pushes you to skip.

Nothing above depends on MonkeyCode. Swap in any model and any runner, and the ledger, the properties, and the fingerprint test behave the same way.

Limits and who should skip this

A ledger without expiry becomes a graveyard. Review the skipped count monthly and treat growth as a bug. Property tests only work when you can state the invariant in one sentence. If you cannot, example tests are honest enough.

This approach fits three groups poorly. Teams with a deterministic suite should fix the flake and move on. Teams that need per-test evidence for compliance should not hide tests behind a skip marker. Teams without a named ledger owner should not start, because the file will rot within a quarter.

Start with one entry and one property. The ledger is not a place to hide failures. It is a record of what you do not know yet, with a date attached.
