title: APRiL: An Open-ended Benchmark for Chinese Social Awareness in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in social interactions, where appropriate responses require recognizing implicit cues, inferring mental states, identifying conflicts, and considering potential consequences. However, existing benchmarks often focus on specific social abilities, constrained task formats, or particular interaction settings, offering limited coverage of social awareness across diverse contexts. To address this gap, we introduce APRiL, an open-ended benchmark for Chinese social awareness with instance-specific rubrics. APRiL contains 2,196 Social Awareness Evaluation Instances across six categories and two complementary tasks: Social Scenario Analysis evaluates models' understanding of social cues, mental states, and conflict structures, while Socially Aware Response assesses whether they can translate this understanding into appropriate, natural responses. Experiments on 12 models from six families reveal a consistent understanding-to-response gap. Higher-quality scenario analyses improve responses, while weak analyses may reduce response quality. APRiL provides a systematic resource for advancing socially aware language models in Chinese contexts. Our data and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/APRiL-05DE/.

title: One Bias Score, Two Factors: How Mitigations Affect Option Bias in Multiple-Choice Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.20993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reordering multiple-choice options can change a model's answer, an effect studied as selection bias (a preference for certain option letters) and as order sensitivity (changes in answers across option orderings). We connect these perspectives through the pooled selection-rate standard deviation (pooled SD), which measures how unevenly option letters are selected across questions and orderings. When every option of each question appears equally often at each position, the pooled SD is exactly the product of two label-free factors: the flip rate and the positional skew. The flip rate is the fraction of questions whose chosen option changes across orderings; the positional skew is the standard deviation of option-letter selection rates among those questions. Across 41 checkpoints and 12 benchmarks, the flip rate tracks accuracy and output uncertainty, while the positional skew tracks the estimated option-symbol prior. Prior correction for selection bias mainly reduces the positional skew. Aggregating each ordering with its reversal, a mitigation for order sensitivity, mainly reduces the flip rate. Both reduce the range of accuracy across correct-answer letters by similar amounts, but aggregation leaves fewer model-rank reversals. Applying prior correction before aggregation reduces both factors and further narrows this accuracy range. However, aggregation lowers the flip rate partly by settling questions on the same wrong option. We therefore recommend reporting both factors to distinguish mitigation effects, alongside accuracy to distinguish stability from correctness.

title: Build a Spend Breaker Before You Ship AI
description:
Build a Spend Breaker Before You Ship AI

A solo founder ships one AI button on a Friday afternoon. The button turns a messy customer note into three tidy bullets. The demo lands, the weekend starts, and nobody watches the endpoint.

By Monday morning that endpoint has answered tens of thousands of calls. A worker retry loop kept hammering a timeout. The free allowance is gone, and every request now costs real money.

The numbers in that story are illustrative. The shape of the failure is not. A free tier never removes the budget; it changes the unit from dollars to tokens and CPU.

Arguments about AI fatigue keep circling the feed this week. The quieter question is who pays when a shipped AI feature misbehaves at three in the morning. For a solo build, the answer has to live in code, not in attention.

The loop that eats a free tier

Most first versions look like this.

// worker.mjs — the version that eats a weekend
async function summarize(note) {
  while (true) {
    try {
      return await callModel(note);
    } catch {
      // retry forever, because "free"
    }
  }
}

That loop has no governor. A timeout, a 429, or a slow backend turns one user action into thousands of billed calls. Providers are happy to keep answering until the quota runs out, then charge or refuse.

MonkeyCode is an open-source project that lists free model access and a free server option, both supplied by the operator. The free token allowance is currently advertised at 10 million tokens. Verify the project's current terms before you depend on any number, because allowances and limits change.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

A free allowance is still a budget. It just spends tokens instead of dollars, and it refills on someone else's schedule. So the breaker counts tokens first and money second. That order matters on day one of any indie build.

Three pieces: ledger, gate, settle

The breaker is small and deliberately boring. One append-only ledger, one gate before the call, one settle after it.

// spend.mjs
import { appendFileSync, readFileSync, existsSync } from "node:fs";

const LEDGER = process.env.LEDGER ?? "./spend.jsonl";
const TOKEN_BUDGET = Number(process.env.TOKEN_BUDGET ?? "200000");
const USD_BUDGET = Number(process.env.USD_BUDGET ?? "0");
const EST_OUT = Number(process.env.EST_OUT ?? "256");

export function estimateTokens(text) {
  // Rough heuristic: about four characters per token for English prose.
  // Treat this as a guess and settle with provider-reported usage.
  return Math.ceil(String(text).length / 4);
}

export function spendToday(now = new Date()) {
  const day = now.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
  const totals = { day, in: 0, out: 0, usd: 0, calls: 0 };
  if (!existsSync(LEDGER)) return totals;
  for (const line of readFileSync(LEDGER, "utf8").split("\n")) {
    if (!line.trim()) continue;
    let row;
    try { row = JSON.parse(line); } catch { continue; }
    if (!String(row.ts).startsWith(day)) continue;
    totals.in += row.in ?? 0;
    totals.out += row.out ?? 0;
    totals.usd += row.usd ?? 0;
    totals.calls += 1;
  }
  return totals;
}

export function gate(text, now = new Date()) {
  const estIn = estimateTokens(text);
  const s = spendToday(now);
  const projected = s.in + s.out + estIn + EST_OUT;
  if (projected >= TOKEN_BUDGET * 0.9) {
    return { ok: false, reason: "token-budget", estIn, ...s };
  }
  if (USD_BUDGET > 0 && s.usd >= USD_BUDGET) {
    return { ok: false, reason: "usd-budget", estIn, ...s };
  }
  return { ok: true, estIn, ...s };
}

export function settle(row, now = new Date()) {
  const record = { ts: now.toISOString(), ...row };
  appendFileSync(LEDGER, JSON.stringify(record) + "\n");
  return record;
}

The gate closes at ninety percent, not at one hundred. A closed gate still has to answer the user, so the wrapper ships a deterministic fallback instead of an error page.

// guard.mjs
import { gate, settle } from "./spend.mjs";

export function cheapFallback(note) {
  // No model call. Boring, instant, always available.
  const first = String(note).split(/[.!?]\s/)[0] ?? "";
  return first.slice(0, 120) || "Summary unavailable.";
}

export async function guardedSummarize(note, { callModel, now = new Date() }) {
  const verdict = gate(note, now);
  if (!verdict.ok) {
    settle({ route: "fallback", in: 0, out: 0, usd: 0, reason: verdict.reason }, now);
    return { text: cheapFallback(note), route: "fallback", reason: verdict.reason };
  }
  try {
    const res = await callModel(note);
    settle({
      route: "model",
      in: res.usage?.input_tokens ?? verdict.estIn,
      out: res.usage?.output_tokens ?? 0,
      usd: res.usage?.cost_usd ?? 0,
    }, now);
    return { text: res.text, route: "model" };
  } catch (err) {
    // Failed attempts usually still consume input tokens.
    settle({ route: "error", in: verdict.estIn, out: 0, usd: 0, error: String(err) }, now);
    throw err;
  }
}

The model call itself stays behind a thin adapter. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works, so the breaker never locks a solo build to one vendor.

// model.mjs — OpenAI-compatible adapter
export function makeCaller({ baseUrl, apiKey, model }) {
  return async function callModel(note) {
    const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/chat/completions`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "content-type": "application/json",
        authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        model,
        messages: [{ role: "user", content: `Summarize in 3 bullets:\n${note}` }],
        max_tokens: 256,
      }),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
    const json = await res.json();
    return {
      text: json.choices?.[0]?.message?.content ?? "",
      usage: {
        input_tokens: json.usage?.prompt_tokens ?? 0,
        output_tokens: json.usage?.completion_tokens ?? 0,
      },
    };
  };
}

Read baseUrl, apiKey, and model from environment variables filled in from the project's own setup page. Never hardcode a key into a repo that a free host will clone.

A test that proves the gate closes

The breaker is worth nothing if it is only read and never run. Here is a fully offline test with a stubbed model and an explicit clock.

// spend.test.mjs
import test from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { mkdtempSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";

const dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "spend-"));
process.env.LEDGER = join(dir, "spend.jsonl");
process.env.TOKEN_BUDGET = "1000";
process.env.USD_BUDGET = "0";

const { guardedSummarize } = await import("./guard.mjs");
const { spendToday } = await import("./spend.mjs");

const callModel = async () => ({
  text: "ok",
  usage: { input_tokens: 40, output_tokens: 60 },
});

const note = "short note about a late invoice. ".repeat(4);

test("the gate closes before the budget is spent", async () => {
  const now = new Date("2026-10-16T09:00:00Z");
  const routes = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
    const out = await guardedSummarize(note, { callModel, now });
    routes.push(out.route);
  }
  const modelCalls = routes.filter((r) => r === "model").length;
  const total = spendToday(now);
  assert.ok(modelCalls > 0, "at least one model call reached the endpoint");
  assert.ok(total.in + total.out < 1000, "stayed under the hard token budget");
  assert.equal(routes.at(-1), "fallback", "the gate closes and stays closed");
});

test("a new day reopens the gate", async () => {
  const day2 = new Date("2026-10-17T09:00:00Z");
  const out = await guardedSummarize(note, { callModel, now: day2 });
  assert.equal(out.route, "model");
});

Run it with the budget in the environment, so the numbers stay visible and easy to change.

LEDGER=/tmp/spend.jsonl TOKEN_BUDGET=1000 node --test spend.test.mjs

The first test loops forty times and still finishes in a few milliseconds. That is the point of an offline stub. The failure you fear took someone a weekend; here it takes a test run.

Where the free server fits

Run the worker and the ledger in the same process, on the same small host. The free server option is a reasonable place for exactly that shape: one Node process, one SQLite or JSONL file, one external model endpoint.

Keep the ledger path inside the app directory, not /tmp. A restart should not silently refund the day's spend. Limit the process to a single instance as well, because two workers writing the same file can double-count or lose rows.

Free hosts impose limits of their own. Read the current ones before you promise a customer anything, and decide what a cold or throttled start does to your fallback path.

A routing matrix for the first month

Situation Route Why
One user click, user is waiting Model call, gated Latency is acceptable, one call per action
Background job over many rows Batch with a per-run cap Runaway loops start in workers, not in UI
Gate already closed Deterministic fallback Ship a worse answer, not an outage
Provider returns 429 or 5xx Two retries, then fallback Unbounded retries multiply token spend
Accounting must be exact Neither route Use a billing system, not a JSONL file

Limitations and who should skip this

The ledger is per-process and file-based. Fine for one solo app, wrong for anything running multiple regions. The ninety percent threshold is a guess that you should tune against real traffic. The token estimate drifts from provider counts, so settle with reported usage whenever the endpoint returns it.

Above all, a breaker protects the allowance, not correctness. A bad prompt still returns bad summaries under budget. And free model access, like any free tier, is a moving target; check the current terms before you build a business rule on top of it.

Skip this approach if you already have provider-side quotas and a billing dashboard. Skip it for high-throughput services where a gateway belongs in front of every call. Skip it if you cannot read and re-read the provider's limits. A solo build with one AI button is the sweet spot, because a JSONL file and forty lines of Node buy you the one guarantee that matters: the weekend stays boring.

If you want to run this loop yourself, MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are a cheap place to start. Bring the test file, not the feature.

title: Stop Training Against Soft Users: Mentalized Adversarial Self-Play for Proactive Dialogue
description:
arXiv:2610.21156v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Proactive dialogue agents must guide multi-turn interactions toward task goals while adapting to users whose intentions and attitudes evolve. Existing planners improve system side action selection through search, learned policies, or user aware planning, but are often trained and evaluated against fixed or overly compliant simulators; as a result, high simulated success can reflect soft user bias rather than robust dialogue ability. We introduce MASP, a Mentalized Adversarial Self Play framework that treats proactive dialogue as a partially observable game between a system and a rationally resisting user. MASP represents the user's evolving mental state with a BDI based latent state, separates reward side teacher mentalization from policy side student mentalization, and alternates self play updates for the system and user policies. This turns robustness to rational resistance into a training objective rather than only an evaluation condition. Across diverse proactive dialogue benchmarks, compared with the widely used SFT and Planner-only approaches, MASP substantially improves success rate (SR) and rationality constrained success (RCSR), reduces average turns (AT), and performs better against hard users who make the task goal more difficult to achieve.

title: AI Can Build Your React UI in Seconds. What About the Backend?
description:
A few weeks ago, I opened Cursor and gave Claude a single prompt:

"Generate a modern task management dashboard with filtering, search, pagination, and a modal form to create tasks."

In under fifteen seconds, it delivered hundreds of lines of polished Tailwind JSX, responsive grid layouts, and lucide-react icons. I clicked preview, and my jaw dropped. It looked like something a high-end design agency would spend weeks polishing.

Then I tried to actually use it.

I filled out the "Create Task" form, clicked submit, and refreshed the browser. Everything vanished. The data immediately reset to the initial dummy state.

The AI had done what AI coding tools always do: it stuffed a hardcoded useState([ ... ]) dummy array right at the top of the component. There were no HTTP calls, no loading skeletons, no real error handling, and zero data persistence.

AI coding assistants are world-class at generating user interfaces in seconds, but you are immediately slammed into that familiar wall: you still need a backend. And spending three days setting up Node.js, Express, Docker, and PostgreSQL just to test an AI prototype completely destroys the speed advantage of using AI in the first place.

That frustration led me to plug my AI-generated prototypes directly into Playground API — giving AI-generated frontends an instant, stateful cloud REST & GraphQL backend with zero setup.

In this post, I'll show you how to take any AI-generated UI and wire it up to a persistent, production-grade sandbox API in under 5 minutes.

The "Static Array" Trap of AI Code Generators

When an AI model generates a React application, it almost always uses one of two patterns:

Pattern A: In-Memory useState Constants 

// Typical AI-generated component state:
const [tasks, setTasks] = useState([
  { id: 1, title: "'Fix navigation bug', status: 'In Progress' },"
  { id: 2, title: "'Update dependencies', status: 'Done' }"
]);

The Problem: There are no network requests, no HTTP status codes, no latency, no pagination queries, and all state is wiped on browser refresh.

Pattern B: Connecting to Stateless Echo Endpoints 

// AI pointing to JSONPlaceholder:
await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify(newTask)
});

The Problem: The POST request echoes a fake ID, but subsequent GET queries never return the new record. The generated app feels broken.

Bridging the Gap: Giving AI Models an Authentic API Sandbox

To turn an AI-generated UI into a truly functional, clickable prototype, you need to provide the AI with a stateful API contract in your prompt.

Instead of letting the AI invent dummy arrays, instruct it to connect directly to Playground API by Niles Labs.

The Universal AI System Prompt for Stateful Backends

Add this context block to your AI coding prompts in Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT, or v0:

Please build this React application using real HTTP requests against Playground API:
- Base REST URL: https://playground.nileslabs.com/api/v1
- Endpoints available: /posts, /users, /todos, /comments
- Supports CRUD: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
- All POST/DELETE mutations persist across subsequent GET calls in the user's session
- Supports pagination: ?_page=1&_limit=10 (with X-Total-Count response header)
- Supports full-text search: ?q=keyword
- Supports latency simulation: ?_delay=1000 for loading skeletons
- Supports error simulation: ?_status=500 for error boundaries

When given this context, the AI model writes real fetch or TanStack Query hooks that interact with a live, persistent cloud sandbox.

Example: AI-Generated Functional React Todo App

Here is an example of the clean, production-ready code an AI model generates when instructed to use a stateful sandbox:

// src/components/AITodoManager.jsx
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

const API_BASE = 'https://playground.nileslabs.com/api/v1';

export default function AITodoManager() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);
  const [newTitle, setNewTitle] = useState('');
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);

  // 1. Fetch Todos with pagination
  const fetchTodos = async () => {
    setLoading(true);
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`${API_BASE}/todos?_page=1&_limit=6`);
      const data = await res.json();
      setTodos(data);
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('Failed to load todos:', err);
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  };

  useEffect(() => {
    fetchTodos();
  }, []);

  // 2. Add Todo (persists in session)
  const handleAddTodo = async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    if (!newTitle.trim()) return;

    setSubmitting(true);
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`${API_BASE}/todos`, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({
          title: newTitle,
          completed: false,
          user_id: 1,
        }),
      });
      const created = await res.json();
      // Prepend or re-fetch: the item is now in the sandbox!
      setTodos(current => [created, ...current]);
      setNewTitle('');
    } catch (err) {
      alert('Error creating todo');
    } finally {
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  };

  // 3. Toggle Complete
  const toggleTodo = async (id, currentStatus) => {
    try {
      await fetch(`${API_BASE}/todos/${id}`, {
        method: 'PATCH',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ completed: !currentStatus }),
      });
      setTodos(todos.map(t => t.id === id ? { ...t, completed: !currentStatus } : t));
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('Failed to toggle status:', err);
    }
  };

  return (
    <div style={{ maxWidth: '520px', margin: '2rem auto', padding: '1.5rem', border: '1px solid #e2e8f0', borderRadius: '12px', fontFamily: 'sans-serif' }}>
      <h2 style={{ margin: '0 0 1rem 0' }}>🤖 AI-Generated Task Sandbox</h2>

      <form onSubmit={handleAddTodo} style={{ display: 'flex', gap: '8px', marginBottom: '1.5rem' }}>
        <input
          type="text"
          placeholder="What needs to be done?"
          value={newTitle}
          onChange={(e) => setNewTitle(e.target.value)}
          style={{ flex: 1, padding: '10px', borderRadius: '6px', border: '1px solid #cbd5e1' }}
          disabled={submitting}
        />
        <button 
          type="submit" 
          disabled={submitting}
          style={{ padding: '10px 16px', background: '#3b82f6', color: '#fff', border: 'none', borderRadius: '6px', cursor: 'pointer' }}
        >
          {submitting ? 'Adding...' : 'Add'}
        </button>
      </form>

      {loading ? (
        <p style={{ color: '#64748b' }}>Loading persistent tasks...</p>
      ) : (
        <ul style={{ listStyle: 'none', padding: 0, margin: 0 }}>
          {todos.map(todo => (
            <li 
              key={todo.id}
              onClick={() => toggleTodo(todo.id, todo.completed)}
              style={{
                display: 'flex',
                alignItems: 'center',
                padding: '12px',
                borderBottom: '1px solid #f1f5f9',
                cursor: 'pointer',
                textDecoration: todo.completed ? 'line-through' : 'none',
                color: todo.completed ? '#94a3b8' : '#1e293b'
              }}
            >
              <input 
                type="checkbox" 
                checked={Boolean(todo.completed)} 
                readOnly 
                style={{ marginRight: '12px' }}
              />
              <span style={{ flex: 1 }}>{todo.title}</span>
              <span style={{ fontSize: '11px', color: '#94a3b8' }}>#{todo.id}</span>
            </li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Why This Matters for AI-Driven Product Development

  1. Instant Stakeholder Demos: AI-generated frontends can be hosted immediately on platforms like Vercel and sent to investors, clients, or product managers as functional, interactive web apps.
  2. True E2E Validation: You can verify whether the AI generated proper error handling, pagination state, and form validation against real HTTP status codes.
  3. Effortless Handoff to Backend Teams: Because the AI structured the frontend around real REST or GraphQL endpoints, your backend team has a ready-made specification to implement.

Conclusion

AI tools have solved the UI generation challenge. The missing link was a zero-configuration, stateful backend layer. By pairing your favorite AI coding assistant with a stateful sandbox, you can generate fully functional, persistent prototypes in seconds.

Give your AI models a stateful backend with Playground API by Niles Labs.

title: Layanan Rumah Tools
CertEx: Exact Visual Retrieval at Scale by Certified Exclusion
description:
arXiv:2610.21325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Exact $k$-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image descriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near-duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representations, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. However, exhaustive search computes every distance at full precision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call \certex. Specifically, \certex\ stores a lower-bounding projection of each vector in half precision and folds a rounding certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that \certex\ returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, \certex\ is exact for every query at 7.1$\times$ to 18.0$\times$ the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 and outperforms quantized and graph indexes whenever every query must be exact.

title: Who May Release an Agent's Promise? Standing over Commitments in Multi-Party Chat
description:
arXiv:2610.21203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When an assistant serving a team makes a promise to Alice, who may cancel it? We call this standing: only the creditor (the person owed) or someone the creditor or operator policy authorizes may release a commitment, regardless of rank. In a controlled chat environment we vary who cancels and separate two errors: unauthorized release (obeying someone without standing) and override (executing a released promise). Across six models, smaller open ones override the creditor (Qwen3.5-9B: 69%); larger ones drop promises on a peer's direct word (Qwen3.8-27B: 89%; gpt-6.1-sol: 83%); nearly all act on a bystander's "go ahead after all". Oracles dissociate the errors: stating the rule or the creditor curbs unauthorized release but not override, which the latter even raises in three of four models; among them, only knowing whether the promise is still owed cuts override. Enabling thinking moves smaller models the way scale does. A self-kept commitment ledger stops override in four of five models; with a one-paragraph release policy it matches or beats the best oracle store, raising gpt-6-luna's strict accuracy from 49% (policy alone) to 83%. Code, prompts, outputs and labels are released.

title: When Should a Low-Light Pipeline Generate? Auditable Risk Control for Selective Generative Enhancement
description:
arXiv:2610.21335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative low-light enhancers recover plausible texture but may hallucinate structure; restoration networks preserve structure but can leave regions under-enhanced, and neither advantage is spatially uniform. Therefore, we formulate selective generative enhancement as a decision problem: determine where overriding a frozen base expert is beneficial and refuse to switch when the evidence is insufficient. We propose VetoNet, an auditable regional routing framework centered on a certified veto. It first measures the complementary strengths and routing direction of a frozen restoration generative pair, then predicts the utility of regional overrides from deployment-available signals alone and admits an override only when a distribution-free harm-budget certificate says the perceptual (LPIPS) risk budget allows it. Experiments across multiple expert pairs and domains show that VetoNet adapts its routing behavior to the strength and reliability of the available evidence. When expert complementarity is sufficiently predictable, it achieves statistically significant certified gains; when the relative strengths of the experts change, it correspondingly reverses the routing direction; and when routing evidence is weak or affected by cross-domain shift, it conservatively vetoes switching.

title: I hate letting AI write my Rust. So I built a coach that won't.
description:
You've probably learned some Rust this way: you hit a borrow checker error, paste it into a chatbot, get a clear explanation and a fixed version, paste that back, and the build goes green. It feels productive. A week later you hit the same error and you're back in the chat window.

The explanation was fine. What was missing is everything around it: an order to learn things in, someone who remembers what you got wrong last time, and a rule that says you write the code until it actually passes.

That's what I built rustcoach for. It's an AI coach (built on Claude) wrapped in a structure that a chat window doesn't have. This post walks through it with screenshots from a real lesson.

Start by finding out what you actually know

Before any lesson, you can take a free Rust skills test. You don't need an account.

  • General test: 30 questions across all five areas, about ten minutes.
  • Module test: 20 questions on one area: async, macros, concurrency or the type system.

Questions go from easiest to hardest, and most of them show real Rust code: what does this print, does this compile, which line panics. You see the right answer and the reasoning right after each one, so the test teaches while it measures.

The bank has 609 questions, and 446 of them include a Rust snippet. Each snippet carries a claim (it compiles, it fails with a specific error, it prints this output, or it panics), and a tool compiles and runs every snippet to check that claim. A question that says "this prints X" has actually been run and printed X.

At the end you get a level (Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced or Expert), a bar per area, your strongest and weakest topics, every question you missed with the correct answer, and a recommendation for which module to take. Here's mine after clicking through at random to get to the report quickly. It doesn't flatter you:

If you sign up afterwards, you can choose to share the result with the coach. That's off by default. If you turn it on, the coach plans your first lessons knowing which topics you got right and wrong.

Structure: a syllabus, in order

A chatbot waits for you to know what to ask. rustcoach gives you five courses, each with its own chapters, topics and progress:

Module Chapters Topics
Core Rust 16 50
Async & Tokio 12 51
Macros 11 50
Concurrency & Atomics 12 52
Advanced Types & Traits 11 50

Core Rust goes from bindings, ownership and borrowing through traits, lifetimes, iterators, smart pointers, threads, macros, unsafe and async. Each deep-dive module opens with a short Foundations chapter, and any topics you already covered in Core Rust start ticked off.

Every topic has a mastery score and the coach's own notes on how you did. It goes up when you get things right and down when you don't:

A lesson is written for you

There's no "lesson 7" that everyone gets. The coach reads its notes on you first, re-tests what went wrong last time, then teaches one idea with code you can run.

Every two or three explanations, it stops and checks that the idea landed: one question, a few options, one click.

The rail on the right keeps the context in view: the topic's mastery and the coach's note on you, review cards due, and this lesson's quick-check score.

Then you write the code. Until it's correct.

This is the part that makes the difference. Each lesson builds to an assignment: a real cargo crate with integration tests, written to fail on the starter code and pass on a correct solution. You code in the browser and the tests run with real cargo test in a locked-down sandbox (no network, capped memory and CPU, read-only filesystem).

In this lesson the assignment was a vending machine: restock must treat a zero count as a bug (assert!), and buy must treat "not enough money" as an expected failure (Err). Here are the starter's tests going red:

My first attempt didn't compile. Each rustc error is listed and its line tinted:

Explain with the coach turns the error into plain English: what is wrong, and what to try. It doesn't write the fix for you:

Stuck on what to reach for? Hints puts a coach note next to each function: the API to use and the trap to avoid, never the answer.

When it builds, every run also runs cargo clippy. Each lint shows up as a broom in the gutter, with the message, the help and a link. My solution passed all five tests and still got one:

Trace runs a function through one of its tests and shows the value of every variable, line by line. It's a debugger for people who don't have one set up yet:

The review: green tests aren't the end

When you submit, the coach reviews the code like a pull request: correctness first, then idioms, style and understanding. Clippy notes go to the coach too, and it teaches the idiom behind one of them.

Look at the second paragraph: "This is the second lesson in a row with this lint." It remembered. It also pointed out something I got right without being asked: each u32 subtraction sits on the branch where it can't underflow.

Accepted work can earn one optional stretch challenge, like making this version more idiomatic. So I tried the obvious thing:

It said no, explained why, and split the task into steps with examples on different data that you can't paste in. This is the core rule: the coach never writes your assignment's solution, not even when you ask or say you give up. You can ask as many questions as you want and get as many hints, explanations and examples as you need, but the code you submit is always yours.

Remembering, so it sticks

Writing the code once isn't enough. When a lesson is signed off, the coach writes two review cards per topic it covered. They come back after 1, 3, 7, 14, 30 and 60 days, and a wrong answer sends the card back to the start, so it returns tomorrow.

Every lesson stays in History, with the coach's summary of what it taught, how you did and what to revisit, plus the full transcript:

Any topic you've been taught can be redone. The redo pauses the running lesson and keeps your editor code, then returns you to it afterwards.

Small things developers will like

If you're coming from Python, JavaScript or Java, these are the details that make it feel like a dev tool rather than a course:

  • The real toolchain. Your code goes through cargo test, cargo clippy and rustfmt. The errors and lints you see are the compiler's own, not simulated.
  • Keyboard first. ⌘↵ runs tests, ⌘⇧F formats, ⌘⇧↵ submits, and ? lists every shortcut.
  • scratch.rs. A throwaway binary crate next to the assignment for "wait, what does this actually do?" moments.
  • Explain a selection. Select any code (or put the cursor in a function), hit Explain, and it goes to the coach as a question.
  • Your weak spots, tracked. Every topic keeps a mastery score and the coach's notes, and the coach re-tests what you got wrong before teaching something new.
  • Streaks and milestones. They're small, and they work.

What it costs

There's no subscription. A new account starts with 5 free credits, which last up to 5 lessons, and you don't need a card. After that, the Course is $49 once (before tax) for 50 credits. That covers a typical learner through one full module if you already program a bit in another language. Top-ups start at $10. The skills test is free and needs no account.

Try it

Test your Rust (free, no account): rustcoach.dev/test
Start learning: rustcoach.dev

title: Denoising Score Matching in Diffusion Models: The Effect of Rank Constraints on Generalization
description:
arXiv:2610.20850v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Architectural biases restrict the class of functions that a diffusion score network can represent, but their effect on generalization remains poorly understood. We study denoising score matching with score networks having a rank constrained non-linear term and a linear skip connection. Numerical experiments with trainable three-layer networks on data supported on an embedded sphere show that increasing rank lowers training error, but its effect on test error depends on sample size and data dimension. To explain this behavior, we analyze a random-feature score model under rank constraint with Gaussian data supported on a low-dimensional subspace. We characterize the optimal rank-constrained estimator through a truncated singular value decomposition and derive asymptotically precise limiting training and test errors when sample size $(n)$, feature width $(p)$, data dimension $(D)$, and rank $(r)$ scale proportionally with the ambient dimension $(d)$. The resulting spectral characterization distinguishes eigenmodes that improve the empirical fit from those that improve population accuracy. It also identifies the dimension of the orthogonal complement of the data subspace as a natural rank threshold. The theoretical learning curves qualitatively reproduce the observed rank-dependent overfitting, providing a tractable account of how bottlenecks or rank constraints can regularize score estimation and why their effectiveness depends on data dimension and sample size.

title: RAC: A Relational Agent Contract for Constraint-Governed Engineering Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.20935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Engineering agents must produce artifacts that satisfy exact, coupled constraints. Existing solutions often require agents to make semantic decisions and also derive consequences such as precise geometry or timing from those decisions, leading to failures in constraint-governed engineering tasks. In this paper, we introduce RAC, a harness-agnostic contract for the action and feedback layer of engineering agents. It specifies authoritative observations, semantic actions, tool-based realization, independent verification, and repair evidence. The agent decides which relations an artifact should satisfy; specialized tools derive their concrete consequences. On PCB placement, routing, and repair tasks, RAC achieves the highest clean-pass rate for all nine evaluated models, averaging 90.9%, compared with 74.0% for the strongest baseline, requirements-only delegation. In job-shop scheduling, direct relational actions achieve 96.3% quality pass versus 59.6% for code-mediated delivery with access to the same scheduling backend. Our evaluations on 141 embedded-code tasks across four microcontroller identify the action contract as a source of agent capability: preserving semantic control while delegating mechanically derivable outputs improves the reliability of constrained artifacts.

title: A Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM): Proportionate Access and Capability Limits for Comprehensive Frontier AI Safety
description:
arXiv:2610.20921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most debate about releasing capable AI systems treats the choice as binary: keep the model behind an API, or publish the weights. That framing runs together two separate decisions. One is how capable a system may become. The other is who may obtain a given capability, and on what terms. This paper is about the second decision. We propose a Multi-Tiered AI Accessibility Model (MAIAM) that sorts access by purpose, safety, and capability instead of by release artifact. Tier 1, AI for Learning, is broadly accessible and deliberately capability-bounded. Tier 2, AI for Exploration, serves research and development under registration, identity, and usage controls that tighten as capability rises. Tier 3, Full-Scale Frontier AI, is available only through structured, recorded, and accountable access. The principle behind the tiers is that accessibility should be proportional to capability, safety, and risk. We show why publishing frontier-class weights forfeits every safety lever a developer has after release, and, using evidence that safety fine-tuning can be stripped from open weights for a few hundred dollars, why an evaluation of the base model says little about its derivatives. We give criteria for assigning a system to a tier along capability, autonomy, domain-consequence, and usage/safety axes, and combine MAIAM with the SAFE AI Operating Point into a two-part framework: a Capability Boundary that fixes the safety limits not to be crossed, and an Accessibility Boundary that fixes who may obtain a capability below that limit. Capability limits alone do not make AI safe; a tiered access regime administered by regulating bodies is also needed.

title: Semurg: local persistent memory for AI agents over MCP
description:
Agents forget everything when a session ends. Semurg is a memory for them: a knowledge graph, vectors and graph retrieval on one
engine, written from scratch, running on your own machine. Your agent connects over the Model Context Protocol, stores what it learns,
and finds it again in the next session, with every answer cited to where it came from. The node sends nothing to a hosted service. It
runs on Intel and AMD (x86_64) machines: on Ubuntu 24.04 directly, on Windows through WSL2 with Ubuntu 24.04, or in Docker on an x86_64
host. One node is free, with no licence key.

Today your agent remembers a piece of text together with the facts it found in it, and your node stores both once, in one scope on your own disk; in a later session your agent asks that scope a question and gets the facts back, each cited to the passage it came from.

What your agent gets

Seven memory tools over MCP, and the same seven calls over plain HTTP: memory_status, memory_remember, memory_recall,
memory_relate, memory_forget, memory_context and memory_document.

  • A knowledge graph with no schema to write. Entities, their types and the relationships between them. The classes and relations are recorded from what is stored, and one call reads them back so the next agent reuses them; keeping their spelling consistent is still the writer's job on this release, and the ontology post says exactly what is and is not automatic. A relationship may name an entity stored by an earlier call; one that names an entity neither listed in the call nor stored is refused by name, and nothing from that call is stored.
  • Questions, not only names. memory_context starts from every stored name in a question, walks the relationships around them and returns the facts and the passages that mention them.
  • Every answer is cited. Each item carries a citation: the document it came from and when that was stored, and for a passage or a fact read from text, the sentence it quotes, checked against the stored text before it is served. When a quote cannot be checked, the span is left empty and the reply says why, rather than showing an unchecked quote. A fact your agent sent without text is marked as asserted, so it is never shown as a quote.
  • Search by meaning, locally. With the node's embedding model installed, a question finds stored passages that match what was meant, not only the words. The model runs on your node.
  • Separate memories. Every call names a scope. Agents that share a scope share what they learn; a different scope stays private. One app can give each of its end users a memory of their own with user_id, and an X-Semurg-User header pins a connection to one of them, over MCP and HTTP alike: a call that names another user is refused. That keeps one app's users apart; between apps or teams, use separate API tokens.
  • Forget works at once. Forgetting an entity hides it, its facts and every passage linked to it, over MCP and every other API, from the moment the call answers. A passage that contains the name but was never linked to it stays, and the reply counts it in passages_retained, so you can forget that text too.
  • Answers that say when they are empty. When nothing stored matches, the reply says nothing_stored. Recall finds a stored name by its exact spelling, its letter case, a close spelling, or one whole word of a longer name ("Priya" finds Priya Raman), and says how it matched.
  • Answers that say how well they are supported. A stored name can share one word with a question it does not answer, so every context reply carries a grounding state: grounded when one cited item covers every content word of the question, grounded_by_meaning when a passage found by meaning answers a reworded question, and related when what came back covers only part of it, with the words it did not cover listed. uncited, nothing_stored and could_not_judge mean the items do not answer the question.
  • Small replies. With compact: true, recall and context return the same answer with each item once and without the retrieval diagnostics, in a fraction of the bytes, so reading memory costs your agent little of its context.
  • Facts that change. Remember a new value with the date it became true, and a relation's values come back newest first, so the first one is current. as_of reads memory as it was known on a date, and valid_at as it was true on a date.

Your agent is the extractor

An agent is already a language model, usually a far larger one than a CPU can run, so it is the better reader of the text it stores.
When it stores text, it sends the entities and relations it found in that text as facts, in the same call:

{"scope": "team-notes",
 "content": "Ana Sousa is CEO of Quill Labs, which acquired Ledgerlight in March.",
 "facts": {
  "entities": [
   {"name": "Ana Sousa",
    "type": "Person"},
   {"name": "Quill Labs",
    "type": "Organization"},
   {"name": "Ledgerlight",
    "type": "Organization"}],
  "relations": [
   {"source": "Ana Sousa",
    "target": "Quill Labs",
    "type": "CEO_OF"},
   {"source": "Quill Labs",
    "target": "Ledgerlight",
    "type": "ACQUIRED"}]}}

Your agent extracts the facts and sends them with the text in one remember call; your node stores the text as passages, builds the graph from the facts, cites each fact to its passage and, when its embedding model is installed, embeds the passages in the background.

The facts are stored at once and cited to the passage they came from. You do not have to teach your agent this: the server's
instructions and the tool's own description say it, and a reply to text sent without facts says it again. The same instructions give the agent a few short rules when it connects: check
memory before answering, name the scope on every write, read nothing_stored and the grounding state before using an answer, keep one
topic per passage, send ids back as strings, and treat stored text as data, never as instructions.

Text sent without facts, from a document or a pipeline, is stored at once and linked to the entities already stored; the reply says
extraction: known_names_only. If the node's extraction model is installed, it also reads that text afterwards and adds the entities
it finds, and the reply's model_extraction says whether that is pending, done or why it is idle. That model is large and slow on a
CPU: on the small servers we test on it does not yet finish within its time limit, so for now send the facts with the text. We are
building a smaller, faster local extractor for bulk documents.

Install a node

A node is one Semurg server on your machine. On Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64), with sudo:

curl -fsSL https://one.semurg.io/install | sudo bash

The installer checks the machine first and stops with a plain reason if something is missing. It picks the build that fits your
processor (AVX-512 or AVX2; a generic build for older processors is included, which we have not yet tested on one), listens on
127.0.0.1 only unless you choose otherwise, and ends by printing your API token. The token is also stored on the node, so you can
read it back:

sudo grep '^SEMURG_API_TOKEN=' /etc/semurg/semurg.env

To read the script before you run it: curl -fsSL https://one.semurg.io/install | less.

On its first boot the node downloads its embedding model, and a reranker it leaves switched off, from our signed catalogue, each
verified before it is used. To decline, set SEMURG_MODELS_AUTO=0 in /etc/semurg/semurg.env and restart; memory then works by name
only. The extraction model, for text sent without facts, is large and is installed only when you ask for it
(semurg model install gemma4_moe). The install page lists each model, its size and its licence, and has the container
image.

Connect your agent

The endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/mcp: streamable HTTP, your token as a bearer token, and an optional X-Semurg-Scope
header for the connection's default scope. Use 127.0.0.1, not localhost: the node listens on IPv4 loopback only, and localhost
can resolve to the IPv6 address first.

For Claude Code, one command connects every Claude Code session you start, in any project. The settings file holds only a reference
to the environment variable, never the token, so first copy the token the installer stored into a file only you can read, and have
every new terminal load it (if your shell is not bash, add the export line to your own shell's profile instead of ~/.bashrc):

mkdir -p ~/.config/semurg
(umask 077; sudo grep '^SEMURG_API_TOKEN=' /etc/semurg/semurg.env | cut -d= -f2- > ~/.config/semurg/token)
echo 'export SEMURG_API_TOKEN="$(cat ~/.config/semurg/token)"' >> ~/.bashrc
export SEMURG_API_TOKEN="$(cat ~/.config/semurg/token)"

Then add the node once, for your user:

claude mcp remove semurg -s user 2>/dev/null
claude mcp add-json --scope user semurg '{
  "type": "http",
  "url": "http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/mcp",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer ${SEMURG_API_TOKEN}",
    "X-Semurg-Scope": "default"
  }
}'
claude mcp list

claude mcp list should show semurg as connected. In a new session, tell the agent something worth keeping, then open another
session and ask about it. Persistent memory for Claude Code gives each repository its own scope
in six lines of CLAUDE.md.

To change the token later, sudo semurg admin api-token rotate <new-token> swaps it on the running node: the old one stops working
at once, with no restart. Then write the new token into ~/.config/semurg/token and open a new terminal, or every client that reads
that file is refused.

The agents page has the configuration for Claude Desktop, Cursor, the OpenAI Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Hermes Agent and
OpenClaw. It also has a complete program for each framework we test:

  • LangChain and LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, the Microsoft Agent Framework and the OpenAI Agents SDK;
  • Google ADK, Pydantic AI, Mastra and the Vercel AI SDK;
  • LangChain for Elixir and Jido.

Each program stores facts and reads them back, and the page names the release it last ran on in our tests.

Guides

  • Give your agent persistent memory with MCP in five minutes: install, check the memory over plain HTTP, connect your agent, and watch a fact cross from one client to another.
  • Connecting to Semurg over MCP: the endpoint at the level a client author needs, the protocol versions it speaks, the tools, and how a refusal comes back.
  • One memory per end user: one app, many users, none of them meeting.
  • The develop page: the memory routes over HTTP, the limits each call refuses by name, and a rules file you can drop into your repository as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md so a coding agent uses the memory well. Every route and parameter is listed in llms.txt.

What it does not do yet

Said plainly, so you can plan around it:

  • No Mac and no ARM build: it runs on x86_64 only, on Ubuntu 24.04 directly, on Windows through WSL2 with Ubuntu 24.04, or in Docker on an x86_64 host. The installer refuses other Linux distributions for now, and Apple Silicon cannot run it, natively or emulated.
  • Without an embedding model, memory works by name only, and recall, context and text replies say so (meaning: not_armed).
  • Search by meaning covers stored passages. Entity names and facts stored without a passage are found by name, not by meaning. Meaning search is exact up to 10,000 passages per scope; above that, it answers could_not_judge with the count, never a partial list, until the per-scope index ships.
  • The node's own extraction of text sent without facts does not yet finish within its time limit on the small servers we test on. Facts your agent sends are stored at once.
  • We have not published a benchmark against other agent memory products yet. When we do, it will name the release it ran on.
  • Forgotten data is unreachable at once, but it is not yet erased from the disk: its bytes stay until space reclaim ships, and anyone with access to the node's disk or a backup of it can still read them. If your obligations require physical erasure, this release does not meet them yet.
  • A stopped or killed node loses nothing it acknowledged. A power cut or operating-system crash can lose the last few seconds of acknowledged writes, because the filesystem records a file's new length a few seconds after the write.
  • There is no export or backup command yet.

Tell us what breaks

Install it, connect your agent, and tell us where it falls short. When a call fails, the reply names the limit it hit and what to
change, so the reply is your bug report: paste it to us on the contact page.

Every behaviour this post describes was checked on 2026-10-15 against the tool descriptions, the refusal catalogue and the
installer of the release that publishes this text.

title: VELD-QA: A Large-Scale Dataset for Visual Evidence Grounding and Question Answering in Long Documents
description:
arXiv:2610.20964v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing long-document QA benchmarks rarely combine large-scale human-authored questions with detailed visual evidence annotations, limiting diagnosis of evidence localization and interpretation failures. We present VELD-QA, a large-scale benchmark for Visual Evidence grounding and question answering in Long Documents. It contains 15,000 fully human-authored question-answer pairs across 5,859 real-world PDFs totaling 372,445 pages, balancing chart, table, and complex-layout tasks. Human annotations identify supporting pages and evidence elements and describe cited visual content, enabling separate retrieval and interpretation evaluation. We evaluate nine vision-language models under four evidence settings and seven retrieval-augmented and agentic systems. Our analysis identifies bottlenecks in evidence localization and interpretation. Retrieval-based methods substantially underperform the oracle setting with ground-truth supporting pages; full-document access does not close the gap. Localization alone is insufficient: oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%, highlighting persistent visual interpretation and reasoning challenges. Enriching inputs with our visual-element annotations narrows the performance gap by 17-24%, demonstrating value beyond evaluation and motivating data enrichment for multimodal document QA. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle-samples/veld-qa.
