title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for HPC Job Scheduling: A Statistical Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.21008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers learned job selection for High-Performance Computing (HPC), but performance against heuristics alone does not establish value beyond action masking. Six DRL treatments are compared: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), and Deep Q-Network (DQN), each with and without masking. Three heuristics and a seed-paired masked uniform random control provide baselines across ten seeds on two real Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) workload traces, one homogeneous and one heterogeneous, under a common non-parametric framework. All masked treatments complete evaluation, whereas unmasked treatments are truncated. On the homogeneous trace, no masked DRL treatment significantly improves average waiting time or average and maximum bounded slowdown over the control. On the heterogeneous trace, MaskablePPO improves all three metrics relative to the control. Its average waiting time is equivalent to that of the three heuristics within a 10% margin, and its maximum bounded slowdown is 22% lower than that of Last-Come, First-Served (LCFS). MaskablePPO has the leading average waiting-time rank among complete treatments on both traces, but Nemenyi comparisons detect no significant difference from MaskableA2C. Among masked variants, MaskablePPO has the lowest recorded mean training time, while MaskableDQN has the lowest mean decision latency. These findings distinguish completion from baseline-specific scheduling gains and support including a masked random control when assessing the value of learned selection.

title: Founders Today vs Indie Hackers for SaaS Founders
description:
If you build a SaaS product, you have probably posted on Indie Hackers or thought about it. Founders Today is a newer community that overlaps with it in some ways and differs in others. The short version: Indie Hackers is better for long, open stories about building a business, and Founders Today is better for a launch page that stays listed and for quick feedback in a feed. Most SaaS founders get more from using both, for different jobs, than from picking one.

This guide compares them on what SaaS founders actually need: useful feedback, a launch, access to buyers, and a post that does not vanish in a day. It also says where each one falls short, including Founders Today, which is younger and smaller. If you landed here looking for an Indie Hackers alternative, start with what is actually missing for you. The answer changes which platform helps.

Founders Today vs Indie Hackers at a glance

Indie Hackers Founders Today
Format Forum threads, groups, interviews, and a podcast A feed of launches, discussions, and opportunities
Strongest at Open revenue stories and long build logs Launch pages that stay listed, and fast builder-to-builder talk
Product pages Product pages with milestones and updates Launch pages with media
Launch day No ranked launch day: you post and engage A launch system, currently in beta
Extra reach Podcast and newsletter Publisher widgets and a weekly newsletter feature
Track record Running since 2016, bought by Stripe in 2017, independent again since Newer, still early
Cost to join Free Free

The Indie Hackers column comes from its own product pages, podcast, and press coverage. The Founders Today column comes from Founders Today's own pages. Both sites change, so check them for anything new before you decide.

What Indie Hackers is best at

Indie Hackers started in 2016 as a place where founders share real revenue numbers and explain how they got there. Stripe bought it in 2017, as TechCrunch reported at the time, and it later returned to independence. Today it is a mix of forum threads, topic groups, interviews, a podcast, and product pages where you can post milestones and updates.

For a SaaS founder the strongest part is the culture of showing numbers. A post that says you went from 12 to 40 paying customers and shows what changed fits the site better than a polished announcement. If you can share your MRR, your churn, a pricing test that failed, or an acquisition channel that cost more than it returned, you are speaking the local language, and people tend to reply in kind.

The archive is the other asset. Years of interviews and build logs mean you can research how someone in your niche reached their first thousand dollars a month before you write a word of your own. Few communities have that depth.

The limits are mostly about format. It is a forum, so a thread gets most of its attention in the first day or two. If you cannot share revenue yet, you have less to talk about. And a bare link with no story or question attached gets ignored.

What Founders Today is best at, and where it is still early

Founders Today is a feed with launches, discussions, opportunities, and toolkits, plus a member directory where you can follow people and message them. For a SaaS founder the useful pieces are the launch page, which stays listed instead of rotating off a one-day leaderboard, and the discussion feed, where a short question can get answers without a long essay first.

It also runs distribution outside the feed. The publisher program places product widgets on partner blogs, and a weekly tools list goes out through newsletter partners. Treat those as channels to measure, not guarantees. Put a tracking link on your launch page and see what actually arrives.

It is fair to say what is not there yet. Founders Today is younger and smaller than Indie Hackers. The launch system is in beta, and push notification partnerships are still being built. There is no deep archive of revenue case studies like the one Indie Hackers has built over years. If archive depth and brand recognition are what you want, that is a real gap, and you should weigh it honestly.

Founders Today vs Indie Hackers on what SaaS founders care about

Getting useful feedback

Feedback quality depends more on how you ask than on where you ask. Both communities respond to specific questions: is this pricing page clear, which step of onboarding lost you, would you pay this much for this. The difference is format. Indie Hackers threads suit longer replies from people who have run a business, so a detailed critique usually comes from there. A feed suits quick reactions, so five fast opinions on a landing page are easy to collect on Founders Today.

Whichever you use, ask one question per post and say what you plan to change based on the answers. People reply more when they can see their reply will matter.

Launching a product

Indie Hackers gives you a product page and a post. There is no ranked launch day, so your launch is whatever you make of the post and the conversation under it. That suits founders who like to tell a story and stay in the comments for a couple of days.

Founders Today gives you a dedicated launch page with images and media that stays listed after launch week, plus the distribution described above. That suits founders who want a page to point people to long after the post has aged.

Either way, prepare assets first: a one-line description, three screenshots, a short demo, and one clear call to action. If you are comparing launch options more widely, the Product Hunt alternative page and the list of free startup launch platforms with active communities cover the rest of the field.

Reaching buyers, not just builders

Be honest about who is reading. Both audiences are mostly builders. If you sell to developers, indie founders, or other SaaS teams, you are posting in front of possible buyers, and either platform can send real signups. If you sell to dentists, recruiters, or HR managers, these communities will give you feedback, credibility, and links, but your buyers are somewhere else.

In that case use founder communities to sharpen the product and the pitch, then spend your selling time where your buyers gather. The best SaaS founder communities list and the SaaS community page can help you find those other rooms.

Founders Today's publisher widgets are the one feature aimed at readers outside the founder crowd, since they sit on third-party blogs. Whether that reaches your buyers depends on which blogs carry them, so ask which ones before you count on it.

How long your work stays visible

Every feed and forum pushes old posts down. On Indie Hackers a thread is live for a day or two, then lives on mostly through search and your product page. On Founders Today the launch page stays listed, but a feed post ages the same way. Plan a follow-up update a week or two later instead of relying on one post.

Credibility and track record

Indie Hackers has history. People know the name, the press has covered it, and a profile there carries weight with some audiences. Founders Today is newer, so its name means less outside its own members. For a SaaS founder, credibility mostly comes from what you show anyway: a clear product, real numbers, and steady updates over months.

Community culture and tone

Indie Hackers leans toward long, personal, number-heavy posts, and a lot of members share what they earn. Founders Today leans toward shorter posts, quick questions, launches, and discussion threads about tools and news. Neither tone is better, but copying the wrong one costs you replies. A three-paragraph business update with figures reads as normal on Indie Hackers and a little heavy in a feed, while a one-line question can look thin on a forum. Read ten recent posts that got plenty of replies on each platform before you write yours, and match the length and the level of detail.

Time cost

Both are free to join, so the real cost is your time. Fifteen minutes a day of useful replies on one platform beats a big post on two. If you have to choose, pick the one where your likely users already spend time.

Which one fits your stage

Idea stage. You need to know if the problem is real. Post a question about the problem, not a pitch for your solution. Ask how people handle it today and what they pay for. Both communities work for this only if the people answering could be your users.

Pre-launch. You need a handful of people who will try the product on day one. Spend a few weeks commenting on other people's posts before you post your own. People check profiles, and a profile with nothing but your own link looks like an ad.

Launch week. You need a page to point to and some people who see it. This is where the two differ most: Indie Hackers for the story, Founders Today for a page that stays listed. Doing both in the same week is fine as long as the posts are different.

First 100 users. Feedback matters more than traffic here. Ask specific questions, like which onboarding step confused someone, and answer every reply. Write down what you hear and what you changed.

B2B pipeline. Use both for credibility and early adopters if your buyers are founders or developers. If they are not, treat both as places to learn, not places to sell.

Three examples of how this plays out

These are made-up scenarios to show the decision, not case studies.

A developer tool. Say you built an API monitoring tool. Your buyers are developers, so both communities sit close to your audience. Post a build log with real numbers on Indie Hackers, then launch on Founders Today so you have a page that keeps listing. Either one can send trial signups, and you can compare them with separate tracking links.

Vertical software for non-founders. Say you built scheduling software for physiotherapy clinics. Founder communities will critique your pricing and onboarding well, but clinic owners are not reading them. Take the feedback, then bring the product to clinic groups, professional associations, and local forums where the buyers are.

A small solo micro-SaaS. Say you make a few hundred dollars a month. Indie Hackers still welcomes small numbers if you are specific about how you got them, and a launch page gives you something to link from your profile everywhere else. You do not need big revenue to be useful in either place. You need a clear story and the patience to reply to people.

How to tell if it is working

Pick three numbers and check them every Friday for a month: signups from each tracking link, replies that included a specific suggestion, and visits to your product or launch page. Replies like 'nice work' feel good but do not change your product. Replies that name a problem do. If a platform gives you suggestions you act on, it is working, even when signups are small. If it gives you neither signups nor suggestions after a month of steady posting, change the format of your posts before you leave.

A four-week plan for using both

Week 1. Set up your profile and product page on both. Write one plain sentence on what you do and who it is for. Spend about 15 minutes a day replying to other people's posts.

Week 2. Share one specific lesson from your build, with a number in it. For example, what you changed after a user interview and what happened next.

Week 3. Ask one pointed question you really need answered, such as whether your pricing page is clear. Reply to every answer, even short ones.

Week 4. Launch. Put the full launch page on Founders Today. On Indie Hackers, tell the story of the launch as a post and link to your product page instead of pitching.

Two rules for all four weeks. Never paste the same post in both places, because the formats reward different things. And use a separate tracking link for each community, so after 30 days you can see which one sent signups and not just visits.

Mistakes that waste a post

  • Posting a link with no story or question attached.
  • Asking for upvotes instead of asking for feedback.
  • Posting once and disappearing, instead of staying in the comments while the post is live.
  • Making claims without numbers, like 'growing fast' with no figure behind it.
  • Treating a founder audience as your buyers when your product is for someone else.
  • Judging a platform after a single post. Give each one a month of steady replies first.

Which one should you start with?

  • You can share revenue and want long-form credibility: start with Indie Hackers.
  • You are about to launch and want a page that keeps listing: start with Founders Today.
  • You sell to non-founders: use both for feedback, then put your selling effort where your buyers are. The list of free places to promote your startup is a good next step.
  • You have no product yet: neither. Talk to ten people who have the problem first. The guide to networking platforms for new founders can help you find them.

For a direct side-by-side with feature rows, see the Founders Today vs Indie Hackers comparison page.

FAQ

Is Founders Today an Indie Hackers alternative or a replacement? Neither, exactly. They do different jobs. Indie Hackers is stronger for long-form transparency and has a much deeper archive. Founders Today is built around launches and a feed. Many founders will want both.

Can I post the same thing on both? You can, but it works badly. Rewrite it for each format. A long build log suits a forum thread. A short update with a link to your launch page suits a feed.

Which is better for B2B SaaS? Neither is a buyer channel by default. If your buyers are founders or developers, both can send signups. If they are not, use both for feedback and credibility and sell elsewhere.

Do links from either community help SEO? Check the link attributes yourself before counting on it. Even where a link is followed, a community post is worth more as a place to get feedback and early users.

How long before I see results? Give each platform a month of steady replies and one launch post, and track signups per link. One post is not enough to judge either.

Is it free? Both are free to join as of writing. Check each site for current plans.

Pick one thing you want feedback on this week, write it as a question with one number in it, and post it where your users spend time. If you have a SaaS ready to show people, you can submit your launch on Founders Today for free.

title: Split Placement: Deciding Which Agent Steps Run Locally, on a Free Server, or on a Free Model Endpoint
description:
02:10, nineteen steps done, thirty-one to go

Picture a nightly triage job. It has sixty steps, it starts at 02:00, and at 02:10 it has finished nineteen of them. Step twenty needs to pull text out of a PDF, and the function that calls the model endpoint has just started returning 429 on every third request.

The job does not fail. It stalls, half-done, with no record of which leaf of the pipeline was running when the wall appeared. (The scenario is illustrative; the numbers describe the shape of the problem, not a benchmark I ran.)

Most writing about free AI tiers answers one question: which provider should the whole job use. That question is too coarse. Inside a single job, different steps belong in different places, and the placement decision is the one you can actually test.

Why placement is a separate question from tier choice

A job card is a promise about a workload. A placement decision is a predicate about one step: does it need a filesystem, does it touch regulated data, is it retry-safe, how tight is its deadline. Two steps in the same job can have identical inputs and still belong on opposite ends of your infrastructure.

Two themes keep showing up in current AI coverage: features moving into the client, and fatigue with generated output. Both push the same direction. Compute that can stay local should stay local, and anything that leaves the machine should leave under an explicit rule rather than a default.

The free tier used as the concrete case below is MonkeyCode's, which its operator describes as including free model access and a free server option.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I have not independently verified the quota figure the operator quotes (described as 10M tokens) or the server specifications, so the harness below treats any quota as unknown and measures consumption instead of assuming headroom.

Glossary: ten terms this tree depends on

Placement leaf — the destination a step is assigned to. This article uses four: LOCAL, FREE_SERVER, FREE_MODEL, ESCALATE.

Data class — the egress sensitivity of a payload. I use three: PUBLIC, INTERNAL, REGULATED.

Deterministic step — a step whose output depends only on its input, so running it twice costs time and nothing else.

Retry-safe (idempotent) — a step that can be re-executed after a transport failure without duplicating a side effect.

p95_seconds — the measured 95th-percentile duration of a step on your hardware. Guessed values make the whole tree decorative.

Quota cliff — the moment a free allowance stops absorbing requests, after which every call is either throttled or billed.

Fallback ladder — the ordered list of endpoints a step may attempt before it escalates.

Outcome class — how a failed attempt should be interpreted: RETRYABLE, FATAL, or OK. Conflating the first two is the most common cause of hot retry loops.

Fixture hash — a short digest over the exact inputs a test used, recorded so a later run can prove it saw the same bytes.

Ledger row — one append-only record per attempt: step, endpoint, attempt index, outcome, elapsed seconds.

The tree: ordered predicates, first match wins 

place(step)
|
+-- 1. data_class == REGULATED? -----------------> LEAF D: ESCALATE
+-- 2. deterministic AND p95 <= 2s AND no disk? --> LEAF A: LOCAL
+-- 3. needs_disk OR not text_only? --------------> LEAF B: FREE_SERVER
+-- 4. INTERNAL AND not retry_safe? --------------> LEAF D: ESCALATE
+-- 5. p95 > 0.5 * deadline? ---------------------> LEAF D: ESCALATE
+-- 6. otherwise (text, retry-safe) --------------> LEAF C: FREE_MODEL

The order is the contract, not a style choice. Move predicate 1 below predicate 6 and you have an egress incident with a passing test suite.

The four leaves, with a worked example each

Leaf A: LOCAL

Worked example: validate 12,000 issue bodies against a JSON Schema before anything else runs. The step is pure, takes under two seconds at p95, and never needs the network.

# placement.py - pure decision logic, no network, no API keys
from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum


class Leaf(str, Enum):
    LOCAL = "local"
    FREE_SERVER = "free_server"
    FREE_MODEL = "free_model"
    ESCALATE = "escalate"


class DataClass(str, Enum):
    PUBLIC = "public"        # safe to send to a third-party endpoint
    INTERNAL = "internal"    # company-internal, not customer data
    REGULATED = "regulated"  # PII, health, payment, or contract-bound


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Step:
    name: str
    p95_seconds: float      # measured on your machine, not guessed
    deterministic: bool
    text_only: bool
    needs_disk: bool
    data_class: DataClass
    retry_safe: bool
    deadline_seconds: float | None = None


def place(step: Step) -> tuple[Leaf, str]:
    """Ordered predicates. First match wins, so order is the contract."""
    if step.data_class is DataClass.REGULATED:
        return Leaf.ESCALATE, "regulated payload: no third-party egress"

    if step.deterministic and not step.needs_disk and step.p95_seconds <= 2.0:
        return Leaf.LOCAL, "cheap pure function: egress would be waste"

    if step.needs_disk or not step.text_only:
        return Leaf.FREE_SERVER, "needs a filesystem or a non-text runtime"

    if step.data_class is DataClass.INTERNAL and not step.retry_safe:
        return Leaf.ESCALATE, "non-idempotent internal call on a shared endpoint"

    if step.deadline_seconds and step.p95_seconds > step.deadline_seconds * 0.5:
        return Leaf.ESCALATE, "free-tier latency variance can eat the deadline"

    return Leaf.FREE_MODEL, "stateless text transform, retry-safe"

Leaf B: FREE_SERVER

Worked example: extract text from 400 PDFs and keep an on-disk cache so a second run is nearly free. This step needs a filesystem and CPU time, not a model.

This is also the leaf where a free server option changes the cost shape. Compute-heavy, non-text steps have no reason to touch a model endpoint at all, and putting them there wastes the resource you are actually short on.

Leaf C: FREE_MODEL

Worked example: classify and summarize issue text, one call per item, no local state. Text in, text out, retry-safe, egress class PUBLIC.

Before this leaf is reachable you need a reason to believe the endpoint tolerates your request rate. That is what the ladder and the ledger below are for.

Leaf D: ESCALATE

Worked example: redact personal data before any summarization happens. The step is a queue write plus a human or in-boundary worker, never a third-party call.

Escalation is a leaf, not a failure. If your tree has no ESCALATE, it is not a decision tree; it is a preference list.

A reproducible harness in five steps

1. Pin the fixture hash. Record the exact bytes a run consumed, so a later result can be tied to a specific input set.

from hashlib import sha256

def fixture_hash(paths):
    h = sha256()
    for p in sorted(paths):
        h.update(p.encode())
        h.update(open(p, "rb").read())
    return h.hexdigest()[:12]

2. Pin the case table. Every leaf needs at least one case, including the ones you expect to be rare.

CASES = [
    (Step("parse_json", 0.3, True, True, False, DataClass.PUBLIC, True), Leaf.LOCAL),
    (Step("extract_pdf", 12.0, False, False, True, DataClass.INTERNAL, True), Leaf.FREE_SERVER),
    (Step("summarize_issue", 3.1, False, True, False, DataClass.PUBLIC, True), Leaf.FREE_MODEL),
    (Step("redact_pii", 4.0, False, True, False, DataClass.REGULATED, True), Leaf.ESCALATE),
]

3. Separate retryable from fatal. A 429 and a schema mismatch must not share a code path.

class Outcome(str, Enum):
    OK = "ok"
    RETRYABLE = "retryable"  # 429, 503, timeout
    FATAL = "fatal"          # 400, 401, schema mismatch


def run_ladder(step, endpoints, call, ledger):
    for attempt, endpoint in enumerate(endpoints, start=1):
        try:
            result = call(endpoint, step)
        except Retryable as exc:
            ledger(step.name, endpoint, attempt, Outcome.RETRYABLE, exc)
            continue
        except Fatal as exc:
            ledger(step.name, endpoint, attempt, Outcome.FATAL, exc)
            return Leaf.ESCALATE, exc
        ledger(step.name, endpoint, attempt, Outcome.OK, None)
        return endpoint, result
    return Leaf.ESCALATE, "ladder exhausted"

4. Prove the ladder with a stub, not with a live quota. A stub that fails on the first endpoint is deterministic, free, and runs in CI.

def test_ladder_falls_through():
    def call(endpoint, step):
        if endpoint == "model-a":
            raise Retryable("429")
        return "ok"

    endpoint, result = run_ladder(step, ["model-a", "free-server"], call, ledger=lambda *a: None)
    assert endpoint == "free-server"
    assert result == "ok"

5. Write a ledger row per attempt. Append-only JSONL is enough, and it is the only artifact that tells you where a quota went when it disappears.

import json, time

def ledger(step_name, endpoint, attempt, outcome, error, path="ledger.jsonl", t0=None):
    row = {
        "step": step_name,
        "endpoint": endpoint,
        "attempt": attempt,
        "outcome": outcome.value,
        "error": type(error).__name__ if error else None,
        "seconds": round(time.monotonic() - t0, 3) if t0 else None,
    }
    with open(path, "a") as fh:
        fh.write(json.dumps(row) + "\n")

Run the whole thing with pytest -q. If you want the leaf distribution for a real job, feed your step table through place() and count the leaves before you deploy anything.

Limitations and what I did not verify

Free tiers move. A tree that encodes this month's allowances will quietly lie next quarter, which is why the harness measures instead of assuming headroom. The p95_seconds values must come from your own runs; copy-pasting mine would produce confident nonsense.

The data-class verdicts are jurisdictional and contractual. REGULATED here means "handled under a reviewed boundary" and nothing more, so the compliance owner decides those rows, not the engineer writing the predicate.

The ladder costs latency. Each retryable failure adds a round trip, and any non-idempotent step placed on FREE_MODEL by mistake can duplicate a side effect instead of failing cleanly. Retry-safety is a property of your step, not of the endpoint.

The described MonkeyCode free tier and its reported quota are operator-supplied statements that I have not independently tested against live rate limits, model behavior, or uptime.

Who should not use this

Teams with hard contractual SLAs should not route deadline-critical steps through any free tier, whatever the tree says. Workloads dominated by large non-text payloads will spend more time uploading than computing and should keep those steps local or on a server you control. Anyone without an owner for the REGULATED branch should stop at the glossary and get one first.

If you have a nightly job with a mixed step table, run place() over it and post the leaf counts. The distribution usually says more about where your budget goes than the tree does, and it is a cheap thing to compare across two teams.

title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
description:
arXiv:2610.21081v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump-like. We study STOCHLOB, a training-only score-matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired alternatives: jump-L\'evy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture, and clipped $\alpha$-stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor $h_t(r)$ is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically held-out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized tail-window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints. Code and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny.

title: Backends on Vercel: Python, containers, and Daemons
description:
Last year, we expanded zero-config support for Python and TypeScript backend frameworks. By this summer, developers could deploy their frontend and backend together with Vercel Services and coordinate background work with queues and durable workflows.

Today at Vercel Ship in San Francisco, we are expanding the backend workloads you can run on Vercel. Python on Vercel is now generally available, container support in Vercel Functions enables custom runtimes and system libraries, and we are introducing Vercel Daemons in Public Beta for background workers that pull work and stay running between jobs.

Python is now generally available

You can build your backend in Python with the Vercel infrastructure and development experience you know from your frontend, including local development, previews, and production deployments. Frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, and Django run on standard CPython with your PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling.

Already, 150,000 teams run Python backends on Vercel, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa.

SDKs for Python let you use Vercel products from your application, whether you’re storing files in Vercel Blob, sending background jobs to Vercel Queues, coordinating durable steps with Vercel Workflows, running untrusted code in Vercel Sandbox, or streaming model responses and handling tool calls with the AI SDK for Python.

Delphi, which builds AI digital minds from books and talks, moved its Python backend from AWS ECS to Vercel. With ten engineers and no dedicated infrastructure role, the team ships to production more than 100 times a day and uses Queues to handle background jobs.

Visit the Python knowledge base for framework details and examples.

Applications in any language with containers

The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel.

Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing, which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing. Vercel Services lets you develop and deploy your backend alongside your frontend, while Vercel CDN serves traffic on your domains, Vercel WAF protects it, logs help you investigate issues, and rollbacks restore earlier deployments.

For example, take a video app that uses a container for background processing, preparing a playback copy and thumbnail for each uploaded clip. This Dockerfile packages the Python processor, its dependencies, and ffmpeg to run with Daemons:

When you deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI, Vercel builds the image and stores it in your Vercel Container Registry. Read our containerized Functions deployment guide to get started.

Background workers with Vercel Daemons

Vercel Daemons lets you deploy containers as continuously running background workers on Fluid compute. You choose the number of instances in each region, and Vercel maintains that capacity by restarting processes when they exit or crash.

Daemons launches with support for pull-based workloads, where your code requests work from another system and processes it as it becomes available. That could mean consuming queue messages or fetching pending jobs from a database.

In our example, Daemons runs the video processor continuously as it pulls jobs from Vercel Queues. In vercel.toml, define the Next.js frontend, route requests to it, and add the processor using Dockerfile:

Follow the Daemons deployment guide to add a background worker to your Vercel project.

Run your backends on Vercel

We’re continuing to invest in backend support so more of your existing application can run on Vercel, using the languages, dependencies, and execution patterns it needs.

title: AutoOnboarder: Autonomously Onboarding LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. It places the agent under the supervision of an intelligent ``Onboarder'' coding agent, which iteratively tailors its foundation model, prompt, and harness source code to simultaneously improve performance and decrease cost. Like a real onboarding process, the Onboarder is only given tens of examples, and all evaluation data is isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. We report the lessons learned from building and testing AutoOnboarder on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission. Autonomously onboarded agents are able to match or exceed the performance of a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29$\times$ lower costs. However, these agents remain imperfect, and the Onboarding process varies greatly in terms of final performance. We conclude that future Onboarding systems require a robust environment for the Onboarder, including a structured thought interface, (controlled) internet access, and a wide model search space.

title: When Go GC Burns 60% CPU: The Container Memory Limit Problem
description:
Banner: Go garbage collection, memory pacing, and the container limits that can make a difference.

A Go service can burn CPU collecting garbage without having a memory leak.

That is the counterintuitive part of Zomato's Go garbage collection story.

The reported symptoms were striking: garbage collection consuming 25–60% of CPU in some services, alongside containers getting OOM-killed without an obvious memory leak.

These look like separate problems. But they can share a common cause: the garbage collector's pacing decisions don't automatically account for the container's actual memory budget.

The problem with doubling the live heap

Go's garbage collector uses GOGC to control when the next collection should happen.

With the default GOGC=100, the GC target is roughly based on the live heap growing by 100% relative to the previous cycle, with additional accounting for GC roots and other implementation details.

In simplified terms:

Next GC target ≈ live heap × (1 + GOGC/100)

At GOGC=100:

Live heap:       500 MiB
Approx. target: 1,000 MiB

That target is reasonable as a starting point when the process has enough memory available.

But containers introduce another constraint: the process has a memory budget imposed from outside the Go runtime.

The GC's heap-growth target and the container's memory ceiling are two different things.

When they aren't coordinated, two failure modes become possible.

Failure mode 1: OOM kills without a leak

Suppose a container has a memory limit of 1 GiB.

The Go process has a live heap of 600 MiB. A simplified GOGC=100 calculation puts the next target around 1,200 MiB.

But the container cannot safely accommodate that much memory. The process also needs room for goroutine stacks, runtime metadata, native allocations, and other memory outside the live heap.

The container can hit its limit before the collector's normal heap target becomes appropriate.

The result can be an OOM kill even when reachable memory isn't growing uncontrollably.

That doesn't mean every OOM without an obvious leak is a GC pacing issue. Transient allocation spikes, native memory, and other causes still need investigation.

The important point is that a heap-growth target alone isn't a container memory budget.

Failure mode 2: Excessive GC CPU

Now consider the opposite situation.

A service has a relatively small live heap and plenty of memory available in its container.

The GC keeps using a target derived from that live heap. Depending on the allocation rate and workload, it may collect frequently even though the container has significant unused headroom.

Every collection consumes CPU.

At fleet scale, unnecessary GC work can become a meaningful compute cost.

This is why the following combination deserves attention:

  • High GC CPU.
  • A relatively flat live-heap graph.
  • No convincing evidence of sustained heap growth.

It is a diagnostic clue, not proof. A service can allocate and discard large volumes of temporary objects while maintaining a flat live heap. Allocation rate, GC frequency, and allocation profiles matter too.

But before treating every high-GC-CPU incident as a memory leak, inspect the collector's pacing and the container's actual memory constraints.

The fix: Give Go a realistic memory limit

Go provides GOMEMLIMIT to let applications communicate a soft memory limit to the runtime.

Unlike GOGC, which controls GC aggressiveness in relation to heap growth, GOMEMLIMIT helps the runtime account for its overall memory footprint when deciding how aggressively to collect.

Conceptually, the runtime must balance two competing costs:

  • Collect too late, and the process risks exhausting its container memory budget.
  • Collect too aggressively, and the application wastes CPU reclaiming memory it could have used safely.

A memory limit gives the runtime another constraint to consider.

In the Zomato case, the reported approach used container metadata to derive a per-container limit, refreshed it periodically, and combined memory tuning with CPU scheduling adjustments.

A limit around 90% of the container ceiling can be a starting point for investigation, not a universal safe value. The correct margin depends on the application's non-heap memory, traffic spikes, allocation behavior, and operational requirements.

The goal is to give the runtime a realistic budget while preserving enough headroom for the rest of the process.

Why GOMEMLIMIT isn't a hard wall

This distinction matters in production.

GOMEMLIMIT is a soft limit, not a strict process-memory cap. The runtime can exceed it when necessary, and it does not guarantee that a container will avoid OOM kills.

The runtime also has to balance memory pressure against GC CPU overhead.

If the limit is too high, it may offer little protection against container memory pressure. If it is too low, the runtime can spend excessive CPU collecting garbage in an attempt to stay within the target.

That is why blindly setting GOMEMLIMIT equal to the container limit is not a complete solution.

A production rollout should account for:

  1. The container's actual memory limit.
  2. Heap and non-heap memory usage.
  3. Peak allocation rates and traffic bursts.
  4. GC CPU and pause behavior.
  5. OOM events and memory headroom after deployment.

Start with representative workloads, observe the results, and tune based on measurements rather than assuming a single multiplier works everywhere.

Don't overlook `

title: Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches
description:
arXiv:2610.21126v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse KV compression reduces long-context inference costs by retaining selected historical states, yet these states typically keep their coordinates from the full history. Under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), gaps left by evicted tokens continue to affect query-key matching, potentially limiting the use of retained evidence. We study post-selection positional geometry on a fixed selector-produced cache, examining how positional organization affects the use of retained information and which coordinate and continuation rules improve answer quality. To reorganize this geometry, we propose RoPERelay, which assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases through inverse rotation and re-rotation, and synchronizes the current query and subsequent generation. It reuses existing K/V without renewed selection, historical re-prefill, or additional cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors, and three long-term memory tasks, RoPERelay improves answer quality in 32 cases. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with BM25 on LongMemEval-S, accuracy increases from 23.6% to 35.4%. Measured complete-request time overhead is approximately 1%-3% in the evaluated configurations. These findings establish positional organization as a distinct optimization dimension for sparse KV caches after content selection.

title: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21267v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern agents select tools from registries, but exposing entire registries incurs high token costs and can impair selection as they grow. We present TRACER, a retrieval front-end that indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks continuations using a learned blend of empirical and contextual priors. On a mixed retail-and-telecom $\tau^2$ environment, TRACER improves GPT-5.4's tool-selection accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing input tokens per step by 80%, exposing just 5 of 128 tools. In autonomous full-turn execution, it matches GPT-5.4's full-registry task success with 61% fewer input tokens per step. Across six environments and four models, TRACER improves tool-selection accuracy over full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs, with average gains of 6 to 10 points; the three exceptions trail by at most 2.2. We analyze failures in both regimes to identify directions for future work.

title: Price Free AI Capacity in Deadline Slack, Not in Tokens
description:
It is 02:14. Your nightly batch window closes at 02:30. The free lane is still running, and the token meter reads zero.

Last week that felt like a win. Tonight the window is gone. Which operational action follows from that evidence?

Not delete the free lane. Price it.

Two numbers, one decision

Most teams measure the wrong number.

  1. Token spend. Cheap, often zero on a free tier.
  2. Deadline slack. Seconds you can spend before an SLO breaks.

Free capacity converts the first into the second. That conversion has a rate. Measure the rate, not the sticker price.

Define slack use per job class:

slack_used = free_p95_duration * (1 + retry_ratio) - paid_p50_duration

Three terms matter. The free lane p95 per attempt. The extra attempts per completed job. The paid baseline you gave up.

What the retry tax actually costs

A retry is not a retry. It is wall-clock time plus a new queue position plus a fresh attempt.

  • Preemption returns the worker mid-attempt. The partial work is gone.
  • Throttling returns a rate-limit signal. The partial work is gone.
  • Worker loss returns nothing at all. You wait for a timeout to notice.

Each event resets the attempt clock. Each event consumes slack, not tokens. That is how a free lane stays cheap and still blows the window.

If your provider returns 429, stop and back off. Do not retry around the limit.

The artifact: a break-even router

Here is a small script. It reads measured job-class statistics from one fixed window and prints a routing decision.

It does not call a model. It prices time.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# breakeven.py - route batch job classes by deadline slack, not list price.
import json
import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class ClassStats:
    name: str
    attempts: int          # free-lane attempt starts in the window
    completed: int         # jobs that finished inside the class deadline
    free_wall_p50: float   # seconds per attempt, free lane
    free_wall_p95: float   # seconds per attempt, free lane
    paid_wall_p50: float   # seconds per job, reserved lane
    paid_cost: float       # currency units per completed job, reserved lane
    slack_budget: float    # seconds of negative slack this class may spend
    miss_penalty: float    # currency units charged when the deadline slips


def retry_ratio(s):
    if s.completed == 0:
        return None
    return max(s.attempts - s.completed, 0) / s.completed


def free_duration_p95(s):
    r = retry_ratio(s)
    return None if r is None else s.free_wall_p95 * (1.0 + r)


def slack_used(s):
    d = free_duration_p95(s)
    return None if d is None else d - s.paid_wall_p50


def miss_proxy(s):
    # Crude upper-bound proxy, not a fitted probability model.
    used = slack_used(s)
    if used is None:
        return 1.0
    if used <= s.slack_budget:
        return 0.0
    return min(1.0, (used - s.slack_budget) / max(used, 1e-9))


def route(s):
    used = slack_used(s)
    if used is None:
        return 'hold', 'no completed jobs in window'
    if used > s.slack_budget:
        return 'reserved', 'p95 slack use exceeds budget'
    risk = miss_proxy(s) * s.miss_penalty
    if risk >= s.paid_cost:
        return 'reserved', 'risk-adjusted free cost >= paid cost'
    return 'free', 'slack within budget and risk below paid cost'


def main(path):
    with open(path) as fh:
        rows = [ClassStats(**json.loads(l)) for l in fh if l.strip()]
    print('class             slack_used  budget  miss_p  free_risk  decision')
    for s in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.name):
        used = slack_used(s)
        decision, why = route(s)
        risk = miss_proxy(s) * s.miss_penalty
        used_s = 'n/a' if used is None else '%ds' % used
        print('%-17s %9s %6ds %7.2f %10.2f  %s' % (
            s.name, used_s, s.slack_budget, miss_proxy(s), risk, decision))
        print('%-17s reason: %s' % ('', why))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 'jobs.jsonl')

Declared workload for the sample fixture

State the conditions before you quote any result.

  • Two job classes, 1,000 and 900 completed jobs in one 24h window.
  • Free lane: one worker pool, no reserved capacity, timing measured per attempt.
  • Paid baseline: p50 per job from the previous week on reserved capacity.
  • No model-quality comparison. This drill prices time, not accuracy.

Run it locally in under a minute

Create the fixture. These are sample values, not published measurements.

{"name":"nightly-embed","attempts":1180,"completed":1000,"free_wall_p50":38.0,"free_wall_p95":96.0,"paid_wall_p50":41.0,"paid_cost":0.42,"slack_budget":120.0,"miss_penalty":180.0}
{"name":"ocr-backfill","attempts":960,"completed":900,"free_wall_p50":22.0,"free_wall_p95":150.0,"paid_wall_p50":24.0,"paid_cost":0.11,"slack_budget":60.0,"miss_penalty":40.0}

Run the router:

python3 breakeven.py jobs.jsonl

Expected output on the fixture above. Label it expected until your own window reproduces it.

class             slack_used  budget  miss_p  free_risk  decision
nightly-embed            72s    120s    0.00       0.00  free
                  reason: slack within budget and risk below paid cost
ocr-backfill            136s     60s    0.56      22.36  reserved
                  reason: p95 slack use exceeds budget

The second class is the interesting one. Its per-attempt p95 is slower, and its retry ratio adds about 7 percent. Slack use lands at 136 seconds against a 60 second budget.

Free is the expensive lane here, and tokens never entered the calculation.

Failure injection: prove the ledger counts

A routing rule you never broke is a guess. Break the lane first.

# worker.py is a throwaway harness, not a model client.
python3 worker.py --class ocr-backfill --concurrency 4 &
WPID=$!
for i in 1 2 3; do
  sleep 60
  pkill -f 'worker.py --class ocr-backfill' -n
  sleep 5
  python3 worker.py --class ocr-backfill --concurrency 4 &
  WPID=$!
done
kill $WPID
python3 breakeven.py jobs.jsonl

Watch one thing: does a killed attempt show up as attempt=fail or does it vanish?

If it vanishes, your attempts counter is wrong. Your retry ratio is then wrong. Your routing decision is then wrong.

A minimal harness so the smoke test runs:

# worker.py - throwaway harness for the ledger drill only.
import argparse, random, time

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument('--class', dest='cls', required=True)
p.add_argument('--concurrency', type=int, default=1)
p.add_argument('--attempt-seconds', type=float, default=30.0)
p.add_argument('--fail-rate', type=float, default=0.15)
a = p.parse_args()

while True:
    time.sleep(a.attempt_seconds)
    ok = random.random() > a.fail_rate
    print('%s attempt=%s' % (a.cls, 'ok' if ok else 'fail'), flush=True)

This harness proves your ledger counts. It proves nothing about any model. Swap in your real worker for that.

Telemetry you must emit

Without these fields the ledger is unreadable a week later.

  • job_class and route at admission time
  • attempt_index per job, starting at 0
  • attempt_started_at, attempt_ended_at
  • attempt_outcome: ok, preempted, timeout, throttled, worker_lost
  • deadline_at and slack_remaining_s at completion
  • tokens_in, tokens_out, even on a free tier
  • worker_id, so a bad host is visible

Keep tokens_in on free runs. You need it later to compute the exchange rate between free capacity and reserved capacity.

Decision table and threshold rationale

Evidence in the window Route Why
p95 slack use under 50 percent of budget free headroom absorbs the retry tax
p95 slack use between 50 and 100 percent free, alert at 70 percent one bad hour breaks it
p95 slack use over budget reserved measured breach, not a guess
risk-adjusted free cost at or above paid cost reserved free is the expensive lane
zero completed jobs hold no data, no route

Why 50 percent as a default? Because retry ratio is usually noisier than wall time. If your retry ratio p95 moves more than your duration p95, tighten the threshold.

If the miss penalty is contractual, do not run the free lane at any threshold. Slack budgets are for engineering tradeoffs, not for contracts.

Cleanup and rollback

Run these in order. Write them down before the drill, not after.

  1. Drain the class. Set free-lane route weight to 0.
  2. Wait for in-flight attempts, or cancel them and record worker_lost explicitly.
  3. Restore the reserved weight from your config store, never from memory.
  4. Keep the window JSONL file. It is the evidence for the next review.
  5. Revert alert thresholds only after two clean windows.

Step 3 matters most. A rollback typed by hand at 02:20 is a second incident.

Where free capacity fits in this drill

The drill needs a free lane before you can price one. MonkeyCode is an open-source project with free model access; the operator states 10M free tokens and a free server option.

I treat both availability claims as operator-supplied. Limits and terms change, so confirm them on the project page before you plan around them.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

In this workflow the free tier is exactly the lane whose retry ratio you are measuring. Point the harness at one small class, run one window, read the ledger. Start with one class and one window on the free tier, then decide.

Limitations and who should not use this

Be honest about the edges.

  • Not for synchronous user traffic with a hard p99. Free lanes are variable by nature.
  • Not for classes where a single miss is contractually unacceptable. Keep those reserved.
  • Not reliable under about 200 completed jobs per window. The p95 is noise below that; widen the window.
  • miss_proxy is a proxy, not a fitted model. Replace it with your own estimator if you have one.
  • Do not use this to justify free capacity against a regulated deadline without a named risk owner.

The threshold question

Every number here is a threshold with a rationale, and yours will differ. The useful question is not whether free capacity is cheap.

It is: how many seconds of slack does a retry buy, and who pays when the budget runs out?

Answer that with a measured window, and routing stops being a mood.

title: Mine, Sample, Render: Test-Time Diversity Alignment Of Generative Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21185v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to do so. We introduce MINE-SAMPLE-RENDER (MSR), a test-time approach that externalizes the diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure. Our pipeline (i) mines an interpretable categorical schema from a corpus of real artifacts and supplies statistics for sampling; (ii) samples attribute configurations from the corpus-derived statistics; (iii) uses a generative model purely as a conditional renderer of a sampled configuration. Across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, we evaluate the diversity and output quality of MSR-guided generation and show that MSR improves alignment with corpus distributions and diversity of generated outputs.

  • Hybrid vector + graph retrieval and graph-only retrieval.
  • Chunk and graph-path citations.
  • Pluggable graph and vector search interfaces.
  • Backfill utilities and a schema migration runner.

Regex-based extraction remains the default. LLM integration is optional.

How we approached parity testing

We compared the Java implementation against the Python ragleap-graph v0.9.0 implementation.

Rather than comparing method names, we exercised behavior using recorded calls, parameters, outputs, and scripted model responses.

The test scenarios covered:

  • 422 string-similarity pairs.
  • 25 extraction-configuration cases.
  • Entity and relation extraction.
  • Graph upserts, including Cypher statements and parameters.
  • Backfills and migration behavior.
  • Retrieval scenarios and retrieval configurations.

We also ran 27 deliberate mutations across the new functionality. Every injected break was caught by the parity tests.

This is evidence for the tested cases, not a mathematical guarantee of complete equivalence.

Why mutation testing matters

A passing test suite can still miss bugs if its assertions are too weak.

Mutation testing deliberately changes behavior to check whether the tests notice. For this release, the 27 deliberate breaks were caught by the parity tests.

That gave us additional confidence that the tests were checking behavior rather than merely executing code paths.

Testing the real release

The full local run used generated parity fixtures and a live Neo4j 5.26.29 Community instance:

  • 129 tests
  • 0 failures
  • 0 skipped tests

After publishing, we resolved the Maven artifact in a clean project and exercised health checks, upserts, backfills, and graph-only retrieval against live Neo4j.

Maven coordinates:

io.github.antonyrag:ragleap-graph:0.2.0\

What still needs testing?

LLM extraction hasn't been verified against a real model provider. Compatibility with other Neo4j deployments also needs more testing, and the optional vector-search adapter hasn't been tested against a live RagLeap facade.

The PostgreSQL audit writer hasn't been ported yet.

Documenting these limitations is part of making a library easier to evaluate responsibly.

Try it and share feedback

Source and release notes:

https://github.com/antonyrag/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-graph-java-v0.2.0

RagLeap is fully open-source and self-hosted, with a wider ecosystem of retrieval, graph, and AI tooling libraries.

If you work with Java or Neo4j, I'd appreciate feedback on the API, compatibility, test coverage, and integration experience.

What integration test would you add before using this library in production?

title: Node.js Duplicate Chat Messages After Reconnect: Trace History and Live Overlap
description:
Short answer: If classroom chat repeats a question after reconnect, overlap history backfill with the live subscription and reconcile both by the same stable message ID. An exact handoff boundary across reconnect is not achievable. For a video lesson, keep this message merge separate from room-token issuance and presence checks. A duplicate delivery does not mean two participants are present.

Option Pick this when Check before committing
Infrai realtime You want a stable REST capability contract while the vendor behind it changes Supply your own history source and test the merge
Ably Dedicated connection recovery and history fit your lifecycle Check recovery behavior and message identity
Pusher Channels Your pub/sub transport is established Pair it with durable history and stable IDs
PubNub Its persistence and presence model fits the roster Test presence separately from message replay

How do you debug duplicate chat messages after reconnect?

Picture an edtech lesson: a teacher starts a video room, issues scoped tokens, and watches the roster while students post questions. A student's connection drops as a question is published. On return, the app loads recent history and resumes live delivery. The question reaches both paths. That's a normal overlap, not evidence that a student sent it twice.

Diagram in words: stored record -> history -> keyed view; that same record -> live event -> the same keyed view. Store and publish the same ID. If each path invents an ID, the client cannot tell that the two arrivals describe one message. A timestamp cutoff won't fix it.

The ID is the boundary.

Keep presence distinct. A roster is not a count of chat events, and a replay does not prove its author is still connected. Scope room tokens and check room membership independently of the displayed message set.

Pick this when the integration boundary matters

Infrai is worth trying for the publish leg if your team wants the backend capability contract to stay put when the vendor behind it changes: one REST API covers multiple backend capabilities with consistent conventions, so changing the provider behind a capability does not require changing your integration code. Infrai uses a single API key across backend services: one key, one wallet, one bill, rather than separate credentials and invoices for each provider. Plain HTTP means no SDK to install. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required; it exposes request and response schemas. Its platform convention also specifies an Idempotency-Key for writes. That gives a publishing integration a concrete way to avoid applying a retried write twice. Neither property removes the need for stable IDs shared by storage and delivery. Define your history source explicitly. The limitation is clear: if your lesson requires a specialist's built-in history and recovery contract, Infrai is not a good fit for that requirement. Ably is the better choice to evaluate first for documented connection recovery and history.

Ably is a stronger candidate when its dedicated realtime recovery and history semantics fit your connection lifecycle. Pusher Channels suits an established channel-event integration where another system owns durable history. PubNub deserves a close look when its persistence and presence semantics align with the lesson roster. Compare those behaviors using your own disconnect sequence, not a generic feature checklist.

For an edtech team that owns its message store and wants one stable integration for realtime publishing alongside room-related capabilities, I recommend trying Infrai for the publish leg, while measuring the client merge and presence independently. Choose a specialist first if built-in recovery or persistence semantics are central to the design.

Run the overlap experiment in Node.js

Use one stored record with ID lesson-42:q-17, one history copy, one live copy, and another distinct record. This runnable TypeScript test operates on normalized data, so it assumes no undocumented provider payload fields. Run it with your TypeScript runner. In production, normalize records from your store and subscription before calling accept. To inspect the associated classroom channel, set INFRAI_API_KEY in your environment; the read-only request below checks its status and surfaces the response body. It does not pretend the channel lookup is a history endpoint or a presence count.

type Message = { id: string; room: string; text: string };

const messages = new Map<string, Message>();
async function inspectChannel(): Promise<string> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!key) throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY");
  const url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/channel/get/lesson-42";
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${key}` },
    });
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
      const seconds = retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)
        ? Number(retryAfter) : 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, seconds * 1000));
      continue;
    }
    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Channel lookup ${response.status}: ${body}`);
    return body;
  }
  throw new Error("Rate limit retry budget exhausted");
}

function accept(message: Message): void {
  if (!message.id || !message.room) throw new Error("Missing message identity");
  const prior = messages.get(message.id);
  if (prior && (prior.room !== message.room || prior.text !== message.text)) {
    throw new Error(`Conflicting content for ${message.id}`);
  }
  messages.set(message.id, message);
}

const question: Message = { id: "lesson-42:q-17", room: "lesson-42", text: "Can you repeat that?" };
const next: Message = { id: "lesson-42:q-18", room: "lesson-42", text: "Got it." };
for (const event of [question, next, question]) accept(event);
if (messages.size !== 2) throw new Error("Reconnect merge failed");
console.log([...messages.values()]);
inspectChannel().then(console.log).catch(error => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Pass: three arrivals display two messages, and replaying an identical record changes nothing. Fail: a repeated ID with different room or text raises an error rather than silently replacing the stored record. This detects an identity conflict; it does not benchmark any service. The channel lookup is an additional live check and requires a valid key and an existing channel; a lookup error cannot invalidate the local merge assertion.

Don't count callbacks.

Next, repeat with your actual store and transport. Log the ID, room, arrival path (history or live), and whether the ID was already seen. Count unique IDs displayed and conflicting IDs, not callback invocations. Disconnect while a question is sent, then vary which path arrives first on reconnect. Observe the room roster separately; never turn a replayed chat event into a participant join.

What should decide the rollout?

Require the persisted record and the published representation to carry the same ID. The UI must show one item per ID in either arrival order. Independently, check the service's presence observations against the membership behavior your lesson requires. A transport that passes the message merge but fails the roster requirement is not the right choice.

This experiment cannot establish a provider's recovery guarantee, retention policy, or video-room behavior. Verify token scope and presence using the service's documented contract. Keep the message store authoritative for history; a live callback alone is not durable history. In particular, do not mistake a successful channel lookup for an accurate class roster: those are different observations with different failure conditions. A sensible rollout exercises all three independently, including a reconnect just before the history response finishes and another just after the live listener starts. Neither ordering should produce an extra displayed question.

References

  • Ably connection recovery.
  • Pusher Channels events.
  • PubNub Message Persistence.
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0.

Further reading

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai realtime documentation and check the live contract before wiring the adapter.

title: RIGen: Beyond Action Following with Reciprocal Interaction in Generative Gameplay
description:
arXiv:2610.20811v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative gameplay requires more than immediate responses to player actions.Actions should have persistent consequences, while the generated world should act according to its own state and rules, shaping the player's situation and subsequent choices. Video generation captures local dynamics, but limited history, partially observed game state, and the need for contextual behavior decisions make such interactions difficult to sustain through audiovisual prediction alone. We introduce \rig (Reciprocally Interactive Generation), a framework for reciprocal interaction in generative gameplay. \rig combines persistent state and configurable rules, contextual interaction reasoning, and action-conditioned audiovisual generation. Together, these components make interaction consequences and actor behavior jointly determine generated content while maintaining consistency between game state and visible outcomes. We construct a Xonotic gameplay dataset to train an audiovisual generator for learning dynamics and interactions. Further post-training enables \rigarena, an interactive generative first-person shooter (FPS) prototype. Experiments demonstrate more reliable combat outcomes and reciprocal interaction between the player and the generated world. Project page: https://murphylmf.github.io/RIGen/.

title: Kubernetes Pod Churn & Node Thrashing: Ephemeral Storage Exhaustion and Eviction Cascades
description:
When background worker pods continuously write temporary scratch files, un-rotated log buffers, or dynamic assets directly to container filesystems without explicit ephemeral storage limits, worker nodes quietly enter local disk pressure states. The kubelet then triggers aggressive pod evictions, sparking cluster-wide pod churn, Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler thrashing, and AWS bill inflation. Here is an architectural deep dive into diagnosing local disk exhaustion and configuring resilient kubelet eviction boundaries.

In high-throughput B2B SaaS platforms running containerized microservices, background processing workloads (e.g., generating PDF reports, processing video/image assets, compiling code, or handling CSV batch imports) frequently rely on local container file systems for temporary scratch space. Under heavy traffic, un-capped ephemeral storage usage creates an invisible cluster-level failure mode: Cascading Node Eviction and Auto-Scaler Thrashing.

1. The Mechanics of OverlayFS and Ephemeral Storage Eviction

By default, when a container writes files to its own filesystem (outside of explicitly mounted Persistent Volumes), those writes land on the node's local disk through the container runtime's writable layer, typically the OverlayFS storage driver. Disk-backed emptyDir volumes and container logs consume the same node disk. If a pod uses significant local disk space without ephemeral storage requests and limits in its manifest, it triggers a chain reaction across the host node.

The Anatomy of a Node Eviction Cascade

  • Unbounded Disk Growth: A burst of PDF generation worker tasks writes 15GB of temporary files to /tmp inside the container overlay filesystem.
  • Kubelet Disk Pressure Breach: The node's disk crosses a kubelet hard eviction threshold (by default, nodefs.available below 10% or imagefs.available below 15%). The kubelet marks the node DiskPressure = True, the node is tainted, and the scheduler stops placing new pods on it.
  • Aggressive Pod Eviction: The kubelet first garbage-collects dead containers and unused images, then starts evicting pods. It ranks pods by whether their disk usage exceeds their ephemeral storage request, then by pod priority, then by usage. With no requests set, every pod counts as over its request, so priority dominates, and lower-priority core services can be evicted before the high-priority worker that is actually filling the disk.
  • Auto-Scaler Thrashing (Karpenter / Cluster Autoscaler): Rescheduled evicted pods flood neighboring nodes, pushing those nodes into disk pressure as well. The autoscaler provisions new EC2 instances for pending pods while consolidation removes others, so nodes churn continuously and compute spend can multiply for the duration of the incident.

2. Diagnosing Ephemeral Storage Bloat in Production

Pod objects do not report disk usage, so kubectl get pods cannot show it. The kubelet's stats summary endpoint does. Run the following diagnostic commands to find which pods are consuming node disk and driving instability (requires jq):

# Top 20 pods by ephemeral storage usage (MiB) across all nodes
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name | cut -d/ -f2); do
  kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$node/proxy/stats/summary" \
    | jq -r --arg node "$node" '.pods[]
        | [$node, .podRef.namespace, .podRef.name,
           ((.["ephemeral-storage"].usedBytes // 0) / 1048576 | floor)]
        | @tsv'
done | sort -t$'\t' -k4 -rn | head -20

# Inspect recent eviction events
kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector reason=Evicted | grep -i "ephemeral"

# Detailed check of Node Disk Pressure conditions
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep -A 8 "Conditions:"

A pod status displaying Evicted with the message The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage confirms your cluster is actively suffering from un-capped container write exhaustion.

3. Production-Ready Remediation: Strict Resource Limits & In-Memory emptyDir

Step 1: Enforce Ephemeral Storage Requests and Limits

Every Kubernetes manifest deployed to production must explicitly define ephemeral-storage resource boundaries alongside CPU and memory parameters. This lets the scheduler place pods according to available disk, and when a container exceeds its storage limit, the kubelet evicts only that pod instead of letting the whole node reach disk pressure.

# PRODUCTION-GRADE DEPLOYMENT MANIFEST WITH EPHEMERAL LIMITS
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: pdf-generator-worker
  namespace: production
spec:
  replicas: 8
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pdf-generator-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pdf-generator-worker
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: registry.internal.net/pdf-worker:v2.1.0
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "2Gi"
            ephemeral-storage: "1Gi" # Scheduler reserves this much node disk
          limits:
            cpu: "2000m"
            memory: "4Gi"            # Includes up to 2Gi of tmpfs scratch below
            ephemeral-storage: "4Gi" # Hard ceiling: kubelet evicts this pod if exceeded
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /tmp/scratch
          name: scratch-volume
      volumes:
      - name: scratch-volume
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory # Back temporary writes with RAM (tmpfs)
          sizeLimit: 2Gi # Cap scratch space so it cannot consume all memory

Step 2: Redirect High-Frequency Scratch Writes to In-Memory tmpfs

For workloads requiring ultra-fast, short-lived file creation (e.g., image resizing or PDF rendering), mount an emptyDir volume backed by RAM (medium: Memory). Writes to this volume bypass the node disk entirely, removing them as a source of disk pressure and speeding up file I/O. One catch: files in a memory-backed emptyDir count toward the container's memory limit, not its ephemeral storage limit. Size the memory limit to cover the application plus the scratch volume, as in the manifest above, or a full scratch directory will get the pod OOM-killed.

4. Tuning Kubelet Eviction Thresholds and Karpenter Node Consolidation

Reduce premature evictions by tuning kubelet eviction settings in your node configuration (for example, the kubelet config in your EKS node group launch template or Karpenter EC2NodeClass user data):

# Kubelet Eviction Configuration Parameters (kubelet-config.json)
{
  "evictionHard": {
    "memory.available": "5%",
    "nodefs.available": "10%",
    "nodefs.inodesFree": "5%",
    "imagefs.available": "15%"
  },
  "evictionSoft": {
    "nodefs.available": "15%"
  },
  "evictionSoftGracePeriod": {
    "nodefs.available": "2m"
  },
  "evictionMaxPodGracePeriod": 60
}

Then slow down Karpenter's consolidation so short traffic spikes don't cause node churn (Karpenter v1 API):

# Karpenter v1 NodePool with churn guardrails
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      expireAfter: 720h # Rotate nodes every 30 days for patching
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 5m # Wait before consolidating so spikes can settle
    budgets:
      - nodes: "10%"     # Never disrupt more than 10% of nodes at once
  • Soft Eviction Grace Periods: With a soft threshold, the kubelet only evicts if disk stays below 15% free for a full 2 minutes. Short spikes that clear on their own (a batch job finishing, logs rotating, image garbage collection) no longer trigger evictions. The hard threshold at 10% still protects the node.
  • Karpenter Consolidation Guardrails: consolidateAfter delays consolidation so nodes are not removed the moment utilization dips, and disruption budgets cap how many nodes Karpenter can replace at once. expireAfter handles routine node rotation; it is not a churn control on its own.

5. Executive Summary & Systems Rules

  • Always Specify ephemeral-storage Requests and Limits: Unbounded container writes will fill host node disks and trigger cascading evictions across unrelated pods.
  • Use RAM-Backed emptyDir for Transient Files: Mount temporary scratch directories with medium: Memory to keep high-frequency file I/O off node disks, and raise the memory limit to cover the scratch size.
  • Set Soft Kubelet Eviction Windows: Configure grace periods on nodes so brief disk spikes can clear before the kubelet evicts pods, and add consolidation delays and disruption budgets to your autoscaler.

Are pod evictions and node churn driving up your Kubernetes bill? I help SaaS teams right-size workloads, tune kubelet and Karpenter settings, and build clusters that stay stable under heavy batch traffic. Book a consultation →

title: AbridgeKV: Compressing Long Reasoning into the KV Cache of Learned Pause Tokens
description:
arXiv:2610.20641v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long chain-of-thought decoding is memory-bound: the KV cache of the generated tokens grows linearly with the test-time compute being spent. Evicting cache entries does not fix this, because a model never trained on a cache with entries removed generates longer, often up to the length limit. We instead train the model to compress its own output. AbridgeKV compresses each completed block of generated text into the KV entries of a few learned pause tokens. These are extra input tokens with trained embeddings that produce no output. Once the pause tokens have encoded the block, AbridgeKV frees the block's original cache; subsequent tokens attend to the pause tokens' KV entries in its place. Three novel choices make this work: the pause tokens' KV entries take positions inside the block they replace, the cache budget is allocated across layers according to the measured value of each layer's entries, and compression operates on relatively large blocks. On 446 competition problems from AIME, HMMT, AMC, BRUMO, CMIMC and SMT with 32K-token generations, keeping a quarter of the generated cache matches an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length; the strongest published evictor at a matched budget writes far longer, and the closest trained compressor, retrained on the same data, loses 10 points. Served in vLLM, the cache is 3.5x smaller per sequence and a saturated H100 finishes a problem 3.2x faster than with full KV.
