title: I kept hitting jq: parse error on AI streams, so I built sjq
description:
If you work with LLMs, you've done this: curl -N <streaming endpoint> | jq. And you've seen this:

jq: parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 9

Column 9. That's where data: ends and the JSON begins. An SSE stream isn't JSON — it's a framing protocol: data: {...} lines separated by blank lines, [DONE] at the end. jq never stood a chance.

So I built sjq — jq, but for AI streaming. A small Rust CLI that parses OpenAI-compatible server-sent event streams (/v1/chat/completions and /v1/responses) and prints one short line per event, showing only what each event added.

What it looks like 

sjq curl -s $BASE/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"gemini-4-argon","stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'

model: gemini-4-argon
role: assistant
data: 'Hi'
data: ' there'
data: ' 👋'
…
time: ttft=0.42s total=3.1s tok/s=258.2

Instead of 99% envelope JSON, you watch the actual content arrive — plus a timing line: TTFT, total, tokens/sec. Run through sjq curl and it also breaks out connect, TLS handshake, and TTFB, which is genuinely useful when you're debugging a slow provider.

It understands tool calls (name + arguments as they stream in), reasoning_content, refusals, logprobs, usage blocks, and multiple choices — each rendered as its own labeled line.

Install 

brew tap vivgrid/tap
brew trust vivgrid/tap  # Homebrew 6+ requires trusting third-party taps
brew install sjq

Or from source: cargo install --git https://github.com/vivgrid/sjq (one dependency: serde_json).

Why not just strip the framing with sed?

You can — sed 's/^data: //' | jq — and plenty of people do. But then you're staring at full envelope objects per chunk: ids, timestamps, object: "chat.completion.chunk", finish_reason: null fifty times over. The signal (the tokens) drowns in the envelope. sjq inverts that: the delta is the output; the envelope gets summarized once.

MIT licensed, single binary. The repo ships 14 test fixtures covering the gnarly edges: multi-line data payloads, mid-stream errors, parallel tool calls, logprobs, CJK/emoji text.

Repo: https://github.com/vivgrid/sjq — feedback and weird streams welcome.

title: LLM-Based Weak Annotation for Cybersecurity Tweet Classification: A Teacher-Student Framework
description:
arXiv:2610.21254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) relies on the timely identification of emerging threats, enabling organizations and security analysts to support situational awareness and decision-making. Social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter) have become valuable CTI sources because vulnerabilities and attack activities are often discussed there before appearing in formal reports. However, the rapid growth of cybersecurity discussions on social media has created more content than domain experts can realistically review and annotate, making labeled data a major bottleneck for developing supervised learning approaches. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as weak annotators in other domains, their effectiveness for cybersecurity tweet classification and downstream training of domain-specific pre-trained language models (PLMs) remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose a Teacher-Student weak supervision framework in which a selected LLM serves as a Teacher to generate weak labels for unlabeled cybersecurity tweets, enabling the training of cybersecurity-specific PLMs without large-scale manual annotation. Experimental results show that PLMs trained solely on LLM-generated labels consistently achieve F1 scores above 0.92, remaining within 3 percentage points of fully human-supervised models across all evaluated architectures. These findings suggest that LLM-based weak annotation offers a practical alternative for constructing cybersecurity-specific training data when expert annotation resources are limited.

title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?
description:
arXiv:2610.20887v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined harmful tasks can induce emergent misalignment (EM) across unrelated domains. While prior work has identified shared misalignment-associated representations across independently fine-tuned models, it remains unclear whether these models rely on common computational components. We investigate this question using three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct trained on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations. Using direction-based activation tracing, we identify three attention-head locations shared among the five highest-ranked heads of all three organisms. Replacing each organism's five selected head contributions with Base contributions reduces free-generation EM from 38.9% to 22.9% for medical, 50.7% to 12.5% for finance, and 41.7% to 11.1% for sports, outperforming layer-matched random interventions without reducing judged coherence. Cross-organism activation transfer further shows that the shared heads exhibit partially interchangeable effects on fixed-response preference. These findings provide evidence that representational convergence in EM extends to shared, causally relevant attention-head components within a common model architecture.

title: INCONVENIENT: A Benchmark to Assess LLM Generalization Capabilities from Convenience Samples
description:
arXiv:2610.21038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning models for tabular prediction typically assume that training data are representative of the population on which they will be deployed. In practice, however, data are often collected based on convenience, availability, or cost, resulting in systematic sampling biases that can distort feature--target relationships and undermine real-world generalization. Existing tabular distribution-shift benchmarks primarily construct out-of-distribution (OOD) settings by partitioning observations across naturally occurring domains. While such partitions may induce changes in P(Y | X), the resulting shifts are neither explicitly controlled nor isolated, and the evaluation distributions themselves are often not representative of the broader target population. We introduce INCONVENIENT, a benchmark designed to study robustness to convenience-sample bias. Rather than relying on naturally occurring domain partitions, INCONVENIENT directly perturbs feature--target relationships in the training distribution while preserving the original population distribution as the deployment environment. This setting more closely reflects real-world scenarios in which models are developed from unrepresentative samples and subsequently deployed on a broader population. The distinction is particularly relevant for large language models (LLMs), whose pretraining may encode population-level knowledge that extends beyond the relationships observed in a biased training dataset. Unlike existing distribution-shift benchmarks, INCONVENIENT provides explicit control over both the direction and severity of relationship shifts, enabling a systematic assessment of robustness to convenience sampling. The benchmark comprises 200 tabular classification and regression datasets spanning diverse application domains and generates around 15,500 shifted training distributions which lead to substantial downstream degradation.

title: Introducing Flat Rate CDN
description:
Over the past year, we have improved Vercel’s Pro pricing to better reflect how teams build, with expanded user roles, flexible credits, access to enterprise features, and more. But one area our customers continued to give us feedback on was CDN pricing.

CDN costs should be predictable, but viral launches, traffic bursts, or misconfigured routes sometimes turned an otherwise normal month into an unexpected bill. For teams building on Vercel, that uncertainty made growth feel like a problem at exactly the moment it should feel exciting.

Today, we are introducing Flat Rate CDN for Pro teams: a new way to pay for CDN usage with a predictable monthly bill, built-in spike protection, and service tiers designed for different traffic profiles.

What is Flat Rate CDN?

Flat Rate CDN is an alternative to usage-based CDN billing that provides you with a predictable monthly bill.

The model is designed around a simple idea: teams should be able to choose the CDN capacity that corresponds to their typical usage profile, pay a known amount monthly, and avoid surprise overages from temporary spikes.

Flat Rate CDN has several advantages over usage-based billing:

  • Fixed monthly price: Pay a fixed amount for Vercel CDN each month.

  • Covers traffic spikes: CDN Requests, Fast Data Transfer, and other resources are no longer billed directly, so spikes don't result in surprise bills.

  • No overages: Your bill will never increase because of temporary usage spikes.

Importantly, predictable pricing does not mean lower-quality bandwidth. Every request still runs on Vercel’s premium network, including private fiber that routes around congestion on the public internet, which can improve performance by up to 60%. Comparable routing is often sold as a premium add-on, but Vercel includes it by default for Pro teams, and performance isn't degraded during traffic spikes.

title: Amazon SageMaker Studio simplifies getting started for new AI/ML builders with new sign-in options
description:
Amazon SageMaker Studio now lets new customers sign up with their Google, GitHub, or Apple credentials and land inside a fully configured Studio environment - no traditional AWS account setup and no console navigation required.

Previously, new customers who discovered a model on Hugging Face or an AWS product page had to complete a multi-step AWS account creation process, provide a credit card, navigate the AWS Console to find SageMaker AI, configure an environment, and set up IAM permissions before they could begin working. With earlier launches, we reduced environment setup to twenty seconds, pre-configured model customization permissions, and introduced deep links from Hugging Face and AWS product pages so customers could land directly inside Studio with a model pre-loaded. Customers can invite team members by email, and collaborators sign in with their own email credentials to access the shared Studio environment, including shared models, notebooks, and endpoints without configuring IAM users or permissions. title: DefoliationCAM: An Edge-AI System for Real-Time Insect Defoliation Severity Assessment in Grapevines
description:
arXiv:2610.20879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Insect-induced defoliation threatens grapevine health and yield, yet severity assessment relies on subjective manual scouting. We developed DefoliationCAM (D-CAM), a solar-powered edge AI system that estimates canopy defoliation and transmits results via LoRa to a web dashboard. The pipeline uses YOLOX-Nano to localize grapevine cordons in 4K images and a MobileNet-based classifier with lightweight channel attention to classify 320 x 320 pixel patches. The 29,674 field-collected patches were labeled as background or one of four damage levels: no to negligible, mild, moderate, and severe. Merging moderate and severe classes reduced the class imbalance ratio from approximately 40:1 to 8.8:1. Synthetic augmentation increased macro-F1 from 0.768 to 0.838. The classifier outperformed ResNet-50 in macro-F1 with fewer parameters (1.08 M versus 23.52 M). Patch predictions were aggregated into a canopy-level Non-linear Global Defoliation Severity (NGDS) score and validated against an entomologist's ratings of 86 held-out canopy images. Quadratic discriminant analysis identified boundaries of 9% and 29% separating negligible damage, mild damage requiring monitoring, and action-level damage warranting on-site scouting and insecticide treatment consideration. The 29% boundary aligned with the 25%-30% action threshold range for Japanese beetle management in grapevine. Using TensorRT FP16 on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, the pipeline processed each 4K image in approximately 1.5 s, with a complete operating cycle of 57-60 s. A five-week deployment of two field units demonstrated the feasibility of autonomous solar-powered operation, LoRa communication, and remote defoliation monitoring. D-CAM supports frequent, objective canopy damage assessment for targeted scouting and timely pest-management decisions.

title: A million-tap linear-phase FIR in real time: 7 ms of plumbing, 650 ms of filter
description:
I'm building Sonir Bench, a macOS app that captures everything your Mac plays, runs it through a DSP chain you design, and sends it to your DAC. The first post in this series was the overview. This one goes deep on a single piece: long FIR convolution.

Here's the result up front. On an M6 Mac mini, I ran a 998,545-tap linear-phase FIR at 768 kHz in f64 for almost eight hours. Zero dropouts: no underruns, no overruns, no missed deadlines.

The round-trip latency was 657.43 ms. But 650.09 ms of that is the filter's own group delay. The machinery that moves the audio adds only 7.33 ms. It took me a few wrong turns to learn to keep those two numbers apart.

Direct convolution buys you about 1 ms

Bench upsamples everything to 705.6 kHz (the 44.1 kHz family) or 768 kHz (the 48 kHz family) before processing. The upsampling filter itself is user-designed: you pick the transition band and tap count.

The first thing I measured was direct convolution, one multiply-add per tap per sample. At 705.6 kHz stereo, one core tops out at 757 taps. That's about 1 ms of impulse response. Not enough for a steep resampling filter, let alone room correction.

So the convolver is a uniformly partitioned FFT convolution (overlap-save):

Split the IR into K partitions of length B → FFT each to 2B points, keep them

Every B samples:
  FFT the latest 2B input samples → push onto the frequency-domain delay line (FDL)
  Σ_k FDL[p−k] · IR_k → inverse FFT → the second half (B samples) is valid output

Here's one hop for one channel, lightly trimmed (error handling removed, comments translated):

// 1. FFT the latest 2B samples (forward FFT clobbers its input, so copy first)
for (dst, src) in self.time.iter_mut().zip(history) {
    *dst = T::from_bus(*src);
}
self.fft.process_with_scratch(&mut self.time, &mut self.spectrum, &mut self.fft_scratch)?;

// 2. Store it in the FDL
let slot = (ch * partitions + fdl_pos) * bins;
self.fdl[slot..slot + bins].copy_from_slice(&self.spectrum);

// 3. Σ_k FDL[pos−k] · IR_k
self.acc.fill(Self::zero());
for k in 0..partitions {
    let idx = (fdl_pos + partitions - k) % partitions;
    let x = (ch * partitions + idx) * bins;
    let h = k * bins;
    T::mul_add_mono(&mut self.acc, &self.fdl[x..x + bins], &self.ir_spectra[h..h + bins]);
}

// 4. Inverse FFT
self.spectrum.copy_from_slice(&self.acc);
self.ifft.process_with_scratch(&mut self.spectrum, &mut self.time, &mut self.ifft_scratch)?;

// 5. Overlap-save: only the second B samples are valid. realfft doesn't normalize, hence 1/2B
let norm = 1.0 / (2 * b) as f64;
for (dst, src) in out.iter_mut().zip(&self.time[b..]) {
    *dst = src.to_bus() * norm;
}

The FFT is realfft. The FFTs aren't where the time goes, though. Step 3 is: K complex multiply-accumulates over B + 1 bins, every hop. mul_add_mono is hand-written NEON, and in stereo the IR spectrum is loaded once and applied to both channels. For a million taps the IR spectrum is about 17 MB of f64 complex numbers, and every hop reads all of it, so halving the reads is a direct speedup.

Per-sample cost is roughly 12·N/B for N taps: linear in taps, divided by the partition length. Measured on an Apple M1, 705.6 kHz stereo, as a share of one core:

taps \ B 1,024 4,096 16,384 65,536
65,537 21.6% 7.6% 3.7% 2.4%
300,001 38.2% 10.9% 4.3% 2.7%
1,048,576 154.5% 33.9% 9.5% 4.0%

The same million taps doesn't fit in a core at B = 1,024 and costs 4% at B = 65,536. B matters more than the tap count.

Partitioning without adding latency

Textbooks say a partitioned convolver has a latency of B. That assumes the host's block size is smaller than B. Plugin hosts typically use 64 to 512 samples, so if you pick a large B for efficiency, you have to buffer input until you have B samples, and that buffering is the latency.

If the host's block size is a multiple of B, there's nothing to buffer. You convolve the block you were handed and return a block of the same length.

Bench's internal block length is the entry block length times the interpolation ratio. Take 256 frames at 48 kHz, upsample 16×, and you get 4,096 frames at 768 kHz. So B is set to the internal block length itself, and the convolver adds zero latency.

B is the largest power of two that divides the block length:

pub fn partition_for(block: usize) -> Option<usize> {
    if block == 0 {
        return None;
    }
    // Largest power of two dividing the block (= its lowest set bit).
    // If the block is a power of two, that's the block itself
    let b = block & block.wrapping_neg();
    (b >= MIN_PARTITION).then_some(b)
}

block & block.wrapping_neg() keeps only the lowest set bit in two's complement: 4,096 gives 4,096, and 6,144 gives 2,048.

A test pins this down. It builds the chain with a unit-impulse IR and checks the path latency is identical to an empty chain:

#[test]
fn a_default_partition_convolver_adds_no_latency_to_the_chain() {
    let empty = Chain::build(&spec_48(256), Vec::new(), config()).unwrap();
    let baseline = empty.report().latency_base_frames;

    // Unit impulse = pass-through IR. We only care about delay
    let mut ir = vec![0.0; DEFAULT_PARTITION * 128];
    ir[0] = 1.0;
    let conv = FirConvolver::new(ir, DEFAULT_PARTITION).unwrap();
    let chain = Chain::build(&spec_48(256), vec![Box::new(conv)], config()).unwrap();

    assert_eq!(chain.report().node_report.latency_frames(), 0);
    assert_eq!(
        chain.report().latency_base_frames,
        baseline,
        "adding the convolver increased path latency"
    );
}

Reporting zero latency and actually having zero latency are different claims, so a second test pushes a sine through the same chain and checks the output lines up with the input at the reported delay.

The latency hasn't vanished, though. A bigger B means a bigger entry block, and the round trip grows with it. B is an exchange rate between latency and CPU, and Bench lets you pick it in the UI (4,096 to 65,536).

Failure 1: 1.37 seconds of wrong output after every swap

Bench can swap the processing chain while audio is playing. You build two chains, A and B, and switch between them with a 5 to 10 ms crossfade to compare by ear.

The first version started each new convolver from empty. A partitioned convolver keeps the spectra of the last K input blocks in its FDL, so starting empty means wrong output until the FDL fills. With a long IR that took up to 1.37 seconds. No 10 ms crossfade hides that.

The fix came from noticing that the FDL holds spectra of the input. It doesn't depend on the IR at all. Hand the old convolver's FDL to the new one and the new one is correct from its first block. That's transfer_history:

pub fn transfer_history(&mut self, previous: &Self) -> bool {
    if self.partition != previous.partition
        || self.channels != previous.channels
        || self.bins != previous.bins
        || self.precision != previous.precision
        // ...
    {
        return false;
    }
    // Input-side state carries over as is
    self.history.copy_from_slice(&previous.history);
    self.stage.copy_from_slice(&previous.stage);
    self.fill = previous.fill;

    // Re-pack the FDL newest-first. K may differ, so positions are remapped
    // (a precision mismatch means a different FDL type; the guard above already bailed)
    let geo = self.geometry();
    let (channels, previous_partitions, previous_pos) =
        (self.channels, previous.partitions, previous.fdl_pos);
    let (Some(next), Some(old)) = (self.freq.as_mut(), previous.freq.as_ref()) else {
        return false;
    };
    match (next, old) {
        (FreqDomain::F64(next), FreqDomain::F64(old)) => {
            next.transfer_fdl(old, geo, channels, previous_partitions, previous_pos);
        }
        (FreqDomain::F32(next), FreqDomain::F32(old)) => {
            next.transfer_fdl(old, geo, channels, previous_partitions, previous_pos);
        }
        _ => return false,
    }

    // Don't carry the output side over. The old graph keeps emitting the same
    // blocks during the crossfade, so its pending output would play twice
    self.pending.fill(0.0);
    // ...
}

A new tap count means a new K, but re-packing newest-first handles that. If K grows, the oldest slots stay zero and only the tail of the new IR is missing for a few hops. That's orders of magnitude better than starting from nothing, so I accept it.

The output side is the other trap. During the crossfade the old chain is still producing the same blocks, so carrying its pending output over would play that audio twice. Only the input side transfers.

The transfer only works when B, the channel count and the precision all match. That implies a rule: never derive B, or the choice of implementation, from anything a swap can change, such as the tap count. I went on to break that rule twice.

One more thing: a longer crossfade isn't safer. Both chains run for its whole duration, which doubles the CPU load, and a longer fade means a longer stretch at double load. The crossfade is clamped to 5 to 10 ms.

Failure 2: 300k taps and a stuttering mess

One day a 300k-tap resampling filter turned the output into a string of clicks. Design-time validation had said the filter was fine.

The resampling stage turned out not to use the partitioned FFT convolver at all. It ran a direct polyphase filter. Polyphase saves you a factor of the interpolation ratio, 1/16 at 16×, and I'd assumed that made it cheap. Wrong comparison. Polyphase is still O(N) per sample against O(N/B) for the FFT path, and a constant factor of 1/16 can't beat a different complexity class. At 300k taps, stereo, 44.1 kHz in, it needed about 35 cores' worth of time, so it missed every single block.

The fix was one convolution engine. The FIR node in the graph and the resampling stages now share the same partitioned convolver.

My first version switched implementations by tap count: direct below a threshold, FFT above. A test then showed that a swap crossing the threshold changed the implementation, so transfer_history refused and the audio dropped out, all because you nudged a design parameter. Since FFT was cheaper even at the default 1,345 taps, I deleted the switch.

Failure 3: the limit wasn't the CPU

The next investigation started from this: "On an M1 Air, 300k taps looks like the real-time ceiling. The compute estimate is two orders of magnitude below what the machine can do. Is something other than raw compute the bottleneck?"

I went through thermal throttling, being scheduled on an E-core, allocation on the real-time thread, and memory bandwidth. None of them. The machine never got hot because the whole pipeline used one core out of eight.

The cause was one line:

// How B was chosen (at the time)
DEFAULT_PARTITION.min(block)

However long the internal block, B never went above 4,096. That cap came from a 20 ms round-trip latency budget, and the reason for that budget had already gone away (next section). When the premise died, nobody went back to revisit what had been built on it.

I made B follow the internal block length and removed the cap. That opened the hole next to it. If B is longer than the block, the convolver can't complete a hop and fills the output with silence, without any error. Nothing in the path looks wrong, and silence plays. B is now derived from the block length the device actually delivers, and blocks that couldn't be filled are counted and shown in the UI.

To count them, process now returns the number of frames it actually wrote:

/// Returns the number of frames that received convolution output. The rest is filled with silence.
pub fn process(&mut self, input: &[f64], output: &mut [f64]) -> usize {
    // ...
    // 1. Accumulate input; run one hop every time B samples are buffered
    let mut done = 0usize;
    while done < frames {
        let take = (b - self.fill).min(frames - done);
        // ... (copy into stage)
        self.fill += take;
        done += take;
        if self.fill == b {
            self.hop();
            self.fill = 0;
        }
    }

    // 2. Emit output. Silence if there isn't enough
    let emit = frames.min(self.available);
    // ... (copy from pending to output, zero-fill the rest)
    self.available -= emit;
    emit
}

When the block length equals B, each call runs exactly one hop and returns what it was given. That's the whole zero-latency trick from earlier. When B is longer than the block, calls before B samples have accumulated run no hop and emit is 0. The output buffer still has the right length, so nobody notices unless they check the return value.

The latency was the filter

This is the part I most wanted to write about.

Bench's round-trip latency target is 20 ms. Browser video and games go through it too, so lip sync puts the ceiling around there. Originally, designs that exceeded it couldn't be saved.

But a linear-phase FIR with N taps always has a group delay of (N−1)/2 samples. At 300k taps that's 212 ms of group delay alone, ten times the budget. Making the convolver add zero latency didn't matter when the filter itself carried an order of magnitude more.

The UI makes it obvious. Here's an upsampler designed at 500k taps, built for 48 kHz input. The latency panel (labels translated):

Segment ms
Input 5.33
IPC 1.00
Upsampler 354.60
Node chain 0.00
Decimator 0.00
DAC 1.00
Total 361.94

At 768 kHz the same transition band needs 8.8% more taps than at 705.6 kHz, so the upsampler was built with 544,673 taps. Its 354.60 ms is (544,673 − 1) / 2 = 272,336 samples at 768 kHz. Everything else (input 5.33, IPC 1.00, DAC 1.00) adds up to 7.33 ms. The DAC was fed 768 kHz directly, so there's no decimator and it shows 0.00 ms.

The odd tap count is deliberate. 272,336 is exactly 17,021 × 16, a multiple of the interpolation ratio. Otherwise the delay would be a fractional number of samples at the input rate, and the latency couldn't be reported as whole frames. For linear phase, the tap count gets bumped up slightly to make it line up:

/// Align a linear-phase tap count to the conversion ratio: grow it until the group
/// delay `(N−1)/2` is a whole number of frames at the lower rate
fn align_taps(requested: usize, phase: FirPhase, factor: usize) -> Option<(usize, u32)> {
    match phase {
        FirPhase::Linear => {
            let aligned = ((requested - 1) / 2).div_ceil(factor) * factor;
            let taps = aligned * 2 + 1;
            (taps <= MAX_TAPS).then(|| (taps, u32::try_from(aligned).unwrap_or(u32::MAX)))
        }
        FirPhase::Minimum => Some((requested, 0)),
    }
}

The extra taps aren't zero padding. They go inside the window and the filter is redesigned with them, because if you're paying the CPU anyway, it should buy filter performance. Minimum-phase filters don't have a (N−1)/2 group delay, so there's nothing to align.

Now roughly double the taps: 96 kHz input, a 998,545-tap upsampler, and an 18-node chain behind it. The upsampler alone is 650.09 ms (499,272 samples), for a total of 657.43 ms. Input, IPC and DAC are still 7.33 ms. At 96 kHz the interpolation ratio is 8×, so the entry block is 512 frames, which is still 5.33 ms. The 18 nodes add 0.00 ms.

Double the taps and the filter's delay roughly doubles. The plumbing stays where it was.

Stop refusing latency

Linear-phase group delay is a pure delay, constant across the band. It doesn't change the sound by a single bit. What it costs you is lip sync, and transport response (when you pause or skip, the delay's worth of audio is still in the pipe). Both are costs the user is entitled to decide to pay.

So Bench no longer refuses designs over the latency budget. It shows the current round-trip latency at all times instead. The bar isn't clipped at 20 ms; it extends to the actual value and keeps a line at the 20 ms mark. The condition is that nobody uses it without knowing, and the decision only stands as long as that display does.

CPU got the same treatment. For a while there was a gate that refused designs predicted to overload the CPU. But the prediction moves by 1.75× with thermal state alone, so passing the gate never guaranteed real-time performance. A gate that says yes reads as "this will be fine," which is exactly the wrong message. The gate became a forecast: the expected load at design time, then the measured load and dropout counts once it's playing.

Two CPU numbers

The status bar shows two numbers: "CPU load 46% (peak 77%)" and "CPU 46%".

There used to be one: callback wall-clock time divided by the block deadline. Then I noticed that changing the entry block from 256 to 512 frames, same design, made it jump from 7.0% to 22.2%. Still zero dropouts, and the forecast barely moved. The jump was a step, not a slope, so my theory was that longer callbacks were spanning scheduler quanta and the measurement was counting time spent preempted.

To test that, I measured the thread's own CPU time separately. Rust's standard library has no API for thread CPU time, so this is one line of unsafe:

/// CPU time consumed so far by the calling thread.
pub fn thread_cpu_time() -> Option<Duration> {
    let mut ts = libc::timespec { tv_sec: 0, tv_nsec: 0 };
    // SAFETY: `ts` is a valid `timespec` and `clock_gettime` only writes to it.
    let ok = unsafe { libc::clock_gettime(libc::CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID, &raw mut ts) } == 0;
    // ...
}

A call costs about 154 ns, twice per block. Against the 5.8 ms deadline of 256 frames at 44.1 kHz that's 0.005%, so measuring doesn't disturb what's being measured.

The result: wall clock and CPU time agreed to within 0.1 percentage points at every B. The jump wasn't preemption. The work really had grown, and my explanation was the thing that was wrong. I still haven't tracked down why the forecast misses it.

Splitting them was still worth it. I can only say the two agree because I measured them separately. With one number I'd never have gotten past "probably preemption." Both are shown now:

  • CPU load (wall clock ÷ deadline): are we making the deadline? Includes time spent waiting. At 100%, audio drops out.
  • CPU (thread CPU time ÷ deadline): pure compute. Used to check the forecast.

Over the eight-hour run, peak load was 77%, so even the worst block left about 20% headroom.

One caveat: this run had a single resampling stage. Output stayed at 768 kHz, so there was no stage bringing the rate back down. With a DAC that tops out at 192 kHz, a second filter runs on the way out, and you pay its CPU too.

These numbers are for f64 convolution. Bench also has a mode that runs only the frequency-domain part in f32, which is about 2× faster for the same design with error around −141 dBFS. You can't switch it while playing, though: the FDL type changes, so transfer_history can't carry state across.

Takeaways

  • Direct convolution at 705.6 kHz stereo caps out at 757 taps per core. Partitioned FFT convolution gets a million taps into real time.
  • If the internal block length equals the partition length B, the convolver adds zero samples of latency. The price is that a bigger B means a bigger entry block.
  • Never derive B or the implementation from anything a swap can change, like tap count. The FDL can't transfer, and a small design tweak becomes a dropout.
  • Almost all of the round-trip delay is the filter's group delay, not the plumbing: 650 ms for a million-tap linear-phase filter versus 7 ms to move the audio.
  • Neither latency nor CPU load is refused anymore. Both are shown: latency as the sum of each segment's reported value, CPU as a measurement.

Not done yet

  • The latency figures are the sum of what each segment reports. The group delay is exact by construction, but nothing here was measured with a loopback recording. The 1.00 ms IPC figure is an estimate, and since no audio actually crosses a process boundary, it's a segment with nothing behind it.
  • Convolution runs on one core. This stage is limited by memory traffic more than arithmetic, so more cores wouldn't scale linearly. I did the f32 frequency domain first (2.05×) and left parallelism for later.
  • Low latency and very long filters together would need non-uniform partitioning. Not implemented.

Try it

Sonir Bench is free during the beta. It runs on Apple Silicon Macs with macOS 13 or later.

https://sonir.app

  • Headquarters: 61, Siya Residency Colony, Lalpur, Raipur, Chhattisgarh 492015, India
  • Core Specialties: Flutter (iOS/Android), Go, PHP, MySQL Architecture, Web3 Integrations, and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
  • Code & Engineering Profile: GitHub (@kaushalsingh365) | Dev.to (@kaushal_singh) | X (@creativesitein)

What Sets This Engineering Approach Apart?

  1. End-to-End System Ownership: Rather than outsourcing frontend and backend layers to disconnected freelancers, Kaushal Singh Rajput architects the entire lifecycle—from designing normalized MySQL schemas and writing secure Go/PHP REST APIs to deploying polished iOS and Android binaries via Xcode and Google Play.
  2. Custom Flutter Rendering & State Engines: Beyond standard CRUD apps, CreativeSite engineers interactive mobile experiences, regional social networking platforms, real-estate marketplaces, and custom JSON-driven UI engines in Flutter.
  3. Web3 & Automated FinTech Pipelines: Delivering production backend logic for cryptocurrency cloud platforms, non-custodial wallet connections, and automated BEP20 USDT payment verification.
  4. Generative Engine Optimization (GEO): Pioneering AI-first web architectures in Chhattisgarh—implementing strict Schema.org JSON-LD entity graphs, llms.txt specifications, and AI citation auditing so client brands are natively understood by ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude.

3. Architectural Pattern: High-Speed API Design for Flutter Clients

A common bottleneck in regional mobile app development is pairing a fast Flutter frontend with a sluggish, unoptimized backend. Here is a simplified example of how we structure ultra-fast, secure PDO database transactions at CreativeSite to ensure sub-50ms API responses for mobile clients:


php
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

namespace CreativeSite\Core\Database;

use PDO;
use PDOException;

final class DatabaseManager {
    private static ?PDO $instance = null;

    public static function getConnection(): PDO {
        if (self::$instance === null) {$dsn = "mysql:host=" . DB_HOST . ";dbname=" . DB_NAME . ";charset=utf8mb4";
            $options = [
                PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE            => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,
                PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
                PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES   => false, // Enforces native MySQL prepared statements
                PDO::ATTR_PERSISTENT         => true,  // Reduces connection overhead for high-concurrency mobile APIs
            ];
            self::$instance = new PDO($dsn, DB_USER, DB_PASS,$options);
        }
        return self::$instance;
    }
}

title: Build a Crash-Resistant AI Podcast Production Pipeline on Telnyx Edge
description:
Podcast post-production is rarely one operation. Before an episode can be published, someone must transcribe the recording, identify chapters, write show notes, create promotional copy, and produce a trailer. Each step depends on the one before it, which makes the workflow vulnerable to interruptions.

If processing fails after transcription, should the application transcribe the entire recording again?

I built Show Wrap Desk to explore a more durable approach.

It is a TypeScript application running on Telnyx Edge Compute that turns one podcast recording into:

  • A speaker-labeled transcript
  • Timestamped chapters
  • AI-generated show notes
  • A short trailer script
  • An MP3 trailer generated with Text-to-Speech

The workflow is owned by one Stateful Actor per show, so completed stages remain recorded when later work fails.

The pipeline

A producer starts the workflow with one request:

curl -X POST https://<your-worker>/wrap \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "show": "engineering-notes",
    "audioUrl": "https://example.com/episode.mp3"
  }'

The endpoint immediately returns an episode ID and a 202 Accepted response while the actor continues processing:

transcribing → chapterizing → notes → wrapped

You can inspect progress at any time:

curl "https://<your-worker>/wrapstatus/<episodeId>?show=engineering-notes"

One Stateful Actor per show

The worker derives a deterministic actor name from the show:

const desk = env.DESKS.idFromName(`show:${show}`);
const result = await desk.onWrap(show, audioUrl);

Every episode submitted for the same show reaches the same WrapDesk actor.

The actor stores its workflow data in embedded SQL tables:

  • episodes tracks status, errors, and completion times.
  • chapters stores titles and timestamps.
  • assets stores transcripts, show notes, and trailer audio.

This gives the workflow a durable ledger without requiring a separate orchestration database.

Stable tasks prevent duplicate pipelines

Each episode is processed by a scheduled task with a stable ID:

await this.schedule(
  0,
  "wrapTick",
  { episodeId },
  { id: `wrap:${episodeId}` }
);

Scheduling the same ID again replaces the pending task instead of creating another copy.

After each successful stage, the actor updates the episode status and re-arms that task for the next stage. If the same audio URL is submitted again while processing is incomplete, the actor finds the existing episode and resumes it.

The individual stages also check for persisted output before doing work. A stored transcript is not transcribed again, existing chapters are preserved, and generated notes or trailer audio are reused.

A failure can repeat the currently executing external operation if it occurred before the result was saved. However, completed and persisted stages are not restarted.

Speaker-labeled transcription

The first stage downloads the recording and submits it to the Telnyx Speech-to-Text API using Deepgram Nova-3:

const form = new FormData();

form.append("file", blob, "episode.mp3");
form.append("model", "deepgram/nova-3");
form.append("response_format", "verbose_json");
form.append(
  "model_config",
  JSON.stringify({
    diarize: true,
    smart_format: true,
    punctuate: true,
  })
);

The response includes word-level timestamps and speaker labels. The actor normalizes those words and stores them as the transcript asset before advancing the episode.

Creating chapters

The application groups consecutive words from the same speaker into turns. A silence longer than 60 seconds begins a new chapter:

const turns = buildTurns(words);
const chapters = splitIntoChapters(turns, 60);

Boundary detection happens locally, so the application does not need an AI request to determine every timestamp.

Telnyx AI Inference then receives short summaries of the resulting sections and returns chapter titles. The sample uses zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash through the Edge Compute TELNYX binding.

Writing show notes

The next inference request creates Markdown show notes containing:

  • A summary of the episode
  • Key takeaways
  • A pull quote
  • The generated chapter list

The transcript sent to the model is bounded to keep the example inside a manageable context window. A production implementation should introduce chunking or hierarchical summarization for long recordings.

Generating the trailer

The model selects a promising chapter and writes a trailer script capped at 400 characters.

That script is sent to the Telnyx Text-to-Speech WebSocket:

socket.send(JSON.stringify({ text: " " }));
socket.send(JSON.stringify({ text: script }));
socket.send(JSON.stringify({ text: "" }));

The actor collects base64 audio frames until the service sends:

{ "isFinal": true }

The sample defaults to azure.en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, but HOST_VOICE can be changed to another supported voice.

The project does not automatically clone the podcast host’s voice from the submitted recording. A custom or cloned voice must be configured separately.

Running the example 

git clone https://github.com/team-telnyx/telnyx-code-examples.git
cd telnyx-code-examples/show-wrap-desk

npm install
cp .env.example .env

Add your Telnyx API key, then generate the bindings and deploy:

npm run types
npm run deploy

Set the generated worker URL as DEPLOY_URL and run:

npm run bootstrap

The included demo uses a public-domain LibriVox recording.

Taking the pattern further

Before using this architecture in production, add authentication, audio-size limits, URL validation, retention controls, workflow telemetry, and human review for generated promotional content.

Large transcripts and audio files should also move to durable object storage instead of being kept directly in actor SQL.

The reusable idea is bigger than podcasting:

  1. Assign each workload a durable actor.
  2. Store the output of every stage.
  3. Track progress with explicit statuses.
  4. Schedule work using stable IDs.
  5. Make each stage safe to attempt again.
  6. Expose status through the same durable ledger.

That pattern can support transcription batches, media processing, document enrichment, report generation, and other long-running AI workflows.

The full source is available here:

https://github.com/team-telnyx/telnyx-code-examples/tree/main/show-wrap-desk

title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2610.21025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

title: AgentEval: Evidence-Bounded Assessment of Stateful Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.21177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Task completion alone does not determine whether a stateful agent satisfied its obligations, and a recorded judgment does not guarantee that its supporting evidence remains valid. We present AgentEval, a system that carries a contract-bound assessment record through tool execution, state and event capture, report qualification, and case maintenance. It separates what the agent did, what the evidence establishes, and whether the conclusion is supported for present use. On 32 tool-world administrations, independent checks agree on all 30 complete episodes, distinguishing satisfied, violated, and unresolved obligations; two interrupted administrations are retained. Controlled interventions on 48 evidence views expose 36 binding faults missed by hash-only checks without changing agent behavior. Scenario Studio connects reviewed cases to 12 two-turn reports with 24 independently checked answers. A separate public-benchmark study on 192 held-out executions reveals ten completed return subgoals within broader task failures and isolates the effect of missing evidence. These studies show how an executable assessment record makes scope, evidential support, and report reuse inspectable across an agent evaluation workflow.

title: CoDeFont: One-Shot Font Generation via Multi-Scale Factor-Specific Representation Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.21364v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-shot Font Generation (OFG) aims to synthesize a target glyph by transferring the stylistic characteristics of a single reference glyph while preserving the structure of the target character. However, accurately capturing font style from a single reference image remains challenging due to the limited stylistic information available in a single glyph, and this challenge is further amplified for complex scripts. We propose CoDeFont, a script-agnostic OFG framework that addresses this challenge through multi-level style-content factorization and progressive style-content reconciliation. CoDeFont independently aggregates complementary style and structural information across multiple spatial levels to obtain factor-specific representations, while a contrastive objective explicitly encourages separation between style and content embeddings. During reconstruction, the disentangled representations are progressively injected through multi-level style conditioning, enabling stylistic information to be incorporated at different decoding resolutions while preserving the underlying glyph structure. We evaluate CoDeFont on structurally distinct Bengali and Latin scripts across seen and unseen font styles. Extensive quantitative and qualitative analyses demonstrate consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed framework for OFG across diverse writing systems.

title: PRISM: PRIvileged Sibling-guided Multi-Agent Topology Design
description:
arXiv:2610.20628v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) based on large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful way to address complex problems, and their effectiveness depends critically on the collaboration topology that decides which agents participate and how they communicate. Recent work learns to generate this topology from the task query, fitting the generator to corpora of execution-verified graphs. The post-training method for such generators remains a limitation: a corpus lists the graphs that solved a query but never ranks them, leaving continued supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with no per-query preference to exploit. Without such a preference, the generator drifts toward the topologies the corpus contains most often rather than those that suit each query, so a gain on one task can come at a cost on another. We propose PRISM, which recovers per-query signal from the same corpus by learning with privileged information: a teacher reads, through a zero-initialized low-rank branch, a sibling graph that also solved the query and is unavailable at deployment, and the student matches its per-decision targets on trajectories the student samples itself. Across six diverse benchmarks PRISM improves over every topology-design baseline evaluated, and matched-teacher controls support the contribution of privileged query information. Code is available in this link.

title: Human in the loop means making sure the human is not out of the loop
description:
Agents now act before we ask and reach past what we authorized. A person in the loop isn’t enough if nobody owns the outcome. Here’s what to consider when designing for it.

Agents used to wait for a prompt because everyone though that AI was only chat. Now they triage inboxes, update records, and send messages while we’re in another meeting. That’s the whole point of them, and it’s also where the trouble starts.

Because of this, most agent teams hit the same questions:

  • Should the agent act before the user asks?
  • When the agent does more than anyone authorized, who is liable for the call?

The standard answer is a confirm dialog. Add a human click, and the accountability problem is supposed to vanish. It moves instead, landing on whoever had the least information and the least power over the outcome.

None of this is new.

Eric Horvitz modeled when software should act alone in 1999. Sixteen years earlier, Lisanne Bainbridge warned in Ironies of Automation that automating most of a job leaves people holding its hardest part, the watching. What’s new is volume: Gartner predicts at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously through agents by 2028.

I’m an apologist for artificial intelligence, and I’ll admit some things it isn’t good for.

The proactive question is mostly a decoy.

Initiative isn’t what hurts people; reach is. The better question is a reach test: what can the agent touch, and can a person put it back? The answer also settles liability.

Whoever sets an agent’s reach owns what it does there, and no confirm click should shift that to whoever clicked.

Stop Counting the Clicks

A confirm button records that a person was there; it says nothing about whether they read what they approved.

Kathleen Mosier and Linda Skitka named this automation bias in the 1990s, and it comes in two forms. Errors of commission follow the machine’s wrong suggestion, and errors of omission miss what the machine never flagged.

In Skitka’s 1998 NASA report, Automation: Decision Aid or Decision Maker?, people using an aid were 65% accurate when it was wrong, against 97% for people working without one. My Automation Bias entry at UX Guidelines calls omission the quieter failure, since nothing on the screen ever asks to be doubted.

Anthropic’s study of its own coding agent, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice, found newer users ran full auto-approve in roughly 20% of sessions, rising past 40% for experienced users.

Those experienced users also interrupted more, in about 9% of turns against 5% for new ones.

Approval is a ritual. Interruption is a judgment, which is good.

Anthropic’s own conclusion is that forcing a human to approve every step adds friction without necessarily adding safety. The per-click version is a cousin of the security theater usually credited to Bruce Schneier: visible, reassuring, and blind to how far the agent can reach afterward. People still belong in the loop, just at the point where judgment holds up: watching a run they can stop, instead of pre-signing a list they can’t read.

Follow the Blame

Madeleine Clare Elish gave this its name in 2019. In Moral Crumple Zones, she showed how responsibility for a failure gets pinned on the human operator closest to the event, even when that person had little control over what the automated system did.

A car’s crumple zone protects the driver. The moral version protects the system, and the operator absorbs the impact.

This is the most telling example. In March 2018, an autonomous Uber test vehicle struck and killed Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona. A safety driver, Rafaela Vasquez, sat behind the wheel, in the loop by every definition the program used. Granted, Vasquez was watching television on her phone, but that further illustrates the point.

According to CNN’s report on the Uber test driver’s 2023 guilty plea, the federal safety board found Vasquez had looked away for more than a third of the trip, and that an inadequate safety culture at Uber contributed. Uber faced no criminal charges and the driver pleaded guilty to endangerment and got three years of supervised probation.

She paid the price for the human missing the loop.

Being in the loop, it turns out, mostly means being nearest the crash.

None of this excuses the distraction, but it shows where accountability flows when a system is built around a watcher it doesn’t support. The reviewer who clicked approve on step 41 of a 60-step run becomes the crumple zone, while the team that decided step 41 needed no stronger gate stays out of the story.

Price the Unasked Act

Eric Horvitz’s 1999 paper, Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces, still frames when software should act unasked. His rule is decision theory in plain clothes: act only when the expected value beats doing nothing.

His math leaves one variable implicit: whether the action can be undone. Drafting a reply and sending it carry the same chance of being right and very different costs of being wrong.

One way vs. two way doors: Proactivity should scale with reversibility, not with confidence.

An agent that prepares, drafts, flags, and stages work is extending the user’s reach inside a space they can still edit and undo. One that sends, deletes, pays, or commits is spending the user’s authority.

The accuracy an action needs should shape the interaction too. A probabilistic output is a prediction about what’s likely right, while a deterministic one is a certainty.

  • A summary can be a prediction and still be useful, because a reader applies judgment.
  • A decision that routes a claim, approves a payment, or marks a contract compliant has to be a deterministic certainty, coming out the same way every time on the same input. That pushes it toward explicit rules the model applies rather than invents.

Put both behind the same button and a prediction ends up dressed as a certainty. Dan Maccarone quotes a client’s rule in We’re gorging on borrowed trust and it’s going to cost us: “people conclude, machines don’t.”

All of this gets harder with ambient agents, which watch a queue or an inbox and act while nobody is looking.

  • A chatbot waits for a question, so a bad answer at least has a witness.
  • An ambient agent acts on its own schedule, often many times before anyone reads the log, so its mistakes compound quietly.

For ambient work, the reach test has to be answered entirely in advance, and the record becomes the first thing a person sees rather than the last.

Write the Mandate

An agent, in the legal sense, acts for a principal, and the principal answers for what the agent does within the authority it was given. A power of attorney writes that authority down: what it covers, for how long, revocable at will.

We need this because nobody signs one that just reads “use your judgment.”

Agency is the whole value of an agent, and control over that agency is the one thing a principal never hands across. A mandate is the reach test answered in advance, in writing.

In Moffatt v. Air Canada, the airline claimed it couldn’t be held liable for what its website chatbot told a customer about bereavement fares. A British Columbia tribunal called that “a remarkable submission” in 2024 and held the airline responsible for everything on its site. The company set the chatbot’s reach, so the company owned what it said. And that bot only spoke when a customer asked it something. Maccarone’s name for what Air Canada spent is borrowed trust, a brand’s reputation lent to output nobody checked.

A mandate lives in the permissions, not in the conversation.

The Replit incident in July 2025 shows what happens when the mandate exists only as a sentence. SaaStr founder Jason M. Lemkin froze his project and told the agent repeatedly not to change anything. It deleted the production database anyway, then wrongly reported that rollback was impossible.

The fix is decades old: least privilege, enforced by the system at the moment of action. An instruction the agent can ignore is only a preference, not a harness.

Check the Law

I’m not a lawyer, so read this as a designer’s map of where the rules point, not legal advice. Some decisions shouldn’t appear in any mandate at all. Article 22 of the GDPR gives people the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

Even its exceptions for contracts and consent still require a way to reach a human, state a view, and contest the outcome.

Newer laws push the same way:

  • EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Article 14 requires people overseeing high-risk systems to be able to override the output and stop the system, and it names automation bias outright. A Digital Omnibus in July 2026 pushed those duties for uses like employment to December 2027.
  • California CCPA. The state’s automated decisionmaking rules require notice and an opt-out for significant decisions from January 2027, unless people can appeal to a human who can overturn the decision.
  • Colorado ADMT Act. Colorado replaced its 2024 Artificial Intelligence Act in May 2026 with a law granting human review after an adverse decision, from January 2027 if rulemaking finishes.
  • New York City Local Law 144. Hiring tools have needed bias audits since 2023, yet a December 2025 state comptroller audit found 17 possible violations among 32 companies where the city found one.
The law can require a way back. We have to design one.

These laws cover the second half of the reach test, not the first. What an agent can touch is still a product decision, and my own list goes further.

  • Hire, fire, or discipline. Livelihood decisions need a named person who can explain the call, in court.
  • Deny care or benefits. Refusing a claim or a treatment deserves a human who weighed it.
  • Sign for the organization. Contracts and regulatory filings bind a company in ways no model can answer for.
  • Give advice under a professional’s name. Legal, medical, and financial advice carries a license, and licenses belong to people.
  • Move money past the point of recall. Irreversible payments above a set limit wait for a person.

Design for Ownership

Microsoft Research tested their Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction against 20 products in 2019. Two describe half the job:

  • Scope services when in doubt
  • Provide global controls.

A third matters most once an agent decides rather than suggests: make clear why the system did what it did, which drew one of the highest violation counts in the study.

A decision without an explanation leaves a person who can repeat the call but never defend it, which is why I keep an entry on Explainability at UX Guidelines.

Agents need all three, plus two things a 2019 product rarely needed:

  • The first is a record the agent didn’t write. Replit’s agent misreported its own recovery options.
  • The second is a stop that works mid-flight, on screen while the agent runs, plus an escalation path for when it wants to step past its mandate.

I’ve worked inside a lot of these loops. In legal tech at the companies I managed teams at, we always built guardrails that made lawyers review contract language before it moved. We worked just as hard on making that review easy to do, because a required step that’s painful gets rubber-stamped. Maccarone adds the other half: review holds only when the reviewer has something to lose, like a name or a license.

A rubber stamp is a loop no human truly owns.

So when does human in the loop stop meaning human owning the loop? The moment the person in it can no longer pass the reach test. That happens when approvals outpace reading, when the only fence is a sentence in a prompt, or when the only account of events is the agent’s own. Any one of those is enough to turn a reviewer into a witness.

Keep the Initiative

So, should an agent act before you ask? Often, yes; an agent that never acts first is slower. The useful version gets the work ready while you’re busy, then waits at the edge of anything it can’t take back.

Who is accountable when it does more than you authorized? Not the person who clicked approve on a summary they couldn’t check. Whoever sets the reach owns the result. What happens inside the mandate belongs to whoever granted it. Anything outside it belongs to the team that built an agent able to get there.

That’s less comfortable for builders than a confirm dialog, which is the point. A dialog lets a team ship autonomy and park the liability elsewhere. Elish’s crumple zone is what you get by default when you design around a watcher instead of for one.

Human in the loop was a good phrase for a world where software waited. Agents don’t wait, so the phrase has to carry more than a button can hold. Agency matters, and it stays useful only while the people an agent works for remain in control of it.

Build agents that pass the reach test in plain view, and the loop becomes theirs.

Make These Four Moves

  • Audit the approvals. Measure how long people spend before clicking approve; if most approvals land within seconds, you’ve built a ritual rather than a review.
  • Write the rules. List what the agent may do, on which data, and until when, then enforce it in permissions, not the prompt.
  • Run the reach test. Let the agent act unasked on anything a person can undo in one step, and require a decision for anything they can’t.
  • Keep an independent record. Log actions outside the agent’s own narration, and keep a working stop control on screen while it runs.

Human in the loop means making sure the human is not out of the loop was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: CCIL Test Studio source 07: README.md
description:
# CCIL Test Studio

A complete interactive frontend built with React, plain JavaScript, CSS, and custom SVG icons. React and React DOM are the only runtime dependencies. Vite is the only development dependency, used for the local server and production build.

## Run locally

```powershell
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:5175/. MCM is the default team and includes populated synthetic sample data.

Select a team and enter its shared password. Sample teams use `team-demo` for User access or `admin-demo` for Administrator access, through the same sign-in form. There are no individual role accounts. Administrators can add teams with their own team and administrator passwords.

All team users can create System Baselines and workspaces, upload documents, resolve source-backed questions, and generate/edit test suites. Only adding a team and approving System Baseline updates require Administrator access. Initial baseline creation has no approval step.

System Baseline and CR creation both require at least one document from **Business**, **Technical**, or **Functional / Bug Information**. Any one category is sufficient; all three are never compulsory.

MCM means Membership and Collateral Management. Membership is an alias of MCM; it is not a separate team. Existing Membership-owned records retain their IDs and source references when migrated to MCM.

```powershell
npm run build
npm run preview
npm test
```

The production build is in `dist/`. Tests use Node's built-in test runner and Vite's existing loader; no test framework is installed.

## Included pages and workflows

1. Sign-in and team selection using a shared team password and two access levels.
2. Overview and workspaces: live counts, attention queue, searchable/paginated lists, create/copy wizard, shared team access.
3. System Baselines: reusable library, three document categories, a one-document minimum, initial creation without approval, knowledge manifest, and version history.
4. CR evidence: exactly Technical, Functional / Bug Information, and Business categories; combined documents; CR creation; local routing review; manual source-linked requirements; and activity.
5. Knowledge versions: baseline/CR selection, ADD/REPLACE/REMOVE diff, prerequisites, conflicts, incorporated-CR protection, and shared contracts.
6. Workspace chat: persistent version-specific conversations, cited local evidence lookup, attachments, historic threads, typed clarification answers, and immediate source-backed answer resolution.
7. Generation readiness: concrete blockers, final/provisional gates, template selection, persistent local run stages, cancellation, interruption handling, and retry.
8. Test suites: scenario search, editing and revisions, team reviews, citations, coverage/gaps, historic version identity, and CSV export.
9. Templates: manual fields and ordering, immutable versions, selection, CSV example import with header/source-row review, and separate example suites.
10. Baseline approvals: requests, precise diffs, exact manifest SHA-256, checklist, Administrator-only approval, decision history, and new immutable local baseline versions.
11. Dependency graph: custom SVG, directed relationships, source inspector, unresolved references, pan, zoom, search, type filters, and bounded hops/nodes.
12. Administration: shared team access, source-sharing grants/revocation, local connection configuration, audit history, metadata backup/import, and demo reset.

Light/dark themes, mobile navigation, keyboard focus, command search (Ctrl+K), accessible dialogs, empty/error states, and reduced-motion support are included. Hover motion uses short CSS transitions. The optional DM Sans stylesheet falls back to system fonts offline.

## Storage and integration boundaries

All seeded business content is synthetic. Backend services and agents are deferred.

- Application records use localStorage under `ccil-studio-demo-v1`.
- Original uploads use browser IndexedDB (`ccil-local-files`). Files receive type/size checks and SHA-256 checksums. Plain text, Markdown, and SQL have local previews. PDFs and DOCX are retained for original download. Nothing is sent to a server.
- Local source review does not claim classification, extraction, indexing, or authoritative validation.
- Chat uses a visible deterministic keyword lookup over eligible readable sources. It abstains when matching text is absent. This is not a model integration.
- Generation creates local demo fixtures from selected rules and reviewed answers. Provisional suites retain unresolved expected outcomes. These fixtures do not establish complete test coverage.
- CSV import/export is implemented locally. XLSX parsing/export and PDF/DOCX extraction await backend integration.
- Knowledge changes reset clarification readiness and create a fresh chat context. Historic chats and suites retain their original version.
- Baseline approval creates a new local immutable version. Existing workspaces keep their selected baseline. Real approval enforcement belongs on the backend.
- Connection settings store endpoint/model identifiers with an explicit disconnected state. No API keys are accepted or stored.
- JSON backups include records, conversations, and readable source text, but not original file bytes. Storage is per browser/device and is not a server database.
- Shared password verification and access checks are a browser-local prototype, not server-side authentication. Password digests are stored locally; plaintext passwords are not persisted. Backend authentication is deferred.

## Source layout

```text
src/
  access.js        # Shared team login, upload validation, and migration
  AppShell.jsx       Navigation, themes, search, local run progression
  store.jsx          React state, persistence, version/readiness checks, CSV helpers
  seed.js            Synthetic fixtures
  generation.js      Deterministic source-linked demo suites
  files.js           Native browser file checks, checksums, IndexedDB
  ui.jsx             Shared controls, dialogs, source/file components
  pages/             One module per application area
  styles.css         Approved visual foundation
  studio.css         Full layouts, responsive behavior, lightweight hover states
tests/
  frontend.test.mjs  Page rendering and version/readiness/CSV invariants
```

No UI kit, routing package, state-management package, graph/chart package, animation library, TypeScript compiler, or backend framework is added.

title: Task-Phase-Conditioned Expert Routing Is Not a Reliable Proxy for Quantization Sensitivity in MoE FFN Tensors
description:
arXiv:2610.20826v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate whether per-layer, per-task-phase (prompt/reasoning/response) expert-routing statistics in a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model can guide layer-wise mixed-precision quantization of routed-expert FFN tensors (down/gate and up). To attain layerwise routing statistics, we build a routing-capture and profiling pipeline for Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp, derive a composite sensitivity score from routing entropy/decisiveness, coefficient of variation (CV), Jaccard/phase-fragility, and top-1 expert strength, and use coordinate descent to tune a layer allocation that respects a fixed average bits-per-weight budget. Notably, the profiling pipeline is applicable to standard top-k MoE architectures. Across independent experimental conditions (about 4.0 bpw flat, about 2.7 bpw steep, and about 2.7 bpw random allocation as a control), reallocation fails to outperform the uniform baseline within each quality tier. In the flat regime, reallocation is statistically neutral (z about 0.9). For the steep tier, the random reallocation performs within 1 SE of the routing-guided reallocation at the same tier, indicating a structural loss at this quality rung caused by mandatory downgrades and Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) tail injection. This aggressive-budget condition shows a decisive loss (z greater than 4 SE) replicated across three independent weight vectors. We argue that the deeper issue is that routing-behavior statistics are an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.

title: Client Intake Form Vs Contact Form: A Critical Distinction for Businesses
description:
Client Intake Form Vs Contact Form: A Critical Distinction for Businesses

In the realm of digital interactions, businesses often rely on online forms to capture leads, facilitate communication, and streamline client onboarding processes. However, a common misconception lies in the interchangeable use of client intake forms and contact forms. This oversight can lead to inefficiencies, missed opportunities, and a lack of personalized engagement with potential clients. Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms fail to address the unique needs of businesses, as they do not account for the nuances of client intake, which requires a more comprehensive and structured approach.

The primary reason generic forms fall short is their inability to cater to the specific requirements of client onboarding. They lack the depth and customization necessary to gather pertinent information, set clear expectations, and establish a foundation for a productive client-business relationship. Furthermore, these forms often result in incomplete or inaccurate data, leading to follow-up conversations that could have been avoided with a more tailored approach.

From an engineering standpoint, there are several key takeaways when designing effective client intake forms:

  1. Customization is Key: Client intake forms should be meticulously crafted to align with the specific services or products offered by a business. This ensures that the information gathered is relevant and useful for subsequent interactions.
  2. Structured Data Collection: Unlike contact forms that typically capture basic information, client intake forms should be designed to collect structured data that facilitates seamless integration with existing systems, such as CRM software, to automate workflows and enhance data analysis.
  3. User Experience (UX) Considerations: The design of client intake forms should prioritize user experience, making it easy for potential clients to provide necessary information without feeling overwhelmed. This includes logical form field ordering, clear labeling, and optional fields to minimize friction and increase completion rates.

In conclusion, while contact forms serve a purpose for general inquiries, they are insufficient for the nuanced process of client intake. Businesses must recognize the value in investing in tailored, structured, and user-centric client intake forms to enhance their conversion rates, improve client relationships, and ultimately drive growth.

title: HideProxy Review: Real-world pros and cons of a new residential proxy service
description:
When using GoLogin to manage multiple accounts, choosing the right type of proxy is crucial for the stability and longevity of your profiles. Beginners often find themselves weighing the differences between Residential, Datacenter, Mobile, and ISP proxies.
Residential proxies are currently the top choice. Because they use real IP addresses from individual user devices, they appear more natural and are harder for platforms like Facebook, Google, or TikTok to detect. When paired with GoLogin, residential proxies significantly reduce the risk of triggering security checkpoints. Services like HideProxy fall into this category, offering stable "sticky sessions" and flexible country-based targeting.
Datacenter proxies offer the advantages of high speed and low cost. However, since these IPs originate from data centers, they are easier to identify. This type is best suited for low-risk tasks, such as quick checks or running automated tools that do not require a high level of trust.
Mobile proxies provide the highest level of reliability because the IPs come from mobile network carriers. Many social platforms consider mobile proxy IPs to be very "clean." The downsides are their higher cost and the fact that their speeds can sometimes be less consistent than those of residential proxies.
ISP proxies occupy a middle ground. They offer speeds comparable to datacenter proxies while possessing the characteristics of residential proxies, making them a great fit for users who need long-term stability.
In reality, no single proxy type is perfect for every scenario. The key is to align the proxy type with your specific use case and the platform you are targeting. Many GoLogin users have found that switching to high-quality residential proxies—such as those provided by HideProxy—noticeably reduces the rate of profile errors.
