title: Does Personalization Break Trust? Open-Set Rejection Calibration Under Few-Shot On-Device Intent Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2610.20652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Always-on virtual assistants increasingly personalize on-device to new user-specific commands via few-shot fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA), but this adaptation is evaluated almost exclusively on whether it learns the new commands, not on whether the assistant can still recognize an input that matches none of its intents - the out-of-scope (OOS) rejection problem. We show that naive few-shot LoRA personalization degrades OOS-rejection AUROC (area under the ROC curve) on every one of five public intent-classification benchmarks (mean drop $0.055$--$0.258$, five seeds each), while in-scope accuracy is preserved. A scorer-invariant check shows part of this drop is an artifact of the standard confidence scorer's own miscalibration under adaptation, though a smaller, genuine effect remains under any scorer; we trace it to a measurable shrinkage of the embedding margin around known-intent regions (pooled Spearman rho=0.61$). A deployment-cheap fix is scoring rejection by Mahalanobis distance instead of softmax confidence without extra training/retraining recovers most of the lost quality on 3 of 5 datasets at no accuracy cost, beats two further OOD scoring baselines, and generalizes across shot count, LoRA rank, and a second base encoder. We report honestly where the fix falls short and release all code for reproducibility.

title: N-CODE AI Studio: Turning Website Audits into a Side Hustle with Open-Weight AI
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.

What I Built

I built N-CODE AI Studio, an open-source AI-powered website auditing platform designed to help freelancers, small businesses, and web development agencies understand website performance and identify opportunities for improvement.

Many small business owners struggle to understand technical reports or know which website problems to fix first.

N-CODE AI Studio aims to turn technical website measurements into clear, actionable recommendations using open-weight AI.

The side hustle idea: Freelancers can use this tool to prepare website health assessments and offer professional performance optimization, accessibility improvements, SEO consulting, and website redesign services.

The product is an early-stage prototype. This business concept has not yet been validated with paying customers.

Demo

Application: https://ncode-ai-studio-hf26.vercel.app/

Case Study: https://ncode-ai-studio-hf26.vercel.app/case-study

Verified Lighthouse + Gemma AI Execution:

https://github.com/Deshan217/ncode-ai-studio-hf26/actions/runs/38784847640

Raw Test Evidence:

https://github.com/Deshan217/ncode-ai-studio-hf26/actions/runs/38784847640/artifacts/11998425425

The verified demonstration runs Lighthouse in a GitHub Actions environment and generates recommendations using Gemma 3 through Ollama.

The hosted Vercel application currently demonstrates the interface and case study. Live cloud AI inference and production PageSpeed API quota configuration remain separate deployment improvements.

Code

The project is publicly available on GitHub under the MIT License.

GitHub Repository:

https://github.com/Deshan217/ncode-ai-studio-hf26

The repository contains the Next.js application, audit processing logic, Ollama integration, test workflows, documentation, and reproducible AI testing configuration.

How I Built It

I used the following technologies:

  • Next.js and React: Application interface and server-side API routes.
  • TypeScript: Typed application and auditing logic.
  • Lighthouse: Website performance, accessibility, SEO, and best-practice analysis.
  • Ollama: Local inference infrastructure.
  • Gemma 3 1B: Open-weight AI model used for verified recommendations.
  • GitHub Actions: Automated builds, testing, and reproducible AI execution.
  • Vercel: Hosting for the application interface.

How the AI Workflow Works

The application is designed to accept a public HTTPS website URL, collect audit findings, and generate an understandable improvement report.

For the verified demonstration, GitHub Actions runs Lighthouse directly in headless Chrome, extracts website audit findings, and provides those findings to a locally running Gemma model through Ollama.

The AI then generates prioritized recommendations that a developer or website consultant can review.

Real Testing Results

I tested the workflow against the N-CODE STUDIO website:

Website: https://ncodest.com/

The October 15, 2026 Lighthouse run produced the following mobile lab scores:

Category Score
Performance 57/100
Accessibility 78/100
SEO 100/100
Best Practices 100/100

The Gemma model successfully generated recommendations related to accessibility, semantic structure, accessible labels, contrast, and performance optimization.

These results come from a single lab run and should not be interpreted as ongoing measurements or a guarantee of user experience. AI-generated recommendations require human review.

Challenges I Faced

One challenge was Google PageSpeed Insights API quota limits.

Although local Gemma inference worked, the first end-to-end attempt could not retrieve audit data because the PageSpeed API quota had been exceeded.

To produce reproducible evidence, I implemented a separate GitHub Actions workflow using Lighthouse directly with headless Chrome, without depending on the PageSpeed API.

This workflow successfully completed both a real Lighthouse audit and real open-weight AI inference.

Another challenge is hosting: an Ollama instance running locally is not automatically accessible to a cloud-hosted Next.js application. A secure production AI service is part of the future roadmap.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation gives independent developers the freedom to experiment, learn, customize, and build useful products without depending entirely on proprietary AI platforms.

Using Gemma through Ollama makes it possible to run the language model under developer control.

For N-CODE AI Studio, this provides several advantages:

  • Ability to inspect and modify the AI prompt and integration.
  • Flexibility to experiment with different open-weight models.
  • Potential to operate local inference without per-request proprietary model API charges.
  • Opportunities for community contributions and improvements.
  • Greater control over where AI processing takes place.

The complete application is shared under the MIT License.

My goal is to make useful AI-assisted website consulting more accessible to independent developers and smaller businesses.

What's Next?

My future plans for N-CODE AI Studio include a securely hosted AI inference service, better audit reporting, user authentication, rate limiting, audit history, and professional client-ready reports.

I also want to collect feedback from freelancers and small business owners to see whether this tool can become a practical, affordable website consulting product.

Built by N-CODE STUDIO for Hacktoberfest 2026.

Thank you to the open-source community and the developers building accessible AI tools!

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma

N-CODE AI Studio uses Google's open-weight Gemma 3 1B model through Ollama to transform real Lighthouse audit measurements into actionable website improvement recommendations.

The model was successfully executed and tested using GitHub Actions, with real inference results and supporting evidence available in the public repository.

title: Building a Headless E-Commerce ERP Integration Engine with Node.js
description:
As modern enterprises shift toward composable commerce architectures, standard point-to-point plugins quickly hit structural bottlenecks. Monolithic e-commerce plugins fail when confronted with complex business logic, custom pricing tiers, multi-warehouse fulfillment, and high-velocity transactional spikes. For engineering leaders, CTOs, and technical directors, designing a scalable headless e-commerce erp integration engine requires moving beyond brittle out-of-the-box connectors toward a resilient, event-driven middleware approach.

At WebVibez, our engineering team regularly designs robust backend architectures for complex enterprise requirements. Whether we are architecting bespoke solutions or delivering scalable Custom Software Development projects, the core challenge remains the same: ensuring absolute data consistency between fast-moving customer-facing storefronts and heavily structured legacy enterprise resource planning (ERP) databases.

The Engineering Challenge: Bridging Decoupled Systems

In a traditional monolithic setup, the database handles both user experience rendering and business logic execution. In a headless paradigm, the frontend (Next.js, Remix, or mobile clients) communicates exclusively via APIs. When an order is placed, or stock levels shift, the system must coordinate state changes across distinct services:

  1. Storefront/API Gateway: Captures user intent and processes payment tokens.
  2. Integration Middleware: Acts as the translator, state manager, and retry orchestrator.
  3. ERP Core: Processes accounting, procurement, manufacturing, and master inventory.

Without a well-architected node.js erp integration architecture, minor network hiccups or unexpected payload mutations can lead to inventory overselling, orphan orders, or silent data drift.

Architectural Blueprint: Node.js & TypeScript Middleware

Building with Node.js and TypeScript offers the ideal balance of asynchronous I/O performance and compile-time safety. Below is a breakdown of how to structure an enterprise-grade integration engine.

1. Webhook Orchestration & Event-Driven Ingestion

Instead of polling the ERP system—which wastes compute resources and causes stale data—rely on webhook-driven ingestion. Your Node.js server should expose high-throughput endpoints to catch events like order/created, inventory/updated, and customer/updated.

import express, { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { verifyWebhookSignature } from './security';
import { orderQueue } from './queues/orderQueue';

const router = express.Router();

router.post('/webhooks/commerce/order-created', async (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const signature = req.headers['x-commerce-signature'] as string;

  if (!verifyWebhookSignature(req.rawBody, signature)) {
    return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid webhook signature' });
  }

  const orderPayload = req.body;

  // Push to persistent queue for resilient async processing
  await orderQueue.add('process-erp-order', orderPayload, {
    attempts: 5,
    backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 5000 },
  });

  return res.status(202).json({ status: 'queued' });
});

2. Strict Type Safety with Zod and TypeScript

TypeScript custom erp backend development requires rigorous payload validation. ERP systems are notorious for strict data schemas (e.g., specific SKU formats, precise decimal handling for currency). Using validation libraries like Zod alongside TypeScript interfaces ensures invalid data is caught at the ingress boundary before hitting downstream queues.

import { z } from 'zod';

export const ErpOrderSchema = z.object({
  externalOrderId: z.string(),
  customerEmail: z.string().email(),
  items: z.array(
    z.object({
      sku: z.string(),
      quantity: z.number().int().positive(),
      unitPrice: z.number().positive(),
    })
  ),
  totalAmount: z.number().positive(),
});

export type ErpOrder = z.infer<typeof ErpOrderSchema>;

Comparing Integration Approaches

Evaluating architectural choices early prevents costly refactoring cycles down the line. The table below outlines the tradeoffs between common integration strategies.

Strategy Latency Scalability Maintenance Overhead Best Suited For
Point-to-Point Plugins Low to Medium Low High (breaks on updates) SMBs with standard product catalogs
Batch FTP/CSV Sync High (Hours/Days) Medium Low Legacy systems with zero API support
Event-Driven Node.js Middleware Real-Time / Near-Instant High Medium (requires active monitoring) Enterprise headless commerce & multi-warehouse setups

Achieving Reliable Real-Time Inventory Sync

One of the most complex requirements in syncing e-commerce platforms with custom erp is preventing overselling during flash sales. To achieve low-latency inventory synchronization, developers must handle concurrency gracefully.

  • Redis Distributed Locks: When stock updates arrive from the ERP, acquire a distributed lock on the specific SKU key in Redis to prevent race conditions across parallel worker threads.
  • Optimistic UI with Background Verification: Allow the e-commerce cart to reserve stock temporarily, backed by a fast cache layer, while asynchronously committing the transaction to the backend ERP database.

For businesses scaling up their digital footprint beyond e-commerce into omnichannel operations, maintaining robust infrastructure is critical. Beyond backend APIs, organizations often require complementary digital touchpoints, such as high-performance Website Development Services and scalable Mobile App Development to unify the complete customer journey.

Conclusion

Mastering headless e-commerce erp integration transforms a brittle operational bottleneck into a competitive advantage. By leveraging Node.js for asynchronous throughput, TypeScript for strict domain modeling, and robust message queues for fault tolerance, engineering teams can build resilient systems capable of handling enterprise-scale transactions without breaking a sweat.

title: TurboMamba: Faster Inference, Faster Training, and Better Prediction with Lexical Memory
description:
arXiv:2610.20682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce TurboMamba, a language-model architecture for faster inference, faster training, and better token prediction. A global Mamba-3 model runs once per completed token block. A small Transformer uses this global context and earlier tokens within the block to predict the next token. Three lightweight additions improve local predictions: direct access to the previous block's last token, a small correction to next-token scores, and a learned mixture with recent-token frequencies. We compare twelve small-scale implementations on public FineWeb-Edu, with comparable parameter counts and shared training-budget caps. The baselines include Transformer, Mamba-3, Jamba, and Zamba. The Jamba and Zamba versions use Mamba-3 in place of their original Mamba modules. TurboMamba achieves the lowest mean test prediction loss (negative log-likelihood, NLL) among all twelve models. Its mean NLL is 9.4% lower than that of Mamba-3, 7.3% lower than that of the Jamba version, and 18.3% lower than that of the Zamba version. End-to-end training throughput is 2.60x that of Mamba-3, 2.81x that of the Jamba version, and 4.82x that of the Zamba version. We measure end-to-end batch latency for a batch of 32 sequences, each with a 256-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. On this workload, TurboMamba achieves a 3.12x speedup over Mamba-3, a 3.53x speedup over the Jamba version, and a 6.21x speedup over the Zamba version.

title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.20881v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While foundation models and vision transformers (ViTs) have redefined visual representations, current active learning (AL) strategies for these backbones largely operate at the patch or region level, where annotation requirements remain high due to extensive pixel labeling. Extending ViT-based AL to the pixel-level, low-budget regime is uniquely challenging: with as little as one pixel query per image, a method must simultaneously identify the most informative locations and train a reliable decoder head from an extremely sparse signal. We introduce TEAL (Token-space Efficient Active Learning), the first pixel-level AL framework built around ViT representations. TEAL uses a frozen ViT backbone and performs diversity-based selection directly on its native token lattice, avoiding the artifacts introduced by interpolating token embeddings to dense pixel resolutions. Our framework applies a two-level MaxHerding strategy over multi-layer token descriptors to select representative candidates, followed by margin-based uncertainty refinement on a finer decoder grid. Across CamVid, Cityscapes, ADE20K, and Pascal Context, TEAL consistently outperforms previous baselines under extreme label scarcity, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +24.36 mIoU with a single labeled pixel (px) per image, and reaching up to 97% of fully supervised performance with just 10 px. To rigorously establish the source of the gains, we further show that the improvements persist when all baselines are equipped with the same DINOv3 backbone, demonstrating that coupling token-space selection with uncertainty refinement on the decoder grid makes ViT token geometry an effective foundation for extremely low-budget active segmentation.

title: GRADS: Graph-Regulated Agentic Data Synthesis with Controllable Difficulty
description:
arXiv:2610.21167v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly deployed to retrieve precise information from large corpora, yet multi-hop, long-horizon tasks remain challenging. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a scalable solution, with existing pipelines typically expanding seed tasks to increase their apparent depth and breadth. However, this expansion does not reliably translate into necessary reasoning: newly introduced evidence may be only weakly coupled to the answer, creating a mismatch between intended and empirical difficulty. To address this problem, we introduce GRADS, a graph-guided agentic data synthesis framework with explicit difficulty control. GRADS runs a closed loop of seed selection, evidence expansion, question--answer construction, and verification while maintaining a graph of the evidence and inference dependencies required to derive each answer. At each step, it conditions generation on a relevant subgraph, preserving indispensable inference without accumulating irrelevant context. Experiments across security, software-engineering, and scientific-document domains show that GRADS consistently generates verified tasks with empirically separated difficulty distributions, as measured by independent solvers. Moreover, under matched training budgets, post-training on this data delivers consistent gains at every level: SFT raises the solution-termination rate to over 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%, RL trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and on our held-out, domain-specific benchmarks, the resulting 4B model matches Sonnet~4 on software engineering and surpasses it on the scientific and security domains.

title: ARIA: Runtime Inspection and Amendment for Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.20780v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, turning a correctable error into a failed task. Diagnosing completed runs or repeatedly re-executing them to search for corrections does not provide a learned policy for intervening while execution is still in progress. We present Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (ARIA), a framework for learning when and how to repair ongoing multi-agent executions. Our key intuition is to turn execution-verified repairs into reusable supervision, moving repair search into data construction and training so that a learned model can intervene at runtime without repeatedly testing alternatives. First, we collect over 24{,}000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi-agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models. From these trajectories, we construct the ARIA dataset, to our knowledge the first large-scale dataset pairing failed multi-agent trajectories with execution-verified repairs. It contains 3{,}953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue. Then, we develop the ARIA framework for MAS-agnostic runtime inspection and amendment, designed to integrate with any MAS that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement. Using verified repairs as training examples, we teach a compact model to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run. The aim is to learn repair strategies that apply to related failures in new configurations, rather than merely reproduce individual corrections. Finally, the trained ARIA model demonstrates strong repair performance in both post-hoc and runtime settings, with generalization to unseen frameworks and host models. Our code is available at https://github.com/LabRAI/ARIA.

title: My React forms expect exactly one error shape: the 422 contract between Laravel and React
description:
I used to handle API errors in React the way most people do: one big try/catch, one generic toast, done. It worked, and every form looked like it was built by someone who had given up.

The fix wasn't a library. It was a contract: Laravel always returns validation failures the same way, so React can always render them the same way.

On the backend, FormRequests do the work. When validation fails, Laravel responds with HTTP 422 and a JSON body shaped like this:

{
  "message": "The email field is required. (and 1 more error)",
  "errors": {
    "email": ["The email field is required."],
    "password": ["The password must be at least 8 characters."]
  }
}

That shape never changes, on any endpoint. That's the whole contract.

On the frontend, my registration form keeps one state object:

const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

And the catch block is a single if/else:

catch (err) {
  if (err.response?.status === 422 && err.response.data?.errors) {
    setErrors(err.response.data.errors);
  } else {
    setErrors({ general: err.response?.data?.message || 'Registration failed. Please try again.' });
  }
}

Each input renders its own error:

{errors.email && <p className="mt-1 text-xs text-rose-600">{errors.email[0]}</p>}

The input border turns rose via a tiny inputClass(field) helper. And the odd-shaped failures — network down, server 500, a route that doesn't exist — collapse into errors.general, the single banner at the top of the form.

Two deliberate choices worth calling out:

  1. I only take the first error per field (errors.email[0]). Showing three stacked messages under one input looks broken. Laravel orders them by rule priority, and the first one is almost always the one that matters.

  2. Non-422 failures never pretend to be validation errors. A 500 doesn't become "the email is invalid" — it becomes a banner. This is the thing most form code gets wrong: it maps every failure onto the same red box and lies to the user about what happened.

The admin user-edit form in my kit uses the exact same pattern — setFormErrors(err.response.data.errors) on 422, general otherwise. One contract, copied across every form, zero decisions left to make per page.

If you're starting a new Laravel + React project and want to skip wiring all of this yourself — the 422 contract, the AuthContext, the token interceptor — I sell a starter kit that has it done: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig. It's $19, one-time, and it's the same code I copy into client projects.

title: KNOU-Flood: Advancing global streamflow forecasting with lead-aware probabilistic machine learning
description:
arXiv:2610.20640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Global streamflow forecasting supports flood preparedness, yet data-driven models trained on reanalysis lose skill when driven by operational forecasts, increasingly so with lead time. AIFL addresses this shift with a two-stage transfer-learning recipe and a deterministic LSTM, but it feeds one forecast lead time into the whole input window and gives no uncertainty. We ask how far this open recipe can be extended without changing its recurrent core. KNOU-Flood keeps a single-layer LSTM and the two-stage training and changes the information around it: a longer input window (424 days), lead-aware forecast inputs, GraphCast as a second forecast source next to ECMWF HRES, and a latent-noise ensemble trained with the fair CRPS. We compare against a re-implementation of the AIFL recipe (its code is not public) under identical data, stations, splits and metrics. Our contributions are threefold. First, over three seeds and 2,099 test basins (2021-2023), KNOU-Flood reaches a median KGE' of 0.65 at LT1 and 0.48 at LT10 against 0.62 and 0.34, with significant gains at all ten lead times under two scoring protocols, also against a 1024-unit baseline and on held-out basins (one seed each). Second, identical weights give an LT10 KGE' of 0.18 or 0.34 depending on how forecasts are fed, so much of the lead-time decay reported for AIFL is an input-protocol effect; the probabilistic head contributes most to the gain, followed by the raw GraphCast channels, the longer window and mixed fine-tuning. Third, the ensembles reach lower CRPS than probabilistic versions of the baseline, are nearly calibrated with inference-time dropout, and detect 1.5- and 2-year floods better than all baselines; the benefit for rarer floods depends on the seed, and an exploratory tail-weighted variant improves 10-year and larger events. KNOU-Flood is a controlled extension of an open recipe, not a new architecture.

title: Expert pruning improves decode throughput up to 1.8 with minimal quality loss
description:
Current MoE inference pipelines still stall on expert traffic during batched decoding, limiting latency improvements despite sparsity. SlimWise shows that pruning experts only in the decode phase and reusing prefill KV caches can boost throughput by nearly twofold without perceptible quality loss.

Earlier serving optimizations either prune the full model—including the costly prefilling step—or accept a trade‑off where speed gains come at the cost of generation fidelity. Those approaches sacrifice the rich context built in the prefill stage, leading to noticeable drops in perplexity or output length when the same pruning ratio is applied during both phases.

On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, SlimWise improves decode throughput by up to 1.81× at 50 % expert pruning with minimal accuracy loss[1]. The system keeps the prefill stage untouched, activates only half of the experts during generation, and still delivers token‑level latency reductions that translate into a roughly 78 % end‑to‑end speedup in typical request patterns.

Without additional training, SlimWise’s KV cache handoff recovers much of the accuracy lost to pruning in many evaluated settings[1]. By feeding the decoder with the full‑model KV cache generated during prefill, the pruned model inherits a high‑quality attention context, so the model’s accuracy remains comparable to the unpruned baseline even when half the experts are disabled.

Because expert pruning preserves the attention architecture and KV cache format, this KV cache handoff requires no KV cache conversion[1]. The unchanged cache layout lets the runtime simply swap the weight mask between phases, eliminating costly data reshaping or additional memory copies that would otherwise erase any latency gains from pruning.

SlimWise’s gains are demonstrated on two MoE backbones and three pruning criteria; performance on larger models or more aggressive pruning ratios remains untested, and the low‑cost distillation stage—while helpful—adds a modest extra training step before deployment. One open question is whether dynamic token‑level expert selection could further tighten the latency–quality curve without requiring a static prune threshold.

Production stacks that serve Mixture‑of‑Experts should replace monolithic decode with a prefill‑decode split and directly feed the full‑model KV cache into a pruned decoder, eliminating the need for costly runtime cache rewrites. Re‑running latency benchmarks under this disaggregated regime will likely reveal hidden speed margins that current end‑to‑end numbers conceal.

References

  1. SlimWise: Decoupling Expert Pruning Across Prefill and Decode for Efficient MoE Serving

title: OpCredit: Operation-Aware Policy Learning for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2610.21345v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering(KGQA) relies on sequences of executable operations, but trajectory-level rewards obscure their individual contributions. Successful trajectories may contain ineffective operations, while failed trajectories may contain useful ones. To assess individual operations, we propose OpCredit, an operationaware policy-learning framework that combines downstream outcome credit with immediate transition credit: Branch Outcome Credit (BOC) reuses ordinary rollouts to compare terminal task rewards observed after different operations under matched navigation contexts; Frontier Transition Credit (FTC) measures operation-induced changes in answer-conditioned frontier potential. The two complementary signals jointly supervise the corresponding decision spans during training, while inference uses only the learned policy and standard KG interface. Experiments on ComplexWebQuestions, WebQSP, and GrailQA across three backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in KGQA performance.

title: A 429 at 02:00: Postmortem for a Quota Outage
description:
A 429 at 02:00: Postmortem for a Quota Outage

Your phone buzzes at 02:07 with a failed staging job, which on its own is survivable, and then four minutes later the production summarizer starts emitting truncated output for real users. You check the model provider's status page and it is a wall of green, so you conclude the model is fine and start hunting through your own prompts instead. That instinct costs you twenty minutes, because the outage was never a model problem — it was a credential and retry problem that the model was merely the first to notice.

A boundary before we go further: this is a teaching postmortem, reconstructed from a well-documented failure class rather than a report on one named company's incident. The timeline is a plausible sequence, the code below is runnable against a fake provider, and the only numbers you should trust are the ones you print on your own machine. That distinction matters, because postmortems copied verbatim from someone else's outage teach you nothing about your own blast radius.

Timeline

Time Observation
02:00 Nightly staging suite begins; it imports the same client library and the same API credential as production.
02:03 Staging's summarization fixtures exhaust the shared quota; the provider starts returning 429.
02:07 Production requests begin returning 429 as well, and the client treats them as generic errors.
02:11 Retry amplification peaks: every in-flight worker retries on the same fixed one-second boundary.
02:19 On-call inspects prompts and model selection, because error dashboards only count 5xx responses.
02:34 A per-environment key rotation in staging stops the bleeding; production recovers without a deploy.
03:10 First honest summary: the feature degraded because our retry policy converted a soft limit into a hard outage.

Contributing factors, in order of leverage

The first factor is shared credentials across environments, which turns a test suite into a production dependency without anyone deciding that on purpose. Nobody wrote a ticket saying “let staging rate-limit production,” but that is precisely what the shared key encoded, and it stayed invisible because both environments succeeded for months. When you cannot attribute a request to an environment, you also cannot revoke or budget it independently.

The second factor is retry without jitter, which is the classic way to convert a temporary throttle into a sustained stampede. Fixed delays look harmless in a single-threaded test and become a synchronized heartbeat in production, where dozens of workers wake at the same millisecond and fire again. Exponential backoff helps only when you also randomize the interval and cap the number of attempts; otherwise you have made each individual client polite while making the fleet as rude as before.

The third factor is alerting that keyed on 5xx only, which meant a 429 looked like success to the dashboard and like failure to the user. Quota pressure is a leading indicator, so if your error-rate panel ignores status 429 you will always learn about exhaustion from the customers instead of the graph. The uncomfortable lesson is that our observability was tuned for crashes, not for throttling.

The fix you can rehearse

The durable fix has four parts, and only the first is infrastructure: environment-scoped keys, a client-side token budget with a hard ceiling, jittered retries with a small attempt cap, and a circuit breaker that fails fast once throttling is sustained. The script below models the difference between a naive client and a jittered client behind a breaker, using a deterministic fake provider so the result is reproducible on any laptop.

"""quota_sim.py — rehearse a retry storm against a capped fake provider.
Run: python quota_sim.py
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
import random


@dataclass
class CappedProvider:
    """Accepts a fixed number of call-units, then returns 429 forever."""
    capacity: int = 100
    cost_per_call: int = 12
    seen: int = field(default=0)
    accepted: int = field(default=0)

    def complete(self) -> int:
        self.seen += 1
        self.capacity -= self.cost_per_call
        if self.capacity < 0:
            return 429
        self.accepted += 1
        return 200


class Breaker:
    """Opens after `threshold` consecutive throttles, stays open for the run."""

    def __init__(self, threshold: int = 4) -> None:
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.failures = 0
        self.open = False

    def record(self, status: int) -> None:
        if status == 429:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.failures >= self.threshold:
                self.open = True
        else:
            self.failures = 0


def naive_client(provider: CappedProvider, rng: random.Random) -> int:
    """Fixed one-second retry, no jitter: every worker resumes together."""
    for _ in range(6):
        status = provider.complete()
        if status == 200:
            return status
        # time.sleep(1.0) — identical across all workers
    return 429


def jittered_client(provider: CappedProvider, rng: random.Random) -> int:
    """Full jitter, three attempts, then a breaker that fails fast."""
    breaker = Breaker()
    for attempt in range(3):
        if breaker.open:
            return 429
        status = provider.complete()
        breaker.record(status)
        if status == 200:
            return status
        base = 0.2 * (2 ** attempt)
        delay = min(2.0, base) * rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5)  # time.sleep(delay)
        _ = delay
    return 429


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for name, fn in (("naive", naive_client), ("jitter+breaker", jittered_client)):
        provider = CappedProvider()
        rng = random.Random(11)
        codes = [fn(provider, rng) for _ in range(40)]
        amplification = provider.seen / max(provider.accepted, 1)
        print(
            f"{name:>15}: requests={provider.seen:>4} "
            f"ok={provider.accepted:>3} failed={codes.count(429):>3} "
            f"amplification={amplification:.2f}"
        )

The invariant worth asserting in CI is directional rather than numeric: the jittered client behind a breaker should issue strictly fewer requests per successful call than the naive client, and it should stop issuing requests entirely once the breaker opens. Your absolute amplification depends on capacity, worker count, and cost per call, so treat the printed table as a knob you tune rather than a benchmark to quote. Add a test that fails when amplification for the naive strategy drops below the jittered one, and you have encoded the lesson instead of just writing it down.

Where a free tier belongs in this workflow

Here is the part that is genuinely useful: you want to rehearse this failure class regularly, and rehearsal that spends real money is rehearsal that quietly stops happening. MonkeyCode offers free model access and a free server option that the project documents on its own pages, which makes it a reasonable place to run disaster drills like the one above without treating production budget as the test fixture. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. I have not measured its quotas, hardware, or long-term availability, and free-tier terms change, so read the current allocation on the project site rather than trusting any number quoted in a blog post, including this one.

Workload Sensible home Reasoning
Retry-storm drills, breaker tests Free tier Failure is the point; nothing of value is lost when the drill trips a limit.
Nightly staging suites Free tier, separate credentials Isolates test load from anything a customer can feel.
Prompt-regression evals on synthetic data Free tier Cheap, repeatable, and easy to throw away when the schema changes.
User-facing generation with an SLO Paid, environment-scoped keys Throttling here is an outage, not a signal.
Anything bound by a data-processing agreement Whatever your legal review approved Free hosting does not change your obligations.

Limitations and who should not do this

A circuit breaker is a blunt instrument that can mask a genuine provider-side regression, because once it opens you stop collecting the evidence you would need to tell throttling apart from a broken deploy. If your team has nobody who owns the shared client library, adding a token budget and breaker to it will produce three divergent copies within a quarter, and the drift will be worse than the original bug. Per-environment keys also add rotation chores, so a two-person team should weigh whether a shared key plus a hard client-side ceiling is enough for now.

You should not adopt this pattern if you need guaranteed throughput, if your latency budget cannot absorb a fail-fast response, or if your prompts carry data your agreements forbid sending to a third-party endpoint of any price. Free model access is excellent for rehearsal and poor for contractual guarantees, and pretending otherwise is how you end up writing a second postmortem about the same night. For everyone else, the sequence is unglamorous: scope the credentials, budget the tokens, jitter the retries, break the circuit, and alert on 429 before your users do.

The 02:00 page was never about which model you picked, and the fix that survived review was fourteen lines in a client library that nobody had looked at in six months. If you want to rehearse that night without spending anything, the free tier is a reasonable place to start, and you can keep the simulation in your repository as the artifact that proves you learned it.

title: Food and Beverage Industry Project Management: A Complete Guide
description:
Food and beverage companies manage projects that connect product development, ingredient sourcing, packaging, quality assurance, manufacturing, and distribution. A new product launch, factory expansion, recipe reformulation, or packaging update may involve several departments, external suppliers, and fixed commercial deadlines.
The challenge is that these activities rarely happen independently. A packaging approval delay can affect printing, production trials, and the launch date. A late ingredient delivery can postpone testing. Meanwhile, the quality assurance specialist needed for approval may already be committed to another project.
Food and beverage project management helps organizations coordinate these dependencies, manage resources, control budgets, and deliver projects on schedule without overlooking quality and food safety requirements.
This guide explores the project lifecycle, common industry challenges, practical management strategies, and software options for food manufacturers, beverage companies, nutrition businesses, and consultants.
What Is Food and Beverage Project Management?
Food and beverage project management is the process of planning, coordinating, executing, and monitoring initiatives related to product development, manufacturing, packaging, quality improvement, and operational expansion.
The objective is to deliver a defined outcome within an agreed scope, schedule, and budget while meeting applicable quality, regulatory, and food safety requirements.
Common projects include:
New product development and commercialization.
Recipe reformulation and ingredient substitutions.
Packaging redesigns and labeling changes.
Production line installation and factory expansion.
Equipment upgrades and automation projects.
Supplier qualification and sourcing changes.
Quality improvement and audit-related initiatives.
ERP, manufacturing execution system (MES), and quality management system (QMS) implementations.
Process standardization across multiple manufacturing facilities.
For example, launching a new beverage flavor may require formulation approval, ingredient sourcing, packaging artwork, shelf-life testing, pilot production, and commercial planning. Project managers must coordinate these activities so that each team completes its work when the next stage is ready to begin.
What Does a Food and Beverage Project Manager Do?
A food and beverage project manager coordinates the people, schedules, decisions, and resources required to deliver a project.
Key responsibilities include:
Scope management: Defining deliverables and controlling changes to project requirements.
Schedule management: Establishing milestones, identifying dependencies, and monitoring deadlines.
Resource planning: Coordinating employees, production equipment, testing facilities, and external suppliers.
Budget management: Tracking planned costs, actual expenditure, and financial forecasts.
Risk management: Identifying potential delays, quality concerns, supplier problems, and capacity constraints.
Stakeholder coordination: Keeping R&D, procurement, quality, operations, marketing, and leadership aligned.
Progress reporting: Communicating project status, outstanding decisions, and corrective actions.
Project management coordinates delivery. It does not replace specialized food safety systems, quality procedures, or regulatory responsibilities.
Project Management Across Food, Beverage, and Nutrition Industries
Different segments share many project management principles, but their schedules are influenced by different technical and commercial requirements.
Industry segment
Typical projects
Main scheduling challenges
Food manufacturing
New products, recipe changes, factory expansions
Ingredient sourcing, shelf-life testing, production trials
Beverage manufacturing
New flavors, bottle or can formats, filling line upgrades
Packaging lead times, production availability, seasonal demand
Nutrition products
Formulation changes, fortified foods, supplements
Ingredient qualification, stability testing, label and claims review
Food packaging
Packaging redesigns, material changes, line modifications
Artwork approval, material availability, equipment compatibility
Food and nutrition consulting
Product development, quality improvement, compliance support
Client approvals, consultant capacity, project budgets
Food processing facilities
Equipment upgrades, automation, process improvement
Installation windows, commissioning, operator training

A standard project template can help maintain consistency, but it should be flexible enough to accommodate the different requirements of each project type.
The Food and Beverage Project Management Lifecycle
A structured lifecycle helps teams move from an initial idea to an approved, operational result.

  1. Project Initiation The first stage defines the business need, expected outcome, scope, stakeholders, and success criteria. For a new snack product, the project team might establish target production costs, customer requirements, ingredient specifications, expected launch timing, and manufacturing constraints. During initiation, identify the people who must approve important decisions, including quality, regulatory, procurement, and operations representatives.
  2. Planning and Feasibility The planning phase converts the project idea into an actionable delivery plan. Teams estimate effort and costs, identify supplier lead times, define milestones, assign responsibilities, and map dependencies. They should also determine whether the project can be completed using existing resources and production capacity. For example, a production line expansion may require equipment procurement, facility modifications, utility upgrades, installation, commissioning, and staff training. These activities need to be scheduled in the correct sequence.
  3. Development and Execution During execution, teams carry out the planned work. Depending on the initiative, this may include formulation development, supplier onboarding, packaging design, equipment installation, process changes, or software implementation. The project manager coordinates activities across departments and monitors whether work is progressing according to the approved plan.
  4. Testing, Review, and Approval Food and beverage projects often require defined testing and review activities before implementation or release. These may include pilot production, product testing, shelf-life studies, packaging checks, equipment commissioning, and quality reviews. Required approvals should be included in the project schedule rather than treated as informal tasks at the end. Teams must follow their applicable food safety plans, quality procedures, and regulatory obligations.
  5. Launch or Operational Handover Once the required acceptance criteria are met, the project moves into launch or operational handover. This may involve transferring approved specifications, training production staff, confirming supplier readiness, documenting operating procedures, and coordinating launch activities.
  6. Monitoring and Lessons Learned After delivery, review the project's schedule, costs, quality outcomes, and original objectives. Identify what caused delays, which estimates were inaccurate, and whether any problems are likely to recur in future projects. These lessons can improve subsequent product launches, facility upgrades, and process improvement initiatives. Why Is Project Management Challenging in the Food Industry? Food and beverage projects face a combination of operational, technical, commercial, and regulatory constraints.
  7. Complex Product Development A product launch may involve R&D, procurement, packaging, marketing, quality, production, and sales. Each department has different deliverables, and a delay in one area can affect the others. What helps: Build an integrated project schedule that connects activities across departments rather than maintaining separate plans.
  8. Ingredient and Supplier Delays Some ingredients have long lead times, limited sources, seasonal availability, or specific storage requirements. Packaging materials and specialized production equipment can also arrive later than expected. What helps: Track supplier commitments, qualification milestones, expected delivery dates, and backup options for critical materials.
  9. Packaging and Labeling Changes A late change to artwork, ingredient information, allergen declarations, or product claims can require additional review and may affect printing and production schedules. What helps: Include artwork approval, label review, print lead times, and final packaging checks as explicit milestones.
  10. Food Safety and Quality Requirements Projects must account for applicable food safety controls and quality requirements. Testing, reviews, and approvals may require specific people, facilities, and lead times. What helps: Involve quality and regulatory teams during planning, and schedule required reviews before dependent activities begin.
  11. Shared Resources Across Projects R&D specialists, quality analysts, engineers, and production teams may support several initiatives at once. A project may appear adequately staffed in isolation but compete with other projects for the same people or equipment. What helps: Review resource demand across the entire project portfolio and resolve conflicts before committing to delivery dates.
  12. Production Downtime and Equipment Installation Factory upgrades often need to fit into limited shutdown windows. If equipment arrives late or installation takes longer than planned, production schedules can be disrupted. What helps: Coordinate procurement, installation, commissioning, maintenance, and training around realistic shutdown and production calendars.
  13. Budget Overruns Unexpected engineering work, supplier price changes, extended testing, and production adjustments can increase project costs. What helps: Establish a budget baseline, monitor actual expenditure, and update forecasts when the scope or schedule changes.
  14. Poor Portfolio Visibility Executives may receive individual project reports without a clear understanding of how projects compete for resources or affect one another. What helps: Use portfolio dashboards that summarize milestones, resource demand, risks, and financial performance across initiatives. Types of Projects in the Food and Beverage Industry Different projects require different plans, approval processes, and success measures. Project type Primary objective Important dependencies Example success measures New product development Launch a new product Formulation, sourcing, packaging, testing Launch date, target cost, approved specifications Recipe reformulation Change ingredients or improve a formula Ingredient qualification, testing, label review Product performance, cost target, approved labeling Packaging redesign Introduce new packaging Artwork, material sourcing, line compatibility Approved design, changeover date, reduced rework Factory expansion Increase production capacity Capital approval, equipment, utilities, commissioning Budget, completion date, production readiness Equipment modernization Upgrade production equipment Vendor delivery, shutdowns, testing, training Installation completion, successful commissioning Quality improvement Address quality problems or strengthen controls Root-cause analysis, corrective actions, verification Actions closed, repeat issues reduced Supplier onboarding Qualify a new supplier Specifications, audits, contracts, trial lots Qualification completed, supply continuity Digital transformation Implement business or manufacturing systems Process design, integration, data migration, training Go-live readiness, adoption, expected benefits Multi-site standardization Align processes across facilities Local requirements, training, change management Consistent processes and reporting

The project plan should reflect the specific risks and dependencies of the initiative instead of applying the same checklist to every project.
8 Best Practices for Food and Beverage Project Management

  1. Standardize Project Intake and Prioritization New project requests can quickly exceed the available capacity of R&D, quality, engineering, and operations teams. Use a standard intake process to capture the business case, expected benefits, estimated costs, resource needs, and target dates. Then evaluate requests against agreed business priorities. For example, a manufacturer considering several new product flavors could prioritize them based on customer commitments, commercial potential, manufacturing capacity, and development effort. Measure: Percentage of approved projects that achieve their original business objectives.
  2. Build Schedules Around Dependencies A list of deadlines does not show whether the project can realistically meet them. Activities must be connected to the work that needs to happen first. For example, packaging printing may depend on final artwork approval, while a production trial may depend on both packaging delivery and formulation readiness. Use Gantt charts, milestone plans, and dependency links to make these relationships visible. Measure: On-time milestone completion rate and the number of missed critical milestones.
  3. Plan Shared Resources Across All Projects Do not allocate resources based only on individual project plans. Review the combined demand for employees, equipment, laboratories, and production lines. If the same quality specialist is needed for two pilot runs during the same week, the project manager can adjust the sequence or arrange suitable additional capacity. Measure: Resource utilization, overallocated periods, and delays caused by resource conflicts.
  4. Involve Quality and Regulatory Teams Early Quality-related activities should be included from the beginning rather than added shortly before launch. Identify required reviews, testing, documentation, and approvals during project planning. This makes their resource needs and expected duration easier to manage. Project schedules should support applicable quality and food safety procedures, not replace them. Measure: Approval cycle time and the number of late-stage changes caused by missed requirements.
  5. Monitor Costs and Forecast Changes Set a budget baseline and track actual spending against planned expenditure. Review major cost categories, such as ingredients, packaging, external services, equipment, and installation. When scope changes or delays occur, estimate their financial impact and revise forecasts as appropriate. Measure: Budget variance and forecast accuracy.
  6. Maintain an Active Risk Register A risk register should identify potential problems, assess their impact, assign owners, and document mitigation actions. Common examples include supplier delivery changes, delayed approvals, equipment commissioning problems, and unexpected production constraints. Review significant risks regularly and define when they must be escalated. Measure: Number of unresolved high-priority risks and average time to close issues.
  7. Improve Supplier Coordination Supplier milestones should be part of the project plan, particularly when materials or equipment have long lead times. Record delivery commitments, qualification requirements, key contacts, and any activities that depend on supplier completion. Regular checkpoints can help identify delays while there is still time to evaluate alternatives. Measure: On-time delivery of project-critical materials and equipment.
  8. Use Standardized Reporting Project teams should report progress using consistent definitions and formats. A practical status report might include schedule performance, budget status, key risks, resource constraints, completed milestones, and decisions needed from management. Dashboards can reduce manual reporting effort and help leaders compare projects more easily. Measure: Time required to prepare reports and the frequency of unexpected project escalations. How to Choose Food and Beverage Project Management Software The best software depends on whether your main need is task coordination, enterprise project governance, production execution, or quality management.
  9. Identify the Problem You Need to Solve Start with your existing process. Are product launches delayed because of disconnected schedules? Are managers unable to see resource conflicts? Are budgets reviewed too late? Or does the organization need better production, inventory, or quality controls? These problems require different categories of software.
  10. Evaluate Scheduling and Dependency Management Look for the ability to build project timelines, connect dependent tasks, track milestones, and update schedules when plans change. For complex initiatives, verify whether dependencies can be tracked across multiple projects.
  11. Review Resource and Capacity Planning Determine whether the platform can show resource availability across projects and identify conflicts involving employees, teams, or equipment. If your organization manages multiple product launches simultaneously, portfolio-level capacity visibility may be particularly valuable.
  12. Check Budget and Risk Management Evaluate how the software tracks planned and actual costs, forecasts expenditure, and records risks and mitigation actions. Confirm whether it can provide the financial reports your project managers and executives need.
  13. Consider Integrations Food manufacturers often use ERP, MES, QMS, PLM, inventory, and finance systems. Project management software should fit into this environment. Ask vendors how information will be exchanged, which integrations are available, and whether additional configuration is required.
  14. Test Realistic Scenarios During a software demonstration, use an example such as a delayed packaging delivery. Ask the vendor to show how the delay affects production trials, staffing, costs, and the launch milestone. Then test how the team can assign corrective actions and communicate the revised plan. This is more useful than evaluating features individually without seeing how they work together. 7 Food and Beverage Project Management Tools Compared Food and beverage organizations may need more than one software category. Enterprise project portfolio management, work management, and manufacturing ERP support different activities. These tools should not be treated as direct equivalents. Some coordinate projects, while others manage business and manufacturing operations. Product features, licensing, and integrations should be verified against your requirements.
How Celoxis Helps Manage Food and Beverage Projects
Celoxis is a project and portfolio management platform that can help food and beverage companies coordinate schedules, resources, budgets, risks, and reporting across multiple initiatives.
It may be particularly useful when product launches, facility upgrades, packaging changes, and process improvement projects compete for the same people and resources.
Project Planning and Scheduling
Gantt charts and task dependencies help teams sequence activities and track milestones.
For a new product launch, the schedule can include formulation development, supplier qualification, packaging approval, pilot production, and commercial readiness.
Resource and Capacity Management
Resource planning helps managers review assignments and workload across projects.
This is useful when quality specialists, engineers, and R&D employees support several initiatives at the same time.
Portfolio Management
Portfolio dashboards provide a consolidated view of multiple projects. Managers can compare progress, identify delayed initiatives, and assess where additional attention or resources may be needed.
Budget and Cost Visibility
Project financial tracking can help teams compare planned costs with actual expenditure and identify potential overruns.
The usefulness of this information depends on accurate project data and appropriate integration with existing financial systems.
Risk and Issue Tracking
Teams can record risks, assign owners, and monitor mitigation activities. This provides a structured way to manage supplier delays, equipment problems, and other issues that could affect delivery.
Reporting and Collaboration
Shared project information and dashboards can help reduce manual status reporting and improve communication across departments.
Celoxis can support project governance and execution, but it does not replace systems responsible for manufacturing execution, inventory, food safety records, or product traceability.
Real-World Example: Goodman Fielder
A published Celoxis customer story describes how Goodman Fielder addressed project planning and prioritization challenges. The company needed better visibility into its project portfolio and resource allocation.
According to the case study, the reported outcomes included:
Three times faster roadmap planning.
30% fewer project prioritization errors.
Centralized project and process information.
Improved visibility into project schedules, resources, costs, and risks.
These results relate to planning and prioritization as reported in the customer story. They should not be interpreted as measured improvements in food safety, manufacturing output, or product quality.
The broader lesson for food and beverage organizations is that centralized portfolio information can help managers make more informed decisions when multiple initiatives compete for limited resources.
Conclusion
Food and beverage project management requires close coordination between product development, sourcing, quality, manufacturing, packaging, and commercial teams. Even a small delay can affect several connected activities when projects share resources and depend on fixed supplier or production dates.
Organizations can improve delivery by using realistic schedules, involving quality teams early, planning shared capacity, tracking risks, monitoring budgets, and standardizing reporting.
Choosing the right software begins with understanding the problem. Work management tools support everyday coordination, manufacturing ERP systems manage operational processes, and project portfolio management platforms help organizations govern complex initiatives across teams.
For food and beverage companies managing several concurrent projects, Celoxis is worth evaluating for project scheduling, resource planning, portfolio visibility, risk tracking, and financial reporting. The right platform should complement existing operational systems and help teams make better decisions throughout the project lifecycle.

title: shadcn/ui switched to Base UI. Here is what actually changes in your code
description:
On 3 July 2026, npx shadcn init started picking Base UI instead of Radix. If you have read the headlines and nothing else, you probably think one of two things: that Radix is dead, or that nothing changed. Neither is true.

I maintain HextaUI, a shadcn/ui registry built on Base UI, so I have spent most of this year inside both primitive layers. This is the guide I wished existed in July: what changed, what did not, every API difference you will hit, and the order to migrate in if you decide to.

What changed, in one paragraph

New shadcn/ui projects get Base UI primitives. Radix is still fully supported. The shadcn team said every update and new component ships for both libraries, unless a component only exists in Base UI. Existing projects are untouched. If you want Radix on a fresh project, you pass one flag:

npx shadcn@latest init -b radix

If you have CI or scripts that call init non-interactively and expect Radix, add that flag now, before a fresh checkout surprises you.

Why the default moved

Two reasons were given. Base UI had reached a stable 1.6.0 with over six million weekly downloads, and projects created through shadcn/create were already choosing Base UI over Radix about two to one. The default followed what people were picking.

Base UI is built by the people behind Radix, Material UI and Floating UI, and the lineage shows. It covers primitives Radix never shipped, such as Combobox, Autocomplete, Number Field, Toast and Preview Card. As of September 2026 it sits at 1.8.0.

Should you migrate an existing app?

Probably not this quarter, and not all at once.

Stay on Radix if the app is stable, you are not blocked on a missing primitive, and nobody on the team has a specific complaint. Nothing you depend on is going away.

Migrate if you need Combobox or Number Field without reaching for a second library, if you are already rewriting the components for Tailwind v4 anyway, or if you want to be on the layer that new shadcn/ui components target first.

Either way, read the next section before you decide, because the differences are not cosmetic.

Every API difference you will actually hit

I grouped these by how they fail. The first group breaks your build. The second group compiles fine and changes behavior silently, which is worse.

Build-breaking changes

asChild becomes render. This is the one everyone meets first.

// Radix
<DialogTrigger asChild>
  <Button>Open</Button>
</DialogTrigger>

// Base UI
<DialogTrigger render={<Button />}>Open</DialogTrigger>

The render prop takes an element or a function. The function form gives you the state, which is useful for things like a trigger that changes its icon when open.

Anchored popups gain a Positioner. Menu, Select, Popover and Tooltip go from Portal > Content to Portal > Positioner > Popup. Dialog has no Positioner; it uses Backdrop and Popup.

Overlay is now Backdrop. Rename and move on.

Select values are nullable. A controlled Select holds Value | null, not string. Your useState<string>("") becomes useState<string | null>(null), and every place that read the value as a string needs a guard.

Accordion and Toggle Group values are always arrays. Even in single mode, value="a" becomes value={["a"]}. Tabs keep a single value.

onOpenChange has a second argument. Radix lets you call event.preventDefault() to stop a close. Base UI passes (open, details) and you call details.cancel(). The details.reason field tells you whether it was the Escape key, an outside press or something else, which is handy for "unsaved changes" dialogs.

Open-state selectors change. data-[state=open]: variants become data-open:. This one hides in your className strings and in cva variants, so grep for data-[state= before you call the migration done.

Silent behavior changes

Tabs activate manually by default. In Radix, arrow keys move focus and activate the tab. In Base UI, arrow keys move focus and you press Enter or Space to activate. If your tests or users expect the Radix behavior, set activateOnFocus on the list.

Checkbox and radio menu items keep the menu open. closeOnClick defaults to false for CheckboxItem and RadioItem. Plain items still close. This is arguably the better default, but it is a change your users will notice.

Navigation menus open faster. Base UI's hover delay defaults to 50ms. Radix's delayDuration defaulted to 200ms. Fast menus feel great until someone sweeps their mouse across the header and three panels fire in a row. Tune it.

A migration order that does not hurt

Keep both libraries installed. Move one component per commit. Run your tests between each. In this order:

  1. Leaf components with no popup: Switch, Checkbox, Slider, Toggle, Progress. Mostly rename work.
  2. Tabs and Accordion. Fix the array values and decide on activateOnFocus.
  3. Dialog and Alert Dialog. Learn the Backdrop and Popup structure and the details.cancel() pattern here, where there is no Positioner to confuse things.
  4. Popover and Tooltip. Add the Positioner.
  5. Select, Combobox, Dropdown Menu, Context Menu. Nullable values, closeOnClick, and the whole popup tree. Do these last, with the most tests.

Replacing a component with the Base UI version is one CLI command, and your source is in git, so review the diff rather than trusting it:

npx shadcn@latest add dialog --overwrite

Then git diff components/ui/dialog.tsx and read every line before you keep it.

What I would not do

I would not run a codemod across the whole tree and hope. The build-breaking changes are easy to find. The silent ones are not, and a codemod cannot tell you that your settings page now needs two keystrokes to switch tabs.

I would also not switch primitive layers and redesign the components in the same PR. The point of shadcn/ui is that you own the code. Owning it means reading the diff.

If you want the migration done for you

HextaUI is a registry you add to a shadcn/ui project. Every component is already written on Base UI, keeps the shadcn/ui names and props, and uses the same theme tokens, so npx shadcn@latest add https://hextaui.com/r/dialog.json --overwrite lands a Base UI Dialog in components/ui next to your other files. The components are MIT and free. The HextaUI vs shadcn/ui page lists what is different and when plain shadcn/ui is the better pick.

FAQ

Is Radix deprecated? No. shadcn/ui ships every component for both libraries, and the team still runs Radix in production.

Can I mix Radix and Base UI components in one project? Yes. You carry both dependencies while you migrate. Many projects will stay mixed for a long time and that is fine.

Do I need to change my theme tokens? No. --background, --primary, --radius and the rest are unchanged. The primitive layer is independent of the Tailwind side.

Does Base UI support React Server Components? Base UI primitives are client components, the same as Radix. Keep the "use client" directive where shadcn/ui puts it.

Where is the official change log? The July 2026 entry is at ui.shadcn.com/docs/changelog/2026-07-base-ui-default.
