title: Four Law Firms Published 79 Email Addresses. Four Tech Companies Published 11
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali, and the other half of my week goes into Apify Actors. One of them does the thing every sales tool claims to do: you give it Jane Doe, acme.com, it gives you back Jane's work address.

Everybody solves this the same way — apply first.last, because roughly half of corporate mail is first.last, and ship it. That is a coin flip dressed as a lookup. The approach I wanted instead rests on one observation: a company that publishes any personal address on its own website has told you the rule for all of them. If the team page says michael.hart@acme.com, you no longer need to guess what the sales director's address looks like.

So the interesting question stopped being "which format should I guess" and became "how often does a company actually publish something I can read". I ran eight companies through it to find out, and the answer splits so hard by industry that it changes who this kind of tool is for.

The run

Eight people at eight companies, company rows on, four pages read per site:

{
  "people": [
    "Patrick Collison, stripe.com",
    "Jason Fried, basecamp.com",
    "Maria Bennett, cliffordchance.com",
    "Daniel Weber, freshfields.com",
    "Daniel Weber, linklaters.com",
    "Daniel Weber, bakermckenzie.com",
    "Daniel Weber, n8n.io",
    "Daniel Weber, hubspot.com"
  ],
  "candidatesPerPerson": 3,
  "checkMx": true,
  "includeCompanyRows": true,
  "maxPagesPerCompany": 4
}

Two of those names are real people; "Maria Bennett" and "Daniel Weber" are probes I invented, because the person is not what is being measured here. The layout belongs to the company, and the same probe name at eight companies isolates it cleanly. 32 pages, plain HTTP, no browser, no proxy: 7.1 seconds and $0.29 for the whole run on 16 October 2026.

Here is what came back, per company:

Domain Addresses on site Usable as evidence Layout Confidence
cliffordchance.com 48 22 first.last high
freshfields.com 21 13 first.last high
linklaters.com 10 7 first.last high
bakermckenzie.com 0 0 — low
n8n.io 6 0 — low
stripe.com 4 1 first.last medium
basecamp.com 1 1 first confirmed
hubspot.com 0 0 — low

79 of the 90 published addresses came from the four law firms. 42 of the 44 usable pieces of evidence did too.

That is not a coincidence and it is not about law. Professional services firms publish staff directories because clients need to reach a named partner — and the same is true of agencies, clinics, brokerages, accountants and consultancies. Companies that sell software route everything through a form and a support queue on purpose. Which means: if your lead list is made of firms, this method mostly works. If it is made of SaaS companies, you are back to guessing, and the honest move is to say so in the output rather than to hide it.

90 addresses found, 44 that say anything

The gap between those two columns is where all the work is. An address only counts as evidence if you can tell which half is the first name — and that is harder than it sounds, because jane.diaz@ and complaints-in@ have the identical shape. One token, a separator, one token. A tool that reads shape alone will conclude that Stripe writes firstname-lastname on the strength of a complaints inbox, which is exactly what an early version of mine did.

So every candidate local part is tested against a list of common given names instead:

jane.diaz                    {"shapes":["first.last"],"strength":1}
esther.chancatlin            {"shapes":["first.last"],"strength":1}
victoria.brewertonowen       {"shapes":["first.last"],"strength":1}
jason                        {"shapes":["first"],"strength":1}
complaints-in                {"shapes":[],"strength":0}
nodes                        {"shapes":[],"strength":0}
nlinklaters                  {"shapes":[],"strength":0}
freshfieldsalumninetwork     {"shapes":[],"strength":0}
20iva.celic                  {"shapes":[],"strength":0}
esther.chan2                 {"shapes":[],"strength":0}
anne-marie.nistoroiu         {"shapes":[],"strength":0}

Those are all real locals from this run. A few things worth pointing at:

esther.chancatlin and victoria.brewertonowen pass because the first half is a recognised name — the surname is never checked against anything, which is what lets compound surnames through intact.

20iva.celic is a scraping artifact: a page number glued to an address by the surrounding text. Clifford Chance's site produced both it and the clean iva.celic. The dirty one is refused by a leading-character rule, which is cheap and right. The clean one is also refused, because neither "iva" nor "celic" is in the given-name list — a false negative, and one I am fine with. The site offered 22 other usable addresses. Being wrong about the format is expensive; skipping one address out of 48 costs nothing.

anne-marie.nistoroiu is the one that annoys me. It contains both a dot and a hyphen, the dot wins the split, and anne-marie is not in the name list as a hyphenated token. It should be read as first.last and is not.

nlinklaters@linklaters.com is the kind of thing that makes you add rules you did not plan for: a token that starts with a letter, contains no separator, and is not a name. Read it as initial-plus-surname and you have "N. Linklaters" working at Linklaters.

The output ships patternEvidence and patternEvidenceCount for exactly this reason. 22 agreeing addresses and 1 are both patternSource: "site", and they are not the same claim.

Stripe's one piece of evidence is a placeholder

Stripe published four addresses: dpo@, privacy@, complaints-in@ — all discarded as department mail — and jane.diaz@stripe.com. So the Actor read Stripe's layout off a single address and returned:

{
  "fullName": "Patrick Collison",
  "email": "patrick.collison@stripe.com",
  "emailPattern": "first.last",
  "emailPatternSource": "site",
  "confidence": "medium",
  "patternEvidence": ["jane.diaz@stripe.com"],
  "patternEvidenceCount": 1,
  "emailStatus": "deliverable",
  "emailProvider": "google",
  "emailMxHost": "aspmx.l.google.com",
  "mailboxVerified": false,
  "alternatives": [
    { "email": "patrick@stripe.com", "pattern": "first" },
    { "email": "pcollison@stripe.com", "pattern": "flast" }
  ]
}

Jane Diaz does not work at Stripe. She is a string in the home page's checkout graphic:

payment-graphic.checkout.email-address-us":"jane.diaz@stripe.com"
payment-graphic.checkout.email-address-de":"damian.michelfelder@example.com"
payment-graphic.checkout.email-address-jp":"taro.yamada@example.com"

The German and Japanese variants of the same mockup use @example.com, which any sane filter drops. The US one uses the company's live domain. That slip is the entire reason Stripe has a site layout rather than a default guess.

The answer is probably still correct — first.last is a common layout and Stripe is a large US company. But it is right by luck, and a tool that reported it as "confirmed from the company's website" would be lying with a straight face. medium plus one visible piece of evidence lets you decide. That is the difference between a confidence column that means something and one that is decoration.

While I was in there: Freshfields came back as "companyName": "Leading global law firm". The name falls back through JSON-LD Organization → og:site_name → the first segment of <title>, and Freshfields has neither of the first two, so an SEO title became the company name. Two scraped fields, two reminders that "it parsed" and "it's true" are different states.

What zero evidence looks like

Baker McKenzie and HubSpot published nothing on four pages. n8n published six addresses — marketing@, license@, nodes@, community@, partners@, legal@ — and not one of them says anything about how a person's address is written. "How many addresses did you find" is the wrong metric; "how many contained a human name" is the one that matters.

All three got first.last, patternSource: "default", confidence: "low", and empty patternEvidence. Same shaped answer, honestly labelled as a guess. Sort by confidence and those rows go to the bottom of the sequence, or nowhere.

One more field earns its place here. The four law firms sit behind mail gateways — Mimecast twice, Proofpoint twice — while Stripe, HubSpot and n8n are on Google. emailProvider and emailMxHost come from an MX lookup, which also means mailboxVerified is permanently false: checking whether a specific mailbox exists requires an SMTP conversation on port 25, and outbound 25 is blocked from Apify's cloud for every Actor there, whatever a listing claims. Domain-level truth and published evidence is what is actually obtainable. If you need address hygiene on a list you already have — role flags, disposable domains, deliverability — that is a different job, and Email Verifier & Phone Number Validator is the one I use for it.

Calling it 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("lergassy/email-finder-api").call(run_input={
    "people": ["Daniel Weber, linklaters.com"],
    "includeCompanyRows": True,
})
for row in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if row["type"] == "person" and row["confidence"] in ("confirmed", "high"):
        print(row["email"], row["patternEvidenceCount"])

peopleList takes pre-split fields from a CRM export, and inputDatasetId reads the people straight out of another Actor's dataset. Error rows are free, which matters when a third of a real list has an unresolvable company.

When not to use this

If your targets are consumer-facing tech companies, expect mostly low and treat the output as a guess with a mail-server check attached. If you need a confirmed mailbox before sending, no Apify Actor can give you that — send to the confirmed and high rows and let the bounce be the verification, with alternatives as the retry. And if what you actually want is every public address on a set of websites rather than one person's address, this is the wrong shape of tool entirely.

The Actor is Email Finder API. If you find a company whose layout it reads wrongly, the company and the expected address is a genuinely useful bug report — the given-name list and the rules above grew almost entirely out of those. anne-marie.nistoroiu is next.

title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
description:
arXiv:2610.20773v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting. In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.

title: Why Host in South America? How Local Infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro Reduces Latency and Boosts App Performance
description:
When building modern applications, the choice of where to host our code is often an afterthought: we select traditional hyperscalers in the US or Europe and assume their infrastructure will handle everything. However, for anyone serving users in South America, network latency (ping) and packet routing quickly become critical performance bottlenecks.

In this article, let's analyze the real impact of server locality and how relying on local infrastructure in South America changes the game for developers, businesses, and growing projects.

The "Distance Cost" Problem (Latency)

Round Trip Time (RTT) is strictly limited by the physics of submarine and terrestrial cables. When a user in Brazil or neighboring countries accesses an application hosted thousands of miles away in the Northern Hemisphere, data packets must travel through multiple network hops.

This results in:

  • Noticeable Increase in Time to First Byte (TTFB): Browsers take longer to start rendering page content.
  • API and Database Bottlenecks: Asynchronous queries and chained HTTP requests suffer from cumulative delays.
  • Degraded User Experience: Real-time applications or interactive dashboards feel sluggish, even on fast local fiber-optic connections.

The Advantage of Local Infrastructure

Hosting close to your target audience brings immediate architectural benefits:

  1. Drastically Reduced Latency: Fewer network hops mean millisecond-level responses for local and regional users.
  2. Optimized Routing: Streamlined connectivity across the eastern coast of South America, facilitating seamless communication with neighboring countries.
  3. Real Infrastructure: Physical data center operations based in Rio de Janeiro, powered by high-performance enterprise hardware and fast NVMe storage.

Meet AzureWeb

If you or your company are looking for a robust alternative to traditional US/EU cloud giants, AzureWeb (azureweb.com.br) delivers reliable infrastructure solutions directly from Brazil.

  • Cloud VPS: Flexible, scalable virtual private servers with dedicated resources, ideal for developers, testing environments, and growing production apps.
  • Cloud Servers: High-performance environments tailored for heavy workloads and demanding system architectures.
  • Web Hosting: Fast, secure, and reliable web hosting plans designed to keep your web applications online 24/7.

Final Thoughts

Choosing a data center should be treated as a core part of your application's engineering design, just like picking a framework or a database. Reducing the physical distance between your server and your end-user is the most cost-effective and impactful way to improve any system's performance.

title: Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally
description:
arXiv:2610.21204v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a speaker says ``some students passed'', listeners infer that not all of them did. Reasoning models now let users decide how long a model thinks before it answers, but we do not know what extra thinking does to such everyday inferences. We study this directly: we keep a model's weights fixed, change only how much it thinks, and record which reading it chooses. A second tool cuts the model's own reasoning at successive points and asks for an answer, showing where the reading changes. Thinking makes models read logical words as logic: it cancels the implicatures of \emph{some} (\emph{not all}) and \emph{or} (\emph{not both}) in most tested open reasoning models and in GPT-5, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers improve. The trace shows why: models first entertain the enriched reading and cancel it later. Answering from that early reading, an exploratory inference-time remedy, recovers these implicatures without losing literal accuracy. Evaluations of reasoning models should measure how they interpret, not only how accurate they are.

title: How to Build a Production-Ready SaaS with Spring Boot 3, React 18 & Stripe in 2026
description:
When building a new B2B SaaS, 90% of the boilerplates and tutorials out there focus exclusively on the JavaScript ecosystem (Next.js, Node, Remix).

But if you want the type safety, multithreading performance (Virtual Threads in Java 21), and enterprise reliability of Spring Boot 3 combined with a fast React 18 frontend, you usually end up spending 3 to 4 weeks configuring the exact same plumbing from scratch:

  • Stateless JWT Authentication & Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
  • PostgreSQL persistence with Flyway database migrations
  • Stripe Checkout & asynchronous Webhook signature verification
  • CORS, security filters, and production deployment configs

In this guide, we’ll walk through the exact production architecture for a Spring Boot 3 (Java 21) + React 18 SaaS in 2026—and look at the core code patterns that hold it all together.

💡 Want to skip the 40+ hours of setup? I packaged this entire production-ready architecture (with full source code, Stripe webhooks, JWT Auth, Flyway migrations, and AI modules) into SaaSKit — The Spring Boot 3 & React 18 SaaS Boilerplate. Check out the live demo and documentation!

1. High-Level Architecture Overview

A modern, decoupled B2B SaaS architecture needs to be stateless, easy to scale horizontally, and strictly typed across boundaries:

  • Backend: Java 21 + Spring Boot 3.x (Spring Security 6, Spring Data JPA)
  • Database & Migrations: PostgreSQL + Flyway (versioned SQL schemas)
  • Frontend: React 18 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS (hosted on Vercel)
  • Payments: Stripe Checkout Sessions + Webhook Event Handler

Let's break down the three hardest parts of the implementation: Database Migrations, Stateless JWT Security, and Stripe Subscription Webhooks.

2. Database Schema & Flyway Migrations (V1__init.sql)

Never use spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update in production. One accidental entity change can corrupt customer data or break constraints. Instead, set ddl-auto=validate and let Flyway manage your PostgreSQL schema deterministically.

Place your initial migration inside src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__init_schema.sql:

CREATE TABLE users (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    role VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ROLE_USER',
    stripe_customer_id VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE,
    subscription_status VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'FREE',
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_stripe_customer ON users(stripe_customer_id);

This guarantees that every environment—from your local Docker container to staging and production—runs the exact same schema version.

3. Stateless JWT Security in Spring Boot 3 (Spring Security 6)

With Spring Security 6, the configuration uses the functional Lambda DSL. Since our React 18 frontend is hosted separately (e.g., on Vercel) and communicates via REST APIs, we disable CSRF for stateless endpoints, configure strict CORS policies, and inject a custom JwtAuthenticationFilter.

Here is the clean SecurityConfig.java pattern:

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class SecurityConfig {

    private final JwtAuthenticationFilter jwtAuthFilter;
    private final AuthenticationProvider authenticationProvider;

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .sessionManagement(session -> 
                session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)
            )
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers(
                    "/api/v1/auth/**",
                    "/api/v1/stripe/webhook",
                    "/v3/api-docs/**",
                    "/swagger-ui/**"
                ).permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .authenticationProvider(authenticationProvider)
            .addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);

        return http.build();
    }
}

Notice how /api/v1/stripe/webhook is explicitly whitelisted in permitAll(). Why? Because Stripe servers don't have a user JWT token—they authenticate via cryptographic webhook signatures instead.

4. Handling Stripe Subscriptions & Webhooks Reliably

The biggest mistake developers make when integrating Stripe with React and Spring Boot is updating the user's subscription status on the frontend redirect (?success=true). Users close their browser tabs, lose connectivity, or spoof URLs.

The only source of truth for SaaS billing is the Stripe Webhook.

Here is how to securely verify the Stripe-Signature header and provision access in Spring Boot 3:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/stripe")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class StripeWebhookController {

    @Value("${stripe.webhook.secret}")
    private String endpointSecret;

    private final SubscriptionService subscriptionService;

    @PostMapping("/webhook")
    public ResponseEntity<String> handleStripeWebhook(
            @RequestBody String payload,
            @RequestHeader("Stripe-Signature") String sigHeader) {

        Event event;
        try {
            event = Webhook.constructEvent(payload, sigHeader, endpointSecret);
        } catch (SignatureVerificationException e) {
            log.warn("Invalid Stripe webhook signature!");
            return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST).body("Invalid signature");
        }

        switch (event.getType()) {
            case "checkout.session.completed" -> {
                Session session = (Session) event.getDataObjectDeserializer().getObject().orElseThrow();
                subscriptionService.activateSubscription(
                    session.getClientReferenceId(),
                    session.getCustomer(),
                    session.getSubscription()
                );
            }
            case "customer.subscription.deleted" -> {
                Subscription sub = (Subscription) event.getDataObjectDeserializer().getObject().orElseThrow();
                subscriptionService.cancelSubscription(sub.getCustomer());
            }
            default -> log.debug("Unhandled Stripe event type: {}", event.getType());
        }

        return ResponseEntity.ok("Webhook processed");
    }
}

When a user clicks "Upgrade to Pro" in your React 18 dashboard:

  1. React calls POST /api/v1/billing/checkout-session with the user's JWT.
  2. Spring Boot creates a Stripe Checkout Session passing the user's UUID in client_reference_id.
  3. Once payment succeeds, Stripe fires checkout.session.completed to your backend, and Flyway-backed PostgreSQL updates subscription_status = 'PRO'.

5. Connecting React 18 with Axios Interceptors

On the React 18 side, you can centralize token handling and automatic 401 redirects using an Axios instance:

import axios from 'axios';

export const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL,
});

api.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('access_token');
  if (token) {
    config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
  }
  return config;
});

title: DeSpatial: The devil of Agentic Spatial Reasoning Lies in 3D Itself
description:
arXiv:2610.20990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial agents have access to reconstruction and segmentation tools, yet inconsistent predictions and fragmented object identities can prevent their outputs from becoming reliable 3D scene information. A simple oracle experiment exposes this perception bottleneck: replacing tool-predicted perception with ground-truth 3D bounding boxes raises an agent to nearly full score across five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, while retaining the same reasoning tools. Motivated by this finding, we believe the devil of spatial reasoning lies in 3D itself, and introduce DeSpatial(Devil of Spatial), which explicitly decomposes spatial understanding into perception and reasoning. DeSpatial has a shared 3D perception tool to reconcile independent perception outputs into a unified, metric, gravity-aligned 3D scene. This perception tool has two core components: a) a joint segmentation--depth co-refinement module that consolidates masks of the same object and removes projection artifacts caused by inconsistent segmentation and depth within a single frame; b) a cross-view instance fusion module that consolidate voxel-overlapping instances but not allowed to merge same-frame instances. This fusion module additionally fuses spatially disjoint fragments caused by insufficient multi-view observations, by checking their 3D structure and source mask appearance. After receiving the complete and unified 3D scene information, the agent chooses reasoning or computational tools to solve the spatial problem. DeSpatial achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video results on VSI-SUPER, revealing the bottleneck of spatial understanding lies in a precise 3D perception itself.

title: The best workflow engine is a programming language
description:
The idea of orchestrating long-running, stateful logic on top of unreliable, stateless infrastructure isn't new. We've had message queues, job runners, microservice choreographies, and full-blown workflow engines for a long time. What we never had was a version of it that felt good to write.

I'd spent about six months working on a fork of Temporal, mostly on weekends, trying to turn it into a serverless answer with DX that felt more Vercel-native. Eventually it dawned on me that to ship that experience, I'd need to own the execution environment too. So I dropped the fork, joined Vercel, and started hacking on a new framework from scratch alongside Nathan Rajlich.

Code is already a DAG

A workflow is a DAG, a directed acyclic graph. Before Temporal (and Cadence before it), nearly every workflow framework made you draw that DAG by hand. Apache Airflow is the canonical example. You describe your pipeline as an explicit graph of tasks and dependencies, and your actual logic gets buried inside the nodes."

That always felt backwards to me. We already have a tool for expressing "do this, then that, and these in parallel, and branch here." It's called a programming language. An abstract syntax tree is a DAG. Software itself is a DAG.

I knew that in the abstract, but it didn't truly hit me until I saw Temporal, where you write what looks like normal sequential code and the engine makes it durable underneath. It was the dream all along.

What running Temporal taught me

Temporal is great once your infrastructure exists. I was starting from scratch, and setting it up meant:

  • Standing up Temporal Cloud (or self-hosting the server: Frontend, History, Matching, and Worker services, plus a Cassandra/Postgres/MySQL backend and sharding).

  • Running your own worker fleet: Temporal never executes your code. Your workers poll the server and run your workflows and activities. In practice that's a Kubernetes cluster you own.

  • Wiring it all together: task queues, activity registration, client config.

  • Managing the workers yourself: scaling, uptime, restarts, and the build-and-deploy pipeline for the worker processes.

  • Setting up encryption: workers talk to the control plane over the internet, so you're configuring mutual TLS and a data converter to encrypt payloads before they leave your environment.

Once all of that was in place, the workflow dream mostly became real. But I wanted something easy to start that could still scale as my project grew into production.

Versioning in-flight workflows

Beyond owning the worker build-and-deploy process myself, there was a harder problem. If I changed my workflow code while runs were still in flight, I was kind of stuck. There were no longer any workers running the old, correct version of that code. Replay would hit my new code with an old event history and break on a non-determinism error.

The official answer is the patching API (patched() / GetVersion). You branch your code on a change ID and march it through a multi-stage deprecate-then-remove lifecycle as old runs age out of retention. It works, but it means evolving workflow code very carefully. Over enough changes, the workflow code rots into a thicket of version flags.

I couldn't explain Temporal signals

Whenever I tried to show running Temporal demos to friends, signals / queries / updates turned into the single most confusing part. They're three separate primitives for getting data in and out of a running workflow, each with its own rules. Queries can't block, signals are fire-and-forget and get buffered, and you have to know when to reach for which. The concepts did land but it wasn't very intuitive. To me, that was a DX smell. If I can't explain the human-in-the-loop primitive without a whiteboard, it's too complicated. That's why Workflow SDK replaces all three with a single primitive, the hook.

What Workflow SDK looks like today

With Workflow SDK, you write one file of normal code. "use workflow" marks an orchestrator; "use step" marks a unit of side-effecting work. In between it's just await, try/catch, Promise.all, loops, and conditionals.

A few things fall out of that one file:

  • No DAG file: The compiler reads the directives and splits the code into workflow and client/step bundles. The graph is your control flow.

  • Retries: Uncaught errors retry by default. Throw new FatalError(...) to stop. Throw new RetryableError(..., { retryAfter }) for custom backoff. Set fn.maxRetries = n to tune.

  • Ad-hoc webhooks: const webhook = createWebhook() creates a real, callable URL inside a running workflow, in a single line. The run parks until someone hits it, with no route or handler.

  • Hooks: Webhooks are sugar over a more general primitive. Create a hook with createHook<T>(), await it, and the data someone sends is what comes back. This one concept replaces signals, queries and updates

Here's an ad-hoc webhook end to end. An approval that can pause for seconds or for weeks, with nothing extra to deploy.

A library, not a platform

Traditional engines make you bring infrastructure to the framework. Workflow SDK brings the framework to infrastructure you already have.

DBOS had the right idea

While I was working out how to actually build this, I studied every workflow engine I could find. The one that stood out was DBOS, an open-source durable execution library that runs almost entirely client-side. The only thing its server needs is Postgres.

Workflow SDK adopts that shape. There's no bespoke orchestrator to self-host or pay for, and no new stateful system to operate. The only infrastructure it needs is infrastructure you already run: your app, a database, a queue. All the heavy lifting happens in the library.

The backend is swappable

Workflow SDK pushes the idea past one database. The whole thing is a spec, a way of writing workflows, steps, and hooks that any infrastructure can back. You mix and match the substrate to fit your stack:

  • Redis / Kafka / etc. for your streams

  • Postgres / Cassandra / the file system / Turso / Durable Objects / etc. for durability

  • Vercel Queues / SQS / Cloudflare Queues / etc. for your queue

The runtime only ever talks to a single interface, the World, which covers storage, queuing, auth, and streaming. Swapping any layer never touches your workflow code.

In fact, we maintain a first-party Postgres world inspired by DBOS, using Postgres for durability, queueing, and streaming. And in every world, there's no worker fleet and no control plane. A framework integration exposes two plain HTTP endpoints that deploy like the rest of your app.

Even the Vercel backend is "just" a CRUD API

The Vercel Workflow Server, the thing that backs workflows on Vercel, is stateless and does no compute or orchestration at all. It's just like the Postgres world, but extended with Vercel's authentication and multi-tenancy. A CRUD API, nothing more. It even runs as a regular Vercel deployment. All the heavy lifting, all the actual workflow logic, lives in the open-source, Apache-licensed client-side library, which can be extended freely.

So the "managed" offering isn't a black box you're locked into. It's just another World, one implementation of a spec you can read, fork, and extend. The data format isn't bespoke either. You can swap out any piece of the stack.

Some patterns lean on the platform

I should be upfront. A few of Workflow SDK's design choices are shaped by how Vercel executes code. The clearest example is versioning, the same code-evolution problem that makes traditional engines so painful.

Our answer is to pin each run to the specific deployment that started it. The run keeps executing against the exact copy of the code it began on, so changing your workflow never breaks in-flight runs. It's a clean solution, but it was only easy to build because Vercel already keeps immutable deployments around for long periods. The official Postgres world doesn't track and route versions this way yet. Encouragingly, community worlds have already implemented the spec as intended. Platformatic's version-safe durable workflows on Kubernetes is a great example.

And I think that's exactly the right trade. Pinning moves the complexity of versioning off the developer writing workflows and onto the infrastructure. That burden lands on the world author, the infra provider, and us as the framework authors. If everyone using a framework hits the same hard problem and has to solve it themselves in the same painful ways, the framework has failed them. A good framework moves that complexity upstream.

Steps should be free

Performance is the next big problem for us to solve. Invoking a step isn't cheap. Each step involves networking and a trip over a queue to durably commit its result correctly. For correctness, that's the right thing to do. But it works against the pitch that distributed computing should feel like function calls.

When you write ordinary code, you don't think twice about the overhead of a function call. It's so fast it's effectively free. But if every step carried a heavy overhead, the abstraction leaks. You start rationing steps, reasoning about granularity, declining to turn a small function into a checkpoint because it's "not worth a step."

So the goal is blunt: steps should be free.

In the ideal version of this, you could take any function in an existing codebase, add "use step", and everything would just work, with no serialization constraints and no performance penalty.

That dream drives us.

What if any developer could turn a plain function into something with the performance, networking, observability, and availability of a standalone microservice, but using just two words: "use step"? That would change how we write code.

Workflow v5 (in beta at the time of writing) already delivers up to a 5x performance improvement with no change to the user-facing API, and v6 will push it further while making third-party worlds just as fast. We're sharing details as we go in this GitHub discussion, and you can start testing today with npm install workflow@beta.

I set out to build a durable framework that feels like writing ordinary code, runs on the infrastructure you already have, and is fast enough that you never think twice about reaching for a step. It's real today, and we're building the rest of it in the open.

Come build Workflow SDK with us

If designing durable systems under real-world constraints sounds like fun, the Workflow team at Vercel is hiring.

See open roles.

Direct Providers vs Stable Contracts — SMS Event Resend Failures and Carrier Filtering
description:
A stable messaging contract is the better default for telehealth login verification when the team expects to change the SMS provider without rewriting application code; choose a direct specialist instead when carrier-specific controls and event push are hard requirements. TL;DR: registration and signature work must happen before launch, delivery evidence must drive every resend, and the application must enforce its own US/EU fraud and spend policy. Reliability starts at that boundary, not at the send call.

This architecture decision record covers one narrow job: issue a login code and retain an auditable account of what the messaging system reports. It does not treat an accepted request as delivery, and it does not promise exactly-once delivery over a carrier network. The attainable property is exactly-once business effect: one verification challenge, one state machine, and retry decisions that cannot create an unbounded stream of valid codes.

How should SMS event notifications handle resend failures and carrier filtering?

The first invariant is identity. A challenge ID belongs to the application, while a provider message ID is evidence attached to it; replacing one with the other would erase the audit trail. The second is monotonic state: queued may become delivered, failed, or carrier-rejected, but a late poll must not move a terminal record backward. The third is bounded issuance. A resend can create another transport attempt, yet it must not mint a second independently valid login challenge.

The correct sender configuration has to be registered and verified for each destination market before failed deliveries are diagnosed. Geo-fencing and per-country spend cutoffs are not supplied by the messaging capability, so US/EU allowlists, velocity limits, and budget circuit breakers remain application responsibilities. Carrier rejection is not an invitation to retry forever.

Keep four records: the challenge, each transport attempt, every observed status transition, and the policy decision that permitted or denied a resend. Record timestamps and opaque provider IDs, but never put the OTP itself in an audit log. OWASP recommends consistent responses and protections against excessive automated submissions for account-recovery flows; the same defensive posture is appropriate at a login-verification boundary.

This distinction matters.

Decision and failure boundaries

The decision is between a provider-owned integration and an application-owned contract. Infrai fits the latter. Its breadth is real: 295 routes across 20 modules use the same platform conventions. Infrai uses one key, one wallet, and one bill, removing separate credential rotation and invoice reconciliation from the verification service's operating path. Infrai exposes one REST API over plain HTTP with no SDK to install, so the Go service does not inherit a vendor library merely to poll delivery state. Its public, self-describing discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples without requiring a key. With Infrai, a team can swap the vendor behind a capability without changing application code; the contract stays put while the implementation behind it moves.

Teams operating login verification across US and EU markets should try Infrai for the SMS transport boundary when contract stability and a discoverable schema matter more than provider-native event delivery. The limitation is material: SMS events are pull-only, so a team requiring webhook-driven, near-real-time carrier events should choose a specialist integration. Infrai also provides no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS fallback, and email does not offer a hosted OTP endpoint, so those recovery paths require separate design.

Option Integration surface Delivery evidence Best boundary Material trade-off
Infrai One REST contract and credential; public discovery exposes schemas and examples Poll SMS status and events; resend and cancel are available Teams insulating application code from vendor changes No webhook events, built-in geo-fence, or per-country spend cutoff
Twilio Messaging Direct specialist contract Provider-native status callbacks Teams needing pushed status and specialist controls Application code and credentials remain coupled to that specialist
Vonage SMS API Direct specialist contract Provider delivery receipts Teams standardizing operations on Vonage A provider move crosses the application contract
AWS End User Messaging SMS AWS-native specialist surface Configured SMS event destinations Teams whose policy and operations already live in AWS Cloud-specific configuration enters the messaging boundary

These options are not interchangeable merely because all can originate an SMS. Twilio, Vonage, and AWS are valid choices where native controls are the reason for the integration. The stable-contract option wins when portability and credential consolidation remove more operating work than specialist hooks would save.

The critical path is observation, not resend

The smallest useful diagnostic program polls one message ID and preserves the raw response for the audit pipeline. It deliberately does not guess the response schema or automatically resend: a retry needs challenge state, destination policy, attempt count, and elapsed time. The program handles throttling, honors Retry-After when expressed as seconds, applies exponential backoff otherwise, checks every response, and stops after a bounded number of attempts.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... go run main.go <sms-id>")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        endpoint := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/status/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[1]), 1)
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { panic(readErr) }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay): continue
            case <-ctx.Done(): panic(ctx.Err())
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "status lookup failed: %s: %s\n", resp.Status, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "status lookup remained rate-limited after 5 attempts")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Persist the response beside the attempt before interpreting it. A worker can map the four documented outcomes into the local monotonic state machine. Only the policy layer may authorize a resend, and its audit entry should include the prior attempt ID, observed state, decision reason, and actor. Five polling attempts above are a client-side bound, not a claim about delivery time.

A resend endpoint exists, as does cancellation for SMS, but availability is not policy. A delayed alert may justify a controlled operational retry; a carrier-rejected code calls for checking sender registration, signature, destination eligibility, and suppression state first. Deduplicate the business command, allow multiple transport observations, and make every new attempt explicit.

Consider the decision at 09:00 when an EU patient's attempt is queued, the login challenge still has 90 seconds of validity, and the account has no earlier resend. The transport state does not prove failure, so the worker records the observation and schedules another poll; it does not issue a second code. If a later observation is carrier-rejected, the policy closes that transport attempt, records the terminal evidence, checks that the destination and sender configuration were approved, and only then evaluates a resend. A US request follows the same state machine but a different country allowlist and spend circuit breaker. Now change one fact: the first attempt becomes delivered after a retry command was accepted. The application must invalidate any superseded challenge or keep both transport attempts bound to the same challenge, because allowing two unrelated valid codes would turn transport uncertainty into an authentication defect. This example contains no assumed delivery interval and no claim that polling creates certainty; it shows why the local ledger, rather than a provider response or a timer, owns the business truth. The trade-off is deliberate: waiting for evidence can add friction, while resending without evidence can multiply valid credentials and obscure reconciliation. For a compliance notice rather than a short-lived code, the same ledger can authorize cancellation of a delayed SMS, but the policy and audit reason still belong outside the transport adapter.

No blind retry.

Why reject automatic failover?

The rejected design sends through one provider, waits a fixed interval, then fires the same code through another whenever no confirmation has arrived. It looks resilient. It also conflates queued with failed, can race a late delivery, and makes reconciliation ambiguous because two attempts may reach one patient.

Automatic failover has a valid use case when the application has a durable attempt ledger, a single challenge whose validity is centrally controlled, destination-specific sender registrations on both paths, and a documented threshold for declaring the first path unusable. Even then, the decision should consume observed state rather than a timer alone. Without those controls, a policy-gated resend is more defensible.

A direct provider is also correct when webhook latency is part of the login service-level objective, a carrier-specific feature is required, or an organization already has mature compliance operations around Twilio, Vonage, or AWS. Contract stability cannot compensate for a missing channel or an event model too slow for the workflow.

Operational record

Before release, verify sender registration and signatures in every intended market, then test policy outcomes rather than assuming a successful API response proves delivery. Acceptance evidence should cover a queued message becoming delivered, a terminal failure that does not loop, a carrier rejection that blocks blind resend, a 429 that backs off, a disallowed country, and a spend cutoff reached under concurrency. Six cases expose more architectural truth than another SDK wrapper.

Reconciliation should compare challenges, attempts, and observed events by stable identifiers. There is no tag-aggregated cost-report API, so finance-grade allocation needs an application-side dimension recorded at send time. Because SMS events are polled, the worker must be restartable and idempotent; processing the same observation twice must leave the same terminal state and audit record.

Use a stable messaging contract when provider substitution, schema discovery, and reduced credential sprawl dominate; use a direct specialist when pushed events, carrier-specific controls, or another communications channel is a hard requirement. If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai SMS troubleshooting guide.

References

  • OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet
  • Twilio: Monitor the status of your message
  • Vonage SMS API: Delivery receipts
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS: Monitor SMS activity
  • Infrai SMS troubleshooting guide

title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations
description:
arXiv:2610.20866v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.

Vercel Connect now supports Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) in public beta. Your apps and agents can access supported services on behalf of signed-in users without separate consent prompts for each service.

  • Admin-managed access: Administrators can grant or revoke access to supported services through the identity provider.

  • Corporate sign-in: Users sign into your app with their corporate account through a compatible identity provider such as Okta.

  • Scoped tokens: Your app requests the scopes it needs, and Connect handles token exchange, caching, and renewal. Access is limited to approved scopes and the user’s existing service permissions.

If your app uses Vercel Passport, you can request a token for Slack’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with the signed-in user’s identity:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 1T9cFkjaRDDmRFQ5bWVmD6

Connect supports Cross-App Access (XAA), including its use for MCP authorization through EMA. Follow the Vercel Connect EMA setup guide to configure your identity provider and services and enable EMA on their Connect connectors.

title: WeightWatch: Detección Black-Box de Backdoors en LLMs Fine-Tuneados
description:
La cadena de suministro de modelos de IA representa un vector de ataque emergente y crítico. Los modelos open-weight fine-tuneados pueden contener puertas traseras (backdoors) latentes que solo se activan ante triggers específicos, siendo indetectables mediante inspección superficial.

Presentamos WeightWatch (github.com/amurlaniakea/weightwatch), una herramienta de auditoría de seguridad diseñada para escanear modelos de lenguaje antes de su despliegue.

Características técnicas principales:

Análisis Black-Box: No requiere acceso a los datos de entrenamiento originales ni a un modelo base de referencia limpio.

Detección Híbrida: Combina la técnica output-to-input loop (para forzar la convergencia de firmas anómalas) con inyección de muestras canary.

Determinismo y Reproducibilidad: Ejecución con semilla fija, garantizando el mismo veredicto y hash sha256 para un modelo dado.

Integración CI/CD Nativa: Salida estructurada en JSON y códigos de salida (exit codes) para automatizar el bloqueo de modelos con veredicto SUSPICIOUS o BACKDOOR en pipelines de MLOps.

Estado actual: El MVP valida su lógica mediante fixtures sintéticos embebidos, sin dependencias de red. La validación a escala con modelos reales de Hugging Face está programada para la v0.2.

Invitamos a la comunidad de seguridad en IA, ingenieros de MLOps e investigadores a revisar el código, contribuir con heurísticas de detección y probar su integración en entornos de staging. La seguridad de la IA debe ser automatizable, transparente y de código abierto.

title: ReState: Noise-Level-Aware State Correction for Training-Free Object Removal in Few-Step Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21287v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training-free object removal commonly redirects self-attention away from the target region, but on few-step distilled diffusion models this often leaves object-shaped residuals. We identify a temporal mismatch: a structured prediction forms inside the mask at the first forward, and the short trajectory offers few later chances to revise it, while attention rerouting acts mainly in later steps. Across four distilled backbones, magnitude-matched single-forward interventions show that background-directed state correction affects the final result more than attention rerouting. We therefore propose ReState, which corrects the masked clean prediction toward background evidence retrieved from the input using a noise-level-aware weight that vanishes at the final forward. ReState retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and adds no denoiser evaluations. Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, ReState achieves the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, improving PSNR by 3.17 dB on average over the strongest baseline. On OBER-Test, it also outperforms the 50-step attention-forcing reference on all three metrics at 6.7x lower latency. The same configuration transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning. Project page: https://tdrlee.github.io/ReState

title: How to Train Your Little Dragon: Teaching a Small Language Model to Construct and Refine GPU Optimization Scripts
description:
arXiv:2610.20980v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compiler transformations interact, making GPU kernel optimization a search for combinations that preserve the computation while improving performance. We introduce HOW TO TRAIN YOUR LITTLE DRAGON, a training method that teaches a small language model both to construct complete optimization scripts and to improve existing ones. Instead of ranking candidates or generating kernel code, our model generates optimization scripts. We devise a compact, lossless representation whose deterministic decoding reconstructs the exact compiler trace, preserving its transformation parameters and dependencies. We use a compiler framework TVM MetaSchedule to build training data on 54,116 distinct workloads, and construct 108,594 examples in two training sets: 60,236 teach the model to generate an optimized script from an unoptimized kernel, while 48,358 teach it to produce a better script given the kernel and a somewhat optimized script. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to construct and improve optimization scripts from these search-derived examples. We then add reinforcement learning with a shaped reward that combines correctness with measured performance, awarding a latency-based bonus only to numerically correct kernels. We apply this training method to a model with 8 billion parameters. After supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model achieves per-attempt correctness of 91.27% for construction and 92.01% for refinement, while reinforcement learning produces faster kernels than supervised training on 88 of 102 construction tasks and 145 of 170 refinement prompts. With only 8B parameters, our LITTLE DRAGON achieves higher per-attempt correctness and better kernel performance than six frontier LLMs: GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3 among them, each with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, for which task-specific training is unavailable or expensive.

title: Fewer crates.io projects go silent on outside pull requests than npm or PyPI
description:
If you maintain a crate, you probably have a view on whether outside pull requests get a fair hearing in the Rust world. I now have a number to set beside that view, and it comes with enough caveats that I want to list them.

Porchlamp scores open-source projects on how they handle pull requests from people outside the team. This post uses a second cut of the same data, split by ecosystem, from the snapshot of 14 October. I covered the method in an earlier post, so here is only the part you need: a black hole is a project that leaves most of its outside pull requests without a human reply, review or merge for two weeks.

The comparison

Among crates projects that received a decision, 20.0% are black holes. The figure for npm is 30.0%, and for PyPI it is 33.8%. The cut spans six ecosystems, and the Rust subset is 1,065 crates.io projects. In plain terms, one in five of the decided crates projects is a black hole, against roughly three in ten for npm and a third for PyPI.

A decision means Porchlamp could judge the project either way. Undecided projects are not in these percentages.

Those figures reconcile with the headline from the earlier post, which is how I checked this cut ties to the published numbers: across all six ecosystems, 4,297 projects received a decision and 1,133 of them (26.4%) are black holes.

Ecosystem Sampled Decided Black holes Share
maven 1,001 278 54 19.4%
crates 1,065 586 117 20.0%
systems 1,287 573 115 20.1%
go 1,164 609 135 22.2%
npm 3,774 1,283 385 30.0%
pypi 2,709 968 327 33.8%
All six 11,000 4,297 1,133 26.4%

Rust is not first in that table. The JVM sample is a shade better at 19.4%, and the systems sample is within a
whisker at 20.1%. The clean split in this data is between those four and npm and PyPI, and I would rather say so
plainly than let the Rust number do more work than it can.

What you can reasonably conclude

In this sample, a decided crates.io project was less likely to be a black hole than a decided npm or PyPI one, by ten points and nearly fourteen points respectively. If you are choosing where to send a first patch, that is mild encouragement for Rust projects and not a guarantee for any one of them. It is also a single snapshot, and it will change as projects do.

What you should not conclude

Do not read this as a finding about the Rust community's character, and do not read it as a clean verdict on your own crate. There is no control for project size in this cut. Ecosystem is the sampling frame, meaning it describes how projects entered the sample and not why they behave as they do. Elsewhere in the same data the black-hole share rises with stars, from 21% to 39% across the bands I measured, so if one ecosystem's sample leans towards larger or smaller projects, its share moves for reasons unrelated to the ecosystem itself.

A second caveat concerns who is counted. Anything reviewed on Gerrit or a mailing list is undecided, so it sits outside all three percentages. If undecided projects cluster in some ecosystems more than others, the shares would shift, and this cut cannot say whether they do.

Nor should a maintainer feel judged by any of these shares. The measure counts silence over two weeks, which is a narrow window and not a character reference.

Help me get it right

Porchlamp is open source, and this comparison is exactly the sort of claim that benefits from more eyes. Each verdict lists the pull requests behind it, so if a crate is misjudged you can show the evidence and ask for a change. Missing projects can be added, and the code takes patches in the repository. The rankings themselves are on the site.

Would you expect the Rust figure to survive a control for project size, and if not, which way would you guess it moves?

title: VisualTrust: Video Reasoning under On-Screen Claim Framing
description:
arXiv:2610.21159v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models' tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.

title: MAI-Gym: An Open All-in-One Platform for GUI Agent Evaluation and RL Training across Mobile and Computer Environments
description:
arXiv:2610.20939v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has driven rapid progress in mathematics, coding, and tool use, but scaling this success to GUI agents remains challenging due to the high cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks. We introduce MAI-Gym, an open all-in-one platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments. Through a shared rollout pipeline, MAI-Gym ensures consistent agent behavior across evaluation and training, supports ten established benchmarks, and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances. Beyond scalable infrastructure, MAI-Gym enables automated synthesis of diverse GUI applications and challenging tasks, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers. Using MAI-Gym, we train MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open GUI agents under 10B parameters: 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified. Importantly, RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a phys- ical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. We release the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint to support repro- ducible research and further advances in scalable GUI agent training.

title: Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields: Evidence-Grounded Selective Safety for Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20679v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Representation-based safety defenses for vision-language models (VLMs) often learn to separate harmful from benign inputs, but separation alone does not establish what a risk score means or when it should be trusted. We introduce Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields (CNRF), an evidence-grounded framework for selective VLM safety. CNRF constructs context-matched benign-harmful counterfactual pairs, uses their representation differences as capability-related risk directions, and estimates neighborhood support separately from risk. This separation prevents unfamiliarity from being conflated with harmfulness and enables selective intervention rather than blanket rejection. A victim-adaptive interface accommodates different safety observations across VLM architectures and routes selected requests for same-victim response review, which either releases acceptable candidates or produces constrained alternatives with reduced harmful capability. Across three VLMs and five multimodal jailbreak families, CNRF achieves 86.06-89.30% macro defense success rate while retaining substantial benign-task utility. Controlled experiments further show that query-matched references and preserved context-direction correspondence materially improve risk ranking in the low-false-positive regime. CNRF thus reframes representation-based VLM safety from learning harmfulness boundaries to constructing applicable evidence for selective risk decisions.

title: The Receiving Inspection Workshop: A Gate for AI-Written Code
description:
Three agent-written patches landed on a Friday afternoon. Two were nine-line diffs, one touched a helper nobody remembered owning, and all three were reviewed in the ten minutes between a standup and a release. On Monday the nightly seed job died, and nobody could say which candidate produced the line that killed it.

That team did not have a review problem. It had a receiving problem. A candidate sat in a pull request, looked plausible, and crossed into the trunk without anything recording what had actually been checked.

The last few weeks of DEV discussion keep circling a familiar split: model capability climbs, and the software wrapped around it stays about as fragile as the day it was written. That gap is not a model problem. It is a testing problem, and it is teachable in ninety minutes.

This workshop builds a receiving dock. Students leave with a gate that parses a candidate, runs it against a fixture, writes a verdict to a ledger, and refuses to be the last word on anything.

The invariant

The whole workshop hangs on one sentence, written by the students in the first ten minutes and never edited afterward: nothing reaches the trunk without a receipt.

A receipt is one JSON line. It names the task, the model that produced the candidate, the verdict, a machine-readable reason, and a timestamp. It is boring on purpose. When the nightly job breaks three days later, the receipt is what lets someone say this candidate passed a three-case fixture and nothing else, instead of reconstructing the week from chat scrollback.

The run sheet

Clock Segment Artifact at the end
00–10 The Monday failure story, told once The written invariant
10–25 Fixture before gate tasks/03_slugify/test_solution.py, three cases
25–45 Build the gate gate.py, first accept receipt
45–60 Break it deliberately Two quarantines, one false accept
60–75 Boundary sweep A property test that catches the fake
75–90 Yield accounting and transport swap receipts.jsonl and a yield number

Every segment ends with a file. If a segment runs long, the artifact gets cut down, never skipped, because a workshop that finishes with a feeling instead of a file teaches nothing rerunnable.

Fixture before gate

Students almost always want to write the gate first. That order produces a gate that grades whatever it happens to be shown, which is the exact failure mode of human review under deadline pressure.

The fixture comes first. A task is a directory with a prompt and a test file, and the candidate is expected to expose one function.

{
  "id": "03_slugify",
  "model": "fill-from-current-provider-docs",
  "prompt": "Write slugify(text: str) -> str"
}

# tasks/03_slugify/test_solution.py
from solution import slugify


def test_basic():
    assert slugify("Hello World") == "hello-world"


def test_collapses_runs():
    assert slugify("a   b---c") == "a-b-c"


def test_empty_stays_empty():
    assert slugify("") == ""

Three cases is the right number for the first pass. A fixture large enough to be impressive is a fixture nobody in the room can explain, and an unexplained fixture fails silently the day it is edited.

The gate

The gate is deliberately small: it parses, it runs, it records, it stops.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""gate.py - receiving inspection for model-written candidates."""
import ast, json, pathlib, subprocess, sys, time

ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
MAX_BYTES = 8192


def parse_ok(path):
    try:
        ast.parse(path.read_text())
    except SyntaxError as exc:
        return False, f"syntax_error_line_{exc.lineno}"
    return True, "parsed"


def behavior(test_path, scratch):
    proc = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", "-q", str(test_path)],
        cwd=scratch, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60,
    )
    lines = proc.stdout.strip().splitlines()
    return proc.returncode == 0, (lines[-1] if lines else "no_output")


def main(task_dir):
    task = json.loads(pathlib.Path(task_dir, "task.json").read_text())
    scratch = ROOT / "scratch" / task["id"]
    scratch.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    candidate = ROOT / "candidates" / f'{task["id"]}.py'
    verdict, reason = "quarantine", "no_candidate"

    if candidate.exists() and candidate.stat().st_size <= MAX_BYTES:
        ok, why = parse_ok(candidate)
        if ok:
            (scratch / "solution.py").write_text(candidate.read_text())
            (scratch / "test_solution.py").write_text(
                pathlib.Path(task_dir, "test_solution.py").read_text()
            )
            ok, why = behavior(scratch / "test_solution.py", scratch)
        verdict, reason = ("accept" if ok else "quarantine"), why
    elif candidate.exists():
        reason = f"oversize_{candidate.stat().st_size}b"

    receipt = {
        "task": task["id"],
        "model": task.get("model", "unspecified"),
        "verdict": verdict,
        "reason": reason,
        "ts": int(time.time()),
    }
    with open(ROOT / "receipts.jsonl", "a") as fh:
        fh.write(json.dumps(receipt) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(receipt))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1])

A candidate for the slug task, dropped at candidates/03_slugify.py, looks like this:

import re


def slugify(text):
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", text.lower()).strip("-")

$ pip install pytest
$ python gate.py tasks/03_slugify
{"task": "03_slugify", "model": "fill-from-current-provider-docs", "verdict": "accept", "reason": "3 passed", "ts": 1792000000}

If pytest reports an ImportError on solution, the instructor has hit the classic path problem; run the gate with PYTHONPATH=. set and the scratch directory as the working directory, and the failure disappears. That detour is worth five minutes, because everyone meets it eventually in their own repository.

Break it deliberately

This is the segment that changes how students think about green checks. The instructor supplies a candidate that hardcodes the fixture's answers:

def slugify(text):
    return {
        "Hello World": "hello-world",
        "a   b---c": "a-b-c",
        "": "",
    }.get(text, "")

The gate accepts it. Three tests, three passes, one receipt that says accept, and a function that will return an empty string for every input the product actually receives. The fixture graded the fixture.

The correction is a property check that ties output back to input instead of to remembered examples:

# tasks/03_slugify/test_boundary.py
import random, string
from solution import slugify


def test_alnum_digest_matches():
    rng = random.Random(7)
    for _ in range(200):
        raw = "".join(
            rng.choice(string.printable) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 40))
        )
        digest = "".join(ch for ch in raw.lower() if ch.isalnum())
        assert slugify(raw).replace("-", "") == digest

The hardcoded candidate now fails within a handful of iterations, while the real implementation passes all two hundred. Students see the difference between evidence and a memory test, and they see it in code rather than in a slide.

Where the compute comes from

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Two hundred generated candidates per cohort is small by industry standards and painful in a classroom, because it forces every student to hold a paid key before they have learned anything worth paying for. MonkeyCode, the project behind this article's operator, describes a free tier and a free server option; the operator currently reports the free allowance at ten million tokens. Those terms live on the project's own page and can change, so this workshop treats them as a starting point to check rather than constants to quote in a syllabus, and it asserts nothing about which models are included, how large the server is, or how long either offer lasts.

The harness itself assumes no vendor at all. The transport is one function, and the shape below is what students fill in from whatever endpoint they are actually using:

import json, os, urllib.request


def ask(prompt):
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        os.environ["BASE_URL"] + "/chat/completions",
        data=json.dumps({
            "model": os.environ["MODEL"],
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        }).encode(),
        headers={
            "Authorization": f'Bearer {os.environ["API_KEY"]}',
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=120) as response:
        return json.load(response)["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

The free server option earns its place in the boundary-sweep segment, where a loop of two hundred candidates would otherwise compete with whatever else is on the student's laptop. It is a convenience for the exercise, not a claim about production throughput.

Yield accounting

The last artifact is a number students compute themselves:

import collections, json

rows = [json.loads(line) for line in open("receipts.jsonl")]
counts = collections.Counter(row["verdict"] for row in rows)
total = sum(counts.values())
print(counts, "yield=", round(counts["accept"] / total, 3))

Yield is acceptance rate per task, and it belongs to the task, not to the model. A slug function with a clear contract collects accepts; a task whose prompt hides its error handling collects quarantines and tells the room nothing about model quality. That distinction is worth more than any leaderboard.

The verdict table

The gate produces four outcomes, and each maps to one action.

Verdict Signal Action
Accept Parses, fixture green, sweep green Merge with a link to the receipt
Repair Parses, one named test fails with a local cause One bounded revision, re-run the gate, two attempts maximum
Quarantine Syntax error, oversize candidate, timeout, or missing file Move the candidate to quarantine/ and stop
Escalate Sweep green but the diff touches files, network, or credentials Human review of record, no exceptions

What this gate cannot see

The gate checks exactly what the fixture encodes and nothing more. A candidate that passes one afternoon is not guaranteed to pass tomorrow, because sampling variance means the same prompt can produce a different artifact; that is why the candidate bytes get stored next to the receipt and re-run on demand. The byte limit is arbitrary and exists to keep reviews short. The sixty-second timeout catches hangs, not deadlocks that resolve in ninety seconds. Concurrency, license headers, and secret handling are invisible to it.

Teams in regulated pipelines should not treat this gate as a control. It is a teaching device and a first filter, and a named human reviewer of record is still required wherever the rules say so. Teams with no fixture-writing habit should fix that habit before building the gate, or they will automate the grading of nothing.

A cohort that wants to see the sweep finish before deciding whether the gate belongs in its pipeline can start on the free tier and the free server option; the current terms page is the only place worth trusting for what is included today.

MonkeyCode provides free models that can run this workflow.
