title: Automatic Sentence Completion Using Bengali Audio Speech with a Transformer-Based Early Speech Recognition System
description:
arXiv:2610.21164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dementia severely impairs communication abilities and turns everyday conversations into challenging experiences. Individuals affected by dementia frequently struggle to express their thoughts or complete sentences, making it difficult for family members and caregivers to understand their needs. This study proposes a novel approach to assist dementia patients by developing an integrated system that detects signs of dementia through Bangla speech and text analysis and provides sentence auto-completion support during conversations. To achieve this, recorded voices from individuals with and without dementia were analysed, and key acoustic features were extracted to capture vocal patterns associated with cognitive decline. A transformer-based model was employed to transcribe voice signals into text for linguistic analysis. In the classification task, several Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models were evaluated using both acoustic and textual representations, and the LSTM model architectures demonstrated strong capabilities for modelling contextual patterns in speech and language data. For the sentence auto-completion task, a sequential learning model based on a Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) network with an attention mechanism was developed to sequentially complete partially expressed Bangla sentences during conversation. This research bridges the gap in dementia analysis in an underrepresented language and implements a sentence auto-completion framework for cognitive disorders.

title: RoPE-Flow: Monocular Vision-based Robot Pose Estimation via 2D Graph-Conditioned 3D Flow Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.21086v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D-3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints. In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras. Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: ropeflow.netlify.app

title: Towards automatic digital garment assembly
description:
arXiv:2610.20651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Creating digital garments from existing two-dimensional patterns remains a time-consuming process. Although patterns are widely available in digital form, their assembly in garment CAD software involves manual definition of sewing operations and arrangement of the pattern panels for drape simulation. We present two learning-based approaches that automate both tasks using the 2D vector pattern as their sole input. Our automatic sewing model operates at the segment level, leveraging a Transformer encoder with multiple prediction heads. Our novel architecture supports many-to-many, ordered segment correspondences, as well as hems, overlapping seams needed for multilayer garments, and construction properties such as seam allowances and stitch types, required for the finished virtual garment but neglected by previous methods. A complementary panel-level model predicts body-region assignments, layers, and placement coordinates to initialize the drape simulation. We evaluate both models on a curated dataset of 4,035 professionally assembled garment instances. The sewing model exactly recovers all seam and hem topologies of 63.3\% of test garments, while the arrangement model meets the specified placement criteria for all panels in 66.2\% of test garments. We also integrate both methods into garment CAD software, demonstrating automatic assembly of successfully predicted garments.

title: Mind the Tail: Data Selection Through Sparse Concepts
description:
arXiv:2610.21007v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test-time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine-grained, spurious-correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset-level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down-weights well-represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out-of-distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data-efficient and robust learning.

title: How to build a shadcn/ui registry that Claude Code and Cursor can actually use
description:
Most shadcn/ui components are now installed by an AI coding agent, not a person typing the command. If you publish a registry, the agent is your user. It needs to find your components, read their props without guessing, and run the right install command. A registry that only works for humans clicking through a docs site is a registry that gets misused.

I run HextaUI, a shadcn/ui registry, and I spent a chunk of this year making it work for Claude Code, Cursor and the shadcn MCP server. This is everything that turned out to matter, in the order I would do it again.

1. Ship a registry that passes validation

Start with the basics. Every item is a JSON file that follows the registry schema, with name, type, files, dependencies and registryDependencies. Put the index at a stable URL and every item at a predictable one:

https://your-site.com/r/registry.json
https://your-site.com/r/button.json
https://your-site.com/r/all.json

Run shadcn build to generate them from a registry.json source, and validate before you deploy. The CLI gained a registry validate step in May 2026. A registry that fails validation fails silently for agents, who will then write the component by hand and get it wrong.

Two details that make a real difference:

  • registryDependencies with full URLs. When your Dialog depends on your Button, point to https://your-site.com/r/button.json, not button, or the CLI pulls the shadcn/ui Button instead.
  • An all.json item that depends on everything. Agents asked to "set up the design system" will reach for it.

2. Register a namespace

Since the registry namespace feature landed, a user adds this to components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@hextaui": "https://hextaui.com/r/{name}.json"
  }
}

And then installs with a short name:

npx shadcn@latest add @hextaui/dialog

Document this snippet on your installation page and in your llms.txt. The short form is what the shadcn MCP server searches across, so a registry without a namespace is invisible to the one tool most agents use to browse registries.

If the registry is private, the object form takes headers with environment variables that the CLI expands and never logs:

{
  "registries": {
    "@acme-pro": {
      "url": "https://acme.com/r/pro/{name}.json",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${ACME_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

3. Give every docs page a Markdown twin

Agents fetch HTML badly. They fetch Markdown well. Make every docs URL answer at .md with the same content: description, install command, full source, usage, examples, keyboard support and the API table.

https://hextaui.com/docs/button      -> HTML for people
https://hextaui.com/docs/button.md   -> Markdown for agents

Do not hand-write the Markdown. Generate it from the same source as the page so the two never drift. On HextaUI the .md route walks the page's React tree and serializes it, so adding an example to the page adds it to the Markdown for free.

The API reference matters most here. An agent that can read a props table does not hallucinate a size="xl" that does not exist.

4. Publish llms.txt and llms-full.txt

llms.txt is a Markdown index at your site root: what the project is, when to use it, when not to, how to install, and one line per docs page with its .md link. llms-full.txt is every docs page concatenated, for agents that want to load everything once.

The "when not to use it" section is the part people skip and the part that saves you support tickets. If your registry is React and Tailwind only, say so, or an agent will try to install it into a Vue project.

Keep the install command in the first ten lines. Agents read the top.

5. Run an MCP server, read-only, no key

The shadcn CLI has its own MCP server (npx shadcn@latest mcp) that searches any registry in components.json. That covers installs. It does not cover docs, keyboard maps or examples.

So I run a second one at https://hextaui.com/mcp, Streamable HTTP, read-only, no API key, with five tools: search_docs, get_component, get_component_api, get_examples and get_install_command. Claude Code connects with one line:

claude mcp add --transport http hextaui https://hextaui.com/mcp

Cursor and VS Code take the same URL in their MCP config. Once connected, "add a HextaUI combobox with async results" turns into a docs search, an API read and the right install command, with no guessing in between.

Make it discoverable too. Publish a server card at /.well-known/mcp/server-card.json and a server.json in the MCP registry format. Agents and the tools around them are starting to look there first.

6. Describe the HTTP surface with OpenAPI and real errors

Everything above is also plain HTTP, and agents increasingly call HTTP directly. Publish an openapi.json with operation ids and typed responses. Return errors as RFC 9457 application/problem+json with a resolution field that says what to do next:

{
  "type": "https://hextaui.com/docs/api#not-found",
  "title": "Component not found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "No component named 'modal'.",
  "resolution": "Try 'dialog' or 'alert-dialog'. The catalog is at /mcp/index.json."
}

An agent that gets a 404 with a hint recovers. An agent that gets an HTML error page writes the component from memory.

7. Ship a skill file

Claude Code and a growing list of agents read SKILL.md files that explain how to use a tool. Put one at /.well-known/agent-skills/<name>/SKILL.md: how to find a component, read its docs, and install it, with the exact commands. It is a page of Markdown and it is the highest-leverage page on the site.

8. Test with the agents, not with yourself

Open a fresh Next.js project in Claude Code with your MCP server connected and no other context. Ask it to "add a date picker from with a range and a disabled weekend rule". Watch what it does. Every wrong guess is a gap in your .md docs or your llms.txt.

Then do the same in Cursor with only llms.txt and no MCP. Then with nothing but the URL. The registry should degrade gracefully through all three.

What this gets you

An agent with the MCP server or the .md docs connected reads the props table instead of guessing it, runs the install command instead of rewriting the component, and installs the dependencies in the right order. The registry side of HextaUI was about a week of work. The agent side took longer, and it is the part that made the registry usable by the people who now do most of the installing.

If you want to see all of it live: hextaui.com/llms.txt, any docs page with .md appended, the MCP docs, and the API docs with the OpenAPI spec.

FAQ

Do I need my own MCP server if the shadcn CLI has one? The shadcn MCP covers search and install across registries in components.json. Your own server covers docs, APIs and examples. Most registries benefit from both.

Should the MCP server require an API key? Not for public docs. Every key you require is an agent that gives up. Keep auth for private items and use bearer tokens through components.json headers.

How do I generate the Markdown docs without duplicating content? Render the same component tree the page uses and serialize it to Markdown. One source, two formats.

What goes in llms.txt? A description, when to use and when not to, the install command, the namespace snippet, and one line per docs page linking to its .md.

title: Planning Commitment of LLM under Partial Observability
description:
arXiv:2610.21108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based planning agents commit to plans of different lengths before interacting with a partially observable environment. Some aggressively commit to a long plan based on assumptions about unobserved states, while others conservatively plan only over what they have observed. Both behaviors emerge implicitly in pre-trained models, whether the LLM outputs a plan directly or generates a PDDL formulation for a classical solver. Aggressive commitment risks costly failures, while conservative commitment risks excessive LLM calls. This choice pits safety against efficiency, a trade-off that has been neither characterized systematically nor made controllable. We investigate aggressive and conservative LLM planners and formalizers on two partially observable domains, where priors are provided as either explicit statistics or common-sense knowledge. Across three LLMs, both strategies reach similar accuracy. Conservative methods achieve fewer failed attempts (safety) at the cost of more API calls (efficiency). Aggressive methods fail more often but replan efficiently only when priors are informative. Interestingly, analysis shows that LLMs treat the provided priors nearly as facts, which risks failure when priors are unreliable. We also explore hybrid strategies with tunable hyperparameters that adjust the balance between safety and efficiency.

title: Sparse Attention for Video Generation Acceleration via Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search
description:
arXiv:2610.21129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.

title: Clinically Interpretable Biological Age Estimation Using CatBoost and SHAP with Continuous and Categorical Features from NHANES
description:
arXiv:2610.20868v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Biological age (BA) captures inter-individual variation in physiological aging beyond chronological age (CA). Although machine-learning models have advanced BA estimation, many rely primarily on continuous laboratory biomarkers, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) dependence plots are typically interpreted visually. We developed a clinically interpretable machine-learning framework for BA estimation using heterogeneous clinical data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2011-March 2020, N = 24,983 adults aged >= 18). A CatBoost regression model incorporated 44 demographic, laboratory, physical examination, and lifestyle predictors to estimate CA, defining model-estimated age as BA. SHAP provided multi-level interpretability. Crucially, building on standard visual inspection, we implemented a prespecified automated procedure directly on SHAP dependence plots to quantify feature-value ranges associated with lowest and highest BA contributions, corresponding adjustment magnitudes, and zero-crossing thresholds. Model-estimated BA strongly correlated with CA in held-out testing data (Pearson r = 0.798, P < 0.001). Population-level SHAP identified blood urea nitrogen, serum glucose, vigorous recreational activity, red cell distribution width, and alanine aminotransferase among the leading predictors, with three categorical variables ranking among the top 25. Automated quantitative SHAP analysis mapped predictor-specific ranges, effect sizes, and inflection points, while waterfall plots enabled individual explanations. By extending qualitative visual interpretation to reproducible quantitative metrics across heterogeneous clinical data, this framework enhances transparency and provides a scalable methodological foundation for biological aging research and precision health.

title: Trajectory Prediction Method for person under WSN with Hierarchical Envelope Adversarial Domain Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2610.21132v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pedestrian trajectory prediction holds significant applications across autonomous driving, intelligent surveillance, and smart cities. However, the complexity and unpredictability of pedestrian interactions make this task a persistent challenge. Current models face two common limitations: 1) Consider only a single type of social coupling. This introduces redundant interactions. More critically, it fails to account for the varying nature of trajectory coupled across different scenarios and between different pedestrians. Consequently, models cannot deeply adapt to diverse scenes. 2) Inadequate domain shift handling. Although very few methods address domain shift, they rely on statistical criterion-based domain distribution alignment. Such approaches exhibit strong dependency on predefined statistical metrics. This leads to significant limitations in complex and dynamic environments. To address these problems, a Hierarchical Envelope Adversarial Domain Adaptation with Loosely-Tightly coupled model (HEADA-LTCTPM) is proposed. First, an envelope sample construction mechanism was proposed. It constructs envelope samples and extends them into graph structures. Secondly, an adversarial domain adaptation module was proposed. This integrates both local and global domain adaptation strategies. It dynamically adapts to diverse coupled relationships across scenarios. These innovations collectively enhance prediction accuracy and robustness. In the experimental section, two representative public datasets were employed for validation and comprehensive comparisons with six relevant baseline algorithms were conducted. Results demonstrate that our model achieves significantly higher accuracy compared to existing methods, with the ADE and FDE metrics reduced by 17.6% and 19.1% respectively. The time overhead meets practical requirements, which verifies the effectiveness of our key innovations.

title: RepoDNA v1.4.1: Preparing Native WinGet Installation and Upgrades for Windows
description:
RepoDNA v1.4.1: Preparing Native WinGet Installation and Upgrades for Windows

Installing developer tools should be straightforward, and keeping them updated should be even easier.

With RepoDNA v1.4.1, I've introduced the packaging and automation needed to prepare RepoDNA for the Windows Package Manager (WinGet) community catalog.

RepoDNA is an open-source, local-first repository intelligence platform that helps developers understand their codebases through architecture analysis, dependency exploration, repository history, and evidence-backed reports.

What's new in v1.4.1?

1. WinGet package manifests

The release introduces manifest generation for two separate Windows packages:

  • SanskarIN.RepoDNA — RepoDNA desktop application.
  • SanskarIN.RepoDNA.CLI — RepoDNA command-line tool.

Both packages are prepared for Windows x64 and ARM64.

2. Preparing native installation and upgrades

Once Microsoft accepts and indexes the packages, Windows users will be able to discover them through WinGet.

For example:

winget source update
winget search --id SanskarIN.RepoDNA --exact

After the community listing becomes available, users will be able to install the package using:

winget install --id SanskarIN.RepoDNA --exact

And when a future package version is published:

winget upgrade --id SanskarIN.RepoDNA --exact

Important: The v1.4.1 release generates the necessary manifest files, but publishing on GitHub does not automatically make a package available in Microsoft's WinGet catalog. The manifests must be submitted, accepted, and indexed.

3. Release integrity and automation

The release process now prepares six YAML manifest files, covering version metadata, locale information, and installer definitions for the two packages.

SHA-256 hashes are calculated from the actual release artifacts rather than entered manually.

An optional GitHub Actions workflow also helps maintainers submit these manifests for Microsoft's review.

4. Regression testing

New tests cover:

  • Generated package hashes.
  • Portable archive executable paths.
  • Supported CPU architectures.
  • Missing input artifacts.
  • Unsupported version strings.

These checks help keep the package generation process consistent as RepoDNA evolves.

Why this matters

RepoDNA already offers desktop, CLI, browser, and WebAssembly-based workflows.

A well-maintained WinGet listing will provide another installation and update path for Windows users.

Future releases will still need their own accepted manifests, but the automation introduced in v1.4.1 makes that process easier to maintain.

Try RepoDNA

GitHub release:
https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.4.1

Live web app:
https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

WinGet documentation:
https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/blob/v1.4.1/docs/winget.md

If you're maintaining a Windows application through WinGet, I'd be interested in hearing how you handle package submissions, installer validation, and upgrade testing.

Thanks for following RepoDNA's development! 🧬

title: The new business case for design systems
description: Design systems have evolved from static libraries to key drivers of business revenue, customer loyalty, and product strategy. Here’s what you need to know about how to track and communicate the value of your design system, based on new research from the Design Executive Council (DXC).

title: Emotion Is Not External Knowledge: Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.21347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model's own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.

title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
description:
arXiv:2610.21170v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with DeepSeek V3.2 and from 50 to 53 with Kimi K2.7 Code. On disjoint ALFWorld unseen tasks, success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%. These results support fine-grained execution evidence as a basis for localized, in-place memory-architecture evolution.

title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Improving the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) often relies on post-training with supervision from stronger models. Two common strategies are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which trains on teacher-generated demonstrations, and on-policy distillation (OPD), which provides teacher feedback on trajectories generated by the student itself. While OPD can be more data-efficient by supervising student-generated trajectories, it is unclear how the teacher's supervision at each state affects the student's learned behavior. To study this question, we conduct a controlled comparison of OPD and filtered SFT across data budgets and tasks where the teacher exhibits different levels of reliability, and analyze how these differences shape student accuracy and completion behavior. Across the two tasks, we find that OPD is effective only when the teacher remains reliable on student-generated trajectories. On ChartQA, where the teacher completes 99% of its solutions, OPD trained on only 10% of the data comes within 1.4 accuracy points of full-data SFT. In contrast, on Geometry3K, where the teacher fails to complete 22% of its solutions, OPD underperforms SFT by 7.9 points, with most of the gap explained by incomplete responses. More strikingly, starting OPD from an SFT student reduces its completion rate from 76% to 62%, effectively erasing the completion behavior learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT's advantage. These results show that on-policy supervision can transfer not only teacher knowledge but also persistent failure modes on student-visited states. Code is available at https://github.com/ffy208/opd-inherits-teacher-vlm.

title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation
description:
arXiv:2610.21114v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.

title: Spectral Indistinguishability and Learning-Curve Identifiability in Quadratic Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.20678v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study what spectral summaries and scalar learning curves reveal about centered quadratic networks. We construct analytic positive input densities with exactly Gaussian one- and two-coordinate marginals. Their complete fourth-moment operators are intertwined by an orthogonal map fixing the entire diagonal teacher algebra, so the corresponding anchored spectral measures agree. For selected common teachers with a nonzero cycle invariant, their factorized loss curves differ because the map does not preserve matrix multiplication. Cycle length $r$, which can be arbitrarily large, gives $O(\varepsilon^r)$ contrast uniformly in training time for each fixed construction. For a supplied pair, noisy scalar loss queries require order $\varepsilon^{-2r}$ observations, while bounded initialization interventions with scalar gradient readouts require order $\varepsilon^{-2}$. A shared-input score, equal to a paired-gradient difference, attains the optimal input-sample exponent without knowing the teacher. An explicit family of diverging auxiliary teacher scales instead admits a nonzero finite limiting contrast at coupling $1/\log L$. Conversely, for Gaussian inputs and a rationally independent teacher spectrum, one exact scalar loss curve identifies the initial predictor up to sign conjugation. Within this rationally independent class, with nonzero diagonal inverse-state error in every coordinate and calibrated time and loss scales, it also identifies the unknown teacher spectrum and active dimension, modulo simultaneous rotations. For fixed dimension and distinct unordered teacher sums, dimension-minimal exact observations give generic joint local recovery. Finite exact global bounds hold for a known teacher and, on the active class, under a blind dimension cap. Exact certificates and full-weight replay verify the construction; numerical inverse checks reveal severe ill-conditioning.

title: Optimal Hydra: Model Heterogeneous Federated Learning for LLMs using Data-Informed Hydra-Nets
description:
arXiv:2610.20753v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on vast amounts of data have demonstrated impressive performance over a range of tasks, but future performance gains will require increasing amounts of data and compute. Federated Learning (FL) facilitates training on decentralized private data, but client resource limitations can make training impractical, particularly as model sizes continue to expand. These resource constraints make the assumption of a shared server-client architecture impractical. Model heterogeneous FL offers a promising alternative by adapting model size to client capabilities; however, previous work is limited to the pre-training setting, and conclusions on sub-network selection do not necessarily hold for fine-tuning. Furthermore, prior approaches create client sub-networks without considering their unique data distributions, thereby overlooking the opportunity to tailor sub-network architecture to local data. Motivated by evidence that attention heads exhibit task dependency within layer defined feature spaces, we propose Optimal Hydra, a transformer based heterogeneous FL framework for fine-tuning that combines global layer selection with client specific attention head selection, aligned with local data distributions. Optimal Hydra makes explicit use of client data to produce client-specific sub-networks we call Hydra-nets. To our knowledge, this is the first model heterogeneous FL approach tailored to LLM fine-tuning. Experiments on three datasets show significant improvements over baseline methods while also reducing local resource demands.

title: Feature Elicitation for SAE Steering of Deceptive Behaviour in Small LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.20638v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Research on deceptive alignment is becoming increasingly urgent as frontier-model capabilities advance and their risk of causing catastrophic harm increases. Alignment faking is a form of deceptive alignment, with the compliance gap serving as a key behavioural indicator. This behaviour remains understudied in small LLMs and prior mechanistic interventions have not been shown to mitigate the compliance gap. We test whether steering SAE (sparse autoencoders) features associated with deontological ethics can mitigate this behaviour. We use a novel bag-of-words feature elicitation pipeline for SAE steering to identify what we construe as concept-level steering directions. Our approach reduced the compliance gap to non-significance in Gemma-3-27B-IT, whereas the tested configurations were not effective in LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct. Analysis of scratchpad traces also revealed deceptive model behaviour which we term deceptive defanging: deliberately degrading the aligned functionality of a response (in this case harmfulness) while preserving the appearance of alignment (in this case helpful compliance with the harmful request), sometimes conditioned on tier, training, or RLHF consequences. These findings provide, to our knowledge, the first evidence that a mechanistic activation-level intervention can mitigate the compliance gap in an alignment faking setup. They also identify a form of deceptive behaviour that may broaden our understanding of the different forms of deceptive behaviour in LLMs.

title: GBase Database Pre-Deployment Checklist: 4 Essential Environment Checks
description:
Before installing GBase Database (GBase 8s), take a few minutes to validate the target Linux environment. Missing dependencies, insufficient disk space, network configuration issues, and incorrect locale settings can all complicate database deployment.

A structured GBase Database pre-installation checklist helps identify these issues before they become troubleshooting sessions.

1. Check Network and Security Settings

Start by checking the firewall, SELinux status, and hostname resolution:

# Check firewall status
systemctl status firewalld

# Check SELinux mode
getenforce

# Review hostname and hosts configuration
hostname
cat /etc/hosts
getent hosts "$(hostname)"

Verify that the required database ports are accessible and hostname resolution works correctly.

Don't automatically disable the firewall or SELinux. Configure the necessary network rules and security policies according to your GBase 8s version and deployment requirements. If troubleshooting requires a temporary security-policy change, follow your organization's security procedures.

2. Verify System Resources

Insufficient temporary disk space or memory can interrupt installation or complicate instance initialization.

# Check temporary directory space
df -h /tmp

# Check available memory
free -h

# Check CPU architecture and core count
uname -m
nproc

# Check available inodes
df -i /tmp

Compare the results against the hardware and operating system requirements for your target GBase Database release. Don't rely on a single resource threshold for every deployment.

3. Validate System Dependencies

Check required libraries and packages before running the installer.

On RPM-based Linux systems, rpm -q can verify whether a specified package is installed. Use the dependency list documented for your particular GBase 8s version and operating system.

Remember that package names vary across Linux distributions, and package presence alone doesn't guarantee library compatibility.

4. Confirm Character Set and Locale

Character-set planning is especially important when migrating existing applications or data.

Check the current locale:

locale
locale -a

Confirm the required database and client locale settings before initialization. Values such as zh_CN.utf8 and en_US.utf8 are examples; select settings supported by the target operating system and compatible with your application requirements.

Changing character-set-related settings after deployment may require substantial migration or reconfiguration work, depending on what needs to change.

Final Takeaway

A reliable GBase Database deployment starts with four checks: network and security, system resources, dependencies, and character-set planning.

For teams working on Xinchuang (China's IT application innovation) migrations, incorporating these checks into deployment documentation helps improve consistency, traceability, and installation readiness.

Do you use a standardized pre-deployment checklist for every GBase Database installation?

title: Predicting Live Birth After Fresh Embryo Transfer in IVF/ICSI: Differential ICM/Trophectoderm Morphology Encoding and a Hybrid Attention--Logistic Regression Ensemble
description:
arXiv:2610.21134v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predicting live birth before fresh embryo transfer could support shared decision-making in IVF/ICSI, but routine clinical data are small, heterogeneous, and contain pathway-dependent variables prone to outcome leakage. We aimed to construct a curated single-centre IVF/ICSI dataset and develop a prediction model suited to small tabular clinical data. \textit{Materials and Methods:} We assembled 616 fresh embryo-transfer cycles (251 live birth, 365 non-live birth) with clinical, laboratory, and embryological predictors, and embryo morphology encoded with a novel differential weighting of the inner cell mass and trophectoderm. After KNN imputation, robust scaling, and selection of 50 features, we developed a Hybrid Attention Network (HAN), a learnable feature-attention gate followed by a compact multilayer perceptron, and a HAN + logistic-regression (LR) ensemble with a validation-tuned weight. Models were benchmarked against classical machine learning, TabPFN, and text-serialized language models on a held-out test set; AUC-ROC was the primary metric. \textit{Results:} The HAN + LR ensemble achieved the highest test AUC-ROC (0.710; accuracy 0.710, F1 0.630), ahead of the HAN backbone alone (0.700), logistic regression (0.667), the TabPFN + LR hybrid (0.666), and TabPFN (0.650). Text-serialized language models performed near chance (AUC $\le$ 0.61). The differentially weighted trophectoderm feature ranked highest by consensus importance across models. \textit{Discussion:} A compact attention network combined with a linear model outperformed both components and strong foundation-model baselines on a small clinical cohort. \textit{Conclusion:} The curated dataset and HAN + LR ensemble offer a transparent, reproducible basis for IVF/ICSI live-birth prediction; external validation is the next step.

title: Go Production Debugging: 3 Checks When Published Events Are Never Seen
description:
TL;DR: When a published device-status event never reaches an e-commerce support room and neither side reports an error, compare the event name with the provider's supported type list first. A typo is a contract mismatch: nothing subscribes, nothing fails loudly, and retries faithfully repeat the wrong publish. Fetch the type list during Go service startup, validate every event constant from one module, and refuse readiness when any constant is unknown.

The page arrives as "video support room live, device status absent." The room may be healthy, its scoped client token may be valid, and other traffic may still flow. The immediate action is narrow: stop retrying the suspect event, inspect the exact emitted name, and test it against supported types. This is an SLO problem because successful publish attempts are an input metric, while visible status transitions are the user outcome.

How should you debug published events that are never seen?

Silent non-delivery is the signature. Suppose checkout support opens a video room so an agent can help diagnose a customer's payment terminal. The backend intends to emit device.status.changed, but the publisher contains a one-character misspelling. No subscriber matches it, and no error has to appear. A dashboard built around HTTP success can remain green while the customer and agent stare at stale state.

The first useful signal should have fired before that page: an invariant check during deployment or process startup. Count attempted publishes for capacity planning, but do not confuse that count with delivery. The operational objective is closer to "a valid device transition becomes observable by the authorized room client"; the event-name contract is one dependency of that objective, alongside token scope, connection state, and the client handler.

This distinction also keeps token debugging disciplined. A scoped token should grant only the room and actions the client needs. Broadening client trust to make a missing event appear is the wrong experiment when the name itself is invalid. Validate the server-side event vocabulary first, then inspect token scope if a known type still does not arrive.

Names first.

Make the vocabulary a startup dependency

Keep event constants in one Go package. Exhaustiveness matters more than cleverness: scattered literals make it impossible to know whether startup validation covered every publisher. This program reads the API base from configuration, calls the verified event-type route, accepts JSON without assuming an undocumented field name, and exits before readiness if a configured name is absent. The discovery call is public, so the program does not send a credential.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var applicationEvents = []string{
    "device.status.changed",
    "support.room.joined",
}

func collectStrings(v any, out map[string]struct{}) {
    switch x := v.(type) {
    case string:
        out[x] = struct{}{}
    case []any:
        for _, item := range x {
            collectStrings(item, out)
        }
    case map[string]any:
        for _, item := range x {
            collectStrings(item, out)
        }
    }
}

func supportedTypes(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, baseURL string) (map[string]struct{}, error) {
    url := strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/") + "/realtime/event/types"
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("event type discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
    }

    var document any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &document); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("decode event types: %w", err)
    }
    types := make(map[string]struct{})
    collectStrings(document, types)
    if len(types) == 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("event type discovery returned no strings")
    }
    return types, nil
}

func main() {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    types, err := supportedTypes(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 6 * time.Second}, baseURL)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    var unknown []string
    for _, name := range applicationEvents {
        if _, ok := types[name]; !ok {
            unknown = append(unknown, name)
        }
    }
    if len(unknown) != 0 {
        sort.Strings(unknown)
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "unsupported realtime event constants: %v\n", unknown)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The parser deliberately treats discovery as a set-membership source instead of binding the application to an unverified response field. In production I would cap startup retries and leave the instance unready, because accepting traffic with an unchecked vocabulary exchanges a visible deployment failure for silent customer impact. Five seconds is an example timeout, not a latency claim or universal setting; set it from the deployment budget and measurements in your environment.

One trap deserves emphasis. Do not "fix" a failed assertion by deleting the constant from applicationEvents. The list must be the single source imported by every publisher, otherwise the check becomes theater. A code-generation step can enforce that relationship in a large repository, but a plain Go package is enough for a small service.

Fail closed.

Trace the alert backward, then change the signal

Start at the page and walk toward the earliest discriminating observation. The on-call sees a live video room, an authorized client, and a missing device update. A publish-success counter says only that a request was accepted; it cannot prove that a subscriber registered the same string. The next check is the emitted name against the supported set. If the name is absent, stop there. The instrumentation change has two layers: startup validation blocks new bad binaries, while runtime telemetry compares accepted device transitions with client-observed transitions over the service's chosen window, partitioned by event type but not by unbounded room or customer identifiers. Alert on sustained outcome loss, and keep the raw startup mismatch as a deployment event that points directly to the bad constant. This catches both vocabulary mistakes and later delivery failures without pretending they share a cause. Capacity planning enters sooner than teams expect because event type is a bounded label and room ID is not; a per-room metric can turn one incident into a monitoring-cardinality incident, raising query cost and weakening the alert needed during a peak support period. Keep room-level correlation in structured logs keyed by a request identifier, and reserve metrics for bounded dimensions. This is a deliberate trade-off: metrics answer whether the SLO is at risk, while logs answer which room needs inspection.

The useful page names the failed outcome and the event type, not merely the publish operation. It should send the responder to the contract diff first. Only after the type is known should the investigation fan out to room membership, scoped-token authorization, client connection state, and handler registration.

Where should offline delivery meet the video room?

A live socket is not durable storage. If the customer briefly loses connectivity while the device changes state, publishing once and hoping the browser is present turns a recoverable disconnect into stale support data. A queue should hold the notification until a worker can attempt delivery; the video-room client receives only the scoped realtime event it is authorized to see. Consumer-side idempotency remains mandatory for an at-least-once standard queue, so the business transition needs a stable identifier even when transport attempts repeat.

Infrai is one plausible combined choice because realtime/RTC and jobs/queues sit behind one REST API, one key, and one bill; fewer credential rotations and invoices are useful to a small platform team, while public self-describing discovery supports the startup assertion above. The trade-off is concentration: one vendor becomes the trust and billing boundary for both durable handoff and live delivery. It is not a good fit when policy requires separate providers or the team wants to replace queue and realtime layers independently.

The platform discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules. That breadth can reduce credential sprawl, but it makes provider review more consequential, not less.

The verified route set used here does not specify a queue enqueue operation or its request schema, so a queue-to-socket request sample would require invented fields. The safe implementation boundary is a durable worker that reads the business transition, checks its idempotency key, and publishes a supported realtime type; generate its exact queue path and payload from live discovery before shipping.

With Pusher plus Amazon SQS, the equivalent stack requires two service signups, two credential sets, two billing relationships, and glue mapping an SQS delivery to a Pusher channel event while handling retries and deduplication. That separation can be desirable: IAM can be narrower, and either side can be replaced without migrating the other. It also increases on-call load.

Option Token scope and client trust Durable handoff Best fit Main limitation
Infrai realtime/RTC plus jobs/queues Backend issues scoped client access; one backend key spans both groups Combined service surface; consumers still need idempotency Small platform teams accepting a unified boundary Provider concentration
Pusher Channels plus Amazon SQS Pusher channel authorization is separate from AWS IAM SQS buffers; application glue delivers AWS teams wanting replaceable components Two signups, credential sets, and bills
Ably plus an external queue Token capabilities constrain client operations Separate queue and worker required Teams prioritizing realtime-specific controls Integration remains yours
PubNub plus an external queue PubNub access controls govern messaging clients Separate queue and worker required Teams wanting a managed pub/sub product Durable workflow spans products
Socket.IO plus a managed queue Application owns authentication and authorization Chosen queue feeds an application worker Teams wanting protocol and hosting control Highest build and on-call ownership

These products are not interchangeable merely because each can appear in the same diagram. Pusher, Ably, and PubNub center managed realtime messaging; Socket.IO gives more application control; the AWS pairing gives explicit infrastructure components. Choose according to the trust boundary the team can explain during review and the systems it can operate at 03:00, not the shortest initial setup.

Pick the boundary deliberately.

Set the threshold with the false-positive budget in view

The final risk is an alert that fires whenever one client disconnects normally. A zero-tolerance ratio over a tiny window will page on ordinary mobile churn; a wide aggregate window may conceal a typo affecting one event type. Segment by the bounded event vocabulary, require enough traffic to make the comparison meaningful, and page only when the sustained gap threatens the customer-facing SLO. Record lower-volume mismatches for investigation without waking someone.

There is no universal number in the available evidence. Derive the window and threshold from observed event volume, reconnect behavior, and the error budget for the support workflow. Then test the alert by introducing an unsupported constant in a non-production contract test: startup should fail, no customer token should be broadened, and no live publish should be necessary.

That closes the trace. The page becomes actionable because the earlier signal identifies a vocabulary mismatch, the startup gate prevents recurrence, and the runtime outcome metric remains available for failures that are not spelling mistakes. The cost of setting the threshold too low is alert fatigue and wasted on-call capacity; the cost of setting it too high is a customer discovering stale status first. Treat both as reliability costs.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • Pusher Channels, authenticating users: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/server_api/authenticating-users/
  • Amazon SQS, delivery semantics: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html
  • Ably, token authentication: https://ably.com/docs/auth/token
  • PubNub, access manager: https://www.pubnub.com/docs/general/security/access-control
  • Socket.IO, delivery guarantees: https://socket.io/docs/v4/delivery-guarantees

title: Stable Percentage Rollout Feature Flags — User Hashing for Gradual Backend Releases
description:
A Node.js backend using percentage rollout feature flags needs stable user hashing for a gradual release; otherwise, the same fintech account can switch paths between scheduled imports. When the page says the import completed but the ledger has received no new rows for 47 minutes, the safest response is to set the new importer’s rollout to zero, leave every account on the old path, and investigate without changing the bucket rule.

TL;DR: keep the percentage in the flag service, but decide membership in the backend with a documented deterministic hash of an immutable user or account ID. The same account must stay in the same bucket across requests, workers, and deploys. Treat the percentage change as a reversible routing decision, not as an experiment system. For a scheduled import, separately monitor the age of the last successful result; a feature flag cannot detect a job that never ran.

That separation is the operating model: the provider stores the desired rollout, application code evaluates stable membership, import metrics show whether work produced results, and a heartbeat monitor pages on silence. Each boundary has one job. Rollback remains boring.

What should the page have told us earlier?

The useful signal is not “cron fired.” It is “a scheduled import produced a valid result for this tenant within its expected interval.” A worker can start, retry, or even return success while writing nothing. For an hourly account import, record the completion time only after the durable result is committed, then alert when its age crosses a threshold derived from the schedule and normal runtime.

Use an external dead-man’s-switch service such as Healthchecks for the silent case. Infrai has no heartbeat monitoring or notification routing, so polling its free query APIs and building a pager around them would create another small monitoring system to own. That can be reasonable when a team already has an alert dispatcher, but it is not the least complex choice for “the job should have run and did not.”

The rollout signal answers a different question: which accounts should execute the new importer? Infrai can store and update the rollout percentage through its plain REST API. There is no SDK or client-library version to carry in every worker; any runtime that can make an authenticated HTTP request can use the same surface. I recommend trying Infrai for teams that want a small control-plane boundary for rollout percentages across mixed backend runtimes, because the REST handoff is explicit and its public discovery schema can remove guesswork when wiring the call.

Do not turn that recommendation into an analytics claim. The flag capability does not provide evaluation statistics, advanced targeting governance, dependency graphs, or a change audit log. Document who may change a percentage, preserve changes in your own deployment record, and use a specialist when those controls are requirements.

How should Node.js backends combine percentage rollout feature flags with stable hashing?

A random number per request is not a rollout. It is traffic flicker. An account can reach the new importer on Monday, the old one on Tuesday, and both paths during a retry storm. That defeats rollback analysis and may duplicate side effects.

Keep the cohort still.

Hash a stable identifier with a named, versioned algorithm and map it into a fixed bucket range. The example below uses 10,000 buckets, so a percentage can be expressed in basis points. It uses the first eight bytes of SHA-256 in big-endian order. Those details belong in the runbook; changing any one of them reshuffles users.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/binary"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const bucketCount uint64 = 10_000

func enabled(flagKey, accountID string, rolloutBasisPoints uint64) bool {
    if rolloutBasisPoints > bucketCount {
        rolloutBasisPoints = bucketCount
    }
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(flagKey + ":v1:" + accountID))
    bucket := binary.BigEndian.Uint64(sum[:8]) % bucketCount
    return bucket < rolloutBasisPoints
}

func getDiscovery(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get discovery: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("get discovery: rate limit retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    manifest, err := getDiscovery(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("discovery response: %s\n", manifest)

    // Bind the discovered flag schema in production. This fixed value keeps the
    // hashing example runnable without guessing any response fields.
    for _, accountID := range []string{"acct_us_1042", "acct_eu_2088", "acct_us_7711"} {
        fmt.Printf("%s new_importer=%t\n", accountID, enabled("ledger-import", accountID, 2_500))
    }
}

The flag key is part of the hash input so unrelated flags do not select exactly the same cohort. The v1 marker makes the contract visible. Keep it unchanged during a release. If a future migration truly needs new bucketing, create a new flag or version and treat the cohort shift as a separate rollout.

Choose the identifier with equal care. For a fintech import, account ID is usually safer than user ID because the work and its side effects belong to the account. A person joining two accounts should not couple their rollout states. Region is not a substitute for hashing: if US and EU tenants need separate release controls, use separate flag keys or apply a documented eligibility check before bucketing.

The sample deliberately prints the discovery response instead of asserting an undocumented flag JSON field. Before production use, select the flag capability from that manifest, bind its documented response schema to a typed structure, validate the resulting percentage as an integer from 0 through 10,000, and pass it to enabled. The public discovery surface needs no key and describes request and response schemas. Authenticated flag calls use Authorization: Bearer <key>, with the key read from an environment variable rather than stored in source. Every documented capability also includes runnable examples in 10 languages, so the Node.js service and Go worker can implement the same boundary without sharing a vendor SDK.

The application flow is short. Read the rollout percentage from the flag system, validate it, evaluate locally, and attach the flag key, bucket algorithm version, and chosen path to the import’s structured result. Cache policy must match the rollback objective. If workers poll every 60 seconds, the operational promise is “rollout changes converge in roughly one polling interval,” not “rollback is immediate.” Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key; for a team already using adjacent backend capabilities, that means this flag poller does not require another credential distribution path or another client dependency.

One trap deserves a runbook line: do not recompute membership from email, mutable customer labels, process-local hash functions, or map iteration. A language upgrade or profile edit can otherwise move accounts with no percentage change.

Trace the page back to the control boundary

When the no-results page fires, the on-call needs enough context to choose a safe first action. Put the account ID, expected schedule, last successful result time, current importer path, flag key, and bucket version in the alert or its linked dashboard. Avoid customer data in those labels. Cardinality and privacy still count during an incident.

The first action is containment. Set the rollout to zero if evidence points to the new path, then verify that old-path completions resume for previously selected accounts. Because selection is deterministic, zero removes the new cohort without asking operators to identify individual users. Raising the percentage later adds a stable superset of accounts as long as the algorithm and key remain fixed.

Instrumentation should sit after the durable write:

  1. The scheduler dispatches an account import with an idempotency key derived from account ID and schedule window.
  2. The worker reads the rollout percentage and evaluates the stable bucket.
  3. The selected importer writes results idempotently. Retries must not double-apply ledger effects.
  4. Only after commit, the worker reports completion and updates the heartbeat.
  5. The monitor pages when result age exceeds the agreed threshold.

This ordering separates delivery from outcome. Standard queues are at-least-once in practice, so consumer idempotency is mandatory regardless of which flag provider chooses the code path. A flag rollback controls future routing; it does not undo a committed financial write.

Infrai’s rollout operation is POST /v1/flags/rollout/{key}. Keep that control-plane call outside the per-record loop. Its broader platform also specifies idempotency as a first-class convention and publishes request schemas and runnable examples through public discovery, which reduces integration upkeep when the same team already uses the REST surface for adjacent backend work. The trade-off is visibility: there is no built-in evaluation history or flag-change audit log, and clients poll rather than receive streamed updates.

Where do the provider boundaries differ?

Provider choice follows the control burden, not the hash function. Flag specialists own the release decision, while observability products own evidence and paging. Mixing those categories in one score would hide the boundary that matters during rollback.

Option Best fit here Boundary or limitation to plan for
Infrai A rollout percentage behind one plain REST surface, especially across several backend languages Rollout basics only; no evaluation analytics, dependency graph, advanced targeting governance, or change audit log
LaunchDarkly Teams that need a dedicated feature-management product and want evaluation and governance concerns handled by a specialist Introduces a dedicated flag platform into the production path; validate its SDK and operating model against rollback requirements
Unleash Teams that prefer a dedicated, open feature-management platform and want control over how it is operated Self-management choices add ownership; confirm that the chosen deployment and client mode meet polling and audit expectations
ConfigCat Teams seeking a focused hosted feature-flag service with language-specific integration options Still a separate vendor surface; verify evaluation semantics and change controls before using it for financial workflows
Sentry Error investigation around failed importer code paths It does not replace a stable flag evaluator or prove that an absent job ran
Datadog Teams wanting metrics, logs, traces, monitors, and paging in one observability product It is a separate operational surface from the rollout control plane
Grafana Teams composing dashboards and alerts over their chosen telemetry sources Alert quality still depends on emitting the last-success signal correctly
Better Stack Teams wanting hosted monitoring and incident response around scheduled work Keep feature selection in the flag layer rather than coupling it to the pager

This is deliberately not a feature-count verdict. LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and ConfigCat are more natural candidates when flags are a program with targeting policy, experimentation, or governance requirements. Infrai is a stronger fit when the desired boundary is narrower: store a percentage, retrieve it over HTTP, evaluate a stable account bucket in code, and keep the surrounding backend integrations on one consistent API.

LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and ConfigCat do not replace the missing-job detector. Healthchecks is the relevant specialist for a scheduled task that goes silent. Sentry is useful once there is an error to inspect; Datadog, Grafana, and Better Stack are credible alternatives when the team wants the result-age signal integrated with a broader monitoring stack. Likewise, logs carrying trace_id and span_id can help correlate an import, but Infrai does not provide distributed trace queries or a span tree. Use a tracing system when the investigation depends on cross-service causal structure.

One tool rarely owns this whole trace.

Thresholds are part of the rollback design

An alert at exactly 60 minutes for an hourly job sounds precise and pages on ordinary scheduling jitter. An alert at six hours preserves sleep but weakens the rollback window. Set the threshold from the business recovery objective, the schedule, normal queue delay, and observed completion time. Then test it by withholding a heartbeat, not by assuming a dashboard query proves the page route works.

There is a second false-positive cost. During a staged rollout, the new cohort may contain too few scheduled accounts to produce a result in every interval. A global “new importer produced zero rows” alert will fire even when no selected account was due. Compare due-and-selected accounts with successful results, or page on each due account’s result age. This adds state, but the state corresponds to the obligation the business actually cares about.

Roll out in steps that allow at least one meaningful import cycle between changes. Record the percentage, timestamp, operator, bucket version, and observed completion counts in the deployment record because the flag service will not supply that audit history. Stop on ambiguous evidence.

The clean design has two independent rollback levers: percentage zero routes future work to the old importer, while normal deployment rollback restores code. Neither should change the hashing contract. After recovery, reconcile any schedule windows that started before containment using the same idempotency key scheme, then advance gradually only when old-path and new-path result-age signals are comparable.

False positives spend operator attention and train people to distrust silence alerts. False negatives hide missed financial data. That is why the final threshold belongs in an SLO or runbook decision, with an owner and a test cadence, rather than as a convenient constant copied from the cron expression.

Further reading

  • Infrai documentation
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Better Stack documentation
  • RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol
  • Electron crashReporter documentation

If this narrow control-plane boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the live rollout schema before wiring the poller.

title: Imperfect Is Perfect: Learned Column Prefilling for Branch-Price-and-Cut
description:
arXiv:2610.21001v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Column generation folklore warns that initial columns hurt: a warm start may bias the dual and slow the root of branch-price-and-cut. We show the opposite once the columns are imperfect in the right way. Preloading the support of the optimal root LP, the best columns one could know in advance, fails to finish on half of our hardest instances; a pool of ordinary routes that need not belong to any optimal solution, held outside the master and priced at the current smoothed dual, speeds the root up. Because the columns need not be optimal, producing them becomes a learning task: a neural edge scorer guides a constructive generator that builds the pool in seconds. A second network predicts the initial center of Wentges smoothing from the instance file, and with it the direction of the smoothed pricing queries; the solver's own updates run unchanged. With prefill and center in place, exact pricing dominates root pricing time, so we rebuild bucket-graph labeling around its dominance test for the GPU and certify on the CPU. Inside RouteOpt, the state-of-the-art exact solver for capacitated vehicle routing, the pipeline reaches the same certified root bound in 13.2% of vanilla RouteOpt's root pricing time over 95 instances with 300 to 1000 customers, prefill alone in 26.1%, and 17.5 times faster in the best case. In an exact branch-price-and-cut solver for unrelated parallel machine scheduling, prefill with smoothing and the learned center certifies all 25 benchmark instances, 12 times faster than the solver's own column generation, which certifies 20 of them.

title: CoViG: Coarsened Vision GNN for Image Classification
description:
arXiv:2610.21321v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although Graph Neural Networks are widely used in various domains, they remained mostly unexplored in computer vision. Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers were leading the field, until the quite recent introduction of Vision Graphs (ViG) that treat images as a set of nodes and apply graph convolution on their k-NN graphs. ViGs show impressive accuracy on image classification but their computational cost remains relatively high. Inspired by optimization methods for GNNs, we present CoViG, a novel approach combining graph coarsening and ViGs. Our method introduces an additional MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks. By simplifying the intermediate graphs and thus decreasing the number of nodes of specific blocks, our approach considerably reduces the computational cost of ViG during inference. We evaluated our approach on ImageNet with several ViG architectures, and we obtained accuracies equivalent to the original ViG models with only about 51\% of FLOPs.
