title: Vercel Ship 2026 recap
description:
For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. The companies that win the next decade will build on infrastructure designed for agents from the start, and thousands of people gathered across London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco to do just that at Vercel Ship 2026.

Agentic infrastructure

Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself.

Agentic infrastructure has three parts:

  • Vercel is where coding agents deploy software. When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform.

  • Vercel is where you build and deploy your own agents. We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale.

  • Vercel itself is automated by agents. Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts.

Vercel exists to put the full force of agentic infrastructure behind you, so that you, your agents, and your software can deploy and run faster than ever.

Vercel is for shipping full-stack apps and agents

In the next keynote, Malte Ubl (CTO, Vercel) showed how frontends, APIs, backend services, containers, MCP servers, and background workers can all run on Vercel, with support for custom runtimes and system dependencies.

He then announced that Python is now generally available on Vercel. Run FastAPI, Flask, or Django with standard CPython, PyPI dependencies, uv, and pyproject.toml. With Vercel Services, your frontend and backend deploy together, with previews of the full app.

Malte also introduced Vercel Daemons, now in public beta, for continuously running background workers. Deploy your code or container image, set the number of instances, and Vercel keeps them running and replaces them if they fail. Bring Celery, Dramatiq, Temporal workers, or your existing worker processes.

Vercel is for shipping agents

Tomo Occhino (CPO, Vercel) walked through the Agent Stack and its latest updates. The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production.

  • eve, our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard.

  • Vercel Connect is generally available, with more than 1,000 connectors. And MCP Events, now in public beta, lets agents respond to events from MCP servers. Connect handles subscriptions, renewals, and secure delivery.

  • AI Gateway now lets you set budgets for API keys, projects, individuals, and teams. You can also choose US-only inference to keep model processing in the United States, or enable Zero Data Retention so providers don’t retain your prompts or responses. He also introduced Vercel Token Pass, now in early access for Pro teams. Get $80 in GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 token credit for $30/month, with more models coming soon.

  • Vercel Drives, now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace.

Vercel is for shipping in the enterprise

Jeanne Grosser (COO, Vercel) focused on what happens when everyone in a company can build. Engineers, marketers, analysts, and sellers need a common place to deploy, with controls over who can ship, who can access an app, which systems agents can use, and how much they can spend. Company building is now agent building.

Vercel for Enterprise brings those controls together, with two additions announced:

  • Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS is now generally available. Your application functions run in your own AWS account, within your security and network boundaries.

  • Enterprise-Managed Authorization for Vercel Connect launched in public beta. With supported services and your identity provider configured, agents can act on employees’ behalf without asking each person to authorize every connection separately.

Ship 2026 in San Francisco

The rest of Ship SF brought more than 2,700 developers, founders, and technical leaders to the Palace of Fine Arts for talks, workshops, startup studio sessions, and agent labs.

Ship day sessions

  • Assaf Elovic from Ora showed how his team tests whether websites work for agents by sending real agents to sign up, integrate, and pay, then tracing every step. Ora built that fleet on eve and used Is-Agentic to score a live site.

  • Katelyn Lesse from Anthropic covered the work that starts after an agent is running: keeping it fast and improving its performance across thousands of production sessions with Claude Managed Agents on Vercel.

  • Prashant Ratanchandani from Meta Superintelligence Labs joined Tomo to discuss building products including Muse on Vercel.

  • Matt Lewis from Vercel and Mala Neti from Slack explained how we built v, our internal agent, around Vercel’s own data and working practices. Connect and Passport secure its access, and Slack gives employees a place to use it where their work already happens.

  • Max Peters from Adapta broke down the router behind Brazil’s largest generative AI platform. Built on AI Gateway, it serves 168 models through one integration, selects a model in under 200 milliseconds, and handles more than three million requests a day with automatic failover and per-user budgets.

  • Sarah Sachs from Notion and Malte Ubl discussed how AI is changing the software teams build and the context agents need to do useful work.

  • Olawale Oladehin from AWS walked through production patterns for agents on AWS and Vercel, from self-correcting agents to multi-agent orchestration, and how BYOC lets teams run application functions within their own AWS environment.

  • Philip Miseldine and Sophia Levens from SAP showed how SAP is using v0, eve, and json-render to build generative interfaces, with a focus on consistent design and government requirements.

  • Aaron Brown and Arty Vohmincevs from Mercor explained how hundreds of employees build internal tools without losing control of access or spending. Apps inherit a managed identity layer, while AI Gateway gives the team visibility into model usage and budgets.

  • Yury Izrailevsky from ClickHouse traced the company’s path from an open-source analytics database to a platform spanning observability, AI engineering, and managed Postgres. His focus was how open source earns developer trust and helps infrastructure expand into new workloads.

Panel: Fast AI

Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, the company behind Jev, and Andrew Feldman, founder and CEO of Cerebras, joined Vercel for a discussion on model reliability, latency, and cost. The panel brought together the model and hardware sides of fast inference, from specialized models to wafer-scale chips.

Closing fireside with Tobi Lütke

Guillermo sat down with Tobi Lütke, CEO of Shopify, for "The Third Customer," a conversation about building for a world where agents research, compare, and buy products on people’s behalf.

Guillermo Rauch: What excites you about agentic commerce?

Tobi Lütke: It’s early, but the opportunity goes beyond handling purchases people already make. Think about project-based commerce: planning Halloween decorations for your house, or a 3D-printing project with your kids, then ordering everything to arrive before the weekend. Agents can help people follow through on things they otherwise wouldn’t have had time to do.

Guillermo Rauch: Where does that leave traditional storefronts?

Tobi Lütke: There’s still room for exceptional shopping experiences. A distinctive, thoughtful storefront can grow, just as a well-executed boutique can. The businesses that will struggle are the ones offering an undifferentiated experience. Quality and originality still matter.

Guillermo Rauch: How is AI changing engineering at Shopify?

Tobi Lütke: We now think of ourselves as verification engineers, building harnesses and acceptance tests that make changes verifiable. We’re rewriting our storefront renderer from Ruby to Rust, where we can compare the output byte for byte before switching over. We also celebrate simplification and code deletion. At a company hackathon, our internal Slack agent, River, topped the code-deletion leaderboard by a wide margin.

Guillermo Rauch: What should developers in this room go build?

Tobi Lütke: Explore the catalog APIs. They give you access to products from Shopify merchants, so you can build new commerce experiences without first recruiting both sides of a marketplace. Product discovery, recommendations, and curation are real business opportunities. People will pay for tools that help them find what they need.

Ship week San Francisco

Fast Forward hackathon

The day before Ship, Vercel and Meta hosted Fast Forward, with support from Shopify and Neon Postgres. Builders worked across three tracks: agents that keep working after you step away, multimodal apps, and immersive VR experiences.

Founder dinners, executive conversations, and Partner Day

Founders, partners, and enterprise leaders gathered throughout the week for dinners, Partner Day, and conversations on building with AI. The executive program focused on what happens when anyone with an idea can build, and how do you govern what ships.

Ship 2026 in London

Ship day keynotes

  • Tomo introduced the Agent Stack, bringing model access, durable execution, sandboxed compute, and messaging together for production agents.

  • Hedi launched Vercel Connect in public preview, giving agents scoped access to external tools and data without storing long-lived provider credentials in environment variables.

  • Shar demoed eve, our open-source agent framework. Each agent lives in a directory, with instructions in Markdown and tools in TypeScript. Durable execution, approvals, subagents, and evals are already wired in.

  • Jeanne introduced Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents, including Vercel Passport in public beta for protecting internal apps with your identity provider, and Bring Your Own Cloud on AWS in private beta.

Ship week London

Our first Ship outside the U.S. ran five days of events leading into the keynote, and an ice cream truck spent the week working its way across the city.

Built in London hackathon

Two hundred builders shipped agents on Codex and Vercel in a hackathon with OpenAI. Three projects stood out. Stella hunts down unclaimed grants for London SMBs, Oscar is a co-pilot that sharpens your prompts before you send them to a model, and Phone Jail blocks distractions and roasts you when you reach for your phone anyway.

Media, Founder, VC, and CTO dinners

Reporters traded story ideas over a media dinner. Twelve founders talked through the future of AI in EMEA at a VC dinner. And a dozen CTOs from teams including Marks & Spencer and Currys went off the record on what it takes to build and scale agents in the enterprise.

Day Zero builder night

Day Zero, the day before the keynote, turned into a 400-person builder night. Enterprise teams Mentimeter, Okta, and MongoDB joined Vercel in a packed room alongside partners DeepMind, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

AI Social Club

A 160-deep waitlist formed for Malte's talk A New Stack for a New Era of Software, followed by Guillermo and Deliveroo's Will Shu's chat on building the agentic enterprise.

Ship day sessions

  • André Balleyguier from Anthropic showed Claude Managed Agents on Vercel, where Anthropic hosts the agent loop while every command the agent runs executes inside a Vercel Sandbox you own, keeping its filesystem, processes, and network egress in your environment.

  • Tomas Jansson from Currys/Elkjøp showed how his team evolved a Nordic retailer's ecommerce stack from storefronts toward shopping agents in three phases, anchored by a Next.js migration that cut time to first byte by 40%. The end state is one where customer intent replaces navigation.

  • Matan Kushner from Vercel broke down how Vertex, Vercel's support agent, now automates 91% of support tickets and saves 5,000 engineer-hours a month without degrading as its context grows.

  • Jas Sagoo and Sam Bellen from Auth0 made the case that getting an agent into production depends more on identity than on model quality. They demoed four standards-based identity patterns on the Vercel AI SDK, Token Vault, CIBA approvals, agents as first-class principals, and on-behalf-of delegation, so every action is scoped and traces back to a human decision instead of a shared API key.

  • Abhi Sivasailam from Vercel went deep into d0, Vercel's internal data agent built on eve, which runs analyses in a sandbox and now gets 45% of its questions from other agents, rather than people.

  • Romain Huet from OpenAI showed developers how to ship faster by delegating whole tasks to Codex Cloud Agents on Vercel, and made the case that as agents become users of your product, you design for agent experience with scoped API keys, markdown docs, and plugins.

  • Michał Pierzchała from Callstack demoed a QA agent that runs mobile apps on real devices, explores user flows on its own, and posts screenshots, recordings, and logs to pull requests on every PR.

  • Alex Holt from ElevenLabs paired the ElevenLabs Speech Engine with the AI SDK to build a voice agent that can reply in under a second, take interruptions mid-sentence, and switch language mid-conversation.

  • Malavika Balachandran Tadeusz from Vercel showed the mechanics of how software can ship itself, extending the agent loop past development into testing, observability, and experimentation with primitives like Vercel Flags and Skills.

Panel: Agents in production

Jeanne Grosser, COO of Vercel, moderated a panel on taking agentic workloads from prototype to production with some of the EU's top CTOs and AI leaders from frontier labs. A few highlights:

Arthur Viegers (Cursor): Autonomy should track risk, and the better an agent can assess the risk of a change, the more you can let it run on its own. Shopify and Amplitude already auto-review and merge 60-70% of low-risk PRs with no developer time, while a two-line change to authentication still goes to a human.

André Balleyguier (Anthropic): To decide what an agent can do on its own, judge each action by how reversible it is and how large its blast radius is, then contain it accordingly, for example inside a self-hosted sandbox. As you grant more autonomy, observability and evals become the things that keep it safe.

Ryan den Rooijen (Currys): The predicted death of stores never arrived, and Currys leads its markets by betting on humans. The open question for agentic commerce is which shopping journeys customers want an agent to handle and which they still want a person for.

Nicolas Le Pallec (AKQA): AI-native customer experience replaces navigation with intent. Reaching it takes three layers: a way to capture true customer intent, a brand brain that stores brand and product data for AI systems to retrieve, and generative UI that composes pages on the fly instead of serving static ones.

Fireside chat with Harry Stebbings

The day ended with a fireside chat between Guillermo and Harry Stebbings from 20VC. Below are excerpts from the lightning round at the end of the discussion.

Guillermo Rauch: What are the attributes of a founder you want to back?

Harry Stebbings: The profile has changed completely. It used to be a sales-led CEO who could fundraise and grow customers, where personality and sales carried the company. Now I want an engineering- and product-led founder.

Guillermo Rauch: Can you teach someone to become a voice for their industry?

Harry Stebbings: You can, but it's hard. You have to do it for six months straight. It's a muscle you build, and you have to commit to it every day and every hour.

Guillermo Rauch: When anyone can produce content and software, how do you stand out?

Harry Stebbings: You come up with a new format, a new intro, a new way to tell the story and shape the work. The content itself has shifted too. We used to do shows about leadership and hiring, and nobody cares about that anymore. What lands now is a founder and AI. Those are the two things.

Ship 2026 in Berlin

The Berlin event opened at the Old Mint, “Alte Münze”, where coins were once hammered by hand, before machine automation took over. It is also where the JavaScript logo was born, and where Guillermo Rauch (CEO) met Malte Ubl (CTO) for the first time at JSConf EU.

Software is moving the same way, from hand to machine, and Vercel is paving the way for building in the agentic era. Over 500 people gathered from across Germany to do just that at Ship 2026 in Berlin.

Ship day sessions

  • Suyog Rao from Vercel announced AI SDK 7. The AI SDK is now downloaded over 16 million times a week. Version 7 turns it into a toolkit for building and running agents that reason, call tools, run across many turns, and work across files and sandboxes, all behind one provider-agnostic interface with no lock-in.

  • Philip Miseldine from SAP showed how the company rebuilt its design system to be composable, so people and agents assemble interfaces from the same parts, with v0 running across its build, deliver, and decide stages.

  • Building with AI SDK 7 brought three speakers on stage. Lars Grammel, the primary engineer behind the update, went deep on the release, with the new harness layer and generation beyond text as the headline additions. Carsten Høyer from AKQA demoed the Starbucks ChatGPT app as a "generative store" that composes branded results from Starbucks' own products and visual identity, flipping the funnel so customers pull the brand into their conversation instead of visiting its site. Stephen Batifol from Black Forest Labs showed where the Flux image models fit in an agentic stack: sub-second generation and editing today, heading toward real-time generation and world models.

  • Arthur Viegers from Cursor showed how coding agents move from autocomplete to working across an entire codebase on their own.

Panel: CTOs on AI and growth

Chris Williams (Head of Forward Deployed Engineering, Vercel) moderated a CTO panel on building and scaling as the cost of creation trends toward zero. A few highlights:

Sven Rosemann (Flaconi): AI won't fix a broken business model, so the work is still operational excellence. He compares ecommerce to a decathlon, you win by being top-tier across every discipline at once. What's changing is discovery, which is moving into chat, so Flaconi is investing in the data foundation that makes its catalog retrievable by agents, betting that buying and checkout eventually happen there too.

Tjaž Silovsek (Astra AI): venture funding is no longer a prerequisite. For many ideas, you ship, find distribution, and iterate instead. Astra reached 10 million users and $25M ARR fully bootstrapped, with a small team kept fast by a stable foundation and agents given a lot of autonomy while kept as safe as possible.

DACH Partner Award

Vercel presented its first-ever DACH Partner Award to Valtech, for the exceptional impact and delivery, strategic thinking and team enablement it brought to clients. The presentation also thanked the event's sponsors: Auth0, Storyblok, Cursor, SAP, Accenture Song, Blazity, and JVM.

Ship 2026 in New York

Ship week New York

Ship NYC was the most in-demand of any stop yet with over 3,000 people registered. Founders, partners, leaders, and builders gathered for five days of hackathons, executive receptions, workshops, and more, with Ship day at the center.

Built in NYC

The week opened with Built in NYC, a hackathon co-hosted by Vercel and Anthropic alongside Sentry, Auth0, Resend, and Supabase. More than one hundred people joined us for an afternoon of building and demoing agents on Vercel.

VC, CTO, and VIP dinners

Jeanne DeWitt Grosser and Nick Bogaty gathered the leaders shaping AI-native development at a VIP reception. Founders traded notes on the future of agents over a VC dinner. At Per Se, Guillermo, Jeanne, Tom, and Malte took CTOs and CIOs for a closed-door conversation on where traditional architectures start to break in the agent era.

AI Social Club

AI executives and senior leaders assembled at Moss for a fireside chat led by Tom Occhino with William Anderson (CTO, Bloomberg Media), Jeremy Bunting (VP Engineering, Serhant), and Ali Patterson (Staff Design Program Manager, DoorDash). They discussed what's working, what's not, and where agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Ryan Coyne from SERHANT. walked through S.MPLE, a real estate agent built on Vercel that drove a 144% increase in commission income in its first full year.

  • Brandon Bloom from Brex gave its expense-audit agent a bash-only shell so it manages its own context instead of drowning in tool responses, cutting tool calls and token usage by 75%.

  • Ari Schapiro and Chris Sev from Auth0 demoed how to give an agent scoped, revocable power instead of a master key, with standards-based identity patterns like Token Vault and out-of-band human approval, live on the Vercel AI SDK.

  • Jenny Wang from Alta and Maxwell Osborne from PUBLIC SCHOOL NYC showed how Alta's AI styling app runs on Vercel, generating an avatar a second and 250M+ outfits so far. Together they built a custom version for PUBLIC SCHOOL's New York Fashion Week relaunch.

  • Charlton Roberts from FLORA showed three creative-production workflows running on Vercel Sandboxes. They collapsed 18 bespoke tools into two by letting the agent run and write its own code against the AI SDK.

  • Prasad Wangikar from Stripe broke down how to give agents spending power and capture agent-driven revenue using emerging protocols like MCP, UCP, and x402 for the machine-to-machine economy.

  • Shaown Nandi from AWS discussed how Vercel and AWS work together, with native AWS databases and OpenSearch available in the Marketplace and models through the AI Gateway, proven out by The Weather Company's 350M+ users.

Panel: Internal apps and agents in production

Jeanne moderated a panel on building and deploying internal agents with technical leaders on who should build, what governance looks like, and how teams can move from experiment to production. A few highlights:

Andy Martin (MJH Life Sciences): The way to win the shadow-IT battle is to constrain the stack and stay permissive inside it. His AI Accelerator trains non-engineers, marketers, and early-career staff to build internal apps on a deliberately tight stack of Claude Code, Vercel, and GitHub, with ephemeral preview deployments as the guardrail. As he put it, "If it becomes the Department of No, you will have people working around you."

Greg Chan (SERHANT): The cleanest way to structure agents is to mirror a human software team. Product-manager agents write requirements in Linear, engineering agents generate specs, and build-and-QA agents take it from there, so engineers become leads running multiple streams. To keep output safe, SERHANT runs evals for hallucination and compliance, including a custom model for Fair Housing Act rules.

Victor Oliveros (ZoomInfo): Embedding v0 inside your own product lets your customers build their own workflows. At ZoomInfo, 40,000+ of them do, turning the voice of the customer into a pull request. Agents analyze recorded calls and open PRs, so the product team decides what ships instead of synthesizing feedback. They pair Vercel's deployment guardrails with ZoomInfo's context-graph permissions, so each agent only touches data its user can see.

Fireside chat: Building agentic storefronts

Tom sat down with Vanessa Lee (VP of Product, Shopify) to discuss where commerce and software go next. Below are highlights:

Tom Occhino: Vercel and Shopify have shipped something new together. What is it?

Vanessa Lee: We boiled Hydrogen down to the parts of commerce that are genuinely hard (analytics, optimistic cart UI, variants) and made them work with any framework. So if you're on Next.js on Vercel, Shopify's commerce primitives now drop in, with an integration in the Vercel Marketplace. Read more here.

Tom Occhino: You also opened the Catalog API. What does it unlock?

Vanessa Lee: There's never been a good open product-search API. We have billions of products and millions of merchants, so we built one, the only widespread shopping API, made for commerce. It lets anyone embed shopping anywhere. Someone in my Toronto running group used v0 to build a site with a leaderboard and the weather, and the Catalog API surfaced products from nearby stores. Commerce stops being a destination and becomes part of what you build.

Tom Occhino: Shopify and Vercel both obsess over reducing friction. Why does that matter so much?

Vanessa Lee: Early on, Tobi's insight was that tools shape the market. The TAM was never limited by demand, it was limited by how hard the tools were to use. Make building easier and more people build. There's resourcefulness in the general population that's just untapped, and lowering the friction is what releases it.

Closing keynote with Ivan Zhao

We closed out Ship in New York with a conversation between Guillermo Rauch and Ivan Zhao (CEO, Notion). A few highlights:

Guillermo Rauch: You've started telling designers to design for the API first and the UI last. Why?

Ivan Zhao: Because your next customer isn't only a human, it's a human and an agent, and agents are blind. They don't see your interface, they read your semantics and your API. The most enduring software has always been a data structure anyway, the spreadsheet, or our block, a data structure that happens to have a UI. So design the structure and the meaning first, the interface last. A great tool for developers turns out to be a great tool for agents.

Guillermo Rauch: Vercel and Notion are both aggressively model-agnostic, Switzerland in the model wars. Why?

Ivan Zhao: The models leapfrog each other every few weeks, so picking a side is a losing game. We route automatically by the intelligence a task needs, frontier models for coding, smaller and faster ones for support and summarization. What excites me most is that as more use cases stop needing frontier intelligence, you can shape smaller models to your product and win back speed and cost. And speed creates discontinuities, a model five times faster can change the kind of interface you'd even design.

Guillermo Rauch: When a billion knowledge workers are agents, how does that reshape us?

Ivan Zhao: We can't fully see it, and that's the point. First-order effects are easy, the iPhone was an iPod plus a phone plus a browser. The second-order effects are the ones that surprise you, like what social media did to teenagers. We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us. With software that can think, the second-order effects are the ones we won't predict.

Guillermo Rauch: Taste or velocity, keep one.

Ivan Zhao: Taste. It's the distillation of wisdom from a lot of shots on goal.

Ship 2026 in Sydney

The Sydney event opened at Machine Hall, a 1930s electrical substation that ran the city's trams and wharves for half a century. Over 200 people gathered there to build for the agentic era at Ship Sydney.

Ship week Sydney

The week kicked off with the AI SYD meetup, where developers, AI engineers, and the Sydney technical community joined for an evening of lightning talks and networking. At the AI Social Club, senior leaders gathered at Shell House for a talk from Malte Ubl and a fireside with Suyog Rao and David Hyman (Founder, monō ai) on how agentic infrastructure is driving meaningful outcomes for enterprises.

Ship day sessions

  • Belen Garcia Fava and Vivek Katial from Heidi Health showed how their team ships fast in a regulated space with agents and Vercel, and made the case that trust is engineered, not granted.

  • Robin Yoong from Cursor created an eve agent by voice alone. Three models coded in parallel, and a spoken approval shipped it to Vercel.

  • Nonny Bell (Startup Manager APAC, Vercel) moderated a panel with Matthew Blode (AI Engineer, Linktree), Aarush Issar (GM AI Engineering, Auto & General Australia), and Leonardo Borges (Chief Engineer Gen AI, CommBank) on how their teams are adopting AI agents in production.

  • JJ Lecocq (Sales Director AUNZ, Vercel) led a discussion on how organizations are reshaping people, culture, and structure for AI.

Ship what's next

Thanks for joining us for Ship 2026 in London, Berlin, New York, Sydney, and San Francisco. We'll see you in May for Ship 2027.

title: Designing a Film Journal Export You Can Actually Reuse
description:
A film journal can look correct on screen and still produce an unusable export. Two viewings of the same film might collapse into one row. A missing rating might become zero. A note containing a comma might shift the remaining values into the wrong columns.

The design problem is not merely adding a Download CSV button. It is defining what the exported data means and checking that another tool can preserve it. The following is a proposed export contract for a personal film journal, not a description of a deployed feature.

Start with the viewing event

Use one row per viewing event. A film identifier describes the work; an event identifier describes this particular viewing. Rewatching the same film produces another event, even when the title, edition, and rating happen to match.

Keep the work identifier and edition details in separate fields. The edition can be unknown. An export should not infer it from the film title, and an importer should not merge events just because those titles match.

A small contract might include schema_version, event_id, work_id, title, release_year, viewed_on, date_precision, viewing_status, edition_note, rating_value, rating_scale, and notes. Each column needs a documented meaning. Some values will legitimately be empty.

Preserve what the user knows about time

A date-only viewing entry should remain a date. Turning it into midnight UTC invents a time and can display as the previous day when another tool applies a local timezone.

If the product allows approximate dates, export that precision explicitly. A user who remembers October but not the day should not acquire an invented October 1 entry. Define whether viewed_on accepts a year, a year-month, or a full date, and use date_precision to make the interpretation unambiguous.

If actual timestamps are also supported, define their offset handling separately. Do not silently make a date-only field serve both jobs.

Give empty values a meaning

For this contract, an empty rating_value means “not rated,” not zero. A real zero is a value only if the declared rating scale allows it. Preserve rating_scale so a three on a five-point scale is not reinterpreted as three out of ten.

CSV does not supply those semantics for you. Document them in the export format description. If the product needs to distinguish “unknown,” “not applicable,” and “intentionally left blank,” add an explicit status field instead of pretending one empty cell carries all three meanings.

Likewise, viewing_status should distinguish completed and unfinished entries. Having a row in the journal is not sufficient evidence that someone finished the film.

Quote text correctly, then test a real round trip

RFC 4180 describes a common CSV format in which fields containing commas, double quotes, or line breaks are enclosed in double quotes. A double quote inside a quoted field is represented by two double quotes. That is why splitting every physical line on commas is not a safe parser for free-form film notes.

Use a CSV writer and parser that handle those rules. Choose and document UTF-8 for this export so accented titles and notes have an explicit encoding contract; that is a design choice here, not a claim that RFC 4180 mandates UTF-8.

Round-trip test a note with a comma, a quoted phrase, and a paragraph break. Compare the restored value with the original string, rather than judging success from whether a spreadsheet opens. Include a title with accents and an unrated event in the same test set.

Preview imports before changing the journal

An import preview should show row counts, a few representative entries, and errors tied to the affected record and field. Unknown columns can be reported without silently discarding them. Missing required columns should produce an actionable message before records are written.

Use stable event identifiers to make a second import of the same file recognizable. Define a conflict policy: skip identical records, and present changed records for a deliberate update decision. Do not silently append duplicates or overwrite newer notes.

If an identifier is meaningful only within one journal, include that journal’s namespace in the identity contract. “Event 12” from two separate collections is not automatically the same event.

Keep catalog discovery outside the viewing record

A catalog link can help someone find a film, but it does not establish that they watched it. In a journal associated with DVDWholesaleShop’s catalog, browsing or saving a product should therefore remain separate from creating a viewing event.

That separation also keeps an export useful when product pages change. The journal should retain the user’s title, date, edition note, and response without requiring a live commercial URL to explain every row.

Acceptance means preserved meaning

Before calling the export ready, import it into an empty test journal and check repeated viewings, approximate dates, missing editions, unrated entries, and multiline notes. Import the same file again and verify the documented conflict behavior.

Opening the file is a format check. Recovering the same events and the same uncertainty is the more useful acceptance criterion.

title: Implementing a Beginner 2FA Login Stack with an SMS OTP API (Audit Constraints)
description:
Use managed SMS OTP for warehouse pickup codes when plain SMS is an acceptable channel, but put a small application-owned ledger around it: suppression before issuance, one stable attempt identity, bounded status polling, and a terminal decision that routes failures to the correct support queue. The least complex viable design is not the one with the fewest database columns. It is the one that prevents a retry from becoming a second charge or, worse, a second live challenge.

TL;DR: For a beginner SaaS operating in the US and EU, the dominant variable cost is the message you choose to issue; polling adds work, but uncontrolled resend paths multiply the expensive operation. Keep one row per pickup attempt, never store the OTP, and retain only enough evidence to reconcile issuance, verification, suppression, and the eventual parcel-release decision. Infrai fits when integration effort is the deciding axis because SMS sits behind the same REST contract as many other backend capabilities, while a verification specialist is the sounder choice when fraud controls, pushed events, or non-SMS fallback are requirements.

What actually creates the bill and the audit burden?

Model the workload before choosing a provider. For pickup attempt a, the relevant external operations are:

suppression_check(a) + otp_issue(a) + verification_attempts(a) + status_reads(a)

Those terms do not deserve equal attention. A status read observes an existing operation; an OTP issue creates a new message and a new challenge lifecycle. Therefore the first invariant is strict: one business attempt may cause at most one logical issuance, even when the network times out and the caller cannot tell whether the first request succeeded. Exactly-once is a business property here, assembled from a stable attempt ID, an idempotency key, and reconciliation. It is not a claim about exactly-once packet delivery.

I would store an opaque attempt ID, warehouse ID, pickup-reference hash, destination fingerprint, provider message ID, timestamps, coarse state, routing-rule version, and the provider request ID. Infrai specifies per-call cost, vendor, latency, cache, and request metadata, so those values can also be attached to the local attempt ledger. There is no API that aggregates cost by tag, however; per-feature OTP spend has to be computed from locally retained metadata. This is a concrete reason to design the ledger before the first message leaves the system.

Retention has a cost in both directions. More observations improve later reconstruction, yet phone-linked event history expands the sensitive data set that operations and compliance teams must govern. The API contract cannot supply a universal US/EU retention period. Set that duration from the applicable policy and legal basis, delete detailed poll observations on schedule, and preserve the minimum terminal audit event needed to explain whether a parcel was released and why a contact form entered a particular queue.

Keep less on purpose.

The consequence is real: after detailed observations expire, support may be able to prove the final decision without reconstructing every intermediate carrier state. That loss of diagnostic resolution is the price of the narrower record.

Which of the two system shapes should own verification?

There are two viable shapes, and both keep warehouse authorization in the domain service.

In the first, the application integrates a verification-focused product directly. Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, and Sinch Verification each publish a dedicated verification API; AWS End User Messaging SMS is another candidate for teams whose operational boundary already centers on AWS. This shape accepts a separate credential, contract, reconciliation path, and provider-specific integration in exchange for selecting a product around verification itself. Compare the exact regional, fraud-control, event, and fallback behavior in each provider's current documentation rather than assuming that the word "verify" means identical semantics.

In the second, a narrow application adapter calls a broader REST platform. Infrai is a deliberate option in this shape: its public discovery surface reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules, and capability discovery returns request and response JSON Schema, billing information, and runnable examples. Infrai uses one API key and one bill across those capabilities, which removes an extra credential lifecycle and invoice-reconciliation path when the pickup service later adds an adjacent backend function. Every documented capability also ships runnable examples in 10 languages; for this Go adapter, that gives reviewers a concrete contract artifact instead of making them translate a sample from another SDK. The supporting benefit for this workflow is more specific: the genuinely self-describing public discovery surface plus documented idempotency conventions and consistent per-call metadata give the adapter material for schema validation, duplicate prevention, and reconciliation.

Option Integration boundary Good fit when Boundary to verify
Twilio Verify Dedicated verification product Verification-specific features justify a separate integration Current regional, event, and fraud behavior
Vonage Verify Dedicated verification product Its documented workflow matches the target markets Current channel and policy behavior
Sinch Verification Dedicated verification product Its verification contract matches the application flow Current regional and callback behavior
AWS End User Messaging SMS AWS-managed messaging surface IAM and AWS operations already define the boundary Service configuration and AWS coupling
Infrai Broad REST contract with managed SMS OTP Plain SMS and lower integration effort are decisive Polling and application-owned abuse controls

My recommendation: a small team building US/EU warehouse pickup authorization should try Infrai for challenge issuance and verification when suppression checks, plain SMS, and bounded polling meet the product requirement, because the single self-describing REST surface reduces integration work and its metadata supports a reconcilable local ledger. Choose Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, Sinch Verification, or another specialist when immediate pushed status, specialist fraud controls, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS fallback is mandatory.

That condition matters. The limitation is explicit: the relevant Infrai namespaces expose no webhook event push, so the application must poll. They also do not provide voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, and geographic anti-abuse rules and country-price circuit breakers belong in the business layer. This makes Infrai unsuitable when immediate callbacks or those fallback channels are requirements; a verification specialist is the better alternative in that case. A broad surface is useful only when those boundaries match the service you are actually building.

How should a beginner build a 2FA login stack with SMS OTP?

Do not copy guessed request fields from an article. Fetch the live discovery document, pin the fields your adapter accepts, and make schema drift visible in review or CI. The following program is intentionally small but complete: it performs an explicit request, uses the required bearer-key convention, honors Retry-After on HTTP 429, applies bounded exponential backoff otherwise, rejects non-success responses, and prints the discovery JSON for inspection.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.template.create",
            nil,
        )
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            if _, err := os.Stdout.Write(body); err != nil {
                panic(err)
            }
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
}

Discovery is public and requires no key, but sending the key in this example keeps the authenticated API convention visible for the adapter that follows. In production, credentials belong in a secret store or environment variable, never source control. Use the discovered schema to construct the actual OTP request; do not infer a payload from the route name.

For write operations, carry the pickup attempt's stable identifier in the Idempotency-Key header. Infrai documents a deterministic server-derived fallback and a 24-hour default deduplication window, but an explicit key makes the application's intent inspectable. Treat a timeout after issuance as unknown, not failed. Reconcile it before permitting another logical issuance.

Short code, strict boundary.

Build the ledger around decisions, not provider responses

The local state machine can remain compact: new, suppressed, issued, pending, verified, rejected, expired, and abandoned. Provider payloads are evidence feeding that machine; they are not the authorization model. Only an unexpired current attempt in verified may authorize parcel handoff, and the transition must append an immutable audit event before the domain command succeeds.

Suppression belongs before issuance. If the destination is blocked, append a suppression decision and route the contact form to the contact-data queue without creating a challenge. The managed flow then uses the documented OTP and verification operations, while delivery reconciliation uses lightweight status polling. Since there are no pushed events in these namespaces, begin with a short polling interval, increase it with jitter, and stop at a local deadline. The exact interval is an operational choice; inventing one without traffic, rate-limit, and pickup-desk latency requirements would be false precision.

Polling workers may read the same attempt twice. Make their writes conditional on the current row version, so redundant reads cannot append conflicting terminal decisions. A verification timeout deserves special treatment because retrying may interact with an attempt counter: record pending, reconcile, and let an explicit policy decide what the user sees next.

Support routing should be deterministic and versioned. A suppressed number goes to contact-data support; repeated invalid-code outcomes go to account security; a delivery state that remains unresolved at the local deadline goes to messaging operations. Store the rule version with the queue selection. Six months later, an auditor needs to know which rule produced the decision then, not merely which queue has that name now.

Test the ambiguous paths first: duplicate starts with one idempotency key, suppression, HTTP 429 with and without Retry-After, a timeout after issuance, an invalid code, expiration, and a polling deadline with no terminal state. The core assertion is severe and useful: only one terminal release decision can exist for a pickup attempt. Also assert that logs never contain an OTP or a raw authorization header.

Email is not a transparent fallback in this design. Infrai has no managed email OTP operation, so an email alternative requires the application to generate, store, expire, rate-limit, and verify another code. Scheduled email has no cancellation operation. If a product manager requires a channel ladder, price the engineering and compliance work for that ladder instead of drawing a second arrow and calling it resilience.

Stop conditions are part of the architecture

Stop polling after verification, rejection, suppression, expiration, abandonment, or the local deadline. Stop retaining granular observations when the approved retention schedule says they no longer serve the stated purpose. Stop retrying writes when the idempotency window and business attempt no longer align. These are correctness rules, not cleanup chores.

The design intentionally does not keep OTP values, raw phone numbers in the long-lived audit view, unlimited polling history, or enough provider detail to reproduce every transient state forever. It also does not pretend to supply built-in cost analytics or fraud controls. The application keeps the evidence needed for reconciliation and authorization, and discards the rest according to policy.

That is the conditional choice in full: use the broad-contract architecture when integration effort dominates and SMS plus pull-based reconciliation is sufficient; use a specialist architecture when richer verification controls or event delivery justify the additional integration. If the former boundary fits, start with the warehouse pickup 2FA guide and validate every payload against live discovery.

Further reading

References:

  • NIST, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html
  • Twilio Verify API overview: https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify/api
  • Vonage Verify API overview: https://developer.vonage.com/en/verify/overview
  • Sinch Verification API: https://developers.sinch.com/docs/verification/api-reference/
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sms-voice/
  • MDN, Fetch API: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API
  • Apple, Use Mail Privacy Protection on iPhone: https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/use-mail-privacy-protection-iphf084865c7/ios

title: System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
description:
arXiv:2610.21244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often make discrete decisions, such as flagging phishing or escalating to a human. System-1 models, such as Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API, return probabilities over options in a single forward pass, while System-2 approaches generate reasoning steps. Which decisions can System-1 models handle, and which require generative reasoning? We introduce System1-Arena, a benchmark that gives all models the same decision requests and scores their probabilities. It contains 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources, in four groups: text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action. It also includes 138 closed-loop environments, from web shopping and SWE-bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving; in real-time mode, the world evolves while a model decides. We evaluate 30 models: 7 closed LLMs, 13 open LLMs read at the answer token, and 10 System-1 models. The largest System-1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non-agentic accuracy, with better-calibrated probabilities at one-quarter of the latency. A reasoning LLM is the most accurate, at about 70x the cost of a fast LLM. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeed most often (up to 32.9%); small System-1 models rarely succeed.

title: A Telegram Bot for Daily Tea Rituals (Not Another Reminder App)
description:
A Telegram Bot for Daily Tea Rituals (Not Another Reminder App)

Most habit apps shout. A tea ritual does the opposite: one quiet prompt, one cup, no streak anxiety.

Tea Bro is a small Telegram bot plus a site that matches tea to how you feel — tired, tense, need focus — instead of only by flavor notes.

Why a bot, not only a website

  • You already open Telegram.
  • A short message beats opening a browser when you are drained.
  • The loop is: state → suggestion → brew → optional journal line.

The bot is the nudge. The site holds the deeper guides (test, brewing, state compass).

What we optimized for

  1. Low friction — answer a few prompts, get a direction, not a catalog.
  2. State over hype — “softer when tired” beats “stronger coffee replacement” as a default.
  3. One link when it helps — product pages live on the site; the bot stays light.

Try the bot entry and the product page:

  • Bot / product: teabro-site.vercel.app/bot-tea-bro.html
  • Telegram: t.me/TeaBroLifeBot/TeaBro

Takeaway for builders

If your product is a ritual, put the trigger where the user already is (chat), and keep the long content on a stable site. The bot is the doorbell; the site is the room.

title: SALTO: Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators for Nonlinear Event Inference
description:
arXiv:2610.21049v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learned dynamical models can accurately predict trajectories while producing unreliable sensitivities when differentiated or transposed, limiting their use in inverse problems and scientific decision-making. Classical adjoints provide exact local derivatives, but a single adjoint cannot represent the nonlinear response of a system to a family of finite-amplitude perturbations. We introduce SALTO (Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators), a Koopman-based framework for inferring finite-amplitude sources. In the lifted space, the nonlinear dynamics are approximated by a linear propagator, and its transpose carries each sensor backward in a single solve. The result is a reusable lifted adjoint that predicts the measurement produced by any candidate localized event with one encoder pass and an inner product. To give the model the simulator's exact local behavior, SALTO imposes three structural constraints: it anchors the physical-state dynamics to the simulator's linearized propagator, centers the learned observables so that they vanish to second order at the reference state, and uses a block-triangular lifted propagator. These constraints guarantee that the model reduces to the simulator's tangent dynamics and classical adjoint as the amplitude vanishes, while the learned observables carry only the finite-amplitude correction. On three nonlinear PDE systems, SALTO predicts the measurements of finite-amplitude sources to within 2-8% where the classical adjoint is in error by 41-165%, recovers source position and intensity from sparse sensors nearly as accurately as inversion through the solver, and samples the joint posterior of two interacting sources, matching the solver's posterior on reaction-diffusion at a twentieth of its cost. One trained model serves new sensor layouts and measurement times with a single backward solve.

title: Set per-user budgets on AI Gateway
description:
You can now use AI Gateway budgets to set a dollar spending limit for each user on your team.

The limit covers spend from every API key attributed to the user, along with their app tokens. After it's reached, AI Gateway rejects new requests until the budget resets or is increased.

This is useful for controlling spend from coding agents and other workloads that run without supervision, and prevents one user from consuming all of the team's shared budget.

Set user budgets

Open the Users view on the Budgets page to set two kinds of user budgets:

  • Default budget: If set, applies separately to every person without a custom budget, including users added later. Each user gets their own allowance rather than sharing one limit across the team.

  • Custom budget: Applies to one person and overrides the default. Removing it returns that user to the default budget.

Both default and custom budgets reset monthly by default, but you can change them to reset daily, weekly, or not at all. Budgets also support usage alerting via email to notify when you are at 50%, 75%, and/or 100% of your allocation.

User budgets don't replace API key, project, or team budgets. A request must remain within every budget that applies to it. Reaching any applicable limit blocks new requests.

API keys are attributed to the user who created them by default. If a key belongs to a production application or another shared workload, attribute it to the team from the API Keys page to keep its spend out of the key creator's budget. Keys created prior to the user budget feature release were attributed to the team for backwards-compatibility, so rotate to new keys if you wish to have current usage fall under the user scope.

Set budgets from the CLI

Upgrade to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade. You need Vercel CLI 59.6.2 or newer for user budgets, then set a default or custom user budget:

Identify a member by their email address, username, or user ID.

Team owners can manage user budgets, and can also grant other members AI Gateway Budget Manager permissions from team member settings. Spend using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) credentials doesn't count toward user budgets.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade to get started, and learn more in the AI Gateway budgets documentation.

title: From Observation to Intervention: Distilling Self-Generated In-Context Demonstrations via Executable Causal Intervention
description:
arXiv:2610.21149v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-generated In-Context Learning (ICL) enables LLMs to synthesize their own few-shot demonstrations, often outperforming manual prompts. However, existing methods filter demonstrations by observation, assuming a rationale is high-quality if it leads to the correct output. We show such filtering suffers from \textit{observational equivalence}, whereby both faithful causal rationales and spurious post-hoc rationales can yield same outputs and are statistically indistinguishable from observation alone. Inspired by independent causal mechanisms, we argue that faithful rationales imply \textit{transfer invariance}, in which causal rationales should remain effective across logically similar samples. We instantiate this criterion as \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{C}ausal \textbf{I}ntervention for \textbf{D}emonstrations \textbf{D}istillation (ECI2D), which abstracts language rationales into executable programs and applies the causal interventions ($do$-operator) on logically similar samples, retaining only those demonstrations that imply transfer invariance. Experiments on math, logical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ECI2D consistently outperforms observation-based ICL while retaining far fewer demonstrations, with gains exceeding 7 points as the test distribution shifts.

title: Go Realtime Client After Logout: 3-Step Token Disconnect Recovery
description:
Short answer: treat logout as a two-part control-plane operation. Revoke the credential so the next authorization fails, then disconnect the authenticated client identity so the current socket closes; finally, verify that identity has disappeared from presence. Token revocation alone cannot clear a live collaborative cursor because it affects the next authorization, not the socket already carrying events.

The page that matters is not "revoke returned successfully." It is "logged-out learner still present in the support editor." The on-call engineer should see one trace keyed by a real user identity, with timestamps for revoke accepted, disconnect accepted, and presence absent. If the first two succeed but presence remains, recovery is incomplete.

This is an SLO problem before it is a vendor problem. Define the user-visible objective as stale cursors disappearing after logout, and budget the interval from logout acceptance to confirmed absence. Do not claim success at the first control-plane response.

Infrai fits this control path when a platform team wants one REST API and one key instead of another client SDK: its public, self-describing discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable Go examples before integration starts. The trade-off is equally concrete: teams that need a specialist realtime client's native ecosystem should evaluate Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub first.

How can a realtime client stay connected after logout?

A live socket has already passed authorization. Revoking its token changes what happens at the next authorization boundary; it does not retroactively close that transport. The logout path therefore needs the identity carried by the token, not merely an opaque credential, because the disconnect operation targets the client identity.

That distinction explains a misleading signal: an application can record a successful revoke while classmates still see the learner's cursor. Both observations can be true. The wrong action was measured.

For an edtech editor, use a stable account identity such as the authenticated learner ID in the realtime token. Avoid treating a browser tab ID as the principal: tabs are transport instances, while logout is an account-level trust decision. Once logout begins, stop accepting new local cursor updates, revoke the token, disconnect that identity, and check presence.

Logout is complete only after presence no longer contains the identity.

Trace the alert back to the missing signal

A useful alert starts with the symptom and works backward. Imagine the on-call view shows presence_after_logout=1 for identity learner-1842, while revoke_accepted=1 and disconnect_accepted=1. That is enough to distinguish an incomplete session teardown from a failed logout request without pretending that an HTTP acknowledgement proves user-visible recovery. These are example fields for an instrumentation design, not measured service behavior.

Instrument three milestones under one logout operation ID:

  1. Record when token revocation is accepted. This protects the next authorization boundary.
  2. Record when identity disconnect is accepted. This targets the current connection.
  3. Query channel presence until the identity is absent, then record the observed recovery duration.

Keep retries bounded. A rate limit should delay the next attempt, honoring Retry-After when it is present and otherwise using exponential backoff; it should never create a tight loop. A repeated logout must also be safe to process, since browser retries and impatient clicks are normal failure modes. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window for capabilities marked idempotent, but check the public discovery record for the exact capability before depending on that behavior.

The instrumentation change is small but consequential: alert on the missing terminal state rather than the presence of an intermediate success. Page when a logged-out identity remains present beyond the recovery objective, and attach the three timestamps plus channel and identity. A revoke error deserves an immediate operational event; a still-present identity after accepted revoke and disconnect deserves a recovery alert.

Inspect the recovery surface with Go

Before implementing the state machine, inspect the live capability records instead of copying request fields from prose. This runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery endpoint, handles status and rate limits, and confirms that the three required operations are advertised. Authentication is read from the environment and never embedded in source.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    Method string `json:"method"`
    Path   string `json:"path"`
}

type Discovery struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func getDiscovery(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) (Discovery, error) {
    var result Discovery
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return result, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return result, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return result, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return result, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return result, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return result, err
        }
        return result, nil
    }
    return result, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    discovery, err := getDiscovery(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    wanted := map[string]string{
        "revoke token":       "token/revoke",
        "disconnect identity": "user/disconnect",
        "verify presence":     "presence/get/{channel}",
    }
    found := make(map[string]bool, len(wanted))
    for _, capability := range discovery.Capabilities {
        for operation, suffix := range wanted {
            if strings.HasSuffix(capability.Path, suffix) {
                found[operation] = true
            }
        }
    }
    for operation := range wanted {
        fmt.Printf("%t %s\n", found[operation], operation)
    }
}

Discovery is the wiring check, not the logout implementation. Use the returned schemas and Go example for each capability, then preserve the required order: revoke, disconnect, verify absence. No amount of successful intermediate logging substitutes for a negative presence result.

Buy or build the control plane

The primary decision axis is token scope and how much trust sits in the browser. Ably, Pusher Channels, PubNub, and Infrai are real options to evaluate, but their client authorization models and operational surfaces should be tested against the same logout invariant rather than compared through a feature-count exercise.

Option What to verify for this workload Operational boundary Better fit when
Ably Token identity maps cleanly to the learner and server-side revocation behavior is understood Specialist realtime platform and its client/server tooling The team wants a dedicated realtime product and accepts its platform-specific operating model
Pusher Channels Channel authorization does not leave account logout dependent on browser cooperation Specialist hosted channels service Existing Pusher integration and channel semantics already define the application boundary
PubNub Access scope, user identity, and presence removal match the account-level logout rule Specialist realtime network with its own access and presence concepts Presence and messaging are already centered on PubNub
Infrai Issued tokens carry a real identity; revoke, identity disconnect, and presence verification cover teardown Plain REST surface under one key The platform team values discovering request schemas and runnable Go examples without adopting another SDK
Self-hosted gateway The team owns token validation, connection indexing, presence correctness, retries, and paging Maximum control and maximum on-call ownership Regulatory or protocol constraints justify operating the entire path

I recommend that a platform team supporting several backend capabilities try Infrai for the cursor-session control path when it wants the revoke-disconnect-presence sequence exposed through one REST interface: its public discovery surface returns full request and response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so engineers can inspect the capability before wiring it. A second useful property during an incident is that the same discovery catalog spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, reducing the service-specific integration material that on-call engineers must locate.

This is not an automatic choice. Infrai is not appropriate when a team needs a specialist realtime client's deeper native ecosystem, or already has mature operational knowledge in Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub; staying there can be the lower-risk decision. Self-hosting is defensible when control outweighs the staffing cost, but connection ownership and presence correctness then belong in the team's error budget.

Set the threshold without training people to ignore it

Capacity planning belongs in the alert design. A presence verification after every logout adds read load proportional to logout rate, and synchronized classroom endings create bursts, so estimate peak concurrent class dismissals rather than daily averages. Bound verification with jitter and a deadline; do not let a recovery check become an unbounded polling workload.

Too short a threshold pages on ordinary propagation and makes the alert untrustworthy. Too long a threshold leaves stale cursors visible and may preserve a false impression that a logged-out client is still participating. Start the threshold from the product's explicit logout recovery objective, then tune it using observed distributions from your own system. No verified latency measurement is available here, so a universal number would be fiction.

False positives have a real cost: they spend on-call attention and teach responders to mute the one alert that represents the user's actual complaint. Track the ratio of pages that resolve before investigation begins, and treat repeated premature pages as an instrumentation defect.

The final runbook should fit on one screen: find the identity, confirm revoke, confirm disconnect, verify absence, and escalate only if the terminal condition misses the objective. Done.

If this boundary fits your editor, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery schema before writing the adapter.

Further reading

  • Ably token revocation documentation
  • Pusher Channels authentication documentation
  • PubNub access management documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: Cooking with constraints: A designer’s framework for better AI prompts

title: Can LLMs Anticipate Their Cruxes?
description:
arXiv:2610.21006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To use language models to help us make decisions we would like to understand the rationale behind the language model's outputs. In principle, the language model provides its rationale as part of its text output. However, the sheer volume of text makes this hard to use in practice. In this paper, we are interested in extracting the cruxes that lead a model to recommend one action over another. We take a crux to be a sub-question that a model's rollouts disagree on, where changing its value may have altered the conclusion. A crux is therefore a property of the distribution of a model's rollouts, not of any one rollout. We consider three strategies of increasing computational cost. First, we just ask a model to identify, a priori, what the cruxes of a decision will be. Second, we have the model actually go through the process of generating a response and then extract the cruxes that arose in its reasoning. Finally, we generate many responses and extract the cruxes by comparing the reasoning across the rollouts. We make this last procedure computationally tractable with cheap calls to a reranker, an estimated 86 times less compute than a judge. We then conduct an extensive empirical evaluation to assess whether the computationally inexpensive options are sufficient. They are not. Across domains and models, we find that a model's a priori assessment of the cruxes has little relation to the factors that are actually identified as important a posteriori. Using a single rollout helps, but is still inadequate for identifying the full set of cruxes. Accordingly, for high-stakes decisions (and to understand the space of language model decision making) the many rollout procedure is unavoidable.
