title: How our agents build on-brand pages with design.md
description:
Across Vercel, we use coding agents to design and build pages that have to look and feel like Vercel. The typography, color, and composition all need to carry the same judgment that we put into the pages we already ship ourselves.

We recently wrote about product-design, our skill that teaches agents how we design when they work in our codebases. The skill lives in each repository alongside the code that it governs, explaining how agents can find and understand our design system as well as product guidelines for whatever they are building.

This works great when agents are working in our codebases, where everything the skill needs is right there. But what about reports, proposals, and the one-off pages that still have to look like Vercel but get made in tools that can't read any of those files? For us, the answer was design.md, one public file any agent can load.

How we approached building design.md

What made product-design work well was that the design system and product guidelines were sitting right there in the repository for agents to read. We needed a way for agents and tools outside that environment to reach the same knowledge, so that the pages coming out the other end would still look like something we designed ourselves. That set two requirements:

  • A single public URL that anyone can point their agents at, regardless of the environment they run in.

  • Guidance covering everything that made product-design useful in the first place, from brand, layout, and copywriting to the design system, responsiveness, and information architecture.

The naive approach we tried first was to simply port product-design into a public prompt, collapsing the skill's reference files into one file any agent could read from a URL. The problem we found was that while the prompt described our visual language just fine, every model reading it interpreted that description differently, generating vastly different pages from the same guidance.

Part of this comes from the fact that design language is subjective. Phrases like "keep the layout clean" can really mean anything. What is "clean"? Beyond that, the bigger problem was everything else the prompt left behind. Inside our codebases, an agent reads product-design surrounded by real components and shipped examples of the things it describes. But a public prompt includes none of that, leaving every model to rebuild our style from just words alone.

So what we needed to do was distill what that environment provided into a single file, and the only way to know whether we were getting closer was to look at the pages coming out. We set the port aside and started writing a new file from scratch, this time testing every change against a repeatable set of eval prompts.

We wrote seven of them, pulled from real use cases and paired with mock inputs:

  • Usage and performance report

  • Renewal proposal

  • Benchmark report

  • Interactive planning page

  • Build-versus-buy brief

  • Security governance brief

  • Presentation deck

The prompts stayed fixed while the file changed, so any difference in the output traced back to the guidance.

The first comparison

These evals gave us a way to measure both what the file was actually doing and how it was being interpreted by different agents. For our first test, we wanted to know whether design.md would actually change what a model produced at all. We ran the renewal proposal eval twice in the same environment with the same model, once without design.md and once with it loaded, keeping the prompt, data, and viewport identical in both runs.

Without design.md, the model generated a generic SaaS dashboard. But with it, the page led with the renewal recommendation itself, pulled the commercial evidence into one grid, put peer values on a single scale so they could actually be compared, and kept supporting detail available without letting it compete with the summary. This allowed us to conclude that the file changed the page’s structure and hierarchy as well, not just the styling like we originally found, giving us enough signal to keep building the guidance like this, one rule at a time.

The three parts that make the system work

As we tested and rebuilt design.md, the scope evolved into a three-part system that made the entire thing work:

  • design.md supplies guidance that shows agents how to frame the reader's job, structure evidence, and choose a composition.

  • A public stylesheet that defines a bounded, documented vocabulary of classes and tokens.

  • An evaluation loop turns repeated human feedback into better guidance and deterministic checks.

Each of these layers covers a different slice of the work that creates a high-quality, on-brand Vercel page. The judgment that gets encoded in design.md gives agents guidance on:

  • Shaping a page for both a quick executive read and a detailed audit.

  • Writing copy with concrete claims and honest caveats.

  • Composing hierarchy, typography, and color so that evidence and prose support each other.

  • How to publish as Vercel, down to the asset rules for our wordmark and the triangle logo.

design.md also names the recurring generated-design patterns that we never want to see, allowing agents to recognize and avoid them far more reliably by giving the patterns names.

We created a stylesheet because agents kept inventing their own typography, spacing, and layout, so we took those decisions away from the model entirely. The stylesheet packages our design system's primitives, such as headers, tables, stat strips, and chart styles, as CSS that any page can use via a public URL. Then design.md documents the class names and tokens that the stylesheet provides, allowing the agent to build the page with those names in the HTML instead of reinventing them.

Another benefit to this is that the agent never actually reads the stylesheet itself. The stylesheet loads when the page renders in your browser, so none of the code enters the model's context, saving more room for design guidance instead.

Last, the evaluation loop is what helps make the other two pieces work. Deterministic checks are used to help catch mechanical failures, such as a table that ignores the width available to it, while people judge the subjective parts that can't be automated, like hierarchy, composition, and whether the page actually gives the reader what they came for.

How guidance made it into the file

Every line of guidance in design.md earned its place through the eval loop. We generated pages from fixed scenarios, reviewed what came back, encoded the corrections we accepted, and reran the scenarios to see whether each change stuck, since a change that helped one artifact could quietly hurt another. Nothing got in any other way.

Scenarios and rounds

Each of the seven prompts becomes a scenario, meaning the prompt is frozen together with its mock inputs and render settings. The renewal proposal, for example, always runs with the same fake customer data with the same viewport settings, keeping design.md as the only thing that changes between runs. A round means generating a fresh page from every scenario against the current version of the file. Full rounds cover all seven scenarios on both Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex with GPT-5.5.

If we want to investigate something specific, such as a rule change that only affects tables, we can rerun the affected scenarios or a single model, keeping iteration loops tight.

Generating all seven pages together also made them easy to compare side by side, and what stood out was that design.md wasn't pushing every page toward one template. The interactive planning page put its controls front and center, because someone opens a planning page to change the numbers and see what happens. The renewal proposal instead led with the recommendation and the commercial comparison behind it, because its reader is deciding whether to renew. Every page used the same Vercel typography, color, and spacing, but each one was structured around what its reader came to do.

Reviewing every run

To review the pages each round produced, we built a local app that displays full-page renders and runs blind A/B comparisons. This app eventually became our eval harness, running each scenario and storing the results. Each stored run keeps the prompt, inputs, model configuration, the version of design.md it used, the screenshots, and whatever feedback the reviewer left about it. Reviewers record every correction against the exact run that produced it.

Turning corrections into rules and checks

Each correction a reviewer records gets landed in the narrowest place that can consistently enforce it. Judgment changes go into design.md as prose, reusable mechanics go into the stylesheet, and anything that we can check mechanically becomes a deterministic check in code. Problems with the harness itself stay in the harness, and when a single model fails in a way the others don't, we keep it out of the rules until it repeats.

Take one of the early renewal proposals. Its commercial terms table came back squeezed to the same width as the prose, even though the page had room for the table to be twice as wide.

During review, we flagged that evidence tables should use the full width available to them. But when looking through previous outputs, we found this same failure everywhere. So this correction ended up going into two places:

  • A rule in design.md stating the intended behavior.

  • A deterministic check in code that catches the same layout failure the next time it appears.

Once this landed, later renewal proposal prompts resulted in pages with correct full-width tables. To verify changes like this one, we reran the affected scenarios after encoding them. At milestones we went further, running blind A/B rounds that put the updated design.md against an earlier version of the file to decide whether to keep, revise, or revert each change.

Measuring whether it worked

Building the file had taken well over 200 runs, counting full rounds, targeted checks, dry runs, and all of the dead ends. Alongside the human reviewers, a model judge wrote critiques for each round, and every round's feedback went into improving the next run.

After all of those runs, we wanted to know whether the corrections we had encoded were actually preventing the failures they were written for. So we picked three desktop scenarios, and for each one we had Codex with GPT-5.5 generate the page twice, once with design.md loaded and once without. We kept the first attempt from every generation, with no re-rolls. Then we ran our deterministic checks over all six pages and counted how many times a known failure, like a table that ignores its available width, showed up in each set. The pages generated with design.md had 39 of those failures. The pages generated without it had 91, which works out to 57% fewer in this test.

Those numbers come with two caveats. The checks can only catch failures we have already seen and written down, so this test says nothing about whether a page is well designed overall. Six pages is also far too small a sample to make claims about quality or reliability, and every one of them, with or without the file, still had at least one failure serious enough to block shipping. But what the test does well is tell us that once we name a failure and encode it, that failure tends to stay gone.

How design.md stays current

The eval loop got the file shipped, but what keeps it current is real usage. Inside our Slack, that usage comes through @design-agent, an agent built on eve that we use for anything from design critiques and copy alternatives to icon recommendations and report sites built from pasted data. Instead of setting up a prompt or hunting down source files, you just mention the agent in a thread. For website requests, it loads the current design.md, builds the page against the published stylesheet, and posts a full-page screenshot and deployment URL back to the thread. Unlike our fixed scenarios, each of these threads captures a real request, a real output, and whatever feedback or steering followed, showing us how the guidance performs out in the wild.

Every week, we gather all of that feedback in one place, the Slack threads along with comments from GitHub reviews and Figma. Automation groups the comments that keep repeating, and each repeated complaint becomes a proposed change. A person then reviews each proposal, checks whether the system already handles it, and decides where the accepted fix belongs, whether that is @design-agent, the product-design skill, design.md, the stylesheet, or a deterministic check. And if people start asking for a kind of page we have never tested, that request becomes a new eval scenario.

To know whether any of this is working, we count how often each kind of complaint shows up in similar work over time. Once we encode a fix, that count should start falling. When it does not, something about the fix is wrong. The rule might be unclear, it might not be loading when it is needed, the stylesheet might not have a primitive that can express it, or it might need a deterministic check instead of prose.

Build your own

You can build the same loop yourself, starting with one recurring artifact and one manual comparison.

1. Pick one repeated artifact

Use a recent task with a real reader and real inputs, like a proposal, performance report, benchmark, or microsite. Avoid broad goals such as "make it on-brand." Before generating anything, write down a short rubric. A good one checks that the supplied facts survived, that the reader's decision is clear, and that the correction you keep making by hand actually got resolved.

2. Save the baseline first

Generate the page once without any new design context, and save the prompt, inputs, configuration, and a screenshot. Keep that first output even if it looks rough, unless the harness itself failed. You cannot tell whether new context helped without a before.

3. Start from your last ten corrections

Collect the feedback you keep giving in design reviews, pull requests, or Slack, and rewrite each correction as something observable. That means writing Let evidence tables use the full available width instead of Make the table feel less cramped, since only one of those can be checked.

Put the decisions in one file with sections for scope, reader and task, observable decisions, and available primitives. That file is your first design.md.

4. Constrain repeatable mechanics

If your outputs keep inventing their own typography, spacing, or layout, publish a stylesheet and document the exact classes and tokens the agent may use. Keep your judgment in prose, and push the repeatable mechanics into CSS or deterministic checks.

5. Run one matched comparison

Generate the page one more time with the same input, model, and viewport, but now with your file loaded. Shuffle it with the baseline and score both against your rubric without knowing which is which.

You do not need a runner or a model judge to start, a single trial can reveal the large, obvious failures. To measure reliability, run multiple independent first-attempt trials (Anthropic's guide to evals for agents) and report how often the result holds.

6. Encode the correction

Review the output alongside whatever follow-up prompts you have to send, and then ask:

  • What did the user have to repeat or steer manually?

  • Is a rule missing or unclear?

  • Can the stylesheet express the correction?

  • Is the failure mechanical enough to check in code?

  • Does the correction generalize beyond this output?

Update the guidance instead of hand-tuning the generated page. Your next comparison tells you whether first attempts actually improved.

Add tooling after the manual loop starts paying off:

  • Include scenarios where the guidance should and should not apply.

  • Keep a small holdout hidden while editing.

  • Record model and guidance versions.

  • Automate mechanical checks.

  • Use multiple blind reviewers.

However far you take the automation, keep final changes human-reviewed.

Then keep the loop running. Collect feedback on a cadence, and watch whether each kind of complaint actually becomes less common after you change the guidance. A passing evaluation matters less if people keep correcting the same mistake in production.

And if you want working examples, ours are public. We load design.md into tools like v0, Codex, and Claude every day to make artifacts that feel like Vercel, and the eve design agent template will get you a Slack design agent like the one we run.

title: DeepUnfolding_Agent: A Classical_Quantum Adaptive Control API
description:
arXiv:2610.20615v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adaptive optimization workflows in machine learning, federated learning, quantum machine learning, and hybrid classical quantum systems often embed controller logic directly inside task specific training scripts. This coupling limits reuse, reproducibility, safety validation, and fair comparison across execution environments. This paper presents DeepUnfolding Agent, a schema-driven FastAPI platform that exposes deep unfolded adaptive control as an external software service. External executors register a strategy schema, submit round-level diagnostic variables, receive schema-bounded control actions, execute one optimization round, and return feedback for controller update. The framework separates controller intelligence from domain specific execution through a strategy registry, diagnostic to state adapter, controller factory, safety guard, executor abstraction, feedback update path, SQLite persistence layer, Docker deployment, and reproducible benchmark scripts. The implementation supports classical, quantum-aware, hybrid, Qiskit Aer, and optional IBM quantum processing execution pathways. We validate the software through unit, schema, API, safety, orchestration, Quantum execution, checkpointing, and Docker tests, and demonstrate external user fixed versus adaptive workflows across finance, healthcare, genomics, transport, noisy quantum simulation, and hardware backed IBM Quantum execution. The results show that DeepUnfolding-Agent provides a reusable and traceable adaptive control layer for heterogeneous optimization workflows. Our quantum experiments are interpreted as API level quantum control and hardware portability evidence.

title: The states shadcn/ui leaves to you: loading, success, error, empty and reduced motion
description:
Search "shadcn button loading state" and you will find a hundred snippets that do the same thing: add an isLoading prop, swap the label for a spinner, disable the button. Ship that and your app will feel worse than before you added it.

That is not a knock on shadcn/ui. It gives you a clean starting point and leaves the states to you, on purpose. But "the states" are where most of the feel of an interface lives, and almost nobody budgets time for them. This is the list of states I handle in every component I ship, and the specific timings that separate "finished" from "works".

1. Loading that does not flicker

The naive loading button shows a spinner the instant you click. Most requests finish in under 200ms, so what the user sees is a flash of spinner and then the result. It reads as jitter.

Two rules fix it:

  • Wait before you show the spinner. If the request finishes within about 150ms, never show it at all.
  • Once shown, keep it up for a minimum time. Around 400ms. A spinner that appears for 30ms is worse than no spinner. 
const spinnerDelay = 150
const minimumSpinnerTime = 400

That is a hook, not a prop. Here is the shape:

const { buttonProps, track } = useButtonFeedback()

<Button {...buttonProps} onClick={() => track(save())}>
  Save
</Button>

track takes the promise. The hook decides whether the request was fast enough to skip the spinner, holds the spinner long enough not to flicker, and moves the button into success or error when the promise settles. The HextaUI useButtonFeedback hook and useDelayedLoading do exactly this, and they are small enough to read in one sitting.

The same delay rule applies to skeletons. A skeleton that appears for 50ms and gets replaced by the content is a flash of grey. Delay it by 150ms, and when the content arrives, fade it in without moving anything around it.

2. Success and error, in place

After a save succeeds, the button should say so. "Saved" with a check, for about two seconds, then back to idle. After it fails, the button should say that too, and hold the error longer, about four seconds, because people need time to read an error and decide what to do.

Two details that matter more than they sound:

  • Do not reset while the pointer is on the button. If someone is hovering, they are reading. Reset after they leave.
  • Ignore clicks while the request is in flight. Not with disabled, which removes the button from the tab order and makes screen readers skip it. Use aria-busy and ignore the click.

A Switch has the same problem in a smaller space. Flip it, send the request, and if the request fails, flip it back. The user needs to see the rollback, so animate it, and show a brief pending state while the save is out.

3. Invalid, without punishing typing

Shake the field when a submit attempt finds it invalid. Never shake while someone is still typing. The rule is the trigger: validation on submit or on blur gets the shake, validation on change does not.

The shake itself should be short, three or four oscillations in about 300ms, and under prefers-reduced-motion it becomes a color change on the border and nothing else.

Native :user-invalid helps here. It only matches after the user has interacted, so you can style the invalid state in CSS without a touched flag in React.

4. Empty is a state, not an absence

An empty list is where new users land first, and the default is a blank area with a header above it. Every empty state needs three things: an icon or illustration so the space reads as intentional, one sentence that says what will appear here, and the action that makes something appear.

This is cheap to build and almost always skipped because the person building the feature has test data. Clear your database once in a while.

5. Reduced motion is not "no motion"

prefers-reduced-motion: reduce is on for a meaningful share of users, and the lazy implementation is a global * { transition: none }. That removes the information motion was carrying. A dialog that snaps open with no fade is harder to parse than one that fades.

The rule I use: anything that moves across the screen becomes a fade. Anything that fades stays a fade. Anything that loops stops. Durations get shorter, not zero.

Put the check in one place so every component reads it:

export function prefersReducedMotion() {
  return window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches
}

And share the easing curves and durations too. If every component picks its own cubic-bezier, the app will feel like it was built by six people, because it was.

6. Motion you can interrupt

Open an accordion, then close it halfway through the opening animation. In a lot of implementations, it finishes opening and then closes, or it jumps. The right behavior is to reverse from wherever it is.

The Web Animations API makes this easy: keep a reference to the running animation, and on the next toggle, read its current time and animate from the current computed height. CSS transitions on height: auto cannot do this, and grid-template-rows: 0fr to 1fr can but is harder to reverse mid-way. Pick the approach that lets you interrupt.

7. Touch targets and the iOS zoom

Two things break on phones that you will never see on a laptop:

  • Inputs under 16px zoom the page on iOS Safari. Keep input text at 16px on coarse pointers even if your theme is 15px elsewhere. A single @media (pointer: coarse) rule covers it.
  • Tap targets under 44px miss. Buttons can be 32px tall on desktop and grow on touch screens through the same media query.

8. Right-to-left

If you ever ship to Arabic or Hebrew users, every ml- and pl- and left- in your components is a bug. Use logical properties: ms-, ps-, start-. shadcn/ui added RTL support in January 2026, so new components you pull are fine, but the ones you copied in 2024 are not.

Where this leaves you

None of these is hard. All of them together is a few weeks of work on a component set the size of shadcn/ui, and the work is invisible when it is done, which is why it gets cut.

I built HextaUI because I kept doing this work on every project. It is a free, MIT-licensed registry you add to a shadcn/ui project. Same CLI, same component names, same theme tokens, and every one of the states above already handled, down to the 150ms spinner delay. If you would rather own the code and write the states yourself, the hooks are standalone and you can install just those.

npx shadcn@latest add https://hextaui.com/r/use-button-feedback.json

FAQ

Should I disable a button while loading? Set aria-busy="true" and ignore clicks. disabled removes it from the tab order and hides it from screen readers mid-action.

How long should a success state show? About two seconds, longer if the pointer is still on the control. Errors about four seconds.

Is a skeleton always better than a spinner? A skeleton is better when you know the shape of what is coming. A spinner is better for actions. Both need the 150ms delay.

Does reduced motion mean I should remove all animation? No. Replace movement with fades, stop loops and shorten durations. Keep the information.

title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20824v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .

title: Same Answer, New Box: How Much of RLVR's Out-of-Domain Gain Is Answer Format?
description:
arXiv:2610.20639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is credited with gains beyond the domain its rewards check, such as higher MMLU accuracy after training on mathematics. Such accuracies are usually read out of the model's text by an answer extractor. A model that learns to write its answer where the extractor looks can therefore score higher without answering better. We measure how much of the gain reported by extractors copied from public code arises this way. We generate outputs from a base model and its RL model and score them twice: with those extractors, and with one extractor of our own that reads a stated answer whether it is in the answer box \boxed{} or in the text. On four released 7B SimpleRL base-RL pairs, 82% of the out-of-domain multiple-choice gain that these extractors report disappears under ours: it is a gain in answer format, not in answers. The base models already state most of their answers in text, and RL moves them into the box, where these extractors look first. Independent LLM readers, in place of our extractor, put the figure at 77%. With a prompt that itself asks for the box, our extractor puts it at 79%. On a 32B pair trained with another recipe, almost none of the reported gain is format gain: its base model boxes its answers when asked, and its RL model rarely does when not. A reported gain is partly a property of the extractor that read it, and re-scoring stored outputs with a second extractor shows how much, without re-running RL.

title: When Judges Agree and Are Wrong: Consistency-Accuracy Dissociation as a Blind Spot for Label-Free Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.21128v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Label-free evaluation methods, such as self-consistency filtering, majority-vote aggregation, and agreement-based reliability scoring, rely on an implicit assumption that consistency can serve as a proxy for correctness when ground-truth labels are unavailable or expensive to obtain. In this paper, we test this assumption directly. Using four financial QA datasets (multiple-choice and free-form), ten consistency dimensions, and two frontier model families, we measure the joint distribution of consistency and accuracy at the level of individual examples rather than in aggregate. We find that 60% of all incorrect answers fall in the high-consistency region (consistency $\geq$ 0.8), and that 77.7% of these show complete answer collapse, i.e. identical wrong answers across all perturbation variants. This high-consistency/incorrect quadrant cannot be detected by any evaluation signal that is built on agreement alone, as the model appears maximally reliable while being wrong. We show that the phenomenon is robust to the choice of consistency threshold t (it persists from t=0.50 to t=1.00), is shared across model families, and is concentrated in specific intersections of perturbation dimension and domain. We map where this quadrant occurs, analyze its stability properties, and discuss the implications for evaluation pipelines that use agreement-based signals in place of human labels.

title: Redis Backup Verification: Turn Recovery Testing Into a Routine
description:
Check This:- Revenant Verify
Introducing a simpler way to validate Redis backups, inspect recovery results, and measure recovery time with Revenant.

Redis plays an important role in modern applications. Teams use it for caching, session management, queues, rate limiting, and other workloads where fast access to data matters.

Keeping Redis available is important. But managing persistence and understanding what happens during recovery are different responsibilities.

A backup may exist, yet teams still need a practical way to check whether it can be restored and whether the recovered data looks as expected.

That's why we're adding Redis Backup Verification to Revenant.

The goal is straightforward: make Redis recovery testing easier to run, easier to understand, and easier to repeat.

Why Redis recovery deserves attention

Redis is frequently introduced as a cache, but its operational importance varies from application to application.

Some applications can rebuild their cache from a primary database. Others depend on Redis for session state, queued work, or data that would be expensive to reconstruct.

The recovery requirements are therefore not identical for every Redis deployment.

A healthy Redis process tells you that the server is responding. A configured persistence policy tells you how Redis is expected to save data. Neither observation alone provides a complete picture of a recovery attempt.

Teams also need to understand how long recovery takes and whether the restored dataset meets their expectations.

That is where repeatable verification becomes useful.

Introducing Redis Backup Verification

Revenant's Redis verification workflow brings several recovery checks into one place.

1. Run verification when you need it

Connect a supported Redis instance and initiate a verification run. Instead of maintaining a separate collection of scripts and manual steps, teams can use a dedicated workflow to organize their checks and results.

Verification can also become part of a recurring operational routine as the workflow matures.

2. Test the restored dataset

The workflow captures a Redis RDB snapshot and tests it in an isolated environment.

This lets the verification process inspect the restored instance rather than relying only on the state of the original Redis server.

The result is a more meaningful view of what the recovery process actually produced.

3. Get understandable validation results

The verification report includes checks such as:

  • Keyspace and database-size comparisons.
  • Relevant Redis configuration settings.
  • A keyspace digest comparison.
  • A clear pass/fail result with supporting information.

Differences need context. Redis keys can expire, and the live dataset can change over time. A count mismatch should therefore be interpreted with appropriate tolerance and investigation, rather than automatically treated as corruption.

The objective is to make recovery results easier to interpret and act on.

4. Understand recovery time

Recovery time is an important operational metric.

If a team has a recovery time objective (RTO), it needs measurements from actual recovery attempts to understand how the process performs.

Revenant records the duration of the verification workflow, helping teams track recovery performance and identify changes over time.

A measured duration is evidence about that particular run; it is not a guarantee that every future recovery will take the same amount of time.

5. Keep evidence when it's useful

Some teams only need to run a verification and inspect its result. Others may want to retain snapshots and review previous reports.

Revenant supports optional artifact retention through managed Cloudflare R2 storage. Retained artifacts have plan-based expiry and automatic cleanup, so customers do not need to configure their own object-storage bucket for this workflow.

This gives teams a choice between running verification without retaining artifacts and keeping them for a defined period when historical evidence is useful.

Designed to reduce operational overhead

Recovery testing should not become another infrastructure system that teams must maintain themselves.

The aim of Revenant's Redis workflow is to make routine verification more accessible by bringing the process and its results together.

Instead of separately tracking a snapshot, a temporary restore, several manual checks, and the duration of each step, engineers can work through a dedicated verification workflow and inspect its report.

The workflow is designed to avoid unnecessary key-by-key inspection of the live dataset. Nevertheless, capturing a snapshot consumes resources, so production load and dataset size remain important considerations.

What this does—and doesn't—prove

A successful verification provides evidence that a particular snapshot was restored and passed the checks performed against the recovered instance.

It does not automatically prove that an entire application can recover, that every key contains the correct business data, or that all downstream dependencies are available.

Those outcomes require additional application-specific validation.

Being precise about this distinction matters. Recovery evidence is useful when it describes exactly what was tested and what the results support.

Where Revenant fits

Revenant is being developed to help teams make database recovery verification a repeatable engineering practice.

Redis extends that goal beyond relational databases by adding a workflow for RDB snapshots, restored keyspace checks, recovery-time measurement, and optional evidence retention.

The free local CLI provides an accessible starting point. Paid plans add capabilities for teams that need more resources, repeated verification, and longer evidence retention.

The Redis workflow is currently being tested, and its capabilities will be presented according to what has been verified.

The bigger goal: make recovery easier to manage

Reliable infrastructure requires more than keeping services online. Teams also need to understand what happens when recovery is necessary.

Redis Backup Verification is another step toward making that work easier to perform and easier to review.

With Revenant, the aim is to help engineers spend less time assembling recovery checks manually and more time understanding the results.

Recovery verification should be a routine engineering task—not a process that begins only when something goes wrong.

title: MSP: Modality Self-Play for Training Multimodal LLMs Without Paired Cross-Modal Data
description:
arXiv:2610.20965v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large multimodal models have achieved remarkable progress by scaling model capacity and training on massive paired multimodal data. However, this paradigm introduces a fundamental bottleneck: aligned multimodal datasets are expensive to curate, difficult to scale across diverse modality combinations, and increasingly constrain further progress. We introduce Modality Self-Play (MSP), a training framework for multimodal foundation models based on proxy-mediated modality composition. Instead of relying on paired cross-modal data, MSP uses anchor-supporting proxy textual descriptions of unseen modalities as semantic bridges during training. Given an observed modality (e.g., image or audio), the model generates proxy descriptions for complementary unseen modalities, which are then encoded and aligned with the observed modality through learned bridges, enabling cross-modal interaction without real paired non-text supervision.
  Our central hypothesis is that proxy text, combined with contrastively trained pretrained encoders, provides sufficient semantic structure for multimodal composition to emerge. We show that MSP enables zero-shot modality composition: models trained only with a real anchor modality and accompanying proxy descriptions can integrate and reason over multiple modalities at inference time despite never observing real paired non-text data during training. Empirically, MSP achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on multiple multimodal benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate that learned bridges improve alignment, while anchor-supporting proxy descriptions enable effective cross-modal composition. MSP removes the need for real paired non-text (e.g., audio-vision) supervision, while continuing to rely on modality-text pairs, pretrained contrastive encoders, and modality-distribution bridge calibration.

title: PiCo: Physics-Informed Concept Probing for Geo-Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2610.20973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geo-foundation models (GFMs) are typically evaluated by downstream task predictive performance, revealing little about which physical features they are sensitive to or use in prediction. This limits developers' ability to test hypotheses about model behaviour and users' ability to select models for new tasks. We propose Physics-Informed Concept Probing (PiCo), a post-hoc framework for explaining GFM predictions. PiCo identifies concept vectors in a GFM's embedding space by generating synthetic multispectral satellite observations from a 3D radiative transfer model coupled with a game engine. These vectors reveal physical sensitivities that inform domain-based hypotheses about downstream performance. Projecting embeddings onto these concept vectors produces low-dimensional representations for quantifying concept importance in making predictions. We evaluate PiCo on three GFMs with different input modalities using seven physical concepts covering forest leaf optics and canopy structure. In ground-cover estimation, RGB restriction reduces dry-matter sensitivity and disproportionately degrades predictions for dry vegetation and bare ground, supporting a hypothesis derived from sensitivity analysis. For hierarchical forest type and tree species classification, concept representations retain 70.0-93.8% of full-embedding accuracy. Models capture similar physical contrasts between classes, such as structural differences between broadleaf forest and cleared ground and leaf-water-content differences between oak and beech, yet differ in the strength of these contrasts and the concepts driving classification. PiCo thus provides a physical basis for hypothesis testing and model assessment, with potential applicability beyond Earth observation wherever forward models enable controlled simulation and pretrained embeddings are accessible for probing.

title: Expanding Attention: A Taylor-Series Route to Linear-Time Transformers with a Fixed Number of Recurrent States
description:
arXiv:2610.20637v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We expand the exponential kernel of attention into a truncated Taylor series of $n$ terms and factorize each term into a tensor-power inner product, which collapses the causal history into exactly $n$ recurrent states, each updated by one rank-one outer product per token and independent of context length $N$. The recursion is lossless with respect to the truncated kernel ($2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ in float64), and the states are additive across chunks ($5.7 \times 10^{-14}$), so prefill admits a parallel scan. Measured exponents are $t \propto N^{2.28}$ for softmax against $N^{0.91}$ for states, with a crossover at $N \approx 728$ and $20.8\times$ at $N = 8192$; per-token decoding latency is constant at $7.3\,\mu$s against $N^{1.04}$ for softmax, giving $76.0\times$ at $N = 65536$. Accuracy improves exponentially in $n$ while cost grows combinatorially, since the $m$-th state is $\binom{d+m-1}{m}$ wide---a bound confirmed by SVD---so the optimum is second order, $n = 3$, at $6.5 \times 10^{-4}$ error and $9{,}945$ elements per head. Query and key normalization is a prerequisite: without it the argument exceeds the convergence radius and adding terms stops helping.

title: Do VLAs Really Follow Instructions? Diagnosing How-Level Instruction Following in Vision-Language-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2610.21251v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.

title: Recursive Offline Distillation via Entropy Gain Sampling and Answer Mixing
description:
arXiv:2610.20914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distillation of reasoning chains from Large Language Models (LLMs) into their smaller siblings is a standard training approach. Frequently, researchers do not have full access to a teacher model and its internal representations, which limits the resulting performance. We propose a recursive offline distillation method combining two components: entropy-based sampling for selective distillation and answer mixing. Specifically, for three open models (3-4B), at each epoch, we sample reasoning chains weighted by entropy difference with an auxiliary medium model (70-72B) and, next, supplement thinking traces with single-token ground truth answers. Our approach consistently outperforms naive distillation with comparable data budgets ($57.15 \pm 1.01$ vs 51.61 on average) and offers a much steeper learning curve. Additionally, we present a comparative analysis of methods to generate and normalize distillation traces.

title: AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go is now generally available
description:
Today, AWS announces the general availability of the AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go, enabling Go developers to build resilient, long-running workflows using Lambda durable functions. With this SDK, developers can create multi-step applications like infrastructure automation, deployment rollouts with approval gates, and pipelines that call AI models and pause for human review directly in their Go code without implementing custom progress tracking.

Lambda durable functions extend Lambda's event-driven programming model with operations that checkpoint progress automatically and pause execution for up to an year when waiting on external events. The AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go provides a native Go experience for building with Lambda durable functions. It includes steps for progress tracking, callback integration for human and agent-in-the-loop workflows, durable invocation for reliable function chaining, and waits for efficient suspension.

The SDK works with the Go tools developers already use. Developers add it to a Go module with go get and deploy their function as a single static binary on the provided.al2023 runtime, like any other Go function on Lambda. Before deploying, they can locally test complete workflows on their own machine with the durabletest package, without requiring network access or AWS credentials, and use the durablelint analyzer to catch code that could break a workflow when it resumes.

To get started, see the Lambda durable functions developer guide and the AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go on GitHub. For Regional availability and pricing details for Lambda durable functions, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page and AWS Lambda Pricing.

title: Plan, Prioritize, and Manage IT Support and Maintenance Activities
description:
Plan, Prioritize, and Manage IT Support and Maintenance Activities

IT support and maintenance rarely make it onto a product roadmap. They are the work that keeps systems running while everyone else builds new features. Yet this work consumes a large share of most engineering and operations teams: patching servers, responding to incidents, renewing certificates, upgrading dependencies, answering tickets, and reviewing backups. When it is unplanned, it becomes a constant interruption. When it is planned well, it becomes predictable, measurable, and far less disruptive to the business.

This article describes a practical approach to planning, prioritizing, and managing IT support and maintenance activities. It covers how to classify work, how to set a priority model that people trust, how to schedule maintenance without surprising the business, and how to measure whether the system is actually improving. Java examples are included where automation or tooling helps.

The problem: reactive work crowds out everything else

Most support teams start in reactive mode. A request arrives, someone handles it, and the next one arrives. Over time three problems emerge:

  • Priorities are implicit. Whoever shouts loudest gets served first, and urgent-looking work displaces important work.
  • Maintenance is deferred indefinitely. Patches, certificate renewals, and dependency upgrades are always "next sprint", until an outage forces them through under pressure.
  • Knowledge stays in people's heads. Recurring problems are solved from scratch each time because nobody recorded the fix.

The cure is not heroic effort. It is a small set of explicit practices: a shared intake, a priority model everyone understands, a maintenance calendar that is treated as seriously as a release calendar, and a feedback loop based on data.

Step 1: Put all work in one place

You cannot prioritize what you cannot see. Support requests arrive through email, chat, phone calls, monitoring alerts, and hallway conversations. The first practice is to route all of them into a single queue, whether that is Jira Service Management, ServiceNow, or a well-configured shared board.

Each item should capture a minimum set of fields:

  • Category: incident, service request, problem, or maintenance task.
  • Affected service or system.
  • Business impact: how many users are affected and what they cannot do.
  • Requester and owner.
  • Creation time and target time.

Keeping the vocabulary consistent matters more than the tool. An incident is an unplanned interruption or degradation of a service. A service request is a standard, low-risk request such as access or a license. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents. Maintenance is planned work that reduces future risk. When these categories blur, every queue becomes a mix of everything, and prioritization becomes guesswork.

Step 2: Prioritize with impact and urgency, not volume

A widely used model combines two dimensions: impact, which is how much damage the issue causes, and urgency, which is how quickly the damage grows or how soon a deadline hits. A simple matrix turns these into a priority:

Low urgency Medium urgency High urgency
High impact P2 P1 P1
Medium impact P3 P2 P1
Low impact P4 P3 P2

The matrix itself is less important than the rules behind it. Write them down. For example, "High impact means a customer-facing service is down or a regulated process is blocked. Medium impact means a team cannot complete its work but a workaround exists. Low impact means cosmetic or single-user issues." When everyone can see these definitions, disagreements become discussions about classification rather than arguments about who is more important.

Maintenance work needs its own treatment. Patching a vulnerability that is being actively exploited is urgent. Upgrading a library that nobody has complained about may be low priority. A reasonable approach is to score maintenance items on three factors: risk reduction (how much exposure the work removes), effort, and deadline (end-of-support dates, certificate expiry, audit requirements). Items with a hard deadline move up regardless of their score.

Step 3: Make the priority score explicit in code

Teams often start with a spreadsheet and graduate to automation. A small Java model is enough to make the rules transparent and testable. The following example scores work items so the queue can be sorted consistently:

public enum Impact { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }
public enum Urgency { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH }

public record WorkItem(
        String id,
        String title,
        String category,       // INCIDENT, SERVICE_REQUEST, PROBLEM, MAINTENANCE
        Impact impact,
        Urgency urgency,
        int riskReduction,     // 1-5, used for maintenance items
        int effortDays,        // estimated effort
        java.time.LocalDate deadline // nullable
) {}

public final class PriorityCalculator {

    public String priorityOf(WorkItem item) {
        // Incidents and classic impact/urgency matrix
        if (!"MAINTENANCE".equals(item.category())) {
            return matrixPriority(item.impact(), item.urgency());
        }
        // Hard deadlines override scoring
        if (item.deadline() != null
                && item.deadline().isBefore(java.time.LocalDate.now().plusDays(14))) {
            return "P1";
        }
        // Score maintenance by risk reduction per unit of effort
        double score = item.riskReduction() / Math.max(1.0, item.effortDays());
        if (score >= 1.0) return "P2";
        if (score >= 0.3) return "P3";
        return "P4";
    }

    private String matrixPriority(Impact impact, Urgency urgency) {
        int i = impact.ordinal();   // 0 = LOW, 2 = HIGH
        int u = urgency.ordinal();
        int level = i + u;          // 0..4
        if (level >= 3) return "P1";
        if (level == 2) return "P2";
        if (level == 1) return "P3";
        return "P4";
    }
}

The point of this code is not the exact thresholds. It is that the rules are written down, reviewed in pull requests, and covered by tests. A few unit tests that encode the policy prevent quiet drift: when someone changes a threshold, the test fails and the change becomes a conscious decision.

Step 4: Plan maintenance as a calendar, not a backlog

Maintenance that lives only in a backlog gets postponed. Maintenance that lives on a calendar gets scheduled. Treat recurring work as a set of commitments with clear cadences:

  • Weekly: review the incident queue for patterns, check backup job results, review failed jobs and alerts.
  • Monthly: apply security patches to non-critical systems, rotate service accounts, review access lists for leavers.
  • Quarterly: test disaster recovery procedures, review capacity trends, review vendor support end dates.
  • Annually: renew certificates and licenses in advance, run a full access review, verify business continuity plans.

Two details make this work. First, schedule maintenance windows with the business, not around it. Publish the windows, explain the expected impact, and agree on rollback criteria before the work starts. Second, reserve capacity explicitly. A common rule is to allocate about 20 percent of the team's time to planned maintenance and small improvements. If the reserved capacity is always consumed by urgent incidents, that is a signal that the problem backlog needs attention, not that maintenance can be dropped.

Change management deserves a light but real process. For standard changes, such as a routine patch that has been done many times, a pre-approved template is enough. For non-standard changes, a short change record should state the purpose, the systems affected, the test evidence, the rollback plan, and the owner. The goal is not bureaucracy. It is making sure that the person on call at 2 a.m. knows what was changed and how to undo it.

Step 5: Turn recurring incidents into problems

One of the highest-leverage practices is problem management. When the same incident happens three times, it is no longer an incident. It is a problem with a root cause that is not yet fixed. Each recurring pattern should open a problem record, assigned to an owner with a target date for a permanent fix or a documented workaround.

A simple trigger works well: any incident category that appears more than three times in a month opens a problem review. The review answers four questions: what keeps happening, what is the root cause, what permanent fix is feasible, and what is the cost of not fixing it. Often the answer to the last question justifies the fix immediately.

Automation can help detect these patterns. The following sketch groups incidents by a normalized signature and flags clusters:

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public record Incident(String id, String service, String errorSignature, java.time.Instant openedAt) {}

public final class ProblemDetector {

    private static final int THRESHOLD = 3;

    public Map<String, List<Incident>> recurringPatterns(List<Incident> incidents) {
        return incidents.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(i -> i.service() + "|" + normalize(i.errorSignature())))
                .entrySet().stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getValue().size() >= THRESHOLD)
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(Map.Entry::getKey, Map.Entry::getValue));
    }

    // Strip volatile parts such as IDs, timestamps, and numbers so similar errors group together
    private String normalize(String signature) {
        return signature
                .replaceAll("\\b[0-9a-fA-F-]{8,}\\b", "<id>")
                .replaceAll("\\d+", "<n>")
                .toLowerCase()
                .trim();
    }
}

Normalization is the part that needs care. Two errors that differ only by a request ID are the same problem. Two errors that differ by the failing dependency are not. Review the grouping output periodically, because over-grouping hides distinct causes and under-grouping hides patterns.

Step 6: Measure what matters

Teams that cannot measure their support work cannot improve it. A small set of metrics is enough to guide decisions:

  • Mean time to acknowledge and mean time to resolve, broken down by priority. Averages hide problems, so look at the distribution, especially the slowest 10 percent.
  • Reopen rate: the share of tickets closed and then reopened. A high rate usually means fixes are superficial.
  • Ratio of planned to unplanned work. If unplanned work dominates, the team is in firefighting mode regardless of how fast it responds.
  • Maintenance completion rate against the calendar. Missed maintenance is a leading indicator of future incidents.
  • Recurring problem count and how many have a permanent fix in place.

Review these monthly with the people who do the work and the people who depend on it. The conversation should focus on trends and decisions, such as "we need to shift 10 percent of capacity to fixing the authentication failures", rather than on blaming individuals for individual tickets.

Step 7: Communicate proactively

Support teams are often judged by how they communicate during disruption. Three habits make a large difference. First, publish a status update at a predictable interval during any priority one incident, even if the update is only "still investigating, next update in 30 minutes". Second, after every significant incident, publish a short review that states what happened, what was done, and what will change. Third, tell the business about planned maintenance early and in plain language. People accept interruptions they understand far more readily than surprises.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating every request as urgent. If everything is P1, nothing is. Enforce the definitions.
  • Maintaining a backlog that nobody reviews. Items older than a set period should be closed, reprioritized, or explicitly accepted as risk.
  • Skipping rollback plans. A maintenance task without a rollback is a gamble.
  • Measuring only speed. Fast closure of tickets that reopen is not progress.
  • Automating before defining. A script that prioritizes according to unclear rules just makes confusion faster.

A roadmap for the first ninety days

Days 1 to 30: Consolidate intake into one queue. Define the category, impact, and urgency vocabulary and publish it. Start tracking time to acknowledge and resolve.

Days 31 to 60: Introduce the priority matrix and the maintenance calendar. Agree maintenance windows with the business. Open problem records for every recurring incident pattern you can identify manually.

Days 61 to 90: Automate the priority calculation and recurring pattern detection. Set up the monthly metrics review. Reserve a fixed share of capacity for planned maintenance and start reporting against it.

By the end of the ninety days, most teams can answer three questions they could not answer before: what is the team working on and why, what is coming next, and whether the system is getting more reliable over time.

Key takeaways

  • Consolidate all incoming work into one queue with a shared vocabulary of categories.
  • Prioritize using impact and urgency with written definitions, and treat maintenance with its own scoring that includes deadlines.
  • Encode priority rules in code and test them, so policy changes are deliberate.
  • Plan maintenance on a calendar, reserve capacity for it, and coordinate windows with the business.
  • Turn recurring incidents into problems with owners and target dates.
  • Measure distribution, reopen rates, and the balance between planned and unplanned work, and review trends monthly.

Reliable IT services are rarely the result of one heroic fix. They come from a steady system of planning, prioritization, and follow-through, and that system is worth building deliberately.

title: Blame Errant Words, Not the Canvas: Defect-Aware Spatial Credit Assignment for Visual Text Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.20794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent reinforcement learning approaches have improved visual text generation, yet generated images still suffer from incorrect wording and malformed glyphs. We identify two coupled limitations: recognition-based rewards often overlook visible glyph defects, while whole-image scalar feedback obscures the uneven quality of individual text regions. These limitations motivate our central principle: $\textit{Blame errant words, not the canvas}$, to effectively preserve local quality distinctions. First, we introduce $\mathbf{TextDART}$, a defect-aware region-targeted reward model that localizes individual text regions and independently evaluates their semantic correctness and glyph quality, providing fine-grained, region-precise feedback. Building on TextDART, we propose $\mathbf{SCANNER}$, which turns these regional judgments into spatially differentiated policy feedback. It normalizes rewards for each text target across sampled images and casts the resulting regional advantages onto the corresponding latent tokens. Extensive experiments on existing benchmarks and our newly established $\textbf{PolyText-Bench}$ demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in text accuracy and glyph fidelity. Project page: https://sujiehu.github.io/textdart-scanner

title: GBase Database Installation Troubleshooting: 5 Common Causes and Fixes
description:
When a GBase Database (GBase 8s) installation fails, don't assume the installation command is the problem. Missing dependencies, insufficient disk space, port conflicts, and incorrect permissions are often better places to start.

Here are five practical checks to help troubleshoot GBase Database installation and startup issues systematically.

1. Missing System Dependencies

Typical error:

error while loading shared libraries: libaio.so.1:
cannot open shared object file

How to check:

On RPM-based Linux systems, verify whether the required package is installed:

rpm -q libaio

If it is missing, confirm that it is required for your GBase 8s version and operating system before installing it:

sudo yum install libaio

Other libraries may also be required, depending on the platform. Check the official dependency list rather than assuming every installation needs the same packages.

2. Insufficient /tmp Space

Typical symptom: Installation stalls or fails while extracting the package.

How to check:

df -h /tmp
df -i /tmp

Check both available disk space and inodes.

If temporary storage is insufficient, use a larger filesystem where supported by the installer:

mkdir -p /opt/tmp
chmod 700 /opt/tmp
export TMPDIR=/opt/tmp

Verify that the installer honors TMPDIR; some installation tools use their own temporary paths.

3. Port Conflict

If the configured database service port is already occupied, the service may fail to bind to it.

How to check:

ss -tlnp

To inspect a specific port, such as 9088:

ss -tlnp | grep ':9088'

Confirm the actual port in your GBase Database connection configuration. If a conflict exists, coordinate a port change or resolve the conflicting service without disrupting other applications.

4. Hostname Resolution or Connection Failure

Typical symptom: dbaccess cannot connect to the database server.

Check hostname resolution:

hostname
getent hosts "$(hostname)"
cat /etc/hosts

Then review the GBase 8s sqlhosts configuration, including the server name, protocol, hostname, and service or port settings.

A connection failure can also result from an inactive instance, incorrect connection parameters, firewall rules, or a service that is not listening. Check these factors before concluding that hostname resolution is the cause.

5. Incorrect Instance Ownership or Permissions

Incorrect ownership can prevent the database account from accessing instance files.

First, inspect ownership and permissions:

ls -ld /home/gbase/gbasedbt
ls -l /home/gbase/gbasedbt

Use the actual instance path and database account for your installation.

Avoid blindly running recursive chown commands. Changing ownership across an entire directory tree can damage permissions or affect unrelated files. Correct only the paths and ownership settings identified by the installation documentation or troubleshooting evidence.

Also, distinguish software installation privileges from instance initialization privileges: follow the procedures specified for your GBase 8s release.

Final Takeaway

Most GBase Database installation problems become easier to diagnose when you follow a consistent troubleshooting order:

  1. Verify dependencies.
  2. Check temporary disk space.
  3. Investigate port conflicts.
  4. Validate hostname and connection settings.
  5. Inspect instance ownership and permissions.

A structured troubleshooting process beats trial and error.

What is the most common GBase Database installation issue you've encountered?

title: Probing Negation Understanding in Vision-Language Models With Object Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.20852v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision-language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye-fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA-1.5-7B displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. Code available at https://github.com/otmive/negation_attention
