title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures
description:
arXiv:2610.21270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.

title: A Status Is Not Proof: The Laptop I Never Received, and the Job I Was Handed Anyway
description:
In October, an online marketplace asked me to return a laptop I never received.

A day later, after looking into it, they agreed I had never received it. Then they asked me to go and fetch it, and send it back myself.

I said no.

This is a small story compared with the ones I usually write about. But it shows, step by step, how one wrong record can travel through a system until a customer who did nothing wrong is first treated as the problem, and then asked to be the fix.

I write about this kind of thing because it is my work. I review how software behaves when something goes wrong, and my standard is called No Silent Failure. In this story, every failure stayed silent until it reached me.

What happened

In August, I ordered a refurbished laptop from a marketplace that sells devices from independent sellers. The order was set for delivery to my home.

It never arrived. Later that month, the order was refunded. As far as I was concerned, that was the end of it.

Two months later, in mid-October, I got an email from the marketplace's customer care team. It said the courier and the seller had both confirmed that the parcel was "successfully collected" from a service point, and that I therefore had both the laptop and the refund. It asked me to send the laptop back, and offered a 10% discount code once the seller confirmed it had arrived.

The same conversation also held a prepaid return label and a checklist for shipping the laptop back, including photographing it from every angle.

I had never been to a service point for this order. I had never asked anyone to collect it for me. I had never seen the laptop.

I wrote back the same day. I explained that the parcel never reached me, that I hadn't collected it or authorized anyone else to, and that under UK consumer law, goods remain the seller's responsibility until they are in the buyer's hands. I asked them to get the courier's proof of collection: the date and time, the service point's address, and the name, signature or ID given at the counter.

Later that day, a second agent replied. They apologized, opened an investigation, and promised an update within one business day.

The next day, the update came. The parcel had never been collected. It was still sitting at the service point.

And then: since the order had already been refunded, would I please go and collect it, and send it back to the seller with the prepaid label? As a goodwill gesture, here was a 10% discount code.

Where it went wrong

I have no view inside any of these systems, so I can only describe what they did from the outside. From the outside, I count six points where a check, a link or a handoff was missing.

1. The refund closed the money, not the parcel

When the order was refunded in August, the money side of the order was finished. The parcel side was not. By the marketplace's own account, the laptop sat at a service point for about two months after the refund, and nothing in the process asked where it was or brought it back to the seller.

A refund on an undelivered order is a moment when two records should agree: the payment and the parcel's location. Here, one record said "done", and the other was never asked.

What would work: when an order is refunded before delivery, the same step tells the courier to return the parcel to the seller, and the case stays open until the seller confirms it has arrived.

2. A status became a statement about me

Somewhere, a record said the parcel had been collected. Both the courier and the seller passed that on. My guess is that both were reading the same tracking entry, which would make two confirmations really one source repeated twice. But that is only a guess.

What I do know is what happened next. "Collected" became "you have the device and the refund". A line in a tracking system turned into a statement about a person, and was sent to that person, without anyone asking where the proof was.

What would work: before telling a customer they have something, attach the evidence: when, where, and who signed. If that evidence can't be found, ask the customer a question instead of telling them a fact.

3. The return started before anyone checked

The message asking me to return the laptop came with everything needed to do it: a prepaid label, a link to the return instructions, and advice on photographing the device. The process had already moved on to the next step, built on a claim nobody had looked at.

Automation is good at taking the next step quickly. That is exactly why steps that assume something about a person need a check in front of them.

What would work: when a return comes from a courier's status rather than from the customer's own request, ask the customer first. Create the label after they confirm, not before.

4. The message lived somewhere I wasn't looking

The email didn't appear on the order in my account. My first job was working out whether it was even real, because an unexpected email saying you have something you shouldn't, with a link and an attachment, is exactly the shape of a scam. Only later did I find the conversation under a separate messages section.

When a company tells someone they are holding something that isn't theirs, that message should be easy to verify and easy to answer. If it is hard to find, the person spends their effort proving the message is genuine before they can even reply to it.

What would work: attach every conversation about an order to that order, so the customer sees it in context and knows it's real.

5. The burden of proof landed on me

I was asked, in effect, to account for something I had never had. That is asking someone to prove a negative, and it is very hard to do. I can't photograph a parcel I never saw.

So I did the one thing I could: I asked for the proof that should have been there from the start. As soon as someone looked for it, the story changed. The parcel had never left the service point.

That is the part I keep coming back to. The truth was available all along. It took a customer asking for evidence before anyone checked.

What would work: the side making the claim holds the evidence. If a system says a customer has something, the system's own records should show it before the customer is ever contacted.

6. The cleanup was handed back to me

Once it was clear I had never had the laptop, the request changed from "send it back" to "go and get it, then send it back". The parcel was with the courier. The laptop belonged to the seller. The one person in the chain who had no part in what went wrong was the person asked to put it right.

It would have meant two trips, carrying a heavy laptop between them, for a parcel I never wanted to see again. It would also have meant signing for it, and that signature would have created exactly the record that started all this: proof that the parcel had been in my hands.

The discount code was offered as goodwill. But a discount on a future purchase isn't payment for work, and this was work that was never mine to do.

What would work: send the physical fix to the parties who have custody. The seller and the courier can return an uncollected parcel between themselves, and the customer only needs to hear that it's done.

What worked

I want to be fair here, because one part of this worked well.

The second agent read what I wrote, apologized, and opened an investigation the same day. They gave me a time frame and kept to it. When the facts came back, they told me plainly that the parcel had never been collected.

That is what a good handoff looks like: a person takes the customer's account seriously, checks it, and reports back. The investigation did its job. What came after it is where the process went wrong, because the system's answer to "the customer was right" was still "so the customer should fix it".

What I said

I said no, politely and in writing. I explained that I wouldn't collect the parcel or sign for it, and that returning it was a matter for the seller and the courier. I asked for three things: for them to arrange the return directly with the seller and the courier, for written confirmation that nothing more is needed from me, and for the note on my account saying I had collected the parcel to be corrected.

The shape of it

Put the six points together, and a familiar shape appears:

  1. A record is wrong.
  2. The system treats it as true and acts on it.
  3. The person on the other end has to show that it's wrong.
  4. When they do, the cost of fixing it still lands on them.

None of this needed anyone to be careless or unkind. Everyone I dealt with was polite. The trouble lives in the joins: between the payment and the parcel, between tracking and customer care, and between "the customer was right" and "who fixes it". Each join is a place where a check could sit, and in this story none did.

That is what I mean by No Silent Failure. A parcel sitting at a service point for two months is a silent failure. A wrong status is a silent failure. Neither made a sound until it reached me, and by then it arrived as an accusation.

My recommendations for businesses

If you run a business that ships things, or any process where a record can be wrong, here is what I'd recommend. None of it is expensive. Most of it is about where you place a check, and who you ask first.

  1. Keep the evidence with the status. A status like "collected" or "delivered" should carry its proof: when, where, and who signed or showed ID. If the proof is missing, the status is a lead to look into, not a fact to act on.

  2. Ask before you tell. When your records and your customer's experience might disagree, start with a question: "Our records show this parcel was collected on this date. Does that match what you saw?" A question invites the truth. A statement makes the customer defend themselves before they can help you.

  3. Give every refund a matching return. When you refund an order that never arrived, the same step should bring the goods back to the seller, and someone should confirm that they arrived. Money and goods should close together.

  4. Pause automation before it points at a person. Automate the routine steps freely. But when a step tells a customer they owe something, have something, or must do something, let a person or a clear rule confirm the facts first.

  5. Watch for things that sit still. A parcel waiting at a service point for two months is a record that stopped moving. Set a normal time for each stage, and flag anything that stays longer, so you notice it before your customer does.

  6. Keep the conversation where the customer looks. Put every message about an order on that order, in the customer's account. Then they can see at a glance that it's genuine, and answer it without first wondering whether it's a scam.

  7. Send the fix to whoever holds the problem. If the goods are with your courier or your seller, the fix belongs to them. The customer's part is simply to be told when it's done.

  8. Make the apology match the mistake. If a customer was told they had something they didn't, say so plainly, correct the record, and confirm it in writing. If you offer a goodwill gesture, make it a thank you for their patience, never a payment for more of their time.

Happy customers don't need a business that never makes mistakes. They need a business that notices its own mistakes first, owns them, and puts them right without handing the work back.

Here is a simple test: count what the customer had to do to fix your error. Every message they wrote, every proof they had to find and every trip they were asked to make shows how much of your process still rests on them. The goal is zero.

A status is not proof. A refund is not a return. And the customer is not the courier.

title: Open weight takes 71.5% of tokens and 23% of spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — October 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from July, August, and September.

October 2026 summary

  • Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June.

  • September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record.

  • Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December.

  • Jev was the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history, reaching 35% of paid teams in its first two weeks, but it accounted for just 0.27% of gateway spend over that same period. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch.

Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22%

In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September.

Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend.

Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend.

In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average.

Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold.

In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year.

Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business.

AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halves

Market share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper.

September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend.

Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record.

Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. The average rose to 26 for teams processing at least 100 million tokens, and 42 for those processing at least a billion.

The model is becoming a replaceable part of a much larger investment. Companies can continuously improve their AI products and workflows while changing which models power them. They can spend more on AI without becoming more dependent on any one lab.

Chinese models are big business for American providers

More than two-thirds of September’s gateway spend on Chinese-origin models went to US-based providers, up from less than a tenth in December. The Chinese lab builds the model; the American provider runs it and sells access.

DeepSeek’s models processed 58% of all gateway tokens for 6.6% of spend. More than four in five of those tokens were served by DeepSeek itself, yet two in five dollars spent on its models went through US-based providers.

Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based lab behind Kimi, accounted for 3.6% of gateway tokens and 13.2% of spend in September. US-based providers served nine in ten of those tokens.

Z.ai, also based in Beijing and the creator of GLM, accounted for 7.2% of all tokens and 4.5% of spend. US-based providers served seven in ten.

Customers can use Chinese models through access sold by American providers. For teams that put more money into Chinese models in September, an average of 53% of their spending on those models went through US-based providers and 41% through China-based ones.

The same Chinese model can compete with US-based models while generating revenue for US-based providers.

September model launch scorecard: Jev, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6

Whether a model launch is successful depends on what you measure: how broadly it’s tried, how much usage and spend it receives, or what share of its initial users return. We ranked every model launch in September with at least two weeks of data by these metrics; the tables show the top ten for each. The full scorecard is at the end of the report.

Jev is the most-adopted and most-called model

In its first two weeks, Jev reached more than a third of paid teams, nearly double the reach of Sonnet 5.5 in second place. This is the fastest adoption of any model in AI Gateway history.

Jev also received the most requests of any model in September, even though it launched halfway through the month. Of the teams that tried Jev in week one, 55.6% returned in week two, the fifth-highest retention rate.

Jev is a decision model. Compared with typical language-model requests, a Jev request is faster, cheaper and uses a fraction of the tokens. So although its adoption was fast and broad, it accounted for just 1% of the month’s tokens and 0.15% of spend.

In September, Jev quickly became a popular model for production while remaining a tiny part of the inference bill.

Opus 5.5 takes more than one in ten gateway dollars

The launch that received the most dollars was Opus 5.5, with more than twice the share of any other September launch, followed by GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash.

Opus 5.5 caught on quickly, with almost nine in ten dollars coming from teams already using Opus 5. Existing customers were trying the new release while the wider Opus family was losing market share.

Across all versions, Opus accounted for almost a third of gateway dollars in September, down from one in two in August. Anthropic’s overall share fell below half of total gateway spend for the first time, dropping from 63.7% to 43.9%.

Luna brought users back; Astra brought spend

GPT-6 Luna reached nearly three out of every twenty paid teams in its first two weeks, in third place behind Jev and Sonnet 5.5. But its return rate was the highest of the month; almost two-thirds of the teams that tried it in its first week came back in the second.

GPT-6 Astra reached a smaller audience but took more budget. In its first two weeks, it accounted for about one in twenty gateway dollars; Luna accounted for less than one in a hundred. Luna reached almost three times as many teams while Astra captured more than five times the share of spend.

OpenAI is attracting more customers with Luna, but capturing far more money with Astra, even though fewer teams use it.

Full September scorecard

  • August 2026

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through September 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, a broader definition than in earlier reports.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million paid tokens in both months. “Most-used” is measured by paid tokens.

  • Provider location means company headquarters.

  • Launch metrics cover external paid teams during each model’s first 14 days. Reach uses paid teams active from the start of the launch month through the data cutoff. Spend share uses total paid gateway spending during the model’s window. Return rate is the share of first-week teams that used it again in week two.

  • Model counts cover December–September, with each version counted separately. Team-size thresholds use total input and output tokens over that period.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

title: CLAD: Keypoint Matching Using Global Line Correspondences
description:
arXiv:2610.21409v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Traditional keypoint descriptors, such as SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) and ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF), are computed from local image patches. They may be unreliable in scenes with repetitive patterns or weak textures, where patches at different locations can look similar. We propose the Contextual Line-Assisted Descriptor (CLAD), a keypoint matching method that addresses this problem by using global geometric context from line correspondences. CLAD represents each keypoint with a vector whose elements indicate its proximity to matched lines. It can therefore use the keypoint's spatial relationships to the lines in the scene. We use HOME (Hough-space One-dimensional Matching of Extrema) to detect both clear and weak linear structures and to establish enough line-to-keypoint associations to represent this context. Evaluations on the TUM RGB-D SLAM dataset and outdoor video sequences show that CLAD provides geometrically consistent matches that complement those obtained with traditional local descriptors. In repetitive scenes, where local descriptors may not distinguish similar patches, CLAD uses global structure to improve matching reliability. The method is computationally lightweight and practical to implement.
